management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus,metrics
  endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true      # /readiness and /liveness, separately
  metrics.tags.application: ${spring.application.name}
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://collector:4318/v1/traces

spring:
  kafka:
    template.observation-enabled: true      # producer spans
    listener.observation-enabled: true      # consumer spans — joins the trace
logging.pattern.correlation: "[%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "
Cardinality killsA metric tagged with orderId or customerId creates millions of time series and takes your monitoring stack down. Tags are for bounded dimensions — endpoint, status, module, outcome. High-cardinality identifiers belong in logs and traces, joined by trace id.

Separate liveness (restart me) from readiness (send me traffic). Conflating them means a slow dependency triggers a restart loop across the whole fleet.

Alert on what the customer feels

CPU alerts wake people for things nobody noticed; symptom alerts wake people for things everybody noticed. Define the SLO first, then derive alerts from its error budget.

JourneySLISLOPage when
Place order% of POST /orders that succeed in < 1.5 s99.9% / 28dBurning the 28-day budget 14× over 1 h
Browse catalog% of product reads < 300 ms99.5% / 28dFast burn only; slow burn is a ticket
Payment capture% captured within 5 min of authorisation99.95% / 28dAny sustained breach — money is involved
Order eventsConsumer lag on orders.placed.v1< 30 s at p99Lag > 5 min or DLT depth > 0

RED, for every endpoint

Rate, Errors, Duration. Three dashboards panels per service that answer "is it working" without domain knowledge.

USE, for every resource

Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — connection pool, thread pool, disk, heap. This is where you look after RED says something is wrong.

Burn-rate alerts

Two windows: fast (1 h at 14× burn → page) and slow (6 h at 6× → ticket). It catches both the outage and the slow bleed, without paging on a single blip.

The four dashboards a team needsJourney (SLOs, customer-visible) · Service (RED per endpoint) · Dependencies (latency and error rate per downstream, circuit-breaker state) · Resources (USE). More than four and nobody opens any of them during an incident.

A test pyramid shaped like your architecture

The mistake is uniform testing: everything through @SpringBootTest, or everything mocked. Match the test type to the layer, and the suite stays fast and meaningful.

LevelToolWhat it provesSpeedShare
Domain unitPlain JUnit, no SpringInvariants and state transitions on the aggregate< 1 ms~60%
ApplicationJUnit + fakes for portsOrchestration and error mapping~5 ms~15%
Web slice@WebMvcTestSerialization, validation, status codes, security rules~1 s ctx~10%
Persistence@DataJpaTest + TestcontainersReal SQL, real constraints, migrations apply~2 s~8%
Module@ApplicationModuleTestA module's behaviour including its events~3 s~5%
Contractoasdiff / schema registryYou did not break a consumer~sgate
End-to-endPlaywright, on a real envThe three journeys that must never breakminutes< 2%
Testcontainers, shared and fast — Boot 4 service connections
import org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer;  // NOT ...containers.KafkaContainer

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ContainersConfig {
    @Bean @ServiceConnection            // wires spring.datasource.* automatically
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine").withReuse(true);
    }
    @Bean @ServiceConnection
    KafkaContainer kafka() {
        return new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka:4.0.0").withReuse(true);
    }
}
// Two classes share the simple name KafkaContainer:
//   org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer      → apache/kafka (KRaft)
//   org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer → confluentinc/cp-kafka
// Pair the wrong one with your image and startup hangs until it times out.

// src/test: one container per build, reused across every test class
@SpringBootTest
@Import(ContainersConfig.class)
class OrderFlowIT { ... }
H2 is not your databaseTesting against H2 while running PostgreSQL means your tests pass on SQL that production rejects — and silently skip the constraints, types and locking behaviour that matter. Testcontainers removed this excuse years ago.
Architecture tests are testsThe ArchUnit rules from slide 8 and modules.verify() from slide 9 run in the same suite. That is what makes the boundary real rather than aspirational.
Flaky E2E destroys trustThree reliable end-to-end journeys beat forty that fail randomly. A suite people re-run "because it's probably flaky" has already stopped being a gate.

One build, one artifact, four environments

The artifact that reaches production is the one that was tested — byte for byte. Anything rebuilt per environment reintroduces the class of bug this rule exists to eliminate.

settings.gradle.kts — modules as Gradle projects, when you want hard walls
rootProject.name = "shop"
include("modules:order", "modules:payment", "modules:inventory",
        "modules:catalog", "modules:shared", "app")

// modules/order/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    api(project(":modules:shared"))
    implementation(project(":modules:payment"))   // sees payment's api only
    // a compile error is now impossible to merge, not just discouraged
}

Trade-off: Gradle modules give compiler-enforced boundaries and faster incremental builds, at the cost of more build files and slower IDE indexing. One source set plus ArchUnit is lighter and usually enough; escalate to Gradle modules when the rules keep getting suppressed.

The pipeline

  1. Build + unit + arch tests — under 5 minutes or people stop watching.
  2. Integration — Testcontainers, module tests.
  3. Contract gates — OpenAPI breaking-change check, schema registry compatibility.
  4. Security — dependency scan (CVE), SAST, image scan, license check.
  5. Package once — bootBuildImage, tagged with the commit sha.
  6. Promote the same digest: dev → test → staging → prod.
  7. Deploy rolling or canary; migrate before, expand/contract always.
Deploy ≠ releaseDeploying the artifact and enabling the behaviour are separate events. Deploy continuously; release with a flag. This is what makes a Tuesday-afternoon deploy boring, which is the actual goal.

Sizing the runtime with arithmetic, not vibes

Connection pools and thread pools are where capacity planning meets reality. Both are answerable with one formula, and both are almost always set by copy-paste instead.

Little's law, applied to a connection pool

Concurrency needed = throughput × time each request holds a connection.

Target
600 orders/min = 10 orders/s
DB time
~40 ms of database work per order (not total request time)
Needed
10 × 0.04 = 0.4 connections average
Peak ×5
~2 connections; set the pool to 10–20 for headroom and bursts

The usual instinct — "set it to 100, to be safe" — makes things worse: PostgreSQL context-switches between 100 backends, latency rises, and each request holds its connection longer, which needs more connections. Pools are queues; oversizing moves the queue somewhere less observable.

Sanity check: total connections across all pods must stay well under the database's max_connections. 40 pods × 20 = 800 is how a healthy service takes down a shared cluster.

Virtual threads (Java 21+, on by default in Boot 4 when enabled)

spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true
  • Helps: IO-bound request handling — thousands of concurrent requests blocked on HTTP or JDBC, without a thread per request.
  • Does not help: CPU-bound work, or throughput limited by the database. It removes a thread ceiling; it does not create capacity downstream.
  • Watch: pooled resources are still the real limit — 10 000 virtual threads contending for 20 connections just queues elsewhere. And pinning on synchronized blocks is largely resolved in modern JDKs, but legacy libraries can still pin.

Startup, when it matters

Baseline
~4–8 s for a large Boot app
Spring Data AOT
repositories generated at build time — a large share of that startup back
CDS / AppCDS
class-data sharing: typically 20–40% off startup, no code change
GraalVM native
~50 ms start, low memory — at the cost of build time, reflection config and a harder debugging story

For a long-running enterprise service, startup matters for rolling deploys and autoscaling, not for cost. Reach for native only when scale-to-zero or per-request billing is genuinely on the table.

What "one deployable" looks like in production

A modular monolith is not one server. It is one artifact deployed many times — and you can already scale, isolate and protect parts of it before extracting anything.

The same jar, three deployments

web
12 pods behind the gateway; handles HTTP only. Kafka listeners disabled by profile.
worker
6 pods; Kafka consumers, outbox relay, schedulers. No ingress at all.
batch
2 pods; nightly reconciliation and exports, with their own resource limits.

A profile decides which listeners and schedulers start. You now scale request traffic and event traffic independently, and a batch job can never starve checkout of threads — most of the benefit people expect from extracting services, without the distribution.

# worker deployment
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod,worker
# order/internal/kafka/OrderPlacedConsumer.java
@Profile("worker")

Production hygiene checklist

  • Liveness and readiness probes distinct; readiness fails while warming.
  • preStop sleep + graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful) so in-flight requests finish.
  • Requests and limits set; -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the JVM respects the container.
  • PodDisruptionBudget, so a node drain does not take the whole service.
  • HPA on a metric that reflects load (RPS or queue depth), not only CPU.
  • Anti-affinity across zones; at least three replicas for anything customer-facing.
Sequencing a release with a migrationMigrate first (expand-only, backwards compatible), then roll the pods. Never run migrations from an init container on every pod — one pod runs them, as a Job, with a lock. Flyway takes the lock for you; the mistake is running the Job concurrently with itself.

Multi-region: three topologies, one hard question

The hard question is never compute — it is where writes happen. Everything else follows from that answer, and picking it is one of the few decisions that is genuinely irreversible.

Things that quietly break when you go multi-regionAuto-increment ids collide — switch to UUIDv7 or region-prefixed sequences. Kafka does not replicate itself; you need MirrorMaker and a consumer-offset story. Caches are per-region and diverge. Scheduled jobs fire twice. Every one of these is discovered after the decision, so raise them during it.

DR: two numbers the business owns, one drill you must run

RTO and RPO are business decisions with engineering price tags. The engineering failure is not choosing wrong numbers — it is having numbers nobody has ever tested.

TierRPO — data you can loseRTO — time to recoverWhat it takesRelative cost
Backup onlyup to 24 hhours–daysNightly backup, restore procedure, somewhere to restore to1×
Warm standbyseconds–minutes15–60 minAsync replication, scaled-down standby, manual promotion1.3×
Hot standbyseconds< 5 minFull-size standby, automated failover, regular drills2×
Active–active~0secondsSynchronous or conflict-resolved replication, global routing2–3× plus design cost

The conversation to have with the business

Not "what RTO do you want" — the answer is always zero. Instead: "one hour of downtime costs roughly £X in lost orders and £Y in remediation. Going from a 4-hour RTO to a 15-minute RTO costs £Z a year. Which do you want?"

That question gets a real answer, gets it signed off, and gives you something to point at when the budget is reviewed. It is also exactly the reasoning an interviewer is listening for.

Untested is untrueA DR plan that has never been executed is a document, not a capability. The common discoveries on a first real drill: the restore takes nine hours, not one; a schema was never being backed up; the runbook references a person who left; the standby's credentials expired six months ago.
Make it routineQuarterly, in business hours, with a rollback plan: fail over to the standby, run for an hour, fail back. Publish the measured RTO. Teams that do this have a boring DR story; teams that do not have an exciting one exactly once.
Do not forget the dependenciesYour service failing over is pointless if the identity provider, the secret store or the payment gateway is single-region. DR is a property of the whole path, and the weakest link sets the real RTO.

Cost is an architectural constraint, not a finance problem

Architecture decisions set the cost curve years before anyone looks at the bill. Being able to express a design in cost per unit of business value is one of the clearest seniority signals there is.

Worked example: cost per 1,000 orders

Volume
1.2M orders/month, peak 40× on sale days
Compute
12 web + 6 worker pods, 2 vCPU / 4 GiB each
Database
primary + replica, provisioned for peak
Kafka
3 brokers, 7-day retention
Egress
the line everyone forgets until the invoice

Divide the monthly total by 1,200 and you have cost per 1,000 orders. Now every proposal has a comparable number: does this cache pay for itself? Does that extra service? Does multi-region?

It also exposes the real bill-driver, which in most enterprise systems is the database provisioned for peak and idle the rest of the month — not the application tier everyone spends time tuning.

Decisions with long cost tails

  • Provisioning for peak. A 40× sale peak sized statically means paying 40× all year. Autoscaling, queueing and load shedding are cost decisions as much as resilience ones.
  • Chatty synchronous calls. Each internal hop costs compute, network and latency budget on every request, forever.
  • Retention. Seven days of Kafka versus thirty is a straight multiple. So is log retention, which is frequently the largest observability line.
  • Cross-AZ and cross-region traffic. Priced per gigabyte, invisible in design reviews, and often the biggest surprise on a first multi-region bill.
  • One service per team, by policy. Each one carries a fixed floor of compute, monitoring and pipeline cost regardless of its traffic.
Capacity planning, minimallyCurrent peak throughput × expected growth × a safety factor, checked against the measured limit from a load test. Re-run quarterly. That is enough to avoid both the surprise outage and the 60%-idle cluster.

Data residency, PII and retention as architecture

In a regulated enterprise these constraints arrive as requirements, not preferences, and each one is far cheaper designed in than retrofitted. All four below are architectural, not operational.

Know where personal data is

A data inventory per module: which fields are personal, what the lawful basis is, how long it is kept, who it is shared with. Without it you cannot answer a regulator, a deletion request, or "does this new report leak anything".

Practical version: annotate the fields. @Pii(category = CONTACT) on the entity, and a test that fails if a @Pii field appears in a log format or an unencrypted export.

Residency shapes the topology

"EU customer data stays in the EU" decides your region strategy, your backup locations, your analytics pipeline and which SaaS vendors you may use. It also rules out a single global database — which is exactly the kind of constraint that must land in level 1 of the decision hierarchy, not level 6.

Deletion must be designed

A deletion request has to reach: the OLTP row, every read model, the search index, the cache, the warehouse, the backups, and the event log. The last two are the hard ones — an immutable event log and a right to erasure are in direct tension.

The usual resolution is crypto-shredding: store personal fields encrypted with a per-subject key, and delete the key. The events remain; their personal content becomes unreadable.

Minimise, then separate

  • Do not collect what you do not need; do not copy it into three services because it was convenient.
  • Pseudonymise in analytics — the warehouse rarely needs a real name.
  • Keep the PCI or PII surface in as few components as possible; that is one of the four legitimate reasons to extract a service.
  • Retention policies enforced by a job, not by a wiki page.
The one that catches everybodyLogs and heap dumps. A team designs beautiful field-level encryption, then logs the whole request body at DEBUG during an incident, and ships a copy to a log aggregator in another jurisdiction with 90-day retention. Privacy controls must cover the diagnostic path, because that is the path people use under pressure.

C4: four zoom levels, and only two of them are for everyone

Most architecture diagrams fail because they mix levels — a box labelled "Customers" next to a box labelled OrderRepositoryAdapter. C4's whole contribution is insisting you pick one altitude per picture.

The test for a good diagramHand it to someone who has never seen the system and ask them to explain it back. If they cannot say what each box does, which arrow carries the user's request, or where data is stored, the diagram is decoration. Adding a legend is usually a sign the encoding is doing too much work.

Documentation that is still true in a year

Every architecture document decays. The only ones that do not are the ones generated from the system, or the ones that record a decision rather than a state.

ArtefactAnswersStays true becauseWhere it lives
System context (C4 L1)What is this, who uses it, what does it depend onIt changes about twice a yearRepo, as diagram source
Container diagram (C4 L2)What gets deployed and how the pieces talkReviewed whenever a deployable is addedRepo, as diagram source
Component diagram (C4 L3)Modules and their dependenciesGenerated from the code by Spring ModulithBuild output
ADRsWhy is it like thisA decision record is history; it is never "out of date"docs/adr/, in the PR that implements it
Module canvasWhat this module exposes, publishes and depends onGenerated by Modulith's DocumenterBuild output
OpenAPI specThe HTTP contractGenerated from controllers; a CI gate diffs itBuild output, committed for diffing
RunbooksWhat to do when this alert firesExercised every time the alert firesLinked from the alert itself
Diagrams as code — reviewed in the PR, diffed like anything else
# docs/architecture/container.puml — C4-PlantUML, rendered in CI
@startuml
!include <C4/C4_Container>
Person(customer, "Customer")
System_Boundary(shop, "Order Platform") {
  Container(spa,  "Storefront",     "Angular",      "Browse and checkout")
  Container(app,  "Order Platform", "Spring Boot",  "8 modules, one deployable")
  ContainerDb(db, "PostgreSQL",     "17",           "Schema per module")
}
System_Ext(gw, "Payment Gateway")
Rel(customer, spa, "Uses", "HTTPS")
Rel(spa, app, "Calls", "JSON/HTTPS")
Rel(app, db, "Reads/writes", "JDBC")

@enduml
Why source beats a drawing toolIt lives beside the code, changes in the same pull request, diffs in review, and renders in CI. A diagram in a slide deck on a shared drive is accurate on the day it was exported and never again — and nobody can tell which day that was.
Write down what is deliberately absentThe most valuable and least written documentation is the list of things you chose not to do, and why: no service mesh yet, no multi-region, no event sourcing. Without it, every new joiner proposes all three in their first month, and the team re-litigates the same decisions annually.
One page per serviceName, owning team, what it does in a sentence, its SLO, its dependencies, its runbook links, how to run it locally. Generated where possible. This is the page people open at 2am, and it is worth more than any architecture deck.

Evolutionary architecture: make the rules executable

A fitness function is any automated check that an architectural property still holds. It is the difference between architecture as a decision and architecture as a description of what the code happened to become.

Property you care aboutFitness functionRuns
Modules do not reach into each other's internalsArchUnit slice rules + ApplicationModules.verify()Every build
The domain stays framework-freeArchUnit: no Spring or JPA imports under ..domain..Every build
No module reads another's tablesA database role per module, granted only its own schemaEvery integration test
The API does not break consumersoasdiff against main; schema-registry BACKWARD compatibilityEvery PR
Hot endpoints stay free of N+1Query-count assertions on the top three endpointsEvery build
Checkout stays within its latency budgetA performance test with a p95 threshold that fails the pipelineNightly
No known-vulnerable dependencies shipCVE scan with a severity gateEvery build
Startup stays fast enough to roll back quicklyAssert boot time under a threshold in an integration testNightly
Nothing writes personal data to logsA test scanning log output for @Pii-annotated field valuesEvery build

How to introduce them into an existing codebase

  1. Baseline, do not block. Record today's violations in a file; fail the build only on new ones.
  2. Ratchet. Every sprint, remove a few from the baseline. The number only ever goes down.
  3. Add one per repeated review comment. If a reviewer catches the same mistake twice, that is a missing fitness function, not a missing reviewer.

A big-bang "turn on all the rules" attempt produces 400 failures on day one and gets disabled by day three.

The reframing worth carryingArchitecture is not the diagram — it is the set of properties you are defending. A property nobody measures is a preference. A property with a failing build behind it is a constraint, and constraints are what actually survive delivery pressure.
Good interview material"How do you stop a modular monolith degrading?" answered with three named, executable checks and a ratcheting strategy is a much stronger answer than "code reviews and discipline" — because the interviewer has watched discipline lose to a deadline before.

Governance that speeds teams up

Enterprise architecture functions fail in one of two ways: a review board everyone routes around, or no standards at all and forty incompatible services. The way out is to make the compliant path the easy path.

The bottleneck model

  • Every design goes to a weekly board; the queue is three weeks.
  • Standards are a 90-page document nobody has read.
  • Compliance is checked by a human, late, at a gate.
  • Architects are separate from delivery and have not run anything in production for years.

Result: teams either wait and resent it, or ship first and seek forgiveness. Both damage the architecture, and the board sees neither.

The paved road model

  • A service template that already has observability, security, CI, health checks and the error model wired in — a new service starts compliant.
  • Shared starters the platform team owns, so a change to the logging standard is a version bump.
  • Fitness functions enforce the rules in the pipeline, not in a meeting.
  • ADRs for anything off the road, reviewed asynchronously in the PR.
  • Architects embedded in delivery, writing some of the code.

Leaving the paved road stays possible — it just requires writing down why.

What a review is actually forNot approving designs — catching the level 1–4 decisions from the hierarchy slide, and spotting the same problem being solved separately by three teams. Review the decisions that are expensive to reverse; let teams own the rest. A board that debates library choices has no time left for the boundary that will cost a quarter.
Measure the function, not the artefactsLead time for a new service to reach production. Number of teams on the current template version. Percentage of services meeting the observability baseline. Those tell you whether governance is working. "Number of designs reviewed" tells you only how busy the board was.
Where this leaves the atlasEverything in this deck is one of three things: a decision (recorded in an ADR), a property (defended by a fitness function), or a default (encoded in the template). Anything that is none of the three is an opinion, and opinions do not survive contact with a delivery deadline.

Twelve anti-patterns, and what each one actually costs

Every one of these is common, defensible in the moment, and expensive later. Recognising them by their symptom is more useful than knowing their names.

Anti-patternWhat you seeWhat it costs
Distributed monolithServices that must be deployed together; a change touches four reposMicroservice cost, monolith coupling — the worst square of the grid
Shared database across servicesTwo services, one schema, nobody may change a columnThe schema becomes the coupling; autonomy is zero
Anaemic domainEntities with only getters; 900-line OrderServiceRules duplicated across services and silently diverging
Chatty sync callsOne page render = 14 internal HTTP callsLatency multiplies, availability multiplies down
Retry without idempotencyA retry annotation on a POSTDuplicate charges, duplicate orders, a finance reconciliation project
God gatewayBusiness rules in gateway YAMLUntested, unversioned logic that cannot run locally
Entity as API contract@Entity returned from a controllerSchema changes break clients; lazy-loading errors in serialization
Everything asyncEvents for things the user is waiting onUnreadable flows, and a UI that must explain eight intermediate states
Library sprawlThree JSON libraries, two HTTP clients, two mappersCVE surface, onboarding cost, inconsistent behaviour at boundaries
Config in the artifactEnvironment-specific values baked into the jarRebuild per environment; the tested artifact is not the shipped one
Dogmatic layeringSix mapper classes to read one lookup tableTeam abandons the architecture wholesale because the tax is uniform
Architecture as a documentA wiki page; no test enforces any of itDrift within one quarter, and nobody can tell you when it happened
The pattern behind the patternsNine of these twelve are failures to make the rule executable. Whenever you write down an architectural rule, ask in the same breath: what test, lint, database grant or CI gate makes it true tomorrow?

Write the decision down while you still remember why

An ADR takes twenty minutes and answers the question every new engineer asks in month two: "why is it like this?" — which is otherwise answered by guessing, and then by an unnecessary rewrite.

ADR-014 · Keep the modular monolith; do not split payment yet

Status
Accepted — 2026-03-11 · supersedes ADR-006
Context
Payments team wants an independent release cadence. Checkout p99 is 780 ms; payment is 240 ms of it. Team is 6 engineers. No separate SLA is contractually required today.
Decision
Keep payment as a module. Extract the gateway adapters into a separate deployable behind PaymentGatewayClient, which isolates the PCI surface and the third-party latency without splitting the domain.
Consequences
+ PCI scope narrows to one small service. + Release cadence unblocked for the adapter, which is what actually changed weekly. − One more deployable to operate. − Revisit if payment needs its own data store.
Revisit
When any of: payment team > 10 engineers · a contractual payment SLA appears · checkout and payment scaling diverge by more than 3×

What makes an ADR useful

  • The context is dated and numeric. "6 engineers, 240 ms" ages visibly; "the team is small" does not.
  • The rejected options are listed, with why. Otherwise someone re-proposes them in a year.
  • Consequences include the negatives. An ADR with only upsides was written to win an argument, not to record one.
  • A revisit trigger. This is the line that turns a decision into a living one.
Where they liveIn the repo, under docs/adr/, in the PR that implements them. A decision record in a wiki nobody opens is a decision record nobody reads.
Worth recordingAnything in levels 1–4 of the decision hierarchy, any library that becomes load-bearing, any deliberate deviation from your own standard, and every "we tried X and it did not work".

The reference architecture, on one page

Everything in this deck, assembled. Copper is the synchronous request path with a latency budget; teal is asynchronous and allowed to lag.

If you are starting on Monday

Order of work for a greenfield enterprise service, or for bringing an existing one under control. Roughly a quarter, and each step makes the next one cheaper.

Weeks 1–2 Make the boundaries real

  • Name the bounded contexts with the business, not in a code review.
  • Create the module packages with api / spi / internal.
  • Add ArchUnit rules and modules.verify() to CI on day one — retrofitting them is what costs.
  • Schema per module, one database role per module, grants enforced.

Weeks 3–6 Make it observable and testable

  • Trace id end to end, including across Kafka; structured JSON logs.
  • Testcontainers from the first integration test; no H2.
  • One vertical slice fully built — controller to database to event — as the pattern everyone copies.
  • Error model (ProblemDetail) and the OpenAPI contract gate.

Weeks 7–10 Make it resilient

  • Timeouts on every outbound client; then retries, breakers, bulkheads in that order.
  • Outbox for every event that must not be lost; idempotent consumers with a DLT.
  • Idempotency keys on every mutating public endpoint.
  • SLOs defined for the top three journeys; burn-rate alerts wired.

Weeks 11–13 Make it operable

  • Expand/contract migration discipline and a rehearsed rollback.
  • Feature flags with expiry; deploy decoupled from release.
  • Four dashboards, not fourteen; a runbook per alert.
  • ADRs for every level 1–4 decision made so far, written while the context is fresh.
Going deeperEric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (contexts and aggregates) · Vaughn Vernon, Implementing DDD (the practical companion) · Sam Newman, Monolith to Microservices (the extraction playbook) · Gregor Hohpe, Enterprise Integration Patterns (still the reference for messaging) · Ford, Richards et al., Fundamentals of Software Architecture and Software Architecture: The Hard Parts (trade-off analysis) · Nygard, Release It! (the resilience patterns, with the outage stories that produced them).

Spring Boot, from the container up

Eight topics, in the order they build on each other: how Boot is put together, what happens between main() and your first request, the starters an enterprise actually pulls in, and three annotation catalogues — core, JPA and security — covering the ones you meet in real code, each with the failure it causes when used wrongly.

3.x

Code targets Spring Boot 3.4/3.5 — Jakarta EE, Spring Security 6, Hibernate 6. What enterprise codebases actually run.

4.0

Boxes marked Boot 4 flag what changed in Spring Boot 4 / Framework 7, so you can speak to both.

56

slides. Same e-commerce order domain as the architecture deck, so the examples line up.

The nine sections

Architecture
the layer cake, auto-configuration, the @Conditional family, how to override it
Lifecycle
application startup · bean · HTTP request · transaction and persistence context
Starters
what a starter is, and the ones enterprises pull: core, messaging, batch, cloud
Core annotations

JPA

Security

Internals
AOP, transaction propagation and isolation, Jackson, Spring Data patterns, SpEL
Production
Actuator, metrics, logging, JVM memory, GC, profiling, leaks, load tests
Reference
the Spring Boot 3 → 4 delta, as one table you can answer questions from
How the annotation slides are writtenEvery entry gets three things: what it does, a real line of code, and the failure it causes when it is wrong. The third one is the reason to read a reference rather than the Javadoc — the Javadoc tells you what an attribute means, not what happens at 2am when you set it badly.

What Spring Boot actually is

Boot is not a framework. It is three things layered on top of Spring Framework: an opinionated dependency set, a conditional configuration engine, and an embedded runtime. Knowing which layer a behaviour comes from is what makes problems diagnosable.

Boot adds no runtime model

There is no "Boot container". It is the same ApplicationContext Spring has always had — Boot just populates it for you and starts a server in main() instead of deploying a WAR.

Opinionated, not locked

Every auto-configured bean backs off the moment you declare your own. That is the single design rule the whole thing rests on — the next three slides are how it works.

Boot 4 finer modules

Boot 4 splits the framework and its own jars into smaller modules. Nothing changes conceptually, but it is the most common upgrade surprise — imports move.

Auto-configuration, mechanically

Three annotations, one file of class names, and a pile of conditions. No reflection tricks, nothing hidden — you can read the whole chain yourself, and you should once.

ShopApplication.java — one annotation, three jobs
@SpringBootApplication      // = the three below, combined
public class ShopApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// @SpringBootApplication expands to:
@SpringBootConfiguration    // a @Configuration, marked as THE primary one
@EnableAutoConfiguration    // pull in auto-config classes
@ComponentScan              // scan this package and below
Inside spring-boot-autoconfigure.jar
META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcAutoConfiguration
...about 150 more, one class name per line
A real auto-configuration class, trimmed
@AutoConfiguration(before = { HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration.class })
@ConditionalOnClass({ DataSource.class, EmbeddedDatabaseType.class })
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(type = "io.r2dbc.spi.ConnectionFactory")
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)   // ← backs off if YOU declared one
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "spring.datasource.type",
                           havingValue = "com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource",
                           matchIfMissing = true)
    HikariDataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties properties) { ... }
}
The order of events1. @EnableAutoConfiguration reads every AutoConfiguration.imports on the classpath. 2. Each class's conditions are evaluated. 3. Surviving classes are ordered by before/after. 4. Their @Bean methods run — but only after your own @Configuration classes are registered, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean can see your beans.
Legacy detail worth knowingBefore Boot 2.7 this list lived in META-INF/spring.factories under an EnableAutoConfiguration key. Boot 2.7 introduced the .imports file and read both; Boot 3.0 removed the spring.factories route entirely. An old in-house starter that never migrated contributes nothing — with no error, because other spring.factories keys still work, so the file looks fine. If a starter mysteriously stopped applying on the 2.x→3.x upgrade, this is why.

The conditions that decide what exists

These are the whole of Boot's "opinion". Nine annotations; you will write three of them yourself the first time you build an internal starter.

AnnotationFires whenTypical use
@ConditionalOnClassA class is on the classpathConfigure Hibernate only if Hibernate was added
@ConditionalOnMissingClassA class is absentFall back when an optional library is not present
@ConditionalOnBeanA bean of that type already existsAdd a JpaTransactionManager only if a DataSource exists
@ConditionalOnMissingBeanNo such bean is definedThe back-off rule. On nearly every auto-configured @Bean
@ConditionalOnPropertyA property has a value (or is absent, with matchIfMissing)Feature toggles in your own starter
@ConditionalOnWebApplicationIt is a servlet or reactive web appSkip MVC config in a batch job
@ConditionalOnResourceA file exists on the classpathLoad config only when a mapping file is shipped
@ConditionalOnExpressionA SpEL expression is trueCompound conditions — use sparingly, it is unreadable
@ProfileAn active profile matchesEnvironment-shaped beans (worker vs web)
Find out why a bean does or does not exist
# run with --debug, or set:
debug: true
# prints the ConditionEvaluationReport:
#
#   Positive matches:
#   -----------------
#   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
#      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource' (OnClassCondition)
#
#   Negative matches:
#   -----------------
#   KafkaAutoConfiguration:
#      Did not match:
#      - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class
#        'org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate' (OnClassCondition)
Read this report before guessing"Why is my DataSource the wrong one?" and "why did my custom ObjectMapper not take effect?" are both answered in full by that output, in about thirty seconds. It is the single most under-used diagnostic in Spring Boot.

Actuator's /actuator/conditions endpoint gives the same report as JSON on a running application — useful when the problem only reproduces in an environment you cannot restart with --debug.

Four ways to take control back

In escalating order of force. Reach for the weakest one that works — each step up moves you further from the defaults that Boot upgrades will keep maintaining for you.

1 · Set a property weakest, best

spring.jpa.open-in-view: false
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 20
server.shutdown: graceful

Covers the large majority of real cases. Nothing to maintain, survives every upgrade.

2 · Declare your own bean

@Bean
ObjectMapper objectMapper() { ... }     // auto-config backs off

Works because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean. The trap: you now own all of Boot's defaults for that bean, which for ObjectMapper means you silently lose the module registrations Boot had configured.

3 · Customise instead of replace usually right

@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer dates() {
    return b -> b.simpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");
}

Boot exposes a *Customizer for most things it builds. You change one setting and keep every default — almost always what you actually wanted in case 2.

4 · Exclude the auto-configuration

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class)

The blunt instrument. Legitimate for a batch app that must not start a web server, or when an in-house starter conflicts. Excluding SecurityAutoConfiguration to "make the 401 go away" is how unauthenticated endpoints reach production.

Writing your own starterAn internal starter is a jar with an @AutoConfiguration class, an entry in AutoConfiguration.imports, and a @ConfigurationProperties record. Name it acme-spring-boot-starter — the spring-boot-starter-* prefix is reserved for the Spring team. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor so your properties get IDE autocomplete; teams notice that immediately.

From main() to "Started ShopApplication in 4.2s"

Ten phases. Knowing which one you are in tells you where a startup failure can be caught, where a property is readable, and why your @PostConstruct ran before the web server was listening.

Which hook to useApplicationReadyEvent for anything that must not run until the app is genuinely serving (warm caches, register with a discovery service). ApplicationRunner for one-off startup work. @PostConstruct only for initialising that bean — never for work that assumes other beans are ready, because ordering is not guaranteed.

Startup hooks, failure analysis, and dying gracefully

Shutdown gets far less attention than startup and causes more customer-visible errors — every rolling deploy exercises it, several times an hour.

Startup hooks, in the order they fire
@Component
class WarmUpRunner implements ApplicationRunner {
    @Override public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        catalogCache.preload();        // context up, server listening
    }
}

@Component
class RegisterOnReady {
    @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)   // after runners, truly ready
    void onReady() { discovery.register(); }
}

@Component
class OrderMetrics {
    @PostConstruct void init() { ... }   // this bean only; no ordering guarantees
    @PreDestroy   void close() { ... }   // on graceful shutdown
}
Graceful shutdown — three settings that matter
server.shutdown: graceful           # stop accepting, finish in-flight requests
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
# Kubernetes: a preStop sleep of ~5s so the endpoint is removed from the
# Service BEFORE the JVM stops accepting — otherwise the last few requests
# are routed to a pod that has already closed its connector.

Shutdown order, and the one that bites

  1. SIGTERM arrives; ContextClosedEvent is published.
  2. Web connector stops accepting new requests; in-flight ones finish.
  3. SmartLifecycle.stop() runs in reverse phase order — Kafka listener containers stop here.
  4. Singletons destroyed in reverse dependency order; @PreDestroy then DisposableBean.

The bite: a Kafka consumer that has read a batch but not committed offsets when the JVM is killed will reprocess it on the next pod. That is normal and correct — and it is why every consumer must be idempotent.

Failure analysersWhen startup fails, Boot's FailureAnalyzers turn a 400-line stack trace into a readable block — "Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use." You can register your own for in-house starters, and it is one of the highest-goodwill things a platform team can ship.
Don't do work in a constructorA bean constructor that calls a database or an HTTP endpoint makes startup depend on that system being up. Boot will fail to start, the pod will crash-loop, and a dependency's blip becomes your outage. Constructors wire; ApplicationReadyEvent works.

The bean lifecycle, and where your proxy appears

Nine steps between "definition" and "usable bean". The one worth memorising is step 7 — it is where @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async and @PreAuthorize all physically come into existence.

Scopes

singleton (default, one per context) · prototype (new every injection; no destroy callback ever runs) · request / session (web, injected as a scoped proxy) · application. A prototype injected into a singleton is created once — use ObjectProvider if you need a fresh one per call.

Circular dependencies

Constructor injection on both sides cannot be resolved and fails at startup — correctly, since it is a design smell. Boot 2.6+ disables the field-injection workaround by default. Fix the design, or use @Lazy on one side only as a stopgap.

Proxy type

JDK dynamic proxy when the bean implements an interface, CGLIB subclass otherwise (Boot forces CGLIB by default). CGLIB cannot proxy final classes or final/private methods — the annotation is silently ignored, which is the worst failure mode there is.

One HTTP request, hop by hop

Where your code can intervene, and — more usefully — which stage an exception was thrown in, because that determines whether your @ControllerAdvice will ever see it.

Customising the security error bodyBecause the security chain sits outside the advice, you shape its responses with authenticationEntryPoint (401) and accessDeniedHandler (403) on the filter chain itself. Doing that is what makes every error in your API one consistent shape — see the ProblemDetail slide in the architecture deck.

The persistence context: open, dirty, flush, commit

Most JPA surprises — "I never called save() and it updated anyway", "my change vanished", "LazyInitializationException" — are this lifecycle, not a mapping problem.

Flush happens three times

Before a query that would read stale data, on flush(), and at commit. So an INSERT can appear far from the save() that caused it — which is why constraint-violation stack traces often point at an unrelated line.

Detached is where lazies die

After commit, a lazy association on a detached entity throws LazyInitializationException. Map to a DTO inside the transaction. open-in-view hides this by keeping the context open for the whole request — set it to false and fix the real cause.

Entity states

Transient (new, no id) → Managed (tracked) → Detached (context closed) → Removed. save() on a detached entity does a merge, which issues a SELECT first — a quiet source of double queries in bulk loops.

A starter is a POM with no code in it

That is the entire trick. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa contains zero classes — it is a dependency list plus a curated set of versions. The behaviour comes from the auto-configuration in the jars it drags in.

What spring-boot-starter-data-jpa actually contains
<dependencies>
  <dependency>spring-boot-starter</dependency>          <!-- core + logging + yaml -->
  <dependency>spring-boot-starter-jdbc</dependency>      <!-- HikariCP + JdbcTemplate -->
  <dependency>hibernate-core</dependency>
  <dependency>spring-data-jpa</dependency>
  <dependency>spring-aspects</dependency>
</dependencies>
<!-- no src/main/java at all -->
The BOM is the other half — and the more valuable one (Maven)
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.0</version>
</parent>
<!-- now: no <version> on any managed dependency, ever.
     Boot has tested this exact combination of ~400 library versions
     against each other. Overriding one is how you find out which
     three others it was holding hands with. -->
The same thing in Gradle — what the rest of this atlas assumes
plugins {
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "3.5.0"
    id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"  // applies the BOM
}
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web")  // no version
}
ext["kafka.version"] = "3.9.1"   // the ONLY safe way to move one library

How to read a dependency problem

  1. mvn dependency:tree / gradle dependencies — find where the version came from.
  2. Override Boot's version only through the property Boot defines (<hibernate.version>, ext["kafka.version"]), never by pinning the artifact directly — that way the whole family moves together.
  3. If you must exclude something, check nothing else on the tree needed it.
The enterprise smellA pom.xml with thirty explicit <version> tags means someone is fighting the BOM. Each one is a CVE-patching job that no longer happens automatically, and a compatibility matrix nobody maintains. Getting a team back onto managed versions is usually a one-day win worth taking.
Boot 4 module splitBoot 4 breaks its own jars into finer modules, so a class you imported from spring-boot-autoconfigure may now live elsewhere. The starters still work unchanged — it is direct dependencies on internal jars that break.

The six on almost every enterprise service

What each one brings, and the first property you will want to change after adding it.

StarterPulls inGives youFirst thing to set
-webSpring MVC, embedded Tomcat, JacksonDispatcherServlet, JSON in/out, error pageserver.shutdown: graceful
-data-jpaHibernate, Spring Data, HikariCP, spring-jdbcRepositories, EntityManager, tx managerspring.jpa.open-in-view: false
-validationHibernate Validator (Jakarta Bean Validation)@Valid on request bodies, @Validated on beansNothing — but know it is not in -web since Boot 2.3
-actuatorMicrometer, health contributors/health, /metrics, /info, /conditionsendpoints.web.exposure.include — and expose it on a separate port
-securitySpring Security 6 filter chainEverything locked down by defaultA SecurityFilterChain bean — the generated password is a dev convenience only
-testJUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, JSONassert, Awaitility@SpringBootTest and every slice annotationAdd Testcontainers alongside it

Actuator on its own port

management.server.port: 8081 keeps health and metrics off the public route entirely, so no gateway rule can accidentally expose /actuator/env. Standard practice in regulated environments.

Swap Tomcat deliberately

Exclude -tomcat and add -undertow or -jetty only with a benchmark in hand. On modern Boot with virtual threads enabled, the difference is rarely the bottleneck.

-web vs -webflux

Pick one. Both on the classpath makes Boot start as a servlet app and quietly ignore your reactive assumptions. Since Boot 3.2's virtual threads, blocking MVC scales far enough that WebFlux needs a specific streaming reason.

Messaging and integration starters

The middleware half of an enterprise stack. Each one auto-configures a template, a listener container, and a set of health indicators you should be alerting on.

Starter / dependencyAuto-configuresUse it forWatch out for
spring-kafkaKafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener containers, DefaultErrorHandlerEvent backbone, high throughput, replayThe container disables auto-commit for you and acks per poll (AckMode.BATCH) — use ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE when each record must be durable before its offset moves
-activemq / -artemis / IBM MQ starterJmsTemplate, @JmsListener, ConnectionFactoryClassic enterprise queues, XA, request/replyJMS transactions are not your JPA transaction unless you configure XA — usually you should not
-amqpRabbitTemplate, @RabbitListener, adminRouting-heavy workloads, work queuesDead-letter exchange must be declared explicitly — it is not automatic
spring-integrationChannels, adapters, IntegrationFlow DSLFile pickup, SFTP, protocol bridging, EIP patternsEasy to build an unreadable flow; keep business logic out of it
spring-cloud-streamBinder abstraction over Kafka/Rabbit, functional handlersSwapping brokers, standardising across many teamsThe abstraction leaks the moment you need broker-specific behaviour
-mailJavaMailSenderNotification moduleNever send inside a transaction — it is not rollback-able
The Kafka settings an enterprise service should not leave at default
spring.kafka:
  bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BROKERS}
  producer:
    acks: all                       # client default since Kafka 3.0 — pin it anyway,
    properties.enable.idempotence: true   # so an inherited config cannot weaken it
  consumer:
    group-id: inventory
    auto-offset-reset: earliest     # default 'latest' SILENTLY skips a backlog
    enable-auto-commit: false       # the container already does this; be explicit
    isolation-level: read_committed
  listener:
    ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE      # container default is BATCH (per poll)
    observation-enabled: true       # propagates the trace across the async hop
The default that still causes real incidentsauto-offset-reset: latest means a brand-new consumer group skips everything already on the topic, so a new service quietly starts from "now" and nobody notices until reconciliation. What is no longer true: acks defaulted to 1 only before Kafka 3.0 — since then the client defaults to acks=all with enable.idempotence=true. Set both explicitly regardless, because the failure mode is someone weakening them for throughput and nobody noticing until a leader election.

Batch, scheduling, and the cloud/ops set

Batch is the half of enterprise Java that architecture decks usually ignore and that runs the business overnight.

Batch & scheduling

-batch
Jobs, steps, chunk-oriented processing, restartability, and the BATCH_* metadata tables that make a failed job resumable from the last commit point. For end-of-day reconciliation, statement generation, bulk file loads.
-quartz
Clustered, persistent scheduling. Use when the schedule must survive restarts and must fire exactly once across a fleet.
@Scheduled
Built into the core — no starter. Fine for a single instance; on N pods it fires N times unless you add a lock (ShedLock, or a database advisory lock).
The classic bug@Scheduled on a service running 6 replicas sends six reminder emails to every customer. Every team meets this once. Design for it: either Quartz clustered, ShedLock, or a dedicated single-replica batch deployment — the third option is the one from the deployment-topology slide.

Cloud & ops

-oauth2-resource-server
Validate incoming JWTs. What your API uses.
-oauth2-client
Obtain tokens to call others — client-credentials for service-to-service.
cloud-config-client
Externalised config with refresh. Weigh against ConfigMaps + a restart, which is simpler and usually enough.
cloud-openfeign
Declarative HTTP clients. Boot 4 Spring's own @ImportHttpServices covers most of this natively now.
resilience4j-spring-boot3
Circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiter with Actuator endpoints. Boot 4 core @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit cover the common cases.
vault-config
Secrets, and — the part that matters — dynamically issued, short-lived database credentials.
-cache
@Cacheable plus a provider (Caffeine local, Redis shared).
A Spring Batch step — chunked, restartable, and the reason batch exists
@Bean
Step reconcilePayments(JobRepository repo, PlatformTransactionManager tx,
                       ItemReader<PaymentRecord> reader,
                       ItemProcessor<PaymentRecord, Reconciliation> processor,
                       ItemWriter<Reconciliation> writer) {
    return new StepBuilder("reconcilePayments", repo)
            .<PaymentRecord, Reconciliation>chunk(500, tx)   // commit every 500 items
            .reader(reader).processor(processor).writer(writer)
            .faultTolerant()
              .skipLimit(50).skip(MalformedRecordException.class)   // tolerate bad rows
              .retryLimit(3).retry(TransientDatabaseException.class)
            .build();
}
// Crash at item 12,300 of 500,000? Restart resumes from the last committed chunk,
// because the BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION table recorded it. That is the whole value.

Stereotypes and configuration

All the stereotypes are @Component underneath. The differences that actually matter are exception translation on @Repository and proxying on @Configuration.

Stereotypes
@Component        // generic managed bean — the base for all of these
@Service          // semantic only; marks application/domain logic
@Repository       // + translates JDBC/Hibernate exceptions into Spring's
                  //   DataAccessException hierarchy. Not cosmetic.
@Controller       // returns view names
@RestController   // = @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method
@Configuration    // bean definitions live here; see proxyBeanMethods below
@ControllerAdvice // cross-controller @ExceptionHandler / @ModelAttribute
Configuration and bean registration
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)   // set this on your own configs
class OrderConfig {

    @Bean                                   // method name = bean name
    OrderService orderService(OrderRepository repo) { ... }

    @Bean(initMethod = "start", destroyMethod = "close")
    ReportGenerator reports() { ... }
}

@Import(SharedInfraConfig.class)      // pull in another @Configuration explicitly
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.retailco.shop",
               excludeFilters = @Filter(type = ASSIGNABLE_TYPE, classes = LegacyJob.class))

proxyBeanMethods — the one people never set

By default, @Configuration is CGLIB-proxied so that calling orderService() from another @Bean method returns the singleton rather than a new object. Convenient, but it costs a proxy per config class at startup.

If your @Bean methods never call each other — which is the norm when you take dependencies as method parameters — set proxyBeanMethods = false. Every Boot auto-configuration class does. Measurably faster startup, and it is what native-image compilation wants.

@Repository is not decorativeWithout it, a unique-constraint violation surfaces as a Hibernate ConstraintViolationException; with it, as Spring's DataIntegrityViolationException. Your catch blocks and your @Retryable rules are written against the second one. Spring Data repositories get this automatically; hand-written DAOs do not.
Scanning@SpringBootApplication scans its own package and below. That is why the main class belongs at the root package — a class in a sibling package is silently never registered, and the symptom is a confusing "no qualifying bean" at startup.

Wiring and externalised configuration

Constructor injection is the only form worth using. Everything else on this slide exists to disambiguate, defer or configure it.

Injection
@Service
class PlaceOrderUseCase {
    private final OrderRepository orders;          // final = immutable, testable
    private final PaymentGateway payments;

    // No @Autowired needed — a single constructor is autowired since Spring 4.3
    PlaceOrderUseCase(OrderRepository orders, PaymentGateway payments) { ... }
}

@Qualifier("primaryGateway")      // pick between several beans of a type
@Primary                          // the default choice when ambiguous
@Lazy                             // create on first use — a circular-dep stopgap
@Scope("prototype")               // new instance per lookup
ObjectProvider<Foo> provider;     // optional / lazy / multiple, without @Lazy tricks
@Order(10)                        // ordering within an injected List<Handler>
Configuration binding
@Value("${shop.order.max-lines:100}")   // single value + default. Avoid at scale.
private int maxLines;

// Prefer this: typed, validated at startup, documented, IDE-completable
@ConfigurationProperties("shop.order")
@Validated
public record OrderProperties(
        @Min(1) @Max(500) int maxLines,
        @NotNull Duration reservationTtl,
        @NotBlank String currency) { }

@EnableConfigurationProperties(OrderProperties.class)   // or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan
Never field injection@Autowired private OrderRepository repo; hides dependencies from the constructor, makes the class untestable without Spring, permits circular dependencies that should have failed, and cannot be final. If a class has eight constructor parameters that is a signal, not a reason to switch to fields.

Why @ConfigurationProperties beats @Value

  • Validated at startup, not on first read — a typo fails the boot, not a 3am payment.
  • Relaxed binding: max-lines, maxLines, MAX_LINES all bind, so an env var Just Works.
  • Type conversion for Duration, DataSize, List, nested records.
  • With spring-boot-configuration-processor, your properties get IDE autocomplete and docs.

Records get constructor binding with no @ConstructorBinding needed since Boot 3.

Profiles@Profile("worker") on a bean, application-worker.yaml for its config, SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod,worker at runtime. This is the mechanism behind "one artifact, three deployments" in the architecture deck. Keep profiles about role (web/worker/batch), not about environment secrets.

Web MVC: mapping, binding, responding

The full set you use on a real controller, plus the two response-shaping annotations that most teams only discover after their error format has already gone inconsistent.

OrderController.java — every common annotation in one place
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")                    // class-level prefix
@Validated                                        // enables @Min/@NotBlank on params
class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    OrderView get(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }

    @GetMapping
    Page<OrderSummary> list(
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "PLACED") OrderStatus status,
            @RequestParam(required = false) @Size(max = 64) String customerRef,
            @RequestHeader(value = "X-Channel", defaultValue = "web") String channel,
            @CookieValue(required = false) String sessionHint,
            @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "placedAt", direction = DESC) Pageable page) { ... }

    @PostMapping(consumes = APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, produces = APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    @ResponseStatus(CREATED)                      // 201 instead of the default 200
    OrderView place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest body,
                    @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") @NotBlank String key,
                    @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) { ... }

    @PatchMapping("/{id}/address")
    ResponseEntity<Void> reroute(@PathVariable UUID id, @RequestBody AddressPatch patch) {
        orders.reroute(OrderId.of(id), patch);
        return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();   // full control when you need it
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(NO_CONTENT)
    void cancel(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }
}

@RestControllerAdvice

Class-level @ExceptionHandler methods shared across controllers. Scope it with @RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "...") when different modules need different error shapes — otherwise one advice quietly owns the whole application.

@ResponseStatus two ways

On a handler method it sets the success status. On an exception class it maps that exception to a status without any advice — convenient for simple cases, but it produces Boot's default error body, not your ProblemDetail.

@CrossOrigin

Works, but scattering it across controllers means CORS rules live in fifteen files. Configure it once in WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings — or at the gateway, which is where it belongs in an enterprise topology.

Return type: DTO or ResponseEntity?Return the DTO directly when the status is always the same — it is cleaner and reads better. Reach for ResponseEntity only when the status, headers or presence of a body genuinely vary at runtime (Location on create, ETag, conditional 304). Mixing both in one controller is fine and normal.

Validation: shape at the edge, rules in the domain

Bean Validation is excellent at "is this well-formed". It is a poor place for business rules, and the boundary between the two is worth being deliberate about.

The constraints you will actually use
record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 100) List<@Valid LineRequest> lines,  // cascades into each
        @NotNull @Valid AddressRequest shipTo,
        @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{3}") String currency,
        @NotBlank @Email String contactEmail,
        @Positive BigDecimal expectedTotal,
        @Future Instant deliverBy,
        @AssertTrue(message = "Terms must be accepted") boolean termsAccepted) { }

// @NotNull  — not null (but "" passes)
// @NotEmpty — not null and not empty (collection, string, map)
// @NotBlank — not null and contains non-whitespace. For strings, this is the one you want.
Two different annotations, two different jobs
@Valid      // Jakarta: cascade validation into this object
@Validated  // Spring: enables method-level validation on a bean,
            //         and is the only one that supports groups
A custom constraint — reusable and testable
@Target(FIELD) @Retention(RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = SkuValidator.class)
public @interface ValidSku {
    String message() default "Not a known SKU format";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

class SkuValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ValidSku, String> {
    public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        return value == null || value.matches("SKU-\\d{4,8}");   // null = @NotNull's job
    }
}
Where the line isShape — "currency is three letters", "at most 100 lines" — belongs here. Rule — "this customer may not ship to that country", "discount cannot exceed the order value" — belongs on the aggregate, where it can be unit-tested without HTTP and cannot be bypassed by a second entry point such as a Kafka consumer or a batch job.
Turning violations into your error shapeHandle MethodArgumentNotValidException (body) and ConstraintViolationException (params) in your advice and emit a ProblemDetail with a errors property listing field and message. Without that, Boot's default body is a shape your frontend has to special-case.

The proxy-driven annotations, and the test set

Everything in the left column works by the proxy from the bean-lifecycle slide — which means every one of them silently does nothing on a self-invocation, on a private method, or on a final class.

Async, scheduling, caching, events, retry
@EnableAsync @EnableScheduling @EnableCaching     // on a @Configuration

@Async("notificationExecutor")                    // ALWAYS name an executor
CompletableFuture<Void> sendConfirmation(OrderId id) { ... }

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *", zone = "Europe/London")
void nightlyReconcile() { ... }
@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "PT30S")            // delay AFTER completion
@Scheduled(fixedRateString = "PT30S")             // every 30s regardless — can overlap

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "product", key = "#sku", sync = true)  // sync = stampede guard
ProductView byKey(String sku) { ... }
@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "product", key = "#p.sku")
@CachePut(cacheNames = "product", key = "#p.sku")              // always executes + caches
@Caching(evict = { @CacheEvict("product"), @CacheEvict("catalog") })

@EventListener                                    // fires immediately, same thread
@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) // fires only if the tx committed
void on(OrderPlaced event) { ... }

// Spring Retry (3.x). @EnableRetry on a @Configuration.
@Retryable(retryFor = TransientException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
           backoff = @Backoff(delay = 100, multiplier = 2, random = true))
@Recover Tax fallback(TransientException e, Basket b) { ... }
Testing — pick the narrowest slice that proves the thing
@SpringBootTest                 // whole context. Slowest; use for real integration tests
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)      // MVC layer only: JSON, validation, security rules
@DataJpaTest                    // JPA + a real DB via Testcontainers; rolls back per test
@JsonTest @RestClientTest @DataRedisTest        // other slices

@MockitoBean  OrderService orders;      // Boot 3.4+ — replaces the deprecated @MockBean
@MockitoSpyBean PricingService pricing;

@TestConfiguration              // extra beans for tests, NOT picked up by component scan
@DynamicPropertySource          // wire container ports into properties
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@Sql("/seed-orders.sql")
@Transactional                  // on a test = rollback after each method
Three traps in one slide@Async without an executor uses a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor that creates an unbounded number of threads — define your own ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy. fixedRate can overlap runs if one takes longer than the interval; fixedDelay cannot. @Transactional on a test rolls back — which means it also hides the constraint violations that only fire at commit.
Boot 4 the retry annotation you know is not the one you getFramework 7 ships its own @Retryable in org.springframework.core.retry, and it is not a drop-in rename. retryFor/noRetryFor become includes/excludes; the nested @Backoff flattens into delay/multiplier/jitter/maxDelay; maxAttempts = 3 becomes maxRetries = 2 — it counts retries, not attempts, so a straight copy silently gives you one extra call; there is no @Recover, so recovery moves to a catch in the caller; and nothing is advised at all without @EnableResilientMethods. @ConcurrencyLimit arrives alongside it for bulkheads. Keep Spring Retry on the classpath if you rely on @Recover.

Entity and column mapping

The annotations on nearly every entity, with the defaults that are wrong often enough to be worth overriding deliberately.

OrderJpaEntity.java — the mapping layer, not the domain model
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders", schema = "order_mgmt",
       indexes = @Index(name = "idx_orders_customer_placed",
                        columnList = "customer_id, placed_at DESC"),
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = { "idempotency_key" }))
public class OrderJpaEntity {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
    private UUID id;

    @Column(name = "customer_id", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private UUID customerId;

    @Column(name = "total_minor", nullable = false)
    private long totalMinor;                    // money as minor units, never double

    @Column(length = 3, nullable = false, columnDefinition = "char(3)")
    private String currency;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)                // NEVER ORDINAL — see the warning
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 32)
    private OrderStatus status;

    private Instant placedAt;                   // java.time — no @Temporal needed on Hibernate 6

    @Embedded                                   // flattens into the same table
    private AddressEmbeddable shipTo;

    @Column(name = "raw_payload", columnDefinition = "text")
    private String rawPayload;                  // NOT @Lob — see the warning below

    @Transient                                  // never persisted
    private transient boolean recalculated;

    @Version                                    // optimistic locking
    private long version;

    protected OrderJpaEntity() { }              // JPA needs a no-arg constructor
}

@Enumerated(ORDINAL) is the default

And it stores 0, 1, 2. Insert a new enum constant in the middle a year later and every historical row silently changes meaning. Always STRING. This is the single most damaging JPA default.

@Column defaults you should set

nullable is true by default and only affects schema generation — the real constraint must be in your Flyway migration. updatable = false on immutable columns is genuinely enforced by Hibernate and catches bugs.

equals/hashCode

Do not use Lombok's @Data on an entity — it generates them over all fields including lazy associations, which triggers loads and breaks Set semantics before the id is assigned. Use the business key, or the id with a stable hashCode.

@Lob on a String, on PostgreSQLEverywhere else @Lob String means "a big text column". On PostgreSQL the JDBC driver maps it to a large object: the column stores an oid and the bytes live in pg_largeobject. The consequences are all unpleasant — SELECT raw_payload in psql returns a number, a plain DELETE orphans the object so the table never shrinks until you run vacuumlo, and reads need an open transaction so you get "Large Objects may not be used in auto-commit mode". Use columnDefinition = "text" (or @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.LONGVARCHAR)) and let Postgres TOAST it, which it does automatically past ~2 kB. Reserve real LOBs for genuine streaming of hundreds of megabytes.
The mapping entity is not the domain modelIn the architecture deck's layering, Order (domain, no annotations) and OrderJpaEntity (this class) are different types with a mapper between them. For a CRUD-shaped module that separation is overhead worth skipping; for the module where the rules live, it is what keeps Hibernate out of your business logic.

Identifiers: the choice that affects insert throughput

Four generation strategies with materially different behaviour under batch inserts, plus the two ways to model a composite key.

StrategyHow it worksBatch insertsUse when
IDENTITYDatabase auto-increment; id known only after the INSERT❌ disabledLegacy schemas you cannot change. Hibernate cannot batch, because it must round-trip per row
SEQUENCEDatabase sequence, pre-fetched in blocks✅ excellentThe default choice on PostgreSQL/Oracle. Set allocationSize to match the sequence's INCREMENT BY
UUIDGenerated in the JVM before insert✅ excellentDistributed id generation, ids needed before persisting, no cross-service collisions
AUTOProvider picks — usually sequence on Hibernate 6~Avoid: what you get depends on the dialect, so behaviour changes with the database
Sequence with a matching allocation size
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = SEQUENCE, generator = "order_seq")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "order_seq", sequenceName = "order_mgmt.order_id_seq",
                   allocationSize = 50)     // must equal the DB's INCREMENT BY
private Long id;

// DB: CREATE SEQUENCE order_mgmt.order_id_seq INCREMENT BY 50;
// Hibernate now fetches one value and hands out 50 ids without another round trip.
// Mismatch here = duplicate key errors that appear only under concurrency.
Composite keys — prefer @EmbeddedId
@Embeddable
record OrderLineId(UUID orderId, int lineNo) implements Serializable { }

@Entity
class OrderLineEntity {
    @EmbeddedId private OrderLineId id;        // one field, typed, reusable

    @MapsId("orderId")                         // the FK column IS part of the key
    @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY)
    private OrderJpaEntity order;
}

UUID: the version matters

Random UUIDv4 primary keys fragment a B-tree index, because every insert lands in a random leaf page. On a large, insert-heavy table that costs real write throughput and index bloat.

Time-ordered UUIDs (v7) insert near-sequentially and largely remove the problem while keeping client-side generation.

// RFC 9562 version 7 — Hibernate ORM 7.0+ only
@Id @UuidGenerator(style = UuidGenerator.Style.VERSION_7)
private UUID id;

Do not reach for style = TIME expecting v7. Hibernate's TIME style is a custom version 1 layout — timestamp plus the host IP, not the Unix-epoch prefix v7 specifies. It is still index-friendly, but it is not the thing your DBA or your Postgres uuidv7() function means, and mixing the two in one column defeats the ordering you wanted. Style.VERSION_7 arrived in Hibernate ORM 7.0 — on 6.6 and earlier the enum has only AUTO, RANDOM and TIME, so generate v7 in the application and assign it yourself.

@IdClass vs @EmbeddedId@IdClass repeats every key field on the entity and in a separate class, so the two drift. @EmbeddedId keeps one definition and gives you a type you can pass around. Use @IdClass only when mapping a legacy schema whose queries you cannot change.
Natural vs surrogateUse a surrogate key even when a natural one exists. Order numbers get reformatted, customer references get reissued, and "this will never change" is a statement about the current business process, not about the data.

Relationships: owning side, cascade, orphans

Four annotations, and about six ways each to get it subtly wrong. The owning side is the concept everything else hangs off: the side without mappedBy owns the foreign key, and only changes to the owning side are written.

The parent — order owns its lines
@Entity
class OrderJpaEntity {

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order",              // ← inverse side: line owns the FK
               cascade = CascadeType.ALL,       // persist/merge/remove flow to lines
               orphanRemoval = true,            // removing from the list DELETEs the row
               fetch = FetchType.LAZY)          // default for *ToMany — keep it
    private List<OrderLineEntity> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    // ALWAYS maintain both sides — the object graph is not self-healing
    void addLine(OrderLineEntity line) {
        lines.add(line);
        line.setOrder(this);
    }
    void removeLine(OrderLineEntity line) {
        lines.remove(line);
        line.setOrder(null);
    }

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)          // EAGER is the default here — override it
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false)
    private CustomerEntity customer;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "order_promotion",
               joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "order_id"),
               inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "promotion_id"))
    private Set<PromotionEntity> promotions = new HashSet<>();

    @OneToOne(mappedBy = "order", fetch = LAZY, optional = false)
    private OrderPaymentEntity payment;
}
Cascade the aggregate, never across aggregatesCascadeType.ALL from Order to OrderLine is right — lines have no life without the order. CascadeType.ALL from Order to Customer means deleting an order deletes the customer. REMOVE is the dangerous one; PERSIST and MERGE are usually what people actually wanted.
@ManyToOne is EAGER by defaultThe spec default, and it is wrong for almost every enterprise entity. Every @ManyToOne without fetch = LAZY adds a join or an extra select to every single load of that entity — and they compound: five eager parents on one entity means loading one row touches six tables.
@ManyToMany: prefer the join entityThe moment the relationship needs an attribute — when the promotion was applied, who applied it — @ManyToMany has to be rewritten as two @OneToManys to an explicit join entity. That request always comes. Also: use Set, not List, or Hibernate deletes and reinserts the whole join table on every change.

Fetching: where the performance actually is

Fetch type is a default, not a plan. The plan is set per query — which is the distinction that separates people who have tuned Hibernate from people who have configured it.

Four ways to control what gets loaded
// 1. @EntityGraph — declarative, composes with Spring Data method names
interface OrderJpaRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, UUID> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = { "lines", "customer" })
    Optional<OrderJpaEntity> findWithLinesById(UUID id);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")
    Page<OrderJpaEntity> findByCustomerId(UUID customerId, Pageable page);
}

// 2. JOIN FETCH — explicit, one collection at a time
@Query("select o from OrderJpaEntity o join fetch o.lines where o.id = :id")
Optional<OrderJpaEntity> loadWithLines(@Param("id") UUID id);

// 3. @BatchSize — turns N+1 into N/size+1 when you cannot restructure
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")
@BatchSize(size = 50)
private List<OrderLineEntity> lines;

// 4. Don't load entities at all — project
@Query("select new com.retailco.OrderSummary(o.id, o.placedAt, o.totalMinor) " +
       "from OrderJpaEntity o where o.customerId = :c")
List<OrderSummary> summariesFor(@Param("c") UUID customerId);
Two join fetch on collections = cartesian productAn order with 10 lines and 10 promotions returns 100 rows, and Hibernate 6 will refuse with MultipleBagFetchException if both are List. Fetch one collection per query and let @BatchSize handle the second, or run two queries.
Pagination + join fetchLogs "firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory" — Hibernate loads every matching row then pages in the JVM. On 40,000 orders that is an OOM. Fix: page over ids first, then fetch the entities for that page. Set hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true so it throws instead of quietly working until it doesn't.
Make it a testCount queries on your three hottest endpoints with datasource-proxy and assert an upper bound. An N+1 introduced six months later then fails the build rather than the Black Friday dashboard.

Inheritance: three strategies, three different tables

Payment types — card, bank transfer, store credit — are the canonical case. The choice is a schema decision you will not casually reverse, so make it on the query pattern.

StrategySchemaWinsCosts
SINGLE_TABLE defaultOne table, all columns, a discriminatorFastest — no joins, polymorphic queries are one scanSubclass columns must be nullable, so the database cannot enforce "card payments must have a last4"
JOINEDParent table + one table per subclass, sharing the PKProperly normalised; NOT NULL works per subclassA join per subclass on every read; polymorphic queries join everything
TABLE_PER_CLASSOne full table per concrete subclassNo joins for a known typePolymorphic queries become a UNION ALL; shared sequences get awkward. Rarely the right answer
@MappedSuperclassNot inheritance at all — column reuseShare createdAt/version across unrelated entitiesCannot query the superclass; it is not an entity
SINGLE_TABLE, the usual enterprise choice
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments", schema = "payment")
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
@DiscriminatorColumn(name = "payment_type", length = 20)
abstract class PaymentEntity {
