2 · MigrateUnchangedEach consumer switches to the new field on its own scheduleWeeks — the long pole
3 · VerifyMetric: is anyone still reading the old field?—Until the metric is zero
4 · ContractStop populating the old field, then remove itUnaffected — nobody reads itOne release

When expand/contract is impossible

A change to the meaning of the topic itself — different granularity, a different key, a fundamentally different shape. Then it is a new topic:

  1. Create orders.order.placed.v2.
  2. Dual-publish to v1 and v2 from the same transaction.
  3. Consumers migrate one at a time and confirm.
  4. Monitor v1 consumer groups until none remain active.
  5. Announce a sunset date, stop publishing v1, delete it later.

The version in the topic name is what makes this routine instead of a coordinated outage.

What not to doChange the schema, tell people in a chat channel, deploy on Friday. The consumers you know about will cope; the batch job that runs monthly and the partner integration nobody documented will fail silently, and you will hear about it in three weeks from a finance reconciliation.
The metric that makes step 3 possibleMonitor active consumer groups per topic and per schema version. Without it, "has everyone migrated?" is answered by asking around, which means v1 is never retired and you maintain both forever.
Dual-publish from one transactionBoth records go into the same outbox transaction, so v1 and v2 can never diverge. Publishing v2 from a separate job that reads v1 introduces lag and a second failure mode at exactly the moment you need confidence.

Living with three versions in flight

During a migration — and after a replay — a consumer sees several versions of the same event type. Handling that deliberately is what keeps the migration a background activity rather than an event.

Upcasting: normalise on the way in, handle one shape
@Component
class OrderPlacedUpcaster {

    /** Every version is converted to the current internal shape at the boundary.
     *  The handler below never sees a v1 payload. */
    OrderPlaced upcast(JsonNode raw) {
        int version = raw.path("eventVersion").asInt(1);
        return switch (version) {
            case 1 -> fromV1(raw);      // v1 had 'total' in major units, no currency
            case 2 -> fromV2(raw);      // v2 added currency, still 'total'
            case 3 -> fromV3(raw);      // v3 renamed to totalMinor
            default -> throw new UnknownEventVersion(version);   // → DLT, loudly
        };
    }

    private OrderPlaced fromV1(JsonNode n) {
        return new OrderPlaced(
            n.get("orderId").asText(),
            Money.ofMajor(n.get("total").asDouble(), "GBP"),    // the assumption, documented
            n.path("occurredAt").asText());
    }
}

One class holds every historical shape, and the business logic holds none. That is the property worth paying for: your handler stays readable even when the topic has four years of history in it.

The tolerant-reader rules

  • Ignore unknown fields. Never fail on a field you did not expect — that turns every additive producer change into your outage.
  • Never assume field order or the absence of new ones.
  • Read only what you need. A consumer that deserialises the whole payload into a mirror of the producer's model is coupled to all of it.
  • Fail loudly on an unknown version, not on an unknown field. One is a real incompatibility; the other is normal evolution.
Upcasters are permanentYou can never delete one while the topic still holds events of that version — and with compaction or long retention, that can be indefinitely. This is the hidden long-term cost of event-driven systems, and it is the main reason event sourcing is a heavier commitment than a plain event stream.
Test every versionKeep a fixture file per historical version and a test that upcasts each one. It takes minutes, it documents the history better than any wiki page, and it is what makes a four-year-old replay safe to run.

Securing an event platform

Four layers, and the one that gets skipped is authorisation — a cluster where every application can read every topic is a data-governance finding waiting to be written.

LayerMechanismProtects againstNote
Encryption in transitTLS on every listenerNetwork interceptionTable stakes. Costs some CPU unless offloaded
AuthenticationmTLS, SASL/OAUTHBEARER, SASL/SCRAMUnknown clientsOAuth aligns Kafka with your existing IdP — Kafka 4.1 added jwt-bearer
AuthorisationACLs per principal, topic and operationKnown clients reading what they should notThe layer most often left wide open
Encryption at restDisk encryption, or field-level in the payloadStolen disks; broker operatorsField-level is the only one that protects data from the platform team
ACLs: least privilege, per application
# inventory service: read orders, write its own events, use its own group
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Read --topic orders.order.placed.v1
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Read --group inventory-order-reservation
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Write --topic inventory.stock.reserved.v1

# Deny by default at the cluster level:
#   allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found = false
# Anything not explicitly granted is refused — the setting that makes ACLs mean something.
Personal data in events is foreverA customer's name and address in a topic with 90-day retention exists in 90 days of segments, in every consumer's local copy, in the lake, and in every backup. A deletion request cannot reach any of it.

Two defences: minimise — put ids in events and let consumers look up what they are entitled to — or crypto-shred: encrypt personal fields with a per-subject key and delete the key. The events remain; their contents become unreadable.

The quiet risk of a shared clusterA topic with no ACL on a permissive cluster is readable by every application in the estate, including ones from other departments with different data-handling obligations. In a bank that is a control failure, not a configuration preference — and it is invisible until an audit.
Principals from the platformUse mTLS certificates issued by a service mesh or a workload-identity system rather than long-lived SCRAM passwords in config. Rotation stops being a project, and a compromised credential expires on its own.

Platform governance: topics, quotas and self-service

A shared Kafka cluster with no rules becomes unusable at around a hundred topics. With the wrong rules it becomes a ticket queue. The paved-road model from the architecture deck applies directly.

Topic provisioning as code

# topics/orders.yaml — in the owning team's repo, applied by CI
- name: orders.order.placed.v1
  owner: checkout-team
  partitions: 24
  replication: 3
  config:
    min.insync.replicas: 2
    retention.ms: 604800000
    cleanup.policy: delete
  schema: schemas/order-placed-v1.avsc
  compatibility: BACKWARD
  consumers: [inventory, payment, search, notification]

Reviewed in a pull request, applied by a pipeline, and the same file generates the catalogue entry. No ticket, no console clicking, and every topic has an owner by construction.

Quotas: stop one client taking the cluster

kafka-configs --alter --entity-type clients --entity-name analytics-backfill \
  --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=10485760,consumer_byte_rate=52428800'

A backfill job replaying six months of history will saturate the cluster and degrade every production consumer. A quota makes it slow instead of making everyone else slow.

The standards worth setting centrallyNaming convention · envelope fields · default partition count and replication · compatibility mode · required ACL model · mandatory DLT per consumer · trace propagation on. Six or seven rules, enforced by the pipeline that provisions topics, cover almost everything that goes wrong.
Orphan topicsTeams reorganise; topics do not. Run a quarterly report of topics with no producer traffic, no active consumer group, or an owner who no longer exists. Deleting them is usually blocked on nobody being willing to confirm they are unused — which is what the consumer-group metric is for.

What to alert on in an event-driven system

The instinct is to alert on broker health. The things that actually hurt customers are further along, and they are all measurable.

SignalMeansPage whenOwner
End-to-end staleness p99How out of date the slowest consumer's view isAbove the stated SLO for that flowThe consuming team
Consumer lag per partitionFalling behind, or one stuck partitionRising trend, or any partition flat and non-zeroThe consuming team
DLT depthBusiness events not happeningGreater than zeroThe consuming team
Oldest unsent outbox rowEvents not reaching the broker at allOlder than ~30 sThe producing team
Rebalance rateAn unstable consumer groupMore than a few per hour with no deployThe consuming team
Under-replicated partitionsA broker is unhealthy or laggingNon-zero for more than a few minutesPlatform
Offline partitionsData unavailable right nowImmediatelyPlatform
Replication slot lag (CDC)WAL not being consumedBefore the disk fills — this can stop the databasePlatform + producing team
Lag alone is a poor alertA lag of 50,000 is fine on a topic doing 20,000/s and a disaster on one doing 5/s. Alert on estimated time to drain — lag divided by consumption rate — which is dimensionally the thing you care about and comparable across every topic.
The two SLIs to put in front of the businessFlow completeness: of the orders placed in the last hour, what fraction reached a terminal state. Flow latency: p99 time from order placed to confirmed. Both are in the product's language, both are measurable from events you already have, and both catch problems that every technical dashboard shows as green.

Consumer lag is climbing — the diagnostic order

Six checks, cheapest first. The mistake is scaling consumers before knowing which of these it is, which usually makes the problem worse by triggering a rebalance.

#CheckIf yes
1Is lag on all partitions or one?One → hot key or a stuck consumer. Do not scale; find that partition
2Did producer volume jump?A legitimate spike — scale out, or let the buffer absorb it if time-to-drain is acceptable
3Is the rebalance rate elevated?The group is thrashing. Look at max.poll.interval vs handler duration, and pod restarts
4Has handler latency risen?A downstream dependency slowed. Fix there; the consumer is a symptom
5Are consumers at the partition count already?You cannot scale further without adding partitions — make handling cheaper instead
6Are errors and retries up?Retries multiply effective processing time. Check the DLT and the retry topics
The commands to run first
# Lag per partition — the single most useful command
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group inventory
#  TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
#  orders  0          918224          918230          6     consumer-1-a3f…
#  orders  7          901003          962847          61844 consumer-4-9cd…   ← here

# Is anything consuming at all?
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group inventory --members

# What is that consumer's thread actually doing?
curl -s localhost:8081/actuator/threaddump | jq '.threads[]
  | select(.threadName | contains("KafkaConsumer")) | {threadName, threadState}'
A consumer with no member idIf --describe shows lag but the CONSUMER-ID column is empty, nothing is consuming that partition — the group has no live member for it. That is a dead or unstarted consumer, not a slow one, and scaling will not help.
The fastest real fix, usuallySwitch to a batch listener with a bulk write. Five hundred individual inserts become one statement, and a consumer that handled 2,000/s handles 20,000/s with no new infrastructure and no partition change. Check this before adding pods.
Do not raise max.poll.interval.ms to stop rebalancesIt hides a slow handler and delays detection of genuinely dead consumers. Reduce max.poll.records so a poll's work finishes quickly instead.

Replay and reprocessing: the playbook

Replay is the superpower of a log-based system and the fastest way to cause a second incident. Four scenarios, each with a different safe procedure.

1 · Drain a DLT after fixing a bug

  1. Fix and deploy the consumer first. Confirm new traffic is clean.
  2. Consume the DLT with a purpose-built job, not the main listener.
  3. Republish to the main topic, or apply directly — whichever preserves idempotency.
  4. Rate-limit. Ten thousand dead letters replayed at full speed becomes a second outage.

2 · Rebuild a projection

  1. Build into a new table with a new consumer group.
  2. Let it catch up; compare against the live table.
  3. Switch reads with a feature flag.
  4. Keep the old table until you are confident.

Never reset the live group and truncate in place — you have no read model at all while it rebuilds.

3 · Backfill a new consumer

  1. Deploy with auto.offset.reset=earliest and a new group id.
  2. Apply a client quota first, so the backfill cannot starve production consumers.
  3. Expect old schema versions — your upcasters must cover them.
  4. Watch downstream systems: replaying a year of events into a database at full speed will find its limits.

4 · Reprocess after a logic bug

  1. Work out what the wrong logic already did. Emails sent, payments taken — replay will not unsend them.
  2. Reset the group to a timestamp, not an offset — timestamps are meaningful to humans and stable across partitions.
  3. Suppress non-idempotent side effects for the replay window, with a flag.
  4. Reconcile afterwards and report the delta.
Resetting a group — the group must be inactive
# Always --dry-run first. It prints what WOULD happen.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --group projection-order-history \
  --topic orders.order.placed.v1 --reset-offsets \
  --to-datetime 2026-09-14T00:00:00.000 --dry-run

# Then --execute. Other options: --to-earliest --to-latest --shift-by -1000
#   --to-offset N   --by-duration PT6H
The rule that prevents the second incidentReplay re-fires every side effect the handler performs. Customers have been emailed their order confirmation four times by a well-intentioned replay. Before any replay, list what the consumer does that is not idempotent, and turn it off for the duration — deliberately, with a flag, and tell the people who own it.

Six failures, and what to do at 3am

Runbook material. Each of these has happened to every team running Kafka for more than a year.

SymptomLikely causeImmediate actionPrevention
Consumer lag rising steadily, no errorsThroughput mismatch, or a slowed dependencyCheck per-partition lag; check handler latency; scale if all partitions are behindAlert on time-to-drain; batch listeners
One partition stuck, others finePoison record blocking, or a hot keyInspect the record at that offset; confirm bounded retries route it to the DLTNon-retryable exception list; retry topics
Group rebalancing repeatedlyHandler exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, or pods restartingLower max.poll.records; check pod restarts and memory limitsStatic membership; cooperative or KIP-848 protocol
Producer errors: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICASISR below min.insync.replicas — a broker is down or laggingThis is the cluster protecting you. Restore the broker; do not lower the setting to "fix" itAlert on ISR shrink; capacity headroom
Consumer restarted and reprocessed everythingOffsets expired, or the group id changedRely on idempotency; if unavailable, stop and reset to a known offsetStable group ids; know your offsets.retention
Events stopped arriving; broker healthyOutbox relay down, or a CDC slot stalledCheck oldest unsent outbox row and replication slot lag — the producer side, not KafkaAlert on both; they are the blind spot
The one that catches everyone"Events stopped arriving" and every Kafka dashboard is green — because the problem is upstream of Kafka entirely. The outbox relay crashed, or the Debezium connector is in FAILED state. Both are invisible from the broker's perspective, and both are why the producer-side metrics belong on the same dashboard as the consumer-side ones.
What to write down before you need itFor each critical flow: which topics, which consumer groups, who owns them, what the SLO is, how to replay safely, and what is not idempotent. One page. Link it from every alert on that flow. The value of a runbook is entirely in it existing before the incident.

Twelve event-driven anti-patterns

Each of these is common, was reasonable when it was introduced, and is expensive to unwind. Recognising them by symptom is more useful than knowing the names.

Anti-patternWhat you seeWhat it costs
Commands disguised as eventsSendEmail on a topic, one consumer, producer knows the outcomeCoupling with no owner for failures. Fan-out you can never use
Database change feed as a "domain event"CDC straight off tables into a shared topicThirty teams coupled to your schema; you can never refactor
Dual writesave(); kafka.send();Silent loss on crash. Found weeks later by reconciliation
Non-idempotent consumerA counter increment in a handlerEvery rebalance, retry and replay corrupts data a little
Unbounded retriesRetry forever, no DLTOne bad record blocks its partition and everything behind it
Event chains as workflowSix services each reacting to the last, no coordinatorNobody can answer "where is order 88421 stuck"
Event sourcing by accidentRebuilding current state by replaying a topic on every readAll the cost of event sourcing, none of the tooling
Shared consumer groupTwo applications, one group idEach sees half the events. Nobody notices for weeks
No schema governanceJSON, no registry, "we'll be careful"A breaking change reaches production and fails asynchronously
Fat events as data dumpsEvery column of the row in the payloadA published contract you can never shrink, plus a PII exposure
Synchronous call inside a consumerHandler calls three services and waitsConsumer throughput now equals the slowest dependency's latency
Events for everythingThe whole request path made asyncEvery screen must model "not yet"; debugging cost with no availability gain
The pattern behind themNine of the twelve come from treating the broker as the architecture. Kafka does not make a system event-driven any more than a database makes it well-modelled. The architecture is the event design — what is a fact, who owns it, what it means — and the broker is how it travels.

Moving an existing system to events

You almost never build event-driven from scratch — you convert something. Six phases, each shipping value on its own, none requiring a big bang.

1–2 Prepare

  • Map the synchronous calls and classify each: must succeed now, or a reaction? Only the second group moves.
  • Add the outbox to the producing service and publish events alongside the existing calls. Nothing consumes them yet.
  • Verify the event stream matches reality — counts, totals, timing — before anyone depends on it.

3–4 Shift one consumer

  • Pick the least critical reaction — search indexing, analytics, notifications.
  • Build the consumer; run it in parallel with the synchronous call, writing to a shadow table.
  • Compare outputs for a week. Then switch with a flag and remove the synchronous call.
  • Repeat for the next consumer. One at a time.

5 Harden

  • Idempotency and a DLT on every consumer before the second one goes live, not after.
  • Trace propagation across the hop — you will need it during phase 6.
  • Reconciliation job comparing source of truth to every consumer's state.
  • Runbook and alerts per flow.

6 Only then, the interesting parts

  • Projections and read models, once the stream is trusted.
  • A saga, once more than one service reacts and someone asks where things are stuck.
  • Streams, once you have a genuine stateful or windowed requirement.

Teams that start at phase 6 are the ones that end up with an event-driven system they cannot debug.

The parallel-run is the whole safety mechanismRunning the event path and the synchronous path together, comparing outputs, and only then switching is what makes this reversible at every step. It costs double processing for a few weeks. That is far cheaper than discovering in production that your event carries a subtly different meaning from the call it replaced.

Kafka, and when something else is better

Kafka is the default for enterprise event backbones and is the wrong choice more often than its popularity suggests. Honest comparison.

TechnologyModelStrong atWeak atPick it when
KafkaPartitioned, replayable logThroughput, replay, fan-out, stream processing, retention as a featurePer-message TTL, priority, complex routing, tiny deploymentsYou need a durable event backbone many consumers read independently
RabbitMQQueues with exchangesFlexible routing, per-message TTL, priorities, low latency, simple opsReplay (messages are consumed), very high throughputWork queues and RPC-style messaging with routing rules
IBM MQ / JMSQueues, transactionalXA transactions, guaranteed once-only delivery, decades of bank toolingFan-out, replay, throughput, costYou are integrating with systems that already speak it — extremely common in banking
AWS SQS + SNSManaged queue + pub/subZero operations, elastic, cheap at low volume, native DLQOrdering (FIFO queues are limited), replay, throughput ceilingsCloud-native workloads where you do not want to run a broker
EventBridge / Pub-SubManaged event busRouting rules, SaaS integrations, schema registry, no opsReplay, cost at high volume, vendor lock-inEvent routing across services and third parties, moderate volume
PulsarLog + queue, tiered by designMulti-tenancy, geo-replication, both queue and stream semanticsSmaller ecosystem, more moving parts (BookKeeper)Strong multi-tenancy or geo-replication requirements
The honest enterprise answerMost large organisations run two: Kafka as the event backbone for domain events and analytics, and an existing MQ estate for transactional integration with systems that will not change. That is not a failure to standardise — it is two different jobs. What matters is a clear rule for which goes where, written down.
Kafka's queue gap has closedKafka historically could not do per-message acknowledgement or competing consumers beyond the partition count. KIP-932 "queues for Kafka" adds share groups that acknowledge individual records and let consumer count exceed partition count. Early access in 4.0, preview in 4.1, GA in Kafka 4.2 behind the share.version feature flag (level 1 by default). On 4.2+ this is a real option for work-queue workloads instead of a second broker.

What an event-driven system costs to run

The line items that appear on the bill and in the on-call rota. Useful for a business case, and for answering "why is this more expensive than the monolith".

Worked monthly estimate

Volume
20,000 events/s × 1 KB ≈ 50 TB/month written
Replication
× 3 for RF=3 → 150 TB of writes
Storage
7 days retained, lz4 at ~4× → ~9 TB on disk
Read amplification
5 consumer groups → 5× read traffic, and cross-AZ reads are charged
Brokers
6 instances sized for network, not CPU
Plus
schema registry, Connect cluster, monitoring, and the consumers themselves

Divide by orders processed and you have cost per 1,000 orders for the event path — directly comparable to the synchronous alternative.

The costs that surprise people

  • Cross-AZ traffic. Replication and consumption across zones is charged per gigabyte and can exceed the compute bill. Rack-aware follower fetching helps.
  • Retention creep. "Let's keep 30 days just in case" quadruples storage and nobody revisits it.
  • Read amplification. Each new consumer group re-reads everything. Ten groups is 10× read cost.
  • Idle consumers. Pods beyond the partition count cost money and process nothing.
  • On-call. A broker estate needs owners, upgrades and a rota. Often the largest real cost.
Three levers that actually move the billCompression — lz4 or zstd typically cuts storage and network 3–5× for a little CPU. Retention per topic — most topics do not need seven days; some need thirty. Decide each one. Tiered storage — long retention on object storage costs a fraction of broker disk, which changes the replay conversation entirely.

The decisions, in the order to make them

Everything in this tab, as a sequence. Each answer constrains the next, and the expensive ones are all near the top.

#DecisionDefault answerCost to reverse
1Does this step need to be synchronous?Yes if the user's action should fail when it fails; otherwise an eventweeks
2Event or command?Event — a past-tense fact with no named consumerweeks
3Thin, fat or delta?Fat, with only the fields the event genuinely meansweeks — it is a contract
4What is the key?The entity whose events must stay orderedweeks — repartitioning is disruptive
5Choreography or orchestration?Choreograph within a context, orchestrate across them and past four stepsweeks
6How does the event get published?Outbox. Always. Polling relay first, CDC when volume justifies itdays
7Partition count?Peak throughput ÷ per-consumer rate, × 3 headroom. Round up generouslyweeks
8Format and compatibility?Avro + registry, BACKWARD, register from CIdays
9Retention?7 days for operational topics; compaction for reference data; long retention if rebuild is requiredhours
10Retry strategy?Bounded retries then a DLT. Non-blocking retry topics if ordering permitshours
11How is the consumer idempotent?Business key, or a dedupe table on the event id. Answer this before writing the handlerhours
12What is the staleness SLO?State a number per flow, measure it, alert on ithours
If you answer only threeMake them 6 (outbox — otherwise you lose events silently), 11 (idempotency — otherwise duplicates corrupt data) and 10 (bounded retries plus a DLT — otherwise one bad record stops a partition). Those three are the difference between a system that degrades gracefully and one that fails invisibly.

Glossary and where to go deeper

The terms that come up in design reviews and interviews, and the sources worth the time.

Terms

Offset
A record's position in a partition. A consumer group's committed offset is its bookmark.
ISR
In-sync replicas — those caught up with the leader. acks=all means all of these.
Consumer group
Both the parallelism unit and the isolation boundary. One partition to one member at a time.
Rebalance
Reassigning partitions when membership changes. Cooperative and KIP-848 make it nearly free.
Compaction
Retain the latest value per key forever. Turns a topic into a snapshot.
Tombstone
A null value on a compacted topic — the key is deleted.
Outbox
Write the event to your database in the same transaction; relay it afterwards.
Saga
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of a rollback.
Projection
A read model maintained by consuming events. Rebuildable by replay.
Upcaster
Converts an old event version to the current shape at the consumer boundary.
EOS
Exactly-once semantics — within Kafka. Elsewhere, idempotency.
Backpressure
What a system does when it cannot keep up. In Kafka, the topic absorbs it until retention does not.

Going deeper

  • Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — chapter 11 on streams is the best explanation of logs, ordering and derived data anywhere.
  • Stopford, Designing Event-Driven Systems — free from Confluent; the enterprise patterns, told well.
  • Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns — the vocabulary everyone still uses, and it predates all of this.
  • Richardson, Microservices Patterns — the definitive treatment of sagas and the outbox.
  • Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design — where domain events come from and what makes one well-formed.
  • The Kafka documentation's design section — genuinely well written, and shorter than people expect.
The three sentences worth being able to say"We design for at-least-once delivery into idempotent consumers, which gives exactly-once effects." · "Every event that must not be lost goes through an outbox, because there is no transaction across the database and the broker." · "Ordering is guaranteed per partition, so we key on the entity whose sequence matters." Those three cover most of what an interviewer is checking for, and most of what a design review needs to establish.

Design the system before you design the classes

High-level design (HLD) is where you decide what the components are, how data moves between them, where it is stored, and what happens when a piece fails or the load grows tenfold. This deck teaches that in three stages: the fundamentals and building blocks, the architectural and cloud patterns built from them, and then twelve interview designs worked step by step. It loosely follows the roadmap.sh system design path, and almost every idea comes with a diagram.

11

topic sections: fundamentals, estimation, the building blocks, reliability, operations, and the patterns built from them.

12

worked designs, from the URL shortener to a distributed key-value store. Each takes six slides and follows the same method.

8

steps in the interview framework. Every sample design is walked through them in order, so the method becomes habit.

How to use it

  • Arrow keys or the buttons move through slides, and C opens the contents. Each worked design is its own section there.
  • Self-study: read one section per sitting, then redraw its diagrams from memory. If you can't redraw a diagram, you can't use it in an interview.
  • Teaching: use sections 02–11 as lectures. Use the designs as exercises: show the requirements slide, let the group sketch a design for 15 minutes, then reveal the rest.

What it assumes

  • You have built and deployed a web service with a database behind it. No distributed-systems background is needed.
  • Nothing is tied to one vendor, but real technology is named (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Cassandra, S3, a CDN), because interviewers want to hear concrete choices.
  • All numbers are rough, and each states its assumptions. In an interview, the reasoning behind a number counts for more than its precision.
The one habit worth buildingName the trade-off every time you choose something. "I'll use a cache" earns nothing. "I'll use a cache-aside Redis in front of the database. Profiles can be up to 60 seconds stale, and in return the database sees about 5% of reads" is the sentence that gets scored.

HLD draws the boxes and arrows; LLD fills in the boxes

It is the same system at three zoom levels. High-level design stops at the service boundary: which services exist, how they talk to each other, and where the data lives. Low-level design opens one service up and decides its classes, interfaces and schema.

High-level designLow-level design
Question it answersWhat are the parts, and how do they cooperate at scale?How is one part built so it is correct and easy to change?
DecisionsServices and their boundaries, datastores, sync vs async, caching, partitioning, replication, consistency level, failure handlingClasses and interfaces, design patterns (Strategy, Factory…), concurrency inside a process, exact schema, algorithms
ArtefactsArchitecture diagram, data-flow and sequence diagrams, capacity estimate, API contract, ADRsClass and sequence diagrams, DDL, interface signatures, pseudo-code
Optimises forScalability, availability, latency, cost, team autonomyReadability, testability, extensibility, correctness
Interview round"System design", 45–60 min, whiteboard"OOD" or "machine coding", 60–90 min, often compiles
Where they meetThe API contract and the data model belong to both. HLD decides that an order service owns the orders and exposes POST /orders. LLD decides the Order aggregate, its invariants, and the columns in the table. In an HLD round, sketch both at the level of resources and fields, not classes and methods.

The roadmap, and where each stop lives in this deck

The roadmap.sh system design path runs from vocabulary to cloud patterns. The deck follows the same arc but groups the stops by building block, and it ends where interviews start: with worked designs. Each stop below is tagged with the section that teaches it.

Beyond the roadmap

§03
Back-of-the-envelope estimation: the numbers to know and a repeatable method.
§08
Reliability: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, rate limiting, multi-region, consensus, unique IDs and clocks.
§09
Security: OAuth2/OIDC, tokens, securing the edge, and alerting on SLOs rather than on CPU.
§10
Architecture styles compared honestly, with a matrix for choosing between them.

Wrap-up: a trade-offs cheat sheet, red flags, and an answer checklist.

A four-week pace

  • Week 1: §01–§04. Learn the vocabulary, estimation, and the edge.
  • Week 2: §05–§08. Data, caching, async and reliability, which is the core of the deck.
  • Week 3: §09–§11 and the first six designs. Do each design yourself before reading it.
  • Week 4: the last six designs, out loud and timed at 45 minutes, then §24.

Eight steps in 45 minutes, and you drive

A system-design round is scored on how you get to an answer, not on reaching one particular diagram. The eight steps make your reasoning visible and keep you from spending 30 minutes on the database schema. Every worked design in this deck follows them in order.

StepWhat you doSay out loud, e.g.
1 · ClarifyFunctional scope (3–5 core features), non-functional targets (scale, latency, availability, consistency), what is out of scope"I'll focus on create and redirect. Analytics can be eventually consistent. Is that fair?"
2 · EstimateDAU → QPS, peak, read:write ratio, storage over 5 years, bandwidth, cache size"100 M writes a day is about 1,200 a second, so one Postgres primary can take it."
3 · APIThe 3–5 endpoints or messages that serve the core features, including idempotency and paging"POST /v1/urls takes an idempotency key, so a retried create can't make two links."
4 · Data modelEntities, key fields, access patterns, then SQL or NoSQL and the partition key"Every read is by short code, so this is a key-value access pattern."
5 · High-level designClients → edge → services → stores → async consumers. Walk one request end to end."A redirect never touches the write path. Here's the read path…"
6 · Deep divesThe two hardest parts: usually the core algorithm and the scaling bottleneck"The interesting problems are generating unique keys and keeping redirects under 10 ms."
7 · BottlenecksHot spots, single points of failure, what breaks at 10×, the failure modes of each dependency"If Redis dies, redirects fall back to the read replicas, which are sized to carry the full read load."
8 · Wrap-upSummarise the trade-offs you made and what you would do next"I chose availability over consistency for reads. Next I'd add multi-region."
What is actually scoredFour things: navigating the problem (did you find the hard part?), the design (does it work end to end?), trade-offs (did you name the alternatives and why you rejected them?), and communication (could the interviewer follow you?). Senior candidates are also expected to raise failure modes and operability without being asked.
The classic ways to loseDesigning before clarifying. Drawing boxes with no data flow. Naming technologies without reasons ("Kafka, because it scales"). Going deep too early. Waiting for the interviewer to drive. And never mentioning what happens when something fails.

Functional requirements say what it does; non-functional ones decide the architecture

Two systems with identical features can need completely different designs. A URL shortener for an internal team fits on one box. The same shortener for a social network needs a CDN, a cache tier and a key-generation service. The non-functional requirements are what separate them, which is why step 1 exists.

If the requirement says……the architecture gets
Reads ≫ writes (100:1), p99 read < 50 msA cache in front of the store, read replicas, CDN for anything static, denormalised read models
99.99% availableNo single points of failure, at least two availability zones, automated fail-over, graceful degradation of non-core features
Strong consistency (money, inventory, bookings)A single leader per record, transactions or compare-and-set, idempotency keys. Accept the latency cost.
Traffic spikes 10× (sales, launches)Queues to absorb bursts, autoscaling on the stateless tier, load shedding and rate limits at the edge
Data must never be lostSynchronous replication or quorum writes, write-ahead logs, backups with tested restores, RPO ≈ 0
Global users, < 100 ms everywhereA CDN, geo-routing, regional read replicas, and possibly multi-region writes with conflict handling
GDPR / data residencyPer-region data stores, a deletion pipeline that reaches caches, logs and backups, encryption and audit trails
Questions worth asking every timeWho are the users, and how many are active each day? What is the read:write ratio? What must be fast, and what may be slow? What is the worst thing that can go wrong: losing data, showing stale data, or being down? Is it one region or global? What is explicitly out of scope?

Slow for one user is a performance problem; slow for many is a scalability problem

A service is scalable if adding resources adds capacity in roughly the same proportion. The two problems need different fixes, so diagnose which one you have before reaching for more servers. More servers won't fix a slow query, and faster code won't fix a single shared lock.

Diagnose performance

Measure one request: trace it, profile it, look at EXPLAIN. The fixes are an index, a batched call, less serialisation, a cache in front of an expensive computation, or a better algorithm.

Diagnose scalability

Load-test at rising load and watch where latency turns upward. Find the resource that saturates first: CPU, connection pool, a DB row lock, one hot partition, or a single-threaded consumer.

Why scaling is never perfectly linear

The Universal Scalability Law names the two taxes. Contention is waiting for shared resources. Coherency is the work of keeping nodes in agreement. The second grows with the square of the node count, which is why "just add nodes" eventually stops helping.

Interviewers probe"What happens at 10× load?" Name the first thing that saturates and what you'd do about it: "The primary database's write throughput. I'd first check whether writes can be batched or queued, then shard by user id." A vague "add more servers" is not an answer.

Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many finish per second

Think of a pipe. Its length is the latency and its width is the throughput. You can widen the pipe (more workers, more partitions) without shortening it, and a pipe running nearly full gets slower for everyone, because requests start queueing. Aim for the most throughput you can get while latency stays acceptable.

Report percentiles, never the mean

A mean of 40 ms can hide a p99 of 2 s. Users experience the tail, and your heaviest users hit it most often. Set targets as p50 / p99 (and p99.9 for critical paths).

Fan-out amplifies the tail

If one request calls 100 backends and each is slow 1% of the time, then 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 63% of requests are slow. Mitigations: hedged requests, tighter per-call timeouts, and returning partial results.

Trading one for the other

Batching raises throughput and adds latency (Kafka's linger.ms, group commit). Parallelism lowers latency and costs throughput headroom. Say which one the requirement values.

Availability multiplies in series and compounds in parallel

Availability is the fraction of time, or of requests, that succeed. Each nine you add cuts the allowed downtime by 10×, and the cost of the system goes up much more steeply than that. Two rules of arithmetic decide most availability arguments in an interview.

AvailabilityDown / yearDown / 30 daysDown / day
99% (two nines)3.65 d7.2 h14.4 min
99.9%8.77 h43.2 min1.44 min
99.95%4.38 h21.6 min43 s
99.99%52.6 min4.3 min8.6 s
99.999%5.26 min26 s0.86 s

MTBF, MTTR, and where the nines come from

Availability = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). You can fail less often (raise the mean time between failures) or recover faster (cut the mean time to recovery). Past three nines, the cheaper lever is usually recovery: automated fail-over, fast rollback, feature flags, and good alerts. At 99.99% there is no time for a human to wake up and log in.

Say it this way"The checkout path has four synchronous dependencies. At 99.9% each, that's about 99.6%. To reach 99.95% I'd make recommendations and loyalty asynchronous and give tax calculation a cached fallback. That leaves two dependencies on the critical path."

During a network partition, choose: refuse to answer, or answer possibly wrong

CAP says a distributed data store cannot be both Consistent (every read sees the latest write, i.e. linearizable) and Available (every request to a live node gets a non-error answer) while a Partition splits the network. Networks do partition, so P is not optional. The real choice is what each node does when it can't reach the others.

CP: correctness over uptime

Use it where a wrong answer costs money or trust: balances, inventory counts at checkout, seat and room bookings, leader election, locks, configuration. etcd ZooKeeper Spanner HBase MongoDB (majority)

AP: uptime over freshness

Use it where stale is fine and down is not: timelines, likes, product views, shopping carts, presence, metrics. You need conflict resolution: last-write-wins, CRDTs, or merging in the application. Cassandra DynamoDB Riak CouchDB

The mature answerChoose per operation, not per system. An e-commerce site can be AP for browsing and the cart, and CP for "decrement stock and take payment". Many stores let you tune this per request, for example Cassandra's QUORUM vs ONE, or DynamoDB's strongly consistent reads.

Partitions are rare; the latency-versus-consistency trade-off is paid on every request

CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC adds the everyday case: if Partitioned, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Waiting for replicas to confirm a write makes it consistent, and it makes the request slower. That trade-off applies on every request, not only during a partition.

PA/EL fast and always up

Cassandra, DynamoDB (default reads), Riak. Writes are acknowledged by one or a few replicas and reads may be stale. Good for feeds, carts, sensor data, and anything that has to be write-heavy and low-latency.

PC/EC correct, and pays for it

Spanner, HBase, etcd / ZooKeeper, VoltDB. Writes wait for a quorum or synchronous replicas. Good for money, metadata, coordination and schedules. Expect cross-zone round-trips on each write.

PA/EC consistent until it can't be

MongoDB, in Abadi's classification: it reads from the primary in normal operation, but during some partitions can serve writes that are later rolled back.

PC/EL fast normally, strict under stress

Yahoo PNUTS, the classic example: it serves reads from the local replica for low latency, but refuses writes to a record whose master is unreachable.

The number to rememberSynchronous replication between availability zones in one region adds roughly 1–2 ms per write, which is usually worth it. Synchronous replication across continents adds 60–150 ms per write, which is why global systems are nearly always EL across regions and EC within one.

"Consistent" is a spectrum: say which guarantee you need

A consistency model is a promise about what reads may return after a write. Stronger promises are simpler to reason about and cost more latency and availability. Most products need strong consistency on a few operations and one of the session guarantees everywhere else.

ModelGuaranteeTypical implementationUse it for
Strong (linearizable)Behaves like a single copy; reads see all completed writesSingle leader + sync replication, consensus (Raft/Paxos), quorum R+W>NBalances, stock at checkout, unique usernames, locks
CausalEffects are never seen before their causesVersion vectors, dependency trackingComment threads, chat (a reply never appears before its message)
Read-your-writesA session sees its own writesRead from the leader for a few seconds after a write, or send a version tokenProfile edits, posting a comment, settings
Monotonic readsA session never sees older data than it already sawSticky replica per user, or reads with a min-versionFeeds, inboxes, anything refreshed
EventualIf writes stop, replicas convergeAsync replication, anti-entropy, last-write-wins or CRDTsLike counts, view counts, DNS, search index, analytics
WeakBest effort; reads may miss writes entirelyFire-and-forget, in-memory cachesVoIP, live video frames, multiplayer positions

Fail-over and replication: keep a second copy ready to take over

There are two ways to survive losing a node. Keep a standby that takes over (active-passive), or have every node serve all the time (active-active). The first is simpler. The second uses all the hardware you pay for, but it needs a way to settle conflicting writes.

StandbyStateRecovery (RTO)Cost
ColdBackups only; provision on failurehourslowest
WarmRunning, replicating, scaled downminutesmedium
HotFully sized, in sync, auto-promotedseconds≈ 2×
Active-activeServing live traffic≈ 0 (reroute)≈ 2×, plus conflict handling

What goes wrong in fail-over

  • Split brain: a network blip makes both nodes think they're the primary. Prevent it with a quorum or a lease, and fence the old primary.
  • Lost writes: with async replication, writes the standby hadn't received are gone. That window is the RPO.
  • Flapping: too-sensitive health checks fail over back and forth. Add hysteresis.
  • Untested standby: a fail-over nobody has rehearsed usually fails. Run game days.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Multi-regionDeck · Disaster recovery

Scale the database up, scale the stateless tier out

Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine. It needs no code change, but it has a ceiling, a single point of failure, and a price that grows faster than the capacity. Horizontal scaling adds more machines, which only works once the machines are interchangeable. So the real work of scaling out is moving state out of the application servers.

Where state hides

In-memory sessions, local file uploads, in-process caches that must be coherent, scheduled jobs that run "on the server", WebSocket connections. Each one needs a home outside the box, or the box can't be replaced freely.

Sticky sessions are a smell

Pinning a user to one server works until that server dies or the load becomes uneven. Prefer a shared session store, or signed tokens (JWT) that carry the state. Keep stickiness for connection-oriented protocols such as WebSockets, where it is inherent.

Autoscaling needs headroom

New instances take 1–5 minutes to boot and warm up. Scale on a leading signal (request rate, queue depth) with a target around 60% utilisation. For known events, pre-scale rather than waiting for the autoscaler to react.

An SLO turns "highly available" into a number you can spend

An SLI is a measurement, e.g. the share of requests served successfully within 300 ms. An SLO is the target for it: 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is the contract with a penalty, set looser than the SLO so you breach the SLO internally before you owe anyone money. The gap between 100% and the SLO is the error budget.

Good SLIs are user-shaped

Measure at the edge, where the user feels it: the success ratio and latency of real requests to a journey ("place order", "load feed"). CPU and memory are causes, not SLIs.

Pick targets you can defend

A target stricter than your dependencies is fiction: you can't be 99.99% on top of a 99.9% database without redundancy. Start from what users tolerate and what you achieve today, then tighten.

Budgets make trade-offs explicit

Budget left over means you can ship faster and run experiments. Budget exhausted means reliability comes first. Product and engineering argue about data instead of opinions.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · SLOs and alerting

The vocabulary, one line each

Use these words precisely. Interviewers notice when "consistent" or "partition" is used loosely, and each one below has a slide later in the deck.

Load and performance

QPS / RPS
Queries or requests per second. Always state average and peak (peak is usually 2–10× average).
DAU / MAU
Daily and monthly active users, the input to most estimates.
p50 / p99
Median and 99th-percentile latency. p99 is what your heaviest users feel.
Tail latency
The slow end of the distribution, which fan-out amplifies.
Throughput
Work completed per unit time, in requests, rows or bytes per second.
Hot spot / hot key
One partition or key getting a disproportionate share of traffic.
Fan-out
One request or event turning into many downstream calls or writes.
Back pressure
A slow consumer signalling upstream to slow down instead of drowning.
Thundering herd
Many clients hitting the same resource at once, e.g. after a cache expiry or a restart.
Head-of-line blocking
One slow item delaying everything queued behind it.

Data and distribution

Replication
The same data copied to several nodes, for availability and read scale.
Partitioning / sharding
Different data on different nodes, for write scale and size.
Network partition
Nodes that are up but can't reach each other. Not the same thing as a data partition.
Quorum
A majority, or R + W > N, needed for an operation to count.
Linearizable
Behaves as if there were one copy. The precise meaning of "strongly consistent".
Eventual consistency
Replicas converge if writes stop; reads may be stale until then.
Idempotent
Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, which is what makes retries safe.
SPOF
Single point of failure: one component whose loss takes the system down.
Split brain
Two nodes both acting as the leader after a partition.
RPO / RTO
How much data you can lose, and how long you can be down.

Memory is fast, the network is slower, and crossing an ocean is slowest

You don't need these to the nanosecond. You need the orders of magnitude, because they decide designs: why a cache in memory beats a database round trip, why chatty services hurt, and why a synchronous call across continents can't sit on a 100 ms path.

Handy conversionsValue
Seconds per day86,400 ≈ 10⁵
Seconds per month / year≈ 2.5 M / ≈ 31.5 M
1 M requests / day≈ 12 / s
1 B requests / day≈ 12,000 / s
2¹⁰ · 2²⁰ · 2³⁰ · 2⁴⁰ · 2⁵⁰KB · MB · GB · TB · PB (thousand … quadrillion)
1 Gbps≈ 125 MB/s
Typical sizesValue
int / long, timestamp / UUID4 B / 8 B / 16 B
A database row with a few columns100 B – 1 KB
A short post or chat message + metadata~0.5–1 KB
Compressed photo / thumbnail200 KB – 2 MB / 10–50 KB
1 minute of 1080p video at 5 Mbps≈ 40 MB
A web page's HTML / all its assets50–100 KB / 1–3 MB

Five numbers, derived the same way every time

Estimation isn't about being right. It tells you which parts of the design matter. Two minutes of arithmetic answers questions like "does this fit on one database?", "do we need a CDN?" and "can the cache hold the hot set?". Say the assumptions out loud, round hard, and write the results where you can point at them later.

Round aggressively

86,400 becomes 10⁵. 365 becomes 400 when you are rounding up. 2.3 becomes 2. Interviewers want the order of magnitude and a clean chain of reasoning, not long division. State "about" and move on.

Compare to one box

Every number means something only next to a capacity. 3,000 writes/s fits one PostgreSQL primary, and 300,000 does not. 2 TB fits one node, and 2 PB needs object storage. That comparison is the reason for doing the estimate.

Separate the hard dimension

Usually only one number is scary: the QPS (feeds), the storage (video), the fan-out (notifications), or the concurrency (chat). Name it. It becomes your first deep dive.

Worked estimate: a photo-sharing app with 100 million daily users

The assumptions, said out loud: 100 M daily active users. Each user views about 50 photos a day, and one user in five uploads one photo a day. An original photo compresses to about 500 KB, and its thumbnails add about 100 KB. A feed-sized image served to a phone is about 100 KB. Peak traffic is 3× the average.

The script, spoken

"100 million users times 50 views is 5 billion a day. Divided by about 10⁵ seconds, that's roughly 50 thousand a second, and about 150 thousand at peak. Each view is about 100 KB, so tens of gigabits per second leave the system. That has to come from a CDN. Uploads are 20 million a day, a few hundred a second, but at 600 KB each that's 12 terabytes a day. So photos go to object storage, and only metadata goes to a database."

Sanity checks worth a sentence

  • Is 50 views a day plausible? It is for a scrolling feed. For a utility app, it might be 5.
  • Storage is often dominated by derived data: thumbnails, transcodes, indexes, replicas. Add it.
  • Retention changes everything: keep forever, or delete after 30 days?
  • Erasure coding (≈ 1.5×) instead of 3 full replicas saves a third of the raw storage at PB scale.

What one well-tuned node can take, to an order of magnitude

An estimate means nothing until it meets a capacity. These ranges are for a commodity cloud node (8–32 cores, SSD, 10 Gbps) doing simple operations. Real numbers depend heavily on payload size, query shape and tuning, so treat them as "which order of magnitude" guides and say so in the interview.

Other limits per nodeRough practical ceiling
Relational DB size1–10 TB before backups, vacuum and migrations get painful
Redis memory25–100 GB per instance; cluster beyond
Concurrent WebSockets per server100 k – 1 M, bounded by memory (~10–50 KB each)
Kafka partition write rate~10 MB/s per partition is a safe planning figure
DB connections (PostgreSQL)a few hundred active; put a pooler in front
Network per instance10–25 Gbps; egress cost often binds first
How to use themSay "roughly" and the order of magnitude: "About 3,000 writes a second at peak. A single PostgreSQL primary handles that with headroom, so I won't shard on day one, but I'll pick a partition key now so sharding later is a migration, not a redesign." Then move on. Nobody will argue about 5k versus 15k.

Follow one request from the browser to the database and back

Nearly every design shares the same front half: name resolution, an edge that caches, a balancer that spreads load, a gateway that enforces policy, and a stateless service in front of a cache and a database. Know that path cold. Then each interview design is mostly a question of what changes behind the service.

HopJobScales byIf it fails
DNSName → IP, and often geo- or latency-based routingManaged, anycastCached answers keep working until their TTLs expire
CDNServe static and cacheable content near the user; absorb DDoSProvider's global edgeFail-open to the origin, which must be sized for it
Load balancerTerminate TLS, spread requests, remove unhealthy instancesManaged or HA pairRedundant pair; DNS fail-over across regions
API gatewayAuthN, rate limits, routing, request loggingStateless replicasEverything behind it is unreachable, so keep it thin
ServiceBusiness logicHorizontal replicasThe LB routes around it; retries with idempotency
Cache / DBHot reads / durable truthCluster / replicas and shardsCache miss storm; DB fail-over (see §05, §06)

DNS turns names into addresses, and it is also your first load balancer

A lookup walks a hierarchy from the root to the top-level domain to the domain's own nameserver, and every answer is cached for its TTL. That caching makes DNS fast and massively scalable. It is also why a DNS change or DNS fail-over is never instant.

Records you'll mention

A/AAAA name → IPv4/IPv6. CNAME is an alias to another name (how you point at a CDN or load balancer). NS delegates to nameservers. MX is mail, TXT holds verification and SPF, and SRV gives a service's host and port.

DNS as traffic management

Managed DNS can answer differently per query. Weighted answers split traffic (canary 5%). Latency or geo answers send users to the nearest region. Fail-over answers stop returning an unhealthy region. That makes it the usual way to route between regions.

TTL is a trade-off

A short TTL (30–60 s) means faster fail-over and more lookups. A long TTL (hours) means fewer lookups and slow changes. Some clients and ISPs ignore TTLs, so plan for a stale tail of traffic after any change, and lower the TTL a day before a planned migration.

A CDN moves bytes close to users so your origin never sees most requests

A content delivery network is a fleet of caching proxies in hundreds of locations. It cuts latency (the edge might be 10 ms away when the origin is 150 ms away) and it absorbs load and DDoS traffic. The main decision is how content reaches the edge: fetched on first request (pull) or uploaded ahead of time (push).

Cache keys and headers

Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 lets the edge cache a response, and private or no-store stops it. The cache key is usually URL plus selected headers, so keep the key small: an unneeded Vary header or a tracking query parameter destroys the hit ratio.

Invalidation

Prefer versioned URLs (app.3f9a.js, /img/v2/…): a new version is a new object, so nothing needs purging. Keep purge APIs for mistakes. For HTML, use short TTLs with stale-while-revalidate.

More than static files

Modern CDNs terminate TLS, run a WAF and absorb DDoS, cache public API responses for seconds, sign URLs for private media, and run small functions at the edge. An origin shield (a mid-tier cache) stops 300 PoPs from all missing to the origin at once.

An L4 balancer routes connections; an L7 balancer routes requests

The layer tells you how much of the packet the balancer can read. A layer-4 balancer sees addresses and ports, so it forwards whole TCP or UDP connections, blindly and very fast. A layer-7 balancer terminates TLS and reads the HTTP request, so it can route on path, header or cookie, at the cost of more CPU per request.

Layer 4Layer 7
Routes onIP, port, protocolHost, path, method, headers, cookies, JWT claims
Unit of balancingConnection: a long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection sticks to one serverRequest: can spread requests from one connection across servers
TLSPass-through (or terminate)Terminates, and can re-encrypt to the backend
ExtrasVery high throughput, low latency, any TCP/UDP protocolRetries, header rewrites, compression, auth hooks, canary splits, WebSocket upgrade
ExamplesAWS NLB, GCP Network LB, IPVS, HAProxy (TCP mode)AWS ALB, Envoy, Nginx, HAProxy (HTTP mode), Traefik
The gRPC gotchagRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. Behind an L4 balancer, each client's connection is pinned to one server, so load ends up badly skewed. Use an L7 proxy that balances per request, or client-side load balancing.

How the balancer picks a server decides whether load actually evens out

If requests cost roughly the same and the servers are identical, the simplest algorithm is fine. Once request costs vary (one search takes 5 ms, another 2 s) or servers differ, you want an algorithm that looks at current load. If a server holds state for a key, such as a cache shard or a WebSocket, you want one that sends that key to the same place every time.

AlgorithmUse whenWeakness
Round robinIdentical servers, uniform short requestsBlind to slow requests and slow servers
Least connections / least requestVariable request cost, long-lived connectionsNeeds per-server state; a fresh server gets flooded (use slow-start)
Weighted (RR or LC)Mixed instance sizes; shifting 5% of traffic to a canaryWeights must be maintained by hand or automation
IP / key hash, consistent hashCache shards, session affinity, stateful connectionsHot keys overload one server; client IPs behind NAT cluster together
Power of two choicesLarge fleets, many independent balancersSlightly worse than a perfect global view, which doesn't exist anyway

A gateway is a reverse proxy that knows about your API

A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and hides them: it terminates TLS, compresses, caches and buffers. An API gateway adds API-aware policy: who is calling, how often they may call, and which of many services should answer. A service mesh applies the same ideas to traffic between services.

Put in the gateway

Cross-cutting, request-level policy that should be identical for every service: token validation, coarse authorisation (scopes), rate limits, request size limits, CORS, request IDs, access logs.

Keep out of the gateway

Business logic, orchestration across services, and anything that needs a database transaction. A gateway full of logic becomes a distributed monolith that every team queues to change.

BFF: one gateway per client

A backend for frontend is a thin gateway per client type (web, iOS, partner). It aggregates and shapes responses for that client, so the mobile app gets one call instead of six, and web and mobile evolve separately.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Gateway, BFF or meshDeck · Gateway configuration

Every new connection costs round trips, so reuse them

TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery and pays for it with handshakes and head-of-line blocking. UDP guarantees nothing and adds nothing. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which rebuilds TCP's reliability on top of UDP with fewer round trips and independent streams. For system design, the lesson is: long-lived, pooled connections, and fewer round trips on the critical path.

TCPUDP
DeliveryReliable, ordered, retransmitsBest effort: may drop, duplicate or reorder
ConnectionHandshake, per-connection stateNone; each datagram stands alone
Flow / congestion controlBuilt inYour job, if you need it
Use forHTTP/1–2, databases, gRPC, anything that must arriveDNS, VoIP, video calls, games, QUIC, metrics (StatsD)
What this means for designsPool connections to databases and services, because a new TLS connection per call adds 2–3 RTT. Keep chatty protocols inside a datacenter. For real-time media, prefer UDP-based transports (WebRTC), where a late packet is worthless and should be dropped, not retransmitted.

REST for public resources, gRPC between services, GraphQL for many-shaped clients

All three can build any API. They differ in who shapes the response, the client or the server, what goes over the wire (text JSON or binary protobuf), and how well caches, browsers and tooling understand them. Here is the same question asked three ways: user 42's name and last three orders.

REST (JSON over HTTP)gRPC (protobuf over HTTP/2)GraphQL
Best forPublic APIs, CRUD resources, anything cacheableInternal service-to-service, low latency, streamingMany client types with different data needs; aggregation layer
ContractOpenAPI (optional, often drifts).proto, required, with code generationSchema, required, introspectable
PayloadText, verbose, human-readableBinary, typically 3–10× smaller, fast to parseJSON, shaped by the query
CachingExcellent: HTTP semantics, CDN, ETagsApplication-level onlyHard at HTTP level (POST); needs persisted queries or client caches
EvolutionVersioned URLs or headers; add fields freelyAdd fields with new numbers; never reuse oneDeprecate fields; no versions
Watch out forChatty clients, over- and under-fetchingBrowser support (grpc-web), L4 load balancingExpensive queries (depth and cost limits), N+1 in resolvers
A defensible default"REST at the public edge, because it's cacheable and every client speaks it. gRPC between internal services, for the typed contracts and efficiency. And a GraphQL or BFF layer only if the mobile and web teams are fighting over response shapes." Also say how you would paginate (cursor, not offset) and make writes idempotent.

Four ways for the server to tell the client something changed

HTTP is request-response: the server can only speak when it's asked. Real-time features (chat, live scores, notifications, collaborative editing) need a way round that. The four options trade simplicity against latency and the number of connections you must keep open.

Short pollingLong pollingSSEWebSocket
DirectionClient pullsServer replies when readyServer → client streamBoth ways
LatencyUp to one intervalNear real timeReal timeReal time
CostMany empty requestsA held request per client, plus reconnectsOne open HTTP response per client; auto-reconnect built inOne open connection per client; stateful servers
Infra frictionNoneProxy timeoutsPlain HTTP; watch proxy buffering; per-origin connection limit on HTTP/1.1LB must support Upgrade; sticky routing; custom heartbeats
Use forRare updates, simplest clientsFallback; legacy clientsNotifications, feeds, dashboards, token streamingChat, multiplayer, collaborative editing, trading
The scaling consequencePersistent connections make the connection tier stateful. A million online users is a million open sockets spread over, say, 20 gateway servers. The system needs a registry of which user is on which gateway, so a message can be routed to the right box. The chat design (§14) builds exactly that.

Instances come and go, so callers look them up rather than hard-coding them

With autoscaling and rolling deploys, the set of healthy instances behind a service changes by the minute. Service discovery is a registry of what's healthy right now, plus a way for callers to use it: either the client asks the registry and picks an instance, or a load balancer does that on the client's behalf.

Health decides membership

An instance should enter the registry only when it is ready (warmed caches, connections open) and leave the moment it starts draining. Liveness ("restart me") and readiness ("send me traffic") are different probes. Mixing them up causes restart loops.

The registry is critical infrastructure

If the registry goes down, nothing can find anything. Registries are replicated consensus clusters (etcd, Consul). Clients cache the last known list, so a registry outage freezes membership instead of breaking calls.

DNS-based discovery caveats

DNS is universal, but clients cache answers, sometimes past the TTL (the JVM's own DNS cache is a classic example), and DNS carries no load information. That is fine for coarse routing. Use a proxy or a client-side balancer for per-request balancing.

Start from the access pattern, not from the database you like

"SQL or NoSQL" is really two questions: do you need relational features (transactions across rows, joins, ad-hoc queries), and does the data or the write rate outgrow one primary? A relational database is the right default until you can name the requirement it fails. NoSQL stores trade that flexibility for scale along one specific access pattern.

Relational (SQL)NoSQL (as a family)
Data modelNormalised tables, schema enforced on writeShaped for the query; schema often enforced by the application on read
QueriesAny query you can write; the optimiser finds a planFast along the designed key; other queries mean a new table or index
TransactionsACID across rows and tablesUsually per item or partition; some offer limited multi-item transactions
Scaling writesVertical, then sharding (hard, manual)Horizontal partitioning built in
ConsistencyStrong on the primaryOften eventual or tunable per request
Pick it whenRelationships and invariants matter; access patterns will changeThe access pattern is known and stable, and the scale or shape demands it

Four data shapes, each optimised for a different question

"NoSQL" covers very different systems. What they share is that you design the data around the queries you will run, often duplicating it, rather than normalising it and letting the query planner work it out. Picture the shape of the data first, then pick the family whose shape matches.

FamilyQuery byStrengthWeaknessTypical uses
Key-valueExact keyLatency, throughput, simplicityNo secondary queries; value is opaqueSessions, caches, counters, rate limits, feature flags
DocumentKey, plus indexed fieldsFlexible schema, aggregate-shaped readsCross-document joins and transactionsCatalogues, user profiles, CMS content, orders
Wide-columnPartition key + clustering-key rangeWrite-heavy scale, time-ordered data, multi-DCQuery-first modelling; no ad-hoc queries; tombstonesMessages, activity feeds, IoT, event logs
GraphTraversals from a start nodeMany-hop relationshipsPartitioning; bulk analyticsSocial graphs, fraud rings, recommendations, access control
Design rule for wide-column and KV storesOne table per query. Write the list of queries first, and give each one a table whose partition key is what the query filters on and whose clustering key is what it sorts by. Duplicate the data across tables at write time. Storage is cheap; a scatter-gather query across every node is not.

B-trees update in place; LSM-trees append and merge later

Under every database is a storage engine, and there are two main families. B-trees (PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB) keep sorted pages on disk and modify them in place, which makes them good at reads and range scans. LSM-trees (Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB, Bigtable) buffer writes in memory and flush them as immutable sorted files, which makes them good at heavy write loads.

B-treeLSM-tree
WritesSlower (random I/O)Faster (sequential)
Point readsPredictable, fastMay touch several files
Range scansExcellentGood within a partition
Hidden costPage splits, fragmentationCompaction I/O spikes, tombstones
Found inPostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL ServerCassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, HBase

Indexes: speed reads, tax writes

  • Primary index: the table is ordered by it (clustered) or points into it.
  • Secondary index: another sorted structure. Every insert updates each one, so five indexes means roughly six writes.
  • Composite (user_id, created_at) serves "user X's latest", but not "all rows since T". Column order matters.
  • Covering index: holds every column the query needs, so the table is never read.
  • Index for your queries, check with EXPLAIN, and drop unused indexes.

One leader takes writes; followers copy its log and serve reads

Single-leader replication is the workhorse (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis). All writes go to one node, so there are no write conflicts. The leader streams its change log to followers, which gives you read scaling and a fail-over target. The design decision is how many followers the leader waits for before it tells the client "committed".

Replication lag bites users

A user updates their profile, the next page reads from a lagging replica, and the old name comes back. Fixes: read your own writes from the leader for a few seconds; send the last-write position (LSN) with the request and wait for a replica that has reached it; or pin a session to one replica for monotonic reads.

Fail-over, step by step

Detect that the leader is gone (missed heartbeats). Choose the most up-to-date follower, ideally the sync standby. Promote it, fence the old leader so it can't accept writes if it returns, and repoint clients. Managed databases do this in 30–120 s.

What it doesn't solve

Write throughput: every follower replays every write, so replicas add read capacity and nothing for writes. When one leader's writes or disk are the limit, you need partitioning (next slides), not more replicas.

More than one node accepts writes, so conflicts become your problem

A single leader is a bottleneck and a single point of failure for writes. Multi-leader puts a leader in each region, so writes stay local. Leaderless (Dynamo-style) lets any replica accept a write and uses quorums. Both buy write availability and latency, and both need a rule for what happens when two writes to the same key collide.

Setting (N = 3)Behaviour
W=2, R=2Balanced; tolerates 1 node down for reads and writes
W=3, R=1Fast reads, but any node down blocks writes
W=1, R=3Fast, available writes; slow reads
W=1, R=1Fastest; eventual consistency only (W + R ≤ N)
Quorums are not magicEven with W + R > N you can see anomalies. Sloppy quorums during failures, concurrent writes resolved by clocks, and a write that failed on some replicas but succeeded on others can all break the overlap guarantee. For real linearizability (unique usernames, balances), use consensus-backed single-leader writes. Cassandra's lightweight transactions and DynamoDB's conditional writes exist for exactly this.

Sharding splits the data so each node holds, and writes, only a part

Partitioning (sharding) is how you scale writes and storage past one machine. Each record lives on exactly one shard, chosen by its partition key. The strategy decides three things: whether load spreads evenly, whether range queries stay on one shard, and how hard it is to add shards later.

Choosing the partition key

Choose a key with high cardinality (many distinct values), even load (no key far hotter than the rest), and that matches the main query, so the common request touches one shard. user_id for user data, conversation_id for messages, tenant_id for SaaS. Never a boolean, a country, or a raw timestamp.

Secondary indexes

Local index: each shard indexes its own rows. Writes stay cheap, but a query by the indexed field must ask every shard. Global index: the index is itself partitioned by the indexed value. Reads go to one place, but each write updates another shard, usually asynchronously.

What you give up

Cross-shard joins, transactions and unique constraints. Design so the common operation stays inside one shard. For the rare cross-shard operation, use a saga or an async job, and denormalise the data a query needs onto the shard that serves it.

Consistent hashing: adding a node moves only its share of keys

With hash(key) % N, going from 3 to 4 nodes changes the answer for about 75% of keys. For a cache that means a sudden wave of misses; for a database it means a massive data migration. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on the same ring and gives each key to the next node clockwise, so a new node only takes keys from its immediate neighbour.

Virtual nodes fix the lumps

Three random points on a ring give very uneven arcs. Each physical node therefore takes 100–256 virtual nodes spread around the ring, which evens out the load. A new node takes a little from everyone rather than a lot from one neighbour, and a bigger machine can simply own more vnodes.

Replication falls out of it

To keep N copies, store the key on the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise. That list is the key's preference list. It is how Cassandra and DynamoDB place replicas without a central directory.

Alternatives worth naming

Rendezvous (HRW) hashing: each key goes to the node with the highest hash(key, node). It's simple and needs no ring. Jump hash: fast, but nodes must be numbered. Fixed hash slots (Redis Cluster uses 16,384) make rebalancing a matter of moving whole slots.

Even perfect hashing can't spread one very popular key

Hashing spreads keys evenly, not traffic. A celebrity's profile, a viral post or a flash-sale SKU can send 1,000× the average load to one key, and so to one shard. Detect hot keys, then split them: spread writes across sub-keys, and spread reads across copies.

Detect before it pages you

Track per-key request counts, e.g. top-K sampling in the proxy or redis-cli --hotkeys, alongside per-shard CPU and latency. A shard at 90% while its siblings sit at 20% is a hot key until proven otherwise.

Reshard without downtime

Choose many logical shards up front and map them to fewer physical nodes, so resharding means moving a logical shard rather than rehashing everything. To move one: copy a snapshot, stream the ongoing changes, cut over reads and writes briefly, then verify. Vitess, Citus and DynamoDB automate this.

Design the key for skew

If you know a few entities will be huge (celebrities, big tenants, famous products), treat them differently from day one: a separate code path, dedicated shards, or precomputed fan-out. The news feed design (§15) does exactly this.

Split the database by function, and copy data where reads need it

Two cheaper moves often come before sharding. Federation (functional partitioning) splits one database into several by domain, so users, products and orders each get their own, with separate load and separate failures. Denormalization stores data redundantly in the shape the read needs, trading write complexity for join-free reads.

Federation is service ownership

In microservices, federation is the norm: each service owns its data and nobody else touches its tables (database per service, §10). The same split works inside a modular monolith, as schema per module. Cross-domain questions are then answered through APIs or read models, never joins.

Some copies are features

Copying the product title and price into the order line isn't really denormalization. It records what the customer actually bought, even if the catalogue changes tomorrow. Separate snapshots, which must never update, from caches of truth, which must.

Materialized views

A denormalized read model maintained automatically, either by the database (a materialized view) or by a consumer of change events (a projection). This is the read side of CQRS (§10). Accept that it lags the source by milliseconds to seconds.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Data ownershipDeck · Read models

Transactions are only as safe as their isolation level

ACID means Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (invariants hold), Isolated (concurrent transactions don't interfere) and Durable (committed means kept). The "I" is a spectrum, and most databases default to a weak level for speed. The two anomalies below cause real incidents in money and booking systems.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatableLost updateWrite skew
Read committed PG default✓ prevented✗ possible✗ possible✗ possible
Snapshot / repeatable read✓✓engine-specific*✗ possible
Serializable✓✓✓✓

The fixes, from cheapest

  • Atomic update: SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30. There is no read-modify-write left to race.
  • Optimistic lock: a version column, … WHERE version = 7. Zero rows updated means someone else won, so retry.
  • Pessimistic lock: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the rows you check. Correct, but it serialises contention.
  • Serializable isolation with automatic retry on a serialization failure. Simplest to reason about, with some throughput cost.

* PostgreSQL's repeatable read aborts one of two conflicting updates. MySQL InnoDB's does not, and a plain read-then-write there still loses an update.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · TransactionsDeck · Concurrency and idempotency

Across services, trade atomic commits for sagas that can undo

Once an operation spans several databases (orders, payments, inventory), no single transaction covers it. Two-phase commit makes the databases agree atomically, by holding locks until a coordinator decides. A saga runs a sequence of local transactions and, if a step fails, runs compensating steps that semantically undo the earlier ones.

Two-phase commitSaga
GuaranteeAtomic: all commit or noneEventually consistent: all complete, or compensations run
IsolationFull, with locks held across the protocolNone between steps; others may see PENDING states
AvailabilityBlocks if the coordinator or any participant is downEach step retries independently; a durable log drives progress
NeedsEvery participant supports XA / prepareIdempotent steps, a compensation for each, a saga state store
UseInside one database cluster (Spanner, CockroachDB do this internally)Across services and third parties (payments, shipping, email)
Order the steps to shrink the undoPut steps that can't be undone last. You can't un-send an email or un-ship a parcel. Do the reversible, likely-to-fail steps first: reserve stock before charging the card, and charge before shipping.
