Orchestrated sagas (a central coordinator) are easier to follow than choreographed ones once there are more than three steps.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · SagasEvents · Sagas with events

Blobs go to object storage; the database keeps only their metadata

Photos, videos, documents, backups and logs belong in an object store (S3, GCS, Azure Blob). It is effectively unlimited, cheap per GB, and designed for eleven nines of durability. Databases are for the small, queryable facts about those objects. The best pattern keeps the bytes off your application servers entirely.

What object stores are

A flat namespace of immutable objects addressed by key, served over HTTP. There is no in-place edit (rewrite the object instead), no rename, and listing is slow. Large objects use multipart upload (parallel, resumable parts). Strong read-after-write consistency is now standard on S3, GCS and Azure.

Cost levers

Lifecycle rules move cold objects to cheaper tiers (infrequent access, then archive) and expire temporary files. Egress is often the biggest bill: serve through a CDN and keep processing in the same region as the bucket.

Security

Buckets are private by default and stay that way. Presigned URLs grant one operation on one key for minutes. Content types are validated and sizes capped at signing time. Scan uploads before anyone else can download them. Keys include an unguessable id, never a user-controlled filename.

Full-text search inverts the data: from each word to the documents that contain it

LIKE '%shoe%' scans every row and knows nothing about relevance. A search engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Solr, or Lucene underneath) builds an inverted index at write time, so a query becomes a few list lookups and a merge. Search is a derived view, fed from your system of record.

Not a source of truth

Write to the database first and index asynchronously, from CDC or events. Search clusters can lose data or need reindexing after a mapping change, so rebuilding from the source must be a routine job, not a crisis.

Scaling a search cluster

Shard by document, so each query fans out to all shards and merges the top-k. Add replicas for query throughput. Keep shards around 10–50 GB. Time-based indexes (logs-2026.09.30) make retention a matter of dropping old indexes.

Where it shows up

Product and content search, typo tolerance and synonyms, faceted filtering ("brand: X, price < 50"), log analytics, geo queries, and autocomplete. For simple prefix autocomplete, a dedicated trie service can be cheaper (§17).

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Search and reporting

Every store trades query flexibility against scale

Stores that answer any question (relational, OLAP) are harder to scale for writes. Stores that scale almost without limit (wide-column, KV, object storage) answer only the questions you designed for. Place the requirement on this map, and name what you give up.

RequirementReach forBecause
Money, orders, inventory, bookingsPostgreSQL / MySQL (or Spanner at global scale)Transactions, constraints, strong consistency
Sessions, counters, rate limits, leaderboardsRedisSub-ms, atomic ops, TTLs, sorted sets
Chat messages, feeds, IoT, event historyCassandra / ScyllaDB / DynamoDBWrite-heavy, partitioned by entity, time-ordered
Images, video, backups, logs archiveObject storage + CDNCheap, durable, unlimited; metadata in a DB
Product search, typo tolerance, facetsOpenSearch / ElasticsearchInverted index, relevance ranking
Dashboards over billions of rowsClickHouse / BigQuery / DruidColumnar storage, vectorised scans
Metrics and time seriesPrometheus / TimescaleDB / InfluxDBCompression, downsampling, time windows

Caches sit at every layer, and the earliest hit is the cheapest

A cache keeps a copy of expensive-to-get data somewhere faster. Between the user and the database there are half a dozen places to keep that copy, each closer, faster and less consistent than the one behind it. A good design caches each kind of data at the earliest layer where its freshness requirements still hold.

What is worth caching

Data that is read far more often than it's written, is expensive to compute or fetch, and can tolerate some staleness. Classic examples: product pages, user profiles, rendered feeds, permission sets, and the results of heavy aggregations.

What isn't

Data that must be exact at the moment you read it: balances at payment time, stock at checkout, a password hash during login. Also anything with a unique key per request (a near-zero hit ratio), and data cheaper to recompute than to fetch over the network.

In-process vs distributed

In-process is the fastest, but each instance holds its own copy, so N servers keep N inconsistent copies and N times the memory. Use it for tiny, slow-changing data or a 1–5 s shield in front of hot keys. Use a distributed cache for everything that must be shared or larger than one heap.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Caching

On a miss, someone has to load from the database: your code or the cache

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default. The application checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, and fills the cache itself. Read-through moves that loading logic into the cache layer, so the application only ever talks to the cache. Both load only what is actually requested, so the cache fills with the hot set.

cache-aside, the whole pattern
def get_profile(user_id):
    key = f"profile:{user_id}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return deserialize(cached)            # hit
    row = db.query("SELECT … FROM profiles WHERE id = %s", user_id)
    if row is None:
        redis.set(key, NOT_FOUND, ex=60)      # cache the miss too
        return None
    redis.set(key, serialize(row), ex=300 + random.randint(0, 60))
    return row

def update_profile(user_id, changes):
    db.update(user_id, changes)               # 1. write the truth
    redis.delete(f"profile:{user_id}")        # 2. then invalidate, don't update

Trade-offs to state

  • Resilient: if the cache dies, reads fall through to the database. That is slower but still correct, provided the database can take it.
  • First request is slow: every miss costs a cache round trip plus a database read. Warm critical keys at deploy time.
  • Stale window: data can be stale until the TTL expires or an invalidation lands. Pick the TTL from how stale the business can tolerate.
  • The random extra TTL (jitter) stops thousands of keys set together from expiring together.

What happens to the cache when data changes is the real design choice

Reads are straightforward. The bugs live in writes. Four strategies decide whether a write goes through the cache, around it, or is buffered in it, and each one fixes the write latency, the freshness of reads, and what you lose if the cache node dies.

StrategyWrite latencyRead-after-writeDurability riskGood for
Cache-aside + delete on writeDB onlyMiss, then freshNoneThe default for most read-heavy data
Write-throughDB + cacheFresh hitNone (DB is written synchronously)Read-after-write heavy data: sessions, carts, profiles
Write-behindCache only (fastest)Fresh hitBuffered writes lost if the cache failsCounters, view counts, metrics, where loss of a few is tolerable
Write-aroundDB onlyMissNoneWrite-heavy data rarely read back (logs, bulk imports)
Refresh-aheadn/aDepends on the write pathNoneA small, predictable hot set (home page, top products)
Delete, don't updateOn a write, delete the cache key rather than setting it to the new value. Two concurrent writers that each update the cache can finish in the opposite order to their database commits, leaving the older value cached indefinitely. A delete is idempotent, and the next read reloads the truth.

A full cache must forget something; the policy decides what

Memory is finite, so a cache evicts entries to make room. The policy is a bet about the future. LRU bets that recently used items will be used again, LFU that frequently used ones will, and TTL expiry that data goes bad after a while regardless. The best policy depends on the access pattern, which is why it's measured, not guessed.

PolicyEvictsGood whenFails when
LRULeast recently usedRecency predicts reuse (sessions, feeds, most web traffic)A one-off scan (a batch job, a crawler) flushes the hot set
LFULeast frequently usedStable popularity (top products, reference data)Popularity shifts and old counts linger, unless counters decay
FIFOOldest insertedSimplicity; data that ages uniformlyHot old keys get evicted anyway
TTL expiryAnything past its time to liveFreshness bounds ("prices at most 60 s old")Used as the only policy: memory still fills
RandomA random keyHuge caches where bookkeeping costs more than precisionSmall caches with a clear hot set
In Redis termsSet maxmemory and a policy. allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache. volatile-lru or volatile-ttl when the same instance also holds keys that must not be evicted (it then evicts only keys with a TTL). And never noeviction for a cache: once memory is full, writes start failing. Watch evicted_keys and the hit ratio together.

Invalidation fails through races, not through forgetting to delete

"Update the database, then delete the key" is correct most of the time. The dangerous case is a slow reader overlapping a writer. The reader loaded the old value before the write, and puts it in the cache after the writer deleted the key. The stale value then stays cached until its TTL expires, and may never be corrected if there is no TTL.

① TTL as the safety net

Choose the TTL from the staleness the business can accept (30 s for prices, 10 min for a profile), and add jitter. Every other technique reduces how often staleness happens. The TTL limits how long it lasts.

② Leases (the Facebook memcache fix)

A miss hands the reader a lease token, and the cache accepts the later SET only with a valid token. A DEL in between invalidates the token, so the late write of v1 is rejected. Leases also throttle stampedes on the same key.

③ Versioned values

Store (version, value) and set conditionally, e.g. with a Lua script that writes only if the incoming version is newer. Because versions come from the database (a row version or LSN), an old value can never overwrite a newer one.

④ Invalidate from the change stream

Instead of every code path remembering to delete, a CDC consumer (for example, Debezium reading the WAL) deletes keys for every committed change, and can delete again a second later to catch late sets. This covers writes made outside your service as well.

Four ways a cache sends a flood to the database

Once the database is sized for a 95% hit ratio, the cache is load-bearing. Anything that suddenly drops the hit ratio becomes a database outage. These four failures have names, and interviewers expect you to name them, together with their fixes.

Say this in the deep dive"The database is sized for about 5% of reads. If the cache goes cold, we'll be at 20× that for a few minutes. So: jittered TTLs, single-flight loading on hot keys, a replicated Redis with warm-up before traffic returns, and a concurrency limit on database-bound queries, so a cold cache degrades latency instead of taking the database down."

If the user doesn't need to wait for it, take it off the request path

In a synchronous chain, latencies add up and availabilities multiply, so every downstream service joins the user's critical path. Putting a queue between the steps that must happen now and the steps that merely must happen is the most useful single move in high-level design.

What you gain

  • Latency: the user waits only for the steps that decide the outcome.
  • Availability: consumers can be down for a while, and messages wait for them.
  • Load levelling: bursts queue up and are processed at a sustainable rate.
  • Decoupling: new consumers subscribe without the producer changing.

What you pay

  • Eventual consistency: the confirmation email may arrive 30 seconds later, so design the UI for it.
  • Duplicates and ordering: at-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent.
  • Harder debugging: you need trace ids carried through messages and alerts on dead-letter queues and lag.
  • Don't make a step async when its result decides what the user sees next.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · What actually changesEvents · When not to

Three messaging shapes: work queue, fan-out topic, replayable log

"Put it on a queue" hides a real decision. A work queue hands each message to exactly one worker and then forgets it. Pub/sub copies each message to every subscriber. A log keeps messages in order for days and lets any number of consumer groups read, and re-read, at their own positions.

NeedChooseWhy
Distribute jobs (resize images, send emails) across workersWork queuePer-message acks, visibility timeouts, dead-letter queue, easy horizontal scaling
Notify several independent systems of an eventPub/sub, or a logFan-out without the producer knowing the consumers
Event streaming, CDC, analytics, rebuilding read modelsLogReplay, ordering per key, very high throughput, many consumer groups
Per-message priority, delays, complex routingQueue broker (RabbitMQ, SQS)Logs have no per-message priority, and a slow message blocks its partition

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · The logEvents · Broker comparison

Messages arrive at least once, so processing must happen effectively once

A consumer can crash after doing the work but before acknowledging it, and the broker cannot tell that apart from never having done it. So it redelivers. Reliable messaging is therefore at-least-once. "Exactly once" in practice means at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer that recognises repeats.

SemanticsHowFailure outcomeUse for
At-most-onceAck (or auto-commit) before processingMessages can be lost, never duplicatedMetrics samples, telemetry, anything where a gap is cheaper than a duplicate
At-least-onceProcess, then ackNever lost; duplicates on crash or retryThe default for business events, paired with idempotent consumers
Effectively-onceAt-least-once + dedupe, or Kafka transactions for read-process-write within KafkaNeither lost nor applied twicePayments, balances, inventory, billing
Idempotency keys at the API edge tooThe same problem appears when a client retries POST /payments after a timeout. The client sends an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the response, and on a repeat key returns the stored response instead of charging again. That is how Stripe's API works, and interviewers expect it on any money-moving endpoint.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · Delivery semanticsEvents · Idempotency

A queue turns a traffic spike into a backlog you work through at your own pace

Without a buffer, the downstream service has to be sized for the peak. With a queue between them, it only has to be sized above the average. Bursts become queue depth, workers drain it at a steady rate, and the database behind the workers never sees the spike. That is queue-based load leveling.

Back pressure: say "slow down"

When a buffer fills, push back instead of growing without limit. Use bounded in-memory queues, 429 or 503 with Retry-After at the edge, consumers that pull at their own rate, and demand signalling in reactive streams. An unbounded queue just moves the out-of-memory crash somewhere else.

Queues are not infinite

Set a maximum depth or a message TTL, and decide in advance what happens when it's reached: reject new work, shed low-priority work, or spill to cheaper storage. Watch for a queue whose drain rate is below its arrival rate on average. It will never catch up.

Scale consumers on lag

Autoscale workers on queue depth or age rather than CPU (KEDA does this on Kubernetes). But cap the workers at what the downstream can handle: fifty workers hammering one database only moves the bottleneck.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · BackpressureEvents · Diagnosing lag

Long work gets a job id now and a result later

Anything slower than a couple of seconds, such as generating a report, transcoding a video or bulk-importing a CSV, shouldn't hold an HTTP request open. Accept the request, put a job on a queue, return 202 Accepted with a URL to check, and let a worker do the work. The client polls, or gets a push when the job finishes.

Event-driven jobs

Triggered by something that happened: an upload finished, an order was placed. Consumers pick them up from a queue or topic. Latency is seconds, and throughput scales with the number of workers.

Schedule-driven jobs

Nightly reports, cleanups, reminders. Don't run cron on every app instance, or it fires N times. Use a single scheduler service, a lock (ShedLock, a DB advisory lock, a Redis lock with a lease), or leader election. Make each run idempotent and resumable.

What a job system needs

Retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue for poison jobs, visibility timeouts so a crashed worker's job reappears, priorities or separate queues so bulk work can't starve urgent work, status and progress tracking, and a limit on how long a job may run.

Writing to the database and the broker separately will eventually lose an event

"Save the order, then publish OrderPlaced" is two writes to two systems, with no transaction spanning them. A crash, timeout or deploy between them leaves the order saved and the event never sent, or the event sent for an order that rolled back. The transactional outbox makes it one write.

Poller vs CDC relay

A poller runs SELECT … FROM outbox WHERE published = false ORDER BY id every few hundred ms. It's simple, and it adds DB load and latency. CDC tails the database log (Debezium on the WAL or binlog): lower latency, no polling load, one more component to run.

Still at-least-once

The relay can publish a row and crash before marking it sent, so the row is published again. The outbox guarantees no loss, not no duplicates. Put a unique event id on every message and dedupe on the consumer side.

The inbox is its mirror

On the consuming side, record each processed event id in the same transaction as its effects (previous slide). Outbox plus inbox gives effectively-once processing across services without distributed transactions.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · The dual-write problemEvents · Outbox and CDC

Order is guaranteed per partition, so key by the thing whose order matters

A log scales by splitting a topic into partitions that are read in parallel. Order holds within a partition, not across them. Messages with the same key always land in the same partition, so choose the key as the entity whose events must stay in sequence, usually the aggregate id.

Choosing the key

Key by the entity whose history must be sequential: order_id, account_id, conversation_id. Avoid keys with a few huge values (a tenant with half the traffic), which create a hot partition, and don't key randomly if anything downstream depends on order.

How order still breaks

Producer retries without idempotence enabled, a consumer that processes one partition with a thread pool, retry topics that re-queue a failed message behind newer ones, and replicas in other regions. Carry a version or sequence number and reject stale updates at the consumer.

Global order is expensive

Total order over everything means one partition, and so the throughput of one consumer. Almost nothing needs it. When something seems to, it usually needs per-entity order plus a timestamp for display.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · OrderingEvents · Partitioning

At scale, something is always broken, so design for partial failure

With 1,000 servers that each fail once every three years, you lose about one a day. Networks drop, delay and reorder packets. A dependency can be up but ten times slower than usual. Reliability doesn't mean preventing failure. It means containing it: one component's failure should degrade one feature, not take down the system.

Timeouts on every remote call

No call waits forever. Set timeouts from the dependency's p99.9 and the caller's own deadline, not from library defaults, some of which are infinite. A missing timeout is how one slow service cascades into a full outage.

Redundancy, and no shared fate

At least two of everything, across failure domains (hosts, zones, regions). Watch for hidden shared fate: the same config push, deploy, certificate, DNS provider or quota can take down all the replicas at once.

Degrade gracefully

Decide in advance what each feature does when a dependency is down. Recommendations disappear, prices come from a cache, reviews show "unavailable", and checkout still works. Write it down as a dependency matrix and test it.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, or your retries become the outage

Retries hide transient failures. But when a dependency is struggling, every client retrying on the same schedule multiplies its load exactly when it can least absorb it. Three rules keep retries helpful: back off exponentially, add random jitter, and cap retries with a budget.

backoff with full jitter
def call_with_retry(op, attempts=3, base=0.1, cap=2.0):
    for n in range(attempts):
        try:
            return op(timeout=remaining_deadline())
        except (Timeout, ServiceUnavailable, ConnectionReset):   # transient only
            if n == attempts - 1 or not retry_budget.try_acquire():
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** n)))
        # 4xx, validation errors, "insufficient funds": never retried

Rules that prevent retry storms

  • Retry only transient errors, and only idempotent operations (or ones carrying an idempotency key).
  • Retry at one layer. Three layers × 3 attempts = 27 calls per user click.
  • Keep a retry budget: retries may add at most 10% extra load, and once it's spent, fail fast.
  • Honour Retry-After and 429. The server knows better than your constant.

Stop calling a dependency that is failing, and check back later

A circuit breaker wraps calls to one dependency and watches their outcomes. When failures or slow calls cross a threshold, it opens and fails subsequent calls immediately, without making them. That protects the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover. After a cool-down it lets a few trial calls through to see whether the dependency is healthy again.

Choose the fallback first

An open breaker is only as good as what you return instead: a cached or default value ("recommended for you" becomes "bestsellers"), a degraded response ("shipping estimate unavailable"), a queued write ("we'll confirm by email"), or, for critical paths, a clear, fast error.

Tune per dependency

Base the window and threshold on each dependency's normal error rate. Count slow calls as failures, not just errors. Use one breaker per dependency (or per endpoint), never one for the whole application. Emit state changes as metrics and alert when a breaker opens.

Where it lives

In-process libraries (Resilience4j, Polly) or in the mesh (Envoy's outlier detection ejects bad hosts from the pool). Combine it with timeouts, which bound each call; retries, which go inside the breaker; and bulkheads, which bound concurrency.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Resilience

Partition resources so one slow dependency can't drain them all

Named after a ship's watertight compartments: a bulkhead gives each dependency or workload its own bounded pool of threads, connections or instances, so a leak in one can't sink the ship. Load shedding is its partner at the front door. When the whole service is saturated, reject the least important requests early, so the important ones still get through.

Kinds of bulkhead

A thread or connection pool per dependency. Separate deployments for API, workers and admin traffic. Separate clusters for your largest tenants (cells, §10). Per-tenant rate limits. The same principle applies at every scale: bound the blast radius.

Sizing a pool

Use Little's law: pool = peak rate × p99 latency × headroom. At 100 req/s to a dependency with a 200 ms p99, that's about 20 slots, so give it 30. A pool that is too big stops being a bulkhead; one that is too small throttles healthy traffic.

Shedding signals

Shed on concurrency or queueing delay (in-flight requests, time spent in queue), not only CPU. Prioritise by request class, carried in a header. Prefer retrying clients' second attempts last. Return 503 with Retry-After so well-behaved clients back off.

Four ways to count requests, each with a different view of bursts

A rate limiter answers one question per request: is this caller over their allowance? The algorithms differ in how much state they keep, how they treat a burst, and how they behave at window boundaries. Pick the one whose burst behaviour matches the contract: "100 per second, bursts to 200" is a token bucket in plain English.

AlgorithmState per keyBurstsAccuracyTypical use
Token buckettokens + last refill timeAllowed up to capacityExactAPI rate limits with a burst allowance (AWS, Stripe, most gateways)
Leaky bucketqueue (or level + time)Smoothed, delayed or droppedExactShaping outbound traffic to a fragile dependency
Fixed window1 counterUp to 2× at boundariesApproximateCoarse quotas (per day), where simplicity wins
Sliding window logA timestamp per requestNone beyond the limitExactLow-volume, high-value limits (login attempts)
Sliding window counter2 countersSmooth~99%, assuming an even spreadHigh-volume per-user limits (Cloudflare's approach)
Where it runsPut a limit at the edge (gateway, per API key or IP) to protect everything, plus per-service concurrency limits on expensive endpoints. The distributed version, with state in Redis updated atomically by a Lua script, and what to do when Redis is down, is worked through in the rate-limiter design (§13).

RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long you can be down

Zones protect you from a data-centre failure. Regions protect you from a regional outage, a bad regional deploy or a natural disaster, at real cost in money and complexity. Size the answer from two numbers agreed with the business. The recovery point objective is the maximum window of lost writes. The recovery time objective is the maximum time until service is restored.

StrategyWhat runs in region BRPORTOCost
Backup & restoreNothing; backups copied cross-regionhourshours–day$
Pilot lightData replicated; compute off or minimalseconds–minutestens of minutes$$
Warm standby (shown)Everything, scaled downsecondsminutes$$$
Active-activeFull traffic share, writes in both≈ 0 – seconds≈ 0 (reroute)$$$$ + conflict handling
Untested DR is a hope, not a planRehearse the fail-over on a schedule (game days), including the fail-back. Automate the decision where you can, but keep a human for "is region A really gone?" to avoid flapping. And check the hidden single-region dependencies: the CI system, the secrets store, the DNS provider, the container registry.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Multi-regionDeck · Disaster recoveryEvents · Multi-region events

Consensus lets a cluster agree on one leader and one log, as long as a majority is up

Many designs need exactly one of something: one primary database, one scheduler, one lock holder. Deciding who, safely, while nodes crash and messages go missing, is the consensus problem. Raft and Paxos solve it with majorities. In practice you rarely implement them yourself. You use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, or a database that runs Raft internally.

Why odd cluster sizes

A majority of 3 is 2, so 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure. A majority of 5 is 3, so 5 nodes tolerate 2. Four nodes also tolerate only 1, while paying more latency per write. Consensus clusters are small (3 or 5 nodes) and kept for metadata, not bulk data.

What to use it for

Leader election (one scheduler, one primary), distributed locks with leases, service registries, cluster membership, configuration, and the metadata of bigger systems. Kafka's KRaft, CockroachDB ranges and Kubernetes' etcd all sit on it.

Its costs

Every write is a round trip to a majority, so cross-region consensus costs cross-region latency. A minority partition can't make progress; that is the CP choice from §02. Leases depend on clocks being roughly right, which is why fencing tokens exist.

Generate IDs without a central counter by putting time and machine in the bits

An auto-increment column works until you have several databases, several regions, or a client that needs an ID before the insert. Distributed ID schemes let every node mint unique IDs with no coordination. The better ones are also roughly time-sortable, which keeps B-tree inserts sequential and makes "latest first" queries cheap.

SchemeSizeSortableCoordinationWatch out for
DB auto-increment8 BYesOne writer per sequenceSingle point of contention; leaks volume ("order 1,000,017"); hard to merge shards
Ticket server / ID ranges8 BRoughlyNodes lease blocks (e.g. 1,000 at a time)The allocator must be HA; gaps after crashes (fine)
Snowflake-style8 BYes (per ms)Assign unique machine ids onceClock going backwards (wait or refuse); running out of sequence in a hot millisecond
UUIDv716 BYes (per ms)NoneTwice the size of a long; exposes creation time
UUIDv416 BNoNoneIndex fragmentation and poor locality on large tables
A good defaultUse UUIDv7 (or ULID) for entity ids: no coordination, and time-ordered, so it's index-friendly. Use a Snowflake-style 64-bit id when size matters at huge volume (tweets, messages). For short public codes (a URL shortener, an order reference), encode a number in base62 and don't make them guessable where that matters (§12).

Wall clocks disagree, so don't use them to decide which write came last

Every machine's clock drifts, and NTP corrects it only to within a few milliseconds, sometimes by jumping backwards. If two nodes timestamp writes and "last write wins", a node whose clock runs fast wins even when it wrote first. Distributed systems order events with logical clocks, and fall back on physical time only with explicit uncertainty bounds.

Lamport clocks

One counter per node, carried on every message. They give a total order consistent with causality (ties broken by node id). They cannot tell you whether two events were concurrent.

Vector clocks / version vectors

One counter per node, kept as a vector. Comparing two vectors tells you "happened before", "happened after", or "concurrent, so this is a conflict". Dynamo-style stores use them to detect siblings that need merging.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC)

Physical time plus a logical counter. The timestamps stay close to wall time (readable, useful for TTLs) but never go backwards and respect causality. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use them.

TrueTime (Spanner)

GPS and atomic clocks expose time as an interval [earliest, latest], and a commit waits out the uncertainty (a few ms) before it becomes visible. Real-time ordering across the globe, paid for in hardware and latency.

Monitor from the user inward: journeys first, machines last

A design isn't finished until you can tell whether it's working. Monitoring works in layers. At the top are the signals users feel, which page a human. Below them are the signals that explain why, which go on dashboards. Alongside sit security and usage monitoring, which answer "who is doing what" rather than "is it up".

Three kinds of health check

Liveness: is the process stuck? Restart it. Readiness: can it take traffic now? Remove it from the load balancer. Deep checks of dependencies belong on dashboards, not in liveness probes. Otherwise a database blip restarts your whole fleet at once.

Measure where the user is

Server metrics miss DNS failures, CDN errors and slow clients. Add synthetic probes (scripted journeys from several regions every minute) and real user monitoring (timings reported by the browser or app).

Instrument once, everywhere

OpenTelemetry SDKs emit metrics, logs and traces with shared resource attributes (service, version, region) and a shared trace id. Put that into platform libraries, so every new service is observable by default.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Observability

Metrics say something is wrong, traces say where, logs say why

Each signal answers a different question at a different cost. Metrics are cheap aggregates you can alert on. Traces follow one request across services and show where its time went. Logs hold the detail of individual events. Tie them together with one trace id, and an incident goes from an alert to a graph to a trace to a log line in a few clicks.

MethodForSignals
Golden signalsAny user-facing systemLatency, traffic, errors, saturation
REDServices and endpointsRate, Errors, Duration (as a histogram)
USEResources: CPU, disks, poolsUtilisation, Saturation (queueing), Errors

Costs to design for

  • Metric cardinality: a label per user id makes millions of series. Keep labels bounded (endpoint, status class, region).
  • Log volume: use structured JSON, sample debug logs, and set retention by tier. Log bills rival compute bills.
  • Trace sampling: keep 1–10% at random, plus every error and slow trace, decided at the tail.

Page on how fast the error budget is burning, not on raw thresholds

"Error rate above 1%" pages too often at night on low traffic, and too late for a slow leak. Burn-rate alerts ask a better question: at this rate, how soon will the month's error budget be gone? A fast burn pages within minutes. A slow burn that would still exhaust the budget pages within hours. Everything else becomes a ticket.

Alert on symptoms

Page on what users feel: error-budget burn on the key journeys, and synthetic checks failing. Causes such as high CPU, a full disk or consumer lag go to dashboards and tickets, unless they predict a symptom soon (a disk full within 4 hours).

Every page must be actionable

If the response is "wait and see", it isn't a page. Each alert links to a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate (roll back, fail over, shed load). Review noisy alerts weekly, and delete or fix them.

Asynchronous systems need their own SLOs

For queues and pipelines, "requests succeed" isn't enough. Add freshness and throughput SLOs: 99% of events processed within 60 s, with the dead-letter queue empty. Alert on the age of the oldest message.

Delegate login to an identity provider; services verify tokens locally

Authentication answers who you are, and authorization answers what you may do. In a modern design, neither lives in each service. An identity provider runs login and MFA and issues signed tokens through OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. Every API verifies the token's signature with a cached public key, so no service stores a password and none calls the identity provider on every request.

Sessions or JWTs

A server-side session (an opaque id plus Redis) can be revoked instantly and is small, but every request needs a lookup. A JWT needs no lookup, but it can't be revoked before it expires. So keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 min), rotate refresh tokens, and keep a deny-list for emergencies. For browsers, a BFF keeping tokens server-side behind an HttpOnly cookie is the safest pattern.

Authorization models

RBAC: roles grant permissions ("admin"). ABAC: rules over attributes ("owner, or same tenant and during business hours"). ReBAC: relationships, as in Google Zanzibar or OpenFGA ("is an editor of this doc's folder"). Coarse scopes are checked at the gateway. Object-level checks belong in the service, and skipping them is the top API vulnerability, BOLA.

Machines and partners

Service-to-service calls use mTLS identities (a mesh with SPIFFE ids) or the OAuth client-credentials flow. Federated identity (SSO over SAML or OIDC) lets enterprise customers log in with their own directory. The IdP brokers it, and your services see the same JWTs either way.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · AuthenticationDeck · Security

Defence in depth: every layer assumes the one in front of it failed

Security in an HLD answer is a set of layers, each stopping a different class of attack. Volumetric floods stop at the edge, malicious payloads at the WAF, and unauthenticated calls at the gateway. Unauthorised access to someone else's data is stopped in the service, and a stolen disk is useless because the data is encrypted. Naming each layer and what it blocks is what interviewers are looking for.

Secrets

No secrets in code, images or environment files in git. Use a secrets manager (Vault, a cloud secrets manager) with short-lived, automatically rotated credentials, and workload identity instead of static keys wherever the platform supports it.

Zero trust inside

A request from inside the network is not trusted for that reason alone. Every service authenticates its callers (mTLS), authorises each call, and logs it. Segment the network so that a compromised pod can't reach the database of another domain.

Privacy by design

Collect less. Keep PII in a few well-guarded stores and pass references or tokens elsewhere. Encrypt sensitive fields at the application level. Build deletion (GDPR erasure) into the design from the start, including caches, search indexes, logs and backups.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Privacy by designDeck · Config and secrets

Ten performance antipatterns and the fix for each

The roadmap's list of performance antipatterns is worth knowing by name. Each is a design smell that works at small scale and fails under load, and each has a standard fix you have already met in this deck. In an interview, spotting one in your own design before the interviewer does is a strong signal.

How to use the listWalk your finished diagram looking for each one. Is anything called in a loop? That's chatty I/O. Is any hot read going to the database every time? No caching. Does one table hold everything? Monolithic persistence. Is there a synchronous call to a slow third party on the request path? Synchronous I/O, and probably a candidate for a queue. Saying "one risk here is chatty I/O between the feed and profile services, so I'd batch those lookups" shows seniority.

Layers separate concerns in the code; tiers separate them onto machines

The oldest and still the most common style. A layer is a logical grouping in the codebase: presentation, business logic, data access. Each layer depends only on the one below it. A tier is a physical deployment boundary: browser, application servers, database. Nearly every system in this deck is a 3-tier system at heart, whatever else it adds.

Why it lasts

It's easy to understand, easy to staff and easy to test layer by layer, and each tier scales independently: stateless app servers out, the database up. Most CRUD-heavy business applications never need anything more.

Where it hurts

Layers slice by technical concern, so a single feature touches every layer. In a large codebase every team edits the same layers, which becomes a "big ball of mud" without module boundaries inside each layer. The database becomes the integration point.

The modern refinement

Keep the tiers, but slice the code by business capability first (modules) and by layer within each module. Put the domain at the centre with ports and adapters, so the database and frameworks are details. That becomes the modular monolith on the next slide.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Layering inside a moduleDeck · Port and adapter in code

How much to split is a spectrum, and the middle is usually the right start

The real axis is not "one process or many". It is how strongly the boundaries between parts of the business are enforced, and what price you pay for that enforcement. A modular monolith enforces boundaries in code at almost no operational cost. Microservices enforce them with the network, which buys independent deploys and scaling, and charges you distributed-systems problems in return.

MonolithModular monolithMicroservices
DeployAll togetherAll togetherIndependently per service
BoundariesConvention (erodes)Enforced by build rules / testsEnforced by the network
DataShared schemaSchema per module, no cross-joinsDatabase per service
ConsistencyLocal transactions everywhereLocal transactions; events between modulesSagas, outbox, eventual consistency
ScalingWhole appWhole app (or run modules in separate deployments)Per service
FitsPrototypes, tiny teamsMost products, up to ~5–8 teamsMany teams needing autonomy; parts with very different scaling or compliance needs

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Four styles, honestly comparedDeck · Modular monolith

Split by business capability, give each service its data, and budget for the cost

Good microservice boundaries follow the business, not the technical layers. Each service owns one capability (catalog, ordering, payments), its data, and its team. It talks to the others through APIs for queries and commands, and through events for facts. Bad boundaries give you a distributed monolith: every feature needs five services deployed in lock-step.

Finding the boundaries

  • Business capability / bounded context: a capability with its own language and rules. "Product" means different things in catalog and in shipping.
  • Data ownership: exactly one service writes each piece of data. Others read it through the owner's API or keep a copy fed by its events.
  • Team ownership: one team per service (Conway's law works for you or against you).
  • Different forces: separate scaling (search), security or compliance (payments), or release cadence.

The cost ledger

  • Network: latency, partial failure, retries, timeouts on every call.
  • Data: no joins or transactions across services, so sagas, outboxes, read models.
  • Operations: CI/CD per service, containers, service discovery, tracing, a platform team.
  • Contracts: API and event versioning, consumer-driven contract tests.
  • If the teams can't afford these costs, a modular monolith gets most of the boundary benefit.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Extracting a serviceDeck · Conway's law in practice

Components react to facts instead of calling each other

In an event-driven architecture, a component announces that something happened ("OrderPlaced") and doesn't know or care who listens. Other components react on their own schedule. It comes in two topologies: a broker topology, where processors chain off each other's events, and a mediator topology, where a central coordinator decides the steps.

Three kinds of event

Event notification: "order 17 placed". Thin, so consumers call back for details. Event-carried state transfer: the event carries the data consumers need, so they keep their own copy and never call back. Event sourcing: events are the database (see two slides on).

Where it shines

Many consumers of the same fact. Fan-out to analytics, search and notifications. Integrating systems owned by different teams. Absorbing bursts. Building new features off an existing stream without touching its producer.

What it costs

Eventual consistency everywhere, and flows that are hard to see without tracing. Duplicates and reordering. Schema evolution across teams, which needs a schema registry and compatibility rules. And the temptation to model a synchronous question as two events.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · Event shapesEvents · Events, commands, queries

For multi-step workflows, decide who knows the plan

A multi-service workflow such as "place an order" can be coordinated in two ways. In choreography, each service listens for events and knows its own next move, and the plan emerges from the reactions. In orchestration, one component, a saga orchestrator or workflow engine, holds the plan as an explicit state machine and tells each service what to do.

A rule of thumb that holds upChoreograph simple fan-out, where one event has many independent reactions and none depends on another. Orchestrate business workflows with an order, compensations or timeouts, such as checkout, onboarding or claims. Workflow engines (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Camunda) give you durable orchestration without writing the state machine yourself.

Elsewhere in the atlasEvents · Choreography vs orchestrationDeck · Sagas

CQRS: one model for changing data, others shaped for reading it

Command Query Responsibility Segregation splits the write side (commands that enforce rules on a normalised model) from the read side (queries served by denormalised views built for each screen or API). The views are updated from change events, so each side scales and evolves on its own, at the cost of reads that lag writes slightly.

Use it when

Reads and writes are very different in shape or volume (a 100:1 ratio, complex screens over simple writes). You need several views of the same data (search, reporting, per-customer history). Or the read side must scale independently, possibly in another store.

Don't use it for

Simple CRUD, where a single model and a couple of indexes are enough. CQRS doubles the moving parts, and the replication lag forces UX changes ("your order will appear shortly") or read-your-writes workarounds.

Make projections rebuildable

A projection is derived data. Version it, make its handlers idempotent, and be able to drop it and replay the event stream or CDC log to rebuild it. That is also how you add a new read model next quarter.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Read modelsEvents · Projections

Store what happened, and derive the current state from it

Instead of overwriting a row with the latest state, event sourcing appends every change as an immutable event to a stream per entity. Current state is a fold over the stream. You get a perfect audit log, the ability to answer "what was true on March 1st", and the freedom to build new read models from history. The price is real complexity.

Where it earns its keep

Domains where history is the product or the regulation: ledgers and accounting, banking, trading, insurance claims, audit-heavy workflows. Also when you'll need read models nobody has thought of yet.

What gets hard

Event schemas are forever, so you need upcasters or versioned events. Queries across entities need projections. The right to erasure needs crypto-shredding. Long streams need snapshots. And the team has to think in events.

Not the same as event-driven

Event-driven means publishing events between services. Event sourcing means using events as a service's own storage. You can have either without the other, and most event-driven systems store state in ordinary tables.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Event sourcing: is it justified?Deck · Event sourcing mechanics

Serverless: pay per event, scale to zero, and give up control of the runtime

In serverless (functions as a service, plus managed backends), you write handlers and the platform runs them on demand: one isolated invocation per event, scaling from zero to thousands in seconds, billed per millisecond. There are no servers to patch or size. In return you accept cold starts, execution limits and tight coupling to one cloud's services.

Great fits

Event glue (resize on upload, react to a DB change), scheduled jobs, spiky or low-traffic APIs, webhooks, prototypes, and fan-out batch work. It also suits teams without a platform team, since nothing needs patching or capacity planning.

Poor fits

Latency-critical paths that can't tolerate cold starts (unless you pay for provisioned concurrency), long-running or stateful work, WebSockets at scale, and steady high throughput, where always-on containers are cheaper per request.

Design gotchas

Thousands of concurrent functions can exhaust a relational database's connections, so use a connection proxy or a serverless-native database. Make handlers idempotent, since platforms retry. Watch cost at scale, and design for vendor-specific triggers from the start.

Cells: copy the whole stack many times so a failure only hits a slice of users

Beyond a certain scale, one big shared system means one big blast radius. A bad deploy, a poisoned cache or a runaway tenant hurts everyone. In a cell-based architecture (Azure calls the units deployment stamps), you run many identical, independent copies of the stack, each serving a fixed subset of customers, behind a thin router.

What you get

A bounded blast radius: a failure or noisy tenant affects one cell. Deploys go in waves, cell by cell, with an automatic halt. Each cell has a fixed, tested maximum size, so scaling becomes "add a cell" rather than pushing one system into untested territory.

What it takes

A partition key that maps cleanly to cells (tenant, account, region). A router that is extremely simple and highly available. Automation to stamp out and upgrade identical cells. And a plan for the rare cross-cell query or tenant migration.

Where you'll see it

Large SaaS (Slack, Salesforce "pods", Azure stamps) and cloud control planes (AWS). In an interview, propose it once the design serves millions of tenants, or when the question stresses blast radius and noisy neighbours.

No style wins everywhere, so pick by the forces you actually have

Architecture styles aren't ranked; each trades some properties for others. Score them against what this system needs now: team size, how fast you must ship, how independently parts must deploy and scale, how strict the consistency is, and how much operational load you can carry. Then name the trigger that would make you change your mind.

A defensible default for most interview designs"I'd start with a modular monolith, or a handful of coarse services, with clear data ownership. I'd use events for fan-out to things like notifications, search and analytics, and managed or serverless components for glue. Then I'd extract a service when a specific force appears: a part with a very different scaling profile, a separate team, or a compliance boundary." Then name that force for the system in front of you.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · The decision hierarchyDeck · Four styles, honestly compared

The cloud design patterns, grouped by the problem they solve

The roadmap ends with the catalogue of cloud design patterns (popularised by Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center). They are named, reusable answers to recurring distributed-systems problems. Many have already appeared in this deck under their mechanism. This map puts the names on them, so you can use the vocabulary interviewers expect.

How to use pattern namesName the pattern and then say what it does in this design, in one breath: "I'd use a claim check here. The 20 MB document goes to object storage, and the message carries only its key." A name without the mechanism sounds memorised, and the mechanism without the name is fine too. Together they sound senior.

Four messaging patterns that turn up in almost every async design

Beyond "put it on a queue", four named patterns cover most async needs. They scale consumers, prioritise urgent work, compose processing steps, and keep large payloads off the broker. A fifth, the sequential convoy, keeps order within a group while still processing in parallel across groups.

Sequential convoy

Some messages must be processed in order, but only relative to their group: all of order 17's events, but not order 17 against order 42. Route by group key to a partition or session (Kafka keys, SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions). Each group is then sequential, and different groups run in parallel.

Trade-offs to mention

Competing consumers break global ordering, so combine them with a convoy if order matters. Priority queues need separate worker pools, or urgent work still waits behind bulk work. Pipes and filters add a hop per step: great for throughput, not for low latency. With a claim check, delete the blob when the message is done (use lifecycle rules).

Make multi-step work finish, or undo it, even when steps fail silently

Distributed workflows fail in awkward ways: a step times out, a remote service accepts a request and never answers, a worker dies mid-step. Scheduler Agent Supervisor gives such a workflow a durable memory and a watchdog. Compensating transaction gives each completed step an undo, so a workflow that can't finish can leave the system consistent.

Make every step idempotent

The supervisor will retry steps whose outcome is unknown, so "book hotel" might run twice. Pass a stable request id per step, so the remote service (or your agent) recognises a repeat.

Deadlines, not just failures

The dangerous case is the step that never answers. Record a deadline for each step. When the supervisor finds it expired, it queries the remote system for the real status before deciding to retry or compensate.

Buy it rather than build it

This is what workflow engines implement: Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, Camunda. They give you durable state, timers, retries and compensation handlers as code. Build your own only if the workflow is trivial.

Shape the data for the read before the read arrives

Three data-management patterns that sharding and caching don't cover. Materialized views precompute expensive query results. Index tables add secondary lookups to stores that only index a primary key. Static content hosting takes whole categories of requests off your compute entirely.

Materialized view

Use it for dashboards, leaderboards and "top N" lists, anywhere the same heavy aggregation is read far more often than its inputs change. Maintain it by scheduled refresh, incrementally from change events, or natively (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY).

Index table

The do-it-yourself secondary index for KV and sharded stores (DynamoDB GSIs are the managed version). It's a second write per change, and it's consistent only if both writes are in one transaction or the index is rebuilt from a change stream.

Static content hosting

Use it for single-page apps, docs sites, images and downloads. Version the file names so CDN caching is safe. Pair it with a valet key (presigned URLs) for private files, and never proxy big downloads through app servers.

One front door: route, aggregate, offload, and shape responses per client

The gateway patterns are three jobs a front door can do, and they are often combined. Routing hides many services behind one endpoint. Aggregation turns several backend calls into one client call. Offloading centralises cross-cutting work such as TLS and auth. A backend for frontend applies all three, separately for each client type.

Keep the gateway thinAn aggregating gateway is on every request's critical path and is shared by every team. Put in it only generic, declarative concerns and simple composition. When composition needs business rules, it belongs in a BFF owned by the client team, or in a proper service. A gateway also needs timeouts per downstream call and partial-result fallbacks, or a slow reviews service makes the whole product page slow.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · Gateway, BFF or mesh

Move cross-cutting plumbing out of the app and into a helper beside it

Every service needs the same plumbing: TLS, retries, metrics, log shipping, config reload. Rebuilding that in every language and framework doesn't scale. A sidecar runs next to the app, in the same pod or host, and provides it. An ambassador is a sidecar specialised in outbound calls. A service mesh is sidecars everywhere, configured centrally.

What a mesh buys

mTLS and service identity everywhere without code changes. Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking as configuration. Traffic splitting for canaries. Uniform golden-signal metrics and traces for every hop, in every language.

What it costs

An extra proxy hop per call (roughly 1 ms of p99 each way), CPU and memory per pod, and a complex control plane to run and upgrade. Debugging now spans app, proxy and configuration. Worth it with dozens of services, rarely with five.

Lighter options

Proxyless gRPC with xDS, eBPF-based meshes (Cilium) that avoid per-pod proxies, or simply shared client libraries when there is a single language. Choose on the number of services, languages, and how badly you need zero-trust networking.

Replace a legacy system one route at a time, behind a facade

Big-bang rewrites of systems with years of encoded business rules fail often and expensively. The strangler fig puts a routing facade in front of the legacy system, moves one capability at a time to new services, and retires the old system when nothing routes to it. An anti-corruption layer translates between the new model and the legacy one, so legacy concepts don't leak into the new code.

Choosing what to move first

Pick a capability that has a clear boundary, real business value and a pain point: it changes often, scales badly or breaks often. Avoid the most entangled core first. Use tracing to see which routes carry traffic and which tables each one touches.

The data is the hard part

Routes move easily, data doesn't. Common approaches: the new service reads legacy tables through an ACL; CDC syncs legacy tables into the new store; dual-write for a transition window with reconciliation. Cut over ownership last, once the reconciliation reports are clean.

Anti-corruption layer

A translator (an adapter, a small service, or an event mapper) that converts legacy formats, codes and concepts into the new domain's language, and back. It keeps "CUST_TYP_CD = 3" out of the new code, and it's also how you integrate third-party systems you'll never control.

Elsewhere in the atlasDeck · The strangler figDeck · Systems you cannot change

Four more reliability patterns to have in your vocabulary

Retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, throttling and deployment stamps each had a slide of their own. Four more round out the catalogue: expose health so something can act on it, keep configuration outside the build, serve users from active nodes everywhere, and pack workloads onto shared compute sensibly.

Geodes vs deployment stamps

Both deploy many copies of the stack. Stamps/cells partition users: each copy owns a subset of tenants, and a user always lands in their cell. Geodes are interchangeable: any copy serves any user, routed by proximity, with data replicated everywhere. Geodes give the lowest latency and survive the loss of a region. Cells give the tightest blast radius.

Consolidation vs isolation

Packing services onto shared nodes (Kubernetes) cuts cost and idle capacity, and it creates noisy-neighbour risk. Protect yourself with resource requests and limits, priority classes, and separate node pools for critical or bursty workloads. It's the bulkhead trade-off again, at the infrastructure level.

Design a URL shortener: a tiny write path and an enormous read path

The classic warm-up question (think bit.ly or tinyurl). It looks trivial, which is the point: the interviewer wants to see whether you find the real problems. Those are generating short unique keys without coordination, and serving redirects in milliseconds at 100× the write rate, with analytics on the side.

Functional

  • Shorten a long URL to a 7-character code.
  • Redirect short.ly/Ab3xK9q to the long URL.
  • Optional custom alias and expiry date.
  • Click statistics per link (may lag by minutes).

Non-functional

  • Redirect p99 < 50 ms, availability 99.99%. A broken link breaks someone else's product.
  • Links are durable: never lost, never re-pointed.
  • Codes are not trivially enumerable.
  • Read-heavy at 100:1; writes may be slightly slower.

Clarify, then scope out

  • "Same long URL twice: same code or new?" Different codes per user is simpler.
  • "Do links ever get edited?" No: immutability helps caching.
  • Out of scope: link previews, QR codes, billing.

Three endpoints and one hot table keyed by code

Every redirect is a lookup by exact key, and links never change once created. That is a key-value access pattern with no joins on the hot path, so the store choice is easy. Click data is append-only and analytical, so it goes to a different store entirely.

API
POST /v1/urls
Idempotency-Key: 7c1e…            # retries can't create duplicates
{ "long_url": "https://…", "alias": "spring-sale", "expires_at": "2027-01-01" }
→ 201 { "code": "Ab3xK9q", "short_url": "https://short.ly/Ab3xK9q" }

GET /{code}
→ 302 Location: https://…          # or 404 / 410 Gone if expired

GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats?from=…&to=…
→ 200 { "clicks": 18234, "by_day": […], "top_countries": […] }

DELETE /v1/urls/{code}             # owner only; tombstones the code

302, not 301 (by default)

A 301 Moved Permanently is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach you. That means less load, but no analytics and no way to expire the link. Use 302 when stats or expiry matter. Offer 301 for "permanent, no stats" links.

Why a KV store fits

Lookup by exact key, no joins, immutable values, 3 TB growing steadily. Any of DynamoDB, Cassandra or sharded PostgreSQL works. Say which and why: "PostgreSQL until a few TB, because the team knows it. The schema is already shard-friendly."

Idempotent creates

A mobile client that retries a timed-out create shouldn't get two codes. The Idempotency-Key maps to the first response for 24 hours. Custom aliases use a conditional insert (INSERT … IF NOT EXISTS), so a collision returns 409.

Split the write path from the read path, and keep redirects in memory

Two services with very different shapes share one table. Shorten is low-volume and needs unique keys. Redirect is 100× busier, needs single-digit-millisecond lookups, and scales independently. Clicks go onto a stream, so analytics never slows a redirect.

Walk the write

① POST /v1/urls reaches Shorten. ② Shorten validates the URL (scheme, length, blocklist) and takes the next id from its in-memory block, fetched from the key generation service 1,000 ids at a time. ③ It encodes the id as base62, inserts (code, long_url, owner), and returns 201. It doesn't write to the cache; the first redirect warms it.

Walk the read

① GET /Ab3xK9q reaches Redirect. ② GET url:Ab3xK9q in Redis: on a hit, go to ④. ③ On a miss, read a DB replica and set the cache with a 24 h TTL (links are immutable). ④ Return 302 plus Cache-Control: private, max-age=0. ⑤ Publish a click event asynchronously, with ip hash, UA and referrer.

Deep dive 1: unique 7-character codes without a coordination bottleneck

This is the heart of the question. You need billions of unique, short, non-guessable codes, minted by many servers at once, with no global lock on the write path. There are three standard approaches, and the interviewer wants to hear why you rejected two of them.

The answer to give"Counter ranges. A small coordination service (a DB sequence or etcd) hands each Shorten instance a block of 1,000 ids, so the write path never waits on it. To stop people enumerating links, I pass the id through a reversible scramble, such as a keyed Feistel permutation over the 62⁷ space, before base62-encoding it. Codes look random and are still guaranteed unique. Custom aliases skip all this and use a conditional insert."

Deep dive 2: a redirect in under 10 ms, and clicks counted without slowing it

The read path carries 99% of the traffic, and every millisecond is someone else's page-load time. Keep it to one memory lookup, keep the database off it, record clicks asynchronously, and decide deliberately what the browser and CDN are allowed to cache.

What may be cached where

Redis: everything, with a long TTL (links are immutable; delete on expiry or takedown). Browser/CDN: only for links marked "no stats", via 301 or max-age. Tracked links use 302 + no-store, or the clicks would vanish into caches.

Counting clicks at 20k/s

Don't UPDATE clicks = clicks + 1 per redirect. That's a hot-row write storm. Stream raw events, aggregate per code per minute in a consumer, and write the rollups to a columnar store. For a live counter, use Redis INCR on sharded keys, flushed periodically.

Hot links

A link shared by a celebrity can take 50k/s on one key, which means one Redis shard. Add a 1–5 s in-process cache in the redirect service (links never change, so staleness is harmless) or replicate hot keys. For "no stats" links, let the CDN absorb it entirely.

What breaks at 10×, what fails, and what interviewers ask next

Finish by stress-testing your own design. Redirects must survive the loss of any single component, so each dependency on the read path needs a fallback. Growth pushes the design towards multi-region reads, but the write path can stay in one region, because links are immutable.

At 10× (200k redirects/s)Response
Redis shard hotRedis Cluster plus an in-process cache for the top keys
DB storage (30 TB)More shards; archive expired links; compress long URLs
Click stream volumeMore Kafka partitions; pre-aggregate at the service
Global latencyMore read regions; edge redirects for "no stats" links

Follow-ups to expect

  • Abuse: phishing and malware links. Scan on create (Safe Browsing API), rate-limit creates per user and IP, and add a takedown flag checked on redirect.
  • Expiry: a lazy check on redirect (410 Gone), plus a nightly sweeper that deletes expired rows and cache keys.
  • Custom domains: the tenant becomes part of the key, (domain, code).
  • Privacy: hash IPs in click events, and set retention limits on raw events.

Design a distributed rate limiter for a public API

Every request to the API must be checked against its caller's allowance, across dozens of gateway instances, adding almost no latency. The limiter must not become the outage it was meant to prevent. The core difficulties are shared, contended counters across machines, and deciding what happens when the counter store itself is unavailable.

Functional

  • Limit by API key, user, IP and endpoint, e.g. "100 req/s, bursts to 200" and "10k/day".
  • Return 429 with Retry-After and remaining-quota headers.
  • Change rules without a deploy, and per customer tier.

Non-functional

  • Adds < 2 ms p99. Must not reduce API availability.
  • Accurate to within a few percent. Briefly exceeding a limit by 5% is fine.
  • Scales linearly with gateways and keys.

Ask about the purpose

  • Protective (keep us up) → fail open if the limiter breaks.
  • Contractual (billing tiers) → accuracy matters, and you may fail closed.
  • This one decision drives the failure design (deep dive 2).

Rules are configuration, counters are tiny keys with a TTL

A rate limiter has two kinds of data with opposite profiles. Rules are small, rarely change, and are read on every request, so they're cached in every gateway. Counters are one small record per (rule, client), updated on every request, and expired when idle.

rules (config store, pushed to gateways)
- id: free-tier-default
  match: { tier: free }
  key: api_key
  algorithm: token_bucket
  rate: 10/s
  burst: 20
- id: pro-search
  match: { tier: pro, route: "GET /v1/search" }
  key: api_key
  algorithm: token_bucket
  rate: 100/s
  burst: 200
- id: login-per-ip
  match: { route: "POST /v1/login" }
  key: client_ip
  algorithm: sliding_window
  limit: 10/min
response on rejection
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 2

Rule evaluation is local

Matching a request to its rules must not need a network call. Gateways hold the full rule set in memory, subscribe to changes, and stamp every decision with the rule version it used. That makes audits and debugging possible.

Multiple rules per request

A request can hit several rules at once: per key, per org, per endpoint, and global. Check them all in one round trip (a single Lua call over several keys, or a pipeline). Reject if any rule rejects, and report the tightest one in the headers.

Shadow mode

New or tightened rules first run in "log only" mode: count what would have been rejected, without rejecting. Promote a rule to enforcement once you've seen whom it would hit. This single feature prevents most rate-limit incidents.

Limit at the edge in layers: coarse per IP first, precise per key at the gateway

Rejecting a request is cheapest as early as possible. The CDN or WAF drops floods by IP before they reach you. The gateway enforces precise per-key and per-endpoint limits against a shared counter store. Services keep a last-line concurrency limit for their own expensive work.

Why at the gateway, not in each service

One place to enforce and observe limits. The check happens before expensive work (auth, fan-out) and uses the authenticated identity. Services stay free of limit logic. The trade-off is that the gateway becomes critical, so the filter must be fast and have a failure mode.

Why a shared store and not local counters

With 50 gateways and a load balancer spreading requests, local counters each see about 1/50 of a key's traffic, so per-instance limits are wildly inaccurate for bursty clients. A shared atomic counter makes the limit exact, at the cost of about 0.5 ms and a dependency. Deep dive 2 shows the hybrids.

Deep dive 1: the check must be one atomic operation

"Read the counter, decide, write it back" from 50 gateways is a textbook race. Two gateways read "1 token left", both allow, and the limit leaks under exactly the concurrent load it exists for. Make the whole refill-check-take step atomic on the shard that owns the key. In Redis that means a Lua script.

token_bucket.lua (runs inside Redis)
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key   ARGV = rate/s, burst, now_ms, cost
local rate, burst, now, cost = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]),
                               tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or burst
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(burst, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)   -- refill
local allowed = tokens >= cost
if allowed then tokens = tokens - cost end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(burst / rate * 1000) * 2)
local wait = allowed and 0 or math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate * 1000)
return { allowed and 1 or 0, math.floor(tokens), wait }

Details that come up

  • Whose clock? Pass now from the gateway (NTP-synced), or read Redis TIME inside the script so every caller shares one clock.
  • Cost: weight expensive endpoints (cost = 10 for an export), so a limit reflects load, not just request count.
  • One round trip: load the script once (EVALSHA). Check several rules in one call when their keys share a hash tag, so they land on the same shard.
  • The TTL lets idle keys vanish, so memory tracks active clients, not every client ever seen.

Deep dive 2: trade accuracy against dependency, and decide how to fail

A shared counter is exact but puts a network hop and a dependency in front of every request. Local counters are free but inaccurate. Real systems pick a point between the two, and then state what happens when Redis, or a whole region, is unreachable.

Multi-region

A synchronous cross-region check on every request would add 60–150 ms, which is unacceptable. Give each region its own counters and a share of the global budget, e.g. split by that region's traffic share, and rebalance the shares every few seconds from an aggregated view. Global limits become approximately right, which is almost always fine.

Say the default

"Central Redis counter with an atomic Lua token bucket, since 0.5 ms is affordable. A 5 ms timeout with a circuit breaker around it. Fail open to a local limiter for protective rules and fail closed for login and OTP. Per-region counters with budget shares. Token leasing only if Redis load or latency becomes a problem."

Limits are product decisions as well as defences

A limiter that works technically can still fail its users. A partner who gets throttled with no warning, fair customers starved by one heavy customer, a limit change that locks out your biggest account. Wrap up with the operational and product sides, and with how the design grows.

RiskMitigation
Redis hot shard (one huge client)Shard that client's key with sub-keys, or give it a lease-based local budget
Limit change locks out a big customerShadow mode first, gradual rollout, per-customer overrides
Clients hammer after 429Retry-After, SDKs with backoff + jitter, stricter limits on repeated violators
Limiter adds latencyKeep Redis local to the region, pipeline multi-rule checks, lease tokens

Follow-ups to expect

  • "Limit concurrent requests, not rate?" A semaphore per key: increment on start, decrement on finish, with a TTL for crashed requests.
  • "Daily quotas for billing?" A separate durable counter, since Redis alone isn't billing-grade. Reconcile from the decision stream.
  • "Distributed DDoS?" That's the edge/WAF layer: anycast, IP reputation, challenges. Not this service.
