Design a chat app: millions of open connections, and no lost or reordered messages

Think WhatsApp or Messenger: 1:1 and group chat, delivered in real time when the recipient is online and on reconnect when they aren't, in order, never lost, and synced across devices. The defining constraints are the huge number of persistent connections and the need to route each message to whichever server the recipient happens to be connected to.

Functional

  • 1:1 and group chats (groups ≤ 256 members).
  • Sent / delivered / read receipts, and online presence.
  • Offline delivery on reconnect, plus a push notification.
  • History synced across a user's devices; images via upload.

Non-functional

  • Delivery p99 < 300 ms when both users are online in-region.
  • Never lose an acknowledged message.
  • Messages ordered within a conversation.
  • Very high availability: chat is the product.

Scope it

  • End-to-end encryption: the server stores ciphertext only (mention it, don't design Signal).
  • Out of scope: voice and video calls, stories, payments.
  • Large broadcast channels (100k+) are a different fan-out problem. Flag it.

A WebSocket protocol for live traffic, REST for history, and messages partitioned by conversation

Live messages, receipts and presence flow over one persistent WebSocket per device. Fetching history, the conversation list and media uploads are ordinary REST calls that can be cached and retried. The store is modelled around the two hottest queries: "latest messages in conversation X" and "my conversations, newest first".

WebSocket frames (JSON or protobuf)
// client → server
{ "t": "send", "client_msg_id": "c-9f1…", "conv": "g-77", "body": "…" }
{ "t": "ack",  "conv": "g-77", "seq": 1042 }        // delivered up to 1042
{ "t": "read", "conv": "g-77", "seq": 1042 }

// server → client
{ "t": "sent", "client_msg_id": "c-9f1…", "seq": 1043 }  // persisted ✓
{ "t": "msg",  "conv": "g-77", "seq": 1043, "from": "u-5", "body": "…", "ts": … }
{ "t": "receipt", "conv": "g-77", "seq": 1043, "user": "u-9", "state": "read" }
REST
GET  /v1/conversations?cursor=…                # my inbox, by last activity
GET  /v1/conversations/g-77/messages?before=1043&limit=50
POST /v1/media/upload-url                      # presigned PUT for images

Why a wide-column store

The workload is write-heavy (700k/s), almost all reads are "latest N in one conversation", and there is a lot of data. That's exactly a partition-per-conversation, clustered-by-sequence table. The month bucket keeps very long-lived chats from growing one partition forever.

Sequence numbers, not timestamps

Each conversation gets a monotonically increasing seq, assigned by the server when the message is persisted. It orders messages, drives "give me everything after 1042" sync, and makes receipts one number: "read up to 1042".

client_msg_id for idempotency

Phones retry on flaky networks. The client generates an id per message, and the server dedupes on (conv, client_msg_id), returning the existing seq. A resend never produces a duplicate bubble.

Stateful gateways hold connections; stateless services decide what to deliver where

Separate the parts that must be stateful from those that needn't be. Gateways hold hundreds of thousands of WebSockets each and do almost nothing else. The chat service persists messages and assigns sequence numbers. Delivery workers look up where each recipient is connected, route the message there, and fall back to a push notification when the recipient is offline.

Why stateful gateways stay thin

Gateways deploy slowly: every restart drops half a million sockets, and those clients must reconnect. So keep business logic out of them. They authenticate the socket, register it, relay frames, and push what delivery workers hand them.

Routing to a connection

The session registry maps user → {gateway, device}. Workers forward to that gateway over RPC, or to a per-gateway pub/sub channel. Entries have a TTL refreshed by heartbeats, so a crashed gateway's entries expire on their own.

Sync covers every gap

Real-time delivery is an optimisation. The source of truth is "messages with seq greater than my last acknowledged one". On every reconnect, each device asks for what it missed, which also repairs any delivery that was dropped.

Deep dive 1: one message from Alice's phone to Bob's, with receipts

Follow a single message through the system. The two properties to protect are durability before acknowledgement (the tick means it's safe) and a single order per conversation (every device shows the same sequence). Both come from one decision: the server assigns each message a per-conversation sequence number as it persists it.

Assigning the sequence

There must be exactly one writer of a conversation's counter. Options: a per-conversation Redis INCR, persisted with the message; a conditional update on the conversation row; or routing every send for a conversation through one Kafka partition, whose single consumer numbers the messages. Never use client clocks.

Acks at every hop

Client → server: "sent" only after the write is durable, and the client retries with the same client_msg_id until it arrives. Server → client: the device acknowledges the highest seq it has, and anything unacknowledged is redelivered or picked up by sync. So delivery is at-least-once, and display is deduped by seq.

Multi-device

Each device is a separate connection with its own "acknowledged up to" position. Alice's own messages are also delivered to her other devices. Read state is per user: reading on the phone clears the badge on the laptop via a receipt to self.

Deep dive 2: fan-out to groups, and presence without a broadcast storm

Groups multiply delivery work by the member count. Presence multiplies it by the number of contacts, on every status change. Both are managed the same way: store once, fan out only to the live connections that need it, batch per gateway, and compute everything else lazily when someone looks.

Storage layout

Messages: partition (conv_id, month), clustered by seq DESC, so "latest 50" and "before seq X" are single-partition slices. Media lives in object storage, and the message holds a URL, size and thumbnail hash. Old months move to cheaper storage tiers.

Typing indicators and receipts

These are ephemeral and high-volume. Deliver them best-effort over the socket and never persist them. Coalesce read receipts to the latest seq, and in big groups show aggregated counts ("read by 12"), not per-member events.

Unread counts

Store last_seq and last_read_seq per member and conversation. The badge is the difference, summed across conversations. Never count by scanning messages. Cache the total per user and adjust it on each message and read event.

Reconnect storms, regions and encryption are where chat designs get tested

The steady state is easy to draw. Interviewers probe the transitions. What happens when a gateway holding 500k sockets dies, or a region fails? How do two users in different regions keep one order? And what changes when the server can't read the messages?

Follow-upAnswer sketch
End-to-end encryptionClients encrypt per recipient device (Signal protocol). The server stores and routes ciphertext and holds public prekeys. Search and moderation move to the client.
Edit / deleteA new event referencing the original seq; clients apply it. Deletes are tombstones, purged later.
Spam and abuseRate limits per sender, reputation scores, reports, and metadata-based detection, since content is encrypted.
Message searchServer-side index if not E2E; otherwise a local index on the device.
Summarise the trade-offs"We chose at-least-once delivery with seq-based dedup over exactly-once. Wide-column storage partitioned by conversation over a relational database. Stateful gateways kept thin, with state in a TTL'd registry. And a home region per conversation for ordering, accepting one cross-region hop for remote members."

Design a news feed: cheap reads for everyone, including followers of celebrities

Think of the Twitter/X home timeline, Instagram or Facebook. Users follow others and open a feed of their posts, newest or best first. It's read-heavy like the URL shortener, but each read gathers posts from hundreds of sources. So the central question is when to do that gathering: when a post is written, or when a feed is read.

Functional

  • Create posts (text plus media), follow and unfollow.
  • Home feed: posts from people you follow, ranked, with infinite scroll.
  • Like and comment counts shown on each post.

Non-functional

  • Feed load p99 < 200 ms. This is the product's front page.
  • New posts visible to followers within seconds (eventual is fine).
  • Authors see their own post immediately (read-your-writes).
  • Handle extreme follower skew: 10 followers to 100 M.

Clarify

  • Chronological or ranked? Ranked, but design so chronological is a special case.
  • Do we store the whole history? Feeds show the last ~800 items; older posts come from profile pages.
  • Out of scope: ads auction, notifications, and search.

Posts are the truth; a feed is just a list of post ids

Keep post content in one place, and keep feeds as lightweight lists of ids per user, fetched and then hydrated in a batch. A feed entry never copies the post body. That's what makes edits and deletes tractable, and it keeps the feed cache small enough to hold for every active user.

API
POST /v1/posts                      { "text": "…", "media_ids": ["m-1"] }
→ 201 { "post_id": "18446…", "created_at": … }

GET  /v1/feed?cursor=eyJzIjo…&limit=20
→ 200 { "items": [ { "post": {…}, "author": {…},
                     "likes": 1204, "liked_by_me": false } ],
        "next_cursor": "eyJzIjo…" }      # opaque: (score, post_id)

PUT    /v1/users/{id}/follow
DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow
POST   /v1/posts/{id}/like              # idempotent per user

Why the graph is stored twice

Fan-out asks "who follows X?" and the profile page asks "whom does Y follow?". Each question needs its own partition key. Write both rows on follow (async repair keeps them in sync), or use a graph service such as Facebook's TAO.

Cursor, not offset

Feeds change while you scroll. Offsets skip and duplicate items. An opaque cursor, (score, post_id) of the last item, resumes exactly, and lets the server change the ranking without breaking pages already loaded.

Counters live apart

A viral post takes 100k likes a minute. Incrementing a column on the post row makes it a hot row. Use sharded counters (N sub-keys summed on read), plus a per-user "liked" set so the like button is idempotent.

Precompute feeds on write, then assemble, hydrate and rank on read

The write path stores a post and hands it to fan-out workers, which push its id into each follower's cached feed. The read path takes the precomputed ids, merges in posts from any celebrities the user follows, fetches the post bodies in one batch, ranks, and returns a page. The expensive work happens asynchronously, off the user's critical path.

Post → visible

① Store the post (durable) and return 201. ② Publish PostCreated. ③ Fan-out workers page through the followers in batches of 1,000 and ZADD into each active follower's feed. A normal author's followers see the post in seconds.

Open the feed

① ZREVRANGE feed:u 0 499. ② Merge the latest posts of followed celebrities, cached per celebrity. ③ Multi-get post bodies, authors and counters. ④ Rank and filter (seen, blocked, deleted). ⑤ Return 20 items and a cursor.

Cold and inactive users

Skip fan-out for users inactive for 30 days: that saves most of the writes. When one returns, rebuild their feed on read (pull from followees), store it, then resume pushing. The first load is slower; every later load is fast.

Deep dive 1: push on write, pull on read, or both

This is the question the interviewer is waiting for. Push (fan-out on write) does the work once per post per follower, so reads are one lookup. Pull (fan-out on read) does the work every time a feed opens. Follower counts are wildly skewed, so real systems use a hybrid: push for most authors, pull for the few with millions of followers.

PushPullHybrid
Work per postO(followers)O(1)O(followers) below the threshold, O(1) above
Work per feed loadO(1)O(followees)O(1) + O(celebrities followed)
FreshnessSeconds (lag grows with fan-out)ImmediateImmediate for celebrities, seconds for the rest
Wasted workWrites to feeds nobody opensNoneSmall; inactive users skipped

Deep dive 2: from 1,500 candidates to 20 ranked posts in under 200 ms

A ranked feed is a funnel. Gather candidates cheaply, filter out what must never show, score what's left with a model, then fetch full content only for the handful you'll return. Each stage cuts the set by an order of magnitude, so the expensive stages see little data.

Chronological is a special case

Score = timestamp and skip ③ and ④. Designing the funnel anyway means switching between "latest" and "top" is a flag rather than a rewrite, and ads or recommendations slot in as just another candidate source.

Features must be precomputed

The ranker can't query ten services per candidate. Author–viewer affinity, post engagement velocity and user embeddings are computed by streaming jobs into a feature store, and read in batches (< 10 ms) at ranking time.

Stable pagination

Rank the first page and cache the ordered candidate list for the session (say 10 minutes), so page two continues that snapshot. Re-ranking on every page would reshuffle items: duplicates, and posts that vanish between scrolls.

Viral posts, degraded dependencies, and deletes that must stick

A feed has many dependencies: graph, cache, ranker, counters, media. The page should get worse gracefully rather than fail when any one of them struggles. The other classic stress is a single viral post that every feed hydrates at once.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Delete or edit a postMark it deleted in the posts store. Filter tombstones at hydrate time (the feed holds only ids), and lazily remove it from caches.
UnfollowStop future fan-out, and filter that author at read until the cached entries age out.
Author sees own post nowMerge the author's own recent posts at read time (read-your-writes), without waiting for fan-out.
New user, empty feedCandidates come from recommendations and popular posts until the follow graph fills in.
The trade-off sentence"We trade write amplification and some staleness for fast, predictable reads. Push for the 99.9% of authors with modest follower counts, pull for the celebrity tail, skip inactive users, and treat the feed as ids hydrated at read time, so edits, deletes and counts stay correct without rewriting millions of feeds."

Elsewhere in the atlasHLD · Hot keys and reshardingHLD · Cache failure modes

Design a notification system: many producers, four channels, and users who must not be spammed

Every product team wants to notify users: order shipped, a login from a new device, "you have 3 new followers", a marketing campaign. A central notification platform gives them one API and handles channels (push, SMS, email, in-app), user preferences, templates, rate limits, retries and delivery tracking. The difficulties are wildly mixed urgency and volume, unreliable third-party providers, and not annoying people.

Functional

  • One API for all producers: send to a user, a list, or a segment, now or scheduled.
  • Channels: iOS/Android push, email, SMS, in-app inbox.
  • Templates with localisation; user preferences per category and channel.
  • Delivery status: sent, delivered, opened, failed.

Non-functional

  • Never lose a notification; never double-send an SMS or OTP.
  • Priority isolation between critical and bulk traffic.
  • Survive a provider outage (fail over to a secondary).
  • Per-user caps and quiet hours enforced centrally.

Clarify

  • Who owns the content? Producers pick a template; the platform renders it.
  • Can users unsubscribe per category? Yes, and that's a legal requirement for marketing.
  • Out of scope: campaign authoring UI and A/B testing.

Producers send intents; the platform decides channel, content and timing

A producer says "tell user 42 their order shipped" with a template and parameters. It doesn't choose between push and email, and it doesn't render text. That keeps preferences, localisation, caps and provider details in one place, and lets you change them without touching fifty services.

API
POST /v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: order-881-shipped            # same key → same notification
{ "recipients": { "user_ids": ["u-42"] },     # or { "segment": "lapsed-30d" }
  "template": "order_shipped", "category": "transactional",
  "priority": "normal",                       # critical | normal | bulk
  "params": { "order_id": "881", "eta": "Thu" },
  "send_at": null }                           # or a timestamp
→ 202 { "notification_id": "n-5f2…" }

GET  /v1/notifications/n-5f2…     → per-channel status timeline
POST /v1/devices    { "token": "…", "platform": "ios" }
PUT  /v1/users/u-42/preferences   { "marketing": { "push": false } }

202, not 200

Sending is asynchronous. The API validates the request, checks idempotency, persists it (or enqueues it durably) and returns a notification id immediately. Producers must never block on an SMS provider's latency.

Segments are expanded later

"Send to segment lapsed-30d" (8 M users) is stored as one job. A campaign worker expands it in pages, at a controlled rate, instead of the API call enqueueing 8 M messages synchronously.

Two different stores

Preferences, devices and templates are small, read constantly and change rarely, so keep them in a relational DB behind a cache. The log is write-heavy, time-ordered and huge, so use a wide-column store with a TTL, and aggregate to analytics for open and click rates.

A pipeline of queues: accept, decide, render, deliver, track

Each stage has one job and a queue in front of it, so it can scale, retry and fail on its own. The key design move is keeping queues separate by priority at the front and by channel at the back. A campaign flooding email can't delay an OTP, and a slow SMS provider can't stall push notifications.

Router workers decide

For each (notification, user): Is it a duplicate? Is the user opted in for this category and channel? Is it quiet hours in their timezone? Are they over their cap? Which devices are live? Then render the template in the user's locale and emit one message per channel.

Channel workers deliver

Batch where providers allow it (FCM multicast, email batch APIs). Respect each provider's rate limits with a token bucket per provider. Retry transient errors, drop permanent ones (invalid token, hard bounce), and record the provider's message id for tracking.

Tracking closes the loop

Providers call back with delivered, bounced or complaint. The SDK and email pixels report opens. Hard bounces and invalid tokens feed back into the device and contact tables, which protects sender reputation and cuts cost.

Deep dive 1: isolate by priority, and route around failing providers

Two things threaten delivery. Load you create yourself, when an 8-million-user campaign lands on the same workers as OTPs. And third parties you don't control, when an SMS provider degrades, rate-limits you or goes down. Separate lanes handle the first. Per-provider limiters, circuit breakers and a secondary provider handle the second.

Throttle bulk on purpose

Send campaigns at a fixed rate (say 20k/s). This protects provider quotas and sender reputation, and it protects your own backend: 8 M pushes in one minute means 2 M people opening the app in the same minute. Spread sends by time zone and "send at local 10 am".

Provider abstraction

Hide providers behind one interface per channel, with health scores, cost and region routing. Fail over automatically on errors or latency. For SMS, route by destination country to the cheapest healthy provider; the costs differ by 10× across providers.

Retries that don't duplicate

Send each attempt with the same idempotency or message id where the provider supports it. A timeout isn't a failure. Query the provider's status before resending an OTP, or users receive two codes and the older one no longer works.

Deep dive 2: the router is a policy engine that mostly says "not now"

The best notification system sends fewer notifications. Each candidate passes a sequence of checks, and most of the product value is in them: duplicates dropped, preferences honoured, quiet hours respected, bursts collapsed into digests, and every channel chosen for this user right now. Critical messages skip the checks that could delay them.

Check late, not early

Preferences and quiet hours are evaluated at send time, not when the notification was requested. A deferred or scheduled message rechecks them, so a user who unsubscribed at 9 pm doesn't get the 8 am campaign.

Caps are counters

Per user, per category, per day: a Redis INCR with a TTL until midnight in the user's timezone. Check and increment atomically. Caps are the single best defence against a buggy producer spamming users in a loop.

Aggregation windows

For bursty events (likes, comments), hold the first event for a short window, say 2 minutes, keyed by (user, post, type), and collapse everything that arrives in it into one message. That's fewer notifications, better copy, and lower cost.

At-least-once delivery, bounded duplicates, and a thundering herd you caused yourself

Wrap up with the guarantees you actually offer, which are at-least-once delivery with deduplication and never exactly-once across third-party providers. Then cover how the system behaves at the edges: a campaign that brings the whole user base back at once, stale device tokens, and compliance.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Stale device tokensAPNs/FCM report invalid tokens: delete them. Prune devices unseen for 60 days.
ComplianceOne-click unsubscribe (email), opt-in consent for SMS (TCPA), consent records, and region-specific data storage.
In-app inboxStore per-user notifications (the log indexed by user) with read state; deliver live over WebSocket if connected.
Multi-regionRegional pipelines; route by user home region; providers by destination country.
Summarise"A durable intake API with idempotency, priority-separated topics, router workers that apply preferences, caps and quiet hours at send time, and channel-specific workers with per-provider limiters, breakers and fail-over. Every state change goes into a notification log, so any message can be traced end to end."

Design search autocomplete: a million prefix lookups a second, each answered in milliseconds

As the user types "how to b", show the eight most popular completions. It has to feel instant, so suggestions must arrive before the next keystroke, and it's called on nearly every keystroke. That makes this a read-latency problem, solved by precomputing answers offline and serving them from memory.

Functional

  • Given a prefix, return the top 8 completions by popularity.
  • Reflect trending queries within about an hour.
  • Filter offensive or legally blocked suggestions.

Non-functional

  • Server p99 < 20 ms; highly available. If it fails, the search box still works, just without suggestions.
  • Eventual consistency is fine: suggestions may be hours old.
  • Heavily read-dominated: suggestions are rebuilt offline.

Clarify

  • Personalised or global? Global first, with a personal blend as a follow-up.
  • Prefix only, or typo-tolerant? Prefix only; fuzzy is a follow-up.
  • One language to start (lowercased, normalised).

One tiny GET, and a trie that stores its answers at every node

The API is a single cacheable GET. The interesting data structure is a trie (prefix tree) in which every node also stores the top-k completions below it. A lookup becomes "walk down one node per character, then return the list stored there". There is no subtree search at query time.

API
GET /v1/suggest?q=car&lang=en&limit=8
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300           # short prefixes are very cacheable
→ 200 { "prefix": "car",
        "suggestions": [ "car insurance", "cars for sale", "cartoon",
                         "car rental", "cardi b", … ],
        "version": "trie-2026-09-30T10" }
client behaviour (half the design)
// debounce 50–100 ms; cancel stale requests; cache per prefix
// "car" then "cart" → if "car" results are complete (< 8 hits), filter locally
// never block typing on the network

Where the counts come from

A query_counts table (query → decayed score), built from search logs by a batch or streaming job. Scores decay exponentially (half-life of about a week), so yesterday's spike fades and evergreen queries stay.

The trie is a build artefact

It isn't a database. It's an immutable snapshot built offline, versioned, stored in object storage and loaded into memory by the serving nodes. Updates arrive as new snapshots, never as in-place writes on the hot path.

Or a KV of prefixes

A flat alternative: precompute prefix → top-8 list for every prefix up to 20 characters and serve it from a KV store or a CDN. It's simpler to shard and cache, and bigger on disk. It's often the pragmatic interview answer after explaining the trie.

A fast in-memory serving path fed by a slow, careful build path

Split the system in two. Serving is stateless apart from a read-only trie in memory: every request is a few pointer hops, heavily cached at the edge. Building is a data pipeline that turns search logs into ranked, filtered snapshots every hour or so and ships them to the servers.

Caching does most of the work

One- and two-character prefixes are few (about 1,000) and account for a large share of requests. The CDN and browser cache them for minutes. The server sees mostly longer, rarer prefixes, and each of those is still a microsecond trie walk.

Sharding the trie

Shard by prefix range so each lookup hits exactly one shard. The ranges are cut by measured traffic, not the alphabet ("s" and "c" are huge, "x" is tiny). Replicate each shard three or more times for throughput and availability.

Safe deploys of data

Load the new snapshot alongside the old one, run canary queries (sizes, blocklist hits, top results for known prefixes), then swap an atomic pointer. Keep the previous version for an instant rollback, since a bad snapshot is a data outage.

Deep dive 1: build the top-k lists bottom-up, and keep the trie small

The trie is built offline, so you can afford to do the work there. Insert every kept query with its score, then compute each node's top-k by merging its children's lists from the leaves up. At query time nothing is searched, only read. The remaining problem is memory, which you control with thresholds, depth limits and path compression.

Query cost

O(len(prefix)) pointer hops to reach the node, then return a precomputed list, no matter how many queries sit below it. That flat cost is the property that lets a million requests a second fit on a modest fleet.

Scoring

Score = decayed frequency plus a small freshness boost, capped so a single viral day can't dominate for weeks. Normalise queries at build time (lowercase, trim, Unicode NFKC) so "Car " and "car" count as one.

Why not just a database

WHERE query LIKE 'car%' ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 8 works with a prefix index at low volume, but at 1 M/s each call is a range scan and a sort. A search engine's completion suggester is fine at moderate scale. At this scale, precompute.

Deep dive 2: fresh enough for breaking news, balanced enough for "s"

A daily rebuild is too slow when something happens in the news: people type it within minutes. Rebuilding the whole trie every minute is too expensive. The answer is layers: a stable base, a periodic delta, and a small real-time trending layer, merged when the query is served. Separately, prefix traffic is very uneven, so shard boundaries follow measured load, not the alphabet.

Trending, cheaply

A streaming job counts query frequency per minute with a count-min sketch (small, approximate) and tracks heavy hitters per short prefix. It emits queries whose rate is far above their baseline. The overlay is tiny: a few thousand entries, replicated to every server.

Safety at every layer

Autocomplete can put words in users' mouths, so it's a trust and legal surface. The blocklist and classifier run in the builder and on the overlay, and a manual kill list is applied at serve time for emergencies, taking effect in seconds.

Personalisation as a blend

Keep a small per-user list of recent searches (on the device or in a KV store) and blend it with the global results: "your recent" first, then global. That needs no per-user trie, just a merge of two short lists.

Most of the latency budget is spent outside your servers

A 1 ms trie lookup doesn't help if the phone waits 80 ms for the network and the UI renders late. Close by walking the end-to-end budget. Then show where each layer of caching removes a round trip entirely, and what you'd add next.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Typo toleranceFuzzy matching within edit distance 1 via n-gram indexes or a search engine's completion suggester; costlier, so use it only if the prefix finds nothing.
Multiple languagesA trie per language or locale, chosen by the request's locale; normalisation rules per script.
Personal resultsBlend a per-user recent list; never leak one user's queries into global suggestions below a k-anonymity threshold.
Business rulesBoost fields and pinned results applied at merge time, not baked into the trie.
Summarise"All the heavy work is offline: decayed counts, filtering, a top-k-per-node trie, and shards cut by load. The serving path is an in-memory lookup behind CDN and client caches, with a trending overlay for freshness. Rebuild failures only make suggestions a little stale, and serving failures only hide suggestions."

Design a web crawler: a billion pages a month, without hammering anyone's server

Start from seed URLs, then fetch pages, extract links and repeat, feeding a search index or an archive. Raw throughput is the easy part. The hard parts are politeness (never overload a host), deduplication (most links point to pages you've already seen) and robustness against a web that is malformed, slow and sometimes adversarial.

Functional

  • From seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, and crawl the new ones.
  • Store raw content for downstream consumers (indexer, archive).
  • Recrawl pages so changes show up; faster for pages that change often.

Non-functional

  • Polite: obey robots.txt; at most one connection and about one request per few seconds per host.
  • Robust: survive bad HTML, slow servers, redirect loops and crawler traps.
  • Scalable and extensible: add nodes and new content types (PDF, images) without a redesign.

Clarify

  • Purpose: search index, archive or data set? It sets priority and freshness.
  • HTML only, or render JavaScript too? Rendering costs 10–100× more per page.
  • Whole web or a list of domains? Keep old versions or only the latest?

No public API: the contracts are internal, and the URL table is the crawler's memory

A crawler is a pipeline, so its "API" is a set of stage contracts: enqueue, next, fetch, store, emit. The data model is small but huge in volume. It holds per-URL state (when you last fetched it, whether it changed, when to come back), per-host state (robots.txt, crawl delay, errors), the raw pages, and the link graph that drives priority.

stage contracts
frontier.add(url, priority, found_on)    # only after the seen-check
frontier.next(worker) -> url             # blocks until a host is ready
fetch(url, etag, last_modified)
    -> 200 body | 304 unchanged | 3xx | 4xx | 5xx | timeout
store.append(warc_record) -> (warc_file, offset)
emit("pages.fetched", {url_hash, warc_file, offset, sha256})
robots.txt (fetched per host, cached ~24 h)
User-agent: *
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /search?
Crawl-delay: 5
Sitemap: https://ex.com/sitemap.xml

Normalise before you hash

Lowercase the scheme and host, drop default ports and #fragments, resolve ../, sort query parameters and strip tracking ones (utm_*, session ids). Without this, one page has dozens of "different" URLs and you crawl it dozens of times.

Two different "seen" questions

URL seen? is checked before fetching and saves bandwidth. Content seen? is checked after fetching, because mirrors and syndicated copies have different URLs but the same body. It saves parsing, storage and index pollution.

Store pages as WARC

Append many fetched responses (headers and body) into large WARC files, around 1 GB each, in object storage. Small objects per page would mean billions of tiny writes. The URL table keeps a pointer (file and offset) to each record.

A loop: frontier, fetch, parse, dedupe, filter, and back to the frontier

Every crawler is the same cycle. Take the next URL the frontier allows, fetch it, parse out text and links, drop duplicate content, filter and normalise the links, keep only URLs never seen before, and feed those back in. Everything else, such as indexing, archiving and analytics, hangs off a stream of fetched pages.

Fetchers are I/O-bound

Most time is spent waiting on remote servers, so use asynchronous I/O with thousands of concurrent connections per node rather than a thread per request. Set strict limits: 10 s timeouts, a 10 MB maximum body, at most 5 redirects, and accepted content types only.

DNS becomes a bottleneck

Resolving each host through a public resolver adds 10–100 ms and can get you rate-limited. Run a local caching resolver per node and cache host → IP in host_state, respecting TTLs. Politeness is often enforced per IP too, since one server can host thousands of domains.

Downstream is decoupled

The crawler's output is a durable stream of pages. The indexer, a link-graph job that feeds priorities back, and an archive can each consume it independently, and a slow indexer never slows the crawl.

Deep dive 1: front queues decide what matters, back queues decide when a host may be hit

A plain FIFO queue fails twice. It crawls unimportant pages as eagerly as important ones, and because pages link mostly within their own site, it fires bursts of requests at a single host. The classic fix, from the Mercator crawler, splits the frontier into two layers: priority in front and politeness behind.

Priority

Score each URL by link-based importance (PageRank from the link graph), domain quality, depth from a seed, and for recrawls how likely the page is to have changed. A biased selector pulls from F1 most often but never starves F3, so low-priority URLs still get crawled eventually.

Politeness

One back queue per host plus a ready-time heap enforces a gap between hits. The adaptive gap, ten times the last response time, backs off automatically when a server slows down. A robots.txt Crawl-delay overrides it when larger, and 429 or 503 responses double the gap.

It doesn't fit in memory

Billions of queued URLs live on disk: append-only files or a KV store per queue, with only the heads buffered in RAM. Reads and writes are sequential at each end, so disk is fast enough. The frontier is also checkpointed so a node can restart without losing its place.

Deep dive 2: don't fetch it twice, don't store it twice, don't fall into a hole

Most discovered links are duplicates, and a large share of fetched pages are copies of other pages. A few sites generate infinitely many URLs, some deliberately. Three cheap structures handle it: a Bloom filter for URLs, fingerprints for content, and hard budgets for traps.

robots.txt, properly

Fetch /robots.txt before a host's first page and cache it for about 24 hours. Obey Disallow and Crawl-delay for your user agent. Under RFC 9309, a 4xx means no restrictions, but a 5xx or unreachable file means assume everything is disallowed until you can read it. Identify yourself with a user agent that includes a contact URL.

Bloom filter trade-offs

A false positive means you skip a new URL, and at 1% that's acceptable for a crawler. A false negative is impossible. Standard Bloom filters can't delete, so rebuild per crawl cycle or use a counting or cuckoo filter. Shard the filter by URL hash across nodes, the same way as url_state.

Where each check sits

The URL check comes before fetching, saves bandwidth, and runs at about 20 k lookups/s. The content check comes after fetching and saves storage and index quality. Trap rules run in the URL filter, cheaply, before a URL ever reaches the frontier.

Partition by host so politeness stays local, and recrawl each page on its own clock

To scale out, give every host to exactly one crawler node. Its frontier, politeness timers, robots cache and DNS cache then need no coordination. Then spend the fetch budget where change actually happens: a news front page changes hourly, an archived page almost never.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
JavaScript-heavy sitesA separate pool of headless browsers for pages whose HTML is an empty shell; it costs 10–100× per page, so detect first and render selectively.
Freshness vs coverageSplit the fetch budget explicitly: a share for recrawls ranked by expected change × importance, and the rest for discovery.
GeographyRun crawler nodes in several regions and assign hosts to the closest one to cut latency and cross-ocean bandwidth.
Hostile contentSize and time limits, parsing in a sandbox, and never executing downloaded code outside the render sandbox.
Summarise"A per-node crawl loop in which the frontier separates priority from per-host politeness, a Bloom filter answers 'URL seen?', fingerprints answer 'content seen?', and budgets defuse traps. Hosts are partitioned across nodes by consistent hashing, pages are appended to WARC files in object storage, and a Kafka stream feeds everything downstream."

Elsewhere in the atlasHLD · Consistent hashingHLD · Object storage

Design an online store: two systems in one, browse at scale and checkout without mistakes

Shoppers search, browse product pages, fill a cart, check out and pay. The numbers split the problem in two. Browsing is a huge, read-heavy workload that tolerates slightly stale data. Checkout is small in volume but must never oversell stock or charge a card twice. Say this early, because it justifies every later choice.

Functional

  • Search and browse the catalog; product pages with price and availability.
  • Cart that survives across devices and sessions.
  • Checkout, payment, order status and history; cancellations and refunds.

Non-functional

  • Browse p99 < 200 ms and highly available; a slightly stale stock badge is acceptable.
  • Checkout: never oversell, never double-charge. Strong consistency where money and stock change.
  • Peaks of 10–20× at sales, which are planned, so scale ahead of time.

Clarify

  • Own stock only, or a marketplace with third-party sellers?
  • Payments through a provider (Stripe, Adyen)? Yes: never store card numbers, to stay out of most PCI scope.
  • Flash sales with contested stock? One region or several?

Checkout is one idempotent POST; stock and money live in separate, strongly consistent tables

Browse endpoints are plain cacheable GETs. The single write that matters is POST /checkout. It carries an idempotency key and returns 202 with an order id, because the work behind it (reserve, pay, confirm) is a multi-step workflow. The data model makes the invariants explicit: an order line records the price paid, and a reservation is a row with an expiry.

API
GET  /v1/search?q=running+shoes&size=10&page=2
GET  /v1/products/{sku}            # catalog + price + stock badge
PUT  /v1/carts/{cartId}/items/{sku}   { "qty": 2 }

POST /v1/checkout
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c9a…
{ "cartId": "c_91", "addressId": "a_4", "paymentMethod": "pm_tok_…" }
→ 202 { "orderId": "o_5521", "status": "PENDING" }

GET  /v1/orders/o_5521   → PENDING | CONFIRMED | CANCELLED | SHIPPED
domain events (via the outbox)
OrderPlaced → StockReserved → PaymentAuthorized → OrderConfirmed
                    └→ ReservationExpired / PaymentFailed → OrderCancelled

Snapshot the price

The order line stores the unit price the customer agreed to. Prices change, and the catalog is not the record of what someone paid. Re-validate price and stock at checkout and show the customer any difference before charging.

Reservations are rows

A reservation is a row with an expiry, not just a decremented counter. That gives you an audit trail, lets a sweeper release expired holds, and lets a reconciliation job compare reserved with the sum of active reservations.

A store per service

Catalog: a document store plus a search index. Carts: a KV store (DynamoDB or Redis) with a TTL. Orders, inventory and payments: PostgreSQL, sharded by order id and by SKU when needed. Each service owns its data and publishes events through an outbox.

A cached read path for browsing, an orchestrated write path for checkout

Draw the two halves separately. Browsing fans out from a page BFF to catalog, pricing, availability and search, each heavily cached and allowed to be seconds stale. Checkout goes through an order service that orchestrates reserve, then pay, then confirm, against transactional stores, and publishes what happened through an outbox.

Product page = a BFF fan-out

One request for the page becomes parallel calls to catalog, price, availability, reviews and recommendations, each with a tight timeout and a fallback. A missing section is hidden, not a 500. Cache the assembled, non-personal part of the page at the CDN for a short time.

Search is a projection

Catalog changes flow through CDC or events into OpenSearch, typically within seconds. Search results can show a stale price or stock badge, which is why checkout re-reads the authoritative values before charging.

Why reserve before pay

Reserving is cheap and reversible: releasing a hold costs nothing. Charging a card is external and harder to undo. Doing the reversible step first means most failures need no refund, only a released hold.

Deep dive 1: a guarded update for everyday traffic, a gate in front of it for a flash sale

Overselling happens when two buyers read "1 left" and both decrement it. The fix is to make check-and-decrement one atomic statement and to hold stock with an expiry rather than subtracting it. That covers normal traffic. A flash sale turns one SKU row into a hotspot, so you add a cheap atomic gate in front of the database and let only the winners through.

No Redis? Split the row

Spread a hot SKU's stock across N bucket rows (for example 10 rows of 1,000). Each attempt tries a random bucket and falls back to others when it's empty. Contention drops about N-fold, and the guarded update is still the thing preventing oversell.

Idempotent, one per customer

Put a unique constraint on (customer_id, sale_id) and an idempotency key on the purchase request, so double clicks, retries and scripts can't take two units. Add per-account and per-device limits at the edge for bots.

Holds must expire

A sweeper, or a delayed message per hold, releases expired reservations. It decrements reserved, marks the row released and returns the token to the gate, all idempotently. Without expiry, abandoned carts quietly make stock "sell out" while nothing is sold.

Deep dive 2: checkout is a saga, with reversible steps first and an idempotency key on every hop

Stock, orders and payments live in different services, and one of them is an external provider, so there is no single transaction to wrap it all in. The order service runs a persisted state machine. It reserves, authorises and confirms, and each step has a compensation if a later one fails. Retries are safe because every call carries a key the receiver deduplicates on.

Orchestrate this one

Checkout has a strict order, compensations and a customer waiting on the result, which suits an explicit orchestrator (the order service, or a workflow engine such as Temporal). Persist the saga state after every step so a crashed instance resumes where it stopped instead of starting over.

Authorise, then capture

At checkout, only authorise: the funds are held, not taken. Capture when the order ships. Cancelling before shipment then means voiding an authorisation rather than refunding a charge, which is cheaper, instant, and has no fees.

Trust, but reconcile

Providers also report outcomes by webhook, and webhooks can arrive late, twice or out of order. Handle them idempotently by provider reference. A daily job compares your payments table with the provider's settlement report and flags any mismatch.

Spend consistency only where money and stock change, and scale for the sale before it starts

The big trade-off is a spectrum, not a switch. Along the shopper's journey, staleness is fine at first (search, product pages) and unacceptable at the end (reserve, pay). The operational trade-off is timing: sales are planned, so capacity should be too. An autoscaler that reacts at 12:00:30 is too late.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Several warehousesAllocate at reserve time: the nearest warehouse with stock, or split the shipment; availability is the sum across nodes.
Price changed after add-to-cartRe-price at checkout, show the difference, and snapshot the agreed price on the order line.
FraudA risk score before authorisation; step-up (3-D Secure) or manual review for risky orders.
Multi-regionCatalog and search replicated everywhere; each SKU's stock has one home region that owns its writes.
Summarise"Browsing is a cached fan-out, allowed to be seconds stale. Checkout is an orchestrated saga: reserve with a guarded update and a TTL, authorise with an idempotency key, then confirm, and publish through an outbox. Flash sales add a waiting room and an atomic gate so that only winners reach the database."

Design video on demand: a batch pipeline to prepare every upload, and a CDN to deliver it

Creators upload videos, and viewers watch them on any device and network, starting quickly and without stalling. The estimate settles the architecture in two lines. Processing uploads is heavy but can take minutes, so it is an asynchronous pipeline. Viewing produces tens of terabits per second of egress, which only a CDN can deliver.

Functional

  • Upload large videos, resumable over flaky networks.
  • Process into streamable renditions, thumbnails and captions.
  • Stream on web, mobile and TV at a quality that suits the network.

Non-functional

  • Never lose an original: it is the only irreplaceable byte.
  • Playback highly available and fast to start; processing may take minutes.
  • Cost-aware: storage and egress dominate the bill, not compute.

Clarify

  • Video on demand only, or live too? VOD first; live is a follow-up.
  • DRM needed (studio content), or only signed URLs?
  • Global audience? Limits on upload size and duration?

Upload in resumable chunks; play back as plain files that any CDN can cache

The upload API hands out a signed, resumable upload URL, so large files go straight to object storage in chunks and a failed chunk is retried on its own. Playback isn't an API call per frame. The video becomes a manifest listing renditions, and each rendition is a list of short segments. Both are ordinary HTTP files, which is exactly what a CDN is good at.

API
POST /v1/uploads   { "filename": "trip.mov", "size": 2147483648 }
→ 201 { "videoId": "v_8Kq", "chunkSize": 8388608,
        "uploadUrl": "https://upload…/v_8Kq?sig=…" }

PUT  {uploadUrl}   Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/2147483648
                   # resumable: retry only the failed chunk
POST /v1/videos/v_8Kq/complete   → 202 { "status": "PROCESSING" }

GET  /v1/videos/v_8Kq
→ { "status": "READY", "duration": 312,
    "manifest": "https://cdn…/v_8Kq/master.m3u8?token=…" }

Upload straight to storage

API servers never proxy gigabytes. They issue a signed resumable URL (S3 multipart, GCS resumable) and the client uploads directly in 8 MB chunks. The complete call, or the storage event, triggers processing. Keep the original forever, in a colder storage tier.

HLS and DASH, one set of segments

HLS (Apple) and DASH (everyone else) differ mainly in the manifest. With CMAF-packaged fMP4 segments, both manifests point at the same segment files, halving storage and CDN cache footprint compared with packaging each format separately.

Metadata is small

Videos and renditions are ordinary rows: tens of millions of videos, a few KB each, in a sharded SQL or wide-column store, heavily cached. View counts are events aggregated asynchronously, never a row update per view.

Uploads flow through an event-driven transcoding pipeline; playback never touches it

Upload and playback share only two things: object storage and the metadata store. The upload side is asynchronous. A stored original emits an event, an orchestrator runs a transcoding DAG on a worker fleet, and the video flips to READY when renditions exist. The playback side is a thin API that hands out a signed manifest URL, and the CDN does the rest.

An event starts the pipeline

The storage "object created" event, or the complete call, publishes video.uploaded. The orchestrator builds a DAG for that video, fans tasks out to a queue and tracks them. Every task is idempotent, keyed by (video, chunk, profile), so a retry overwrites instead of duplicating.

Signed, short-lived URLs

The playback API authorises the viewer (region rights, age, subscription) and returns a manifest URL with a token valid for a few hours. The CDN checks the token at the edge, so authorisation stays centralised while bytes stay local. Studio content adds DRM on top.

An origin shield protects storage

Hundreds of edge locations missing on the same new segment would each hit origin. A regional shield layer collapses those into one fetch and caches it. Origin load becomes the number of regions, not the number of edges.

Deep dive 1: split the video into chunks, then encode chunks × renditions in parallel

Encoding one long file serially on one machine takes about as long as the video itself for every rendition, and a crash means starting over. Instead, split the original at keyframes into short chunks. Each chunk × rendition pair is then an independent, retryable task, and the whole thing finishes in minutes on a large pool of cheap workers.

Why chunking works

Each chunk starts on a keyframe, so it can be encoded without its neighbours. Parallelism turns wall-clock time from "length × renditions" into roughly "one chunk". A failed task retries only its 10 seconds of video, and slow stragglers can be speculatively re-run on another worker.

Per-title bitrate ladders

A cartoon needs far fewer bits than a football match at the same quality. Analyse complexity first and pick each video's ladder (resolutions and bitrates) to match. Encode popular videos in efficient codecs such as AV1 or HEVC later, when viewing numbers justify the extra compute.

Cheap, preemptible compute

Transcoding is batch work that can be retried, which is ideal for spot or preemptible instances at a fraction of the price. Use priority queues so a partner's premiere is processed before a backlog of long-tail uploads, and autoscale the fleet on queue depth.

Deep dive 2: the player adapts every few seconds, and the CDN keeps the popular head close

Smooth playback comes from two cooperating pieces. On the client, an ABR algorithm chooses the rendition for each next segment from measured throughput and how much video is buffered. In the network, a tiered CDN serves the few popular videos, which get most of the views, from caches near the viewer, and fetches the long tail on demand.

ABR algorithms

Throughput-based algorithms pick the highest bitrate below the recent measured throughput, with a safety margin. Buffer-based ones (BOLA) pick from buffer occupancy, which is more stable. Production players blend both and add switch penalties so quality doesn't oscillate every segment.

Start fast

Time to first frame is what users notice. Fetch the manifest while the title card shows, start at a low rendition with short first segments, preconnect to the CDN host, and serve the first seconds of popular videos from the edge.

Multi-CDN

At tens of Tbps, one CDN is both a single point of failure and a weak negotiating position. Steer each session to a CDN by measured performance and cost, and fail over mid-stream. Segments are plain files, so any CDN can serve them.

The bill is storage and egress, so trade compute for bytes where views pay it back

Most of the trade-offs here are about money. Keep every rendition of every video hot and storage grows without bound. Encode everything in the most efficient codec and compute costs explode. The answer for both is to let popularity decide: tier storage by age and views, and spend expensive encoding only on videos that will be watched enough to earn it back in egress savings.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Live streamingIngest over RTMP or SRT, transcode in real time, and publish short CMAF parts (LL-HLS) for 2–5 s latency. Manifests refresh continuously and the CDN caches very briefly.
DRM and piracyEncrypt segments once (CENC) and license through Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady; use forensic watermarks for leaks.
View countsPlayer events go to a stream processor that dedupes and filters bots; counts are approximate in real time and exact in a daily batch.
Resume where I left offA per-user KV of (video → position), written every ~10 s and read at play time.
Summarise"Resumable uploads go straight to object storage. An event-driven DAG splits each video into chunks and encodes chunks × renditions in parallel on spot capacity, then packages CMAF with HLS and DASH manifests. Playback is signed manifests plus ABR over a tiered, multi-CDN edge. Storage is tiered by age, and costly codecs are used only where views repay them."

Design ride-hailing: a firehose of moving points, and a trip record that must never double-book

Riders request a trip, the system finds a nearby driver, both follow the trip live on a map, and the rider pays at the end. Two very different workloads hide in that sentence. Driver locations are a huge, ephemeral write stream where only the latest point matters. The trip itself is low-volume state that must be strongly consistent: one driver per trip, one trip per driver.

Functional

  • Riders see nearby cars and an ETA, then request a ride.
  • Match to a driver, who accepts or declines within seconds.
  • Live tracking during pickup and trip; fare and payment at the end.

Non-functional

  • Match within a few seconds; locations at most a few seconds stale.
  • Never assign one driver to two trips, or one trip to two drivers.
  • Highly available per city: an outage in one city mustn't spread.

Clarify

  • Ride types (standard, XL)? Shared rides (pooling) are a follow-up.
  • Surge pricing in scope? Payments through a provider?
  • How many cities and regions? Is data residency required?

Locations stream in over a persistent connection; trips are guarded rows

Drivers push a location every few seconds, so use a long-lived connection (WebSocket or MQTT) rather than a new HTTPS request each time. Riders create a trip with one idempotent POST and then receive updates by push. The data splits along the ephemeral/durable line: locations are latest-value-wins data with a TTL, and trips are transactional rows with a status and a version.

API
# driver app: one persistent connection, a message every ~4 s
WS  /v1/driver/stream   → { "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194,
                            "heading": 90, "seq": 1841, "ts": … }
                        ← { "type": "offer", "offerId": "of_3", "ttl": 10 }

POST /v1/rides   Idempotency-Key: 5d1e…
{ "pickup": {…}, "dropoff": {…}, "product": "standard" }
→ 202 { "rideId": "r_77", "status": "MATCHING" }

POST /v1/offers/of_3/accept         # driver, within 10 s
GET  /v1/rides/r_77  → status, driver, car, ETA   (+ push updates)

Sequence numbers, not trust

Mobile networks deliver updates late and out of order. Each update carries a per-driver seq, and the server drops anything older than the last one applied. Clients buffer points while offline and send them in a batch for the route history, but only the newest point updates the live index.

Update less often, when you can

Four seconds is for moving drivers. A parked, available driver can report every 15–30 s, and the app can skip updates that moved less than about 20 m. That cuts the write rate a lot during quiet periods at no cost in matching quality.

Offers expire

An offer is a short-lived record (Redis, TTL 10 s) linking a trip and a driver. The driver's accept is valid only while it exists and only if the trip is still MATCHING, which the database checks, not the app.

A location pipeline and a ride pipeline that meet only at the geo index

Drivers hold persistent connections to a gateway fleet. Their locations update an in-memory geo index and flow on to a stream for everything else: ETAs, surge, trip tracking and history. Ride requests go through a matching service that queries the index, ranks candidates by ETA and pushes an offer down the driver's open connection. The trip service records the outcome with a guarded write.

The gateway fleet is stateful

Millions of long-lived sockets need a connection registry (driver → gateway node) so matching can push an offer to the right node. It's the same pattern as chat presence. When a gateway node dies, its drivers reconnect elsewhere and re-register within seconds.

Why the stream matters

One point feeds many consumers: the rider's live map during the trip, ETA models, surge computation per cell, fraud checks for teleporting phones, and the fare's distance. A topic keyed by driver id lets each consume independently and keeps per-driver order.

Rider updates by push

While matching and during the trip, the rider's app receives status changes and the driver's position (every few seconds) over its own socket or push channel. Don't poll GET /rides, which multiplies reads for no benefit.

Deep dive 1: turn "drivers near this point" into "drivers in these few cells"

A database scan over latitude and longitude doesn't scale to a million moving points. Instead, divide the map into cells, keep a set of driver ids per cell, and answer "nearby" by reading the rider's cell and its neighbours. The three common cell schemes trade simplicity, adaptiveness and uniform distances.

Redis GEO, or your own index

GEOADD and GEOSEARCH store points in a sorted set scored by a 52-bit geohash. That's simple and fast per city. At larger scale, matching services keep an in-process map of cell → drivers for their shard of cells, fed directly from the location stream.

250 k writes/s is mostly overwrites

A driver changes cell only every few updates. Update the position in place, and move the id between cell sets only when the cell changes. Shard by city, then by cell range within big cities, so no single node sees more than tens of thousands of writes a second.

"Cars near me" is a cache

Riders browsing the map don't need an exact live query. Publish a per-cell snapshot every 2–5 s, including jittered positions for driver privacy, and serve it from a cache. A million reads a second become cheap cache hits.

Deep dive 2: rank by road ETA, offer one driver at a time, and let a guarded write settle races

The closest driver in a straight line is often not the fastest to arrive, because of rivers, one-way streets and highways. Matching ranks candidates by ETA from a routing engine, then offers the trip to the best one under a short lock. The trip itself is a state machine whose transitions are conditional updates, so two drivers accepting at the same instant can never both win.

One offer at a time, or a few?

Offering to one driver at a time is fair and simple but adds up to 10 s per decline. Offering to the top 2–3 at once is faster, but all but one of them see "taken", which frustrates drivers. Many systems offer sequentially with short timeouts, and widen when demand is high.

Batch matching

Greedy matching (each request takes its best driver immediately) is locally optimal but globally poor. Collecting requests for 1–2 s and solving an assignment over the batch, minimising total ETA, noticeably cuts average pickup time in busy areas.

Idempotent everything

Ride creation uses an idempotency key, so a double tap makes one ride. Accepts are keyed by offer id, so a retried accept is a no-op. Driver status (free or on trip) is derived from the trip row, not maintained as a separate flag that can drift.

Cities are natural cells, and surge pricing is a control loop you must damp

Almost every ride starts and ends in one metro area. That makes the city the natural unit of sharding and of failure: each city (or cluster of small cities) runs its own location, matching and trip stack, and only accounts, payments and analytics are global. The other thing interviewers probe is surge pricing, a feedback loop between price, demand and supply that oscillates if nobody damps it.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Shared ridesMatching becomes route insertion: add a rider to a moving trip only if every passenger's detour stays under a limit.
Accurate ETAsA routing engine over a road graph with live traffic (contraction hierarchies for speed), corrected by ML trained on past trips.
GPS spoofingReject impossible speeds and teleports, cross-check with network location, and use device attestation.
PaymentAuthorise an estimate at request time, capture the final fare at completion; tips are a separate later capture.
Summarise"Drivers stream locations over sockets into a per-city in-memory cell index and a Kafka stream. Matching reads nearby cells, ranks candidates by road ETA, and offers under a short lock. The trip is a state machine whose assignment is a guarded write with one active trip per driver. Cities are cells, so failures stay local, and surge is a damped loop fed by the streams."

Design Dropbox: keep every device's folder identical, without re-sending what hasn't changed

Users drop files into a folder, and the same folder appears on their other devices and on their collaborators' machines, with version history and offline edits. The estimate points at the key idea. Split files into content-addressed blocks so an edit re-sends only the changed block, and keep the small, transactional metadata completely separate from the enormous, immutable bytes.

Functional

  • Upload, download, and sync changes to all of a user's devices automatically.
  • Shared folders across users; version history and restore.
  • Work offline; sync when back online.

Non-functional

  • Never lose or corrupt data: eleven nines of durability, with every block verified by hash.
  • Every device converges to the same state; changes propagate within seconds.
  • Frugal with bandwidth, battery and server storage.

Clarify

  • Largest file size? (Tens of GB.) Mobile clients as well as desktop?
  • Real-time co-editing? No: that's a different design (OT or CRDTs).
  • How are conflicts handled: last writer wins, or keep both copies?

A file is a list of block hashes; a change is an append to a per-namespace journal

The client splits a file into blocks (about 4 MB) and hashes each one. It first asks which hashes the server lacks, uploads only those, then commits the new block list against the revision it started from. Every commit appends a row to an ordered journal for that namespace, a user's root or a shared folder. Other devices sync by reading the journal from their last cursor.

API
POST /v1/blocks/check  { "hashes": ["a1f3…", "9c0e…", "77ab…"] }
→ 200 { "missing": ["9c0e…"] }             # upload only what's new
PUT  /v1/blocks/9c0e…   <4 MB>            # content-addressed, idempotent

POST /v1/files/commit
{ "ns": "ns_42", "path": "/docs/plan.key", "parentRev": 17,
  "blocks": ["a1f3…", "9c0e…", "77ab…"], "size": 11534336 }
→ 200 { "rev": 18 }
→ 409 { "latestRev": 18 }                 # someone committed first

GET  /v1/changes?ns=ns_42&cursor=c_9912   → entries since cursor
GET  /v1/notify?cursors=…                 # long-poll: "something changed"

Content addressing

A block's name is its hash, so uploads are idempotent (the same bytes give the same name), deduplication is automatic, and every read can be verified end to end. A version is just a new block list. Unchanged blocks are shared with the previous version at no cost.

Blocks before commit

Upload blocks first, then commit metadata. A commit that references a missing block is rejected. The journal therefore never points at bytes that don't exist, even when a client crashes halfway through an upload.

Shard by namespace

All journal rows for a namespace live on one shard, so a commit is a single-shard transaction and the sequence numbers are gap-free. Very large shared team folders are the hot keys to watch, and may need a dedicated shard.

Bytes through a block service, truth through a metadata service, and a poke to everyone else

The client does much of the work: it watches the folder, chunks and hashes files, and keeps a local database of what it believes is synced. On the server, the block service stores immutable blocks in blob storage and the metadata service commits journal entries. A notification service tells other devices that a namespace changed. They then pull the changes and fetch any blocks they lack.

The client is half the system

The watcher debounces bursts of events (an editor saving through a temp file and a rename). The local state database remembers the last synced revision and hash per path. That is how the client tells "I changed this" from "the server changed this", and how it avoids re-uploading after a restart.

Notifications are cheap to hold

Hundreds of millions of devices keep one long-poll or WebSocket open to the notification service, not to the metadata service. A commit publishes to a pub/sub channel per namespace, and only the notification servers holding subscribers wake up.

Blocks and metadata scale apart

Blob storage grows with bytes and is optimised for throughput and durability. The metadata tier grows with operations and is optimised for transactional commits. Different teams can scale, tune and fail over each one independently.

Deep dive 1: pick block boundaries so that an edit changes as few blocks as possible

Delta sync works only if an edit leaves most block hashes untouched. Fixed 4 MB blocks manage that for in-place edits but fail badly on insertions, because every later boundary shifts. Content-defined chunking puts boundaries where the content itself has a certain pattern, so they move with the content and an insertion disturbs only the chunk it lands in.

Dedup, and its privacy catch

Identical blocks are stored once, with a reference count, across files and versions. Deduplicating across users saves more but leaks information: if an upload is skipped, the file already exists somewhere. Many services therefore deduplicate only within an account or namespace.

Pipeline the upload

Hash, compress and upload blocks concurrently as a stream, rather than one file at a time. Progress is recorded in the local database, so a crash or reboot resumes where it stopped. A 20 GB file commits once, after its last block is stored.

Delta on the way down, too

A downloading device first checks which of the new version's hashes it already has, from the previous version or another file, and fetches only the rest. It assembles the new file in a temporary path and renames it atomically, so a half-written file never appears.

Deep dive 2: an ordered journal and cursors for sync, parent revisions for conflicts

Metadata consistency rests on one structure: an append-only, gap-free journal per namespace. A device is always "caught up to seq N". Being told something changed only prompts it to pull from its cursor. Concurrent edits are caught with optimistic concurrency. A commit names the revision it started from, and if that's no longer the latest, the server refuses and the client keeps both copies.

Why not last-writer-wins?

LWW by timestamp silently discards someone's work, and device clocks disagree anyway. Revision numbers assigned by the server give a total order per file. parentRev detects the conflict exactly, and "keep both" guarantees nothing is lost. Text formats could be merged, but only by apps that understand them.

Moves and deletes are edits too

A rename is recorded as one journal entry (old path to new path), not a delete plus an add, so clients move the local file instead of re-downloading it. A delete keeps the old blocks for the retention window, which is what makes restore possible.

Garbage-collect carefully

When no version references a block any more, its refcount reaches zero, but don't delete it immediately: an in-flight commit may be about to reference it. Mark-and-sweep with a grace period (days) is the safe pattern. An accidental block deletion means permanent data loss.

Pay for durability with erasure codes, and treat big shared folders as hot keys

At exabyte scale, storage overhead dominates the budget: three full replicas cost more than twice the raw disk of an erasure-coded layout with better fault tolerance. On the metadata side, the sharp edge is fan-out. One busy team folder with tens of thousands of members turns every commit into tens of thousands of pokes, unless notifications are coalesced.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Smart / selective syncShow placeholders for cloud-only files and fetch blocks on open; sync only the selected folders to small disks.
EncryptionAt rest per block with keys in a KMS, TLS in transit. End-to-end encryption on the client disables server-side dedup, preview and search.
Version retentionKeep journal entries and blocks for 30–180 days by plan; restore is "commit an old block list as new".
MobileNo constant background sync: upload the camera roll on Wi-Fi and charging; fetch on demand.
Summarise"Clients chunk and hash files, upload only the blocks the server lacks, and commit a block list against a parent revision. Metadata is an append-only journal per namespace in sharded SQL, and devices sync from cursors after data-free pokes. Conflicts keep both copies. Blocks are content-addressed and deduplicated, replicated while hot and erasure-coded after that."

Design a distributed key-value store: always writable, horizontally scalable, tunably consistent

This is the question that tests the whole fundamentals section at once. Build get and put over hundreds of nodes, with no single point of failure, surviving node and network failures, and letting each caller trade consistency against latency. The standard answer is the Dynamo recipe, used in Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB's ancestors: partition with consistent hashing, replicate N ways, coordinate with quorums, and repair in the background.

Functional

  • get(key), put(key, value), delete(key); optional TTL.
  • Values are opaque bytes, up to about 1 MB.
  • Consistency chosen per request (ONE, QUORUM, ALL).

Non-functional

  • No single point of failure; add or remove nodes while serving.
  • Highly available for writes, even during partitions.
  • Durable once acknowledged; self-repairing replicas.

Clarify

  • Is strong consistency ever needed, or is eventual with a quorum enough?
  • Range scans? If not, hash partitioning; if so, range partitioning.
  • One datacenter or several? LWW acceptable, or keep siblings?

Three calls, and a hidden context that makes conflicts detectable

The API is deliberately tiny. The subtle part is the context: a version (a vector clock) returned by get and passed back on put, so the store knows which version a write was based on. Placement is pure computation. Hash the key to a token, and the next N distinct nodes clockwise on the ring are its replicas. No lookup service is needed.

API
get(key, consistency=QUORUM)
    -> [(value, context), ...]      # >1 entry = concurrent siblings
put(key, value, context=None, consistency=QUORUM, ttl=None)
    -> context'                     # context from a prior get
delete(key, context)                # writes a tombstone, not a hole

# per request: ONE | QUORUM | ALL   (N fixed per keyspace, e.g. 3)
placement
token = murmur3(key)                # 64-bit position on the ring
replicas = walk_clockwise(token, n=3, distinct_racks=True)

Virtual nodes

Each physical node owns many small token ranges (vnodes, e.g. 16–256) scattered around the ring rather than one big arc. Load evens out, a joining node takes small slices from everyone, and a failed node's load spreads across the cluster instead of landing on one neighbour.

Rack- and zone-aware replicas

Walking clockwise, skip nodes in a rack or zone that already holds a replica. Three replicas in three availability zones means a whole zone can go down and every key still has two live copies, enough for QUORUM.

Deletes are writes

A delete writes a tombstone that replicates like any value. If replicas simply dropped the key, a replica that missed the delete would "resurrect" it during repair. Tombstones are purged after a grace period (for example 10 days) longer than any repair cycle.

A ring of identical nodes: any one coordinates, N replicate, W or R must answer

There is no master. A client, or a partition-aware driver, sends a request to any node, and that node coordinates. It computes the key's replicas from the ring, forwards the request to all N, and replies as soon as W acknowledge a write or R answer a read. Every node runs the same stack, so the cluster grows by adding identical machines.

Membership by gossip

Every second, each node exchanges its view of the cluster (who's up, which tokens they own, their heartbeat counters) with a few random peers. Changes reach all nodes in O(log n) rounds, with no central registry to fail. Seed nodes only help new nodes join.

Failure detection is a suspicion level

Instead of a fixed timeout, a phi-accrual detector turns the heartbeat inter-arrival history into a suspicion level. That adapts to slow networks. A suspected node is routed around, and no data moves until an operator or a policy decides it is permanently gone.

Adding a node

A new node takes vnode ranges from existing owners and streams those ranges in the background while the old owners keep serving. Only about 1/n of the data moves (n nodes), which is the whole point of consistent hashing compared with hash mod N.

Deep dive 1: overlapping quorums, writes that survive a down replica, and versions that expose conflicts

Three mechanisms define how the store behaves under failure. Quorum overlap (W + R > N) makes a read see the latest acknowledged write. A sloppy quorum with hinted handoff keeps writes available when a replica is down. Vector clocks tell "newer" apart from "concurrent", so the store never silently throws away one side of a conflict.

Quorums aren't linearizability

Even with W + R > N, edge cases remain: sloppy quorums, a write that failed after reaching one replica, and clock-based LWW. Don't promise strong consistency from quorums alone. If you truly need it for a key (a lock or a counter), use consensus (Raft or Paxos) or a lightweight transaction.

Read repair

When the replicas queried for a read disagree, the coordinator returns the newest version and writes it back to the stale replicas, synchronously or asynchronously. Frequently read keys stay consistent without any background job. Rarely read keys need anti-entropy.

LWW or siblings?

Cassandra chose last-writer-wins with timestamps: simple, but concurrent writes lose data and clock skew decides the winner. Dynamo and Riak chose vector clocks and siblings: nothing is lost, but clients must merge. CRDTs (counters, sets) merge automatically where the data type allows it.

Deep dive 2: an LSM tree makes writes sequential, and Merkle trees find divergence cheaply

Inside each node, a log-structured merge tree turns random writes into sequential appends. A write goes to a commit log and a sorted in-memory table, which is flushed to immutable sorted files and compacted in the background. Between nodes, replicas drift apart (missed hints, dropped messages), and Merkle trees let two replicas locate the few key ranges that differ without comparing every key.

Durable before acknowledged

A replica acknowledges only after the commit-log append, and the memtable is rebuilt from that log after a crash. Group commit (fsync every few milliseconds for a batch of writes) keeps throughput high. The coordinator's W then counts durable copies, not just copies in RAM.

Three kinds of repair

Hinted handoff fixes short outages. Read repair fixes keys that are read. Anti-entropy with Merkle trees catches everything else, including long outages and bit rot. Each covers what the others miss, and together they make eventual consistency actually converge.

Compaction is the hidden workload

Merging SSTables rewrites data many times (write amplification), competing with foreground traffic for disk bandwidth. Rate-limit compaction, leave 30–50% of the disk free for it, and watch pending compactions: a growing backlog shows up next as slow reads.

Every knob trades one thing for another: consistency levels per request, compaction per table

The strength of this design is that it exposes its trade-offs as settings. Callers choose how many replicas to wait for, so they trade latency and availability against staleness on each request. Operators choose a compaction strategy per table, trading write amplification against read and space amplification. Close the interview by walking both dials.

Follow-upAnswer sketch
Hot keyCache it at the client or coordinator, spread reads across all replicas, or split the key (key#0..7) and merge on read.
Large valuesStore the blob in object storage and keep a pointer; large values stall compaction and repair streams.
Range queriesHash partitioning can't do them. Use range partitioning (with hot-range splitting) or a separately maintained index table.
Compare-and-setA per-partition consensus round (Paxos lightweight transactions), much slower, so use it only where it's needed.
Summarise"A leaderless ring. Consistent hashing with vnodes places keys on N zone-aware replicas, and any node coordinates with tunable W and R. Hinted handoff keeps writes available, vector clocks or LWW settle conflicts, and read repair plus Merkle anti-entropy converge replicas. Each node is an LSM engine with a commit log. It is AP by default, and QUORUM on both sides gives read-your-latest-ack."
