LC 167 · Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted · clean
class Solution {
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        int sum(int[] a) { return a[l] + a[r]; }
    }

    public int[] twoSum(int[] numbers, int target) {
        // A two-pointer loop is a state machine on (l, r).
        // Stream.iterate runs it; findFirst stops at the hit.
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(0, numbers.length - 1),
                        p -> p.sum(numbers) < target
                                ? new Pair(p.l() + 1, p.r())
                                : new Pair(p.l(), p.r() - 1))
                .filter(p -> p.sum(numbers) == target)
                .findFirst()
                .map(p -> new int[]{ p.l() + 1, p.r() + 1 })
                .orElseThrow();
    }
}
LC 15 · 3Sum · clean
class Solution {
    // (l, r) closes in on a[l] + a[r] == want; a hit moves both
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        Pair next(int[] a, int want) {
            int s = a[l] + a[r];
            return new Pair(s <= want ? l + 1 : l,
                            s >= want ? r - 1 : r);
        }
    }

    public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        // Fix the first value; keep every hit of the (l, r)
        // scan. distinct() replaces the duplicate-skip loops.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length - 2).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> triplets(nums, i))
                .distinct()
                .toList();
    }

    static Stream<List<Integer>> triplets(int[] a, int i) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(i + 1, a.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> p.next(a, -a[i]))
                .filter(p -> a[p.l()] + a[p.r()] == -a[i])
                .map(p -> List.of(a[i], a[p.l()], a[p.r()]));
    }
}
LC 16 · 3Sum Closest · clean
class Solution {
    // One inner scan: first index i, then l and r closing in
    record Scan(int i, int l, int r) {
        int sum(int[] a) { return a[i] + a[l] + a[r]; }
        Scan next(int[] a, int target) {
            return sum(a) < target ? new Scan(i, l + 1, r)
                                   : new Scan(i, l, r - 1);
        }
    }

    public int threeSumClosest(int[] nums, int target) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        Comparator<Integer> byGap = Comparator.comparingInt(
                x -> Math.abs(x - target));
        // Every sum any scan visits; the answer is the nearest.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length - 2).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> scan(nums, i, target))
                .map(s -> s.sum(nums))
                .min(byGap)
                .orElseThrow();
    }

    static Stream<Scan> scan(int[] a, int i, int target) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Scan(i, i + 1, a.length - 1),
                s -> s.l() < s.r(), s -> s.next(a, target));
    }
}
LC 18 · 4Sum · clean
class Solution {
    // (l, r) closes in on a[l] + a[r] == want; a hit moves both
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        Pair next(int[] a, long want) {
            long s = (long) a[l] + a[r];
            return new Pair(s <= want ? l + 1 : l,
                            s >= want ? r - 1 : r);
        }
    }

    public List<List<Integer>> fourSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int n = nums.length;
        // Two flatMaps fix a pair of values; the (l, r) scan
        // finds the rest. Sums are long: 4 × 10⁹ overflows int.
        return IntStream.range(0, n).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> IntStream.range(i + 1, n).boxed()
                        .flatMap(j -> rest(nums, i, j, target)))
                .distinct()
                .toList();
    }

    // every a[i], a[j], a[l], a[r] summing to target, j < l < r
    static Stream<List<Integer>> rest(int[] a, int i, int j,
                                      long target) {
        long want = target - a[i] - a[j];
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(j + 1, a.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> p.next(a, want))
                .filter(p -> (long) a[p.l()] + a[p.r()] == want)
                .map(p -> List.of(a[i], a[j],
                                  a[p.l()], a[p.r()]));
    }
}
LC 11 · Container With Most Water · clean
class Solution {
    record Pair(int l, int r) {}

    public int maxArea(int[] height) {
        // Start at both ends. The shorter wall moves in: no
        // container still using it can be any better. Every
        // state is a candidate, so score each and keep the max.
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(0, height.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> height[p.l()] < height[p.r()]
                                ? new Pair(p.l() + 1, p.r())
                                : new Pair(p.l(), p.r() - 1))
                .mapToInt(p -> (p.r() - p.l()) * Math.min(
                        height[p.l()], height[p.r()]))
                .max().getAsInt();
    }
}
LC 42 · Trapping Rain Water · clean
class Solution {
    // l, r close in; level = the water line reached so far
    record State(int l, int r, int level) {
        int lower(int[] h) { return Math.min(h[l], h[r]); }

        // water above the bar this state is about to settle
        int water(int[] h) {
            return Math.max(level, lower(h)) - lower(h);
        }

        State next(int[] h) {
            int lv = Math.max(level, lower(h));
            return h[l] < h[r] ? new State(l + 1, r, lv)
                               : new State(l, r - 1, lv);
        }
    }

    public int trap(int[] height) {
        // Each state settles the lower of its two end bars. The
        // water line only rises, so it is one running maximum.
        int n = height.length;
        return Stream.iterate(new State(0, n - 1, 0),
                              s -> s.l() <= s.r(),
                              s -> s.next(height))
                .mapToInt(s -> s.water(height))
                .sum();
    }
}
The idiom worth keepingStream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) is the pure way to run any loop whose state fits in a record. Put the step on the record as a method, as every solution here does, and the pipeline reads like the loop's specification: the states, which ones to keep, what to compute from them. The same shape runs binary search, fast and slow pointers, and rolling DP later in this deck.
The one trapThe three-argument iterate calls next once more on the last state it emits, and only then does hasNext reject the result. That is harmless here, because next reads a[l] and a[r] of a state that already passed the test. When a step reads one index past its state, as a fold over an array does, use Stream.iterate(seed, f).skip(n).findFirst() instead: it applies f exactly n times.

You cannot go back, so send a scout ahead

A linked list gives you no indices, no length and no way to step backwards. Two pointers moving at different speeds, or the same speed with a fixed gap, recover all three — in one pass and O(1) space.

The invariant — two speeds

Move slow one node and fast two per step. Two consequences follow, and both are used constantly:

  • When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle — the length was never needed.
  • If there is a cycle, fast must eventually lap slow. Inside the cycle the gap closes by exactly one node per step, so they cannot jump past each other: a meeting is guaranteed.

That "closes by exactly one" is the whole reason the algorithm terminates, and it is what interviewers ask you to justify.

The invariant — fixed gap

Move fast ahead by n nodes first, then advance both at the same speed. The gap is preserved, so when fast hits the end, slow sits exactly n from the end.

This is how "nth node from the end" becomes one pass instead of two: you never learn the length, you just carry the offset.

Both forms are O(n) time and O(1) space, which is almost always the stated constraint. If a problem says "using only constant extra space" about a list, it is naming this pattern.

Applies when

Singly linked lists, and any structure where "next" is a function you can only follow forwards — including an array read as i → nums[i], which turns index-chasing into exactly this cycle problem.

Does not apply when

You need to move backwards, or need the k-th node from the start (that is a plain loop). If the list is doubly linked, the problem is usually easier and this pattern is overkill.

Complexity

O(n) time — phase 1 is at most L + C steps, phase 2 exactly L. O(1) space, which is the constraint these problems exist to enforce. A HashSet of visited nodes also solves 141/142 in O(n) space; say so, then give this.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"determine if the linked list has a cycle" · "return the node where the cycle begins" · "the middle node" · "the n-th node from the end" · "in one pass" · "using O(1) memory" · "the lists intersect". The pairing of linked list with O(1) space or one pass is effectively the problem naming this pattern for you.

LC 142 traced on 3 → 2 → 0 → −4 → (back to 2)

Four nodes; the tail links back to index 1, so the cycle is 2 → 0 → −4 → and the entrance is the node holding 2. Here L = 1 and C = 3. Watch phase 1 meet at −4 — not at the entrance — and phase 2 convert that into the answer in a single step.

PhaseStepslowfastWhat just happened
10A (3)A (3)Both start at the head. The loop tests after moving, so this does not count as a meeting.
11B (2)C (0)slow enters the cycle; fast is one node ahead of it around the loop.
12C (0)B (2)fast wraps D → B. The gap measured along the cycle is now 2.
13D (−4)D (−4)Gap closes by one per step, so it hits zero exactly. Meeting point M = D.
21B (2)B (2)One pointer restarts at the head. After L = 1 step both stand on the entrance. Return node B.
Why they cannot step over each otherOnce both pointers are inside the cycle, fast gains exactly one node on slow per step, so the gap runs … 3, 2, 1, 0 and must land on zero — it can never skip from 1 to −1. This is why the speeds must be 1 and 2. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap falls by two, and on an even-length cycle with an odd starting gap the two pointers can pass each other forever without meeting.

Four skeletons, and a dummy node that prevents half the bugs

Two speeds for cycles and midpoints, a fixed gap for offsets from the end, and a head-swap trick for aligning two lists. The dummy node in skeleton B is not a style choice — it is what makes deleting the head require no special case.

Skeleton A · two speeds — cycle and midpoint (LC 141, 142, 876)
// The guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` covers BOTH
// the odd and even length cases. Getting it wrong is the
// number one NullPointerException in this whole family.
ListNode middle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    return slow;        // even length: the SECOND of the two middles
}

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;   // compare AFTER moving
    }
    return false;                        // fast fell off: no cycle
}
Skeleton B · fixed gap from the end (LC 19)
// `dummy` sits one before the head, so deleting the head
// needs no special case: slow simply stops on the dummy.
ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode fast = dummy, slow = dummy;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) fast = fast.next;   // open the gap

    while (fast.next != null) {                     // preserve it to the end
        fast = fast.next;
        slow = slow.next;
    }

    slow.next = slow.next.next;   // slow is the node BEFORE the target
    return dummy.next;            // not `head` — it may have been deleted
}
Skeleton C · aligning two lists by swapping heads (LC 160)
// Each pointer walks its own list, then the other. Both therefore
// travel exactly lenA + lenB before meeting, which cancels the
// length difference without ever measuring either length.
//
//   a: A A A A | B B B          both cover the same total,
//   b: B B B   | A A A A        so they arrive together.
//
// If the lists never intersect, both become null at the same
// moment and the loop ends with a == b == null. The null case
// is handled by the SAME code, which is why this beats the
// "measure both lengths and skip the difference" version.
ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
    ListNode a = headA, b = headB;

    while (a != b) {
        a = (a == null) ? headB : a.next;
        b = (b == null) ? headA : b.next;
    }
    return a;
}
Skeleton D · reverse in place — the other half of LC 234
// Three pointers, and the order of the four lines never changes.
// Write them in this order every time and it cannot go wrong.
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null, cur = head;

    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;   // 1 · save what is ahead
        cur.next = prev;            // 2 · flip this link
        prev = cur;                 // 3 · advance prev
        cur = next;                 // 4 · advance cur
    }
    return prev;                    // the new head
}

Which skeleton, and why

"has a cycle"
A, returning a boolean. Compare after moving, never before, or both pointers start equal and you return true immediately.
"where the cycle begins"
A for phase 1, then the reset walk for phase 2. Never return the meeting point.
"the middle"
A. Decide up front whether you want the first or second middle on an even length — starting fast at head.next gives the first.
"nth from the end"
B, with a dummy. Also the right shape for "remove the head under a condition".
Two lists
C. It handles the no-intersection case with no extra branch.
The three bugs that actually happenGuard written as fast.next != null && fast != null — the order matters; testing fast.next first throws on a null fast. Comparing before moving — slow and fast both begin at the head, so a pre-move comparison reports a cycle on every list. Returning head after a deletion — if the head itself was removed, head now points at a detached node; always return dummy.next.

Six lists, four skeletons, one shared constraint

Every one of these has an easy O(n)-space solution with a HashSet or an ArrayList. Say that solution out loud first — it shows you see the trade-off — then give the O(1)-space pointer version, which is what the problem is actually testing.

Anchor 1 · LC 142 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Walk the list putting every node into a HashSet; the first node already present is the entrance. O(n) time, O(n) space, and completely correct — offer it first.
The constraint
The follow-up asks for O(1) space, which rules the set out and forces the pointer argument.
Phase 1
Two speeds guarantee a meeting somewhere inside the cycle. That point depends on L and C and is not the entrance.
Phase 2
From 2(L + k) = L + k + nC you get L = nC − k: the head-to-entrance distance equals the meeting-point-to-entrance distance. Walk both at speed one and they collide there.
LC 142 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;

            if (slow == fast) {          // PHASE 1 · a meeting exists
                ListNode p = head;

                // PHASE 2 · L = nC - k, so both walk L steps
                // and land together on the entrance.
                while (p != slow) {
                    p = p.next;
                    slow = slow.next;
                }
                return p;
            }
        }
        return null;                     // fast ran off the end: no cycle
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 234 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Copy the values into an ArrayList and check it with two pointers. O(n) time, O(n) space, three lines. Always say this first.
The constraint
O(1) space. You cannot index a list, and you cannot walk it backwards — so make a piece of it point backwards.
The decomposition
Three known sub-procedures, in order: find the middle (skeleton A), reverse from the middle (skeleton D), then walk the two halves in step. Naming the three parts before coding is what makes this tractable under pressure.
Why the odd case is free
With an odd length the middle node ends up in both halves, and comparing it against itself always succeeds. No special case is needed — which surprises most people.
The professional touch
Mention that this mutates the input, and that a production version would reverse the second half back before returning. Interviewers notice.
LC 234 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
        // 1 · middle — skeleton A
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }

        // 2 · reverse from the middle onwards — skeleton D
        ListNode prev = null;
        while (slow != null) {
            ListNode next = slow.next;
            slow.next = prev;
            prev = slow;
            slow = next;
        }

        // 3 · walk both halves. `prev` heads the reversed tail,
        //     which is the SHORTER half, so it controls the loop.
        ListNode a = head, b = prev;
        while (b != null) {
            if (a.val != b.val) return false;
            a = a.next;
            b = b.next;
        }
        return true;
    }
}

876 · Middle of the Linked List skeleton A

Path: the obvious solution counts the length, then walks half of it — two passes. The two-speed loop does it in one without ever knowing the length.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim, returning slow. The problem asks for the second middle on even lengths, which is exactly what fast = head gives; starting fast = head.next would give the first.

Watch for: this is the sub-procedure inside 234, and inside any routine that has to split a list in half. Make it automatic.

141 · Linked List Cycle skeleton A

Path: a HashSet of visited nodes is the natural first answer, O(n) space. The follow-up forces O(1).

Delta: skeleton A with an identity comparison after each move. Compare with == on references, not .val — two distinct nodes can hold the same value.

Watch for: the loop guard must test fast before fast.next. Reversing those two terms throws on any list of even length with no cycle.

19 · Remove Nth Node From End skeleton B

Path: the two-pass version measures the length, then walks len − n nodes. Perfectly correct; the follow-up asks for one pass, which is the fixed-gap idea.

Delta: gap, not speed. Advance fast by n, then move both until fast.next == null, leaving slow on the node before the target.

Watch for: without the dummy, removing the head needs its own branch. With it, the code is uniform — and you must return dummy.next, not head.

160 · Intersection of Two Linked Lists skeleton C

Path: the explicit version measures both lengths, advances the longer list by the difference, then walks in step. Correct, and worth describing — the head-swap is just that idea written in four lines.

Delta: when a pointer runs off its list, send it to the other head. Both then cover lenA + lenB and arrive together.

Watch for: the no-intersection case terminates because both hit null on the same step and null == null ends the loop. Do not add a guard for it — the guard is what breaks it.

If you only drill twoDo 142 and 234. 142 is the one piece of algebra here, and phase 2 is the half people get backwards; 234 is the composite that proves you can chain three list procedures without losing a pointer.

A list is already a stream; two pointers are one record

Stream.iterate(head, Objects::nonNull, x -> x.next) turns any list into a stream of its nodes. Two pointers moving at different speeds become a record whose step method moves both, and filter(…).findFirst() stops on the state you are after: the meeting point, the middle, or the node before the one to delete. Five of the six keep the loop's O(1) space. Only the palindrome check copies the values out.

LC 876 · Middle of the Linked List · clean
class Solution {
    record Ptrs(ListNode slow, ListNode fast) {
        boolean canStep() {
            return fast != null && fast.next != null;
        }
        Ptrs step() {
            return new Ptrs(slow.next, fast.next.next);
        }
    }

    public ListNode middleNode(ListNode head) {
        // Slow moves one node, fast two. The first state where
        // fast cannot move again has slow on the middle. step()
        // only ever runs on states that failed the filter.
        return Stream.iterate(new Ptrs(head, head), Ptrs::step)
                .filter(p -> !p.canStep())
                .findFirst().get().slow();
    }
}
LC 141 · Linked List Cycle · clean
class Solution {
    record Ptrs(ListNode slow, ListNode fast) {
        boolean canStep() {
            return fast != null && fast.next != null;
        }
        Ptrs step() {
            return new Ptrs(slow.next, fast.next.next);
        }
    }

    public boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
        // Floyd: in a cycle, fast gains a node per step, so it
        // must land on slow. With no cycle, fast hits the end,
        // canStep() fails, and the stream simply stops.
        return Stream.iterate(new Ptrs(head, head),
                              Ptrs::canStep, Ptrs::step)
                .skip(1)
                .anyMatch(p -> p.slow() == p.fast());
    }
}
LC 142 · Linked List Cycle II · clean
class Solution {
    // a always moves 1 node; b moves 2 in phase 1, 1 in phase 2
    record P(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        boolean met() { return a == b; }
        boolean canRun() { return b != null && b.next != null; }
        P run() { return new P(a.next, b.next.next); }
        P walk() { return new P(a.next, b.next); }
    }

    public ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
        // Phase 1: Floyd finds a meeting point in the cycle.
        ListNode meet = Stream.iterate(new P(head, head),
                                       P::canRun, P::run)
                .skip(1)
                .filter(P::met)
                .findFirst().map(P::a).orElse(null);
        if (meet == null) return null;
        // Phase 2: from head and from the meeting point, at
        // equal speed, the pointers meet exactly at the entry.
        return Stream.iterate(new P(head, meet), P::walk)
                .filter(P::met)
                .findFirst().get().a();
    }
}
LC 19 · Remove Nth Node From End of List · clean
class Solution {
    // fast first opens a lead of n + 1, then both walk together
    record Gap(ListNode slow, ListNode fast, int lead) {
        Gap step(int n) {
            return lead <= n
                    ? new Gap(slow, fast.next, lead + 1)
                    : new Gap(slow.next, fast.next, lead);
        }
    }

    public ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
        // When fast falls off the end, slow is n + 1 behind it:
        // on the node just before the one to remove.
        Gap end = Stream.iterate(new Gap(dummy, dummy, 0),
                                 g -> g.step(n))
                .filter(g -> g.fast() == null)
                .findFirst().get();
        end.slow().next = end.slow().next.next;
        return dummy.next;
    }
}
LC 160 · Intersection of Two Linked Lists · clean
class Solution {
    record P(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        // at its list's end, each pointer jumps to the other
        P next(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
            return new P(a == null ? headB : a.next,
                         b == null ? headA : b.next);
        }
    }

    public ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA,
                                        ListNode headB) {
        // Both pointers walk m + n nodes, so they line up on
        // the shared tail, or on null together if there's none.
        return Stream.iterate(new P(headA, headB),
                              p -> p.next(headA, headB))
                .filter(p -> p.a() == p.b())
                .findFirst().get().a();
    }
}
LC 234 · Palindrome Linked List · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
        // Copy the values out, then compare mirrored pairs.
        // int[], not List<Integer>: == on boxed values past 127
        // compares references.
        int[] v = Stream.iterate(head, Objects::nonNull,
                                 x -> x.next)
                .mapToInt(x -> x.val)
                .toArray();
        return IntStream.range(0, v.length / 2)
                .allMatch(i -> v[i] == v[v.length - 1 - i]);
    }
}
Why fast.next.next never throws hereOn an infinite Stream.iterate(seed, f), filter(test).findFirst() applies f only to states that failed the test. So a step that would throw on the last state is safe, because the last state is the one the filter returns. The three-argument form applies its step once more on the last state it emits, so there (141, 142) the step must be safe on every state that passes hasNext, and canStep guarantees exactly that.
Where streams stop234's O(1)-space answer reverses the second half in place, and every problem in the linked-list pattern later in this deck is that kind of pointer surgery. A stream can walk the nodes and work out where each should go, but it must not rewire them while it walks: that is interference with its own source. It computes an order, and the rewiring happens once, afterwards.

Stop searching for a value; search for a boundary

Most people learn binary search as "find the target, return −1 if absent", then rewrite it badly for every variant. Learn it once as find the first index where a monotone predicate becomes true, and equality, insert position, first occurrence, last occurrence and rotated arrays all become the same eight lines.

The invariant — a half-open range

Maintain [l, r): left inclusive, right exclusive. Throughout the loop:

  • Every index below l is known false.
  • Every index at or above r is known true.
  • The boundary lies somewhere in [l, r).

When l == r the range is empty and the boundary is pinned: l is the answer. It needs no post-loop adjustment, which is where nearly all binary-search bugs live.

Start with r = n, not n − 1. That is deliberate: n is the legitimate answer meaning "no index satisfies the predicate", and it is exactly the insert position.

The one precondition — monotonicity

The predicate applied across the array must read F F F F T T T: once true, true forever. It flips exactly once.

A sorted array gives this for free with a[i] >= target. But the array is not what matters — the predicate is. That distinction is what lets the same eight lines work on input that is not sorted at all.

Before writing any binary search, state the predicate in words and check that it is monotone. If it is not, the loop will converge confidently on the wrong index.

Applies when

The array is sorted, or is locally reconstructible as sorted — a rotated sorted array still has one sorted half at every midpoint, and a mountain array is monotone on each side of the peak.

Does not apply when

The predicate is not monotone. Searching an unsorted array for a value is O(n) with a hash set, not O(log n). Duplicates in a rotated array break the sorted-half test — when both ends and the midpoint are equal you cannot tell which side is ordered, and the worst case degrades to O(n).

Complexity

O(log n) time — the range halves every iteration, so at most ⌈log₂ n⌉ ≈ 17 steps for n = 10⁵. O(1) space when written iteratively. Always write it iteratively; recursion adds an O(log n) stack for nothing.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"sorted array" plus "O(log n) runtime" (the problem naming the pattern outright) · "first / last position of" · "insert position" · "rotated sorted array" · "find the minimum" on rotated input · "peak element" · "the array is guaranteed to have no duplicates" — that guarantee exists precisely so the sorted-half test stays decidable.

LC 34 traced on [5,7,7,8,8,10], target 8

Find the first and last index of 8. Both come from the same function: the first position is lowerBound(8), and the last is lowerBound(9) − 1. Two calls, one template, no second implementation to get wrong.

Calllrmida[mid]predicateactionresult

lowerBound(8)03177 ≥ 8 → falsel = 2, mid dropped—

Why lowerBound(target + 1) − 1 gives the last occurrencelowerBound(9) returns the first index holding something ≥ 9, which is the first index past the run of 8s. Step back one and you are on the last 8. This works even when the target is absent: then both calls return the same index, the range is empty, and you return [−1, −1] after a single equality check. No separate "upper bound" function is ever needed.

Write lowerBound once; derive the rest

One function, eight lines, no post-loop fixups. Everything else in this family is either a call to it with a different target, or the same loop with a different way of deciding which half to keep.

The one template worth memorising
/**
 * The first index in [0, n] at which the predicate becomes true.
 * Requires monotonicity:  F F F T T T  — it must flip exactly once.
 *
 * Invariant, maintained by every iteration:
 *     everything <  l  is FALSE
 *     everything >= r  is TRUE
 * so when l == r, that index IS the boundary.
 *
 * Returns n when no index satisfies the predicate — which is
 * exactly the insert position, not an error case.
 */
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length;          // r = n, NOT n - 1

    while (l < r) {                   // strict <, so it ends with l == r
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;    // NOT (l + r) / 2 — that overflows near Integer.MAX_VALUE

        if (a[mid] >= target) r = mid;     // mid may be the boundary: keep it
        else                  l = mid + 1; // mid is definitely not: drop it
    }
    return l;
}

// Everything else falls out of that one function:
int firstOccurrence(int[] a, int t) { int i = lowerBound(a, t);
                                      return (i < a.length && a[i] == t) ? i : -1; }
int lastOccurrence (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t + 1) - 1; }
int countOf        (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t + 1) - lowerBound(a, t); }
int insertPosition (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t); }          // LC 35, verbatim
boolean contains   (int[] a, int t) { int i = lowerBound(a, t);
                                      return i < a.length && a[i] == t; } // LC 704
Variant · rotated array, target search (LC 33)
// A rotated sorted array is not monotone, so no single predicate
// works. But at ANY midpoint, at least one half is still sorted —
// and in a sorted half you can decide containment in O(1).
int search(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;      // closed range here: we want an exact hit

    while (l <= r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;

        if (a[l] <= a[mid]) {                     // LEFT half is sorted
            if (a[l] <= target && target < a[mid]) r = mid - 1;   // it must be in there
            else                                   l = mid + 1;
        } else {                                  // RIGHT half is sorted
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[r]) l = mid + 1;
            else                                   r = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
Variant · compare against a neighbour, not a target (LC 153, 162)
// When there is no target, compare a[mid] with something that
// tells you which side the answer lies on.

// LC 153 — minimum of a rotated array. Compare with a[r], never a[l]:
// on an unrotated array a[mid] > a[l] is true yet the min is at 0.
int findMin(int[] a) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] > a[r]) l = mid + 1;   // min is strictly right of mid
        else               r = mid;       // mid could BE the min
    }
    return a[l];
}

// LC 162 — any peak. Walk uphill; the edges count as -infinity,
// so an uphill step can never run off the end.
int findPeakElement(int[] a) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] < a[mid + 1]) l = mid + 1;   // ascending: a peak lies right
        else                     r = mid;       // descending: mid could be it
    }
    return l;
}

The knobs

Range
[0, n) half-open for boundary questions; [0, n−1] closed only when you need an exact hit and will return from inside the loop, as in LC 33.
Predicate
The only genuinely problem-specific line. Say it in words first, then check it reads F…F T…T left to right.
Comparator
Against a target (34, 35, 704), against the right end (153), or against a neighbour (162). Choosing the wrong comparison partner is the classic LC 153 failure.
Return
l for a boundary, a[l] for a value, l − 1 for the last element below the boundary. Never adjust after the loop for any other reason.
The three bugs that actually happenmid = (l + r) / 2 — overflows once l + r exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE. This is the famous bug that sat in the JDK's own Arrays.binarySearch for nine years; always write l + (r - l) / 2. r = mid - 1 in the half-open template — discards the very index you were looking for, and the result is silently off by one. Mixing the two range conventions — while (l < r) with r = n - 1 never examines the last element; while (l <= r) with r = mid loops forever. Pick one convention per function and never blend them.

Six searches, one template and two rotations

704 and 35 are the template unmodified. 34 is two calls to it. 153 and 162 change what mid is compared against. 33 is the one that needs real thought — and it is the one that gets asked.

Anchor 1 · LC 34 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Linear scan for the first and last hit. O(n) — and the problem explicitly demands O(log n), so it is rejected by the statement itself.
The tempting wrong turn
One binary search for any occurrence, then linear expansion outwards. On [8,8,8,…,8] that expansion is O(n), so the whole thing is O(n). Interviewers reach for exactly that input.
The observation
Both endpoints are boundaries, not values. The first 8 is the boundary of "≥ 8"; the position after the last 8 is the boundary of "≥ 9".
The result
Two calls to one function. Nothing is duplicated, and there is no descending variant to get wrong.
Edge case
Target absent: both calls return the same index, so check a[first] == target before returning and emit [−1,−1] otherwise. Also guard first == a.length.
LC 34 · O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        int first = lowerBound(nums, target);

        // Absent if we ran off the end, or landed on a different value.
        if (first == nums.length || nums[first] != target)
            return new int[]{ -1, -1 };

        // The first index past the run of `target`, minus one.
        int last = lowerBound(nums, target + 1) - 1;

        return new int[]{ first, last };
    }

    /** First index with nums[i] >= target; nums.length if there is none. */
    private int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = nums.length;

        while (l < r) {
            int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[mid] >= target) r = mid;
            else                     l = mid + 1;
        }
        return l;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 33 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Linear scan, O(n). The statement demands O(log n).
Two-pass idea
Binary search for the rotation point (that is LC 153), then binary search the correct half. Two passes, both O(log n), and completely acceptable — say it, because it decomposes into a problem you have already solved.
The observation
You do not need the pivot. Split at any mid and at least one half is guaranteed sorted — a rotation can only break the order in one place.
Deciding the half
a[l] <= a[mid] means the left half is sorted. Inside a sorted half, "is the target here?" is a single range check; if it is not, it must be in the other half.
Why <= and not <
When l == mid — a two-element range — the left half is trivially sorted. Writing < misclassifies it and drops the answer. This is the single most common LC 33 failure.
LC 33 · O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = nums.length - 1;   // closed range: we return on an exact hit

        while (l <= r) {
            int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;

            // A rotation breaks the order in exactly one place,
            // so at least one half is always properly sorted.
            if (nums[l] <= nums[mid]) {              // LEFT half sorted
                // Inside a sorted half, containment is one range test.
                if (nums[l] <= target && target < nums[mid]) r = mid - 1;
                else                                          l = mid + 1;

            } else {                                 // RIGHT half sorted
                if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[r]) l = mid + 1;
                else                                          r = mid - 1;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

704 · Binary Search template

Path: there is no path — this is the baseline. Its value is as a memory test: you should be able to type the template correctly with no compile-and-fix cycle.

Delta: lowerBound, then i < n && a[i] == target. Many people write the closed-range version here instead; either is fine, but pick one and use it everywhere.

Watch for: if you cannot write this from memory, do not move on. Every later pattern in this deck assumes it.

35 · Search Insert Position template

Path: the problem asks where the target "would be if inserted in order" — which is the definition of a lower bound. No adaptation at all.

Delta: none. return lowerBound(nums, target); is the entire solution, and the n return case handles "larger than everything" without a branch.

Watch for: this is the clearest demonstration that "not found" is a legitimate answer rather than an error — the mental shift the whole pattern depends on.

153 · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array neighbour

Path: a linear scan is O(n); the rotation means there is exactly one place where a[i] < a[i-1], and that is the minimum.

Delta: compare a[mid] against a[r]. If a[mid] > a[r] the break lies strictly right, so l = mid + 1; otherwise r = mid, because mid may itself be the minimum.

Watch for: comparing against a[l] instead fails on an unrotated array such as [1,2,3,4], where a[mid] > a[l] yet the minimum is at index 0.

162 · Find Peak Element neighbour

Path: the input is not sorted, which makes O(log n) look impossible. It is not: the predicate "a peak exists at or left of mid" is monotone even though the array is not.

Delta: compare a[mid] with a[mid + 1]. Ascending means a peak lies to the right; descending means mid itself could be one. The stated a[-1] = a[n] = −∞ guarantees the uphill walk always terminates on a peak.

Watch for: this is the clearest proof in the family that binary search needs a monotone predicate, and never a sorted array.

If you only drill twoDo 34 and 33. 34 forces you to internalise the boundary formulation that makes every other variant free; 33 is the most-asked binary search in real interviews and the one where the <= versus < detail separates a working solution from a nearly-working one.

Binary search is the best fit for a stream in the whole deck

Binary search runs in log n steps over a two-field state. Its step is a pure function and its stop condition is a single test, which is exactly the shape Stream.iterate handles well. So all six solutions share one helper: firstTrue(lo, hi, ok) halves a [lo, hi) record until it is empty and returns the first index where ok holds. Each problem then comes down to choosing that predicate and the range.

#ProblemThe stream moveFitStreamsLoop
704Binary SearchfirstTrue over nums[m] >= target, then check that the value is really there.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
35Search Insert PositionThe same lower bound. It already is the insert position.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
34Find First and Last Position of ElementTwo lower bounds: of target, and of anything greater, minus one.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
153Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted ArrayfirstTrue over nums[m] <= last: the rotation point is where values stop exceeding the last one.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
162Find Peak ElementThe same halving with nums[m] > nums[m+1]. The test is not monotone, but a peak always lies on the side the slope points to.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
33Search in Rotated Sorted Array153's rotation point, then an ordinary lower bound in whichever sorted half can hold the target.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 704 · Binary Search · clean
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // A (lo, hi) record, halved by Stream.iterate.
        int i = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        return i < n && nums[i] == target ? i : -1;
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}

LC 34 · Find First and Last Position of Element · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // Two lower bounds: of target, and of anything greater.
        int first = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        if (first == n || nums[first] != target)
            return new int[]{ -1, -1 };
        int last = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] > target) - 1;
        return new int[]{ first, last };
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 153 · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array · clean
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length, last = nums[n - 1];
        // Left of the rotation point every value exceeds the
        // last one; from it onwards none does. The minimum is
        // at the first index with nums[m] <= last.
        return nums[firstTrue(0, n - 1, m -> nums[m] <= last)];
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 162 · Find Peak Element · clean
class Solution {
    public int findPeakElement(int[] nums) {
        // Not a monotone test, and it need not be: whichever
        // way the slope at mid points, a peak lies on that
        // side, so halving towards it keeps one in range.
        return firstTrue(0, nums.length - 1,
                         m -> nums[m] > nums[m + 1]);
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 33 · Search in Rotated Sorted Array · clean
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length, last = nums[n - 1];
        // 1 · the rotation point k, exactly as in 153
        int k = firstTrue(0, n - 1, m -> nums[m] <= last);
        // 2 · values <= last live in [k, n), the rest in [0, k)
        int lo = target <= last ? k : 0;
        int hi = target <= last ? n : k;
        int i = firstTrue(lo, hi, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        return i < hi && nums[i] == target ? i : -1;
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
What the record buys youThe loop version makes three off-by-one decisions every time you write it: < or <=, mid or mid − 1, return lo or hi. The Range record answers all three once. The range is half-open, the step keeps ok(mid) inside it, and the answer is the point where it closes. Every problem above is only a predicate and a range, so there is nothing left to get wrong per problem.
Say this in the interview"I'll write the loop, but binary search is where a stream version genuinely reads better: the state is two ints, the step is pure, and it stops the moment the range is empty." Then write the loop. Naming the invariant is what scores. The helper is the invariant written down.

Guess the answer, then check whether it works

The highest-yield pattern in this deck, and the one most people never recognise. Nothing here is sorted. What is monotone is feasibility: if a capacity of 5 is enough, so is 6. Binary search that, and an apparently intractable optimisation becomes an O(n log V) loop around a ten-line simulation.

The inversion

The question "what is the smallest capacity that works?" is hard. The question "does capacity 7 work?" is usually easy — a single greedy pass.

So stop optimising and start checking. Binary search over the range of possible answers, using the easy question as the predicate. You never derive the answer; you converge on it.

Cost: O(log V) checks, each O(n). With values up to 10⁹ that is 30 checks — the log factor is essentially free, which is why this beats almost any clever direct construction.

Three questions, in this order

  1. What exactly is the answer, and what range must it lie in? Pick lo as a value that obviously fails or is the smallest legal one, and hi as one that obviously works. Sloppy bounds are the main source of wrong answers here.
  2. Can I check one candidate in O(n)? Write feasible(x) as a literal simulation of the problem statement. Resist cleverness — it should read like the English.
  3. Is feasibility monotone? If x works, must x + 1 work? Say the argument out loud. If the answer is no, this pattern does not apply.

Answer those three and the code writes itself — it is an ordinary boundary search whose array comparison has been replaced by feasible(mid).

Applies when

The answer is a single number in a known range; you are asked to minimise a maximum or maximise a minimum; and checking one candidate is a straightforward greedy pass. The constraint shape "small n, huge values" is the giveaway.

Does not apply when

Feasibility is not monotone — for example "exactly k parts" where a larger cap can force fewer parts than required. Reformulate it as "at most k" first, or the search converges on a value that is not actually achievable.

Complexity

O(n log V) where V is the width of the answer range — typically 30 iterations for values to 10⁹, so about 30n. Space is O(1). For real-valued answers, use a fixed 100 iterations rather than an epsilon comparison.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"minimise the maximum…" or "maximise the minimum…" (decisive on their own) · "the smallest X such that…" · "within D days" · "at most k operations" · "the minimum eating speed" · "split into k subarrays" · "the minimum capacity". Add the constraint tell: n ≤ 10⁵ next to value ≤ 10⁹ means the search is over the values, not the array.

LC 875 traced on piles = [3,6,7,11], h = 8

Koko eats at k bananas per hour; each pile takes ceil(pile / k) hours because she never moves on mid-pile. Find the smallest k finishing within 8 hours. The answer range is [1, 11] — one banana per hour at worst, and the largest pile at best.

Setting the bounds correctlylo = 1, because a speed of zero never finishes. hi = max(piles), because eating faster than the biggest pile cannot beat one hour per pile — and with h ≥ piles.length guaranteed by the statement, that speed always works. Picking hi = sum(piles) also terminates correctly and costs only a handful of extra iterations; picking hi too small is the error that silently returns a wrong answer.

One template, three blanks to fill

The loop is an ordinary boundary search; the array comparison becomes feasible(mid) and you are done. All the thinking moves into feasible, which should be a direct transcription of the problem statement — deliberately dull code.

The template — fill in three blanks
/**
 * Smallest x in [lo, hi] for which feasible(x) holds.
 * Requires monotone feasibility:  F F F T T T over the answer range.
 *
 * BLANK 1 · lo   — a value that fails, or the smallest legal one
 * BLANK 2 · hi   — a value that obviously works
 * BLANK 3 · feasible(x) — an O(n) simulation, as literal as possible
 */
int solve(int[] a, int limit) {
    int lo = 1, hi = 0;
    for (int v : a) hi = Math.max(hi, v);        // BLANKS 1 and 2

    while (lo < hi) {                            // an ordinary boundary search
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

        if (feasible(a, mid, limit)) hi = mid;   // mid might be the answer: keep it
        else                         lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;                                   // lo == hi == the smallest feasible x
}

/** BLANK 3 · read this straight off the problem statement. */
private boolean feasible(int[] a, int speed, int limit) {
    long hours = 0;
    for (int pile : a) {
        hours += (pile + speed - 1) / speed;     // ceil without floating point
        if (hours > limit) return false;         // early exit: cheap and avoids overflow
    }
    return hours <= limit;
}

// MAXIMISING instead? Mirror it: keep a feasible mid on the RIGHT.
//     if (feasible(mid)) lo = mid;  else hi = mid - 1;
//     mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2;   // round UP, or this loops forever
feasible() for the four shapes you will meet
// 1 · COUNT THE UNITS — LC 875, 1283
//     "how many hours / how large a sum at this rate?"
long units = 0;
for (int v : a) units += (v + x - 1) / x;
return units <= limit;

// 2 · GREEDY PACKING — LC 410, 1011
//     "how many groups do I need if each is capped at x?"
int parts = 1; long cur = 0;
for (int v : a) {
    if (cur + v > x) { parts++; cur = v; }   // start a new group
    else               cur += v;
}
return parts <= limit;

// 3 · COUNT WHAT QUALIFIES BY TIME x — LC 1482
//     "how many runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers exist by day x?"
int made = 0, run = 0;
for (int day : bloom) {
    if (day <= x) { if (++run == k) { made++; run = 0; } }
    else          run = 0;                   // the run is broken
}
return made >= m;

// 4 · REAL-VALUED ANSWER — LC 774
//     No integer grid, so iterate a FIXED number of times.
//     100 halvings drives the interval below 1e-30 — far past
//     any 1e-6 tolerance — and cannot loop forever the way an
//     epsilon comparison can.
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    double mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid;
}
return hi;

Choosing the bounds

Capacity / speed
lo = max(a) when every element must fit somewhere on its own (LC 410, 1011); lo = 1 when elements may be consumed over several steps (LC 875, 1283).
Upper
hi = sum(a) for packing — one group holds everything. hi = max(a) for rates. Too generous costs a few iterations; too tight returns a wrong answer.
Time-style answers
[min(day), max(day)], and check feasibility at hi first — LC 1482 can be impossible outright, and returns −1.
Overflow
Accumulate in long. With n = 10⁵ and values to 10⁹ the sum reaches 10¹⁴, which overflows int long before the search goes wrong.
The three bugs that actually happenlo set below the largest element in a packing problem — capacity 3 can never hold an item of size 7, and the greedy check loops or reports nonsense. Forgetting to round up — pile / speed is floor division, so a pile of 7 at speed 6 reports one hour instead of two; use (v + x - 1) / x. The maximising mirror without rounding mid up — with lo = mid and a floor midpoint, a two-element range never shrinks and the loop hangs.

Six problems that are the same problem

875, 1011, 410 and 1283 differ only in what feasible counts. Once you see that 1011 and 410 are literally the same algorithm with the inputs renamed, the family collapses into one thing to remember.

Anchor 1 · LC 875 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every speed from 1 upwards and stop at the first that fits. O(max · n) — with piles to 10⁹ that is 10¹⁴ operations.
The constraint tell
n ≤ 10⁴ but piles[i] ≤ 10⁹. A tiny array with gigantic values means the search is over the value range, not the array.
The observation
Eating faster never takes more hours. So feasibility is monotone in speed, and the brute-force scan is a linear search over a sorted-by-feasibility axis — exactly what binary search replaces.
The check
sum(ceil(pile / k)) ≤ h. She never moves on mid-pile, which is why it is a ceiling — that sentence in the statement is the whole modelling step.
Edge cases
Use long for the hour total. Round up with integer arithmetic, never Math.ceil on doubles — at 10⁹ the division loses precision.
LC 875 · O(n log maxPile) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int lo = 1, hi = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hi = Math.max(hi, p);   // fastest useful speed

        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

            if (canFinish(piles, mid, h)) hi = mid;      // maybe the answer
            else                          lo = mid + 1;  // definitely too slow
        }
        return lo;
    }

    private boolean canFinish(int[] piles, int speed, int h) {
        long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) {
            hours += (p + speed - 1) / speed;   // ceil(p / speed), integer only
            if (hours > h) return false;        // early exit
        }
        return true;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 410 — the path to the solution

The DP solution
dp[i][j] = best split of the first i elements into j parts. O(n²k) time, O(nk) space. It is the textbook answer and it passes — mention it, then beat it.
The inversion
Stop asking "what is the smallest possible largest sum" and ask "with a cap of M, how many parts do I need?" That second question is a single greedy pass.
Why greedy is optimal here
Fill each part as full as the cap allows before starting the next. Closing a part early can never reduce the total count, so the greedy count is the minimum. Say this — it is the step interviewers push on.
Monotonicity
A larger cap never needs more parts, so partsNeeded(M) ≤ k reads F F F T T T in M.
Bounds
lo = max(nums) — no part can be smaller than its largest element. hi = sum(nums) — one part holds everything. Starting lo at 0 or 1 is the classic error.
Same problem
LC 1011 is this with "parts" renamed "days" and "cap" renamed "capacity". Identical code.
LC 410 · O(n log sum) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
        long lo = 0, hi = 0;
        for (int v : nums) {
            lo = Math.max(lo, v);   // a part can never be smaller than one element
            hi += v;                // one part holding everything always works
        }

        while (lo < hi) {
            long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

            if (partsNeeded(nums, mid) <= k) hi = mid;
            else                             lo = mid + 1;
        }
        return (int) lo;
    }

    /** Greedy: fill each part to the cap before opening the next. */
    private int partsNeeded(int[] nums, long cap) {
        int parts = 1;
        long cur = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            if (cur + v > cap) { parts++; cur = v; }   // open a new part
            else                 cur += v;
        }
        return parts;
    }
}

1011 · Capacity To Ship Packages greedy packing

Path: identical to 410 in every respect — only the vocabulary differs. Recognising that equivalence out loud is itself worth points.

Delta: lo = max(weights) (a package must fit on one ship), hi = sum(weights). feasible(cap) counts days by the same greedy fill.

Watch for: packages must ship in order, which is what makes the greedy valid. If reordering were allowed this would be bin packing, and NP-hard.

1283 · Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold count units

Path: the same shape as 875 with "hours" renamed "sum of quotients". If you solved Koko, you can write this in two minutes.

Delta: lo = 1, hi = max(nums) — at that divisor every term is 1, so the sum is n, and the statement guarantees threshold ≥ n. feasible(d) is sum(ceil(v/d)) ≤ threshold.

Watch for: the ceiling again. Math.ceil((double) v / d) works here but integer arithmetic is faster and exact — build the habit.

1482 · Min Days to Make m Bouquets count runs

Path: the answer is a day, not a size — the first cue that the answer space is a time axis. By day x, the bloomed flowers form fixed runs, and each run of length L yields L / k bouquets.

Delta: feasible(x) scans once, tracking the current run of flowers with bloomDay ≤ x and resetting it at every unbloomed flower.

Watch for: check (long) m * k > n up front and return −1 — the multiplication overflows int at the stated limits, and it is the only impossible case.

774 · Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station real-valued

Path: a heap-based greedy that repeatedly splits the widest gap looks natural but is wrong — it is locally greedy and misses the optimum. Binary searching the distance is both simpler and correct.

Delta: the answer is a double, so there is no integer grid to converge onto. Run a fixed 100 iterations instead of comparing against an epsilon. feasible(d) sums (int)(gap / d) extra stations per gap and tests against k.

Watch for: while (hi - lo > 1e-6) can spin forever when the two doubles become adjacent representable values. The fixed count cannot.

Premium: this one is behind LeetCode's paywall. LC 1552 is a free substitute: the same "maximise the minimum distance" shape, and it drills the mirrored template.

If you only drill twoDo 875 and 410. 875 teaches the recognition — small n, huge values, "minimum speed". 410 teaches the inversion in its purest form: a Hard problem with a well-known DP solution that collapses to twenty lines once you binary search the answer instead of constructing it. That collapse is the single most transferable move in this deck.

The search is one helper; the feasibility test is a pipeline

Binary search on the answer has two parts: a search over candidate values, and a yes-or-no test for one candidate. The search is the sorted-data pattern's firstTrue helper, unchanged. The test is nearly always a sum or a count over the input, which makes it a single pipeline. Even the greedy packing in 1011 and 410 becomes a pure fold over a three-field record.

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 875 · Koko Eating Bananas · clean
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(piles).max().getAsInt();
        // Hours only shrink as the speed grows, so "fits in h"
        // is monotone: search for the first speed that fits.
        return firstTrue(1, max, k -> Arrays.stream(piles)
                .mapToLong(p -> (p + k - 1) / k)  // ceil(p/k)
                .sum() <= h);
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1011 · Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days · clean
class Solution {
    public int shipWithinDays(int[] weights, int days) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(weights).max().getAsInt();
        int sum = Arrays.stream(weights).sum();
        // The least capacity whose greedy packing fits in days.
        return firstTrue(max, sum,
                         cap -> need(weights, cap) <= days);
    }

    // Greedy packing as a fold: one package per step, carrying
    // the days used so far and the load on the current day.
    record Pack(int i, int days, int load) {
        Pack add(int w, int cap) {
            return load + w > cap
                    ? new Pack(i + 1, days + 1, w)
                    : new Pack(i + 1, days, load + w);
        }
    }

    static int need(int[] w, int cap) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pack(0, 1, 0),
                              p -> p.add(w[p.i()], cap))
                .skip(w.length)   // exactly n steps
                .findFirst().get().days();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1283 · Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold · clean
class Solution {
    public int smallestDivisor(int[] nums, int threshold) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(nums).max().getAsInt();
        // The sum of ceil(x / d) only falls as d grows. Sum in
        // long: at d = 1 it can reach 5·10¹⁰.
        return firstTrue(1, max, d -> Arrays.stream(nums)
                .mapToLong(x -> (x + d - 1) / d)
                .sum() <= threshold);
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1482 · Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets · clean
class Solution {
    public int minDays(int[] bloomDay, int m, int k) {
        if ((long) m * k > bloomDay.length) return -1;
        int max = Arrays.stream(bloomDay).max().getAsInt();
        return firstTrue(1, max,
                day -> bouquets(bloomDay, day, k) >= m);
    }

    // Unbloomed flowers cut the row into runs, and a run of
    // length len makes len / k bouquets. Read the runs off the
    // gaps between consecutive cuts: nothing is carried.
    static long bouquets(int[] bloom, int day, int k) {
        int n = bloom.length;
        int[] cut = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(-1),
                IntStream.concat(IntStream.range(0, n)
                                .filter(i -> bloom[i] > day),
                        IntStream.of(n)))
                .toArray();
        return IntStream.range(1, cut.length)
                .mapToLong(j -> (cut[j] - cut[j - 1] - 1) / k)
                .sum();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 410 · Split Array Largest Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(nums).max().getAsInt();
        int sum = Arrays.stream(nums).sum();
        // 1011 in disguise: the least cap on each piece's sum
        // whose greedy split needs at most k pieces.
        return firstTrue(max, sum,
                         cap -> pieces(nums, cap) <= k);
    }

    // Greedy split as a fold: pieces so far, current load.
    record Pack(int i, int pieces, int load) {
        Pack add(int x, int cap) {
            return load + x > cap
                    ? new Pack(i + 1, pieces + 1, x)
                    : new Pack(i + 1, pieces, load + x);
        }
    }

    static int pieces(int[] a, int cap) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pack(0, 1, 0),
                              p -> p.add(a[p.i()], cap))
                .skip(a.length)
                .findFirst().get().pieces();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 774 · Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station · clean
class Solution {
    record Real(double lo, double hi) {}

    public double minmaxGasDist(int[] stations, int k) {
        int[] gap = IntStream.range(1, stations.length)
                .map(i -> stations[i] - stations[i - 1])
                .toArray();
        // New stations needed so that no gap exceeds d
        DoubleToLongFunction need = d -> Arrays.stream(gap)
                .mapToLong(g -> (long) Math.ceil(g / d) - 1)
                .sum();
        // A real-valued answer has no "empty range" to stop on,
        // so run a fixed 100 halvings: 10⁸ / 2¹⁰⁰ is far below
        // the 10⁻⁶ tolerance.
        double hi = Arrays.stream(gap).max().getAsInt();
        return Stream.iterate(new Real(0, hi), r -> {
                    double mid = (r.lo() + r.hi()) / 2;
                    return need.applyAsLong(mid) <= k
                            ? new Real(r.lo(), mid)
                            : new Real(mid, r.hi());
                })
                .skip(100)
                .findFirst().get().hi();
    }
}
The fold idiomJava 17 has no foldLeft. Stream.iterate(seed, step).skip(n).findFirst() works as one. It applies step exactly n times, so a record can index the array with its own counter and never read past the end. 1011 and 410 use it for the greedy packing, and the DP patterns later in this deck use it for rolling state.
The pattern, restated as codeSuppose the question asks for the smallest X that still works, and working only gets easier as X grows. Then the answer is firstTrue(lo, hi, x -> works(x)). Writing works as a pipeline makes you state it as a pure function of x. That purity is exactly the monotonicity argument the interviewer is waiting to hear.

Buy O(1) lookup with O(n) memory

The simplest trade in the deck and the one that removes the most nested loops. Any time the inner loop is asking "have I seen this?", "how many of these?" or "which of these belong together?", that loop is a hash lookup and the O(n²) collapses to O(n).

The three questions a hash answers

Membership
HashSet. "Have I seen x?" — LC 217 and LC 128.
Counting
HashMap<T, Integer> or int[]. "How many x?" — LC 242 and 347.
Grouping
HashMap<Key, List<T>>. "Which items share a property?" — LC 49. The craft is entirely in choosing the key.

A fourth use is the complement: instead of searching for a pair, store what you have seen and ask whether the partner you need has already gone by. That is LC 1, and it is one pass rather than two loops.

The canonical key

Grouping problems reduce to: find a function key(x) that is identical for items that belong together and different otherwise. Once you have it, the grouping is four lines.

For anagrams, two keys work. Sorting each string is O(L log L) and obvious. A 26-slot count vector is O(L) and strictly better — and generalises to alphabets where sorting is meaningless.

Say both in an interview. Reaching for the count vector unprompted signals that you think about the key rather than just calling sort.

Applies when

Order does not matter to the answer, and the inner loop is a lookup, a count or a grouping. Also when you need original indices, which sorting would destroy.

Does not apply when

You need order, rank or a range query — that is a sorted structure or a TreeMap. Also when O(1) extra space is required: the map is the O(n).

Complexity

O(n) time on average, O(n) space. Java's HashMap degrades to O(log n) per operation under collisions, not O(n), since Java 8 — buckets become red-black trees past eight entries.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return the indices" (order matters, so no sorting) · "group the anagrams" · "contains a duplicate" · "the k most frequent" · "the longest consecutive sequence" · "you may return the answer in any order" · "O(n) runtime" stated on a problem that looks quadratic. That last one is the strongest signal in this deck: a demanded O(n) on a pairing problem almost always means a hash map.

LC 128 traced on [100,4,200,1,3,2]

Longest consecutive sequence, in O(n), on unsorted input. Sorting would be O(n log n) and is explicitly ruled out by the follow-up. The trick is a single guard: only start counting from a value that begins a run — one whose predecessor is absent.

The amortisation argument, stated properlyA value is walked over only by the head of its own run, and every value belongs to exactly one run. So across the entire algorithm the inner while executes at most n times in total — not n times per element. Total work is O(n) probes for the head guard plus O(n) for all walks combined. Being able to state it is what turns "I think it's O(n)" into an answer the interviewer accepts.

Four idioms, and the Java methods worth knowing

The code is short, so the leverage is in fluency: merge, computeIfAbsent and getOrDefault remove the null-checking that makes hash solutions look clumsy under time pressure.

The four idioms
// 1 · MEMBERSHIP — "have I seen it?"
//     Set.add returns false when the element was already there,
//     so the check and the insert are a single operation.
boolean containsDuplicate(int[] a) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (int v : a) if (!seen.add(v)) return true;
    return false;
}

// 2 · COUNTING — merge is the whole idiom
Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (int v : a) freq.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);       // no getOrDefault dance
freq.merge(v, -1, Integer::sum);                      // and to decrement
if (freq.get(v) == 0) freq.remove(v);                 // keep size() honest

//     For a known small alphabet, an array beats a map outright —
//     no boxing, no hashing, and it is what a window state should use.
int[] count = new int[26];
count[c - 'a']++;

// 3 · GROUPING — computeIfAbsent creates the bucket on first use
Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value);

// 4 · COMPLEMENT — store as you go, ask for the partner you need
Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
    if (j != null) return new int[]{ j, i };
    seen.put(a[i], i);        // AFTER the lookup — see the note below
}
Bucket sort by frequency — top-K in O(n), no heap (LC 347)
// A heap gives O(n log k). But a frequency can never exceed n,
// so index an array BY the frequency and read it from the top:
// O(n), and simpler than the heap version once you have seen it.
int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int v : nums) freq.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);

    // bucket[f] = every value occurring exactly f times
    List<Integer>[] bucket = new List[nums.length + 1];
    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
        int f = e.getValue();
        if (bucket[f] == null) bucket[f] = new ArrayList<>();
        bucket[f].add(e.getKey());
    }

    int[] out = new int[k];
    int idx = 0;
    for (int f = nums.length; f >= 1 && idx < k; f--) {
        if (bucket[f] == null) continue;
        for (int v : bucket[f]) {
            out[idx++] = v;
            if (idx == k) break;
        }
    }
    return out;
}

Picking the container

int[26]
Lowercase letters. Fastest, and no boxing at all. Reach for it before a map whenever the alphabet is fixed.
int[128]
ASCII. Covers mixed case and punctuation without thought.
HashMap
Arbitrary or unbounded keys. The default when values are ints up to 10⁹.
HashSet
Membership only. Say !set.add(v) rather than contains then add.
TreeMap
Only when you need order or range queries — floorKey, ceilingKey, subMap. O(log n), so do not reach for it by default.
The three bugs that actually happenInserting before looking up in LC 1 — on [3,3] with target 6, the element finds itself and you return [0,0]. Always probe first, then insert. Leaving zero counts in the map — size() then over-reports distinct keys, which silently breaks every "at most K distinct" window. Using == on boxed Integer — it compares references, and Java only caches −128 to 127, so the comparison works on small tests and fails at 1000. Use .equals, or unbox to int first.

Six lookups, from one line to the amortisation argument

217 and 242 are warm-ups you should be able to write without thinking. 1 and 49 are the idioms in their standard form. 347 introduces bucket sort. 128 is the one with a real idea in it.
