Anchor 1 · LC 1 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Two nested loops over all pairs, O(n²). It passes on small inputs, which is why this is rated Easy and still worth getting exactly right.
Why not two pointers
Sorting would give O(n log n) — but the answer is the original indices, and sorting destroys them. You would have to carry index pairs alongside the values. The hash keeps them for free.
The inversion
Do not search forward for a partner. Remember what you have passed, and at each element ask whether its required partner target − a[i] is already behind you.
The ordering detail
Probe before inserting. On [3,3] with target 6, inserting first lets index 0 match itself and returns [0,0]. Probing first returns the correct [0,1].
Why it is still one pass
If i < j form the answer, then when the loop reaches j the value at i is already stored. Every pair is discovered at its second element.
LC 1 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        // value -> the index where we saw it
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            // PROBE FIRST. Inserting first would let nums[i]
            // pair with itself when 2 * nums[i] == target.
            Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);
            if (j != null) return new int[]{ j, i };

            seen.put(nums[i], i);
        }
        return new int[]{};   // the statement guarantees this is unreachable
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 128 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each value, walk upwards checking membership with a linear scan. O(n³) — or O(n²) with a set.
The obvious fix
Sort, then scan for the longest adjacent run. O(n log n), genuinely correct, and easy to write. Say this first — the follow-up asking for O(n) is what rules it out.
First O(n) attempt
Put everything in a set and walk upwards from every value. Still O(n²): on [1,2,…,n] the walk from 1 covers n, from 2 covers n−1, and so on.
The observation
A walk starting mid-run recomputes a suffix of a walk that another start already covers. So only walk from a head — a value v with v − 1 absent. Every run has exactly one.
The result
Each element is walked over exactly once across the whole algorithm, so the nested loop is O(n) in total. One continue is the entire optimisation.
Edge case
Duplicates are absorbed by the set. The empty array must return 0, so initialise best at 0 rather than 1.
LC 128 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int v : nums) set.add(v);      // duplicates collapse here

        int best = 0;

        for (int v : set) {
            // THE ONE LINE THAT MATTERS.
            // If v-1 exists, v is mid-run and the head will cover it.
            if (set.contains(v - 1)) continue;

            // v begins a run: walk it once.
            int len = 1;
            while (set.contains(v + len)) len++;

            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;   // 0 for an empty array
    }
}

217 · Contains Duplicate membership

Path: nested loops are O(n²); sorting and scanning neighbours is O(n log n) with O(1) extra space. The set is O(n) time for O(n) space — name that trade, because it is the entire point of the problem.

Delta: if (!seen.add(v)) return true;. Set.add already reports whether the element was new, so a separate contains call is redundant work.

Watch for: if the interviewer adds "O(1) space", the answer becomes sort-then-scan, and you must say you are mutating the input.

242 · Valid Anagram counting

Path: sorting both strings and comparing is O(n log n) and perfectly acceptable. Counting is O(n) and strictly better.

Delta: one int[26]. Increment for s, decrement for t, then confirm every slot is zero — or bail early if any goes negative. Compare lengths first and return immediately if they differ.

Watch for: the Unicode follow-up. int[26] no longer works; switch to a HashMap<Integer, Integer> keyed on code points, since a Java char cannot hold one.

49 · Group Anagrams grouping

Path: comparing every pair for anagram-hood is O(n²·L). Replacing the comparison with a computed key makes it one pass.

Delta: the key. Sorting each word is O(L log L); a 26-slot count vector rendered via Arrays.toString is O(L) and better. Build the map with computeIfAbsent, then return new ArrayList<>(map.values()).

Watch for: do not concatenate raw counts into a string — "1,11" and "11,1" would collide. Keep the separators that Arrays.toString supplies.

347 · Top K Frequent Elements buckets

Path: count, then sort by frequency — O(n log n). A size-k min-heap improves that to O(n log k), which is the expected answer and worth presenting.

Delta: then beat it. A frequency is at most n, so it can index an array directly: bucket the values by count and read downwards from n. That is O(n), with no comparator.

Watch for: new List[n + 1] raises an unchecked-generic-array warning. It is correct and conventional here; say so rather than working around it.

If you only drill twoDo 1 and 128. 1 is the complement idiom, and it is the one you will reuse most often. 128 teaches the amortisation argument in a setting where forgetting it costs you the stated complexity target.

Hashing is what collectors were built for

Every problem here is a membership test, a count or a grouping, and each of those is one collector: distinct, groupingBy with counting(), or toMap with a merge function. These are the six where a pipeline reads as well as the loop, often better, and none of them pays for it in time.

LC 217 · Contains Duplicate · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean containsDuplicate(int[] nums) {
        // distinct() keeps a hidden HashSet: the loop's O(n) /
        // O(n), minus the early exit on the first repeat.
        return Arrays.stream(nums).distinct().count()
                < nums.length;
    }
}
LC 242 · Valid Anagram · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean isAnagram(String s, String t) {
        // Equal letter counts. codePoints() also answers the
        // Unicode follow-up: a char is not a code point.
        return counts(s).equals(counts(t));
    }

    private static Map<Integer, Long> counts(String s) {
        return s.codePoints().boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        c -> c, Collectors.counting()));
    }
}
LC 1 · Two Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // value -> the LAST index holding it. Two passes, so
        // the probe-before-insert trap cannot happen: on [3,3]
        // the first 3 finds the second 3's index, not its own.
        Map<Integer, Integer> last = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(i -> nums[i], i -> i,
                                          (a, b) -> b));
        // the partner's index, or i itself when there is none
        IntUnaryOperator mate =
                i -> last.getOrDefault(target - nums[i], i);
        int i = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .filter(k -> mate.applyAsInt(k) != k)
                .findFirst().getAsInt();
        return new int[]{ i, mate.applyAsInt(i) };
    }
}
LC 49 · Group Anagrams · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] strs) {
        // All the work is the key; groupingBy does the rest.
        return new ArrayList<>(Arrays.stream(strs)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Solution::key))
                .values());
    }

    // A 26-slot count vector: O(L), where sorting is O(L log L)
    private static String key(String s) {
        int[] c = s.chars().collect(() -> new int[26],
                (a, ch) -> a[ch - 'a']++,
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        return Arrays.toString(c);  // "1,11" ≠ "11,1"
    }
}
LC 347 · Top K Frequent Elements · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Long> freq = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        v -> v, Collectors.counting()));
        // Invert: frequency -> the values that have it
        Map<Long, List<Integer>> byFreq = freq.keySet().stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(freq::get));
        // Read the buckets from n down: no comparator, no sort.
        return LongStream.iterate(nums.length, f -> f > 0,
                                  f -> f - 1)
                .mapToObj(f -> byFreq.getOrDefault(f,
                                                   List.of()))
                .flatMap(List::stream)
                .limit(k)
                .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 128 · Longest Consecutive Sequence · clean
class Solution {
    public int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        Set<Integer> set = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toSet());
        // Walk only from run heads (v - 1 absent): every value
        // is then walked exactly once, so the total is O(n).
        return set.stream()
                .filter(v -> !set.contains(v - 1))
                .mapToInt(v -> (int) IntStream
                        .iterate(v, set::contains, x -> x + 1)
                        .count())
                .max().orElse(0);
    }
}
Why all six are cleanA collector is a mutable reduction whose container the stream owns. The HashMap inside groupingBy is created, filled and handed back by the pipeline, and nothing outside it ever sees it half-built. That is the whole difference from a lambda writing into an outer map. It is also why hashing is the pattern where streams are the idiomatic answer rather than a trick.
The one thing the loop does betterShort-circuiting. The loop for 217 returns at the first repeat, while distinct().count() reads everything. When that matters, !Arrays.stream(nums).allMatch(seen::add) stops early, but seen then lives outside the pipeline, which makes the solution stateful. The same trade-off, early exit against purity, comes back in almost every pattern after this one.

Pay once up front, answer every range for free

Build an array where P[i] is the sum of everything before index i. Then the sum of any range [l, r] is P[r+1] − P[l] — one subtraction, O(1), no matter how wide the range. That single identity is the whole pattern.

The invariant

P[0] = 0, and P[i] = a[0] + … + a[i−1]. The leading zero is not decoration: it is what makes ranges starting at index 0 need no special case.

So P has length n + 1. Sizing it n is the most common implementation error here, and it forces an if (l == 0) branch that then gets the boundary wrong.

Build is O(n) once; every subsequent range query is O(1). The trade is O(n) extra memory, which is almost always worth it the moment there is more than one query.

The second move — counting with a map

Range lookup is only half the pattern. The other half answers "how many subarrays sum to K?" without examining any range at all.

A subarray (l, r] sums to K exactly when P[r] − P[l] = K, that is when P[l] = P[r] − K. So as you sweep r, ask a hash map how many earlier prefixes equalled P[r] − K and add that count.

This works with negative numbers, which is exactly the case a sliding window cannot handle — there the window has no valid shrink rule, because extending it may raise or lower the sum.

Applies when

Repeated range sum queries on a static array, or any "count the subarrays whose sum has property X" question — including sums that are negative, where a window has no valid shrink rule.

Does not apply when

The array is updated between queries — that needs a Fenwick or segment tree, since every update would rebuild O(n) of the prefix array. Also when the question is about a longest run rather than a count and all values are positive; a window is cheaper there.

Complexity

O(n) to build, O(1) per range query. The counting variant is O(n) total with O(n) map space. Always accumulate in long: 10⁵ values of 10⁹ overflows int.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the sum of the elements between indices left and right" · "multiple queries" or "called many times" · "how many subarrays sum to k" · "divisible by k" · "a subarray whose sum is a multiple of" · "the pivot index" · and critically "nums[i] can be negative", which is what rules out a window and leaves this.

LC 560 traced on [1,2,3,-3,1,2], k = 3

Count the subarrays summing to 3. There are six, and several overlap — which is why the running total is a sum of counts rather than a simple tally. The negative value at index 3 is the reason no window can solve this.

inums[i]running sumneeds prefixmatchestotalthe subarray(s) just counted
——0seed the map with {0:1}—0the empty prefix

Why the map must be updated after the lookupInsert sum into the map after querying for sum − k. With k = 0 the two are equal, so inserting first would let a prefix match itself and count an empty subarray that does not exist. The same ordering rule applies to every complement-style hash lookup.

Two skeletons: build-and-query, and sweep-and-count

The first materialises the prefix array because there will be many queries. The second never stores it at all — it keeps one running sum and a map, because it only ever needs to compare the current prefix against earlier ones.

Skeleton A · build once, query O(1) (LC 303, 724)
// P has length n + 1 and P[0] = 0. That leading zero is what
// removes every "does the range start at index 0?" special case.
class PrefixSum {
    private final long[] P;

    PrefixSum(int[] a) {
        P = new long[a.length + 1];          // n + 1, never n
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i];          // long: 1e5 * 1e9 overflows int
        }
    }

    /** Inclusive on both ends. */
    long range(int l, int r) {
        return P[r + 1] - P[l];              // one subtraction, any width
    }
}
Skeleton B · sweep and count (LC 560, 930, 974, 523)
// No prefix ARRAY is built. One running sum, one map of
// "how many times has this prefix value occurred so far".
int countSubarraysSummingTo(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    seen.put(0L, 1);                    // the empty prefix — never omit this

    long sum = 0;
    int count = 0;

    for (int v : a) {
        sum += v;

        // LOOK UP FIRST. With k == 0 the key equals `sum`,
        // so inserting first would let a prefix match itself.
        count += seen.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);

        seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return count;
}
The modular variant — when the question is "divisible by k" (LC 974, 523)
/**
 * A subarray sum is divisible by k exactly when its two end
 * prefixes have the SAME remainder mod k:
 *     (P[r] - P[l]) % k == 0   is the same as   P[r] % k == P[l] % k
 *
 * So the map is keyed on the remainder, not on the sum itself,
 * and it never grows beyond k entries.
 */
int subarraysDivByK(int[] a, int k) {
    int[] seen = new int[k];        // remainders are 0..k-1, so an array beats a map
    seen[0] = 1;                    // the empty prefix again

    int sum = 0, count = 0;

    for (int v : a) {
        sum += v;

        // Java's % returns a NEGATIVE remainder for negative operands,
        // so -1 % 5 is -1, not 4. This normalisation is mandatory,
        // and forgetting it is the single most common failure here.
        int r = ((sum % k) + k) % k;

        count += seen[r];
        seen[r]++;
    }
    return count;
}

Choosing the skeleton

Many range queries
Skeleton A. Build the array once in the constructor; the whole point is that the queries are then free.
Count subarrays
Skeleton B. Do not build the array — you only ever need the current prefix and a tally of earlier ones.
Divisible by k
The modular variant, keyed on the normalised remainder. An int[k] beats a HashMap.
A multiple of k, length ≥ 2
Store the first index at which each remainder appeared rather than a count, so you can enforce the minimum length.
Balance point
Compare left against total − left − a[i] as you sweep. No map and no array at all.
The three bugs that actually happenOmitting the {0:1} seed — every subarray that starts at index 0 goes uncounted, and the answer is quietly too low on exactly the inputs where the prefix first equals k. Negative remainders — Java's % can return a negative value, so seen[sum % k] throws or silently mis-buckets; always normalise with ((x % k) + k) % k. int accumulation — 10⁵ elements of 10⁹ overflows long before anything looks wrong, and the count comes back plausible but incorrect.

Six prefixes, three different keys

303 and 724 use the array directly. 560 and 930 key the map on the sum. 974 and 523 key it on the remainder — the same skeleton with one line changed.

Anchor 1 · LC 560 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every pair (l, r) with a fresh inner sum. O(n³), or O(n²) if the inner loop accumulates as it goes.
Why not a window
Because nums[i] may be negative. Extending the window can raise or lower the sum, so "shrink while too large" is not a valid rule. Say this out loud — it is the step that shows you chose the pattern rather than guessed it.
The reformulation
A subarray ending at r sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equalled P[r] − k. That turns a search over ranges into a lookup on a single number.
Why counts, not positions
Several earlier prefixes may share a value, and each one yields a distinct subarray. Step 5 of the trace adds two at once for exactly this reason.
Edge cases
Seed {0:1}. Look up before inserting, which matters when k = 0. Accumulate in long.
LC 560 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // prefix value -> how many times it has occurred
        Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1);            // the empty prefix

        long sum = 0;
        int count = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            sum += v;

            // Every earlier prefix equal to (sum - k) marks the
            // start of a distinct subarray ending here.
            count += seen.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);

            // Insert AFTER the lookup: with k == 0 the keys coincide.
            seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return count;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 974 — the path to the solution

Brute force
All O(n²) subarrays, testing each sum for divisibility. Too slow at n = 3×10⁴.
The observation
(P[r] − P[l]) % k == 0 is the same statement as P[r] % k == P[l] % k. So the question becomes "how many earlier prefixes share my remainder?" — the counting skeleton with the key changed.
Why an array beats a map
There are only k possible remainders, so int[k] is exact, faster, and needs no boxing.
The real difficulty
Java defines % to take the sign of the dividend, so -1 % 5 is -1, not 4. Indexing an array with that throws; using it as a map key silently splits one remainder class into two and returns a wrong count.
The fix
((sum % k) + k) % k. Write it every time, even when the input looks non-negative — the running sum can still go negative.
LC 974 · O(n) time, O(k) space
class Solution {
    public int subarraysDivByK(int[] nums, int k) {
        // There are only k possible remainders, so index them directly.
        int[] seen = new int[k];
        seen[0] = 1;                // the empty prefix

        int sum = 0, count = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            sum += v;

            // Java's % takes the sign of the dividend: -1 % 5 == -1.
            // Normalise into [0, k) or this indexes out of bounds.
            int r = ((sum % k) + k) % k;

            // Every earlier prefix with the same remainder gives a
            // subarray whose sum is divisible by k.
            count += seen[r];
            seen[r]++;
        }
        return count;
    }
}

303 · Range Sum Query — Immutable skeleton A

Path: summing the range per call is O(n) each, and the problem says sumRange is called up to 10⁴ times. The word immutable in the title is the hint: the array never changes, so precomputing is safe.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim. Build P in the constructor, return P[r+1] − P[l].

Watch for: sizing P at n instead of n+1. It compiles, and then l = 0 needs a branch that is easy to get wrong.

724 · Find Pivot Index skeleton A, streamed

Path: computing both sides for every candidate is O(n²). One total plus a running left sum makes it O(n) with no array.

Delta: take total first, then sweep keeping left. The right side is total − left − nums[i]; return i the first time the two match.

Watch for: index 0 is a legal pivot with an empty left side summing to 0 — so test before adding nums[i] to left, not after.

930 · Binary Subarrays With Sum skeleton B

Path: the values are only 0 and 1, so the prefix sum is non-decreasing and bounded by n. That means the map can be a plain array.

Delta: skeleton B with int[n + 1] in place of the HashMap, indexed by the prefix sum itself. Everything else is unchanged.

Watch for: goal may be 0, which makes the lookup key equal the current sum — the look-up-before-insert ordering is what keeps that correct.

523 · Continuous Subarray Sum skeleton B, modular

Path: same remainder reformulation, but the problem demands a subarray of length at least two, so a raw count is not enough.

Delta: store the first index at which each remainder appeared, not a count. On a repeat, return true only when i − firstIndex ≥ 2. Seed with remainder 0 at index −1 so a qualifying prefix from the start still works.

Watch for: record the index only when the remainder is new — overwriting it destroys the earliest occurrence and loses valid answers.

If you only drill twoDo 560 and 974. 560 is the counting reformulation in its plainest form, and the look-up-before-insert ordering it teaches applies to every problem on this slide. 974 adds the one piece of Java-specific knowledge in this pattern — that % can return a negative remainder — which is the difference between a correct submission and a runtime exception.

Java 17 has no scan, so keep the state to one line

Every problem here starts from the running total, and a running total is a scan: each output depends on the one before it. Java 17 streams have no scan stage, so the prefix array comes from a map over a one-element array. That is the only lambda in these solutions that carries state, and everything after it reads the finished array and is clean. 930 avoids the scan altogether.

LC 303 · Range Sum Query — Immutable · stateful
class NumArray {
    private final int[] p;   // p[i] = sum of the first i values

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        // Java 17 streams have no scan, so the running total is
        // a stateful map, run once and in order.
        int[] run = {0};
        p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        return p[right + 1] - p[left];
    }
}
LC 724 · Find Pivot Index · stateful
class Solution {
    public int pivotIndex(int[] nums) {
        int total = Arrays.stream(nums).sum();
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
        // left = p[i], right = total - p[i] - nums[i]; equal
        // exactly when 2·p[i] + nums[i] == total.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length)
                .filter(i -> 2 * p[i] + nums[i] == total)
                .findFirst().orElse(-1);
    }
}
LC 560 · Subarray Sum Equals K · stateful
class Solution {
    public int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // 1 · the only stateful line: the running-total scan
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
        // 2 · clean from here on: prefix value -> its indices,
        //     ascending (groupingBy keeps encounter order)
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> at = IntStream
                .rangeClosed(0, n).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> p[i]));
        // subarrays ending at j: earlier i, p[i] == p[j] - k
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                .map(j -> below(at.get(p[j] - k), j))
                .sum();
    }

    // how many indices in the ascending list are below j
    static int below(List<Integer> idx, int j) {
        if (idx == null) return 0;
        int pos = Collections.binarySearch(idx, j);
        return pos >= 0 ? pos : -pos - 1;
    }
}
LC 930 · Binary Subarrays With Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int numSubarraysWithSum(int[] nums, int goal) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // No scan: the positions of the ones, fenced by -1, n
        int[] one = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(-1),
                IntStream.concat(IntStream.range(0, n)
                                .filter(i -> nums[i] == 1),
                        IntStream.of(n)))
                .toArray();
        if (goal == 0)        // all-zero runs: z(z+1)/2 each
            return IntStream.range(1, one.length)
                    .map(j -> one[j] - one[j - 1] - 1)
                    .map(z -> z * (z + 1) / 2)
                    .sum();
        // Ones i .. i+goal-1: the left end sits in the gap
        // before them, the right end in the gap after them.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, one.length - 1 - goal)
                .map(i -> (one[i] - one[i - 1])
                        * (one[i + goal] - one[i + goal - 1]))
                .sum();
    }
}
LC 974 · Subarray Sums Divisible by K · stateful
class Solution {
    public int subarraysDivByK(int[] nums, int k) {
        // Prefix remainders; floorMod keeps them in [0, k).
        int[] s = {0};
        IntStream rems = Arrays.stream(nums)
                .map(v -> s[0] = Math.floorMod(s[0] + v, k));
        Map<Integer, Long> byRem = IntStream
                .concat(IntStream.of(0), rems).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        x -> x, Collectors.counting()));
        // Equal remainders at both ends make a divisible sum,
        // and order stops mattering: c prefixes give c(c-1)/2.
        return (int) byRem.values().stream()
                .mapToLong(c -> c * (c - 1) / 2)
                .sum();
    }
}
LC 523 · Continuous Subarray Sum · stateful
class Solution {
    public boolean checkSubarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // Prefix remainders mod k (long: k can be 2^31 - 1)
        long[] run = {0};
        int[] rem = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(
                        v -> (int) (run[0] = (run[0] + v) % k)))
                .toArray();
        // The FIRST index each remainder appears at
        Map<Integer, Integer> first = IntStream
                .range(0, rem.length).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(i -> rem[i], i -> i,
                                          (a, b) -> a));
        // A repeat two or more positions later is a subarray of
        // length >= 2 whose sum is a multiple of k.
        return IntStream.range(0, rem.length)
                .anyMatch(j -> first.get(rem[j]) < j - 1);
    }
}
Why the scan is statefulmap(v -> run[0] += v) gives the right answer only because a sequential stream calls it in encounter order. Add .parallel() and the totals are garbage. Keep that lambda to one line with one job, and the rest of the pipeline stays pure. The one-pass map version of 560 is shorter and O(n), but it puts the entire loop body inside a single lambda, and at that point it is the loop wearing a costume.
Counting pairs is a grouping974 counts pairs of equal remainders, and for pairs the order no longer matters. c prefixes that share a remainder give c·(c−1)/2 subarrays, so groupingBy(counting()) is the whole algorithm. 560 cannot do the same, because when k ≠ 0 the order i < j matters. That is why it pays for a binary search per end.

Record the edges of a range, not its contents

Adding v to every element of [l, r] costs O(r − l). Do that a hundred thousand times and you have an O(n·q) solution that times out. A difference array records each update as two numbers — a rise at l and a fall at r+1 — and reconstructs the whole array once at the end with a single prefix sum.

The invariant

D[i] holds the change between position i−1 and position i. Running a prefix sum over D therefore rebuilds the original array exactly.

So a range update becomes: D[l] += v and D[r+1] -= v. The first says "from here on, everything is v higher"; the second cancels it once the range ends.

Every update is O(1) regardless of range width. One O(n) sweep at the end turns all of them into the final array.

Why r + 1, and why size n + 1

The range is inclusive of r, so the cancellation must land on the first index after it. Writing D[r] -= v silently drops the last element of every range.

That means r + 1 can equal n, so D needs length n + 1. The extra slot is a deliberate overflow bin: it is written but never read, which removes the bounds check entirely.

This is the exact inverse of a prefix sum. One turns an array into its running totals; the other turns running totals back into an array.

Applies when

Many range updates land before any read. Also for interval occupancy — "is any point covered more than C times?" — where each interval contributes +1 at its start and −1 just past its end.

Does not apply when

Reads and writes interleave, since every read needs a fresh O(n) rebuild. That case wants a Fenwick or segment tree with lazy propagation. Also when the coordinate range is enormous and sparse — then sort the events instead of allocating an array.

Complexity

O(1) per update, O(n) for the single rebuild, so O(q + n) overall. Space is O(n). Use long when many updates can stack on one index.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"add v to all elements between i and j" · "apply all the updates and return the final array" · "bookings[i] = [first, last, seats]" · "passengers get on at from and off at to" · "does the capacity ever exceed" · "shift the letters in the range". The decisive shape is a list of intervals with a value, combined with the fact that nothing is read until every update has been applied.

LC 1109 traced on three bookings over five flights

Bookings are [[1,2,10], [2,3,20], [2,5,25]] with n = 5, and flight labels are 1-indexed. Each booking touches exactly two cells of D, whatever its width. One prefix sweep at the end produces all five answers.

StepWrites to DD after the stepWhy
start—[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]Length n+1 = 6; flight k lives at index k−1.
[1,2,10]D[0] += 10, D[2] −= 10[10, 0, −10, 0, 0, 0]Rise at flight 1, cancel just past flight 2.
[2,3,20]D[1] += 20, D[3] −= 20[10, 20, −10, −20, 0, 0]Rise at flight 2, cancel just past flight 3.
[2,5,25]D[1] += 25, D[5] −= 25[10, 45, −10, −20, 0, −25]Two rises now stack at index 1. The cancel lands in the bin.
sweeprunning total[10, 55, 45, 25, 25]10 → 10+45 → 55−10 → 45−20 → 25+0.
The two rises stacking at index 1Bookings [2,3,20] and [2,5,25] both start at flight 2, so D[1] accumulates 45. Nothing special is needed for that — += already composes. It is the reason the pattern handles overlapping intervals without any sorting or merging, which is what separates it from the interval-merging pattern.

Two writes per update, one sweep at the end

The core is four lines. The variants differ only in what the array counts — seats, passengers, coverage, or a letter shift — and in whether you check a condition during the sweep or afterwards.

The template — apply many range updates, then rebuild once
/**
 * Apply q range updates in O(q), then rebuild in O(n).
 * D[i] holds the CHANGE between position i-1 and position i,
 * so a prefix sum over D reconstructs the array.
 */
int[] applyRangeUpdates(int n, int[][] updates) {
    // n + 1, not n: r + 1 can equal n, and that slot is a
    // deliberate overflow bin — written, never read.
    long[] D = new long[n + 1];

    for (int[] u : updates) {
        int l = u[0], r = u[1], v = u[2];

        D[l]     += v;      // from here on, everything is v higher
        D[r + 1] -= v;      // r + 1, NOT r — the range includes r
    }

    int[] out = new int[n];
    long running = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        running += D[i];            // the running total IS the value
        out[i] = (int) running;
    }
    return out;
}
Variant · check a capacity during the sweep (LC 1094)
// When the question is "does it ever exceed C?", you do not need
// the finished array — bail out the moment the running total breaks.
boolean carPooling(int[][] trips, int capacity) {
    int[] D = new int[1001];        // the statement bounds locations at 1000

    for (int[] t : trips) {
        int num = t[0], from = t[1], to = t[2];

        D[from] += num;
        D[to]   -= num;             // NOT to + 1: the passenger leaves AT `to`,
                                    // so that stop is already free.
    }

    int onboard = 0;
    for (int v : D) {
        onboard += v;
        if (onboard > capacity) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
Variant · sparse coordinates, so sort events instead (LC 1943)
// When positions run to 1e9, you cannot allocate the array.
// Keep only the endpoints in a TreeMap and sweep the keys in order.
List<List<Long>> splitPainting(int[][] segments) {
    TreeMap<Integer, Long> d = new TreeMap<>();

    for (int[] s : segments) {
        d.merge(s[0],  (long) s[2], Long::sum);
        d.merge(s[1], -(long) s[2], Long::sum);
    }

    List<List<Long>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    long running = 0;
    Integer prev = null;

    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Long> e : d.entrySet()) {
        // The stretch from prev to this key carries the previous total.
        if (prev != null && running != 0) {
            out.add(List.of((long) prev, (long) e.getKey(), running));
        }
        running += e.getValue();
        prev = e.getKey();
    }
    return out;
}

The knobs

Array size
n + 1 whenever the range is inclusive of r. If the statement bounds coordinates directly, size to that bound plus one.
Where the fall goes
r + 1 for an inclusive range; r when the interval is half-open, as it is for a passenger who gets off at a stop. Read the statement carefully — this one line decides correctness.
Dense or sparse
An array when coordinates are bounded by roughly 10⁶; a TreeMap of events when they run to 10⁹.
When to read
After the sweep if you need the whole array; during it if you only need to test a threshold, which lets you exit early.
Element type
long when many updates can stack on one index. The trace above reached 55 from three bookings; 10⁵ bookings of 10⁴ seats overflows int.
The three bugs that actually happenD[r] -= v instead of D[r + 1] -= v — silently drops the last element of every range, so the answer is wrong only at the boundaries and passes small tests. Sizing D at n — throws the moment a range ends at the final index, which the example above does. Mixing 1-indexed input with a 0-indexed array — flight k lives at index k−1, and forgetting that shifts every answer by one position.

Six range updates, one idea

370 and 1109 are the template unmodified. 1094 checks a threshold during the sweep. 1893 and 2381 change what the array counts. 1943 replaces the array with sorted events because the coordinates are too large to allocate.

Anchor 1 · LC 1109 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each booking, loop the flights it covers and add the seats. O(q · n), which at 2×10⁴ bookings over 2×10⁴ flights is 4×10⁸ — too slow, and the natural first attempt.
The observation
Nothing is read until every booking has been applied. So the intermediate arrays are wasted work: only the net effect matters.
The reformulation
Record where each booking starts contributing and where it stops. That is two cells regardless of how many flights it spans.
The indexing detail
Flights are 1-indexed in the statement and the array is 0-indexed, so flight f sits at f − 1. The rise goes at first − 1 and the fall at last, which is already (last − 1) + 1.
Edge case
A booking ending at flight n writes to index n, which is why the array has n + 1 slots.
LC 1109 · O(q + n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] corpFlightBookings(int[][] bookings, int n) {
        // n + 1 so that a booking ending at flight n has somewhere
        // to put its cancellation.
        long[] D = new long[n + 1];

        for (int[] b : bookings) {
            int first = b[0], last = b[1], seats = b[2];

            // Flights are 1-indexed; the array is 0-indexed.
            D[first - 1] += seats;   // rise at the first flight
            D[last]      -= seats;   // (last - 1) + 1 — just past the last
        }

        int[] out = new int[n];
        long running = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            running += D[i];         // the running total is the seat count
            out[i] = (int) running;
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 1094 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each trip, add its passengers to every location it spans, then scan for a violation. O(q · M).
The alternative worth naming
Sort the pick-up and drop-off events and sweep them with a running count. That is the same algorithm; the difference array is simply the version that does not need a sort, because the statement bounds locations at 1000.
The detail that decides correctness
A passenger boards at from and leaves at to, so they are not in the car at to — the interval is half-open. The fall therefore goes at to, not to + 1.
Why that matters
Without it, two trips where one ends exactly where the next begins are counted as overlapping, and a car that is actually fine is reported as over capacity.
The early exit
You never need the finished array — only whether the running total ever breaks the limit. Return as soon as it does.
LC 1094 · O(q + M) time, O(M) space
class Solution {
    public boolean carPooling(int[][] trips, int capacity) {
        // The statement bounds locations at 1000.
        int[] D = new int[1001];

        for (int[] t : trips) {
            int num = t[0], from = t[1], to = t[2];

            D[from] += num;
            // The interval is HALF-OPEN: the passenger is gone by `to`,
            // so the fall lands on `to` itself, not to + 1. This is what
            // lets one trip end exactly where the next begins.
            D[to]   -= num;
        }

        int onboard = 0;
        for (int delta : D) {
            onboard += delta;
            if (onboard > capacity) return false;   // no need to finish
        }
        return true;
    }
}

370 · Range Addition template Premium

Path: the statement is the pattern with no story around it — apply k range additions to a zero array and return the result.

Delta: none. The template verbatim, with 0-indexed inclusive ranges, so the fall goes at r + 1.

Premium: locked behind LeetCode's paywall. 1109 above is the same problem and is free — solve that instead and you have covered this one entirely.

1893 · Check if All Integers in a Range Are Covered template

Path: checking each value against every interval is O(q · range), which is fine at these limits — but the difference array makes it one pass and generalises.

Delta: the array counts coverage rather than a value, so each interval contributes +1 and −1. After the sweep, the answer is "was the running total ever zero inside [left, right]?"

Watch for: values run 1 to 50, so size the array 52 and use inclusive ranges — the fall at end + 1.

1943 · Describe the Painting sparse events

Path: the coordinate range makes a dense array wasteful, and the output is a list of maximal stretches rather than per-index values.

Delta: a TreeMap keyed on endpoints replaces the array; iterating it in key order is the sweep. Between consecutive keys the running total is constant, and that stretch becomes one output segment.

Watch for: emit a segment only when the running total is non-zero — gaps between painted regions must not appear in the output. Sums reach 10⁹, so accumulate in long.

2381 · Shifting Letters II template

Path: applying each shift character by character is O(q · n). The accumulated shift per position is exactly what a difference array computes.

Delta: a shift is +1 or −1 depending on the direction flag, so the update value is direction == 1 ? 1 : -1. During the sweep, the running total is the net shift for that character.

Watch for: the net shift can be large and negative, so normalise with ((shift % 26) + 26) % 26 before adding it to the letter — the same signed-remainder trap that appears whenever Java's % meets a negative operand.

If you only drill twoDo 1109 and 1094. 1109 is the template in its cleanest form and forces you to get the 1-indexed-to-0-indexed shift right. 1094 is the one that teaches the half-open distinction — whether the fall belongs at r or r + 1 — which is the only genuinely subtle decision this pattern ever asks you to make.

Build the difference array with a collect; only the sweep carries state

Each update touches two cells of a difference array. Accumulating those is a textbook mutable reduction: a supplier makes the array, an accumulator applies one update, and a combiner adds two partial arrays, so it is even safe in parallel. The sweep that turns differences back into values is a scan, and it is the one stateful line in each solution.

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 370 · Range Addition · stateful
class Solution {
    public int[] getModifiedArray(int length, int[][] updates) {
        // The difference array is a mutable reduction with a
        // real combiner: +inc at start, -inc just past the end.
        int[] diff = Arrays.stream(updates).collect(
                () -> new int[length + 1],
                (d, u) -> {
                    d[u[0]] += u[2];
                    d[u[1] + 1] -= u[2];
                },
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        // Sweeping back to values is a scan: the stateful line.
        int[] run = {0};
        return Arrays.stream(diff, 0, length)
                .map(d -> run[0] += d)
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 1109 · Corporate Flight Bookings · stateful
class Solution {
    public int[] corpFlightBookings(int[][] bookings, int n) {
        // 370 with 1-indexed flights: +seats at first - 1,
        // -seats at last (just past the range, 0-indexed).
        int[] diff = Arrays.stream(bookings).collect(
                () -> new int[n + 1],
                (d, bk) -> {
                    d[bk[0] - 1] += bk[2];
                    d[bk[1]] -= bk[2];
                },
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        int[] run = {0};
        return Arrays.stream(diff, 0, n)
                .map(d -> run[0] += d)
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 1094 · Car Pooling · stateful
class Solution {
    public boolean carPooling(int[][] trips, int capacity) {
        // Pick-ups add at "from", drop-offs subtract at "to":
        // a passenger is out of the car at the stop they leave.
        int[] diff = Arrays.stream(trips).collect(
                () -> new int[1001],
                (d, t) -> { d[t[1]] += t[0]; d[t[2]] -= t[0]; },
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        // Sweep the load and stop at the first overload.
        int[] load = {0};
        return Arrays.stream(diff)
                .allMatch(d -> (load[0] += d) <= capacity);
    }
}
LC 1893 · Check if All the Integers in a Range Are Covered · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean isCovered(int[][] ranges, int left,
                             int right) {
        // At most 50 points × 50 ranges: brute force is clean,
        // instant, and needs no difference array at all.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(left, right)
                .allMatch(x -> Arrays.stream(ranges)
                        .anyMatch(r -> r[0] <= x && x <= r[1]));
    }
}
LC 1943 · Describe the Painting · stateful
class Solution {
    public List<List<Long>> splitPainting(int[][] segments) {
        // position -> net colour change. Keep every key, even a
        // zero: a mix can change while its sum stays the same.
        TreeMap<Integer, Long> delta = Arrays.stream(segments)
                .flatMap(s -> Stream.of(
                        new long[]{ s[0], s[2] },
                        new long[]{ s[1], -s[2] }))
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> (int) e[0],
                        TreeMap::new,
                        Collectors.summingLong(e -> e[1])));
        List<Integer> at = new ArrayList<>(delta.keySet());
        // mix[i] = colour sum on [at[i], at[i+1]): the scan
        long[] run = {0};
        long[] mix = delta.values().stream()
                .mapToLong(d -> run[0] += d).toArray();
        return IntStream.range(0, at.size() - 1)
                .filter(i -> mix[i] > 0)
                .mapToObj(i -> List.of((long) at.get(i),
                        (long) at.get(i + 1), mix[i]))
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 2381 · Shifting Letters II · stateful
class Solution {
    public String shiftingLetters(String s, int[][] shifts) {
        int n = s.length();
        // +1 forward, -1 backward, over [start, end]
        int[] diff = Arrays.stream(shifts).collect(
                () -> new int[n + 1],
                (d, t) -> {
                    int v = t[2] == 1 ? 1 : -1;
                    d[t[0]] += v;
                    d[t[1] + 1] -= v;
                },
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        // The sweep to each letter's net shift is the scan.
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] shift = Arrays.stream(diff, 0, n)
                .map(d -> run[0] += d).toArray();
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(i -> s.charAt(i) - 'a' + shift[i])
                .map(x -> 'a' + Math.floorMod(x, 26))
                .collect(StringBuilder::new,
                         StringBuilder::appendCodePoint,
                         StringBuilder::append)
                .toString();
    }
}
A collect with a real combiner is cleanArrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]) merges two partial difference arrays correctly, so the accumulation is safe in parallel. That is exactly what the three-argument collect is for. The contrast is the sweep after it: in Java 17 it has no correct combiner, because each output needs everything before it. So the one stateful line is always the sweep, never the build.
1943's trap is the same in a streamDrop the zero-change keys, or sum into a HashMap and rebuild the order some other way, and you merge two different colour mixes that happen to have the same sum. The TreeMap collector keeps every event point, so each output segment really is a single mix.

Throw away everything that can never win again

Keep a stack whose values are sorted. When a new element arrives that dominates what is on top, that top can never be the answer for anything further right — so pop it, and settle its answer on the way out. Each element is pushed once and popped once, which is why the whole thing is O(n) despite the inner loop.

The invariant

The stack is always monotone — strictly increasing or strictly decreasing from bottom to top, depending on the question. Everything on it is still waiting for its answer.

A new element a[i] arrives. While it beats the top, the top has found what it was waiting for: pop it and record i as its answer. Then push i.

Anything left on the stack at the end never found an answer — those get the default, usually 0 or −1.

Why it is O(n), not O(n²)

The while loop looks quadratic. It is not: an index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so across the entire run the inner loop body executes at most n times in total — not n times per iteration.

Total work is 2n operations, amortised O(1) per element. Being able to state that in one sentence is worth more than the code: it is the follow-up interviewers ask when the loop looks nested.

Store indices, not values. You almost always need the distance i − stack.peek(), and an index gives you the value for free while the reverse is not true.

Applies when

Every element needs to know about the nearest element to one side that is bigger or smaller than it. Also for rectangle problems, where a bar's reach is bounded by the first shorter bar on each side.

Does not apply when

You need the nearest element by position under some other predicate, or the maximum over a sliding window of fixed width — a stack cannot evict from the bottom, which is what that requires.

Complexity

O(n) time by the push-once, pop-once argument. O(n) space worst case, when the input is already sorted so nothing is ever popped until the end.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the next greater element" · "how many days until a warmer temperature" · "the first element to the right that is larger" · "the largest rectangle" · "the span" · "the nearest smaller value". The giveaway is "nearest" or "first … to the right/left" combined with a size comparison. If the comparison is by position only, it is not this pattern.

LC 739 traced on [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73]

For each day, how many days until a warmer one? The stack holds days still waiting for warmth, and it stays strictly decreasing in temperature. Watch step 6: one arriving value settles two waiting days at once, and step 7 settles two more.

Why the leftovers get zero for freeIndices 6 and 7 are still on the stack when the loop ends, meaning no warmer day ever arrived. Because Java initialises new int[n] to zeros and the problem defines "no warmer day" as 0, they need no handling at all. When the default is −1 instead — as it is for next-greater-element problems — fill the array first, or drain the stack explicitly at the end.

One loop, four questions, two places to record

Flip the comparison to switch between greater and smaller. Record on pop for "next", record from peek() before pushing for "previous". That is the entire configuration space.

The template — next greater element, by index
/**
 * For each i, the index of the first j > i with a[j] > a[i].
 * Stack holds INDICES whose answer is still unknown, and their
 * values are strictly DECREASING from bottom to top.
 *
 * Each index is pushed once and popped at most once  ->  O(n).
 */
int[] nextGreater(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] ans = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(ans, -1);                  // default when nothing is ever greater

    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // ArrayDeque, never java.util.Stack

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

        // a[i] dominates the top, so the top's wait is over.
        while (!stack.isEmpty() && a[stack.peek()] < a[i]) {
            ans[stack.pop()] = i;          // settle it ON THE WAY OUT
        }

        stack.push(i);                     // now i waits its turn
    }
    // Anything still on the stack never found a greater element,
    // and keeps the -1 default.
    return ans;
}
The four configurations
// NEXT greater  — settle on pop, decreasing stack
while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[i]) ans[st.pop()] = i;
st.push(i);

// NEXT smaller  — same shape, comparison flipped
while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] > a[i]) ans[st.pop()] = i;
st.push(i);

// PREVIOUS greater — read peek() BEFORE pushing
while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] <= a[i]) st.pop();
ans[i] = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
st.push(i);

// PREVIOUS smaller — same, comparison flipped
while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] >= a[i]) st.pop();
ans[i] = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
st.push(i);

// CIRCULAR (the array wraps) — walk 2n and take i % n.
// Push only during the first pass, so nothing is settled twice.
for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
    int j = i % n;
    while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[j]) ans[st.pop()] = a[j];
    if (i < n) st.push(j);
}
The rectangle variant — both boundaries at once (LC 84)
// A bar of height h extends left until the first SHORTER bar and
// right until the next shorter bar. The pop moment gives you both:
// the new element is the right boundary, and the item beneath the
// popped one is the left boundary.
int largestRectangleArea(int[] h) {
    Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
    int best = 0, n = h.length;

    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        // A virtual bar of height 0 at index n forces the stack
        // to drain, so no case needs separate handling afterwards.
        int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : h[i];

        while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] >= cur) {
            int height = h[st.pop()];

            // Left boundary is the item now on top; if the stack is
            // empty this bar reached all the way to index 0.
            int left  = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
            int width = i - left - 1;

            best = Math.max(best, height * width);
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return best;
}

The knobs

Direction of the stack
Decreasing for "greater" questions, increasing for "smaller". Get this backwards and the stack drains immediately, giving every element the same wrong answer.
Where you record
On pop for "next"; from peek() just before push for "previous".
Strict or not
< versus <= decides how equal values are treated. For rectangles it does not change the maximum — an equal-height bar is handled by its twin — but for "strictly greater" questions it does.
Sentinel
Iterating to n inclusive with a virtual 0 drains the stack automatically and removes the post-loop cleanup entirely.
Index or value
Push indices. You can always read the value, and only the index gives you the width.
The three bugs that actually happenUsing java.util.Stack — it is synchronised, slower, and iterates bottom-to-top which is the reverse of what you expect; use ArrayDeque. Pushing values instead of indices — then the width i − left − 1 is uncomputable and the rectangle problems become impossible. Forgetting the empty-stack case for the left boundary — when the stack empties, the bar reaches index 0, so the left boundary is −1 and the width is i, not i − 1.

Six stacks, four of them the same loop

739, 496, 503 and 901 are the template with the comparison or the traversal adjusted. 84 uses the pop moment to recover both boundaries of a rectangle, and 85 reduces to 84 applied row by row.

Anchor 1 · LC 739 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each day, scan forward for the first warmer one. O(n²), which at n = 10⁵ is 10¹⁰ and hopeless.
What the brute force wastes
On a long cold spell, every day rescans the same run of cold days. The scan is repeatedly re-deriving something already known.
The observation
If day j is warmer than day i and comes after it, then day i can never be the answer for anything to the right of j — j is closer and warmer. So i can be discarded permanently the moment j appears.
What "discard" means
A stack of days still waiting, kept decreasing in temperature. Each arriving day pops everything it beats, settling those answers.
Why indices
The answer is how many days, so you need i − poppedIndex. Storing temperatures alone makes that impossible.
Edge case
Days never warmed stay on the stack and keep the 0 default — which is exactly what the problem asks for.
LC 739 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] temperatures) {
        int n = temperatures.length;
        int[] ans = new int[n];                    // zeros are the correct default

        // Indices of days still waiting; their temperatures
        // decrease from the bottom of the stack to the top.
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

            // Today is warmer than the day on top, so that day's
            // wait ends here. Settle it and keep going — today may
            // settle several days at once.
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && temperatures[stack.peek()] < temperatures[i]) {
                int day = stack.pop();
                ans[day] = i - day;                // the distance, hence indices
            }

            stack.push(i);
        }
        // Days left on the stack never warmed: ans stays 0.
        return ans;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 84 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every pair (l, r), taking the minimum height between them. O(n³), or O(n²) carrying a running minimum.
The reframing
Stop enumerating rectangles. Instead ask, for each bar, what is the widest rectangle whose height is exactly that bar? Every maximal rectangle is limited by its shortest bar, so this enumeration is complete.
What that needs
For each bar, the first shorter bar to its left and the first shorter bar to its right. Those two indices give the width directly.
The insight
Both boundaries fall out of a single pass. When a bar is popped, the arriving element is its right boundary, and the item now exposed on the stack is its left boundary. No second pass is needed.
The sentinel
Iterate to n inclusive with a virtual bar of height 0. It forces every remaining bar to pop with the correct right boundary, removing the drain loop and the bugs that live in it.
Width, carefully
i − left − 1, where left is −1 when the stack empties. Deriving that from the trace once is worth more than memorising it.
LC 84 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int largestRectangleArea(int[] heights) {
        int n = heights.length, best = 0;
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

        // i == n is a VIRTUAL bar of height 0 that drains the stack.
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : heights[i];

            while (!stack.isEmpty() && heights[stack.peek()] >= cur) {
                int height = heights[stack.pop()];

                // Right boundary is i. Left boundary is whatever the
                // pop exposed — or -1 if this bar reaches index 0.
                int left  = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
                int width = i - left - 1;

                best = Math.max(best, height * width);
            }
            stack.push(i);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

496 · Next Greater Element I next greater

Path: the nested-loop version is O(n·m) and passes at these limits, so say it first. The point of the problem is the decomposition, not the speed.

Delta: run the template over nums2 to get every element's next greater, storing results in a HashMap<value, answer> — the statement guarantees distinct values, which is what makes keying by value safe. Then map nums1 through it.

Watch for: elements left on the stack have no greater element, so their map entry must be −1. Easiest is to drain the stack after the loop.

503 · Next Greater Element II circular

Path: the naive fix duplicates the array and runs the template on 2n elements. That works and costs O(n) extra space — worth mentioning before the cleaner version.

Delta: loop i from 0 to 2n and index with i % n. Push only while i < n: the second pass exists solely to settle leftovers, and pushing again would let elements wait forever.

Watch for: the answer here is the value, not the distance, so record a[j] rather than j.

901 · Online Stock Span previous greater

Path: keeping every price and scanning back is O(n) per call, O(n²) overall. The span is really "distance to the previous greater price", which is this pattern in streaming form.

Delta: the stack is a field, surviving between calls. Push (price, span) pairs; when popping, absorb the popped span into your own — that merged count is what makes the amortised O(1) work without storing the whole history.

Watch for: pop while topPrice <= price, inclusive. The problem counts days with a price equal to today's as part of the span.

85 · Maximal Rectangle rectangle × rows

Path: enumerating all sub-rectangles is O((rows·cols)²). The reduction is the whole problem: treat each row as the base of a histogram whose bar heights are the counts of consecutive 1s above.

Delta: maintain one heights[] array across rows — heights[c] = matrix[r][c] == '1' ? heights[c] + 1 : 0 — and call the LC 84 routine on it after each row.

Watch for: the reset to 0 on a '0' cell is what makes the histogram correct; incrementing unconditionally silently merges rectangles across gaps. Solve 84 first — this problem is unreasonable without it.

If you only drill twoDo 739 and 84. 739 makes the push-once-pop-once argument concrete and forces you to store indices. 84 is where the pattern earns its reputation: the realisation that a single pop yields both boundaries is the idea that makes the Hard tag disappear, and 85 becomes a ten-line wrapper once you have it.

No stack: jump along the answers you have already found

A monotonic stack is state that every element both reads and changes, and no Java 17 stream stage can hold that. But the stack's contents can be read out of the answer array itself. To find the next warmer day after i, start at i + 1 and keep jumping to that day's own next warmer day: every day a jump skips was no warmer than the day it left from. Fill the answers right to left, and each one becomes a short, pure chain over answers already written, with the total work still O(n).

LC 739 · Daily Temperatures · stateful
class Solution {
    public int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t) {
        int n = t.length;
        int[] next = new int[n];   // next warmer day, or n
        // Right to left. From i + 1, jump along answers already
        // found: a jump from j to next[j] skips only days no
        // warmer than t[j], so none of them can beat t[i].
        IntStream.iterate(n - 1, i -> i >= 0, i -> i - 1)
                .forEach(i -> next[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i + 1, j -> next[j])
                        .filter(j -> j == n || t[j] > t[i])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(i -> next[i] == n ? 0 : next[i] - i)
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 496 · Next Greater Element I · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] nextGreaterElement(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
        int n = nums2.length;
        Map<Integer, Integer> pos = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(i -> nums2[i],
                                          i -> i));
        // At most 1000 × 1000: scan right of each value's
        // position for the first greater one. O(m·n), and pure.
        return Arrays.stream(nums1)
                .map(x -> IntStream.range(pos.get(x) + 1, n)
                        .map(j -> nums2[j])
                        .filter(v -> v > x)
                        .findFirst().orElse(-1))
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 503 · Next Greater Element II · stateful
class Solution {
    public int[] nextGreaterElements(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length, m = 2 * n;
        // Unroll the circle: position p holds nums[p % n]. Then
        // it is 739's jumps over 2n positions, right to left.
        int[] next = new int[m];   // next greater, or m
        IntStream.iterate(m - 1, i -> i >= 0, i -> i - 1)
                .forEach(i -> next[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i + 1, j -> next[j])
                        .filter(j -> j == m
                                || nums[j % n] > nums[i % n])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(i -> next[i] == m ? -1 : nums[next[i] % n])
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 901 · Online Stock Span · stateful
class StockSpanner {
    private final List<Integer> price = new ArrayList<>();
    // prev.get(i) = the last day before i with a higher price
    private final List<Integer> prev = new ArrayList<>();

    public int next(int p) {
        int i = price.size();
        // Jump left along answers already stored. Each day a
        // jump skips was <= the day it left from, so <= p too.
        int j = IntStream.iterate(i - 1, k -> prev.get(k))
                .filter(k -> k < 0 || price.get(k) > p)
                .findFirst().getAsInt();
        price.add(p);
        prev.add(j);
        return i - j;
    }
}
LC 84 · Largest Rectangle in Histogram · stateful
class Solution {
    public int largestRectangleArea(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        int[] left = new int[n];    // previous lower bar, or -1
        int[] right = new int[n];   // next lower bar, or n
        // Two jump fills in opposite directions, as in 739.
        IntStream.range(0, n)
                .forEach(i -> left[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i - 1, j -> left[j])
                        .filter(j -> j < 0 || h[j] < h[i])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        IntStream.iterate(n - 1, i -> i >= 0, i -> i - 1)
                .forEach(i -> right[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i + 1, j -> right[j])
                        .filter(j -> j == n || h[j] < h[i])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        // Bar i is the lowest across (left[i], right[i]).
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(i -> h[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1))
                .max().getAsInt();
    }
}
LC 85 · Maximal Rectangle · stateful
class Solution {
    // Column heights of the '1' runs ending at row "row" - 1
    record Hist(int row, int[] h) {
        Hist next(char[][] m) {
            int[] nh = IntStream.range(0, h.length)
                    .map(c -> m[row][c] == '1' ? h[c] + 1 : 0)
                    .toArray();
            return new Hist(row + 1, nh);
        }
    }

    public int maximalRectangle(char[][] matrix) {
        // Each row's histogram is a pure function of the one
        // above it; then every row is 84 on its own.
        int cols = matrix[0].length;
        return Stream.iterate(new Hist(0, new int[cols]),
                              s -> s.next(matrix))
                .skip(1)
                .limit(matrix.length)
                .mapToInt(s -> largest(s.h()))
                .max().getAsInt();
    }

    // 84, unchanged: jump fills for the lower bars either side
    static int largest(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        int[] left = new int[n], right = new int[n];
        IntStream.range(0, n)
                .forEach(i -> left[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i - 1, j -> left[j])
                        .filter(j -> j < 0 || h[j] < h[i])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        IntStream.iterate(n - 1, i -> i >= 0, i -> i - 1)
                .forEach(i -> right[i] = IntStream
                        .iterate(i + 1, j -> right[j])
                        .filter(j -> j == n || h[j] < h[i])
                        .findFirst().getAsInt());
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(i -> h[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1))
                .max().getAsInt();
    }
}
Why the jumps are still O(n)A jump from j to next[j] skips a block that every later chain skips as well, so no element is walked over twice. It is the stack's amortisation argument, with the answer array playing the stack's part. The fill order is what makes it work: right to left for "next", left to right for "previous". The harness checks sorted, reverse-sorted, flat and sawtooth inputs of 10⁵, and each runs in milliseconds.
Stateful is the honest labelforEach writes next[i] and later iterations read it. That makes next a memo table, and the order of the outer stream carries the correctness, so never make it parallel. What the jumps buy you is that each answer comes from a pure inner pipeline over finished entries, rather than a while loop mutating a Deque inside a lambda. In the interview, still write the stack: it is the version the interviewer is looking for.

A sorted spine that can also drop its oldest element

A monotonic stack discards what is dominated. A monotonic deque does that too, but adds a second eviction rule: elements that have fallen out of the window are removed from the front. Two eviction rules, two ends, and the maximum of every window becomes available in O(1).

The invariant

The deque holds indices whose values are decreasing from front to back. Two consequences follow, and both are used on every step:

  • The front is always the maximum of the current window — no scan needed.
  • Anything smaller than an arriving element is useless forever, because the newcomer is both larger and stays in the window longer.

That second point is the whole justification. A smaller, older element can never be the answer again — so it is not merely delayed, it is dead.

Three moves, always in this order

  1. Expire the front while it has fallen outside the window. This is the rule a stack cannot express.
  2. Evict the back while it is dominated by the arriving value, then push the new index.
  3. Read the front — that is the window's answer.

Each index is pushed once and removed once, from one end or the other, so the total work is 2n — amortised O(1) per element despite two inner loops.

Store indices, never values: the expiry test needs positions.

Applies when

You need the max or min over a sliding range, or a DP transition of the form dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j]) over a moving band of j. The deque replaces the inner max with an O(1) read.

Does not apply when

Arbitrary elements are removed, or you need the k-th largest rather than the largest — those want a heap or a balanced tree. Also when the range is not contiguous.

Complexity

O(n) time by push-once, remove-once, and O(k) space for a window of width k. A heap-based solution is O(n log n) / O(n) — say that first, then beat it.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the max sliding window" · "for each window of size k" · "the absolute difference between any two elements is at most limit" (needs two deques, one for max and one for min) · "at most k steps forward" in a DP · "the shortest subarray with sum at least k" where negatives rule out a plain window. The signal is a max or min over a moving range, evaluated at every position.

LC 239 traced on [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3

The maximum of every window of width 3. The deque never holds more than three indices here, and the front is read directly as each answer — no scanning, no comparison across the window.

Why the expiry test uses <=The window covering index i starts at i − k + 1, so an index is stale exactly when it is <= i − k. Writing < i − k keeps one element too many and silently reports a maximum from outside the window. The test fires at most once per step because only one index can newly expire, but write it as a while anyway — it costs nothing and it is the form that survives when the window width varies.

Expire, evict, read — in that order, every time

The order is not stylistic. Expiring before evicting keeps the deque small; reading last guarantees the front is both in-window and maximal. Swap any two and the answer is wrong on some input.

The template — maximum of every window of width k
/**
 * Deque holds INDICES whose values DECREASE from front to back.
 * front = the maximum of the current window.
 *
 * Each index is added once and removed once (from one end or
 * the other), so the two inner loops still total O(n).
 */
int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] out = new int[n - k + 1];

    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

        // 1 · EXPIRE — the front has slid out of the window.
        // Window covering i starts at i-k+1, so <= i-k is stale.
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) {
            dq.pollFirst();
        }

        // 2 · EVICT — anything smaller than a[i] is dead forever:
        // a[i] is bigger AND outlives it.
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) {
            dq.pollLast();
        }
        dq.offerLast(i);

        // 3 · READ — only once the window is actually full.
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return out;
}
Variant · two deques for max AND min (LC 1438)
// "Absolute difference at most limit" means max - min <= limit,
// so run one decreasing deque and one increasing deque side by
// side. The window is invalid while their fronts differ too much.
int longestSubarray(int[] a, int limit) {
    Deque<Integer> maxD = new ArrayDeque<>();   // decreasing
    Deque<Integer> minD = new ArrayDeque<>();   // increasing
    int l = 0, best = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        while (!maxD.isEmpty() && maxD.peekLast() < a[r]) maxD.pollLast();
        maxD.offerLast(a[r]);
        while (!minD.isEmpty() && minD.peekLast() > a[r]) minD.pollLast();
        minD.offerLast(a[r]);

        // Here the left edge moves for VALIDITY, not for age.
        while (maxD.peekFirst() - minD.peekFirst() > limit) {
            if (maxD.peekFirst() == a[l]) maxD.pollFirst();
            if (minD.peekFirst() == a[l]) minD.pollFirst();
            l++;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
Variant · deque as a DP accelerator (LC 1696, 1425)
// dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[i-k] .. dp[i-1])
// The inner max over a moving band is exactly what the deque gives
// in O(1), turning an O(n*k) DP into O(n).
int maxResult(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    dp[0] = a[0];

    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();   // indices, dp decreasing
    dq.offerLast(0);

    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        // expire: only the last k positions may be jumped from
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() < i - k) dq.pollFirst();

        dp[i] = a[i] + dp[dq.peekFirst()];    // best reachable predecessor

        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dp[dq.peekLast()] <= dp[i]) dq.pollLast();
        dq.offerLast(i);
    }
    return dp[n - 1];
}

The knobs

Direction
Decreasing for a maximum, increasing for a minimum. Both at once when the question is about a spread.
Expiry rule
By age for a fixed-width window (index <= i - k); by validity when the left edge is driven by a condition, as in the two-deque variant.
What you store
Indices when you need positions or an age test; raw values when the eviction is purely by comparison, as in LC 1438.
When to read
Guard with i >= k - 1 for fixed windows, or the first few outputs come from an incomplete window.
< or <= on eviction
<= keeps the deque shorter by discarding equal values. Both are correct for a maximum; prefer <=.
The three bugs that actually happenReading before the window is full — without the i >= k - 1 guard the first k−1 answers are maxima of partial windows. Expiring with < instead of <= — keeps one stale index, so the reported maximum can come from just outside the window. Using peek() on an ArrayDeque and expecting the back — peek() is peekFirst(); always write peekFirst and peekLast explicitly here, because both ends are in play.

Six moving ranges, one sorted spine

239 is the template. 1438 runs two deques. 1696 and 1425 use it to accelerate a DP. 862 and 1499 combine it with prefix sums, which is where the pattern stops looking like a window problem at all.
