Anchor 1 · LC 98 — the path to the solution

The wrong first attempt
Check left.val < node.val < right.val at every node. This is the single most common wrong answer in the whole BST family, and it passes the problem's own first example.
Why it fails
The BST property is about entire subtrees, not immediate children. A node can satisfy its parent while violating an ancestor several levels up, exactly as in the traced tree.
Solution one — the range
Carry (lo, hi) down. Descending left tightens hi to the current value; descending right tightens lo. Every node must lie strictly inside its inherited interval.
Solution two — in-order
A valid BST emits a strictly increasing in-order sequence, so keep a prev pointer and fail the moment prev.val >= node.val. Same complexity, and it generalises to LC 99.
The overflow trap
Use long bounds. A tree consisting of one node holding Integer.MIN_VALUE is valid, but val > Integer.MIN_VALUE rejects it — and that case is in the test set.
Duplicates
Invalid by LeetCode's definition, so the comparisons are strict on both sides.
LC 98 · O(n) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
        // long bounds: a node may legitimately hold Integer.MIN_VALUE
        // or Integer.MAX_VALUE, which int sentinels would reject.
        return valid(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    private boolean valid(TreeNode node, long lo, long hi) {
        if (node == null) return true;

        // Strict on both sides — duplicates are not allowed.
        if (node.val <= lo || node.val >= hi) return false;

        // Descending LEFT tightens the upper bound to this value;
        // descending RIGHT tightens the lower bound. That inherited
        // bound is what a parent-only comparison cannot see.
        return valid(node.left,  lo, node.val)
            && valid(node.right, node.val, hi);
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 99 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Collect the in-order values, sort a copy, compare position by position, and swap back the two that differ. O(n log n) time and O(n) space — correct, and worth stating first.
The reframing
The in-order sequence should be sorted. Swapping two elements of a sorted sequence creates a very specific defect, so you do not need to sort anything — just find it.
The two cases
If the swapped nodes are non-adjacent in the sequence, there are exactly two inversions: take the first element of the first and the second element of the last. If they are adjacent, there is exactly one inversion, and both culprits are in it.
Handling both uniformly
On the first inversion, record first = prev and second = node. On any later inversion, overwrite second = node only. That single rule covers both cases with no branching.
The final step
Swap the two values. The statement forbids changing the structure, so moving nodes is not allowed.
Edge cases
Exactly two nodes are swapped, as guaranteed. The O(1)-space follow-up is Morris traversal — mention it, but the stack version is what to write.
LC 99 · O(n) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    private TreeNode first, second, prev;

    public void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
        inorder(root);
        // Swap VALUES — the structure must not change.
        int tmp = first.val;
        first.val = second.val;
        second.val = tmp;
    }

    private void inorder(TreeNode node) {
        if (node == null) return;

        inorder(node.left);

        // In-order should be strictly increasing. An inversion here
        // means one of the two swapped nodes is involved.
        if (prev != null && prev.val > node.val) {
            // First inversion: BOTH candidates come from it.
            if (first == null) first = prev;
            // Every inversion updates `second`. If the nodes were
            // adjacent there is only one inversion, and this line
            // still captures the right node.
            second = node;
        }
        prev = node;

        inorder(node.right);
    }
}

700 · Search in a BST engine A

Path: scanning the whole tree is O(n) and ignores the ordering. One comparison per level discards half the remaining tree.

Delta: a three-line while loop. Prefer the iterative form — it is O(1) space, and the recursive version buys nothing here.

Watch for: return the node, not a boolean. The subtree rooted there is the expected answer, and returning null when absent is correct rather than an error.

235 · Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST engine A

Path: the general-tree algorithm is O(n) and works, but ignores the ordering entirely. The BST version is O(h) and much shorter.

Delta: while both targets are on the same side of the current node, walk that way. The first node where they split — or that equals one of them — is the answer.

Watch for: a node is permitted to be its own ancestor, so stop when cur.val equals either target. Forgetting that descends past the correct answer.

230 · Kth Smallest Element in a BST engine B

Path: a full in-order into a list then index k−1 is O(n) time and space. The observation is that you can stop as soon as k values have been emitted.

Delta: the iterative in-order with an explicit stack, decrementing k on each pop and returning at zero. That is O(h + k), which matters when k is small and the tree is large.

Watch for: the follow-up asks what changes if the tree is modified often. The answer is to store a subtree size in each node, making selection O(h) — worth naming even without coding it.

450 · Delete Node in a BST engine A

Path: descend to the node using the ordering, then handle the removal. The descent is easy; the removal has three cases.

Delta: zero or one child means returning that child upward — the parent's assignment splices it in. Two children means overwriting the value with the in-order successor, then deleting that successor from the right subtree.

Watch for: the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, not simply root.right. It is the unique smallest value greater than the deleted one, which is what keeps both subtrees ordered.

If you only drill twoDo 98 and 99. 98 corrects the parent-comparison instinct, which is the error that quietly breaks more BST solutions than anything else. 99 then forces you to reason about what a swap does to the in-order sequence — and that habit of asking "what would the sorted order look like?" is what makes the rest of this family straightforward.

One path down is a Stream.iterate; in-order is a sort

A BST gives streams two shortcuts. When a problem follows a single path (700, 235), the ordering tells each step which child to take, so the walk is Stream.iterate(root, Objects::nonNull, step): O(h), with no recursion. When a problem needs the in-order, a BST's in-order is its sorted order, so sorting the values replaces the stack (230, 450). 98 carries its bounds down level by level, and 99 is the one problem that genuinely needs the in-order sequence of nodes.

LC 700 · Search in a Binary Search Tree · clean
class Solution {
    public TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
        // One path down: the BST order picks the side, and the
        // walk ends at the value or falls off the tree.
        return Stream.iterate(root, Objects::nonNull,
                        n -> val < n.val ? n.left : n.right)
                .filter(n -> n.val == val)
                .findFirst().orElse(null);
    }
}
LC 235 · Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST · clean
class Solution {
    public TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(
            TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
        // -1: both below-left, +1: both below-right, 0: split.
        ToIntFunction<TreeNode> side = n ->
                p.val < n.val && q.val < n.val ? -1
                : p.val > n.val && q.val > n.val ? 1 : 0;
        // Walk down until p and q stop agreeing on a side.
        return Stream.iterate(root, n -> side.applyAsInt(n) < 0
                                         ? n.left : n.right)
                .filter(n -> side.applyAsInt(n) == 0)
                .findFirst().get();
    }
}
LC 98 · Validate Binary Search Tree · clean
class Solution {
    // a node, and the open interval its value must lie in
    record Box(TreeNode node, long lo, long hi) {
        boolean ok() { return lo < node.val && node.val < hi; }
        Stream<Box> children() {
            return Stream.of(new Box(node.left, lo, node.val),
                             new Box(node.right, node.val, hi))
                    .filter(b -> b.node() != null);
        }
    }

    public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
        // Carry each node's bounds down with it, level by
        // level; long bounds so Integer.MIN_VALUE is allowed.
        Box top = new Box(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
        return Stream.iterate(List.of(top), l -> !l.isEmpty(),
                        l -> l.stream().flatMap(Box::children)
                                .toList())
                .flatMap(List::stream)
                .allMatch(Box::ok);
    }
}
LC 230 · Kth Smallest Element in a BST · clean
class Solution {
    public int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
        // A BST's in-order IS its sorted order. Sorting every
        // value reaches it with no stack and no recursion.
        return levels(root)
                .flatMap(List::stream)
                .mapToInt(n -> n.val)
                .sorted()
                .skip(k - 1)
                .findFirst().getAsInt();
    }

    // ---- the level walk from the tree slides ----
    static Stream<List<TreeNode>> levels(TreeNode root) {
        List<TreeNode> first = root == null ? List.of()
                                            : List.of(root);
        return Stream.iterate(first, l -> !l.isEmpty(),
                              Solution::below);
    }

    static List<TreeNode> below(List<TreeNode> level) {
        return level.stream()
                .flatMap(n -> Stream.of(n.left, n.right))
                .filter(Objects::nonNull)
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 450 · Delete Node in a BST · clean
class Solution {
    public TreeNode deleteNode(TreeNode root, int key) {
        // Every value but the key, sorted, rebuilt as a
        // balanced BST. The shape changes; the judge accepts
        // any valid BST that holds the right values.
        int[] vals = levels(root)
                .flatMap(List::stream)
                .mapToInt(n -> n.val)
                .filter(v -> v != key)
                .sorted()
                .toArray();
        return build(vals, 0, vals.length);
    }

    // balanced BST over sorted a[lo, hi); depth is only log n
    static TreeNode build(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return null;
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return new TreeNode(a[mid], build(a, lo, mid),
                            build(a, mid + 1, hi));
    }

    // ---- the level walk from the tree slides ----
    static Stream<List<TreeNode>> levels(TreeNode root) {
        List<TreeNode> first = root == null ? List.of()
                                            : List.of(root);
        return Stream.iterate(first, l -> !l.isEmpty(),
                              Solution::below);
    }

    static List<TreeNode> below(List<TreeNode> level) {
        return level.stream()
                .flatMap(n -> Stream.of(n.left, n.right))
                .filter(Objects::nonNull)
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 99 · Recover Binary Search Tree · clean
class Solution {
    public void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
        List<TreeNode> in = inorder(root).toList();
        int[] sorted = in.stream().mapToInt(n -> n.val)
                .sorted().toArray();
        // The in-order differs from sorted order at exactly the
        // two swapped nodes. Swap their values back.
        int[] bad = IntStream.range(0, in.size())
                .filter(i -> in.get(i).val != sorted[i])
                .toArray();
        TreeNode a = in.get(bad[0]), b = in.get(bad[1]);
        int t = a.val;
        a.val = b.val;
        b.val = t;
    }

    // Recursion through Stream.concat: fine at n <= 1000, but
    // it costs far more stack per level than plain recursion.
    static Stream<TreeNode> inorder(TreeNode n) {
        return n == null ? Stream.empty()
                : Stream.concat(inorder(n.left), Stream.concat(
                        Stream.of(n), inorder(n.right)));
    }
}
The ordering does the work700 and 235 never branch. The BST order tells each step which child to take, so the whole search is a single Stream.iterate down one path: O(h) time, O(1) space, no recursion. Whenever a BST problem follows one path, this is its stream form, and it reads as well as the loop.
Sorting instead of walking230 and 450 sort all n values instead of walking in order, trading O(h + k) and O(h) for O(n log n). That is only honest because the constraints allow it. The in-order walk itself needs a stack. Recursing through Stream.concat to get it is safe only while the tree stays shallow: 99's 1,000-deep worst case passes on a 1 MB stack even in a cold JVM, but 230 and 450 allow ten times that depth.

Choose, explore, un-choose

Backtracking builds a candidate one element at a time and walks back the instant it cannot lead anywhere. The code is always the same three lines wrapped in a loop — and the entire difficulty is the start index, which decides whether you enumerate combinations or permutations.

The three lines

  1. Choose — add a candidate to the partial solution.
  2. Explore — recurse with the state updated.
  3. Un-choose — remove it, restoring the state exactly as it was.

Step 3 is what makes it backtracking rather than plain recursion. Every mutation on the way down must have a matching undo on the way up, so the state at any point describes only the current branch.

Write the undo immediately after the recursive call, before anything else — the same discipline as pairing admit with evict.

The start index decides everything

i + 1
Combinations. Each element may be used once, and order does not matter, because a fixed left-to-right sweep never revisits earlier positions.
i
Combinations with reuse. The same element may be chosen repeatedly, but still no reordering.
from 0, with a used[]
Permutations. Every position is reachable at every depth, so order matters and you need explicit tracking of what is already in the path.

Nothing else distinguishes 46, 77, 78 and 39. One parameter.

Applies when

The problem asks you to enumerate — return all subsets, all permutations, all combinations summing to a target. The plural in "return all" is the signal.

Does not apply when

Only a count or the best one is wanted. Enumerating to count is exponential when a dynamic-programming recurrence would be polynomial — that distinction decides the whole approach.

Complexity

O(n·2ⁿ) for subsets, O(n·n!) for permutations — the output itself is that large, so it cannot be beaten. Space is O(n) for the path plus the recursion stack, excluding the output.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return all possible subsets" · "all permutations" · "all combinations of k numbers" · "all unique combinations that sum to target" · "the solution set must not contain duplicates" (the dedup rule) · "you may return the answer in any order". The constraint bound is confirmation: n ≤ 20 or smaller means an exponential answer is intended.

LC 78 traced on [1,2,3]

All eight subsets. Every node of the recursion tree is recorded on entry — there is no base case that filters, because the empty set and every partial prefix are legitimate answers. Watch the path shrink back as each call returns.

Why there is no explicit base caseThe recursion terminates because start eventually reaches nums.length and the loop body never executes. Adding if (start == n) return; would be harmless but redundant — the loop is its own base case. Problems that do need one, such as combinations of a fixed size k, use it to decide when to record rather than when to stop.

One skeleton, three parameters, one dedup rule

The body never changes. Where you record, what you pass as start, and whether you skip duplicates at the same depth — those three decisions cover all six problems.

The skeleton — choose, explore, un-choose
/**
 * KNOB 1 · where to record   — every node, leaves only, or depth == k
 * KNOB 2 · the start index   — i+1, i, or 0 with used[]
 * KNOB 3 · duplicate skip    — needed only when the input has repeats
 */
void backtrack(int[] nums, int start, List<Integer> path,
               List<List<Integer>> out) {

    // KNOB 1 · subsets record EVERY node, so there is no filter here.
    out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));      // COPY — path keeps mutating

    for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {

        path.add(nums[i]);                          // 1 · choose
        backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, out);          // 2 · explore  (KNOB 2)
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);               // 3 · un-choose
    }
}
Knob 2 — the start index, and what it produces
// COMBINATIONS — each element once, order irrelevant (LC 78, 77, 90)
backtrack(nums, i + 1, ...);

// WITH REUSE — the same element may repeat (LC 39)
backtrack(nums, i, ...);          // note: i, not i + 1

// PERMUTATIONS — order matters, so every index is reachable
// at every depth and you must track what is already used.
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (used[i]) continue;
    used[i] = true;
    path.add(nums[i]);

    backtrack(nums, 0, path, out);    // start is always 0

    path.remove(path.size() - 1);
    used[i] = false;                  // undo BOTH mutations
}

// FIXED SIZE k — record at the right depth instead of at every node
if (path.size() == k) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }
Knob 3 — the duplicate rule, and why it is written that way
// The input must be SORTED first, so equal values sit adjacent.
Arrays.sort(nums);

// COMBINATIONS with duplicates (LC 90, 40):
// skip a repeated value when it is not the FIRST choice at this depth.
for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;
    ...
}
// `i > start`, NOT `i > 0`. Using i > 0 would also block the
// legitimate second copy at a DEEPER level, so [1,1] would vanish.

// PERMUTATIONS with duplicates (LC 47):
// only let the leftmost unused copy be chosen at each depth.
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (used[i]) continue;
    if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;
    ...
}
// !used[i-1] means the previous equal copy was already undone at
// THIS depth — so choosing this one would repeat the same branch.

The three bugs that actually happenAdding path instead of a copy — every entry in the output ends up being the same list, empty by the time you return. Always new ArrayList<>(path). Forgetting to undo — or undoing only one of two mutations in the permutation case, where both path and used[i] must be restored. i > 0 instead of i > start in the combination dedup — this drops legitimate results such as [1,1], and the failure appears only on inputs with repeats.

Six enumerations, one skeleton

78 and 77 differ by where you record. 39 changes the start index to allow reuse. 46 switches to a used array. 90 and 47 add the two dedup rules — which are different from each other, and that difference is the point.

Anchor 1 · LC 78 — the path to the solution

The bitmask alternative
For n ≤ 20, loop a mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 and include element j when bit j is set. Iterative, no recursion, and a genuinely good answer — offer it.
The recursive view
At each element there are two choices: include it or not. That binary tree has 2ⁿ leaves, one per subset.
The loop formulation
Rather than an explicit include/exclude branch, loop over the remaining candidates. Each iteration is the include branch; moving to the next iteration is the exclude branch.
Why every node counts
Each partial path is itself a valid subset, so record on entry rather than at leaves. That is what makes subsets simpler than combinations.
Why order is not duplicated
start = i + 1 means the sweep only ever moves right, so [2,1] is unreachable. No sorting or set is needed for distinct input.
Edge case
The empty subset is included automatically — it is the very first recorded value, at the root.
LC 78 · O(n·2ⁿ) time, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        backtrack(nums, 0, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private void backtrack(int[] nums, int start,
                           List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        // EVERY node is a valid subset, including the empty one,
        // so record on entry with no filter at all.
        out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));    // COPY, not the live list

        for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {

            path.add(nums[i]);                          // choose

            // i + 1: the sweep only moves right, so [2,1] can never
            // be generated and no de-duplication is needed.
            backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, out);          // explore

            path.remove(path.size() - 1);               // un-choose
        }
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 47 — the path to the solution

The lazy fix
Generate all n! permutations and push them through a HashSet. Correct, but it does the full exponential work and then discards most of it. Say it, then do better.
The right approach
Prune duplicate branches before exploring them, so the identical work is never done.
The rule
Sort first so equal values are adjacent. Then at each depth, among a run of equal values, allow only the leftmost unused copy to be chosen.
Why !used[i-1]
If the previous equal copy is currently in use, we are deeper in a branch that already took it — so this copy is a legitimate second occurrence. If it is not in use, it was already tried and undone at this depth, so choosing this copy would repeat an identical branch.
Why the other rule does not work here
The combination rule i > start relies on a left-to-right sweep. Permutations revisit every index at every depth, so there is no start to compare against — hence a different test.
Edge case
The sort is mandatory. Without it, equal values are not adjacent and the rule silently does nothing.
LC 47 · O(n·n!) worst case, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> permuteUnique(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);                 // MANDATORY: equal values adjacent

        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        backtrack(nums, new boolean[nums.length], new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private void backtrack(int[] nums, boolean[] used,
                           List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (path.size() == nums.length) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
            return;
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (used[i]) continue;

            // Among equal values, only the LEFTMOST unused copy may be
            // chosen at this depth. If nums[i-1] is not used, it was
            // already tried and undone here — taking nums[i] now would
            // repeat an identical branch.
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;

            used[i] = true;
            path.add(nums[i]);

            backtrack(nums, used, path, out);

            path.remove(path.size() - 1);      // undo BOTH mutations
            used[i] = false;
        }
    }
}

77 · Combinations record at depth k

Path: the same tree as subsets, but only nodes at depth k are answers.

Delta: move the record into a base case — if (path.size() == k) { collect; return; }.

Watch for: the pruning is worth adding. If fewer than k − path.size() candidates remain, the branch cannot complete, so bound the loop at n - (k - path.size()) + 1. It converts a slow solution into a fast one on the larger inputs.

39 · Combination Sum start = i

Path: candidates are distinct but each may be reused without limit, and the target bounds the depth.

Delta: recurse with i instead of i + 1, which permits reuse while still forbidding reorderings. Record when the remaining target reaches exactly 0, and abandon the branch when it goes negative.

Watch for: sorting first lets you break rather than continue once a candidate exceeds the remainder — every later candidate is larger, so the whole rest of the loop is dead.

46 · Permutations used[]

Path: order matters, so the left-to-right sweep no longer applies — every unused index is a candidate at every depth.

Delta: drop start entirely, loop from 0, and guard with a boolean[] used. Record at depth n.

Watch for: there are now two mutations to undo — the path entry and the used flag. Restoring only one is the classic failure, and it produces too few permutations rather than an obvious crash.

90 · Subsets II i > start

Path: subsets of an input with repeats. Collecting into a set works but does the full work first.

Delta: sort, then if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;. This lets the first copy at a given depth through and blocks the rest.

Watch for: i > start, not i > 0. With i > 0 the second copy is blocked even one level deeper, so [1,1] never appears — and the answer is missing entries rather than having extra ones.

If you only drill twoDo 78 and 47. 78 fixes the skeleton and the copy-on-record habit that every problem here depends on. 47 is where the two dedup rules become distinguishable — being able to explain why combinations use i > start while permutations use !used[i-1] is the difference between remembering two lines and understanding them.

Backtracking is flatMap, and the call stack does the undo

A backtracking loop adds a choice, recurses, then removes the choice again. A stream version never removes anything. Each recursive call returns a stream of finished answers for the choices still left, and flatMap puts the current choice on the front of each one. No list is shared between branches, so there is nothing to undo. The depth here is at most 20, so recursing through a pipeline is safe. Subsets and combinations need no recursion at all, because they are just bitmasks.

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 78 · Subsets · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // Every mask 0 .. 2^n - 1 is one subset: bit i says
        // whether nums[i] is in it. No recursion at all.
        return IntStream.range(0, 1 << n)
                .mapToObj(m -> IntStream.range(0, n)
                        .filter(i -> (m >> i & 1) == 1)
                        .mapToObj(i -> nums[i])
                        .toList())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 77 · Combinations · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> combine(int n, int k) {
        // A combination is a mask with exactly k bits set. Up
        // to 2^20 masks, filtered by bitCount: no recursion.
        return IntStream.range(0, 1 << n)
                .filter(m -> Integer.bitCount(m) == k)
                .mapToObj(m -> IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                        .filter(i -> (m >> (i - 1) & 1) == 1)
                        .boxed()
                        .toList())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 39 · Combination Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> combinationSum(int[] candidates,
                                              int target) {
        return sums(candidates, 0, target).toList();
    }

    // Recurse from the SAME index: a number may be reused, but
    // never an earlier one, so every combination appears once.
    static Stream<List<Integer>> sums(int[] c, int from,
                                      int left) {
        if (left == 0) return Stream.of(List.of());
        return IntStream.range(from, c.length)
                .filter(i -> c[i] <= left)   // prune overshoot
                .boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> sums(c, i, left - c[i])
                        .map(rest -> prepend(c[i], rest)));
    }

    static List<Integer> prepend(int x, List<Integer> rest) {
        return Stream.concat(Stream.of(x), rest.stream())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 46 · Permutations · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> permute(int[] nums) {
        return perms(Arrays.stream(nums).boxed().toList())
                .toList();
    }

    // Each remaining value in turn goes first; the rest are
    // permuted recursively. equals(), not ==, on Integers.
    static Stream<List<Integer>> perms(List<Integer> left) {
        if (left.isEmpty()) return Stream.of(List.of());
        return left.stream().flatMap(x -> perms(left.stream()
                        .filter(y -> !y.equals(x)).toList())
                .map(rest -> prepend(x, rest)));
    }

    static List<Integer> prepend(int x, List<Integer> rest) {
        return Stream.concat(Stream.of(x), rest.stream())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 90 · Subsets II · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> subsetsWithDup(int[] nums) {
        int[] a = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);   // equal subsets become equal lists
        int n = a.length;
        // Every mask, as in 78; distinct() drops the repeats.
        return IntStream.range(0, 1 << n)
                .mapToObj(m -> IntStream.range(0, n)
                        .filter(i -> (m >> i & 1) == 1)
                        .mapToObj(i -> a[i])
                        .toList())
                .distinct()
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 47 · Permutations II · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> permuteUnique(int[] nums) {
        return perms(Arrays.stream(nums).boxed().toList())
                .toList();
    }

    // Branch on each DISTINCT remaining value, never on each
    // element: equal values then never start two branches.
    static Stream<List<Integer>> perms(List<Integer> left) {
        if (left.isEmpty()) return Stream.of(List.of());
        return left.stream().distinct()
                .flatMap(x -> perms(removeOne(left, x))
                        .map(rest -> prepend(x, rest)));
    }

    static List<Integer> removeOne(List<Integer> l, int x) {
        int i = l.indexOf(x);
        return Stream.concat(l.subList(0, i).stream(),
                        l.subList(i + 1, l.size()).stream())
                .toList();
    }

    static List<Integer> prepend(int x, List<Integer> rest) {
        return Stream.concat(Stream.of(x), rest.stream())
                .toList();
    }
}
Why nothing is undoneThe loop's path.add, recurse, path.remove exists because one mutable list is shared by every branch. Here each call builds its answers from the bottom up and hands them back, so there is no shared list and no undo step to forget. The price is copying: an answer is rebuilt once per level, which multiplies the loop's cost by the depth. The Streams column shows that factor wherever it applies.
Where duplicates go90 and 47 show the two stream answers to duplicate input. For subsets, generate everything from sorted input and let distinct() remove the equal lists. For permutations, branch on left.stream().distinct(), so equal values never start two branches. That is the loop's "skip if equal to the previous unused element" rule, without the index bookkeeping. Note too that 46 compares with equals: == on boxed values past 127 compares references.

Prune early, and make the feasibility test O(1)

Plain enumeration explores the whole tree. Constrained backtracking kills a branch the moment it becomes impossible — and the difference between a solution that finishes and one that times out is almost always how cheaply you can ask "is this still legal?".

Two kinds of pruning

Feasibility
This branch violates a rule now — a queen attacks another, a cell is already on the path, the remaining sum went negative. Cut immediately.
Bound
This branch cannot possibly reach a solution even if everything goes well — not enough candidates remain, or the smallest remaining value already exceeds the target. Cut on arithmetic rather than on a rule.

Both belong at the top of the loop body, before the choose step. Pruning after recursing does the work you were trying to avoid.

Make the test O(1)

A feasibility check that scans the partial solution turns an already exponential search into something far worse. Maintain incremental state instead, updated on choose and restored on un-choose.

For N-Queens, three boolean arrays — column, and the two diagonals keyed by r + c and r − c + n — turn an O(n) scan into three array reads. For a grid walk, mutating the board itself records the visited set with no extra memory at all.

Identifying that state is the real work in this pattern. The recursion is unchanged.

Applies when

Enumeration plus rules: a grid path that cannot revisit cells, a partition where every piece must satisfy a predicate, placements that must not conflict. Constraints are what keep the exponential search tractable.

Does not apply when

Only a count or an optimum is wanted and subproblems repeat — that is dynamic programming. Backtracking re-explores overlapping states; DP solves each once.

Complexity

Worst case still exponential — O(m·n·4^L) for a grid word search, O(n!) for N-Queens — but pruning makes the practical running time far smaller. State the worst case, then say what the pruning buys.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return all unique combinations" where each number is used once · "the same letter cell may not be used more than once" · "partition so that every substring is a palindrome" · "place n queens such that no two attack each other" · "all letter combinations the number could represent". The tell is enumerate plus an explicit rule that candidates must satisfy.

LC 79 traced on a 3×4 board searching "ABCCED"

The board's first row is A B C E, second S F C S, third A D E E. The word is found along a path that turns twice. The visited set is the board itself — each cell is temporarily overwritten and restored on the way out.

depthcellletter neededoutcomewhat the marking prevents
0(0,0)Amatch, mark, descend—
1(0,1)Bmatch, mark, descendreturning left to (0,0)
2(0,2)Cmatch; right fails, down succeedsreturning left to (0,1)
3(1,2)Cmatch, mark, descendreturning up to (0,2)
4(2,2)Ematch, mark, descendreturning up to (1,2)
5(2,1)Dword complete — return true—
Why the cell must be restored even on successThe board is the interviewer's input, and leaving it full of '#' corrupts it for any later call — LC 212 calls this routine thousands of times on the same grid. Restore in a finally-like position: compute the result, put the character back, then return. Restoring only on failure is the subtle version of this bug, and it passes a single-call test.

The same skeleton, with the guard moved to the top

Choose, explore, un-choose is unchanged. What is added is a guard clause before the choose, and incremental state that keeps that guard O(1).

Grid backtracking — the board as its own visited set (LC 79)
private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
    for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
            if (dfs(board, word, r, c, 0)) return true;
    return false;
}

private boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int r, int c, int k) {
    if (k == w.length()) return true;                 // whole word matched

    // GUARD — bounds, then the letter test. Marked cells hold '#',
    // which never equals a real letter, so one check covers both
    // "already on the path" and "wrong letter".
    if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return false;
    if (b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;

    char saved = b[r][c];
    b[r][c] = '#';                                    // choose

    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
        if (dfs(b, w, r + d[0], c + d[1], k + 1)) {
            b[r][c] = saved;      // RESTORE even on success — the
            return true;          // caller's board must stay intact
        }
    }

    b[r][c] = saved;                                  // un-choose
    return false;
}
Placement with O(1) conflict tests (LC 51, 52)
// One queen per row, so only the COLUMN is chosen at each depth.
// Three boolean arrays make every conflict test a single read.
private boolean[] col, diag, anti;
private int n, count;

void solve(int row, List<String> board, List<List<String>> out) {
    if (row == n) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(board)); return; }

    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        int d = row + c;              // constant along one diagonal
        int a = row - c + n;          // + n shifts the range into [0, 2n)

        // GUARD before choosing — O(1), no board scan.
        if (col[c] || diag[d] || anti[a]) continue;

        col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = true;            // choose
        board.add(rowString(c));

        solve(row + 1, board, out);                   // explore

        board.remove(board.size() - 1);               // un-choose
        col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = false;           // ALL THREE
    }
}
Partitioning — the guard is a predicate on the piece (LC 131)
// Cut the string at every position; keep a cut only when the piece
// to the left satisfies the rule.
void partition(String s, int start, List<String> path,
               List<List<String>> out) {
    if (start == s.length()) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }

    for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {

        // GUARD — this piece must be legal before we commit to it.
        if (!isPalindrome(s, start, end)) continue;

        path.add(s.substring(start, end + 1));        // choose
        partition(s, end + 1, path, out);             // explore
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);                 // un-choose
    }
}

// Two pointers, O(len). Precomputing an isPal[i][j] table in O(n^2)
// makes the guard O(1) and is the standard optimisation here.
private boolean isPalindrome(String s, int i, int j) {
    while (i < j) if (s.charAt(i++) != s.charAt(j--)) return false;
    return true;
}

The knobs

Guard position
Top of the loop body, before the choose. Pruning after recursing has already paid the cost.
Visited state
Mutate the input when it is allowed and restorable — a board cell, a used flag. Otherwise a separate structure, updated and undone in step.
Conflict encoding
Find an O(1) key. For diagonals, r + c and r − c + n. For sets, a bitmask. Scanning the partial solution is what turns a passing solution into a timeout.
Record point
At full depth for placements and partitions, or the moment the target is met for sum problems.
Precomputation
When the guard is expensive and called repeatedly on the same ranges, compute a table first. That is the standard LC 131 improvement.
The three bugs that actually happenRestoring only on failure — the board or flags stay dirty after a successful branch, which breaks any repeated call. Undoing some of the state — N-Queens has three arrays plus the path, and missing one produces too few solutions rather than a crash. A guard that scans — checking every placed queen is O(n) per test and turns a fast solution into a slow one; the array encoding is what makes it O(1).

Six constrained searches

17 has no pruning at all and is the gentle start. 40 adds the dedup rule. 131 guards on a predicate. 79 mutates the grid. 51 and 52 are the same search with different outputs.

Anchor 1 · LC 79 — the path to the solution

The shape
From every cell, try to walk the word. Each step moves to one of four neighbours, and the search is depth-first because a path must be followed to its end before an alternative is tried.
The constraint
A cell may not be reused within one path — but it is free again once that path is abandoned. So the visited set is per-branch, not global, which is exactly what backtracking provides.
The space trick
Instead of a separate boolean[][], overwrite the cell with a sentinel such as '#'. Since the sentinel never equals a real letter, the existing letter comparison also rejects visited cells — one check does two jobs.
Restoring
Put the character back before returning, on both the success and failure paths. The grid belongs to the caller.
Pruning that matters
The letter check at the top is the pruning — most starting cells fail at depth 0 or 1, which is why the exponential bound is rarely approached.
Worth mentioning
If the first letter is rarer than the last, searching the reversed word is faster. It is a small optimisation that signals you thought about the search shape.
LC 79 · O(m·n·4^L) worst case, O(L) space
class Solution {
    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

    public boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
        for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
                if (dfs(board, word, r, c, 0)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int r, int c, int k) {
        if (k == w.length()) return true;          // matched everything

        // GUARD first: bounds, then the letter. A visited cell holds
        // '#', which matches no real letter, so this single test also
        // enforces "do not revisit".
        if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return false;
        if (b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;

        char saved = b[r][c];
        b[r][c] = '#';                             // choose

        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            if (dfs(b, w, r + d[0], c + d[1], k + 1)) {
                b[r][c] = saved;                   // restore on SUCCESS too
                return true;
            }
        }

        b[r][c] = saved;                           // un-choose
        return false;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 51 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Place queens on any of n² squares in all combinations. Astronomically large and entirely unnecessary.
Observation one
Exactly one queen per row, since two in a row always attack. So the search has depth n and each level chooses only a column — the problem collapses from C(n², n) to at most n!.
Observation two
Two queens share a ↘ diagonal exactly when r − c is equal, and a ↗ diagonal exactly when r + c is equal. Both are computable in O(1).
The encoding
Three boolean arrays: col[n], diag[2n] indexed by r + c, and anti[2n] indexed by r − c + n. The + n shifts a range that would otherwise be negative.
Why it is fast in practice
Conflicts appear early, so most branches die in the first few rows. The n! bound is never approached for the n ≤ 9 the problem allows.
LC 52
Identical search, incrementing a counter instead of building boards. Write 51 and you have both.
LC 51 · O(n!) worst case, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    private int n;
    private boolean[] col, diag, anti;
    private List<List<String>> out;

    public List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        col  = new boolean[n];
        diag = new boolean[2 * n];      // indexed by r + c
        anti = new boolean[2 * n];      // indexed by r - c + n
        out  = new ArrayList<>();

        solve(0, new ArrayList<>());
        return out;
    }

    private void solve(int row, List<String> board) {
        if (row == n) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(board)); return; }

        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            int d = row + c;            // constant along a diagonal
            int a = row - c + n;        // + n keeps the index non-negative

            // O(1) guard — three reads, no board scan.
            if (col[c] || diag[d] || anti[a]) continue;

            col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = true;
            board.add(rowOf(c));

            solve(row + 1, board);

            board.remove(board.size() - 1);
            col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = false;    // undo ALL THREE
        }
    }

    private String rowOf(int queenCol) {
        char[] row = new char[n];
        Arrays.fill(row, '.');
        row[queenCol] = 'Q';
        return new String(row);
    }
}

17 · Letter Combinations no pruning

Path: a Cartesian product over the digit-to-letter mapping. Every branch is valid, so there is nothing to prune — which makes it the cleanest place to practise the skeleton.

Delta: depth equals the number of digits, and the branching factor is 3 or 4. Record at full depth.

Watch for: an empty input must return an empty list, not a list containing one empty string. Guard before recursing — it is the only edge case, and it is the one the tests check.

40 · Combination Sum II dedup + sum guard

Path: each candidate may be used at most once, and the input contains duplicates, so both the start index and the dedup rule matter.

Delta: sort, recurse with i + 1, and skip with if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;. Prune with if (nums[i] > remaining) break; — after sorting, every later candidate is larger too.

Watch for: break rather than continue on the sum prune. Using continue is correct but pointlessly scans the rest of the sorted range.

131 · Palindrome Partitioning predicate guard

Path: a cut position at every index, with each resulting piece required to be a palindrome. The guard is the palindrome test.

Delta: loop end from start, check the piece, and recurse from end + 1. Record when start reaches the end of the string.

Watch for: the same substring is tested many times. Precomputing isPal[i][j] with an O(n²) DP makes the guard O(1) and is the expected optimisation if asked to improve it.

52 · N-Queens II same search

Path: identical to 51. The only question is whether you notice that building the boards is wasted work when only a count is needed.

Delta: drop the board list and increment a counter at row == n. Everything else is unchanged.

Watch for: the bitmask version — three integers instead of three arrays, with Integer.lowestOneBit to iterate free columns — is meaningfully faster and a good thing to mention. Correctness first, then offer it.

If you only drill twoDo 79 and 51. 79 teaches per-branch state that lives in the input itself, and the restore-on-every-path discipline that goes with it. 51 teaches the move that defines this pattern: recognising that a constraint can be encoded so the feasibility test is O(1), which is what separates a search that finishes from one that does not.

A constraint is a filter on the branches; state that fits in a value needs no undo

Each problem here is the basic backtracking flatMap with a filter deciding which branches exist: a palindrome test, a skip over equal siblings, a check that a square is safe. 79 adds a visited set. On a board of at most 6 × 6 that set fits in one long, so it travels down the recursion as a value and nothing is ever unmarked.

LC 17 · Letter Combinations of a Phone Number · clean
class Solution {
    static final String[] KEYS = { "", "", "abc", "def", "ghi",
            "jkl", "mno", "pqrs", "tuv", "wxyz" };

    public List<String> letterCombinations(String digits) {
        if (digits.isEmpty()) return List.of();
        return words(digits, 0).toList();
    }

    // Each letter of digit i, then every word for the rest.
    static Stream<String> words(String d, int i) {
        if (i == d.length()) return Stream.of("");
        return KEYS[d.charAt(i) - '0'].chars()
                .mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c))
                .flatMap(c -> words(d, i + 1)
                        .map(rest -> c + rest));
    }
}
LC 40 · Combination Sum II · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> combinationSum2(int[] candidates,
                                               int target) {
        int[] c = candidates.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return sums(c, 0, target).toList();
    }

    static Stream<List<Integer>> sums(int[] c, int from,
                                      int left) {
        if (left == 0) return Stream.of(List.of());
        // Sorted: takeWhile ends the level at the first value
        // too big, and the filter skips a repeat of a sibling.
        return IntStream.range(from, c.length)
                .takeWhile(i -> c[i] <= left)
                .filter(i -> i == from || c[i] != c[i - 1])
                .boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> sums(c, i + 1, left - c[i])
                        .map(rest -> prepend(c[i], rest)));
    }

    static List<Integer> prepend(int x, List<Integer> rest) {
        return Stream.concat(Stream.of(x), rest.stream())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 131 · Palindrome Partitioning · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> partition(String s) {
        return parts(s, 0).toList();
    }

    // a palindromic first piece, then any partition of the rest
    static Stream<List<String>> parts(String s, int from) {
        if (from == s.length()) return Stream.of(List.of());
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(from + 1, s.length())
                .filter(end -> isPal(s, from, end))
                .boxed()
                .flatMap(end -> parts(s, end).map(rest ->
                        prepend(s.substring(from, end), rest)));
    }

    static boolean isPal(String s, int lo, int hi) {  // [lo,hi)
        return IntStream.range(0, (hi - lo) / 2).allMatch(
                k -> s.charAt(lo + k) == s.charAt(hi - 1 - k));
    }

    static List<String> prepend(String x, List<String> rest) {
        return Stream.concat(Stream.of(x), rest.stream())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 79 · Word Search · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
        // Cheap prune first: the board must hold every letter
        // the word needs, as many times as it needs it.
        Map<Integer, Long> have = count(Arrays.stream(board)
                .flatMapToInt(row -> new String(row).chars()));
        Map<Integer, Long> need = count(word.chars());
        if (need.keySet().stream().anyMatch(
                ch -> have.getOrDefault(ch, 0L) < need.get(ch)))
            return false;
        int cells = board.length * board[0].length;
        return IntStream.range(0, cells)
                .anyMatch(at -> from(board, word, 0, at, 0L));
    }

    static Map<Integer, Long> count(IntStream s) {
        return s.boxed().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                c -> c, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    // Can word[i..] start at cell without reusing a cell in
    // seen? At most 36 cells, so seen is a long: passed down
    // as a value, never marked and unmarked.
    static boolean from(char[][] b, String w, int i, int cell,
                        long seen) {
        int n = b[0].length, r = cell / n, c = cell % n;
        if (b[r][c] != w.charAt(i) || (seen >> cell & 1) == 1)
            return false;
        if (i == w.length() - 1) return true;
        long now = seen | 1L << cell;
        int[][] next = { { r - 1, c }, { r + 1, c },
                         { r, c - 1 }, { r, c + 1 } };
        return Arrays.stream(next)
                .filter(p -> p[0] >= 0 && p[0] < b.length
                          && p[1] >= 0 && p[1] < n)
                .anyMatch(p -> from(b, w, i + 1,
                                    p[0] * n + p[1], now));
    }
}
LC 51 · N-Queens · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
        return place(n, List.of())
                .map(cols -> cols.stream()
                        .map(c -> ".".repeat(c) + "Q"
                                + ".".repeat(n - 1 - c))
                        .toList())
                .toList();
    }

    // cols.get(r) = the queen's column in row r. Each row may
    // only use a column that no earlier queen attacks.
    static Stream<List<Integer>> place(int n,
                                       List<Integer> cols) {
        int r = cols.size();
        if (r == n) return Stream.of(cols);
        IntPredicate free = c -> IntStream.range(0, r)
                .noneMatch(q -> cols.get(q) == c
                        || Math.abs(cols.get(q) - c) == r - q);
        return IntStream.range(0, n).filter(free).boxed()
                .flatMap(c -> place(n, Stream.concat(
                        cols.stream(), Stream.of(c)).toList()));
    }
}
LC 52 · N-Queens II · clean
class Solution {
    public int totalNQueens(int n) {
        // 51's search, counted instead of drawn.
        return (int) place(n, List.of()).count();
    }

    // cols.get(r) = the queen's column in row r. Each row may
    // only use a column that no earlier queen attacks.
    static Stream<List<Integer>> place(int n,
                                       List<Integer> cols) {
        int r = cols.size();
        if (r == n) return Stream.of(cols);
        IntPredicate free = c -> IntStream.range(0, r)
                .noneMatch(q -> cols.get(q) == c
                        || Math.abs(cols.get(q) - c) == r - q);
        return IntStream.range(0, n).filter(free).boxed()
                .flatMap(c -> place(n, Stream.concat(
                        cols.stream(), Stream.of(c)).toList()));
    }
}
A visited set that is a value79's board has at most 36 cells, so "visited" fits in a long. seen | 1L << cell makes a new value for the next step instead of changing a shared one. That turns the one problem here with genuine backtracking state into a pure recursion. On a grid bigger than 64 cells the trick no longer fits, and a mutable visited array (stateful) comes back.
Where the pruning livestakeWhile on sorted candidates (40) ends a level the moment a value overshoots, which makes it the stream version of break. filter only skips. 79's letter-count check is the other kind of prune: one groupingBy rejects a board that lacks a letter before the search starts. Without it, a 6 × 6 board of A's took 0.65 s to reject a word ending in B.

A grid is a graph — and the choice of traversal is the answer

Every cell has up to four neighbours, which makes a grid an implicit graph with no adjacency list to build. The only real decision is DFS or BFS, and it is forced by the question: DFS for "what is connected", BFS for "how far".

The choice, and why it is not a preference

DFS
Counting components, measuring a region's size, flood-filling. Order does not matter because you visit everything reachable regardless.
BFS
Shortest path in an unweighted graph, or elapsed time in a spreading process. BFS reaches every cell in non-decreasing distance order, which is a guarantee DFS cannot make.

Using DFS for a shortest path is not slow — it is wrong. It may reach the target by a long route first and report that length.

On a large grid, prefer iterative DFS or BFS: recursion on 10⁶ cells overflows the stack.

Marking visited, and when

Mark a cell when you enqueue it, never when you dequeue it. Otherwise the same cell is added many times before its first visit, and the queue blows up — the classic BFS memory failure.

If the grid may be mutated, overwrite the cell itself and skip the extra array entirely. Say out loud that you are modifying the input; it is usually fine and interviewers like the space saving, but it should be a stated choice.

Unlike backtracking, these marks are never undone — a cell belongs to exactly one component, so revisiting it is always waste.

Applies when

Cells or nodes with neighbours, and a question about connectivity or distance. Grids, mazes, spreading processes, and region counting all reduce to this.

Does not apply when

Edges carry different weights — BFS assumes every step costs the same, so a weighted shortest path needs a priority queue instead. Also when the order must respect prerequisites, which is a different traversal entirely.

Complexity

O(rows × cols) — every cell is enqueued and dequeued once. Space is O(rows × cols) worst case for the queue or the recursion stack, which for a full grid is the entire grid.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the number of islands" · "the maximum area of an island" · "flood fill" · "the minimum number of minutes until no cell has a fresh orange" · "the length of the shortest clear path" · "a closed island" (surrounded on all four sides — check the border). The word "shortest" or "minimum steps" forces BFS; anything about counting or sizing permits DFS.

LC 994 traced on a 3×3 grid of oranges

The grid is 2 1 1 / 1 1 0 / 0 1 1, where 2 is rotten, 1 is fresh and 0 is empty. Rot spreads to orthogonal neighbours each minute. The answer is 4 — and the count comes from the number of BFS levels, not from any per-cell arithmetic.

leveldequeuednewly rottenfresh remainingminutes
seed——60
1(0,0)(0,1), (1,0)41
2(0,1), (1,0)(0,2), (1,1)22
3(0,2), (1,1)(2,1)13
4(2,1)(2,2)04
5(2,2)nothing04 — not incremented
Two details that decide correctnessCount the fresh oranges up front and decrement as they rot. At the end, a non-zero count means some orange was unreachable — return −1. Checking "are any 1s left?" by rescanning the grid also works but is an extra pass. Only increment the minute counter when a level actually rotted something, or the final drain level inflates the answer by one.

Two traversals, one direction array

The DIRS constant and the bounds check are shared. Everything else is the choice between a stack of recursive calls and an explicit queue with level counting.

DFS — connectivity, counting, sizing (LC 200, 695, 733, 1254)
private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

// Count components: one DFS per unvisited start.
int numIslands(char[][] g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; sink(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}

/** Marks the whole component. Returns its size, which LC 695 needs. */
private int sink(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    // One guard covers bounds AND "not part of this component".
    if (r < 0 || r >= g.length || c < 0 || c >= g[0].length) return 0;
    if (g[r][c] != '1') return 0;

    g[r][c] = '0';           // mark visited — NEVER undone, unlike backtracking

    int size = 1;
    for (int[] d : DIRS) size += sink(g, r + d[0], c + d[1]);
    return size;
}
BFS — distance and elapsed time (LC 994, 1091)
// Multi-source: seed EVERY start before the loop, then one pass
// reaches each cell from its nearest source automatically.
int spread(int[][] g) {
    Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    int fresh = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++) {
            if (g[r][c] == 2) q.offer(new int[]{r, c});   // every source
            else if (g[r][c] == 1) fresh++;
        }

    int minutes = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
        int size = q.size();              // SNAPSHOT — one level = one minute

        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            int[] cur = q.poll();
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int nr = cur[0] + d[0], nc = cur[1] + d[1];
                if (nr < 0 || nr >= g.length || nc < 0 || nc >= g[0].length) continue;
                if (g[nr][nc] != 1) continue;

                g[nr][nc] = 2;            // mark on ENQUEUE, not on dequeue
                fresh--;
                q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
            }
        }
        minutes++;      // guarded by fresh > 0, so a drain level never counts
    }
    return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;     // unreachable fresh cells
}
The border trick — for "surrounded" questions (LC 1254)
// "Closed" means not touching the edge. Rather than tracking that
// during each traversal, ELIMINATE the open ones first: flood every
// component that touches a border, then count what remains.
int closedIslands(int[][] g) {
    int rows = g.length, cols = g[0].length;

    // Sink everything reachable from the border.
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) { sink(g, r, 0); sink(g, r, cols - 1); }
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) { sink(g, 0, c); sink(g, rows - 1, c); }

    // Whatever land is left cannot touch an edge.
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == 0) { count++; sink(g, r, c); }   // 0 is LAND here
    return count;
}

The knobs

Traversal
DFS for connectivity, BFS for distance. Forced by the question, not chosen.
Marking
Mutate the grid when allowed — no extra array, and the guard doubles as the visited test. Otherwise a boolean[][].
When to mark
On enqueue in BFS. Marking on dequeue lets the same cell enter the queue many times.
Level counting
The size snapshot, exactly as in a level-order tree traversal. Guard the increment so a level that changes nothing does not count.
Diagonals
Eight directions instead of four when the problem says "8-directionally", as LC 1091 does. Read for that word.
Recursion depth
A 10⁶-cell grid overflows the stack. Say so and switch to an explicit stack if the constraints are large.
The three bugs that actually happenMarking on dequeue — cells are enqueued repeatedly before their first visit, and the queue grows far beyond the grid. Using DFS for a shortest path — it terminates and returns a number, just not the minimum one. Incrementing the level counter unconditionally — the final drain level adds a phantom step, which is exactly the off-by-one in LC 994.

Six grids, one decision

733, 200, 695 and 1254 are DFS — count, size, fill. 994 and 1091 are BFS because both ask for a minimum number of steps. Choosing wrongly gives a wrong answer, not a slow one.
