Why a match takes the diagonal and never considers the alternativesWhen the two characters agree, pairing them is never worse than skipping either one — any subsequence that skips a matched pair can be rewritten to include it without getting shorter. So the maximum is unnecessary and dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 is taken unconditionally. That exchange argument is worth being able to state, because interviewers ask why the match branch has no max.

One table, and the rule that changes per problem

The loops and the index offset never vary. What varies is the base row, what a match contributes, and how a mismatch combines its two neighbours.

The template — longest common subsequence
/**
 * dp[i][j] = the answer for the first i chars of a and first j of b.
 *
 * The table is (m+1) x (n+1) because row 0 and column 0 represent
 * the EMPTY prefix — a real base case, not padding.
 *
 * Index offset: dp[i][j] compares a.charAt(i-1) with b.charAt(j-1).
 */
int longestCommonSubsequence(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    // Base row and column are 0: nothing in common with an empty string.

    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                // MATCH: pairing them is never worse than skipping
                // either, so take the diagonal with no comparison.
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
            } else {
                // MISMATCH: drop one character from one string.
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}
The rule per problem
// LC 1143 — longest common subsequence
match:    dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
mismatch: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
base:     row 0 and col 0 are 0

// LC 72 — edit distance. THREE options on a mismatch.
match:    dp[i-1][j-1]                       // free, no operation
mismatch: 1 + min(dp[i-1][j],                // delete from a
                  dp[i][j-1],                // insert into a
                  dp[i-1][j-1])              // replace
base:     dp[i][0] = i  and  dp[0][j] = j    // deleting down to empty

// LC 115 — count distinct subsequences of s equalling t
match:    dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]          // use this char, OR skip it
mismatch: dp[i-1][j]                         // can only skip
base:     dp[i][0] = 1                       // the empty target: one way
          dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0             // empty source: no way

// LC 583 — minimum deletions to make the strings equal
// Reduces to LCS: delete everything not in the common subsequence.
answer:   m + n - 2 * lcs(a, b)
Single-sequence problems in disguise (LC 1312)
// "Minimum insertions to make s a palindrome."
// A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, so the
// characters you can KEEP are exactly the longest common
// subsequence of s and its own reverse. Everything else must be
// paired with an inserted character.
int minInsertions(String s) {
    String rev = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
    return s.length() - longestCommonSubsequence(s, rev);
}

// LC 97 — interleaving. Here the SECOND index is derived, not free:
// having used i chars of s1 and j of s2, you must be exactly at
// position i+j in s3. So the table is still 2D, not 3D.
boolean isInterleave(String s1, String s2, String s3) {
    int m = s1.length(), n = s2.length();
    if (m + n != s3.length()) return false;      // cheap rejection

    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];
    dp[0][0] = true;

    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) {
            if (i > 0 && dp[i - 1][j]
                     && s1.charAt(i - 1) == s3.charAt(i + j - 1)) dp[i][j] = true;
            if (j > 0 && dp[i][j - 1]
                     && s2.charAt(j - 1) == s3.charAt(i + j - 1)) dp[i][j] = true;
        }
    return dp[m][n];
}

The knobs

Base row and column
0 for a length, i or j for a distance, 1 for a count against the empty pattern. Getting these wrong shifts every value in the table.
Match contribution
+1 for a length, +0 for a distance, a sum for a count.
Mismatch combiner
max for longest, min for cheapest, and for a count only one neighbour is even valid.
Reductions
Deletions and palindrome insertions both reduce to LCS. Spotting that is faster than deriving a new recurrence.
Space
Two rolling rows, or one row plus a saved diagonal. Halve the table by iterating over the shorter string.
The three bugs that actually happenThe index offset — dp[i][j] compares charAt(i−1), not charAt(i). Using i throws at the last row or silently compares the wrong characters. Wrong base row — edit distance with a zero base row reports 0 for converting anything into an empty string. Overwriting the diagonal in the rolling form — you must save dp[j−1] from the previous row before writing dp[j], or the match branch reads the current row instead.

Six tables, one grid

1143 is the base. 583 and 1312 reduce to it outright. 72 adds the third option. 115 changes the match branch to a sum. 97 derives the second index from the first.

Anchor 1 · LC 1143 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Generate every subsequence of one string and test membership in the other. 2^m subsequences — impossible at m = 1000.
The recursive view
Compare the last characters. If they match, both are consumed and the problem shrinks by one on each side. If not, you must drop one of them — so try both and take the better.
Why memoisation applies
The recursion reaches the same (i, j) pair along many routes, which is exactly the overlapping-subproblem condition. A table of m × n entries solves each once.
Why a match needs no max
If the characters agree, pairing them is never worse than skipping either — any solution that skips a matched pair can be rewritten to include it without shortening. So take the diagonal outright.
The base row
Nothing is in common with an empty string, so row 0 and column 0 are 0 — which Java's array initialisation already gives you.
Space
Each cell reads only the previous row and the cell to its left, so two rows of length n + 1 suffice.
LC 1143 · O(mn) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int longestCommonSubsequence(String text1, String text2) {
        int m = text1.length(), n = text2.length();

        // Two rolling rows. Base row is all zeros: nothing is in
        // common with an empty prefix.
        int[] prev = new int[n + 1];
        int[] cur  = new int[n + 1];

        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

                // NOTE the offset: dp index i maps to charAt(i - 1).
                if (text1.charAt(i - 1) == text2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    // Pairing a match is never worse than skipping
                    // either side, so no comparison is needed.
                    cur[j] = prev[j - 1] + 1;
                } else {
                    // Drop one character from one of the strings.
                    cur[j] = Math.max(prev[j], cur[j - 1]);
                }
            }
            int[] swap = prev; prev = cur; cur = swap;   // roll the rows
        }
        return prev[n];      // after the final swap, prev holds row m
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 72 — the path to the solution

The state
dp[i][j] = the fewest operations to turn the first i characters of word1 into the first j of word2.
The base cases
dp[i][0] = i — deleting i characters reaches the empty string. dp[0][j] = j — inserting j characters builds it up. These are not zeros, and getting them wrong is the most common failure.
Match
The characters already agree, so no operation is needed: inherit the diagonal unchanged.
Mismatch — three options
Delete from word1 → dp[i−1][j]. Insert into word1 → dp[i][j−1]. Replace → dp[i−1][j−1]. Each costs one, so take 1 + min of the three.
Naming them matters
Attaching an operation to each source cell makes the recurrence derivable rather than memorised — and interviewers ask you to explain the three terms.
Space
Two rolling rows again, but the base column must be re-seeded at the start of every row: cur[0] = i.
LC 72 · O(mn) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int minDistance(String word1, String word2) {
        int m = word1.length(), n = word2.length();

        int[] prev = new int[n + 1];
        int[] cur  = new int[n + 1];

        // Base ROW: turning an empty prefix into j chars costs
        // j insertions. NOT zero.
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) prev[j] = j;

        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
            // Base COLUMN: turning i chars into nothing costs
            // i deletions. Re-seed it every row.
            cur[0] = i;

            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

                if (word1.charAt(i - 1) == word2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    cur[j] = prev[j - 1];          // already equal — free
                } else {
                    cur[j] = 1 + Math.min(prev[j],            // delete
                                 Math.min(cur[j - 1],         // insert
                                          prev[j - 1]));      // replace
                }
            }
            int[] swap = prev; prev = cur; cur = swap;
        }
        return prev[n];
    }
}

583 · Delete Operation for Two Strings LCS reduction

Path: deriving a fresh recurrence works, but there is a shortcut worth seeing. The characters you keep must form a common subsequence, and keeping the longest one minimises the deletions.

Delta: answer = m + n − 2·lcs(a, b). Each string deletes everything outside the common subsequence, hence the factor of two.

Watch for: the direct DP is dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] on a match and 1 + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]) otherwise — it is edit distance without the replace option, which is a nice way to see the connection.

1312 · Minimum Insertion Steps for a Palindrome LCS reduction

Path: a Hard problem that collapses once you see the reduction. Characters that already form a palindromic subsequence need no partner; everything else needs one inserted.

Delta: the longest palindromic subsequence of s is the LCS of s with its reverse, so the answer is n − lcs(s, reverse(s)).

Watch for: the reduction is the entire difficulty. Once stated, the code is three lines on top of the LCS routine — so lead with the reasoning, not the code.

115 · Distinct Subsequences counting

Path: count how many distinct subsequences of s equal t. It is a counting problem, so the match branch adds rather than choosing.

Delta: on a match you may either use this character of s (dp[i−1][j−1]) or skip it (dp[i−1][j]), and both are valid — so sum them. On a mismatch only skipping is possible.

Watch for: the base cases are asymmetric. dp[i][0] = 1 — there is exactly one way to match the empty target, by deleting everything. dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. Counts overflow int, so use long or the problem's stated modulus.

97 · Interleaving String derived index

Path: the instinct is a 3D table over all three strings. That is unnecessary and is the main trap.

Delta: if you have consumed i characters of s1 and j of s2, you must be exactly at position i + j in s3. The third index is derived, so the table stays 2D and boolean.

Watch for: reject immediately when s1.length() + s2.length() != s3.length() — without it the index arithmetic runs off the end. The cell is true if either source could have supplied the next character.

If you only drill twoDo 1143 and 72. 1143 fixes the table shape, the index offset and the match-or-skip split that every problem here inherits. 72 adds the third option and the non-zero base cases — and being able to name each of its three source cells as delete, insert or replace is what turns this whole family from recalled formulas into a recurrence you can rebuild from scratch.

Low-level design: from a one-line prompt to classes that run

This tab prepares you for the low-level design round, sometimes called object-oriented design or machine coding. You get a prompt such as "design a parking lot" and turn it into requirements, a class diagram and working Java in under an hour. It starts with the principles and the 23 patterns, works seven classic problems end to end, and ends with concurrency, scale and the interview itself.

7

problems solved in full: parking lot, library, ATM, chess, elevator, movie booking and Splitwise. Each has its requirements, a class diagram, runnable code and the follow-up questions interviewers ask.

23

Gang of Four patterns. The common ones get a slide each with running code; the rest share slides. One slide shows which patterns are easy to confuse and how to tell them apart.

21

JDK 21 is the baseline. Features added after Java 17 carry a since 21 tag, so you know which to avoid if your interview runs on an older JDK.

The eighteen sections

Orientation
this slide, and the seven problems at a glance
Foundations
what LLD is, the OO pillars, class relationships, how to read the diagrams, value objects, the Java 21 toolkit
SOLID and friends
the five SOLID principles, DRY/KISS/YAGNI, coupling, cohesion, Demeter, GRASP
Design patterns
the catalogue, then creational, structural and behavioural patterns, with code

one section each, five or six slides, from requirements to follow-ups
Concurrency
locks, atomics, virtual threads, a thread-safe LRU cache, a token-bucket rate limiter
Scale and distribution

Interview strategy

Interview questions

How to use it

  • Arrow keys move through slides; C opens contents, where each problem is its own section.
  • New to LLD? Read Foundations and SOLID first. The problem sections assume you know the vocabulary.
  • Short on time? Read the 45-minute plan, then do two problems with the code covered: write your own version, then compare.
  • Class diagrams are drawn as text, in the notation on Reading the class diagrams, because that is what you can draw in a shared editor.
How the code is writtenA code label that starts with a file name, such as ParkingLot.java · 1 of 3, is a complete Java file, or one numbered part of one. The parts join in slide order into a file that compiles with javac --release 21 -Xlint:all without warnings. The block labelled Output on JDK 21 is what that file actually printed. Demos use a fixed clock and ordered maps, so they print the same thing on every run.

Seven problems, chosen for the ideas each one forces

These seven cover most LLD prompts. A new prompt is usually one of them in disguise: a hotel booking is the movie-booking problem, a vending machine is the ATM, a snake-and-ladder game is a smaller chess. Learn what each one teaches, not just its code.

ProblemThe idea it forcesPatterns usedThe hard follow-upStart

Requirements

The same five steps each time

Each problem runs through the same slides: requirements, class diagram and responsibilities, the domain model in code, the services with a demo and its output, then the decisions and follow-ups. That is the order to use in the interview, too.

Scoped to fit the hour

Each solution is the size you can write in a 45 to 90 minute round: about 150 to 250 lines. The last slide of each problem lists what was left out and how you would add it, which is usually the interviewer's next question.

How to practise

Read only the requirements slide. Spend 40 minutes on your own diagram and code. Then compare, looking first at the responsibilities (which class owns which decision), not the syntax.

Low-level design turns a requirement into classes and the code inside them

Low-level design (LLD) decides which classes exist, what each one is responsible for, how they relate, and what their key methods do. Its output is code a teammate could extend without breaking: an interface where the behaviour varies, an enum where the values are fixed, and one owner for each piece of state.

Machine coding round

60 to 120 minutes to write a working program at your own machine, often with a console demo or unit tests. The interviewer then reads the code and asks for a change. Scored on correctness, structure and how easily it extends.

runnable code

Object-oriented design interview

45 to 60 minutes at a whiteboard or in a shared editor: requirements, a class diagram, and the code for the two or three methods that matter. Scored on the model and the reasoning, not on compiling.

diagram + key code

Design discussion in a coding round

A coding question with a design follow-up: "now support three pricing rules", "make it thread-safe". Scored on whether your first version bends or has to be rewritten.

extension

What you hand over by the end

  1. Requirements: the use cases in scope, the ones you left out, and the assumptions you made.
  2. Entities: the nouns that hold state, and the enums and value objects around them.
  3. Class diagram: the classes, their relationships and multiplicities, and the interfaces where behaviour varies.
  4. Code: the model, the service that runs the main use case, and a demo or test that proves it.
  5. Trade-offs: what you would change for concurrency, persistence, or the next requirement.

What it is not

  • Not system design. No load balancers, no sharding, no capacity estimates, unless you are asked how the design scales.
  • Not a pattern quiz. Patterns are a vocabulary for the choices you made. Using five of them where one would do costs marks.
  • Not a database schema. Tables may come up, but the model is objects and behaviour, not rows.
  • Not an algorithm puzzle. Each problem has one algorithmic core (the elevator scheduler, the debt simplifier), but most of the marks are for the structure around it.
One sentence to rememberA good low-level design puts each decision in exactly one place, so when the requirement changes, one class changes.

High-level design draws the boxes; low-level design writes what is inside one

High-level design (HLD, or system design) picks the services, stores and channels, and the way data flows between them. LLD zooms into one of those boxes and designs its classes. The two rounds need different preparation and are scored on different things.

High-level designLow-level design
Typical promptDesign Twitter's timeline. Design a URL shortener for 100M users.Design a parking lot. Design Splitwise. Design an elevator controller.
Unit of designServices, databases, caches, queues, CDNsClasses, interfaces, enums, methods
What you drawBoxes and arrows for request and data flowA class diagram with relationships and multiplicities
What you writeAPIs, a data model, back-of-envelope numbersCompilable code for the core use cases
Key questionsHow many requests per second? What happens when this node dies? Where is the bottleneck?Who owns this state? What changes when a new vehicle type arrives? Is this method thread-safe?
Main trade-offsConsistency against availability, latency against cost, SQL against NoSQLInheritance against composition, flexibility against simplicity, lock granularity
Classic failureNo numbers; one database for everything; no failure handlingOne god class; a switch on type in five places; getters and setters and nothing else
Where they meetAn LLD question often ends with a scale follow-up: "the parking lot now spans 200 sites". The right answer is not to redraw everything. Say which object becomes a service, which in-memory map becomes a table, and which lock becomes a database constraint. Scale and distribution covers this.
Elsewhere in the atlasThe System design tab is the high-level round, the Reference deck is high-level design for one Spring Boot system, and the Event-driven tab covers the channels between services. This tab stays inside one process until section 16.

It is the round closest to the job you will actually do

Most engineering time goes into adding a feature to code someone else designed. An LLD round shows, in an hour, whether your code will make that easy or hard for the next person. Many product companies run a machine-coding round for mid-level hires, and senior loops often use an object-oriented design question alongside system design.

Modelling

Can you find the right nouns, and put state and behaviour together? A candidate who makes ParkingSpot decide whether a vehicle fits has modelled. One who writes a ParkingManager that asks every object for its fields has not.

Handling change

Every interviewer has a second requirement ready: a new vehicle type, a weekend price, a new split rule. They are watching whether the change touches one class or ten.

Code quality under time pressure

Names, small methods, immutability, validation at the boundary, no duplicated logic. Nobody expects perfect code in an hour, but the habits show.

Communication

Asking the right questions before designing, saying why you chose an interface over an enum, and saying what you would do with more time. A silent correct answer scores lower than a spoken, slightly incomplete one.

LevelWhat a pass usually looks like
JuniorA sensible set of classes, correct code for the main use case, and clear names. Patterns are optional.
Mid-levelClean responsibilities, interfaces at the points of variation, edge cases handled, and a working demo. Can name the patterns they used and why.
SeniorAll of that, plus concurrency, failure modes and extensibility, raised without prompting. Explains what they deliberately left out.

The four pillars, and how each one goes wrong

Interviewers rarely ask for the definitions. They check whether your design uses the pillars: state that only its owner can change, callers that depend on what an object does rather than how, and behaviour that varies by type without a switch on the type.

Encapsulation

An object guards its own state, and the only way to change it is through methods that keep it valid.

Goes wrong as a setBalance that lets any caller skip the overdraft rule.

Abstraction

Callers see what an object does and none of how. An interface is the cleanest form.

Goes wrong as a PaymentService whose callers must know which gateway sits behind it.

Inheritance

A subtype reuses and specialises a supertype. It is the strongest coupling Java has: the child depends on its parent's internals.

Goes wrong as Square extends Rectangle, or a hierarchy four levels deep.

Polymorphism

One call, many behaviours, chosen by the runtime type. It replaces conditionals on type.

Goes wrong as if (v instanceof Truck) … else if (v instanceof Car) repeated in five classes.

All four in one listing
interface Shape {                          // abstraction: what, not how
    double area();
}

final class Circle implements Shape {      // polymorphism: its own area()
    private final double r;                // encapsulation: private, final
    Circle(double r) {
        if (r <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("radius");
        this.r = r;                        // valid from construction on
    }
    public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}

abstract class Account {                   // inheritance: shared rule
    private long balanceCents;             // no setter: change goes through
    void withdraw(long cents) {            // a method that keeps it valid
        if (cents > balanceCents + overdraftLimit())
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balanceCents -= cents;
    }
    abstract long overdraftLimit();        // the part subtypes specialise
}

double total = shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::area).sum();
// no switch on type: a new Shape needs no change here
The test interviewers applyAdd a new type. If the new class is the only file you touch, polymorphism is doing its job. If you also have to edit a switch somewhere else, you have found the design's weak point, so say so before the interviewer does.

Six relationships, and the one question that separates them: who owns the lifetime?

Each relationship is a different amount of coupling. Pick the weakest one that works. In Java, several of them look identical in code (a field), so the difference is in who creates the object, who else can hold it, and whether it outlives its holder.

RelationshipMeansJava shapeLifetimeExample
Dependency ┄┄>Uses it brieflyA parameter or a local variableOnly for the callFeeCalculator uses a Ticket passed to fee(ticket)
Association ──>Knows about itA field, set from outsideIndependentA Loan refers to a Member
Aggregation ◇──Has it, as a part that can exist aloneA collection field, filled from outsideThe part outlives the wholeA Group has Users; deleting the group keeps the users
Composition ◆──Owns it, as a part that cannot exist aloneA field the owner creates and never hands outThe part dies with the wholeA ParkingFloor owns its ParkingSpots
Inheritance ──▷Is a kind of itextendsOne objectBishop extends Piece
Realisation ┄┄▷Fulfils its contractimplementsOne objectHourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy
The same field, three relationships
final class ParkingFloor {                 // composition: creates its spots,
    private final List<ParkingSpot> spots; // never exposes the list
    ParkingFloor(int n) {
        spots = IntStream.range(0, n).mapToObj(ParkingSpot::new).toList();
    }
}

final class Group {                        // aggregation: users come from
    private final Set<User> members = new LinkedHashSet<>();
    void add(User u) { members.add(u); }   // outside and outlive the group
}

final class Loan {                         // association: one reference
    private final Member member;           // to an independent object
    Loan(Member member) { this.member = member; }
}
Why interviewers ask"Is that composition or aggregation?" is really "who deletes it, and can anyone else change it?" Answer with the lifecycle: "The floor creates its spots and never hands the list out, so it is composition. When a floor is closed, its spots go with it." Nobody will mark you down for the diamond's colour; they will for a spot that two floors can both mutate.

The text notation every class diagram in this tab uses

In an interview you draw in a shared editor or on a whiteboard, so the diagrams here are plain text in a small subset of UML. Use the same notation in the interview, and say what an arrow means the first time you draw one.

Legend
Stereotypes «interface» «abstract» «enum» «record» «sealed» Visibility + public - private # protected ~ package-private Relationships read left to right A ──▷ B A extends B inheritance A ┄┄▷ B A implements B realisation A ◆── B A owns B; B dies with A composition A ◇── B A has B; B lives on aggregation A ──> B A holds a reference to B association A ┄┄> B A uses B in a method dependency Multiplicity written at the far end 1 exactly one 0..1 optional * zero or more 1..* at least one
An example, read aloud underneath
ParkingLot - floors : List<ParkingFloor> - pricing : PricingStrategy + park(Vehicle) : Ticket + leave(Ticket, Instant) : Receipt ◆── 1..* ParkingFloor ──> 1 PricingStrategy ParkingFloor ◆── 1..* ParkingSpot «interface» PricingStrategy + fee(Ticket, Instant) : Money ┄┄▷ HourlyPricing ┄┄▷ FlatWeekendPricing "A lot owns one or more floors; each floor owns one or more spots. The lot holds exactly one pricing strategy, and there are two kinds."

Draw less

Leave out getters, setters, constructors and toString. Show the fields that carry the design and the methods that do the work.

Arrows point at the dependency

A ──> B means A knows B, and B does not know A. If the arrow goes both ways, ask whether it has to: two-way links are where bugs hide.

Mark the variation points

Every «interface» on the diagram should answer "what might change?" If you cannot say what a second implementation would be, you probably do not need the interface.

Inherit from a class only when you control it and it was designed for it

A subclass depends on how its parent is implemented, not just on what it promises. In the classic example below, the parent's addAll calls add internally, so a subclass that counts in both methods counts every element twice. Wrapping the set instead of extending it removes that dependency.

CountingSet.java · extending against wrapping
import java.util.*;

@SuppressWarnings("serial")
class InstrumentedHashSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {   // inheritance
    private int addCount;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return super.add(e);
    }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);     // HashSet inherits addAll, which calls add()
    }
    int addCount() { return addCount; }
}

final class WrappingSet<E> {                        // composition
    private final Set<E> inner;
    private int addCount;
    WrappingSet(Set<E> inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    boolean add(E e) { addCount++; return inner.add(e); }
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return inner.addAll(c);     // inner's add() is not ours: no double count
    }
    int addCount() { return addCount; }
}

public class CountingSet {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var inherited = new InstrumentedHashSet<String>();
        inherited.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        var wrapped = new WrappingSet<String>(new HashSet<>());
        wrapped.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println("extends HashSet: " + inherited.addCount());
        System.out.println("wraps a Set:     " + wrapped.addCount());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · CountingSet.java
extends HashSet: 6
wraps a Set:     3
UseWhen
InterfaceThe default for a point of variation. A class can implement many. Default methods can share small helpers.
Abstract classSubtypes share state or a fixed algorithm with steps to fill in (template method). A class can extend only one.
Sealed interfaceThe set of subtypes is closed and known, and you want exhaustive switch. Records make good permitted types.
CompositionYou want to reuse behaviour from a class you do not own, or switch it at runtime.
The rule of thumbInheritance is fine for a genuine "is-a" inside one module you control: Bishop extends Piece. Across a boundary, or just to reuse code, compose. A good line to say in the interview: "I'd rather hold a PricingStrategy than be one, so it can change at runtime."

Value objects are equal by value; entities are equal by identity

A value object such as Money, Seat or Position has no identity: two with the same fields are the same value. Make it immutable, and a record gives you equals and hashCode for free. An entity such as Member or Booking keeps its identity while its fields change, so it is equal by its id alone.

ValueObjects.java · money, an entity, and the mutable-key trap
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.*;

record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {     // value object
    Money {                                              // compact constructor:
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");        // validate, then
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");    // normalise the scale
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(),
                                 RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    }
    static Money of(String amount, String code) {
        return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), Currency.getInstance(code));
    }
    Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
}

final class Member {                                     // entity
    private final String id;
    private String email;                                // may change
    Member(String id, String email) { this.id = id; this.email = email; }
    void changeEmail(String email) { this.email = email; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Member m && id.equals(m.id);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return id.hashCode(); }
    @Override public String toString() { return id + "<" + email + ">"; }
}

final class MutablePoint {                               // the trap
    int x, y;
    MutablePoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof MutablePoint p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}

public class ValueObjects {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("double 0.1 + 0.2       = " + (0.1 + 0.2));
        System.out.println("Money  0.10 + 0.20     = "
                + Money.of("0.10", "USD").plus(Money.of("0.20", "USD")));
        System.out.println("BigDecimal 10.5 vs 10.50: "
                + new BigDecimal("10.5").equals(new BigDecimal("10.50")));
        System.out.println("Money      10.5 vs 10.50: "
                + Money.of("10.5", "USD").equals(Money.of("10.50", "USD")));

        Set<Member> members = new HashSet<>();
        Member ana = new Member("M-1", "ana@old.example");
        members.add(ana);
        ana.changeEmail("ana@new.example");
        System.out.println("entity found after edit: " + members.contains(ana));

        Set<MutablePoint> points = new HashSet<>();
        MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
        points.add(p);
        p.x = 5;                                          // hash changes
        System.out.println("mutable key found:       " + points.contains(p)
                + " (size " + points.size() + ")");
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · ValueObjects.java
double 0.1 + 0.2       = 0.30000000000000004
Money  0.10 + 0.20     = Money[amount=0.30, currency=USD]
BigDecimal 10.5 vs 10.50: false
Money      10.5 vs 10.50: true
entity found after edit: true
mutable key found:       false (size 1)

The rules the demo shows

  • Never use double for money. Use BigDecimal with a fixed scale, or a long of minor units (cents).
  • BigDecimal.equals compares scale too, so 10.5 and 10.50 differ. Normalise the scale in the constructor, or compare with compareTo.
  • Validate in the compact constructor. Then no invalid Money can exist anywhere in the program.
  • Base an entity's equals on its id only, and make the id final. Editing an email must not change which member it is.
  • Never put a mutable object in a hash set or use it as a map key if the fields in its hashCode can change. The object is still in the set, but contains looks in the wrong bucket and cannot find it.

Records, sealed types and pattern matching make models shorter and safer

Modern Java changes what an LLD answer looks like. A value object is one line. A closed family of types is a sealed interface, and a switch over it must handle every case or it does not compile. Say what you are using and why: "sealed, so adding a vehicle type breaks the build instead of silently falling through".

FeatureSinceWhat it replaces in a design
Records16Hand-written value objects with equals, hashCode, toString
Sealed classes and interfaces17Open hierarchies that anyone can extend; default branches that hide missing cases
Pattern matching for instanceof16The cast after the check
Switch expressions14Fall-through bugs; a variable assigned in every branch
Text blocks15Concatenated multi-line strings in demos and tests
Pattern matching for switchsince 21An instanceof chain; the visitor pattern for closed hierarchies
Record patternssince 21Calling accessors after matching; nested matching
Sequenced collectionssince 21list.get(list.size() - 1); reversing by copying
Virtual threadssince 21Thread pools sized to avoid running out of threads on blocking I/O
Toolkit.java · sealed types, record patterns, sequenced collections
import java.util.*;

sealed interface Vehicle permits Car, Motorbike, Truck {
    String plate();                        // records implement it for free
}
record Car(String plate, boolean electric) implements Vehicle {}
record Motorbike(String plate) implements Vehicle {}
record Truck(String plate, int axles) implements Vehicle {}

enum SpotSize { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }

public class Toolkit {
    static SpotSize sizeFor(Vehicle v) {
        return switch (v) {                // exhaustive: no default, and a
            case Motorbike m -> SpotSize.SMALL;  // new Vehicle will not compile
            case Car c       -> SpotSize.MEDIUM;
            case Truck t     -> SpotSize.LARGE;
        };
    }

    static int hourlyRate(Vehicle v) {
        return switch (v) {
            case Car(String p, boolean e) when e -> 3;   // record pattern + guard
            case Car c                           -> 4;
            case Motorbike m                     -> 2;
            case Truck(String p, int axles)      -> 5 + 2 * axles;
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Vehicle> queue = List.of(new Car("KA-01", false),
                new Car("KA-02", true), new Motorbike("KA-03"),
                new Truck("KA-04", 3));
        Map<SpotSize, List<String>> bySize = new EnumMap<>(SpotSize.class);
        for (Vehicle v : queue) {
            bySize.computeIfAbsent(sizeFor(v), k -> new ArrayList<>())
                  .add(v.plate());
            System.out.println(v + " -> " + hourlyRate(v) + "/h");
        }
        System.out.println(bySize);
        System.out.println("first " + queue.getFirst().plate()
                + ", last " + queue.getLast().plate()
                + ", reversed " + queue.reversed().stream()
                        .map(Vehicle::plate).toList());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · Toolkit.java
Car[plate=KA-01, electric=false] -> 4/h
Car[plate=KA-02, electric=true] -> 3/h
Motorbike[plate=KA-03] -> 2/h
Truck[plate=KA-04, axles=3] -> 11/h
{SMALL=[KA-03], MEDIUM=[KA-01, KA-02], LARGE=[KA-04]}
first KA-01, last KA-04, reversed [KA-04, KA-03, KA-02, KA-01]
Sealed type or interface with a method?Both are right for different problems. Use a sealed type and switch when the set of types is fixed but operations keep being added (pricing, sizing, reporting). Use an ordinary interface and polymorphic methods when new types keep arriving and the operations are fixed. Say which axis you expect to change; that is the design decision. The visitor slide returns to this.

S · A class should have one reason to change

"One reason to change" means one group of people who would ask for the change. It does not mean one method. An invoice class that calculates tax, saves to a database and emails a PDF changes when finance changes a rule, when the DBA changes the schema, and when marketing changes the email. Three groups, so three classes.

Before · one class, three reasons to change
class InvoiceService {
    Invoice create(Order order) {
        BigDecimal tax = order.subtotal()
                .multiply(new BigDecimal("0.18"));        // finance rule
        Invoice inv = new Invoice(order.id(), order.subtotal(), tax);
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO invoice VALUES (?,?,?)", // storage
                inv.id(), inv.net(), inv.tax());
        mail.send(order.email(), "Your invoice",          // delivery
                pdf.render(inv));
        return inv;
    }
}
After · each rule has one home
final class TaxPolicy {                     // changes with finance
    BigDecimal taxOn(BigDecimal net) { return net.multiply(RATE); }
}
interface InvoiceRepository { void save(Invoice inv); }   // with storage
interface InvoiceNotifier { void issued(Invoice inv); }   // with delivery

final class InvoiceService {                // only coordinates
    private final TaxPolicy tax;
    private final InvoiceRepository repo;
    private final InvoiceNotifier notifier;
    // constructor omitted

    Invoice create(Order order) {
        var inv = new Invoice(order.id(), order.subtotal(),
                              tax.taxOn(order.subtotal()));
        repo.save(inv);
        notifier.issued(inv);
        return inv;
    }
}

How to spot a violation

The class name ends in Manager, Helper or Util. It imports from three unrelated packages. Describing it needs the word "and". Its tests need a database and a mail server.

How far to split

Split by who asks for changes, not until every class has one method. Invoice can still compute its own total, because that is invoice logic. Ten classes of three lines each is its own smell.

In the LLD round

The usual violation is one ParkingLotManager that finds spots, prices tickets and prints receipts. Put the fit rule on ParkingSpot, the price in a PricingStrategy, and keep the service thin.

O · Open for extension, closed for modification, at the points you expect to change

When a requirement you expected arrives, such as a new pricing rule, you should be able to add a class rather than edit a working one. That needs a seam: an interface at the point of variation. You cannot be closed against every change, so choose the seams from the requirements, and say which ones you chose.

Before · every new rule edits this method
long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) {
    long hours = t.hoursUntil(exit);
    switch (t.lot().pricingMode()) {
        case "HOURLY":  return hours * 40;
        case "WEEKEND": return isWeekend(exit) ? 100 : hours * 40;
        case "EVENT":   return 300;
        // next month: "EV_DISCOUNT" goes here, and the tests
        // for the other three rules must run again
        default: throw new IllegalStateException();
    }
}
After · a new rule is a new class
interface PricingStrategy {
    long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit);
}
final class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    public long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) { return t.hoursUntil(exit) * 40; }
}
final class FlatEventPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    public long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) { return 300; }
}
// EV discount: a decorator that wraps any strategy, no edits
final class EvDiscount implements PricingStrategy {
    private final PricingStrategy inner;
    EvDiscount(PricingStrategy inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) {
        long base = inner.fee(t, exit);
        return t.vehicle().electric() ? base * 80 / 100 : base;
    }
}
The honest versionSomething still has to choose which strategy to use: a factory, a configuration map, or the composition root in main. That one place is allowed to change. OCP moves the change to where it is cheap and safe; it does not remove it.
When a switch is the better answerIf the types are fixed (a sealed Vehicle) and operations keep being added, a switch over the sealed type is closed in a different way: the compiler finds every switch that needs a new case. Say which axis you expect to change. See the Java 21 toolkit.

L · A subtype must keep every promise its supertype makes

Code written against a type must still work when handed any subtype. The test is behaviour, not whether the types compile. A square is a rectangle in geometry, but a mutable Square breaks a promise a mutable Rectangle makes: that setting the width leaves the height alone.

LiskovDemo.java · the broken subtype, then the fix
import java.util.*;

class Rectangle {
    protected int w, h;
    void setWidth(int w)  { this.w = w; }     // promise: height unchanged
    void setHeight(int h) { this.h = h; }     // promise: width unchanged
    int area() { return w * h; }
}

class Square extends Rectangle {              // compiles, and is wrong
    @Override void setWidth(int s)  { w = s; h = s; }
    @Override void setHeight(int s) { w = s; h = s; }
}

sealed interface Shape permits Rect, Sq { int area(); }
record Rect(int w, int h) implements Shape {  // immutable: no setter
    public int area() { return w * h; }       // promise to break
}
record Sq(int side) implements Shape {
    public int area() { return side * side; }
}

public class LiskovDemo {
    static void resize(Rectangle r) {         // written for Rectangle
        r.setWidth(5);
        r.setHeight(4);
        System.out.println(r.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + ": expected 20, got " + r.area());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        resize(new Rectangle());
        resize(new Square());

        List<Shape> shapes = List.of(new Rect(5, 4), new Sq(4));
        shapes.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s + " area " + s.area()));

        List<Integer> fixed = List.of(1, 2);  // the JDK's own compromise
        try { fixed.add(3); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("List.of(..).add -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · LiskovDemo.java
Rectangle: expected 20, got 20
Square: expected 20, got 16
Rect[w=5, h=4] area 20
Sq[side=4] area 16
List.of(..).add -> UnsupportedOperationException
A subtype may notExample
Demand more of its inputsAn override that rejects a null the parent accepted
Promise less about its resultA sort override that sometimes leaves the list unsorted
Break an invariantA Square whose sides can no longer be set separately
Throw what the parent does notA ReadOnlyAccount.withdraw that throws UnsupportedOperationException
The fix is usually in the hierarchyIf a subtype has to refuse a method, it is not really that type. Make the shapes immutable, or give them a common interface with only the operations every one supports. Java's List.of breaks LSP on purpose, and documents the "optional operation"; your design should not need to.

I · No client should depend on methods it does not use

A fat interface forces every implementer to provide methods it cannot support, and every caller to depend on methods it never calls. Split interfaces by client, the way each caller uses them. It is LSP's partner: most UnsupportedOperationExceptions mean an interface is too wide.

Before · one interface for every machine
interface OfficeMachine {
    void print(Document d);
    void scan(Document d);
    void fax(Document d, String number);
}

final class BasicPrinter implements OfficeMachine {
    public void print(Document d) { /* works */ }
    public void scan(Document d) {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException();   // LSP broken too
    }
    public void fax(Document d, String n) {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException();
    }
}
After · one role per interface
interface Printer { void print(Document d); }
interface Scanner { void scan(Document d); }
interface Fax     { void fax(Document d, String number); }

final class BasicPrinter implements Printer {
    public void print(Document d) { /* works */ }
}
final class MultiFunctionDevice implements Printer, Scanner, Fax {
    public void print(Document d) { }
    public void scan(Document d) { }
    public void fax(Document d, String number) { }
}

final class PayslipJob {             // needs printing and nothing else
    private final Printer printer;
    PayslipJob(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; }
}

In the library problem

A reference book can be read but not borrowed. Give the catalogue item a Borrowable role instead of a borrow() that throws for reference books.

In the ATM problem

The customer screen and the maintenance panel use the same machine through different interfaces: CustomerSession and MaintenanceOps. A customer can never reach refillCash.

How narrow is too narrow

One interface per method is rarely right. Group methods that the same client always uses together. Comparable has one method and is perfect; Collection has fifteen and is fine because its callers use them together.

D · Business rules depend on interfaces they own, and never on the details

The high-level class (OrderService) declares the interface it needs (PaymentGateway), and the low-level class (the vendor adapter) implements it. The source-code arrow now points from detail to policy, the reverse of the call direction. That is what lets you swap the vendor, or test with a fake, without editing the business rule.

DipDemo.java · the policy owns the interface
import java.util.*;

record Order(String id, long amountCents) {}
record Charge(String orderId, long amountCents, String reference) {}

interface PaymentGateway {                  // declared by the order module
    Charge charge(String orderId, long amountCents);
}

final class OrderService {                  // high-level policy
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;   // injected, never created here
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) {
        this.gateway = Objects.requireNonNull(gateway);
    }
    String checkout(Order o) {
        if (o.amountCents() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount");
        Charge c = gateway.charge(o.id(), o.amountCents());
        return "order " + o.id() + " paid, ref " + c.reference();
    }
}

final class FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway {        // tests, demos
    final List<Charge> charges = new ArrayList<>();
    public Charge charge(String id, long cents) {
        var c = new Charge(id, cents, "FAKE-" + (charges.size() + 1));
        charges.add(c);
        return c;
    }
}

final class CardNetworkGateway implements PaymentGateway { // the detail
    public Charge charge(String id, long cents) {          // would wrap the
        return new Charge(id, cents, "ch_" + id.toLowerCase()); // vendor SDK
    }
}

public class DipDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {               // composition root
        var fake = new FakeGateway();
        var underTest = new OrderService(fake);
        System.out.println(underTest.checkout(new Order("A-1", 2500)));
        System.out.println(underTest.checkout(new Order("A-2", 990)));
        System.out.println("recorded: " + fake.charges.stream()
                .map(Charge::reference).toList());

        var live = new OrderService(new CardNetworkGateway());
        System.out.println(live.checkout(new Order("B-7", 4200)));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · DipDemo.java
order A-1 paid, ref FAKE-1
order A-2 paid, ref FAKE-2
recorded: [FAKE-1, FAKE-2]
order B-7 paid, ref ch_b-7
Call direction OrderService ──calls──> CardNetworkGateway Source dependency, inverted OrderService ──> «interface» PaymentGateway ▲ ┆ implements CardNetworkGateway
Inversion is not injectionDependency injection is how the object arrives: through the constructor, from main or from Spring. Dependency inversion is who owns the interface. Injecting a concrete CardNetworkGateway is injection without inversion, and still couples the policy to the vendor.

DRY, KISS and YAGNI keep SOLID from turning into over-engineering

SOLID pushes you towards more interfaces and more classes. These three push back. In an interview the right amount of design is whatever the stated requirements, plus the one change you can see coming, need. Anything beyond that is time you did not spend on the working code.

DRY · Don't repeat yourself

Every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative home. The late-fee rule lives in one place, not in the checkout screen and in the nightly job.

Misread as "never write similar code twice". Two methods that look alike today but change for different reasons are not duplication. Merging them creates the wrong abstraction, which is worse than the copy.

KISS · Keep it simple

Choose the simplest structure that meets the requirement. If vehicle types differ only in a size, an enum with a field beats a class hierarchy. If there is one pricing rule, a method beats a strategy interface.

Misread as "no design". Simple means few concepts, not one giant method.

YAGNI · You aren't gonna need it

Do not build for requirements you imagined. Multi-currency, plug-in loading and a rules engine are rarely asked for in an hour.

Misread as "no seams". Leaving an interface where the prompt hints at change ("pricing may vary") is not speculation; it is reading the requirements.

KISS · when behaviour is only data, use an enum
enum VehicleType {
    MOTORBIKE(SpotSize.SMALL, 20),
    CAR(SpotSize.MEDIUM, 40),
    TRUCK(SpotSize.LARGE, 90);

    final SpotSize needs;
    final int hourlyRate;
    VehicleType(SpotSize needs, int hourlyRate) {
        this.needs = needs;
        this.hourlyRate = hourlyRate;
    }
}
// Promote to classes only when the types start to
// behave differently, not just carry different numbers.
What to say out loud"I'll keep vehicle types as an enum, because right now they differ only in size and rate. If you tell me trucks need a permit check, I'll turn it into a sealed interface. That's a ten-minute change, because nothing outside VehicleType switches on it." That one sentence shows KISS, YAGNI and an awareness of OCP together, and interviewers notice it.

Low coupling, high cohesion, and knowing which class should own a job

Coupling is how much one class knows about others; keep it low. Cohesion is how closely the parts of one class belong together; keep it high. The Law of Demeter and the GRASP patterns are practical rules for getting both, and GRASP's information expert is the most useful single rule in an LLD round.

Law of Demeter · talk to your friends, not their friends
// Before: the caller walks the object graph, and
// breaks when any link in the chain changes
long rate = ticket.getSpot().getFloor().getLot()
                  .getPricing().getHourlyRate();

// After: tell, don't ask. The ticket knows its lot
// and asks it; the caller knows only the ticket.
long fee = ticket.feeAt(exitTime);
Demeter, preciselyA method may call methods on this, its parameters, objects it creates, and its own fields. Chains on value objects and fluent builders (stream().map().toList()) are fine, because they return the same kind of thing rather than reaching into another object's parts.
GRASP patternThe question it answers
Information expertWho should do this? The class that has the data. ParkingSpot.canFit(vehicle), not Manager.fits(spot, vehicle).
CreatorWho creates B? The class that contains, aggregates or closely uses B. A ParkingFloor creates its spots.
ControllerWho first receives a use case from the UI? A thin service per use case, such as BookingService.
Low coupling · high cohesionThe two tests every choice is scored against.
PolymorphismHow to handle behaviour that varies by type? Subtypes, not conditionals.
Pure fabricationNo domain class fits? Invent one: a repository, a DebtSimplifier.
IndirectionHow to decouple two classes? Put an intermediary between them, such as an interface or an event.
Protected variationsHow to protect code from change? Wrap the unstable part behind a stable interface. This is OCP by another name.

Every principle as a smell, a fix, and a sentence to say

You will not be asked to recite these. You will be asked why you made a class or an interface, and the answer is usually one of these rows. Learn the smell column: it is how you notice the problem in your own code while the interviewer watches.

PrincipleSmell in your codeFixSay it like this
SRPA …Manager with methods for three concernsSplit by who asks for the change"Pricing changes for business reasons, so it gets its own class."
OCPA switch on a type or mode that grows every monthAn interface at the point of variation"A new rule is a new class; nothing that works gets edited."
LSPAn override that throws, or ignores its inputReshape the hierarchy; prefer immutability"If a subtype has to refuse a method, it isn't that type."
ISPUnsupportedOperationException in an implementationSplit the interface by client"The customer screen never sees the maintenance methods."
DIPnew VendorClient() inside a business classThe policy declares an interface; inject the detail"I can test booking with a fake payment gateway."
DRYThe same rule in two places, changed in oneOne home for each piece of knowledge"The late-fee rule lives in one class."
KISS · YAGNIInterfaces with one implementation and no reason for a secondInline them; add the seam when the need appears"I'll add a strategy when a second rule arrives."
Demetera.getB().getC().doIt()Tell, don't ask: move the behaviour to a"The ticket computes its own fee."
Information expertA service that reads every field of an object to decide somethingMove the method to the object that owns the data"The spot knows whether a vehicle fits."
CompositionInheriting only to reuse codeHold the helper as a field"I'd rather have a strategy than be one."

The 23 Gang of Four patterns, and the ones LLD rounds actually use

The 1994 Design Patterns book named 23 recurring solutions in three families: creational (how objects get made), structural (how objects are put together) and behavioural (how objects share work). About ten of them come up in almost every LLD round. The core ones are worth knowing well enough to write from memory.

CreationalIntent
SingletonOne instance, one global access point. Mostly an anti-pattern now.
Factory method coreLet a method decide which class to instantiate.
Abstract factoryCreate families of related objects that must match.
Builder coreBuild a complex object step by step, validated once.
PrototypeCreate by copying a configured instance.
StructuralIntent
Adapter coreMake an existing interface fit the one you need.
BridgeVary an abstraction and its implementation independently.
CompositeTreat a tree of objects and a single object alike.
Decorator coreAdd behaviour by wrapping, without subclassing.
FacadeOne simple entry point to a subsystem.
FlyweightShare immutable state across many small objects.
ProxyA stand-in that controls access: lazy, cached, remote, guarded.
BehaviouralIntent
Chain of resp.Pass a request along handlers until one deals with it.
Command coreA request as an object: queue it, log it, undo it.
InterpreterA grammar as a class per rule. Rare in LLD rounds.
IteratorWalk a collection without exposing its structure.
MediatorObjects talk through a hub, not to each other.
MementoSave and restore state without exposing it.
Observer coreNotify subscribers when something changes.
State coreBehaviour that changes with internal state.
Strategy coreSwap an algorithm behind an interface.
Template methodA fixed algorithm with steps subclasses fill in.
VisitorAdd operations to a closed type hierarchy.
How each pattern slide is laid outThe problem it solves, a complete program that compiles and runs, what it printed, and when not to use it. Patterns cost classes. Use one when it removes a conditional that would otherwise be repeated, or isolates a change you expect.

Start from the symptom in the requirements, never from the pattern

Interviewers mark down "I'll use the factory, strategy and observer patterns" said in the first minute, before any requirement justifies them. Mark them up for "pricing varies by lot and may change, so it goes behind an interface; that is the strategy pattern". The pattern name comes last, as a label for a decision you already made.

When the requirement says…Reach forSeen in
"The rule may differ", "pricing depends on…", "support several algorithms"StrategyParking fees, split types, elevator scheduling, seat pricing
"It behaves differently when it is…", a status field checked in every methodStateATM, vending machine, booking lifecycle, elevator
"Notify", "when X happens, update Y and Z"ObserverDisplays, reservation alerts, waiting lists
"Undo", "replay", "queue the request", "audit every action"CommandChess moves, editor, ATM transaction log
"Create the right kind of X from input"Factory method, or a static factoryVehicles, pieces, notifiers, splits
Many optional fields; an object that must be valid once builtBuilderSearch queries, bookings, test fixtures
"Integrate with the vendor's library"AdapterPayment gateways, SMS providers
Add-ons that stack: "plus a discount, plus logging, plus retry"DecoratorPricing rules, notifier retry, I/O streams
"Try each handler until one accepts", approval levelsChain of responsibilityATM note dispensing, request validation, expense approval
A part-whole tree that should be treated uniformlyCompositeFile systems, menus, group expenses
"One entry point for the client" over several servicesFacadeBooking service over seats, payments and notifications
Pattern-itisA VehicleFactoryFactory, an observer with one listener that will never have a second, a strategy interface with one implementation. Each adds a class and an indirection, and buys nothing. If you cannot name the second implementation, leave the interface out.
Lambdas are patterns tooIn modern Java a strategy with one method is often just a Function or a custom functional interface filled by a lambda. The same goes for commands (Runnable) and observers (Consumer). Give the interface a domain name when it carries domain meaning, such as PricingStrategy.

Singleton: one instance, created safely, and usually better injected

A singleton guarantees one instance of a class and a global way to reach it. Interviewers ask for it for two reasons: to see whether you can write a thread-safe one, and to see whether you know why you usually should not. There are three correct ways to write it. Most of the code people write from memory is a fourth, broken way.

SingletonDemo.java · enum, holder idiom, double-checked locking
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

enum IdGenerator {                       // 1. enum: simplest, and safe against
    INSTANCE;                            //    reflection and serialization
    private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(1);
    long nextId() { return next.getAndIncrement(); }
}

final class Config {                     // 2. holder idiom: lazy, no locks.
    private Config() { System.out.println("Config created"); }
    private static final class Holder {  // the JVM runs Holder's static init
        static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();   // once, on first use
    }
    static Config get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}

final class Registry {                   // 3. double-checked locking
    private static volatile Registry instance;    // volatile is essential
    private Registry() {}
    static Registry get() {
        Registry r = instance;           // one volatile read on the fast path
        if (r == null) {
            synchronized (Registry.class) {
                r = instance;            // check again: another thread
                if (r == null) instance = r = new Registry();  // may have won
            }
        }
        return r;
    }
}

public class SingletonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("before the first get()");
        System.out.println("same Config: " + (Config.get() == Config.get()));

        Set<Registry> registries = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        Set<Long> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    registries.add(Registry.get());
                    ids.add(IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId());
                });
            }
        }                                // close() waits for every task
        System.out.println("Registry instances seen: " + registries.size());
        System.out.println("unique ids from 10,000 threads: " + ids.size());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · SingletonDemo.java
before the first get()
Config created
same Config: true
Registry instances seen: 1
unique ids from 10,000 threads: 10000
The broken version people write from memory
private static Registry instance;         // not volatile
static Registry get() {
    if (instance == null)                 // two threads both see null
        instance = new Registry();        // and both create one; or one
    return instance;                      // sees a half-built object
}
Why volatile mattersWithout it, the write to instance can become visible to another thread before the constructor's writes do, so that thread sees a non-null reference to an object that is not fully built. volatile forbids that reordering. The demo uses virtual threads since 21; the pattern itself works on any Java since 5.
Which to writeSay "enum" first: it is one line and handles serialization and reflection for you. Use the holder idiom if the class must extend something, since an enum cannot.

How a singleton breaks, and why dependency injection replaced it

A private constructor does not guarantee one instance. Reflection can call it, and deserialization creates a new object without calling it at all. Only the enum form survives both. The bigger problem is not a second instance, though. A singleton is hidden global state, and it makes the classes that use it hard to test.

SingletonBreak.java · reflection and serialization against three singletons
import java.io.*;
import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;

final class Naive implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    static final Naive INSTANCE = new Naive();
    private Naive() {}
}

final class Guarded implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    static final Guarded INSTANCE = new Guarded();
    private Guarded() {
        if (INSTANCE != null) throw new IllegalStateException("already created");
    }
    private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }   // replace the copy
}

enum EnumSingleton { INSTANCE }

public class SingletonBreak {
    static String reflect(Class<?> type, Object one) {
        try {
            Constructor<?> c = type.isEnum()
                    ? type.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class, int.class)
                    : type.getDeclaredConstructor();
            c.setAccessible(true);
            Object copy = type.isEnum() ? c.newInstance("COPY", 1) : c.newInstance();
            return copy == one ? "same instance" : "SECOND INSTANCE";
        } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
            return "blocked: " + e.getCause().getMessage();
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException | IllegalArgumentException e) {
            return "blocked: " + e.getMessage();
        }
    }

    static String serialize(Object one) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        var bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(bytes)) { out.writeObject(one); }
        try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(
                new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray()))) {
            return in.readObject() == one ? "same instance" : "SECOND INSTANCE";
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object[][] cases = { { Naive.class, Naive.INSTANCE },
                { Guarded.class, Guarded.INSTANCE },
                { EnumSingleton.class, EnumSingleton.INSTANCE } };
        for (Object[] c : cases) {
            Class<?> type = (Class<?>) c[0];
            System.out.printf("%-13s reflection: %s%n", type.getSimpleName(),
                    reflect(type, c[1]));
            System.out.printf("%-13s serialize:  %s%n", "", serialize(c[1]));
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · SingletonBreak.java
Naive         reflection: SECOND INSTANCE
              serialize:  SECOND INSTANCE
Guarded       reflection: blocked: already created
              serialize:  same instance
EnumSingleton reflection: blocked: Cannot reflectively create enum objects
              serialize:  same instance
Cost of a singletonWhy
Hard to testA class that calls PaymentGateway.getInstance() cannot be given a fake.
Hidden dependencyThe constructor does not show that the class needs the gateway.
State leaks between testsOne test's data is still there in the next.
One per class loaderTwo web apps in one server each get their own "single" instance.
What to say about the parking lot"There is one ParkingLot in this program, but I'll create it in main and pass it in, not make it a singleton. Then a test can build a small lot with two spots." In Spring, a bean is a singleton by default (one per container), which gives you the single instance without the global access.

Factory method: one place decides which class to create

Callers ask for "a notifier for this channel" and never name the concrete class. There are two forms. A static factory is a method that picks the class from its input, and it is what LLD answers use most. The GoF factory method is an abstract method that a subclass overrides to choose the class used inside a fixed algorithm.

FactoryDemo.java · a static factory, and the GoF factory method
import java.util.List;

enum Channel { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }

interface Notifier { String send(String to, String message); }

record EmailNotifier() implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String m) { return "email " + to + ": " + m; }
}
record SmsNotifier(int maxLength) implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String m) {
        String body = m.length() <= maxLength ? m : m.substring(0, maxLength - 3) + "...";
        return "sms   " + to + ": " + body;
    }
}
record PushNotifier() implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String m) { return "push  " + to + ": " + m; }
}

final class Notifiers {                    // static factory: the only code
    private Notifiers() {}                 // that names concrete classes
    static Notifier forChannel(Channel c) {
        return switch (c) {                // exhaustive over the enum
            case EMAIL -> new EmailNotifier();
            case SMS   -> new SmsNotifier(20);
            case PUSH  -> new PushNotifier();
        };
    }
}

interface RowFormat { String header(); String join(List<String> cells); }

abstract class ReportExporter {            // GoF factory method
    final String export(List<List<String>> rows) {  // the fixed algorithm
        RowFormat f = createFormat();      // the subclass picks the class
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(f.header());
        rows.forEach(r -> out.append(f.join(r)).append('\n'));
        return out.toString();
    }
    protected abstract RowFormat createFormat();   // the factory method
}

final class CsvExporter extends ReportExporter {
    protected RowFormat createFormat() {
        return new RowFormat() {
            public String header() { return ""; }
            public String join(List<String> c) { return String.join(",", c); }
        };
    }
}

final class MarkdownExporter extends ReportExporter {
    protected RowFormat createFormat() {
        return new RowFormat() {
            public String header() { return "| plate | fee |\n|---|---|\n"; }
            public String join(List<String> c) { return "| " + String.join(" | ", c) + " |"; }
        };
    }
}

public class FactoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Channel c : Channel.values())
            System.out.println(Notifiers.forChannel(c)
                    .send("ana", "Your car is ready at gate B"));

        var rows = List.of(List.of("KA-01", "120"), List.of("KA-02", "80"));
        System.out.print(new CsvExporter().export(rows));
        System.out.print(new MarkdownExporter().export(rows));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · FactoryDemo.java
email ana: Your car is ready at gate B
sms   ana: Your car is ready...
push  ana: Your car is ready at gate B
KA-01,120
KA-02,80
| plate | fee |
|---|---|
| KA-01 | 120 |
| KA-02 | 80 |
What it buys youOnly Notifiers names the concrete classes. Adding WHATSAPP touches the enum and the factory, and the exhaustive switch will not compile until you add the case. No caller changes.
Where people overdo itA factory that wraps a single new with no choice in it is noise. So is a VehicleFactory interface with one implementation. Add the factory when there is a real decision to make, or when construction needs rules the caller should not know.
In the problemsThe chess setup builds pieces from a layout string through a factory, and Splitwise builds the right Split from the request type. In both cases the parsing code never names a concrete class.

Abstract factory: create a family of objects that must match

Use it when several objects vary together and mixing them would be a bug. A checkout in India needs a UPI authoriser, 18% GST and rupees. A checkout in Germany needs SEPA, 19% VAT and euros. One factory per region makes each checkout internally consistent, and the checkout code never names a region.

AbstractFactoryDemo.java · one kit per region
interface Authorizer { String authorize(long minor); }
interface TaxRule { long taxOn(long minor); }

interface RegionKit {                       // the abstract factory
    Authorizer authorizer();
    TaxRule taxRule();
    String currency();
}

final class IndiaKit implements RegionKit {
    public Authorizer authorizer() { return m -> "UPI mandate for " + m; }
    public TaxRule taxRule() { return m -> m * 18 / 100; }      // GST
    public String currency() { return "INR"; }
}

final class GermanyKit implements RegionKit {
    public Authorizer authorizer() { return m -> "SEPA debit for " + m; }
    public TaxRule taxRule() { return m -> m * 19 / 100; }      // VAT
    public String currency() { return "EUR"; }
}

final class Checkout {                      // knows only the interfaces
    private final RegionKit kit;
    Checkout(RegionKit kit) { this.kit = kit; }
    String pay(long netMinor) {
        long gross = netMinor + kit.taxRule().taxOn(netMinor);
        return kit.authorizer().authorize(gross) + " " + kit.currency();
    }
}

public class AbstractFactoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (RegionKit kit : new RegionKit[] { new IndiaKit(), new GermanyKit() })
            System.out.println(new Checkout(kit).pay(10_000));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · AbstractFactoryDemo.java
UPI mandate for 11800 INR
SEPA debit for 11900 EUR
Factory methodAbstract factory
CreatesOne productA family of related products
Chosen byAn argument, or a subclassWhich factory object you hold
Adding a variantA new case or subclassA new factory class
Adding a productA new methodA new method on every factory
When it earns its placeRarely in a one-hour LLD round. It shows up in "support multiple regions", "support light and dark themes" and "support two database vendors". If there is only one product, you want a factory method; if nothing has to match, you want separate strategies.

Builder: many optional fields, one validated, immutable result

A constructor with seven parameters, four of them optional, is unreadable at the call site (new ShowSearch("Pune", d, null, null, true, 0, false)) and easy to call with two arguments swapped. A builder names every argument, takes the required ones up front, and checks the rules that span several fields once, in build().

BuilderDemo.java · required fields first, cross-field rules in build()
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.*;

final class ShowSearch {
    private final String city;
    private final LocalDate date;
    private final List<String> languages;
    private final Integer maxPrice;             // null means no limit
    private final boolean imaxOnly;

    private ShowSearch(Builder b) {             // only the builder calls this
        city = b.city;
        date = b.date;
        languages = List.copyOf(b.languages);   // defensive, immutable copy
        maxPrice = b.maxPrice;
        imaxOnly = b.imaxOnly;
    }

    static Builder in(String city, LocalDate date) {   // required up front
        return new Builder(city, date);
    }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return "ShowSearch[" + city + " " + date + " " + languages
                + (maxPrice == null ? "" : " max " + maxPrice)
                + (imaxOnly ? " IMAX" : "") + "]";
    }

    static final class Builder {
        private final String city;
        private final LocalDate date;
        private final Set<String> languages = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        private Integer maxPrice;
        private boolean imaxOnly;

        private Builder(String city, LocalDate date) {
            this.city = Objects.requireNonNull(city, "city");
            this.date = Objects.requireNonNull(date, "date");
        }
        Builder language(String l) { languages.add(l); return this; }
        Builder maxPrice(int p) {
            if (p <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxPrice must be > 0");
            maxPrice = p;
            return this;
        }
        Builder imaxOnly() { imaxOnly = true; return this; }

        ShowSearch build() {                    // rules across fields
            if (imaxOnly && maxPrice != null && maxPrice < 300)
                throw new IllegalStateException("no IMAX show costs under 300");
            return new ShowSearch(this);
        }
    }
}

public class BuilderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate day = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 2);
        System.out.println(ShowSearch.in("Pune", day)
                .language("Hindi").language("English").maxPrice(450).build());
        System.out.println(ShowSearch.in("Pune", day).imaxOnly().build());
        try {
            ShowSearch.in("Pune", day).imaxOnly().maxPrice(200).build();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · BuilderDemo.java
ShowSearch[Pune 2026-10-02 [Hindi, English] max 450]
ShowSearch[Pune 2026-10-02 [] IMAX]
rejected: no IMAX show costs under 300

Why the object is immutable

Once build() returns, no one can break the rules it checked. The builder is mutable, but it never escapes the method that uses it.

Records instead

With three or four fields, all required, a record with a compact constructor is shorter and just as safe. Reach for a builder when there are optional fields or cross-field rules.

Say where it goesBuilders fit query objects, bookings with optional add-ons, and test fixtures. Lombok's @Builder writes the boilerplate, but it does not do the build() validation, which is the part the interviewer is looking for.

Prototype: copy a configured object, and copy it deeply enough

Create new objects by copying one that is already set up: a board in its opening position, a document template, a default configuration. The pattern is simple. The hard part is the copy: a shallow copy shares its mutable insides, so changing the copy changes the original. Chess engines hit this when they copy the board to try a move.

PrototypeDemo.java · a shallow copy leaks, a deep copy does not
import java.util.*;

final class Board {
    private final char[][] cells;
    private Board(char[][] cells) { this.cells = cells; }

    static Board parse(String... rows) {
        char[][] c = new char[rows.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) c[i] = rows[i].toCharArray();
        return new Board(c);
    }

    Board shallowCopy() {                  // new Board, same arrays
        return new Board(cells.clone());   // clone() on 2-D copies row refs
    }

    Board deepCopy() {                     // copy constructor semantics
        char[][] c = new char[cells.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < cells.length; i++) c[i] = cells[i].clone();
        return new Board(c);
    }

    void move(int r1, int c1, int r2, int c2) {
        cells[r2][c2] = cells[r1][c1];
        cells[r1][c1] = '.';
    }

    String row(int r) { return new String(cells[r]); }
}

public class PrototypeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Board> prototypes = new LinkedHashMap<>();   // registry
        prototypes.put("mini", Board.parse("rnbk", "pppp", "....", "PPPP", "RNBK"));

        Board original = prototypes.get("mini");
        Board shallow = original.shallowCopy();
        shallow.move(3, 0, 2, 0);          // try a pawn move on the copy
        System.out.println("after shallow try, original row 3: " + original.row(3));

        Board fresh = Board.parse("rnbk", "pppp", "....", "PPPP", "RNBK");
