        Board deep = fresh.deepCopy();
        deep.move(3, 0, 2, 0);
        System.out.println("after deep try,    original row 3: " + fresh.row(3));
        System.out.println("                   copy row 3:     " + deep.row(3));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · PrototypeDemo.java
after shallow try, original row 3: .PPP
after deep try,    original row 3: PPPP
                   copy row 3:     .PPP
Ways to copyVerdict
Cloneable + clone()Avoid. Shallow by default, bypasses constructors, clashes with final fields, and throws a checked exception.
Copy constructor or copy() methodPreferred. You decide what is deep, and it can keep fields final.
Immutable objectsBest of all: nothing to copy. A new board per move, sharing the unchanged rows, is how persistent data structures work.
Where it appears in LLDChess move validation (try the move on a copy, then ask "is my king in check?"), undo by snapshot (see memento), and seat-map templates that each show copies of. Say "deep copy" out loud, and say which fields are deep.

Adapter: make the vendor's interface fit the one your design wants

Your domain declares the interface it needs, such as PaymentGateway.charge(orderId, paise). The vendor's SDK has a different shape: amounts in rupees as strings, results in a map, failure as a status code. An adapter implements your interface by translating to theirs, so the vendor's quirks stay in one class.

AdapterDemo.java · translating units, results and errors
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;

record PaymentResult(boolean ok, String reference, String error) {}

interface PaymentGateway {                    // what our domain wants
    PaymentResult charge(String orderId, long amountPaise);
}

final class LegacyPayClient {                 // the vendor SDK: we cannot
    Map<String, String> doTxn(String ref, String rupees) {   // change it
        if (new BigDecimal(rupees).compareTo(new BigDecimal("50000")) > 0)
            return Map.of("status", "E42", "msg", "limit exceeded");
        return Map.of("status", "00", "txnId", "LP-" + ref);
    }
}

final class LegacyPayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final LegacyPayClient client;     // composition: object adapter
    LegacyPayAdapter(LegacyPayClient client) { this.client = client; }

    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, long paise) {
        String rupees = BigDecimal.valueOf(paise, 2).toPlainString(); // units
        Map<String, String> r = client.doTxn(orderId, rupees);
        return "00".equals(r.get("status"))                          // result
                ? new PaymentResult(true, r.get("txnId"), null)
                : new PaymentResult(false, null,                     // errors
                        r.get("status") + " " + r.get("msg"));
    }
}

public class AdapterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentGateway gateway = new LegacyPayAdapter(new LegacyPayClient());
        System.out.println(gateway.charge("A-1", 125_050));      // 1250.50
        System.out.println(gateway.charge("A-2", 6_000_000));    // 60000.00
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · AdapterDemo.java
PaymentResult[ok=true, reference=LP-A-1, error=null]
PaymentResult[ok=false, reference=null, error=E42 limit exceeded]

Object adapter

Holds the adaptee as a field, as above. Works with final classes and can adapt a whole family. This is the one to write.

Class adapter

Extends the adaptee and implements the target. Java allows only one superclass, and it exposes all the adaptee's methods, so it is rarely right.

Keep the translation completeUnits, time zones, enums, null conventions and exceptions all get translated at the adapter. If a vendor exception type leaks past it, the vendor is back in your domain. In DDD this layer is the anti-corruption layer.
In the JDKArrays.asList adapts an array to List; InputStreamReader adapts bytes to characters; Collections.enumeration adapts a collection to the old Enumeration.

Decorator: stack behaviour by wrapping, in any combination

A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, delegates to it, and adds something before or after. Three add-ons as subclasses would need up to seven classes to cover every combination. As decorators they need three, combined at runtime. The order of wrapping is part of the behaviour, so choose it on purpose.

DecoratorDemo.java · parking pricing with stackable rules
import java.time.*;

record Stay(boolean electric, LocalDateTime in, LocalDateTime out) {
    long startedHours() {                       // any part hour counts
        long minutes = Duration.between(in, out).toMinutes();
        return Math.max(1, (minutes + 59) / 60);
    }
}

interface Pricing {
    long fee(Stay s);
    String describe();
}

record Hourly(long rate) implements Pricing {
    public long fee(Stay s) { return s.startedHours() * rate; }
    public String describe() { return "hourly " + rate; }
}

record WeekendSurcharge(Pricing inner) implements Pricing {     // +25%
    public long fee(Stay s) {
        long base = inner.fee(s);
        DayOfWeek d = s.out().getDayOfWeek();
        boolean weekend = d == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY || d == DayOfWeek.SUNDAY;
        return weekend ? base * 125 / 100 : base;
    }
    public String describe() { return inner.describe() + " > weekend+25%"; }
}

record EvDiscount(Pricing inner) implements Pricing {           // -20%
    public long fee(Stay s) {
        long base = inner.fee(s);
        return s.electric() ? base * 80 / 100 : base;
    }
    public String describe() { return inner.describe() + " > ev-20%"; }
}

record DailyCap(Pricing inner, long cap) implements Pricing {
    public long fee(Stay s) { return Math.min(inner.fee(s), cap); }
    public String describe() { return inner.describe() + " > cap " + cap; }
}

public class DecoratorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var sat = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 3, 10, 0);          // a Saturday
        var stay = new Stay(true, sat, sat.plusHours(3).plusMinutes(20));

        Pricing[] rules = {
            new Hourly(40),
            new WeekendSurcharge(new Hourly(40)),
            new EvDiscount(new WeekendSurcharge(new Hourly(40))),
            new DailyCap(new EvDiscount(new WeekendSurcharge(new Hourly(40))), 150),
            new EvDiscount(new DailyCap(new WeekendSurcharge(new Hourly(40)), 150)),
        };
        System.out.println("stay: " + stay.startedHours() + " started hours, EV, Saturday");
        for (Pricing p : rules)
            System.out.printf("%4d  %s%n", p.fee(stay), p.describe());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · DecoratorDemo.java
stay: 4 started hours, EV, Saturday
 160  hourly 40
 200  hourly 40 > weekend+25%
 160  hourly 40 > weekend+25% > ev-20%
 150  hourly 40 > weekend+25% > ev-20% > cap 150
 120  hourly 40 > weekend+25% > cap 150 > ev-20%
Order is behaviourThe last two lines use the same three rules and give different fees. Capping before the EV discount lets electric cars pay less than the cap. Whether that is right is a business question, so ask it, and build the chain in one place (a factory) so the order is decided once.
Decorator or strategy?A strategy replaces the algorithm; a decorator adds to whatever it wraps. Hourly and flat-rate pricing are strategies. The weekend surcharge and EV discount are decorators, because they apply on top of either.
In the JDKnew BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))) is three decorators. Collections.unmodifiableList and synchronizedMap are decorators too.

Proxy: a stand-in with the same interface that controls access to the real object

A proxy looks exactly like the real object to its callers but decides when, whether and how the real one is reached. The common kinds are caching (skip a slow call), virtual (create the real object lazily), protection (check permissions first) and remote (hide the network). Java can generate a proxy for any interface at runtime, which is how Spring adds @Transactional.

ProxyDemo.java · a caching proxy, wrapped in a dynamic logging proxy
import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
import java.util.*;

interface SeatMapService { List<String> freeSeats(String showId); }

final class RemoteSeatMapService implements SeatMapService {
    int calls;                                   // stands in for a slow call
    public List<String> freeSeats(String showId) {
        calls++;
        return showId.equals("S1") ? List.of("A1", "A2", "B7") : List.of("C3");
    }
}

final class CachingSeatMap implements SeatMapService {    // caching proxy
    private final SeatMapService target;
    private final Map<String, List<String>> cache = new HashMap<>();
    CachingSeatMap(SeatMapService target) { this.target = target; }
    public List<String> freeSeats(String showId) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(showId, target::freeSeats);
    }
    void invalidate(String showId) { cache.remove(showId); }  // on booking
}

public class ProxyDemo {
    static <T> T logging(T target, Class<T> type, List<String> log) {
        Object proxy = Proxy.newProxyInstance(type.getClassLoader(),
                new Class<?>[] { type },
                (p, method, args) -> {           // runs for every call
                    log.add("-> " + method.getName() + Arrays.toString(args));
                    Object result = method.invoke(target, args);
                    log.add("<- " + result);
                    return result;
                });
        return type.cast(proxy);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var remote = new RemoteSeatMapService();
        var cached = new CachingSeatMap(remote);
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
        SeatMapService seats = logging(cached, SeatMapService.class, log);

        seats.freeSeats("S1");
        seats.freeSeats("S1");
        seats.freeSeats("S2");
        cached.invalidate("S1");
        seats.freeSeats("S1");

        log.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("calls that reached the remote service: " + remote.calls);
        System.out.println("proxy class is generated: "
                + Proxy.isProxyClass(seats.getClass()));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · ProxyDemo.java
-> freeSeats[S1]
<- [A1, A2, B7]
-> freeSeats[S1]
<- [A1, A2, B7]
-> freeSeats[S2]
<- [C3]
-> freeSeats[S1]
<- [A1, A2, B7]
calls that reached the remote service: 3
proxy class is generated: true
Proxy, decorator or adapter?All three wrap an object. An adapter changes the interface. A decorator keeps it and adds behaviour the caller asked for, stacked by the client. A proxy keeps it and controls access, usually without the caller knowing, and usually creates or owns the real object itself.
The Spring self-invocation trapSpring's @Transactional and @Cacheable are proxies like the one above. A call from one method of a bean to another method on this never goes through the proxy, so the annotation on the second method is silently ignored. The Spring Boot tab covers it on AOP limits.

Facade: one simple entry point in front of several collaborating services

Booking a ticket touches seat inventory, payments and email, in a set order, with a compensating step when payment fails. Callers should not have to know that sequence. A facade offers one method, book(user, seats), and keeps the choreography in one place. The subsystems stay public for callers who need more control.

FacadeDemo.java · hold, charge, then confirm or release
import java.util.*;

final class SeatInventory {
    private final Map<String, String> holds = new TreeMap<>();  // seat -> user
    private final Set<String> sold = new TreeSet<>();
    boolean hold(String user, List<String> seats) {
        for (String s : seats)
            if (sold.contains(s) || holds.containsKey(s)) return false;
        seats.forEach(s -> holds.put(s, user));
        return true;
    }
    void confirm(List<String> seats) {
        seats.forEach(s -> { holds.remove(s); sold.add(s); });
    }
    void release(List<String> seats) { seats.forEach(holds::remove); }
    String state() { return "sold " + sold + ", held " + holds.keySet(); }
}

final class Payments {
    boolean charge(String user, long amount) { return !user.equals("bob"); }
}

final class Mailer {
    final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();
    void ticket(String user, List<String> seats) { sent.add(user + " " + seats); }
}

final class BookingFacade {
    private static final long PRICE = 250;
    private final SeatInventory inventory;
    private final Payments payments;
    private final Mailer mailer;
    BookingFacade(SeatInventory i, Payments p, Mailer m) {
        inventory = i; payments = p; mailer = m;
    }

    String book(String user, List<String> seats) {
        if (!inventory.hold(user, seats))
            return user + ": seats unavailable";
        if (!payments.charge(user, PRICE * seats.size())) {
            inventory.release(seats);                 // compensate
            return user + ": payment declined, seats released";
        }
        inventory.confirm(seats);
        mailer.ticket(user, seats);
        return user + ": booked " + seats;
    }
}

public class FacadeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var inventory = new SeatInventory();
        var mailer = new Mailer();
        var booking = new BookingFacade(inventory, new Payments(), mailer);

        System.out.println(booking.book("ana", List.of("A1", "A2")));
        System.out.println(booking.book("bob", List.of("B1")));
        System.out.println(booking.book("cy", List.of("A2", "A3")));
        System.out.println(booking.book("cy", List.of("A3", "B1")));
        System.out.println(inventory.state());
        System.out.println("emails: " + mailer.sent);
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · FacadeDemo.java
ana: booked [A1, A2]
bob: payment declined, seats released
cy: seats unavailable
cy: booked [A3, B1]
sold [A1, A2, A3, B1], held []
emails: [ana [A1, A2], cy [A3, B1]]
Facade or god class?A facade coordinates; it does not decide. Seat rules stay in SeatInventory and the charge in Payments. If the facade starts computing prices and checking seat adjacency, it has become the god class the pattern was meant to prevent.
It is the service layerIn LLD answers the facade is usually the application service (BookingService, ParkingLotService): the one class the demo's main talks to. Name it after the use case, not after the pattern.
This version is single-threadedhold checks and then writes, so two threads could both hold A3. The movie booking problem makes the hold atomic.

Composite: treat one item and a whole tree of items the same way

A directory's size is the sum of its children's sizes, and a child can be a file or another directory. A composite gives leaves and containers one interface, so size(), print() or find() work on any node, and the recursion is in the data structure rather than in every caller. It is the standard answer to "design a file system".

CompositeDemo.java · a file tree with a sealed node type
import java.util.*;

sealed interface Node permits FileNode, Dir {
    String name();
    long size();
}

record FileNode(String name, long size) implements Node {}

final class Dir implements Node {
    private final String name;
    private final List<Node> children = new ArrayList<>();
    Dir(String name) { this.name = name; }
    Dir add(Node child) { children.add(child); return this; }
    public String name() { return name; }
    public long size() {                          // recursion lives here
        return children.stream().mapToLong(Node::size).sum();
    }
    List<Node> children() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(children); }
}

public class CompositeDemo {
    static void print(Node n, String indent) {
        switch (n) {                              // pattern switch, sealed
            case FileNode f -> System.out.printf("%s%s (%d)%n", indent, f.name(), f.size());
            case Dir d -> {
                System.out.printf("%s%s/ (%d)%n", indent, d.name(), d.size());
                d.children().forEach(c -> print(c, indent + "  "));
            }
        }
    }

    static Optional<Node> find(Node n, String name) {
        if (n.name().equals(name)) return Optional.of(n);
        if (n instanceof Dir d)
            for (Node c : d.children()) {
                Optional<Node> hit = find(c, name);
                if (hit.isPresent()) return hit;
            }
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dir root = new Dir("root")
            .add(new FileNode("notes.txt", 120))
            .add(new Dir("src")
                .add(new FileNode("Main.java", 2_400))
                .add(new Dir("util").add(new FileNode("Ids.java", 800))))
            .add(new Dir("empty"));
        print(root, "");
        System.out.println("src size: " + find(root, "src").map(Node::size).orElse(-1L));
        System.out.println("missing:  " + find(root, "nope").isPresent());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · CompositeDemo.java
root/ (3320)
  notes.txt (120)
  src/ (3200)
    Main.java (2400)
    util/ (800)
      Ids.java (800)
  empty/ (0)
src size: 3200
missing:  false
«sealed interface» Node + name() : String + size() : long ┄┄▷ FileNode «record», a leaf ┄┄▷ Dir the composite Dir ◆── * Node children: files or dirs
Where the add method goesThe classic GoF version puts add on the shared interface, so a file has an add that throws. That breaks ISP. Putting add only on Dir, as here, is the safer choice; callers who build trees know they are holding a directory.
Other compositesMenus and sub-menus, an org chart, a UI component tree, a pricing rule made of sub-rules, and group expenses in Splitwise, where a group can contain sub-groups.

Bridge splits two dimensions of variation; flyweight shares what never changes

Bridge: when a type varies in two independent ways, such as kind of alert and delivery channel, a subclass per pair means m × n classes. Hold the second dimension as a field instead, and you need m + n. Flyweight: when a program has thousands of small objects with the same intrinsic state, share one immutable instance and pass the rest (the position, the owner) in from outside.

BridgeFlyweight.java · alerts × channels, and shared chess glyphs
import java.util.*;

interface Channel { String deliver(String to, String text); }  // implementor
record Email() implements Channel {
    public String deliver(String to, String t) { return "[email " + to + "] " + t; }
}
record Sms() implements Channel {
    public String deliver(String to, String t) { return "[sms " + to + "] " + t; }
}

abstract class Alert {                          // abstraction: holds the bridge
    protected final Channel channel;
    Alert(Channel channel) { this.channel = channel; }
    abstract String send(String to);
}
final class OutageAlert extends Alert {
    OutageAlert(Channel c) { super(c); }
    String send(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "OUTAGE: lift 2 down"); }
}
final class ReminderAlert extends Alert {
    private final String what;
    ReminderAlert(Channel c, String what) { super(c); this.what = what; }
    String send(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "Reminder: " + what); }
}

record Glyph(char symbol, String name) {}       // flyweight: intrinsic state

final class Glyphs {                            // the flyweight factory
    private static final Map<Character, Glyph> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
    private static final Map<Character, String> NAMES = Map.of('K', "king",
            'Q', "queen", 'R', "rook", 'B', "bishop", 'N', "knight", 'P', "pawn");
    static Glyph of(char c) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(c, k ->
                new Glyph(k, NAMES.get(Character.toUpperCase(k))));
    }
}

record PlacedPiece(Glyph glyph, int square) {}  // extrinsic state

public class BridgeFlyweight {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Alert> alerts = List.of(new OutageAlert(new Email()),
                new OutageAlert(new Sms()), new ReminderAlert(new Sms(), "book return"));
        alerts.forEach(a -> System.out.println(a.send("ana")));

        String setup = "RNBQKBNRPPPPPPPPpppppppprnbqkbnr";
        List<PlacedPiece> pieces = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < setup.length(); i++)
            pieces.add(new PlacedPiece(Glyphs.of(setup.charAt(i)), i < 16 ? i : i + 32));
        Set<Glyph> distinct = Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>());
        pieces.forEach(p -> distinct.add(p.glyph()));
        System.out.println(pieces.size() + " pieces share " + distinct.size() + " glyph objects");
        System.out.println("Integer.valueOf(127) shared: " + (Integer.valueOf(127) == Integer.valueOf(127)));
        System.out.println("Integer.valueOf(128) shared: " + (Integer.valueOf(128) == Integer.valueOf(128)));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · BridgeFlyweight.java
[email ana] OUTAGE: lift 2 down
[sms ana] OUTAGE: lift 2 down
[sms ana] Reminder: book return
32 pieces share 12 glyph objects
Integer.valueOf(127) shared: true
Integer.valueOf(128) shared: false
Bridge in one sentence"Alert type and channel vary independently, so the alert holds a channel instead of extending one." Adding WhatsApp is one class, not one per alert type. It is composition over inheritance applied to two axes.
Flyweight rulesThe shared object must be immutable, since everyone holds the same instance. The extrinsic state (here, the square) lives outside it. The JDK's Integer.valueOf caches -128 to 127, which is why == on boxed integers works in tests and fails in production.
Only when there are manyFlyweight is a memory optimisation. Mention it for 10⁶ map tiles or characters in an editor; for 32 chess pieces it is a talking point, not a need.

Strategy: put a varying algorithm behind an interface and choose it at runtime

The most used pattern in LLD rounds. Whenever the prompt says the rule "may vary" (fares, parking fees, how to split a bill, which elevator answers a call), the context class holds a strategy and delegates to it. In modern Java a one-method strategy is a functional interface, so a new rule can be a lambda, an enum constant or a class.

StrategyDemo.java · fares as lambdas, a factory, and an enum
import java.util.*;

record Trip(int km, int minutes, boolean shared) {}

@FunctionalInterface
interface FareStrategy {                      // domain name, one method
    long fare(Trip t);
}

final class FareCalculator {                  // the context
    private static final long MINIMUM = 50;   // a rule every strategy shares
    private FareStrategy strategy;
    FareCalculator(FareStrategy strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
    void use(FareStrategy s) { strategy = Objects.requireNonNull(s); }
    long quote(Trip t) { return Math.max(MINIMUM, strategy.fare(t)); }
}

enum Plan implements FareStrategy {           // strategies as enum constants
    STANDARD { public long fare(Trip t) { return 12L * t.km() + 2L * t.minutes(); } },
    POOL     { public long fare(Trip t) {
                   long base = STANDARD.fare(t);
                   return t.shared() ? base * 70 / 100 : base; } }
}

public class StrategyDemo {
    static FareStrategy surge(int percent) {  // a strategy factory
        return t -> Plan.STANDARD.fare(t) * percent / 100;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, FareStrategy> byName = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        byName.put("standard", Plan.STANDARD);
        byName.put("pool", Plan.POOL);
        byName.put("surge 150%", surge(150));
        byName.put("flat airport", t -> 799);  // a one-off rule, as a lambda

        var trips = List.of(new Trip(10, 25, true), new Trip(2, 6, false));
        var calc = new FareCalculator(Plan.STANDARD);
        for (var e : byName.entrySet()) {
            calc.use(e.getValue());           // swap at runtime
            System.out.printf("%-13s %s%n", e.getKey(),
                    trips.stream().map(calc::quote).toList());
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · StrategyDemo.java
standard      [170, 50]
pool          [119, 50]
surge 150%    [255, 54]
flat airport  [799, 799]
FareCalculator the context - strategy : FareStrategy + quote(Trip) : long ──> 1 FareStrategy «interface» FareStrategy + fare(Trip) : long ┄┄▷ Plan.STANDARD, Plan.POOL ┄┄▷ lambdas: surge(p), flat
Where the shared rule goesThe minimum fare applies to every strategy, so it lives in the context, not copied into each one. If a rule applies to some strategies but not others, it is a decorator.
Who picks the strategy?Say it explicitly: a factory from configuration, the lot's settings, or the user's choice. "Strategy" without a chooser is half an answer.

Observer: tell the interested parties, without knowing who they are

A subject keeps a list of listeners and calls them when something happens. The subject depends only on the listener interface, so adding a new reaction (an email, a metric, a display update) is a new subscriber, not an edit to the subject. The real design work is in the details: ordering, a listener that throws, and unsubscribing.

ObserverDemo.java · a small typed event bus
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

record BookReturned(String isbn, String title) {}

final class EventBus<E> {
    private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
        return () -> listeners.remove(listener);  // handle to unsubscribe
    }

    void publish(E event) {
        for (var l : listeners) {                 // snapshot: safe even if a
            try {                                 // listener unsubscribes
                l.accept(event);
            } catch (RuntimeException ex) {       // one bad listener must not
                System.out.println("  listener failed: " + ex.getMessage());
            }                                     // starve the others
        }
    }
}

final class Catalogue {                           // the subject
    private final EventBus<BookReturned> returned;
    Catalogue(EventBus<BookReturned> returned) { this.returned = returned; }
    void giveBack(String isbn, String title) {
        System.out.println("returned " + title);
        returned.publish(new BookReturned(isbn, title));
    }
}

public class ObserverDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var bus = new EventBus<BookReturned>();
        var waiting = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of("ana", "bo"));
        int[] returns = {0};

        bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("  notify " + waiting.poll()
                + ": '" + e.title() + "' is ready"));
        bus.subscribe(e -> returns[0]++);
        AutoCloseable flaky = bus.subscribe(e -> {
            throw new IllegalStateException("SMS gateway down");
        });

        var catalogue = new Catalogue(bus);
        catalogue.giveBack("978-0134685991", "Effective Java");
        flaky.close();                            // unsubscribe
        catalogue.giveBack("978-0201633610", "Design Patterns");
        System.out.println("returns counted: " + returns[0]);
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · ObserverDemo.java
returned Effective Java
  notify ana: 'Effective Java' is ready
  listener failed: SMS gateway down
returned Design Patterns
  notify bo: 'Design Patterns' is ready
returns counted: 2
DecisionChoices to state
Push or pullSend the event data (push, as here), or just "changed" and let listeners query (pull).
Sync or asyncSynchronous is simple and ordered, but a slow listener slows the subject. Async needs an executor and loses ordering.
FailureIsolate each listener, as here. Never let one exception stop the loop.
LifetimeListeners that are never removed leak memory. Return an unsubscribe handle.
Thread safetyCopyOnWriteArrayList suits lists that are read often and changed rarely.
Across servicesBetween processes the same idea becomes a message broker, with delivery guarantees to think about. See the Event-driven tab. In Spring, ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener are an in-process observer.

Command: turn a request into an object you can store, undo and replay

A command object holds everything needed to perform an action later: the receiver, the arguments, and enough state to reverse it. Once requests are objects you can keep a history (undo and redo), queue them (a job scheduler), log them (an audit trail) or send them elsewhere. Chess moves, editor edits and ATM transactions are all commands.

CommandDemo.java · an editor with undo and redo
import java.util.*;

interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

final class Document {                          // the receiver
    final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
    @Override public String toString() { return "\"" + text + "\""; }
}

record Insert(Document doc, int at, String s) implements Command {
    public void execute() { doc.text.insert(at, s); }
    public void undo()    { doc.text.delete(at, at + s.length()); }
}

final class Delete implements Command {
    private final Document doc;
    private final int from, to;
    private String removed = "";                // captured for undo
    Delete(Document doc, int from, int to) { this.doc = doc; this.from = from; this.to = to; }
    public void execute() {
        removed = doc.text.substring(from, to);
        doc.text.delete(from, to);
    }
    public void undo() { doc.text.insert(from, removed); }
}

final class Editor {                            // the invoker
    private final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Command> redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }
    boolean undo() {
        if (undo.isEmpty()) return false;
        Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c);
        return true;
    }
    boolean redo() {
        if (redo.isEmpty()) return false;
        Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c);
        return true;
    }
}

public class CommandDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var doc = new Document();
        var ed = new Editor();
        ed.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "hello world"));   System.out.println("insert  " + doc);
        ed.run(new Delete(doc, 5, 11));             System.out.println("delete  " + doc);
        ed.run(new Insert(doc, 5, ", LLD"));        System.out.println("insert  " + doc);
        ed.undo();                                  System.out.println("undo    " + doc);
        ed.undo();                                  System.out.println("undo    " + doc);
        ed.redo();                                  System.out.println("redo    " + doc);
        ed.run(new Insert(doc, 0, ">> "));           System.out.println("insert  " + doc);
        System.out.println("redo after a new edit: " + ed.redo());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · CommandDemo.java
insert  "hello world"
delete  "hello"
insert  "hello, LLD"
undo    "hello"
undo    "hello world"
redo    "hello"
insert  ">> hello"
redo after a new edit: false
Two ways to undoEach command stores what it needs to reverse itself, as Delete stores the removed text. Or the invoker stores a snapshot of the whole state before each command (memento). Reverse operations are cheap; snapshots are simpler and always correct. Chess uses the first: a Move remembers the captured piece.
The redo ruleA new command after an undo must clear the redo stack. Otherwise redo replays an edit on top of text it was never meant for. Interviewers test this exact case.
Command or strategy?Both are objects holding behaviour. A strategy answers how to do something the context always does. A command is a request: it knows its receiver and arguments, and can be stored and undone.

State: when every method starts with a check on the status field, make the status an object

A vending machine answers "select item" differently when it has no money, has money, or is sold out. Written with an enum and ifs, every method re-checks the status and the rules for one state are spread across all of them. With the State pattern each state is a class that handles every event, and returns the next state. Each state's rules live in one class.

StateDemo.java · a vending machine
import java.util.*;

interface State {                                   // each event, with a
    default State insert(Machine m, int coin) {     // safe default
        m.say("coin returned: " + coin); return this;
    }
    default State select(Machine m, String item) {
        m.say("insert money first"); return this;
    }
    default State cancel(Machine m) { return this; }
}

final class Idle implements State {
    public State insert(Machine m, int coin) { m.credit += coin; return new HasCredit(); }
}

final class HasCredit implements State {
    public State insert(Machine m, int coin) { m.credit += coin; return this; }
    public State select(Machine m, String item) {
        int price = m.price(item);
        if (m.stock(item) == 0) { m.say(item + " sold out"); return this; }
        if (m.credit < price) { m.say("need " + (price - m.credit) + " more"); return this; }
        m.vend(item, price);
        return m.empty() ? new SoldOut() : m.credit > 0 ? this : new Idle();
    }
    public State cancel(Machine m) { m.refund(); return new Idle(); }
}

final class SoldOut implements State {
    public State insert(Machine m, int coin) { m.say("sold out, coin returned"); return this; }
    public State cancel(Machine m) { m.refund(); return this; }
}

final class Machine {                                 // the context
    private final Map<String, int[]> items = new TreeMap<>();   // price, stock
    private State state = new Idle();
    int credit;

    Machine add(String item, int price, int stock) { items.put(item, new int[] { price, stock }); return this; }
    void insert(int coin)      { state = state.insert(this, coin); show(); }
    void select(String item)   { state = state.select(this, item); show(); }
    void cancel()              { state = state.cancel(this); show(); }

    int price(String item) { return items.get(item)[0]; }
    int stock(String item) { return items.get(item)[1]; }
    boolean empty() { return items.values().stream().allMatch(v -> v[1] == 0); }
    void vend(String item, int price) { items.get(item)[1]--; credit -= price; say("vend " + item); }
    void refund() { if (credit > 0) say("refund " + credit); credit = 0; }
    void say(String s) { System.out.print(s + "; "); }
    private void show() {
        System.out.println("[" + state.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", credit " + credit + "]");
    }
}

public class StateDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var m = new Machine().add("chips", 20, 1).add("cola", 30, 1);
        m.select("cola");
        m.insert(20);
        m.select("cola");
        m.insert(20);
        m.select("cola");
        m.select("chips");
        m.select("cola");
        m.cancel();
        m.insert(10);
        m.select("chips");
        m.insert(10);
        m.select("chips");
        m.insert(5);
    }
}

insert money first; [Idle, credit 0]
[HasCredit, credit 20]
need 10 more; [HasCredit, credit 20]
[HasCredit, credit 40]
vend cola; [HasCredit, credit 10]
need 10 more; [HasCredit, credit 10]
cola sold out; [HasCredit, credit 10]
refund 10; [Idle, credit 0]
[HasCredit, credit 10]
need 10 more; [HasCredit, credit 10]
[HasCredit, credit 20]
vend chips; [SoldOut, credit 0]
sold out, coin returned; [SoldOut, credit 0]
Transitions Idle ──insert──> HasCredit HasCredit ──insert──> HasCredit HasCredit ──select──> Idle no credit left HasCredit change remains SoldOut last item gone HasCredit ──cancel──> Idle refund SoldOut ──insert──> SoldOut coin returned
State or strategy?The classes look the same. The difference is who changes them. A strategy is chosen from outside and stays until someone swaps it. A state changes itself: each handler returns the next state, so the transitions are part of the design.
Enum with a switch is fine for small machinesWith three states and two events, an enum plus a switch is shorter and easy to read. Move to state classes when states have their own data, or the switch appears in more than one method. The ATM uses state classes.

Template method: fix the algorithm's skeleton, let subclasses fill in the steps

A base class defines the order of steps in a final method and leaves some steps abstract. Subclasses supply those steps but cannot reorder or skip the skeleton. Use it when several variants share the same sequence and differ in a few steps: importers, report generators, a game's turn loop, a chess piece's move generation.

TemplateDemo.java · two importers, one skeleton
import java.util.*;

abstract class Importer<T> {
    final String run(List<String> lines) {          // the template method
        List<T> good = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        int start = hasHeader() ? 1 : 0;
        for (int i = start; i < lines.size(); i++) {
            try {
                T record = parse(lines.get(i).split(","));
                validate(record);                    // hook
                good.add(record);
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException | ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
                errors.add("line " + (i + 1) + ": " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
        save(good);
        return name() + ": " + good.size() + " saved, errors " + errors;
    }
    protected abstract String name();
    protected abstract T parse(String[] cells);      // required step
    protected abstract void save(List<T> records);   // required step
    protected void validate(T record) {}             // hook: optional
    protected boolean hasHeader() { return true; }   // hook: optional
}

record Member(String id, String email) {}
record Book(String isbn, int copies) {}

final class MemberImporter extends Importer<Member> {
    final List<Member> db = new ArrayList<>();
    protected String name() { return "members"; }
    protected Member parse(String[] c) { return new Member(c[0], c[1]); }
    protected void validate(Member m) {
        if (!m.email().contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad email " + m.email());
    }
    protected void save(List<Member> ms) { db.addAll(ms); }
}

final class BookImporter extends Importer<Book> {
    final List<Book> db = new ArrayList<>();
    protected String name() { return "books"; }
    protected boolean hasHeader() { return false; }
    protected Book parse(String[] c) { return new Book(c[0], Integer.parseInt(c[1])); }
    protected void save(List<Book> bs) { db.addAll(bs); }
}

public class TemplateDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var members = new MemberImporter();
        System.out.println(members.run(List.of("id,email", "M1,ana@x.io", "M2,bo-at-x", "M3")));
        var books = new BookImporter();
        System.out.println(books.run(List.of("111,2", "222,two", "333,1")));
        System.out.println(members.db + " " + books.db);
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · TemplateDemo.java
members: 1 saved, errors [line 3: bad email bo-at-x, line 4: Index 1 out of bounds for length 1]
books: 2 saved, errors [line 2: For input string: "two"]
[Member[id=M1, email=ana@x.io]] [Book[isbn=111, copies=2], Book[isbn=333, copies=1]]

Abstract step

Every subclass must provide it: parse, save.

Hook

An optional step with a default that subclasses may override: validate, hasHeader.

Make the template finalOtherwise a subclass can override run and skip validation, and the guarantee is gone. The Hollywood principle ("don't call us, we'll call you") describes the flow: the base class calls the subclass, never the reverse.
The composition alternativeTemplate method is inheritance, with its coupling. If the steps vary independently (any parser with any store), pass them in as strategies instead: new Importer<>(parser, validator, store). Choose template method when the steps belong together.

Chain of responsibility: pass the request along until a handler takes it

Each handler either deals with the request or hands it to the next one. The sender knows only the first handler, and the chain can be reordered or extended without touching it. Approval limits, request validation, servlet filters and the ATM's note dispenser (50s, then 20s, then 10s) are all chains.

ChainDemo.java · expense approval, then the same chain as functions
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

record Expense(String who, long amount, String category) {}

abstract class Approver {
    private Approver next;
    Approver then(Approver next) { this.next = next; return next; }   // fluent

    final String handle(Expense e) {
        String verdict = decide(e);
        if (verdict != null) return verdict;                  // handled
        return next != null ? next.handle(e)                  // pass it on
                            : "rejected: nobody can approve " + e.amount();
    }
    protected abstract String decide(Expense e);              // null = pass
}

final class PolicyCheck extends Approver {
    protected String decide(Expense e) {
        return e.category().equals("gift") ? "rejected by policy" : null;
    }
}

final class Limit extends Approver {
    private final String role;
    private final long max;
    Limit(String role, long max) { this.role = role; this.max = max; }
    protected String decide(Expense e) {
        return e.amount() <= max ? "approved by " + role : null;
    }
}

public class ChainDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Approver chain = new PolicyCheck();
        chain.then(new Limit("team lead", 1_000))
             .then(new Limit("manager", 10_000))
             .then(new Limit("director", 100_000));

        var expenses = List.of(new Expense("ana", 400, "travel"),
                new Expense("bo", 7_500, "hardware"), new Expense("cy", 250, "gift"),
                new Expense("di", 60_000, "training"), new Expense("ed", 250_000, "travel"));
        expenses.forEach(e -> System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "%-3s %,8d  %s%n",
                e.who(), e.amount(), chain.handle(e)));

        List<Function<Expense, Optional<String>>> handlers = List.of(   // the
            e -> e.category().equals("gift") ? Optional.of("policy") : Optional.empty(),
            e -> e.amount() <= 1_000 ? Optional.of("team lead") : Optional.empty(),
            e -> Optional.of("finance review"));                   // lambda form
        System.out.println("functional: " + handlers.stream()
                .map(h -> h.apply(expenses.get(1)))
                .flatMap(Optional::stream).findFirst().orElseThrow());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · ChainDemo.java
ana      400  approved by team lead
bo     7,500  approved by manager
cy       250  rejected by policy
di    60,000  approved by director
ed   250,000  rejected: nobody can approve 250000
functional: finance review

Pure chain

Exactly one handler deals with the request and the rest never see it, as with approval limits above.

Pipeline

Every handler does its part and passes it on: servlet filters, Spring Security's filter chain, middleware. Each can still stop the request.

Say what happens at the endA request that falls off the end of the chain must produce a defined result, like the "nobody can approve" line above. Silent drops are the classic bug. Build the chain in one place so its order is visible.
In the ATMDispensing from ₹500, ₹200 and ₹100 slots is a chain: each slot takes as many notes as it can and passes the remainder on. With limited notes, "as many as it can" is not always right, so the ATM's chain backs off and retries. See ATM · the model.

Four patterns you should recognise, and write when asked

These come up less often as the centre of a design, but interviewers use them as follow-ups. "How would you let callers walk your collection?" is iterator. "The flights all talk to each other" is mediator. "Add undo without exposing the state" is memento. "Add operations to this closed hierarchy" is visitor, which Java 21's pattern-matching switch mostly replaces.

FourPatterns.java · 1 of 2 · iterator and mediator
import java.util.*;

record Range(int from, int to, int step) implements Iterable<Integer> {
    public Iterator<Integer> iterator() {          // ITERATOR: callers walk
        return new Iterator<>() {                  // it, never see its insides
            private int next = from;
            public boolean hasNext() { return next < to; }
            public Integer next() {
                if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
                int v = next;
                next += step;
                return v;
            }
        };
    }
}

final class Tower {                                // MEDIATOR: flights talk
    private final List<Flight> flights = new ArrayList<>();   // to the tower,
    private Flight onRunway;                                  // not each other
    void register(Flight f) { flights.add(f); }
    void requestLanding(Flight f) {
        if (onRunway == null) { onRunway = f; f.hear("cleared to land"); }
        else f.hear("hold, runway busy with " + onRunway.id());
    }
    void landed(Flight f) {
        onRunway = null;
        for (Flight o : flights) if (o != f) o.hear(f.id() + " has vacated the runway");
    }
}

record Flight(String id, Tower tower) {
    void land()   { tower.requestLanding(this); }
    void landed() { tower.landed(this); }
    void hear(String msg) { System.out.println("  " + id + " <- " + msg); }
}
FourPatterns.java · 2 of 2 · memento and visitor
final class TextBox {                              // MEMENTO: the originator
    private String text = "";
    private int cursor;
    void type(String s) {
        text = text.substring(0, cursor) + s + text.substring(cursor);
        cursor += s.length();
    }
    Snapshot save() { return new Snapshot(text, cursor); }
    void restore(Snapshot s) { text = s.text; cursor = s.cursor; }
    @Override public String toString() { return text + " (cursor " + cursor + ")"; }

    static final class Snapshot {                  // opaque to the caretaker:
        private final String text;                 // no public accessors
        private final int cursor;
        private Snapshot(String text, int cursor) { this.text = text; this.cursor = cursor; }
    }
}

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul {
    <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v);                // VISITOR: double dispatch
}
record Num(int v) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> x) { return x.num(this); } }
record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> x) { return x.add(this); } }
record Mul(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> x) { return x.mul(this); } }

interface ExprVisitor<R> { R num(Num n); R add(Add a); R mul(Mul m); }

final class Show implements ExprVisitor<String> {  // one operation per class
    public String num(Num n) { return String.valueOf(n.v()); }
    public String add(Add a) { return "(" + a.l().accept(this) + " + " + a.r().accept(this) + ")"; }
    public String mul(Mul m) { return a(m.l()) + " * " + a(m.r()); }
    private String a(Expr e) { return e.accept(this); }
}

public class FourPatterns {
    static int eval(Expr e) {                      // the Java 21 alternative:
        return switch (e) {                        // a sealed switch with
            case Num(int v) -> v;                  // record patterns
            case Add(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) + eval(r);
            case Mul(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) * eval(r);
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> seen = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i : new Range(0, 10, 3)) seen.add(i);
        System.out.println("iterator: " + seen);

        System.out.println("mediator:");
        var tower = new Tower();
        var a = new Flight("AI101", tower);
        var b = new Flight("6E202", tower);
        tower.register(a); tower.register(b);
        a.land(); b.land(); a.landed(); b.land();

        var box = new TextBox();
        box.type("hello");
        var saved = box.save();
        box.type(" world");
        System.out.print("memento: " + box);
        box.restore(saved);
        System.out.println(" -> " + box);

        Expr e = new Mul(new Add(new Num(2), new Num(3)), new Num(4));
        System.out.println("visitor: " + e.accept(new Show()) + " = " + eval(e));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · FourPatterns.java
iterator: [0, 3, 6, 9]
mediator:
  AI101 <- cleared to land
  6E202 <- hold, runway busy with AI101
  6E202 <- AI101 has vacated the runway
  6E202 <- cleared to land
memento: hello world (cursor 11) -> hello (cursor 5)
visitor: (2 + 3) * 4 = 20
Visitor in modern JavaThe visitor exists because older Java could not switch on type safely. With a sealed hierarchy, eval above does the same job in five lines, and the compiler still rejects a switch that misses a new subtype. Mention the visitor, then say you would use the sealed switch since 21. Keep the visitor for code that must compile on Java 17 or earlier.

Patterns that share a class diagram, and the question that tells them apart

Several patterns have almost the same structure: an interface, an implementation, and a class that holds one. What differs is the intent, meaning who creates the object, who changes it, and why. "Isn't that just a strategy?" is a common follow-up, and these are the answers.

PairSame shapeThe differenceAsk yourself
Strategy vs StateA context delegates to an interfaceA strategy is chosen from outside and stays put. A state replaces itself as events arrive.Who decides the next implementation: the client, or the current one?
Strategy vs Template methodVary part of an algorithmStrategy uses composition and can change at runtime. Template method uses inheritance and is fixed per subclass.Do the varying steps belong together, or mix and match?
Strategy vs CommandAn object wrapping behaviourA strategy is how the context does its job. A command is a request, with its receiver and arguments, that can be stored, queued and undone.Would you ever put it in a history list?
Decorator vs ProxySame interface, wraps the targetA decorator adds behaviour and is stacked by the client. A proxy controls access (lazy, cached, remote, secured) and usually manages the target itself.Does the caller know, and choose, the wrapping?
Adapter vs FacadeA class in front of other codeAn adapter makes one interface look like another. A facade makes many classes look like one simpler interface.One object translated, or many coordinated?
Adapter vs BridgeAn abstraction holding an implementorAn adapter is applied after the fact to make existing code fit. A bridge is designed up front to let two hierarchies vary independently.Retrofitting, or planning?
Composite vs DecoratorRecursive composition of one interfaceA composite holds many children and aggregates them. A decorator holds exactly one and adds to it.One wrapped object, or a tree?
Observer vs MediatorObjects are decoupled from each otherObserver broadcasts one-way from a subject to anyone listening. A mediator holds the coordination logic between peers.Is there logic in the middle, or just a list?
Factory method vs Abstract factory vs BuilderCreation is hidden from the callerA factory method picks the class of one product. An abstract factory creates a matching family. A builder assembles one complex product step by step.Which class? Which family? Or which fields?
The honest answer is often "both"The parking-fee rule is a strategy, wrapped in decorators for discounts, created by a factory from the lot's configuration. Naming each role, and why it is there, is a better answer than choosing one label.

Parking lot: pin the scope down before drawing a single class

"Design a parking lot" is the most common LLD opener because it looks easy and has many directions to go wrong in. Spend the first five minutes asking questions and writing the answers down. The answers below are the ones this solution assumes. Say yours out loud, because the interviewer will often change one of them later.

Functional requirements

  1. The lot has several floors; each floor has spots of three sizes: small, medium, large.
  2. Vehicles are motorbikes, cars and trucks, needing small, medium and large spots.
  3. A vehicle may take a larger spot when its own size is full, but never a smaller one.
  4. Entry assigns the smallest free spot that fits, lowest floor first, and issues a ticket.
  5. Exit takes the ticket, frees the spot and computes the fee: an hourly rate per vehicle type, with part hours rounded up and a one-hour minimum.
  6. The lot can switch pricing (for example to a flat event rate). A ticket keeps the pricing in force when it was issued.
  7. Show free spots per floor and size, for the entrance display.
  8. Reject a vehicle whose plate is already inside, and a ticket used twice.

Questions to ask first

One lot or many?
One lot, one process. Many lots is a scale follow-up.
Entry gates?
Several, so park is called concurrently.
Payment?
Out of scope: compute the fee, assume it is paid.
Reservations?
No. Drive-up only.
EV charging, disabled spots?
Not now; the design should allow them.
Lost ticket?
Out of scope; mention a daily maximum as the usual rule.

Nouns, and what they become

ParkingLotParkingFloorParkingSpotTicketReceipt Vehicle · recordVehicleType · enumSpotSize · enum PricingStrategy · interfaceClock · injected

Not classes: gate, attendant, display board. They are callers of the lot, not parts of its model. Payment is out of scope.

Why vehicle type is an enum hereMotorbikes, cars and trucks differ only in which spot they need and what they pay, and both are data. A class hierarchy would add three classes with no behaviour. If trucks later need a permit check, promote the enum to a sealed interface. See KISS.

Parking lot: four classes with state, two enums, one strategy

The lot coordinates, each floor manages its own free spots, and a spot guards its own occupancy. The fee rule sits behind an interface because the requirements say it changes. Everything else is concrete, because nothing else was said to vary.

ParkingLot the service: entry and exit - floors : Map<Integer, ParkingFloor> - pricing : PricingStrategy volatile: swapped at runtime - active : Map<String, Ticket> ticket id → ticket - platesInside : Set<String> - clock : Clock + park(Vehicle) : Optional<Ticket> + leave(ticketId) : Receipt + changePricing(PricingStrategy) + availability() : List<String> ◆── 1..* ParkingFloor ──> 1 PricingStrategy ◇── * Ticket ParkingFloor - free : EnumMap<SpotSize, Deque<ParkingSpot>> + claim(Vehicle) : Optional<ParkingSpot> synchronized + release(spotId) synchronized ◆── 1..* ParkingSpot ParkingSpot - id : String - size : SpotSize - vehicle : Vehicle (0..1) + occupy(Vehicle) + vacate() «record» Ticket id, vehicle, floor, spotId, entry, pricing «record» Receipt ticketId, plate, spotId, stayed, fee «record» Vehicle plate, type ──> VehicleType «enum» VehicleType MOTORBIKE, CAR, TRUCK each needs a SpotSize «enum» SpotSize SMALL < MEDIUM < LARGE declaration order = size «interface» PricingStrategy + fee(VehicleType, Duration) : long ┄┄▷ HourlyPricing rate per type, started hours ┄┄▷ FlatPricing event days
ClassOwns the decision
ParkingLotWhich floor to try, issuing and redeeming tickets, one plate inside at a time
ParkingFloorWhich of its free spots to hand out; keeping the free lists consistent
ParkingSpotWhether it is free, and whether a vehicle fits
PricingStrategyWhat a stay costs
TicketNothing: an immutable record of the entry, including the pricing in force
Free lists, not a scanEach floor keeps a queue of free spots per size, so finding a spot is a few queue polls rather than a loop over every spot. With 2,000 spots per floor and a busy morning, that is the difference the interviewer asks about when they say "can it be faster?"
No singletonThere is one lot, but it is created in main and passed in, so a test can build a lot with three spots. See Singleton: how it breaks.

Parking lot: the model, where each object guards its own state

The spot refuses to be double-booked and refuses a vehicle that does not fit, so no caller can break those rules. The floor is the only class that touches its free lists, and both of its public methods are synchronized, so two entry gates cannot claim the same spot.

ParkingLotDemo.java · 1 of 3 · the model
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

enum SpotSize { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }          // declared smallest first

enum VehicleType {
    MOTORBIKE(SpotSize.SMALL), CAR(SpotSize.MEDIUM), TRUCK(SpotSize.LARGE);
    final SpotSize needs;
    VehicleType(SpotSize needs) { this.needs = needs; }
}

record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) {
    Vehicle {
        Objects.requireNonNull(type, "type");
        if (plate == null || plate.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("plate");
    }
}

final class ParkingSpot {
    private final String id;
    private final SpotSize size;
    private Vehicle vehicle;                    // null while free

    ParkingSpot(String id, SpotSize size) { this.id = id; this.size = size; }
    String id() { return id; }
    SpotSize size() { return size; }

    void occupy(Vehicle v) {
        if (vehicle != null) throw new IllegalStateException(id + " is taken");
        if (size.compareTo(v.type().needs) < 0)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(v.type() + " does not fit " + id);
        vehicle = v;
    }
    void vacate() {
        if (vehicle == null) throw new IllegalStateException(id + " is already free");
        vehicle = null;
    }
}

final class ParkingFloor {
    private final int number;
    private final Map<String, ParkingSpot> spots = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<SpotSize, Deque<ParkingSpot>> free = new EnumMap<>(SpotSize.class);

    ParkingFloor(int number, Map<SpotSize, Integer> layout) {
        this.number = number;
        for (SpotSize size : SpotSize.values()) {
            Deque<ParkingSpot> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
            for (int i = 1; i <= layout.getOrDefault(size, 0); i++) {
                var spot = new ParkingSpot("F" + number + "-" + size.name().charAt(0) + i, size);
                spots.put(spot.id(), spot);
                queue.addLast(spot);
            }
            free.put(size, queue);
        }
    }

    int number() { return number; }

    synchronized Optional<ParkingSpot> claim(Vehicle v) {
        for (SpotSize size : SpotSize.values()) {          // smallest that fits
            if (size.compareTo(v.type().needs) < 0) continue;
            ParkingSpot spot = free.get(size).pollFirst();
            if (spot != null) {
                spot.occupy(v);
                return Optional.of(spot);
            }
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    synchronized void release(String spotId) {
        ParkingSpot spot = spots.get(spotId);
        spot.vacate();
        free.get(spot.size()).addFirst(spot);              // reuse near spots first
    }

    synchronized String freeSummary() {
        StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder("F" + number + " free");
        free.forEach((size, q) -> s.append(' ').append(size).append('=').append(q.size()));
        return s.toString();
    }
}

record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, int floor, String spotId,
              Instant entry, PricingStrategy pricing) {}

record Receipt(String ticketId, String plate, String spotId, Duration stayed, long fee) {
    @Override public String toString() {
        return ticketId + " " + plate + " from " + spotId + ", "
                + stayed.toMinutes() + " min, pays " + fee;
    }
}
Why the size check lives in the spotInformation expert: the spot has the size, so it answers "does this fit?". The floor uses the same ordering to pick which queue to poll, and the spot's check is the last line of defence if the floor ever gets it wrong.
Why SpotSize relies on declaration ordercompareTo on an enum compares declaration order, so "fits" is one comparison and the claim loop tries sizes from smallest up. Put a comment on the enum, because reordering the constants would change behaviour silently. A rank field is the more defensive choice; say which you picked.
Why the ticket is a recordA ticket never changes after it is issued. It stores the floor and spot id, not the spot object, so it can be printed, stored or sent to a gate device without dragging the model along. It does store the PricingStrategy, because the rate in force at entry is part of the deal with the customer.
One lock per floorTwo gates claiming on different floors never wait for each other. A single lock for the whole lot would also be correct, and simpler; name the trade-off rather than picking silently. The decisions slide covers the race on the last spot.

Parking lot: the pricing strategies, the lot service, and a run through every rule

The lot tries floors in order, records the ticket, and on exit removes the ticket before anything else, so a ticket can be redeemed only once even if two exit gates scan it together. Time comes from an injected Clock, so the demo can move time forward and print the same fees on every run.

ParkingLotDemo.java · 2 of 3 · pricing and the lot
interface PricingStrategy {
    long fee(VehicleType type, Duration stayed);
}

final class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    private final Map<VehicleType, Long> perHour;
    HourlyPricing(Map<VehicleType, Long> perHour) { this.perHour = new EnumMap<>(perHour); }
    public long fee(VehicleType type, Duration stayed) {
        long hours = Math.max(1, (stayed.toMinutes() + 59) / 60);  // started hours
        return hours * perHour.get(type);
    }
}

record FlatPricing(long amount) implements PricingStrategy {
    public long fee(VehicleType type, Duration stayed) { return amount; }
}

final class ParkingLot {
    private final Map<Integer, ParkingFloor> floors = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;
    private volatile PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Set<String> platesInside = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
    private final AtomicInteger nextTicket = new AtomicInteger(1);

    ParkingLot(List<ParkingFloor> floors, PricingStrategy pricing, Clock clock) {
        floors.forEach(f -> this.floors.put(f.number(), f));
        this.pricing = Objects.requireNonNull(pricing);
        this.clock = Objects.requireNonNull(clock);
    }

    void changePricing(PricingStrategy p) { pricing = Objects.requireNonNull(p); }

    Optional<Ticket> park(Vehicle v) {
        if (!platesInside.add(v.plate()))                  // atomic check-and-add
            throw new IllegalStateException(v.plate() + " is already inside");
        for (ParkingFloor floor : floors.values()) {
            Optional<ParkingSpot> spot = floor.claim(v);
            if (spot.isPresent()) {
                var t = new Ticket("T-%03d".formatted(nextTicket.getAndIncrement()), v,
                        floor.number(), spot.get().id(), clock.instant(), pricing);
                active.put(t.id(), t);
                return Optional.of(t);
            }
        }
        platesInside.remove(v.plate());                    // full: undo
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    Receipt leave(String ticketId) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);                // first: one use only
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown or used ticket " + ticketId);
        floors.get(t.floor()).release(t.spotId());
        platesInside.remove(t.vehicle().plate());
        Duration stayed = Duration.between(t.entry(), clock.instant());
        return new Receipt(t.id(), t.vehicle().plate(), t.spotId(), stayed,
                t.pricing().fee(t.vehicle().type(), stayed));
    }

    List<String> availability() {
        return floors.values().stream().map(ParkingFloor::freeSummary).toList();
    }
}

final class MutableClock extends Clock {                   // a clock the demo moves
    private Instant now;
    MutableClock(Instant start) { now = start; }
    void advance(Duration d) { now = now.plus(d); }
    @Override public Instant instant() { return now; }
    @Override public ZoneId getZone() { return ZoneOffset.UTC; }
    @Override public Clock withZone(ZoneId zone) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
ParkingLotDemo.java · 3 of 3 · the demo
public class ParkingLotDemo {
    static final Map<String, String> ticketOf = new HashMap<>();   // plate -> id

    static void park(ParkingLot lot, Vehicle v) {
        String result = lot.park(v).map(t -> {
            ticketOf.put(v.plate(), t.id());
            return t.id() + " at " + t.spotId();
        }).orElse("lot full for " + v.type());
        System.out.println("park  " + v.plate() + ": " + result);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var clock = new MutableClock(Instant.parse("2026-10-02T09:00:00Z"));
        var lot = new ParkingLot(List.of(
                new ParkingFloor(1, Map.of(SpotSize.SMALL, 1, SpotSize.MEDIUM, 1)),
                new ParkingFloor(2, Map.of(SpotSize.MEDIUM, 1, SpotSize.LARGE, 1))),
            new HourlyPricing(Map.of(VehicleType.MOTORBIKE, 10L,
                    VehicleType.CAR, 40L, VehicleType.TRUCK, 100L)),
            clock);

        var bike = new Vehicle("BIKE-1", VehicleType.MOTORBIKE);
        park(lot, bike);
        park(lot, new Vehicle("CAR-A", VehicleType.CAR));
        park(lot, new Vehicle("CAR-B", VehicleType.CAR));
        park(lot, new Vehicle("TRUCK-1", VehicleType.TRUCK));
        park(lot, new Vehicle("CAR-C", VehicleType.CAR));        // no room

        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(130));
        System.out.println("leave " + lot.leave(ticketOf.get("CAR-A")));
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(40));
        System.out.println("leave " + lot.leave(ticketOf.get("TRUCK-1")));

        lot.changePricing(new FlatPricing(250));                 // event starts
        park(lot, new Vehicle("CAR-C", VehicleType.CAR));
        park(lot, new Vehicle("CAR-D", VehicleType.CAR));        // takes LARGE
        try { lot.park(bike); }
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("park  rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        System.out.println(lot.availability());

        clock.advance(Duration.ofHours(3));
        System.out.println("leave " + lot.leave(ticketOf.get("CAR-C")));   // flat
        System.out.println("leave " + lot.leave(ticketOf.get("CAR-B")));   // hourly
        try { lot.leave(ticketOf.get("CAR-B")); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("leave rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        System.out.println(lot.availability());
    }
}
