> EXPENSE cy 999.99 PERCENT ana=50 dee=50
  E3 shares: ana 500.00, dee 499.99
> EXPENSE dee 100.00 EQUAL ana bo dee
  E4 shares: ana 33.34, bo 33.33, dee 33.33
> EXPENSE ana 600.00 SHARES bo=1 cy=2
  E5 shares: bo 200.00, cy 400.00
> EXPENSE ana 500.00 EXACT bo=100.00 cy=100.00
  error: exact amounts add up to 200.00, not 500.00
> EXPENSE ana 500.00 PERCENT bo=60 cy=30
  error: percents add up to 90
> SHOW
  ana owes dee 33.34
  bo owes ana 300.00
  bo owes dee 33.33
  cy owes ana 300.00
  cy owes bo 500.00
  dee owes cy 499.99
> SIMPLIFY
  dee pays ana 433.32
  cy pays bo 166.67
  cy pays ana 133.34
> SETTLE cy ana 300.00
> SHOW
  ana owes dee 33.34
  bo owes ana 300.00
  bo owes dee 33.33
  cy owes bo 500.00
  dee owes cy 499.99

Splitwise: the choices to defend, and why "fewest payments" is harder than it looks

The greedy simplifier never needs more than n − 1 payments, and it is what most answers use. It is not always optimal, though. The true minimum is found by splitting people into as many groups as possible whose balances sum to zero, which is NP-hard. Knowing that, and having a small counterexample ready, is the strongest answer to the last question of the round.

DecisionWhy, and the alternative
Paise in a longExact, fast, and the rounding rule is explicit. BigDecimal everywhere also works; a double never does.
One rounding functionEqual, share and percent splits all call byWeight, so they cannot disagree about the extra paisa.
Sealed split rulesA closed set the parser must handle; records validate themselves.
Debts netted per pairThe app shows one line per friend; the reverse direction is never stored.
Expenses keptThe ledger is derivable from the expense list, which makes edit and delete possible (rebuild) and gives an audit trail.
Greedy simplifierO(n log n), at most n − 1 payments, easy to explain. Exact search is exponential; use it only for small groups.
Greedy is not optimal: balances +6 +4 −4 −3 −3 greedy, biggest with biggest −4 pays +6: 4 +6 now +2 −3 pays +4: 3 +4 now +1 −3 pays +2: 2 −3 now −1 −1 pays +1: 1 4 payments optimal: two zero-sum groups {+6, −3, −3} → 2 payments {+4, −4} → 1 payment 3 payments
How to find the optimum, if askedThe number of payments is n minus the number of zero-sum groups, so maximise the groups. For up to about 20 people, a DP over subsets finds it: mark each subset whose balances sum to zero, and combine them. Say it, and say you would ship the greedy one.
Follow-upWhat changes
GroupsA Group owns its own Ledger; a user's overall balance is the sum across groups. Simplify within a group, never across groups, because people expect group debts to stay in the group.
Several payers on one expenseAn expense gets a payments map as well as a shares map; each person's position is paid minus share, recorded against the payers pro rata.
Edit or delete an expenseRecord a reversing expense (an accountant's approach, and an audit trail), or rebuild the ledger from the expense list.
Multiple currenciesMoney becomes a value object with a currency; ledgers are per currency, and conversion happens only at settlement, at a recorded rate.
Concurrent edits from phonesEach expense carries a client-generated id, so a retried upload is recorded once; the ledger's methods are already synchronized for one process. See idempotency.
Notify on new expenseThe ledger publishes ExpenseAdded; a notifier subscribes. The ledger stays free of email code.

Concurrency in an LLD round: three questions, asked about every piece of shared state

"Make it thread-safe" is the most common follow-up in LLD, and the weakest answer is synchronized on every method. The strong answer starts by naming what is shared, the invariant that must hold, and the smallest set of changes that must happen together. Pick the tool after that.

1 · What is shared?

Which objects can two threads reach at once? A parking floor's free lists, a show's seat claims, a bank account. Objects confined to one thread, and immutable objects, need nothing.

2 · What is the invariant?

The rule that must never be seen broken: a spot has at most one vehicle; a seat has at most one live hold; a balance never goes negative.

3 · What must be atomic?

The smallest group of reads and writes that keeps the invariant: "find a free spot and occupy it"; "check the balance and debit it". That group is your critical section.

ProblemShared stateInvariantWhat this tab used
Parking lotFree-spot queues per floorA spot is handed to one vehiclesynchronized per floor; atomic Set.add for plates; ConcurrentHashMap.remove for tickets
LibraryCopies, members, waiting listsLoan counts match loans; a copy has one borrowerOne lock on the service: low traffic, many objects per operation
ATMAccounts in the bankA balance never goes below zerosynchronized bank methods; the ATM itself is single-user
Movie bookingSeat claims per showA seat has one live hold or one saleLock-free: putIfAbsent, replace, remove(k, v); a small lock per booking
ElevatorCars and their stopsA car is never given a stop mid-stepOne lock on the controller
SplitwiseThe pairwise debt mapDebts net to zero across everyonesynchronized ledger methods
Coarse first, then justify going finerOne lock around the whole service is always a correct first answer, and often the right final one. Go finer (per floor, per seat, lock-free) only for a reason you can state: "a release-day show has 500 users on one seat map, and one lock would serialise them all". Every step finer adds a way to get it wrong.

The toolbox, and the check-then-act bug every tool exists to prevent

Almost every concurrency bug in an LLD answer is a check-then-act: read something, decide, then write, while another thread changes it in between. The demo forces that interleaving with two latches, so it goes wrong on every run. It then does the same withdrawals 10,000 times from virtual threads, safely.

RaceDemo.java · a forced lost update, then two fixes
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

final class Account {
    private int balance;
    Account(int balance) { this.balance = balance; }
    synchronized boolean withdraw(int amount) {    // check and act, one lock
        if (balance < amount) return false;
        balance -= amount;
        return true;
    }
    synchronized int balance() { return balance; }
}

public class RaceDemo {
    static int unsafeBalance = 100;

    static void await(CountDownLatch l) {
        try { l.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var aChecked = new CountDownLatch(1);
        var bDone = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Thread a = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
            if (unsafeBalance >= 80) {              // A checks: 100 >= 80
                aChecked.countDown();
                await(bDone);                       // A is paused here...
                unsafeBalance -= 80;                // ...and acts on a stale check
            }
        });
        Thread b = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
            await(aChecked);
            if (unsafeBalance >= 80) unsafeBalance -= 80;   // B: 100 -> 20
            bDone.countDown();
        });
        a.join();
        b.join();
        System.out.println("check-then-act, no lock: balance " + unsafeBalance);

        var account = new Account(5_000);
        var ok = new AtomicInteger();
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
                pool.submit(() -> { if (account.withdraw(1)) ok.incrementAndGet(); });
        }
        System.out.println("synchronized: " + ok.get() + " withdrawals, balance " + account.balance());

        var counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>();
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                String key = i % 3 == 0 ? "fizz" : "other";
                pool.submit(() -> counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum));   // atomic per key
            }
        }
        System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap.merge: " + new TreeMap<>(counts));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · RaceDemo.java
check-then-act, no lock: balance -60
synchronized: 5000 withdrawals, balance 0
ConcurrentHashMap.merge: {fizz=3334, other=6666}
ToolUse it for
synchronizedThe default. Short critical sections on one object. Re-entrant, released automatically.
ReentrantLockWhen you need tryLock with a timeout, interruptible waits, or several conditions.
ReadWriteLockMany readers, rare writers, and reads that really do not mutate. Not an LRU cache, where every read moves an entry.
AtomicInteger, AtomicReferenceA single variable updated with compare-and-set. LongAdder for hot counters.
ConcurrentHashMapMaps shared between threads. compute, merge, putIfAbsent are atomic per key; get then put is not.
CopyOnWriteArrayListListener lists: read constantly, changed rarely.
BlockingQueueHand-offs between producer and consumer threads, with back-pressure.
SemaphoreLimit how many threads do something at once, such as calls to a slow service.

Virtual threads: a thread per task is cheap again, but the downstream is not

Java 21 made virtual threads final since 21. A virtual thread that blocks on I/O or sleep unmounts from its carrier thread, so a program can hold millions of them. In an LLD answer this means "one virtual thread per request" is a reasonable design, and a fixed thread pool is no longer the default. The limit moves to the service you call, so bound that explicitly.

VirtualThreads.java · one thread per task, a semaphore for the slow dependency
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class VirtualThreads {
    static final Semaphore priceApi = new Semaphore(3);    // it allows 3 at once
    static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger();
    static final AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger();

    static int quote(String showId) throws InterruptedException {
        priceApi.acquire();
        try {
            peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(20));           // blocking: unmounts
            return showId.length() * 100;
        } finally {
            inFlight.decrementAndGet();
            priceApi.release();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> shows = IntStream.range(0, 50).mapToObj(i -> "SHOW-" + i).toList();
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<Integer>> quotes = shows.stream()
                    .map(s -> executor.submit(() -> quote(s))).toList();
            int total = 0;
            for (Future<Integer> f : quotes) total += f.get();
            System.out.println("quoted " + quotes.size() + " shows, total " + total);
        }
        System.out.println("peak concurrent calls to the price API: " + peak.get());

        var slept = new AtomicInteger();
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(100));
                    return slept.incrementAndGet();
                });
        }                                                   // waits for all
        System.out.println(slept.get() + " virtual threads each slept 100 ms");

        Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().name("booking-", 1).unstarted(() -> { });
        System.out.println(t.getName() + " is virtual: " + t.isVirtual());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · VirtualThreads.java
quoted 50 shows, total 34000
peak concurrent calls to the price API: 3
10000 virtual threads each slept 100 ms
booking-1 is virtual: true
RuleWhy
Never pool virtual threadsThey are cheap to create; a pool only adds a queue. Create one per task.
Limit the resource, not the threadsA Semaphore or a connection pool protects the database or API. Ten thousand threads will otherwise open ten thousand connections.
Avoid blocking inside synchronized on 21On JDK 21 to 23 it pins the carrier thread. Use ReentrantLock around blocking calls. JDK 24 removed most pinning (JEP 491).
Use ThreadLocal sparinglyA million threads mean a million copies. Scoped values are the replacement, and are final from JDK 25.
CPU-bound work gains nothingVirtual threads help waiting, not computing. Use a pool sized to the cores, or parallel streams.
Structured concurrency, on its wayStructuredTaskScope runs subtasks as a unit: if one fails, the others are cancelled, and none outlive the block. It is a preview API on JDK 21 through 25, so it needs --enable-preview and is not used in this tab's code. Mention it for "fetch price and seat map in parallel, fail fast".

LRU cache: a hash map for O(1) lookup, a linked list for O(1) recency

"Design an LRU cache" is asked as a coding question and as an LLD question. Both want get and put in O(1), with the least recently used entry evicted when the cache is full. The LLD version adds "and make it thread-safe", which has a trap: in an LRU cache, get is a write.

HashMap<K, Node> finds a node in O(1) Doubly linked list orders nodes by recency head ⇄ [d] ⇄ [a] ⇄ [c] ⇄ tail most recent least recent get(a) index → node a; unlink; add after head put(e) full? unlink tail.prev (c), remove from index add [e] after head, put in index head and tail are sentinel nodes: no null checks at the ends, so unlink and add are four lines each
The two-minute version, when allowed
class LruMap<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruMap(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);            // accessOrder = true
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) {
        return size() > capacity;          // evict after each put
    }
}
// thread-safe: Collections.synchronizedMap(new LruMap<>(100))
Thread-safety optionTrade-off
One lock around every operationCorrect and simple. All threads contend on one lock; fine up to moderate load. The next slide builds this.
Read-write lockWrong. get moves the node, so two readers under a shared read lock corrupt the list.
Striped: N independent LRU segments by key hashN times less contention. Eviction is per segment, so it is only approximately LRU overall.
ConcurrentHashMap + buffered recencyRecord reads in a lock-free buffer and apply them to the order in batches. This is how Caffeine works; near-LRU at very high throughput.
Use a libraryIn production, Caffeine. Say so; then build the simple version, because that is the question.
The trap, stated onceIf an interviewer offers "use a read-write lock, since reads are common", the right answer is to decline and explain that an LRU read changes the order. It is one of the most reliable ways to show you understand what your lock protects.
Related variantsLFU (least frequently used) adds a frequency per node and a list per frequency, still O(1). TTL expiry adds a timestamp per node and a check in get. Both reuse this structure.

LRU cache: the hand-written version, one lock, and a check that the structure survives contention

Every public method takes the lock, does its O(1) work on the map and the list together, and releases it in finally. The demo first shows the eviction order, then runs 20,000 random operations from virtual threads. Which keys survive varies from run to run, so it checks the invariants instead: the map and the list agree, and the size never exceeds capacity.

LruCacheDemo.java · the cache and its demo
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

final class LruCache<K, V> {
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> prev, next;
        Node(K key, V value) { this.key = key; this.value = value; }
    }

    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node<K, V>> index = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node<K, V> head = new Node<>(null, null);  // sentinels
    private final Node<K, V> tail = new Node<>(null, null);
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private long hits, misses, evictions;

    LruCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    Optional<V> get(K key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
            if (n == null) { misses++; return Optional.empty(); }
            hits++;
            moveToFront(n);                      // a read is a write
            return Optional.of(n.value);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    void put(K key, V value) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
            if (n != null) { n.value = value; moveToFront(n); return; }
            if (index.size() == capacity) {
                Node<K, V> lru = tail.prev;
                unlink(lru);
                index.remove(lru.key);
                evictions++;
            }
            n = new Node<>(key, value);
            index.put(key, n);
            addFront(n);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    List<K> keysByRecency() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            List<K> keys = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Node<K, V> n = head.next; n != tail; n = n.next) keys.add(n.key);
            return keys;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    boolean consistent() {                       // for tests
        List<K> keys = keysByRecency();
        lock.lock();
        try {
            return keys.size() == index.size() && keys.size() <= capacity
                && index.keySet().containsAll(keys);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    long lookups() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return hits + misses; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    private void unlink(Node<K, V> n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
    }
    private void moveToFront(Node<K, V> n) { unlink(n); addFront(n); }
}

public class LruCacheDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var cache = new LruCache<String, Integer>(3);
        cache.put("a", 1); cache.put("b", 2); cache.put("c", 3);
        cache.get("a");                           // a becomes most recent
        cache.put("d", 4);                        // evicts b, the least recent
        System.out.println("recency: " + cache.keysByRecency());
        System.out.println("get b: " + cache.get("b") + ", get c: " + cache.get("c"));
        System.out.println("recency: " + cache.keysByRecency());

        var shared = new LruCache<Integer, Integer>(100);
        var gets = new AtomicInteger();
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 20; t++) {
                long seed = t;
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    var random = new Random(seed);
                    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                        int key = random.nextInt(300);
                        if (random.nextBoolean()) shared.put(key, i);
                        else { shared.get(key); gets.incrementAndGet(); }
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("after 20,000 concurrent ops: consistent " + shared.consistent()
                + ", size " + shared.keysByRecency().size()
                + ", lookups counted " + (shared.lookups() == gets.get()));
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · LruCacheDemo.java
recency: [d, a, c]
get b: Optional.empty, get c: Optional[3]
recency: [c, d, a]
after 20,000 concurrent ops: consistent true, size 100, lookups counted true
Why ReentrantLock and not synchronizedEither is correct here. ReentrantLock leaves room for tryLock with a timeout, and on JDK 21 it does not pin a virtual thread's carrier if a loader is later called inside the lock. The try/finally is mandatory: an exception between lock() and unlock() would otherwise leave the cache locked forever.
Why test invariants, not contentsUnder concurrency the final contents depend on scheduling, but the invariants must hold after every run. Tests that assert invariants catch torn updates reliably; tests that assert exact contents are flaky. The same approach applies to the booking race.
The follow-up: a loading cache"On a miss, load from the database, but only once per key even if a hundred threads miss together." Do not load while holding the cache lock. Keep a ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> of in-flight loads: the first thread starts one with computeIfAbsent, and the rest wait on the same future.

Rate limiter: a token bucket per client, refilled from the clock, never by a timer

A bucket holds up to capacity tokens and gains rate tokens per second. Each request takes one token, or is refused if none are left. Bursts up to the capacity are allowed and the long-run average is the rate. Refill is computed from the elapsed time whenever a request arrives, so there is no background thread, and an injected clock makes it testable to the nanosecond.

RateLimiterDemo.java · integer arithmetic, a fake clock, one bucket per user
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

final class TokenBucket {
    private static final long NANOS = 1_000_000_000L;
    private final long capacity, perSecond;
    private final LongSupplier nanoTime;
    private long tokens, lastRefill;

    TokenBucket(long capacity, long perSecond, LongSupplier nanoTime) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.perSecond = perSecond;
        this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
        this.tokens = capacity;                    // start full: allow a burst
        this.lastRefill = nanoTime.getAsLong();
    }

    synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        refill();
        if (tokens == 0) return false;
        tokens--;
        return true;
    }

    private void refill() {                        // lazy: no timer thread
        long now = nanoTime.getAsLong();
        long earned = (now - lastRefill) * perSecond / NANOS;
        if (earned == 0) return;                   // keep the fraction for later
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + earned);
        lastRefill = tokens == capacity ? now : lastRefill + earned * NANOS / perSecond;
    }
}

final class RateLimiter {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, TokenBucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final long capacity, perSecond;
    private final LongSupplier nanoTime;
    RateLimiter(long capacity, long perSecond, LongSupplier nanoTime) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.perSecond = perSecond; this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
    }
    boolean allow(String client) {
        return buckets.computeIfAbsent(client,
                k -> new TokenBucket(capacity, perSecond, nanoTime)).tryAcquire();
    }
}

public class RateLimiterDemo {
    static long now = 0;                           // the fake clock, in nanos

    static void burst(RateLimiter limiter, String client, int requests) {
        StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) s.append(limiter.allow(client) ? 'Y' : 'n');
        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "t=%.2fs %-4s %s%n", now / 1e9, client, s);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var limiter = new RateLimiter(5, 2, () -> now);   // burst 5, then 2 per second
        burst(limiter, "ana", 7);
        burst(limiter, "bo", 1);
        now += 500_000_000L;
        burst(limiter, "ana", 2);
        now += 250_000_000L;
        burst(limiter, "ana", 1);
        now += 250_000_000L;
        burst(limiter, "ana", 1);
        now += 3_000_000_000L;
        burst(limiter, "ana", 7);
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · RateLimiterDemo.java
t=0.00s ana  YYYYYnn
t=0.00s bo   Y
t=0.50s ana  Yn
t=0.75s ana  n
t=1.00s ana  Y
t=4.00s ana  YYYYYnn
AlgorithmBehaviour
Fixed windowCount per calendar minute. Simple; allows 2× the limit across a window boundary.
Sliding logKeep every timestamp. Exact; memory grows with the limit.
Sliding window counterWeight this window and the last. Close to exact, two counters per client.
Token bucketBursts up to capacity, then a steady rate. Two numbers per client. The usual answer.
Leaky bucketA queue drained at a fixed rate. Smooths output; adds latency instead of refusing.
Why integer maths, and why the fraction is keptWith a double, 0.5 s × 2 tokens/s can come out as 0.999…, and a request that should pass is refused. Integer nanoseconds are exact. Advancing lastRefill only by the time actually converted into tokens keeps the leftover fraction, so at t = 0.75 s the half-token earned since 0.5 s is not lost.
Across many serversEach server has its own buckets, so ten servers allow ten times the rate. Keep the bucket in Redis and update it with one Lua script (read, refill, take, write), which runs atomically. Or give each server 1/n of the rate and accept the imprecision.

Producer-consumer with a bounded queue, and the lock ordering that prevents deadlock

Many LLD systems hand work between threads: orders to a fulfilment worker, notifications to a sender. A bounded BlockingQueue makes producers wait when consumers fall behind (back-pressure), and a poison pill per consumer shuts them down cleanly. The other classic is deadlock. Two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders, and each waits for the other forever.

ProducerConsumer.java · three producers, two consumers, clean shutdown
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    record Order(int id, long amount) {}
    static final Order POISON = new Order(-1, 0);       // a sentinel, compared by ==

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<Order> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);   // bounded
        int producers = 3, consumers = 2, perProducer = 1_000;
        var processed = new AtomicInteger();
        var total = new LongAdder();

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<?>> made = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int p = 0; p < producers; p++) {
                int base = p * perProducer;
                made.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 1; i <= perProducer; i++)
                        queue.put(new Order(base + i, i));   // blocks when full
                    return null;
                }));
            }
            for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    while (true) {
                        Order o = queue.take();              // blocks when empty
                        if (o == POISON) return null;
                        processed.incrementAndGet();
                        total.add(o.amount());
                    }
                });
            }
            for (Future<?> f : made) f.get();                // all produced
            for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) queue.put(POISON);
        }                                                    // all consumed
        System.out.println("processed " + processed.get() + " orders, total " + total.sum());
        System.out.println("queue empty: " + queue.isEmpty());
    }
}
Output on JDK 21 · ProducerConsumer.java
processed 3000 orders, total 1501500
queue empty: true
Deadlock, and the fix: always lock in a global order
// Thread 1: transfer(a, b)  locks a, then waits for b
// Thread 2: transfer(b, a)  locks b, then waits for a   → both wait forever
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) {
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;   // same order for
    Account second = from.id() < to.id() ? to : from;   // every caller
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(amount);
            to.credit(amount);
        }
    }
}
Deadlock needs all fourBreak it by
Mutual exclusionLock-free structures, or immutable data
Hold and waitTake every lock at once, or tryLock and back off
No preemptiontryLock(timeout): give up and retry
Circular waitA global lock order, as above. The usual answer.

From one JVM to many: every in-memory guarantee needs a new owner

An LLD answer lives in one process: a synchronized method, a ConcurrentHashMap, an AtomicInteger for ids. Run three copies behind a load balancer and each of those guarantees silently covers only a third of the traffic. The scale follow-up is asking one thing: for each guarantee, what now enforces it?

In one JVMAcross manyIn this tab's problems
synchronized check-then-actA conditional write the database checks: UPDATE … WHERE state = 'FREE', a unique constraint, or a version columnClaiming a parking spot; debiting an account
ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsentINSERT with a unique key; Redis SET … NXSeat claims; one active ticket per plate
AtomicInteger idsA database sequence, a UUID, or a time-ordered id (UUIDv7, Snowflake-style)Ticket, booking and transaction ids
An in-memory map as the source of truthA table, with the JVM holding at most a cacheActive tickets, loans, the Splitwise ledger
In-process observerA message broker, fed by an outbox tableHold-ready notifications, arrival displays
Clock from the JVMDatabase time for anything compared across servers; clocks driftHold expiry; parking fees
A per-process rate limiterA shared counter (Redis), or a per-instance share of the limitAPI rate limits; the booking waiting room
A singletonOne per instance. If only one must run (a sweeper job), use leader election or a leaseHold-expiry and overdue-reminder jobs

Keep the model

The classes do not change. ParkingSpot.occupy still validates; the repository behind it now saves with a condition. The domain model survives; only its guardians move.

Push the invariant down

The database is the one thing all servers share. An invariant it enforces (a unique key, a check constraint, a conditional update) cannot be bypassed by a server with stale memory.

Say what becomes eventual

Seat maps, free-spot displays and balances shown to other users can lag by a second. Claims, debits and bookings cannot. Name which is which.

Idempotency keys make retries safe; version columns make concurrent edits safe

Across a network every call can time out without telling you whether it worked, so clients retry, and the server must treat a repeat as the same request. And two servers can read the same row and both write it back; the second write must fail rather than overwrite the first. These two techniques cover most of the correctness follow-ups in LLD.

Idempotency key · the client picks it, the server remembers it
-- client sends: POST /bookings/BK7/confirm   Idempotency-Key: 9f1c…
CREATE TABLE idempotency (
  key        VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,   -- unique: the second insert fails
  response   TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

-- in the same transaction as the real work:
INSERT INTO idempotency(key, created_at) VALUES (:key, now());
--   duplicate key?  return the stored response, do nothing else
UPDATE booking SET status = 'CONFIRMED' WHERE id = :id AND status = 'HELD';
UPDATE idempotency SET response = :json WHERE key = :key;
Where it goes in the problemsPayment charges and refunds (the ATM's debit request id), booking confirmation (a payment webhook delivered twice), Splitwise expenses uploaded twice from a phone on a bad network. The ATM's reverse already works this way: a second reversal of the same id does nothing.
Optimistic locking · read the version, write only if unchanged
SELECT id, vehicle, version FROM parking_spot WHERE id = 'F1-M1';
--   id=F1-M1 vehicle=NULL version=41

UPDATE parking_spot
   SET vehicle = 'CAR-A', version = version + 1
 WHERE id = 'F1-M1' AND version = 41;
--   1 row  → we won
--   0 rows → someone else changed it: re-read, retry or pick another spot
The same thing in JPA
@Entity
class ParkingSpot {
    @Id String id;
    String vehicle;
    @Version long version;   // Hibernate adds "AND version = ?" to every update,
}                            // and throws OptimisticLockException on 0 rows
OptimisticPessimistic
HowVersion check on writeSELECT … FOR UPDATE
Best whenConflicts are rareConflicts are common and retries are costly
CostRetries on conflictBlocked transactions; deadlock risk
More on bothThe Event-driven tab treats idempotent consumers in depth on Idempotency, and the Spring Boot tab shows @Version with transactions on Isolation levels.

Distributed locks: prefer a conditional write, and if you must lock, use a lease with a fencing token

A lock across servers is harder than it looks. The holder can pause (a long GC, a network partition) past the lock's expiry, wake up, and write, not knowing another server now holds the lock. Most LLD scale questions do not need a lock at all, because a conditional write in the database already makes the decision atomic. When one is needed, it must expire, and the resource it guards must reject stale holders.

OptionHowWatch out for
No lock: conditional writeThe unique key or WHERE clause decides the winnerNothing, which is the point. Try this first.
Database row lockSELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transactionHeld for the whole transaction; keep it short
Redis leaseSET lock:seat:B1 <owner> NX PX 30000; release with a script that deletes only if the value is still yoursExpiry during a pause; a failover losing the key. Not safe on its own for correctness.
ZooKeeper / etcdEphemeral node or lease, with a monotonically increasing revisionMore infrastructure; the revision gives you a fencing token for free
Why a lease alone is not enough t0 A gets lease, token 33 t1 A pauses (GC) lease expires t2 B gets lease, token 34 t3 B writes with token 34 accepted t4 A wakes, writes with token 33 storage: 33 < 34 seen rejected Fencing: every write carries the token, and the resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has already seen.

Seat holds

A hold is a lease: SET seat:S1:B1 BK7 NX PX 480000 claims with an expiry. The booking row is the source of truth, and confirmation checks it conditionally, so a late Redis key cannot sell a seat twice.

One sweeper job

Hold expiry and overdue reminders should run on one instance. Take a lease named after the job; the holder runs it and renews; if it dies, the lease lapses and another instance takes over.

What to say

"I'd avoid a distributed lock by making the write conditional. If I needed one, I'd use a lease with a fencing token checked by the database, not a bare Redis lock."

When one use case spans services: publish through an outbox, coordinate with a saga

In one JVM, the booking facade holds seats, charges the card and sends the email in one method, and compensates on failure. Split into a booking service, a payment service and a notification service, that method becomes a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event, with a compensating step for each. The events must be published reliably, and that is the outbox's job.

The dual-write problem tx: UPDATE booking SET status='HELD' commits kafka.send(BookingHeld) crashes before this → the booking exists; nobody heard about it The outbox fix tx: UPDATE booking SET status='HELD' INSERT INTO outbox(event) VALUES ('BookingHeld') one commit: both or neither relay: read outbox → publish → mark sent at least once consumers: dedupe by event id idempotent
Booking saga, choreographed booking HELD ──BookingHeld──> payment charge ──PaymentSucceeded──> booking CONFIRMED ──PaymentFailed────> booking CANCELLED seats released compensation notify on BookingConfirmed: send ticket
ChoreographyOrchestration
Who drivesEach service reacts to eventsOne orchestrator sends commands and tracks state
Good forTwo or three stepsMany steps, timeouts, visible progress
RiskThe flow is spread over services; hard to seeThe orchestrator becomes a god service
LLD shapeObserversA state machine (the State pattern) persisted per saga
Compensation is not rollbackA refund is a new transaction, visible on the card statement, not an undo. Every step needs a compensating action designed up front, and some steps (an email already sent) cannot be compensated, so they go last.
Elsewhere in the atlasThe Event-driven tab covers these in depth: the dual-write problem, sagas with events and delivery semantics.

Caching and sharding: find the natural partition key, and cache only what can be stale

Every LLD problem has an aggregate that transactions never cross: a parking lot, a show, a Splitwise group, a building's elevators. That is the shard key, because every invariant lives inside one of them. Caching is then a question of which reads may be a few seconds old. The seat map may be; the seat claim may not.

ProblemShard bySafe to cacheNever from cacheHot spot
Parking lotLot idFree-spot counts for displaysClaiming a spotA stadium lot at kick-off
LibraryBranch idCatalogue search, book detailsCopy status at checkoutA newly released bestseller's waiting list
ATMAccount id (at the bank)Nothing about moneyBalance before a debitPayday withdrawals
Movie bookingShow idMovie details, the seat map read modelSeat claims, confirmationA blockbuster's opening night: one show, 10,000 users
ElevatorBuilding idCar positions for displaysDispatch decisionsMorning lobby traffic
SplitwiseGroup idSimplified-debts viewRecording an expenseA large trip group

A hot key cannot be sharded away

One show is one shard, however many servers there are. Spread the load in front of it: a waiting room that admits users in batches (a rate limiter), per-seat keys instead of one show row, and a read model for the map.

Cache-aside, with invalidation on write

Read: cache, then database, then fill the cache. Write: database, then delete the cache entry, so the next read refills it. Expiry (TTL) is the safety net for invalidations that get lost.

Consistent hashing, in one line

Put shards and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next shard clockwise. Adding a shard moves only about 1/n of the keys, instead of nearly all of them as with hash % n.

How much to say in an LLD roundTwo or three sentences: the shard key and why, what is cached and why it may be stale, and where the hot spot is. The rest belongs to a system-design round, and the Reference deck covers it.

The 45-minute plan: requirements, model, code, then change

Most failed LLD rounds fail on time, not on knowledge: twenty minutes on a perfect class diagram and no code, or code from minute two with the wrong model. Fix the time box before the round and say it at the start: "I'll spend five minutes on requirements, ten on the design, and most of the rest on code." Interviewers like a candidate who manages the clock.

MinutesPhaseWhat you produceWhat the interviewer is checking
0–5ClarifyA short list of in-scope use cases, out-of-scope items and assumptions, written where both can see itDo you ask before you build? Do you scope, or try to build everything?
5–10EntitiesNouns to classes, enums and value objects; the one or two points of variationIs the model right? Title versus copy, spot versus vehicle
10–15Class diagramClasses, key fields and methods, relationships, interfaces. Text is fine.Responsibilities: who owns each decision
15–35CodeModel first, then the service, then a demo or test for the main flowClean, working code; naming; validation; no god class
35–40Run itThe happy path and two edge cases, run or walked throughDo you test your own code, unprompted?
40–45ExtendTheir change request, done or described class by class; concurrency if askedDoes the design bend, or break?

Machine-coding rounds (90–120 min)

Same phases, longer code phase. The output must run. Budget 15 minutes at the end for the demo, the input parser they specified, and reading your own code for bugs.

If you are behind at minute 25

Say so, and cut: "I'll finish the main use case and describe the reservation flow rather than code it." A working core beats three half-built features.

If you are ahead

Offer the follow-up before they ask: thread safety, a second strategy, or a test for the edge case you noticed. Raising your own design's weak spot is the strongest senior signal.

Clarifying requirements: the questions that change the design, and none that do not

A good clarifying question has an answer that changes a class, a relationship or a lock. "What colour are the cars?" changes nothing. "Can a car park in a bigger spot?" changes the allocation rule. Ask five or six questions of the first kind, write down the answers, and state your own assumption for anything the interviewer leaves open.

Ask aboutExampleIt decides
Actors"Who uses it: customers, staff, other systems?"Which interfaces and permissions exist
Core use cases"The three things it must do, in priority order?"What gets coded first
Variation"Can the pricing rule change? Per lot, or per day?"Where the interfaces go
Cardinality"One lot or many? Several copies of a title?"Multiplicities, and the title/copy-style splits
Lifecycle"Does a hold expire? Can a booking be cancelled after payment?"States and transitions
Concurrency"Several entry gates? Many users on one show?"Locks and atomic operations
Failure"What if payment fails, or the dispenser jams?"Ordering and compensation
Scale, briefly"In memory for now, or should I assume a database?"Repositories, ids and time
Write it down like this, where both of you can see it
IN SCOPE
  1. park: assign smallest free spot that fits, issue ticket
  2. leave: fee = hourly rate by vehicle type, part hours round up
  3. show free spots per floor

OUT OF SCOPE
  payments, reservations, EV charging

ASSUMPTIONS
  - larger spot allowed if own size is full
  - several gates call park() concurrently
  - one lot, in memory
Two ways to get this phase wrongAsking nothing and designing the parking lot you once read about, which the interviewer then changes under you. Or asking twenty questions and reaching minute twelve with no classes. Five to six questions, then "I'll assume the rest; stop me if any of that is wrong."

From nouns to classes: underline the nouns, then throw half of them away

Noun extraction is the classic technique: the nouns in the requirements are candidate classes and the verbs are candidate methods. The skill is in the filtering. Some nouns are attributes, some are actors outside the system, some are the same thing under two names, and some are values that deserve a record rather than a class.

A noun that is…BecomesExample
A thing with identity and changing stateA class (an entity)ParkingSpot, Copy, Booking
A value, equal by its fieldsA recordPosition, Money, Ticket
A fixed set of options with dataAn enumVehicleType, Tier, SeatCategory
A rule that variesAn interface with implementationsPricingStrategy, Dispatcher
A property of something elseA fieldcolour, licence plate, due date
A person or system outsideA caller, not a classattendant, gate, librarian
A process, not a thingA method, or a service class"checkout", "settlement"

Then assign every verb to one class

  • Information expert: give the method to the class that holds the data it needs. "Does it fit?" goes on the spot.
  • Creator: the class that contains a thing creates it. The floor creates its spots.
  • Controller: each use case enters through a thin service method that coordinates.
  • If a verb needs data from three classes, it goes in the service, and the three classes each answer one question.
CRC cards, in your headFor each class, one line: its Class name, its Responsibilities, and its Collaborators. If a class has no responsibility beyond holding fields, merge it or make it a record. If it has more than three, split it. It takes thirty seconds per class and prevents the god class.
The anaemic modelClasses with only getters and setters, and a Manager that does everything with them, is the most common LLD failure. Interviewers read it as procedural code in class-shaped files. Behaviour belongs next to its data.

Writing the code live: inside out, compiling as you go, talking the whole time

Write in the order things depend on each other: values and enums, then entities with their rules, then interfaces, then the service, then the demo. Each layer compiles on its own, so if time runs out you have a working model rather than a service that calls methods you never wrote.

StepWriteMinutes
1Enums and records: VehicleType, SpotSize, Vehicle, Ticket3
2Entities with their invariants: ParkingSpot.occupy throws if taken5
3The variation points: PricingStrategy and one implementation3
4The service: park and leave, validating input first7
5main or a test: the happy path, then two edge cases4

Habits that score

  • Names from the domain. claim, release, heldUntil, not process, handle, data.
  • Fields private and final where possible; no setters for state with rules.
  • Validate at the boundary, in constructors and service entry points, then trust the data inside.
  • Small methods. A method longer than the screen is hiding a class.
  • Inject time and ids. Clock, id generators: tests and demos stay deterministic.
  • Exceptions with messages the caller could show a user: "A4 is held", not "error".
Narrate decisions, not keystrokes"I'm making the ticket a record because it never changes after issue." "This lock is per floor so gates on different floors don't wait." One sentence per decision. Silence reads as stuck; typing commentary ("now I'm writing a for loop") reads as filler.
Stubs are allowed; say soIf the payment gateway would take five minutes, write the interface and a one-line fake, and say "the real one is an adapter over the vendor's SDK". Interviewers want the seam, not the HTTP client.

Testing and extending on the spot: prove it works, then show it bends

Before the interviewer asks, run your code or walk it through: the main flow, then the edges. Then the change request arrives. Treat it as the real test of the design. Say which classes change before touching the keyboard; if the answer is "one new class and one line in the factory", say that too, because it is the point of the whole exercise.

Edge cases worth one line each

  • Empty and full: no spots left; nothing to undo; an empty waiting list.
  • Twice: the same ticket redeemed twice; the same plate entering twice; a double click on "book".
  • Boundaries: exactly one hour; exactly at heldUntil; an amount of zero.
  • Rounding: ₹100 split three ways; a percentage that does not divide.
  • Order: cancel after confirm; return a copy that is not on loan.
  • Concurrency: two threads on the last spot or seat.
A concurrency test worth writing, in JUnit 5
@Test
void onlyOneOfManyUsersHoldsTheLastSeat() throws Exception {
    var service = new BookingService(pricing, fakeGateway, fixedClock);
    var winners = new AtomicInteger();
    try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            String user = "u" + i;
            pool.submit(() -> service.hold(user, show, List.of("B1"))
                                     .ifPresent(b -> winners.incrementAndGet()));
        }
    }
    assertEquals(1, winners.get());          // an invariant, not a schedule
}
The change requestA good first sentence
"Add a new vehicle type""One enum constant; the allocation loop and pricing map already handle it."
"Weekend pricing""A new PricingStrategy, or a decorator around the hourly one. Nothing else changes."
"Make it thread-safe""The shared state is the free lists; the invariant is one vehicle per spot; I'll make claim atomic per floor."
"Notify users when…""The domain publishes an event; a notifier subscribes. The domain doesn't learn about email."
"Persist it""Maps become repositories behind interfaces; check-then-act becomes a conditional update."
"Add undo""Actions become command objects that know how to reverse themselves."
When the change does not fitSometimes the request cuts across your design. Say so plainly: "This touches three classes, because I modelled X as Y. With this requirement I'd restructure like this." Recognising a design limit calmly scores better than forcing the change in.

What interviewers score, and what each score looks like from their side of the table

Rubrics differ by company, but the dimensions are stable. Most interviewers write notes under five or six headings and decide from the pattern. Knowing the headings tells you where the minutes should go: a flawless diagram with no code scores well on one heading and badly on three.

DimensionWeak signalStrong signal
RequirementsStarts coding at once; or asks twenty questionsFive sharp questions, a written scope, stated assumptions
Object modellingA god class; anaemic entities; one class for title and copyBehaviour next to data; values as records; the right splits
Design principlesPatterns named with no reason; or a switch on type everywhereInterfaces exactly at the stated variation points, and a reason for each
Code qualityPublic fields, setters for everything, double for money, no validationEncapsulated state, validated boundaries, clear names, small methods
CorrectnessNever runs it; misses the double-redeem or the rounding caseDemo or test for the main flow and two edges, unprompted
ExtensibilityThe change request touches everythingNames the classes that change before editing; the change is local
Concurrency (mid/senior)synchronized on everything, or nothingNames shared state, the invariant and the atomic unit; picks the tool
CommunicationSilent typing, or defensive when challengedNarrates decisions, invites correction, handles pushback with trade-offs
By levelJunior: modelling and working code carry the decision. Mid-level: add clean principles and edge cases. Senior: all of that plus concurrency, failure handling and extension, raised by you rather than drawn out by questions. See Why companies interview for it.
The tie-breakerWhen two candidates both produce working designs, the one who pointed out a weakness in their own design, and said how they would fix it, almost always gets the stronger write-up.

Common mistakes, and the fix for each that you can apply mid-interview

Most of these are recoverable if you notice them yourself. Saying "this manager class is getting too big; let me move the fee rule out" costs thirty seconds and turns a mistake into a demonstration of judgement.

Modelling mistakesFix
A …Manager or …System class with every methodMove each rule to the object that owns its data
Classes with only getters and settersReplace setters with intent-named methods that enforce rules
Inheritance for code reuse (Car extends Vehicle extends ParkingThing)Enum or composition; inheritance only for real "is-a"
A subclass per value (RedCar, SmallSpot)A field or an enum
One class where two lifecycles exist (book and copy)Split by identity: what gets borrowed versus what gets searched
Bidirectional references everywhereKeep the direction the use cases need; look the other way up by id
Process and code mistakesFix
Patterns announced before requirementsIntroduce each pattern when a requirement needs it
Twenty minutes on the diagramTime-box it; the diagram is a sketch, the code is the answer
double for moneylong minor units or BigDecimal
LocalDateTime.now() inside the logicInject a Clock
Check-then-act on shared mapsputIfAbsent, compute, or one lock around both
Singletons for the main serviceCreate it in main and pass it in
Never running the codeA main with the happy path and two edge cases
Arguing when challenged"Good point. The trade-off is… Here is what I'd change."

A two-week practice plan: an hour or two a day, ending with timed mocks

LLD improves with repetition under a clock more than with reading. The plan below works through the tab in order, then spends the second week solving problems cold, in 45 minutes, before comparing with the solutions. Always compare responsibilities first ("who owns this decision?"), then code.

DayStudyPractise
1FoundationsRewrite one of your own classes with records, sealed types and an injected clock
2SOLID and friendsFind one violation of each principle in code you have written
3Creational and structural patternsWrite builder, decorator and adapter from memory
4Behavioural patternsWrite strategy, state, command and observer from memory; explain the look-alikes aloud
5Parking lot, LibraryRead requirements only; solve in 45 minutes; then compare
6ATM, ChessSame method. For chess, add castling yourself
7Elevator, Movie booking, SplitwiseSame method. For booking, write the 100-thread test first
8ConcurrencyLRU cache and token bucket from memory, with a concurrent test for each
9Scale and distributionFor each of the seven problems, say the shard key and the conditional write aloud
10–13New problems, cold: vending machine, hotel booking, snake and ladder, food delivery, a logger, a file system, a cab-booking app, an online auction45 minutes each, timed, out loud, ideally with a friend playing interviewer and adding a requirement at minute 35
14Interview questionsAnswer each in 30 seconds, then review your weakest two problems
Map new problems to known onesA vending machine is the ATM's state machine. A hotel is movie booking with dates. Snake and ladder is a smaller chess. Food delivery is the elevator's dispatcher with drivers instead of cars. A logger is chain of responsibility plus observers. Name the parent problem in the first minute and borrow its structure.

Three principle questions that open many LLD rounds

These twelve questions are the conceptual ones that come up around a design problem, before it or as follow-ups. Each has a 30-second answer to give first and a go deeper paragraph for the follow-up. The links go to the slides that cover the topic; the browser's Back button returns you here.

How to practise with theseRead the question, look away, and answer out loud for thirty seconds with an example from one of the seven problems. Then compare. An answer with a concrete class name in it ("the ticket keeps the pricing strategy") is worth more than a textbook definition.
Q1

Composition or inheritance: how do you choose?

30-second answerDefault to composition: hold the collaborator as a field behind an interface, so it can be swapped at runtime and tested with a fake. Use inheritance only for a genuine "is-a" inside code you control, where the parent was designed to be extended, such as chess pieces sharing a move-generation loop. Inheriting just to reuse code couples you to the parent's implementation.

Go deeper: Give the classic failure. A HashSet subclass that counts additions in both add and addAll double-counts, because addAll calls add internally, a detail the subclass never agreed to. A wrapper does not have the problem. Then say where inheritance is right: a sealed hierarchy where the loop is shared and only the data differs, as with sliding and stepping pieces.

In this tabComposition over inheritanceChess pieces

Q2

What does the open/closed principle mean in practice?

30-second answerWhen a change you expected arrives, you add a class instead of editing working code. In practice that means an interface at each point the requirements say will vary: a new pricing rule is a new PricingStrategy, not another case in a switch. You cannot be closed against every change, so choose the seams from the requirements and say which ones you chose.

Go deeper: Be honest that one place still changes: whatever picks the strategy, whether a factory, configuration or main. OCP moves change to where it is cheap. Then give the other axis. If the types are fixed and the operations grow, a sealed type with an exhaustive switch is closed in a different way, because the compiler finds every switch that needs a new case.

In this tabOpen/closedSealed types

Q3

Interface or abstract class, in modern Java?

30-second answerAn interface is the default for a point of variation: a class can implement several, and default methods cover small shared helpers. Choose an abstract class when subtypes share state or a fixed algorithm with steps to fill in, which is the template method pattern. Choose a sealed interface when the set of implementations is closed and you want exhaustive switches.

Go deeper: Name the constraints. Interfaces cannot hold instance state or constructors; abstract classes can, but a class extends only one. Since Java 8 the gap is smaller, so the question is really about state and about who may implement it. Records implement interfaces but cannot extend classes, which pushes value types towards interfaces.

In this tabInterface or abstract classTemplate method

Three pattern questions, each really about telling two things apart

Pattern questions are rarely "define X". They are "how is X different from Y", or "should you use X at all". The answers turn on intent: who creates the object, who changes it, and why.

Q4

What is the difference between the strategy and state patterns?

30-second answerThey have the same structure: a context delegating to an interface. A strategy is chosen from outside and stays until someone swaps it; it answers "how do I do this job?" A state is replaced by the state itself as events arrive; each handler returns the next state, so the transitions are part of the design. Pricing is a strategy; the ATM's idle, card-inserted and authenticated are states.

Go deeper: Mention the smell each one removes. Strategy removes a switch on a configuration value; state removes a switch on a status field repeated in every method. Then say when not to bother: with three states and two events, an enum and one switch is clearer. State classes pay off when states carry their own data, like the ATM's PIN attempt counter, which lives and dies with CardInserted.

In this tabLook-alikesATM states

Q5

Write a thread-safe singleton. Should you use one?

30-second answerThe simplest safe singleton is an enum with one constant: thread-safe, lazy enough, and immune to reflection and serialization. If it must extend a class, use the holder idiom, where a static nested class holds the instance and the JVM initialises it once. Double-checked locking works only with volatile. But usually don't: create one instance in main or let Spring manage it, and pass it in, so it can be replaced in tests.

Go deeper: Explain why volatile matters: without it, another thread can see a non-null reference before the constructor's writes are visible. Then list the costs of singletons: hidden dependencies, state leaking between tests, and one instance per class loader rather than per JVM. A Spring bean is a singleton per container, reached by injection, which keeps the single instance without the global access.

In this tabThe safe waysHow it breaks

Q6

Decorator, proxy and adapter all wrap an object. How do they differ?

30-second answerAn adapter changes the interface: it makes the vendor's SDK look like your PaymentGateway. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour, and the client chooses and stacks the wrappers, as with pricing add-ons or BufferedReader. A proxy keeps the interface and controls access (caching, lazy loading, security, remoting), usually without the caller knowing, as Spring's @Transactional does.

Go deeper: Point out that decorator order is behaviour. Capping a fee before or after an EV discount gives different prices, so build the chain in one place. For proxies, name the self-invocation trap: a call from one method of a Spring bean to another on this skips the proxy, so the second method's @Transactional is ignored.

In this tabDecoratorProxyAdapter

Three modelling questions that test how you think, not what you remember

These come up at the start of a round ("how would you approach this?") or after it ("why is this an enum?"). Answer with the method, then one example from a problem you know well.

Q7

How do you get from a problem statement to classes?

30-second answerFirst pin down the use cases and assumptions. Then list the nouns and filter them: things with identity and changing state become classes, values become records, fixed options become enums, varying rules become interfaces, properties become fields, and outside actors become callers. Then give each verb to the class that has the data it needs, and keep a thin service per use case to coordinate.

Go deeper: Show a filtering decision that matters. In the library, "book" is two things: a Book you search and reserve, and a Copy you borrow. In the parking lot, "attendant" and "gate" are callers, not classes. Then mention the check against a god class: one line of responsibilities per class, split any class with more than three, and merge any with none.

In this tabFrom nouns to classesLibrary

Q8

Enum, class hierarchy or sealed interface: how do you choose?

30-second answerAn enum when the variants differ only in data: vehicle types that differ in spot size and rate. A sealed interface with records when the set is closed but each variant carries different data, and operations are added by switching over it. An open interface with classes when new variants keep arriving and each brings its own behaviour, such as pricing strategies.

Go deeper: Frame it as which axis changes. New types but fixed operations favours polymorphic methods on an interface. Fixed types but new operations favours a sealed type and switch, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness. Say the migration path out loud: "an enum now; if trucks need their own rules, it becomes a sealed interface, and only the classes that switch on it change."

In this tabJava 21 toolkitKISS

Q9

How do you handle money and time in a design?

30-second answerMoney is never a double. Use a long of minor units or BigDecimal with a fixed scale, inside a value object that validates and knows its currency, and make rounding an explicit rule that keeps totals exact. Time is never read from inside the logic. Inject a Clock, so fees, expiries and due dates can be tested by moving time rather than sleeping.

Go deeper: Give a rounding example: ₹100 three ways is 33.34, 33.33, 33.33, with the extra paisa assigned by a stated rule. Mention BigDecimal.equals comparing scale, so 10.5 and 10.50 differ unless you normalise. For time, name the distributed version: compare expiries against database time, because server clocks drift.

In this tabValue objectsSplitwise rounding

Three questions that separate mid-level from senior answers

These are the follow-ups asked once the design works. A strong answer names the shared state, the invariant and the atomic step before naming any tool, and says what changes when the design leaves a single JVM.

Q10

Two users book the same seat at the same moment. What happens in your design?

30-second answerExactly one wins, because claiming a seat is a single atomic operation: putIfAbsent on the show's claim map, or an insert against a unique key in the database. A multi-seat hold claims seats in sorted order and releases everything on the first conflict, so there are no partial holds. Holds carry an expiry that is checked whenever someone wants the seat, so an abandoned hold frees itself.

Go deeper: Cover the payment race. Charge first, then confirm under the booking's own lock only if the hold is still alive; if it expired during payment, refund. "Confirm" and "expire" cannot both succeed, because both go through that lock. For many servers, the same three steps are an insert on a unique key, a conditional update that takes over a dead hold, and a delete that releases only your own claim.

In this tabBooking modelBooking decisions

Q11

Design a thread-safe LRU cache.

30-second answerA hash map from key to node for O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list of nodes in recency order, with sentinel head and tail. get moves the node to the front; put adds at the front and evicts from the back when full. For thread safety, one lock around each operation, because get modifies the list. That also rules out a read-write lock.

Go deeper: Offer the scaling options: striped segments (approximate LRU, less contention), or a concurrent map with buffered recency updates, which is Caffeine's approach and what you would use in production. Mention the loading-cache follow-up: never load while holding the lock, and use a map of in-flight futures so a hundred concurrent misses trigger one load.

In this tabLRU designLRU code

Q12

Your design now runs on ten servers. What changes?

30-second answerThe classes stay; their guardians move. In-memory maps become tables, and the database becomes the source of truth. Every check-then-act becomes a conditional write or a unique constraint, which enforces the invariant for all servers at once. Ids come from sequences or UUIDs, not an AtomicInteger. Retries need idempotency keys, and in-process events go through an outbox to a broker.

Go deeper: Name the shard key: the aggregate no transaction crosses, such as the lot, the show or the group. Name what may be stale (seat maps, free-spot displays) and what may not (claims, debits). Say you would avoid distributed locks by making writes conditional, and if you needed one, use a lease with a fencing token. Finally, name the hot spot a shard cannot fix, such as a blockbuster's opening night, and put a waiting room in front of it.

In this tabFrom one JVM to manyIdempotencyLeases

Core Java: the language, the collections, concurrency and the JVM, with the failure behind each

A reference for the parts of Java that every Spring Boot service stands on and every Java interview probes: how the language resolves types and methods, how the collections work inside, how threads share memory, what the executors and concurrent collections do, and what the JVM does with your code at run time. Every claim comes with a program that shows it, and the output that program printed.

Eight primitives, eight wrappers, and boxing that converts between them without a word

A primitive holds a value. A wrapper is an object: it can be null, it lives in collections, and it has identity. The compiler boxes and unboxes for you, so a == that compares objects, an unboxed null and a remove(1) that removes the wrong element all compile cleanly.

Boxing.java · the cache, unboxing null, the overload, silent narrowing
import java.util.*;

public class Boxing {
    static Integer discount;                          // a field nobody set: null

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
        System.out.println("127 == 127     " + (a == b));      // the same cached object
        System.out.println("128 == 128     " + (c == d));      // two different objects
        System.out.println("128 equals 128 " + c.equals(d));

        Long total = 128L;
        System.out.println("Long 128 equals int 128   " + total.equals(128));   // 128 boxes to Integer
        System.out.println("Long 128 equals long 128  " + total.equals(128L));

        Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
        try {
            int left = stock.get("SKU-1");                   // auto-unboxing a null
            System.out.println(left);
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("NPE: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        boolean member = false;
        try {
            Integer off = member ? 10 : discount;            // int ? int : Integer is an int
            System.out.println(off);
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("NPE: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        List<Integer> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
        ids.remove(1);                                       // remove(int index): drops 20
        ids.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));                     // remove(Object): drops 10
        System.out.println("after both removes " + ids);

        System.out.println("(byte) 200      " + (byte) 200);
        System.out.println("'a' + 1         " + ('a' + 1));
        System.out.println("(char) ('a' + 1) " + (char) ('a' + 1));
        System.out.println("7 / 2 = " + (7 / 2) + ", 7 / 2.0 = " + (7 / 2.0));
        short s = 1;
        s += 70_000;                                         // compound assignment narrows silently
        System.out.println("short 1 += 70000 " + s);
    }
}

== on wrappersIt passes every test that uses small numbers, because Integer.valueOf returns cached objects from −128 to 127. Real order IDs are bigger, and == compares two different objects. Compare wrappers with equals, or unbox first.
The ternary that unboxesmember ? 10 : discount mixes an int and an Integer, so the whole expression is an int and discount is unboxed even though only the else branch was chosen. The helpful NPE message (Java 14+) names the field.
Long is not IntegerLong.equals(128) is false because 128 boxes to an Integer. The same bug makes Map<Long, Order>.get(5) return null. Boxing in a hot loop costs allocations too: see resource and memory bugs.

Java passes everything by value; for an object, the value is a reference

A call copies each argument into the new stack frame. For an int the copy is the number. For an object the copy is the reference, so caller and callee point at the same object: the callee can change that object, but reassigning its parameter only moves its own copy. There is no way to write swap(a, b) in Java.

PassByValue.java · every method gets copies
import java.util.*;

public class PassByValue {
    static void bump(int n) { n++; }                                  // changes the copy
    static void rename(StringBuilder sb) { sb = new StringBuilder("renamed"); }
    static void append(StringBuilder sb) { sb.append(" + appended"); }  // through the copy
    static void swap(Integer x, Integer y) { Integer t = x; x = y; y = t; }
    static void replace(List<String> list) { list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("new")); }
    static void clear(List<String> list) { list.clear(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int count = 1;
        bump(count);
        System.out.println("int after bump        " + count);

        var sb = new StringBuilder("original");
        rename(sb);
        System.out.println("after rename          " + sb);
        append(sb);
        System.out.println("after append          " + sb);

        Integer a = 1, b = 2;
        swap(a, b);
        System.out.println("after swap            a=" + a + " b=" + b);

        List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y"));
        replace(items);
        System.out.println("after replace         " + items);
        clear(items);
        System.out.println("after clear           " + items);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · PassByValue.java
int after bump        1
after rename          original
after append          original + appended
after swap            a=1 b=2
after replace         [x, y]
after clear           []
Inside the methodDoes the caller see it?
Change a primitive parameterNo. It changed a copy.
Call a mutating method on an object parameterYes. Both references point at that object.
Assign a new object to the parameterNo. Only the callee's copy now points elsewhere.
Swap two parametersNo, and it cannot be done. Return a value, or pass a holder object.
What lives whereLocals and parameters live in the frame: primitives as values, objects as references. Every object lives on the heap, as far as your code can tell. The JIT may allocate a non-escaping object on the stack or remove it altogether, which changes the speed but never the result: see the JIT compiler.

Strings never change, so the JVM can share them, pool the literals and cache the hash

Every method that seems to modify a String returns a new one. That one rule makes strings safe to share between threads, safe as map keys, and safe to pass to security checks. It also explains the two classic traps: == that works only for literals, and += in a loop that copies the whole string on every pass.

Strings.java · identity, the pool, compact strings, concatenation cost
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;

public class Strings {
    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
    static long allocated() { return MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String a = "order";
        String b = "order";
        String c = new String("order");
        String d = "ord" + "er";                 // folded by javac into "order"
        final String prefix = "ord";
        String e = prefix + "er";                // a constant too: prefix is final
        String part = "ord";
        String f = part + "er";                  // built at run time
        System.out.println("a == b            " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("a == new String   " + (a == c));
        System.out.println("a == \"ord\"+\"er\"   " + (a == d));
        System.out.println("a == final+\"er\"   " + (a == e));
        System.out.println("a == part+\"er\"    " + (a == f));
        System.out.println("a == f.intern()   " + (a == f.intern()));
        System.out.println("a.equals(c)       " + a.equals(c));

        String s = "total";
        s.concat("!");                           // returns a new string, discarded
        s.toUpperCase();
        System.out.println("still             " + s);

        System.out.println("\"Aa\".hashCode()   " + "Aa".hashCode() + ", \"BB\".hashCode() " + "BB".hashCode());

        long before = allocated();
        String latin = "a".repeat(1_000);
        long latinBytes = allocated() - before;
        before = allocated();
        String euro = "€".repeat(1_000);
        long euroBytes = allocated() - before;
        System.out.println("1000 x 'a' allocates " + latinBytes + " bytes, 1000 x '€' " + euroBytes
                + " (lengths " + latin.length() + ", " + euro.length() + ")");

        before = allocated();
        String joined = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < 5_000; i++) joined += i + ",";
        long plusBytes = allocated() - before;
        before = allocated();
        var builder = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5_000; i++) builder.append(i).append(',');
        String built = builder.toString();
        long builderBytes = allocated() - before;
        System.out.printf("+= in a loop: %,d bytes; StringBuilder: %,d bytes; same result: %b%n",
                plusBytes, builderBytes, joined.equals(built));
    }
}

LineWhy

"ord" + "er", finalConstant expressions: javac folds them into the literal "order".

57.8 MB vs 98 KBEach += copies everything so far: O(n²) bytes for n appends.
AddedString API worth knowing

== on stringsLiterals are pooled, so == passes tests that compare literals. A string from a request, a file or a database is a new object, and the same comparison fails. Use equals, or "ACTIVE".equals(status) when status may be null.
Where the pool livesIn the heap since Java 7, so pooled strings are collected like anything else. Calling intern() yourself is rarely worth it; G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication shares duplicate backing arrays without code changes.

Initialisation runs in a fixed order, and a constructor that calls an overridable method sees null

A class is initialised once, lazily, the first time it is really used: static initialisers in source order, superclass first. Each new then runs the superclass constructor, then this class's field initialisers and instance blocks in source order, then the rest of the constructor. A method called from the superclass constructor runs before the subclass has assigned a single field.

InitOrder.java · numbered in the order the lines run
public class InitOrder {
    static String log(String step, String value) { System.out.println(step); return value; }
    static void log(String step) { System.out.println(step); }

    static class Base {
        static { log("1  Base static block"); }
        private final String tag = log("3  Base field initialiser", "B");
        { log("4  Base instance block"); }
        Base() {
            log("5  Base constructor body, tag=" + tag);
            describe();                          // calls the subclass override
        }
        void describe() { log("   Base.describe"); }
    }

    static class Order extends Base {
        static final String PREFIX = "ORD-";     // compile-time constant: inlined by javac
        static String region = log("2  Order static field", "EU");
        private final String id = log("7  Order field initialiser", PREFIX + 1);
        Order() { log("8  Order constructor body, id=" + id); }
        @Override void describe() { log("6  Order.describe sees id=" + id); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        log("main reads Order.PREFIX = " + Order.PREFIX + " (no class initialised yet)");
        log("-- new Order()");
        new Order();
        log("-- new Order() again: no static lines this time");
        new Order();
        log("Order.region was set once: " + Order.region);
    }
}
