Line 6: id=nullBase() calls describe(), which dispatches to Order.describe before Order's field initialiser has run. Never call an overridable method from a constructor. javac 21 can catch it: -Xlint:this-escape warns when a public class's constructor lets this escape to code a subclass could override.
The first line: no initialisationPREFIX is a compile-time constant, so javac copied "ORD-" into main. Reading it does not touch Order. The catch: change a constant and every class that uses it must be recompiled, or it keeps the old value.
ModifierOnMeansDoes not mean
finallocal, parameterAssigned once. Lambdas and inner classes may capture only final or effectively final locals.That the object it refers to is immutable
finalfieldAssigned exactly once, by the end of the constructor. The memory model guarantees other threads see it fully set once construction finishes (happens-before).A final List cannot be modified
finalmethod, classCannot be overridden, cannot be extended: String, the wrappers and every record are final.Faster: the JIT inlines non-final methods as well
staticfield, methodOne per class (per class loader), shared by every instance. Static methods are hidden, never overridden.Thread-safe: a static mutable field is shared state
staticnested classNo hidden reference to an outer instance: the default for nested types.

Four kinds of nested class, and the hidden reference the inner ones carry

A class declared inside another is either static nested, an ordinary class that happens to live in another's namespace, or one of the three inner kinds: member, local and anonymous. Created in an instance context, an inner class gets a hidden field pointing at the outer object. That field is what lets it read outer state, and it is also how an inner class keeps a large object alive by accident.

Nested.java · all four kinds, and a lambda for contrast
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class Nested {
    private int openOrders = 3;

    static class Totals {                          // static nested: no outer instance
        String hello() { return "static nested: needs no Nested instance"; }
    }

    class Inner {                                  // inner: tied to one Nested instance
        String hello() { return "inner reads the outer field: openOrders=" + openOrders; }
    }

    Supplier<String> anonymous() {
        return new Supplier<>() {                  // a class, so 'this' is the anonymous object
            @Override public String get() { return "anonymous: this is " + this.getClass().getName(); }
        };
    }

    Supplier<String> lambda() {
        return () -> "lambda: this is " + this.getClass().getName();   // the enclosing Nested
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Nested outer = new Nested();
        System.out.println(new Totals().hello());
        Nested.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
        System.out.println(inner.hello());
        for (Field f : Inner.class.getDeclaredFields())
            System.out.println("hidden field in Inner: " + f);
        System.out.println(outer.anonymous().get());
        System.out.println(outer.lambda().get());

        int base = 10;                             // effectively final, so it can be captured
        record Line(String sku, int qty) { }       // local records are implicitly static
        class Pricer { int total(Line l) { return base + l.qty(); } }
        System.out.println("local class: " + new Pricer().total(new Line("SKU-1", 5)));
    }
}

this$0 is a strong referenceA listener, a cache entry or a task built from an inner class keeps its whole outer object reachable for as long as it lives itself. Since JDK 18, javac leaves the field out when the inner class never uses the outer instance. Declare nested classes static unless they really need it.

equals and hashCode are a contract with every hash-based collection, and the compiler only warns

Every class inherits equals, hashCode, toString and clone from Object. The defaults use identity. Override equals and you must override hashCode to match, or HashSet and HashMap stop working for that type. The four bugs below compile; only the first gets a warning, and only with -Xlint.

ObjectContract.java · four ways to break the contract
import java.util.*;

public class ObjectContract {
    static final class Sku {                         // equals, but no hashCode
        final String code;
        Sku(String code) { this.code = code; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Sku s && s.code.equals(code); }
    }

    static class Point {
        final int x, y;
        Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Point p && p.x == x && p.y == y; }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
    }
    static class ColorPoint extends Point {
        final String color;
        ColorPoint(int x, int y, String color) { super(x, y); this.color = color; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof ColorPoint c && super.equals(c) && c.color.equals(color);
        }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y, color); }
    }

    static class Basket implements Cloneable {
        List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea"));
        @Override public Basket clone() {
            try { return (Basket) super.clone(); }     // field-by-field copy: shares the list
            catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Sku> skus = new HashSet<>(List.of(new Sku("A-1"), new Sku("A-1")));
        System.out.println("equal Skus in a HashSet: " + skus.size());

        Point p = new Point(1, 2);
        ColorPoint cp = new ColorPoint(1, 2, "red");
        System.out.println("p.equals(cp) " + p.equals(cp) + ", cp.equals(p) " + cp.equals(p));

        List<String> key = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
        Set<List<String>> seen = new HashSet<>();
        seen.add(key);
        key.add("b");                                  // its hashCode just changed
        System.out.println("mutated key: contains " + seen.contains(key) + ", size " + seen.size());

        Basket original = new Basket();
        Basket copy = original.clone();
        copy.items.add("milk");
        System.out.println("clone shares state: original now " + original.items);
    }
}

    static final class Sku {                         // equals, but no hashCode
                 ^
1 warning

BugWhat went wrong
2 equal SkusEqual objects with identity hash codes land in different buckets, so the set never compares them.
SymmetryPoint accepts any Point; ColorPoint accepts only ColorPoint. Mixing instanceof equality with subclasses that add fields cannot be made symmetric.
Mutated keyThe set filed the list under its old hash. It is still inside, unreachable by contains or remove.
cloneObject.clone copies fields, so both baskets share one list.

The rules

equals is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal ones may collide. Neither may depend on a field that changes while the object sits in a hash collection.

The practical fix

Use a record for anything compared by value: it generates all three methods from its components. For a class, make it final and use the same fields in both methods. Value objects in the LLD tab shows the pattern.

The other two

Default toString is getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode()). Avoid clone: write a copy constructor or factory. finalize is deprecated for removal 18; use try-with-resources or a Cleaner.

Immutable means nothing can change it after construction, including the caller who passed the list in

final fields and no setters are not enough. If the constructor keeps the caller's list, the caller can still change it; if a getter returns that list, every reader can. An immutable class copies every mutable input on the way in and never hands out anything mutable on the way out.

Immutable.java · the leaky version, the fixed class, the record
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.*;

public class Immutable {
    // Looks immutable: final fields, no setters. It is not.
    static final class LeakyOrder {
        private final List<String> lines;
        private final Date placed;
        LeakyOrder(List<String> lines, Date placed) { this.lines = lines; this.placed = placed; }
        List<String> lines() { return lines; }
        Date placed() { return placed; }
        @Override public String toString() { return lines + " @ " + placed.toInstant(); }
    }

    // Immutable: final class, final fields, copies in, nothing mutable out.
    static final class Order {
        private final List<String> lines;
        private final Instant placed;              // immutable type instead of Date
        Order(List<String> lines, Instant placed) {
            this.lines = List.copyOf(lines);       // copy in (and reject nulls)
            this.placed = Objects.requireNonNull(placed);
        }
        List<String> lines() { return lines; }    // already unmodifiable: safe to return
        Instant placed() { return placed; }
        Order withLine(String line) {              // "modification" returns a new object
            var next = new ArrayList<>(lines);
            next.add(line);
            return new Order(next, placed);
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return lines + " @ " + placed; }
    }

    // The same guarantees as a record
    record OrderRecord(List<String> lines, Instant placed) {
        OrderRecord {
            lines = List.copyOf(lines);
            Objects.requireNonNull(placed);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var input = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea"));
        var when = new Date(0);
        var leaky = new LeakyOrder(input, when);
        input.add("milk");                         // the caller still holds the list
        leaky.lines().add("sugar");                // and the getter hands it out
        when.setTime(86_400_000L);                 // Date is mutable too
        System.out.println("leaky   " + leaky);

        var input2 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea"));
        var order = new Order(input2, Instant.EPOCH);
        input2.add("milk");
        try {
            order.lines().add("sugar");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("order.lines().add -> UnsupportedOperationException");
        }
        System.out.println("order   " + order);
        System.out.println("with    " + order.withLine("milk") + "  (original " + order.lines() + ")");

        var input3 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea"));
        var rec = new OrderRecord(input3, Instant.EPOCH);
        input3.add("milk");
        System.out.println("record  " + rec);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · Immutable.java
leaky   [tea, milk, sugar] @ 1970-01-02T00:00:00Z
order.lines().add -> UnsupportedOperationException
order   [tea] @ 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
with    [tea, milk] @ 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z  (original [tea])
record  OrderRecord[lines=[tea], placed=1970-01-01T00:00:00Z]

The checklist

  1. Final class, or a private constructor with factories, so no subclass can add mutable state or override accessors.
  2. Private final fields, all assigned in the constructor.
  3. No setters. A change is a method that returns a new object, like withLine.
  4. Copy mutable inputs in: List.copyOf, Map.copyOf. Prefer immutable types such as Instant over Date.
  5. Never return mutable internals. A list from List.copyOf is already unmodifiable, so it is safe to return as it is.
  6. Check the elements. List.copyOf copies the list, not the objects in it. Immutability is only as deep as the types you hold.
What it buysThread safety with no locks, because there is nothing to race on. Safe sharing and caching. Stable hashCode, so it is a safe map key. Final fields also make it safely published to other threads once the constructor returns.
Records do most of itA record is final with private final fields and no setters. You still write the defensive copy, in the compact constructor, as OrderRecord does. Without it, the record holds the caller's list.
copyOf is not a viewCollections.unmodifiableList wraps the original, so changes to the original show through. List.copyOf takes a snapshot, and returns its argument unchanged if that is already an unmodifiable list. See unmodifiable collections.

The compiler picks an overload from static types; the JVM picks an override from the object

Overloading means several methods with one name and different parameters; javac chooses one at compile time from the declared types of the arguments. Overriding means a subclass replacing an inherited method; the JVM chooses at run time from the actual class of the receiver. Mixing the two up explains most "why did it call that one?" questions.

Overloads.java · overload resolution, overrides, hiding, covariant returns
public class Overloads {
    static String pay(Object o)  { return "pay(Object)"; }
    static String pay(Number n)  { return "pay(Number)"; }
    static String pay(Integer i) { return "pay(Integer)"; }
    static String pay(long l)    { return "pay(long)"; }
    static String pay(int... xs) { return "pay(int...)"; }

    static class Shape {
        String name = "shape";
        String area() { return "Shape.area"; }
        Shape copy() { return new Shape(); }
        static String kind() { return "Shape.kind"; }
    }
    static class Circle extends Shape {
        String name = "circle";                       // hides the field: no override
        @Override String area() { return "Circle.area"; }
        @Override Circle copy() { return new Circle(); }   // covariant return type
        static String kind() { return "Circle.kind"; }     // hides the static method
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int i = 5;
        short s = 5;
        Object boxed = 5;
        System.out.println("pay(int 5)     -> " + pay(i));        // widening beats boxing
        System.out.println("pay(short 5)   -> " + pay(s));
        System.out.println("pay(Integer 5) -> " + pay(Integer.valueOf(5)));
        System.out.println("pay(Object 5)  -> " + pay(boxed));    // the static type decides
        System.out.println("pay()          -> " + pay());

        Shape shape = new Circle();
        System.out.println("shape.area()   -> " + shape.area());  // runtime type decides
        System.out.println("shape.name     -> " + shape.name);    // fields: static type
        System.out.println("shape.copy()   -> " + shape.copy().getClass().getSimpleName());
        System.out.println("Shape.kind()   -> " + Shape.kind() + ", Circle.kind() -> " + Circle.kind());
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · Overloads.java
pay(int 5)     -> pay(long)
pay(short 5)   -> pay(long)
pay(Integer 5) -> pay(Integer)
pay(Object 5)  -> pay(Object)
pay()          -> pay(int...)
shape.area()   -> Circle.area
shape.name     -> shape
shape.copy()   -> Circle
Shape.kind()   -> Shape.kind, Circle.kind() -> Circle.kind

How javac picks an overload

  1. Phase 1: methods applicable by subtyping or widening alone. No boxing, no varargs.
  2. Phase 2: only if phase 1 found nothing, allow boxing and unboxing.
  3. Phase 3: only then, allow varargs.

Within a phase the most specific method wins, and a tie is a compile error. That is why pay(5) calls pay(long): widening is phase 1 and boxing to Integer is phase 2. And pay(boxed) calls pay(Object) although the object is an Integer: overload choice never looks at the runtime class.

OverloadingOverriding
ChosenAt compile time, from argument typesAt run time, from the receiver's class
SignatureSame name, different parameters. The return type plays no part.Same name and parameters. The return type may be a subtype (covariant).
AccessAnythingSame or wider: public cannot become protected
Checked exceptionsAnythingNone new or broader than the overridden method's
static, private, finalCan all be overloadedStatic methods are hidden, private ones are not inherited, final ones are locked
FieldsNever polymorphic. A subclass field with the same name hides the other, and the static type picks: shape.name is "shape".
Always write @OverrideMistype the parameter, as in equals(Order other), and you have written an overload. It compiles, and HashSet keeps calling Object.equals(Object). With @Override the same mistake is a compile error. Equality and hashing bugs shows it failing.

Five invoke instructions, and how a virtual call finds the method it runs

javac compiles every method call into one of five bytecodes. Only invokevirtual and invokeinterface choose the method at run time, from the receiver's class. The JIT then removes most of that cost: a call site that only ever sees one class becomes a direct call, and usually an inlined one.

Dispatch.java · one call of each kind
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

interface Priced { long price(); }

public class Dispatch {
    static class Item implements Priced {
        public long price() { return 100; }
        private long cost() { return 60; }
        long margin() { return price() - cost(); }
    }
    static class Discounted extends Item {
        @Override public long price() { return super.price() - 10; }
    }
    static long tax(long amount) { return amount / 5; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Item item = new Discounted();
        Priced priced = item;
        long a = item.price();                     // class type: invokevirtual
        long b = priced.price();                   // interface type: invokeinterface
        long c = tax(a);                           // static: invokestatic
        long m = item.margin();
        LongSupplier later = () -> a * 2;          // lambda: invokedynamic
        String line = "price=" + a;                // concatenation: invokedynamic
        System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + c + " " + m + " " + later.getAsLong() + " " + line);
    }
}
javap -c -p Dispatch Dispatch$Item Dispatch$Discounted · the invoke lines

        11: invokevirtual #12                 // Method Dispatch$Item.price:()J
        16: invokeinterface #18,  1           // InterfaceMethod Priced.price:()J
        24: invokestatic  #21                 // Method tax:(J)J
        30: invokevirtual #27                 // Method Dispatch$Item.margin:()J
        36: invokedynamic #30,  0             // InvokeDynamic #0:getAsLong:(J)Ljava/util/function/LongSupplier;
        44: invokedynamic #34,  0             // InvokeDynamic #1:makeConcatWithConstants:(J)Ljava/lang/String;
        63: invokeinterface #44,  1           // InterfaceMethod java/util/function/LongSupplier.getAsLong:()J
        70: invokedynamic #48,  0             // InvokeDynamic #2:makeConcatWithConstants:(JJJJJLjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
        75: invokevirtual #51                 // Method java/io/PrintStream.println:(Ljava/lang/String;)V
         1: invokevirtual #11                 // Method price:()J
         5: invokevirtual #17                 // Method cost:()J
         1: invokespecial #7                  // Method Dispatch$Item.price:()J

InstructionEmitted forTarget chosen
invokestaticStatic methodsOnce, when the call is linked
invokespecialConstructors and super.m()Exactly the named method, with no lookup: super.price() above
invokevirtualCalls through a class type, including private methods since JDK 11 (cost above)Per call, from the receiver's class: a vtable slot
invokeinterfaceCalls through an interface typePer call: an itable search, since one class can implement many interfaces
invokedynamicLambdas, string concatenation 9, record methods, pattern switchOn first execution a bootstrap method links the call site; later calls go straight there

What the JIT does with a virtual call

  • Monomorphic (one class seen): a class check, then the method inlined.
  • Bimorphic (two): two checks, both inlined.
  • Megamorphic (three or more): a real vtable or itable call, and no inlining.
  • If only one implementation is loaded, class hierarchy analysis inlines it with no check, and deoptimises if a subclass loads later. final is not needed for speed.
Where this shows upHot loops over many implementations of one interface, such as serializers, rule engines and visitors, pay for megamorphic calls. Typical service code does not. More on compilation in the JIT compiler.

Interfaces carry behaviour since Java 8; abstract classes still own the state and the constructor

Default, static and private methods let an interface ship code, so "an interface has no implementation" is out of date. What an interface still cannot have is instance state or a constructor, which means it cannot protect an invariant. When two interfaces supply the same default, three rules decide which one runs, and if none applies the class must choose.

Interfaces.java · default-method conflicts, and what only a class can do
public class Interfaces {
    interface Shippable {
        int MAX_KG = 30;                                    // implicitly public static final
        default String label() { return "ship: " + describe(); }
        private String describe() { return "parcel up to " + MAX_KG + " kg"; }   // since 9
        static Shippable standard() { return new Shippable() { }; }             // since 8
    }
    interface Giftable {
        default String label() { return "gift"; }
    }

    // Two defaults with the same signature: the class must choose.
    static class Order implements Shippable, Giftable {
        @Override public String label() { return Shippable.super.label() + " + " + Giftable.super.label(); }
    }

    // Rule 1: a method from a class beats any default.
    static class Base { public String label() { return "Base.label"; } }
    static class Special extends Base implements Giftable { }

    // Rule 2: the more specific interface wins.
    interface FragileGift extends Giftable {
        @Override default String label() { return "fragile gift"; }
    }
    static class Vase implements Giftable, FragileGift { }

    // Abstract classes keep state and constructors; interfaces cannot.
    abstract static class Payment {
        private final long cents;
        protected Payment(long cents) {
            if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cents must be positive");
            this.cents = cents;
        }
        final String receipt() { return method() + " " + cents; }   // template method
        abstract String method();
    }
    static class Card extends Payment {
        Card(long cents) { super(cents); }
        @Override String method() { return "card"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Order().label());
        System.out.println(new Special().label());
        System.out.println(new Vase().label());
        System.out.println(Shippable.standard().label());
        System.out.println(new Card(1250).receipt());
        try {
            new Card(0);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · Interfaces.java
ship: parcel up to 30 kg + gift
Base.label
fragile gift
ship: parcel up to 30 kg
card 1250
rejected: cents must be positive

Which default runs

  1. A class wins. A method inherited from a superclass beats any default: Special prints Base.label.
  2. The more specific interface wins. FragileGift extends Giftable, so its default is used.
  3. Otherwise it does not compile. Override the method, and call Shippable.super.label() to reuse one.

1 error

The design questionWhich one to reach for in a model, and why composition usually beats both, is on composition over inheritance in the LLD tab. A common shape uses both: an interface as the type, and an abstract class that implements it as an optional convenience, as List and AbstractList do.

A record is a final class whose state is its components, and the compact constructor guards it

Declare the components and javac writes the private final fields, the canonical constructor, the accessors and value-based equals, hashCode and toString since 16. The compact constructor runs before the fields are assigned, so it can validate and normalise the arguments. What a record cannot do is hide a mutable component: it is only as immutable as the types it holds.

Records.java · validation, normalisation, generic records, the two traps
import java.util.*;

public class Records {
    record Money(long cents, String currency) {
        static final Money ZERO_EUR = new Money(0, "EUR");      // static fields are allowed
        Money {                                                // compact canonical constructor
            if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + cents);
            currency = currency.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);      // normalise before assignment
        }
        Money(long cents) { this(cents, "EUR"); }               // others must delegate
        Money plus(Money other) {
            if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
            return new Money(cents + other.cents, currency);
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return String.format("%d.%02d %s", cents / 100, cents % 100, currency); }
    }

    record Batch(String sku, int[] quantities) { }             // array component: a trap
    record Basket(List<String> items) { }                      // no defensive copy
    record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) { }                   // records can be generic

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Money a = new Money(1250, "eur");
        System.out.println(a + " plus " + new Money(99) + " = " + a.plus(new Money(99)));
        System.out.println("equal by value: " + a.equals(new Money(1250, "EUR"))
                + ", same hash: " + (a.hashCode() == new Money(1250, "EUR").hashCode()));
        try {
            new Money(-1, "EUR");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        Batch b1 = new Batch("A-1", new int[] {1, 2});
        Batch b2 = new Batch("A-1", new int[] {1, 2});
        System.out.println("batches with equal arrays equal? " + b1.equals(b2));
        System.out.println("batch toString: " + b1.toString().replaceAll("@[0-9a-f]+", "@…"));

        var items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea"));
        Basket basket = new Basket(items);
        items.add("milk");
        System.out.println("basket after the caller's add: " + basket);

        var pair = new Pair<>("SKU-1", 3);
        System.out.println(pair + ", components: " + Arrays.stream(Pair.class.getRecordComponents())
                .map(c -> c.getName() + ":" + c.getType().getSimpleName()).toList());
        System.out.println("is a record, final: " + Money.class.isRecord() + ", "
                + java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isFinal(Money.class.getModifiers())
                + ", superclass " + Money.class.getSuperclass().getName());
    }
}

A record canA record cannot
Implement interfacesExtend a class: it already extends java.lang.Record
Declare static fields, static methods, nested typesDeclare instance fields beyond its components
Add constructors that delegate to the canonical oneBe extended: it is implicitly final
Override an accessor, keeping its public signatureMake a component mutable: every field is final
Be generic, local or nested (nested ones are static)Be abstract
Array componentsThe generated equals compares each component with equals, and for an array that means identity. Two batches with equal contents are unequal, and toString prints [I@…. Hold a List instead, or override all three methods.
Shallow immutabilityBasket kept the caller's list, so the caller's later add changed the record. Copy in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items), as on writing an immutable class.
Where records fitDTOs, API payloads, query projections, map keys, events and messages. Not JPA entities, which need a no-argument constructor, mutable state and subclassing proxies. Jackson binds records through the canonical constructor, and Java serialization calls it too, so validation also runs on deserialization.

A sealed hierarchy lets the compiler prove that a switch handles every case

A sealed interface lists every type allowed to implement it since 17. A switch over it can then match on type, deconstruct records and add guards since 21, with no default branch. Add a new permitted type and every switch that forgot it stops compiling, instead of falling into a default that hides the gap.

Sealed.java · type patterns, record patterns, guards, case null
import java.util.List;

public class Sealed {
    sealed interface Payment permits Card, Wallet, BankTransfer { long cents(); }
    record Card(long cents, String network) implements Payment { }
    record Wallet(long cents, String provider) implements Payment { }
    record BankTransfer(long cents, String iban, boolean instant) implements Payment { }

    static long feeCents(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {                                  // exhaustive: no default needed
            case Card c when c.network().equals("AMEX") -> c.cents() * 3 / 100;
            case Card c                                  -> c.cents() * 2 / 100;
            case Wallet w                                -> 25;
            case BankTransfer(long cents, String iban, boolean instant) when instant -> 50;
            case BankTransfer t                          -> 0;
        };
    }

    static String describe(Object o) {
        return switch (o) {
            case null                    -> "nothing";       // since 21: null gets a case
            case Integer i when i > 100  -> "big int " + i;
            case Integer i               -> "int " + i;
            case String s                -> "string of " + s.length();
            case Payment p               -> "payment of " + p.cents();
            default                      -> "other " + o.getClass().getSimpleName();
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Payment> payments = List.of(new Card(10_000, "VISA"), new Card(10_000, "AMEX"),
                new Wallet(4_000, "PayPal"), new BankTransfer(90_000, "DE89...", true),
                new BankTransfer(90_000, "DE89...", false));
        for (Payment p : payments) System.out.println(p + " -> fee " + feeCents(p));

        for (Object o : new Object[] {null, 7, 500, "refund", new Wallet(1, "X"), 2.5})
            System.out.println(describe(o));

        Object order = "ORD-42";
        if (order instanceof String id && id.startsWith("ORD-"))   // pattern variable in scope
            System.out.println("order number " + id.substring(4));
    }
}

SealedMissing.java · a Voucher type the switch does not handle
public class SealedMissing {
    sealed interface Payment permits Card, Wallet, Voucher { long cents(); }
    record Card(long cents) implements Payment { }
    record Wallet(long cents) implements Payment { }
    record Voucher(long cents) implements Payment { }        // the new type

    static long feeCents(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {
            case Card c   -> c.cents() * 2 / 100;
            case Wallet w -> 25;
        };                                                     // Voucher is not handled
    }
}

RuleDetail
Who may be permittedSubtypes in the same module, or the same package when there is no module. Each must be final, sealed or non-sealed; records are final already. permits may be left out when they are all in the same file.
ExhaustivenessRequired for every switch expression, and for any switch that uses patterns or case null.
Order and dominanceCases are tried top to bottom. A case that can never match because an earlier one covers it is an error, shown below.
nullA switch without case null throws NullPointerException on null, as switches always have.
Separate compilationIf a new permitted type arrives in a jar and the switch is not recompiled, it throws MatchException at run time.
Sinceinstanceof patterns 16 · sealed 17 · switch and record patterns 21 · unnamed _ 22 · primitive patterns in preview in 25
javac · Dominance.java, a String case after CharSequence
Dominance.java:5: error: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label

                 ^
1 error
Sealed switch or polymorphic method?Use a sealed type and a switch when the set of types is fixed and new operations keep coming. Use a method on the interface when new types keep coming. The LLD tab's Java 21 toolkit applies this to a parking-lot model.

An enum is a fixed set of singleton objects, so it can carry fields, behaviour and a checked switch

Each constant is created once, when the enum class is initialised, and no code can create another, not even reflection or deserialization. Constants can hold fields, and each can override methods. Two habits cause the bugs: storing ordinal(), and assuming every constant's class is the enum's class.

Enums.java · state machine, stable codes, EnumSet and EnumMap
import java.util.*;

public class Enums {
    enum Status {
        PLACED("P") {
            @Override Status next() { return PAID; }
        },
        PAID("A") {
            @Override Status next() { return SHIPPED; }
        },
        SHIPPED("S") {
            @Override Status next() { return this; }
            @Override boolean isFinal() { return true; }
        };

        private final String code;                         // a stable code for storage
        Status(String code) { this.code = code; }          // constructors are always private
        abstract Status next();                            // each constant implements it
        boolean isFinal() { return false; }

        private static final Map<String, Status> BY_CODE = new HashMap<>();
        static { for (Status s : values()) BY_CODE.put(s.code, s); }
        static Status fromCode(String code) {
            Status s = BY_CODE.get(code);
            if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown status code " + code);
            return s;
        }
    }

    enum Region { NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Status s = Status.PLACED; ; s = s.next()) {
            System.out.println(s + " ordinal=" + s.ordinal() + " code=" + s.code
                    + " class=" + s.getClass().getName());
            if (s.isFinal()) break;
        }
        System.out.println("fromCode(\"A\") = " + Status.fromCode("A"));
        try {
            Status.valueOf("paid");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("values() is a new array each call: " + (Status.values() != Status.values()));

        EnumSet<Region> south = EnumSet.range(Region.EAST, Region.WEST);
        EnumMap<Region, Integer> orders = new EnumMap<>(Region.class);
        orders.put(Region.WEST, 12);
        orders.put(Region.NORTH, 7);
        System.out.println("range " + south + ", complement " + EnumSet.complementOf(south) + ", map " + orders);

        Status s = Status.PAID;
        String label = switch (s) {                         // exhaustive over the constants
            case PLACED -> "awaiting payment";
            case PAID -> "packing";
            case SHIPPED -> "on its way";
        };
        System.out.println(label + "; PAID compareTo SHIPPED = " + Status.PAID.compareTo(Status.SHIPPED));
    }
}

FactConsequence
A constant with a body is an anonymous subclassgetClass() is Enums$Status$1. Use getDeclaringClass() to get Status.
ordinal() is the declaration positionInsert a constant and every stored ordinal now means something else. Store a stable code or the name.
valueOf matches the exact nameWrong case or an unknown value throws IllegalArgumentException. Map external codes yourself.
values() clones an array per callCache it, or build a lookup map once, as BY_CODE does.
compareTo uses ordinal orderDeclare constants in a meaningful order, or do not rely on it.
Ordinals in the databaseJPA's EnumType.ORDINAL stores 0, 1, 2. Someone adds CANCELLED between PLACED and PAID, and every paid order is now cancelled. Use EnumType.STRING or an AttributeConverter with a code.
EnumSet and EnumMapAn EnumSet is a bit vector: one long for up to 64 constants. An EnumMap is an array indexed by ordinal. Both iterate in declaration order and beat HashSet and HashMap for enum keys.
The safest singletonA single-constant enum cannot be duplicated by reflection or serialization, which breaks the other singleton forms. See singleton, the safe ways.

Generics are checked by the compiler and erased from the objects, but not from the declarations

javac checks every type argument, inserts the casts, then compiles List<String> and List<Integer> to the same ArrayList class. That kept Java 5 binary-compatible with older code. At run time an object does not know its type argument. Fields, method signatures and superclass declarations keep theirs in the class file, which is how Jackson and Spring recover them.

Erasure.java · what is erased, and what survives
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.*;

public class Erasure {
    static List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();               // declarations keep their types

    record Money(long cents) implements Comparable<Money> {
        @Override public int compareTo(Money o) { return Long.compare(cents, o.cents); }
    }

    // A "super type token": a subclass records its type argument in the class file.
    abstract static class TypeRef<T> {
        final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0];
    }

    static <T> T[] newArray(Class<T> type, int n) {               // new T[n] does not compile
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        T[] array = (T[]) Array.newInstance(type, n);             // so pass the Class in
        return array;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
        List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
        System.out.println("same class at run time: " + (strings.getClass() == numbers.getClass())
                + " (" + strings.getClass().getName() + ")");

        Field f = Erasure.class.getDeclaredField("names");
        System.out.println("field type " + f.getType().getName() + ", generic type " + f.getGenericType());

        Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() { }.type;
        System.out.println("captured by the token: " + t);

        for (Method m : Money.class.getDeclaredMethods())
            if (m.getName().equals("compareTo"))
                System.out.println("compareTo(" + m.getParameterTypes()[0].getSimpleName() + ") bridge=" + m.isBridge());

        String[] slots = newArray(String.class, 2);
        System.out.println("array made at run time: " + slots.getClass().getSimpleName() + " length " + slots.length);
    }
}

same class at run time: true (java.util.ArrayList)
field type java.util.List, generic type java.util.List<java.lang.String>
captured by the token: java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>>
compareTo(Money) bridge=false
compareTo(Object) bridge=true
array made at run time: String[] length 2
LineWhy
Same classOne ArrayList class serves every type argument. There is no ArrayList<String>.class.
Generic typeThe field's declaration keeps List<String> as a signature attribute, readable by reflection.
The tokenAn anonymous subclass of TypeRef<…> fixes the argument in its superclass declaration. Jackson's TypeReference and Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference use this trick.
Bridge methodcompareTo(Money) erases differently from Comparable.compareTo(Object), so javac adds a synthetic compareTo(Object) that casts and delegates.
Because of erasure, you cannotDo this instead
Write new T() or new T[n]Pass a Class<T>, a Supplier<T> or an IntFunction<T[]>, as newArray and toArray(String[]::new) do
Test o instanceof List<String>Test instanceof List<?>, then check the elements
Overload f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>)Give them different names: both erase to f(List), which is a compile error
Use a primitive as a type argumentBox it, or use IntStream, int[], or a primitive collection library
Catch a generic exception type, or read T in a static contextKeep type parameters on instances and methods

Producer extends, consumer super: wildcards make generic methods accept what they should

Generic types are invariant: a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>, because otherwise you could add a Double to a list of integers. Wildcards win the flexibility back safely. ? extends T means you can read Ts out; ? super T means you can put Ts in. Arrays chose covariance instead, and pay for it at run time.

Pecs.java · extends to read, super to write, and why arrays differ
import java.util.*;

public class Pecs {
    // Producer: we only read from it, so accept any list of a Number subtype.
    static double total(Collection<? extends Number> amounts) {
        double sum = 0;
        for (Number n : amounts) sum += n.doubleValue();
        return sum;
    }

    // Consumer: we only write Integers into it, so accept a list of any supertype.
    static void fillIds(List<? super Integer> sink, int count) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) sink.add(i);
    }

    // The JDK's shape: read from src (extends), write to dest (super).
    static <T> void copyInto(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) {
        for (T item : src) dest.add(item);
    }

    // Comparable<? super T>: works when the comparison is inherited from a superclass.
    static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T largest(List<? extends T> items) {
        T best = items.get(0);
        for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;
        return best;
    }

    static class Amount implements Comparable<Amount> {
        final long cents;
        Amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; }
        @Override public int compareTo(Amount o) { return Long.compare(cents, o.cents); }
        @Override public String toString() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + "(" + cents + ")"; }
    }
    static class Refund extends Amount {               // a Comparable<Amount>, not Comparable<Refund>
        Refund(long cents) { super(cents); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> ints = List.of(1, 2, 3);
        List<Double> doubles = List.of(0.5, 1.5);
        System.out.println("total ints " + total(ints) + ", total doubles " + total(doubles));

        List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
        List<Object> objects = new ArrayList<>();
        fillIds(numbers, 3);
        fillIds(objects, 2);
        copyInto(objects, doubles);
        System.out.println("numbers " + numbers + ", objects " + objects);

        List<Refund> refunds = List.of(new Refund(500), new Refund(1200), new Refund(90));
        System.out.println("largest refund " + largest(refunds));

        // List<Number> wide = ints;                  // does not compile: generics are invariant
        Object[] slots = new String[2];               // arrays are covariant, so this compiles
        try {
            slots[0] = 42;                            // and fails at run time
        } catch (ArrayStoreException e) {
            System.out.println("ArrayStoreException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

total ints 6.0, total doubles 2.0
numbers [1, 2, 3], objects [1, 2, 0.5, 1.5]
largest refund Refund(1200)

Declared asAcceptsYou can
List<Number>Exactly List<Number>Read Numbers, add any Number
List<? extends Number>List<Integer>, List<Double>, …Read Numbers. Add nothing but null.
List<? super Integer>List<Integer>, List<Number>, List<Object>Add Integers. Read only Objects.
List<?>Any listRead Objects, call size, clear

PECS in the JDK

Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src). addAll(Collection<? extends E>). forEach(Consumer<? super T>). Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>). Parameters get wildcards; return types should not, or every caller inherits them.

Why Comparable<? super T>

Refund inherits compareTo from Amount, so it is a Comparable<Amount>, not a Comparable<Refund>. With <T extends Comparable<T>>, largest(refunds) would not compile. That is why Collections.max is declared with ? super T.

Covariant arraysObject[] slots = new String[2] compiles, so every store into an array of references is checked at run time, and the wrong one throws ArrayStoreException. Generics moved that check to compile time. It is also why generic arrays are not allowed.

Generic methods declare their own type parameters, and inference fills them in from the call

A generic method puts <T> before its return type and can be generic in a class that is not. javac infers T from the arguments and from the type the result is assigned to (target typing), which is what lets Comparator.comparing(String::length) compile without a single type written. var uses the same inference, and with a diamond it falls back to Object.

Inference.java · inference, witnesses, var, self-typed builders
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class Inference {
    static <T> T firstOr(List<? extends T> items, T fallback) {
        return items.isEmpty() ? fallback : items.get(0);
    }

    static <K, V extends Comparable<? super V>> Optional<K> keyOfMax(Map<K, V> map) {
        return map.entrySet().stream().max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).map(Map.Entry::getKey);
    }

    // A self-referential bound lets a base builder return the subclass type.
    abstract static class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> {
        final Map<String, String> fields = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        B with(String k, String v) { fields.put(k, v); return self(); }
        abstract B self();
    }
    static final class OrderBuilder extends Builder<OrderBuilder> {
        OrderBuilder express() { fields.put("shipping", "express"); return this; }
        @Override OrderBuilder self() { return this; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = firstOr(List.of(), "none");                 // T inferred as String
        Number n = firstOr(List.of(1, 2), 2.5);                // T inferred from both: Number
        System.out.println(s + " " + n);

        List<String> empty = Collections.<String>emptyList();  // an explicit type witness
        System.out.println("witness " + empty + ", max key " + keyOfMax(Map.of("a", 3, "b", 9)));

        var orders = new ArrayList<String>();                  // var + explicit type argument
        var anything = new ArrayList<>();                      // var + diamond: ArrayList<Object>
        anything.add(1);
        anything.add("two");
        orders.add("ORD-1");
        System.out.println("var with diamond holds " + anything + ", orders " + orders);

        Comparator<String> byLength = Comparator.comparing(String::length);  // target typing
        Function<Integer, String> label = i -> "#" + i;
        System.out.println(byLength.compare("aa", "b") + " " + label.apply(7));

        Iterator<Integer> countdown = new Iterator<>() {        // diamond on anonymous classes: 9
            int left = 3;
            @Override public boolean hasNext() { return left > 0; }
            @Override public Integer next() { return left--; }
        };
        while (countdown.hasNext()) System.out.print(countdown.next() + " ");
        System.out.println();

        var order = new OrderBuilder().with("id", "ORD-7").express().with("note", "gift");
        System.out.println(order.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + order.fields);
    }
}

3 2 1 
OrderBuilder {id=ORD-7, shipping=express, note=gift}
CallWhat javac inferred
firstOr(List.of(), "none")T = String, from the fallback
firstOr(List.of(1, 2), 2.5)T = Number: the most specific type that fits Integer and Double
Collections.<String>emptyList()Nothing: the witness states T. Needed only when there is no target type, such as in a chained call
var anything = new ArrayList<>()ArrayList<Object>, so it accepts 1 and "two"
new OrderBuilder().with(…).express()with returns B = OrderBuilder, so express() is still reachable
var and the diamondvar 10 takes its type from the right-hand side, and a diamond with no target type infers Object. Write the type argument on one side: var orders = new ArrayList<String>().
Self-referential boundsB extends Builder<B> lets a base class return the subclass type from fluent methods. The JDK uses the same shape in Enum<E extends Enum<E>> and Comparable<T> bounds.
When inference gives upLong chains such as Comparator.comparing(o -> o.total()).reversed() lose the target type, because reversed() is called on the result before anything is assigned. Use a method reference, a typed lambda parameter or a witness. The comparator slide shows the fix.

Every unchecked warning is a ClassCastException somewhere else, later

Raw types, unchecked casts and generic varargs all switch the compiler's checks off for one line. The program still compiles. The wrong object then travels until some code that trusts the generic type reads it, and the ClassCastException names that innocent line, not the one that caused it. javac warns about every one of them if you let it.

GenericsTraps.java · heap pollution, three ways
import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.*;

public class GenericsTraps {
    static void legacyAdd(List list) {                    // a raw type: generics switched off
        list.add(42);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    static <T> T unsafeCast(Object o) { return (T) o; }   // erased to Object: checks nothing

    static <T> T[] toArray(T... items) { return items; }  // hands out the varargs array
    static <T> T[] pair(T a, T b) { return toArray(a, b); }   // here T[] is made as Object[]

    @SafeVarargs                                          // safe: it only reads the array
    static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) {
        List<T> list = new ArrayList<>(items.length);
        for (T item : items) list.add(item);
        return list;
    }

    static String brief(ClassCastException e) {           // drop the module details
        return e.getMessage().substring(0, e.getMessage().indexOf(" ("));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ana"));
        legacyAdd(names);                                 // compiles, with a warning
        System.out.println("names holds " + names.size() + " elements: " + names);
        try {
            String second = names.get(1);                 // the failure surfaces here, later
            System.out.println(second);
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println("1 " + brief(e));
        }

        try {
            String text = unsafeCast(LocalTime.NOON);     // javac's checkcast sits on this line
            System.out.println(text);
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println("2 " + brief(e));
        }

        try {
            String[] both = pair("a", "b");
            System.out.println(both.length);
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println("3 " + brief(e));
        }

        System.out.println("4 " + listOf("a", "b") + " " + listOf(1, 2));
    }
}

Make the build enforce itCompile with -Xlint:all -Werror, or set options.compilerArgs in Gradle, and none of these reach main. In legacy code, wrap raw APIs once at the boundary with a checked copy: Collections.checkedList(list, String.class) fails at the bad add instead of the later read.

Checked exceptions are a compiler rule, not a JVM one, and Errors are not yours to catch

Everything throwable descends from Throwable, which splits into Error, meaning the JVM itself is in trouble, and Exception. javac forces every caller to catch or declare an Exception, unless it is a RuntimeException. The JVM never checks this. That is why Kotlin, and Lombok's @SneakyThrows, can throw an IOException that no signature declares.

Hierarchy.java · ancestry, a failing static initialiser, multi-catch
import java.io.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Hierarchy {
    static String chain(Class<?> c) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Class<?> k = c; k != Object.class; k = k.getSuperclass()) names.add(k.getSimpleName());
        return String.join(" < ", names);
    }

    static class TaxTable {                                   // a static initialiser that fails
        static final Map<String, Integer> RATES = load();
        static Map<String, Integer> load() { throw new IllegalStateException("rates file missing"); }
    }

    static int parseQuantity(String raw) throws IOException {
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(raw);
        } catch (NumberFormatException | NullPointerException e) {   // multi-catch: unrelated types
            throw new IOException("bad quantity: " + raw, e);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Class<?> c : List.of(FileNotFoundException.class, InterruptedException.class,
                TimeoutException.class, NumberFormatException.class, ConcurrentModificationException.class,
                UncheckedIOException.class, OutOfMemoryError.class, StackOverflowError.class))
            System.out.println(chain(c));

        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 2; attempt++) {
            try {
                System.out.println(TaxTable.RATES);
            } catch (Throwable t) {
                System.out.println("attempt " + attempt + ": " + t.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + t.getMessage()
                        + (t.getCause() != null ? " / cause: " + t.getCause().getMessage() : ""));
            }
        }

        try {
            parseQuantity("12x");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage() + " <- " + e.getCause());
        }
    }
}

UseFor
CheckedA condition the caller can reasonably handle, at a boundary that can fail: I/O, a remote call, a timeout.
UncheckedProgramming errors (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException) and failures no caller can fix. Spring translates checked JDBC exceptions into unchecked DataAccessExceptions for this reason.
ErrorDo not catch it, except once at the top of a thread to log it. After an OutOfMemoryError the program may be in an inconsistent state.
A failed static initialiser is permanentThe first access throws ExceptionInInitializerError with the real cause. Every later access throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class, and the class stays unusable until the JVM restarts. Recent JDKs attach the first failure as the cause; older ones leave you only the second error, so search the log for the first.
Multi-catchcatch (NumberFormatException | NullPointerException e) 7 handles unrelated types in one block; listing a type together with its subclass is a compile error. Catch blocks are tried in order, so a subclass must come before its superclass, or it does not compile.

try-with-resources closes in reverse order and keeps both failures; finally keeps only the last

When the body throws and then close() throws too, there are two exceptions and one can propagate. try-with-resources 7 propagates the body's, which is the one that explains what happened, and attaches the other with addSuppressed. A hand-written finally lets the close failure replace the original, so the log shows the symptom and loses the cause.

Resources.java · close order, suppressed exceptions, two finally traps
public class Resources {
    static final class Res implements AutoCloseable {
        private final String name;
        private final boolean failOnClose;
        Res(String name, boolean failOnClose) {
            this.name = name;
            this.failOnClose = failOnClose;
            System.out.println("open  " + name);
        }
        @Override public void close() {
            System.out.println("close " + name);
            if (failOnClose) throw new IllegalStateException("close " + name + " failed");
        }
    }

    static void withResources() {
        try (Res conn = new Res("connection", false);
             Res stmt = new Res("statement", true)) {        // closed first: reverse order
            System.out.println("body  uses " + conn.name + " and " + stmt.name);
            throw new RuntimeException("query failed");
        }
    }

    static void withFinally() {                               // the pre-Java 7 way
        Res stmt = new Res("statement", true);
        try {
            throw new RuntimeException("query failed");
        } finally {
            stmt.close();                                     // its exception replaces the real one
        }
    }

    static int returnsFromFinally() {
        try {
            throw new IllegalStateException("lost forever");
        } finally {
            return -1;                                        // discards the exception
        }
    }

    static String finallyOnReturn() {
        try {
            return "from try";
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally runs before the return completes");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            withResources();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
            for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) System.out.println("  suppressed: " + s.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            withFinally();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage() + " (the query failure is gone)");
        }
        System.out.println("returnsFromFinally() = " + returnsFromFinally());
        System.out.println(finallyOnReturn());
    }
}

The rules

  • Resources close in reverse order of opening, after the body and before that try's own catch and finally run.
  • A resource whose constructor threw was never opened, so it is not closed; the ones opened before it are.
  • An effectively final variable can be the resource: try (conn) 9.
  • finally runs on normal exit, on exceptions and on return. It does not run on System.exit, a JVM crash or kill -9.
return in finallyA return, break or throw in finally throws away whatever exception was in flight. returnsFromFinally returned -1, and nobody ever learns about the failure. javac's [finally] lint is the only warning you get.
Write close() to be idempotentCloseable.close must do nothing if called twice; AutoCloseable.close is only encouraged to. Wrappers often close what they wrap, so the inner resource can be closed twice.
Everything that holds a handleStreams, readers, JDBC connections and statements, Files.lines, ExecutorService 19, HttpClient 21. A leak of any of them shows up as "too many open files" or an exhausted pool, hours later: see resource and memory bugs.

A good exception carries a cause, the data to act on, and no more cost than it needs

Exceptions cross layers: a SQLException from the repository becomes a domain failure in the service, and an HTTP status at the edge. Each translation must keep the cause, or the stack trace that explains the incident stops at the layer that translated it. Creating an exception is also not free: filling in the stack trace costs far more than the allocation.

ExceptionDesign.java · translation, lost causes, interrupts, cost
import java.io.*;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class ExceptionDesign {
    // A domain exception: unchecked, with the data a caller needs, and always a cause.
    static class PaymentDeclinedException extends RuntimeException {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private final String orderId;
        PaymentDeclinedException(String orderId, String reason, Throwable cause) {
            super("payment declined for " + orderId + ": " + reason, cause);
            this.orderId = orderId;
        }
        String orderId() { return orderId; }
    }

    // An exception used for flow control: no stack trace to capture.
    static class OutOfStock extends RuntimeException {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        OutOfStock(String sku) { super(sku, null, false, false); }   // no suppression, no trace
    }

    static void gatewayCall() throws SQLException { throw new SQLException("connection reset", "08S01"); }

    static void chargeKeepingCause(String orderId) {
        try {
            gatewayCall();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new PaymentDeclinedException(orderId, "gateway unavailable", e);   // translate, keep cause
        }
    }

    static void chargeLosingCause() {
        try {
            gatewayCall();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage());       // the original stack trace is gone
        }
    }

    static void waitForStock() {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(10_000);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();               // restore the flag before translating
            throw new IllegalStateException("interrupted while waiting for stock", e);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try {
            chargeKeepingCause("ORD-9");
        } catch (PaymentDeclinedException e) {
            var trace = new StringWriter();
            e.printStackTrace(new PrintWriter(trace));
            trace.toString().lines().filter(l -> !l.contains("ExceptionDesign.main")).forEach(System.out::println);
        }
        try {
            chargeLosingCause();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("lost: " + e + ", cause " + e.getCause());
        }

        Thread waiter = new Thread(ExceptionDesign::waitForStock);
        waiter.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> System.out.println(
                "uncaught in " + t.getName() + ": " + e.getMessage() + ", interrupted flag restored: " + t.isInterrupted()));
        waiter.setName("stock-waiter");
        waiter.start();
        waiter.interrupt();
        waiter.join();

        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) new IllegalStateException("x");
        long withTrace = System.nanoTime() - t0;
        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) new OutOfStock("x");
        long without = System.nanoTime() - t0;
        System.out.printf("1M exceptions: %d ms with stack traces, %d ms without (one run)%n",
                withTrace / 1_000_000, without / 1_000_000);
    }
}

	at ExceptionDesign.gatewayCall(ExceptionDesign.java:22)

	... 1 more

DoInstead of
Translate at a boundary, passing the cause: new X(msg, e)new X(e.getMessage()): "cause null" above, and no trace to follow
Put identifiers in the message and in fields: orderId()"Payment failed", with no way to find which one
Restore the flag before translating InterruptedExceptionSwallowing it, so the thread keeps running after a shutdown request
Log once, where the exception is handledLog and rethrow, so the same failure appears five times
Catch the specific type you can handlecatch (Exception e) {}, which hides the next bug too
Exceptions as control flowCapturing a stack trace walks the whole stack: more than ten times the cost of the object itself here. For an expected outcome such as out of stock, return a result type (a sealed Result, an Optional), or use the four-argument constructor with writableStackTrace = false, as OutOfStock does.
Checked or unchecked for domain errorsUnchecked, as most modern Java code and every Spring API does, with the class name stating the business meaning. A checked exception in a widely used signature forces every caller, and every lambda that calls it, to deal with it.
At the edgeMap exception types to one HTTP error body in one place, not in every controller. The reference deck shows the shape: one error shape. Helpful NullPointerException messages 14 name the null expression for free.

Pick the collection by the operation you do most, then by the order you need

The interfaces say what a collection promises: List keeps positions, Set rejects duplicates, Queue hands out elements in some order, Map looks up by key. The implementation decides what each operation costs. In practice three classes cover most code: ArrayList, HashMap and ArrayDeque. The others earn their place with one specific property.

Iterable └─ Collection ├─ List ArrayList, LinkedList, CopyOnWriteArrayList ├─ Set HashSet, LinkedHashSet, EnumSet │ └─ SortedSet → NavigableSet TreeSet, ConcurrentSkipListSet └─ Queue PriorityQueue, the BlockingQueues └─ Deque ArrayDeque, LinkedList, ConcurrentLinkedDeque Map HashMap, LinkedHashMap, EnumMap, IdentityHashMap, │ WeakHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap └─ SortedMap → NavigableMap TreeMap, ConcurrentSkipListMap // Java 21: SequencedCollection sits above List, Deque, LinkedHashSet and // SortedSet; SequencedMap above LinkedHashMap and SortedMap.
How to chooseNeed positions or duplicates: ArrayList. Lookups by key: HashMap, or HashSet for membership. Insertion order on iteration: the Linked variants. Sorted order or range queries: TreeMap, TreeSet. Stack, queue or both ends: ArrayDeque. Smallest or largest first: PriorityQueue. Enum keys: EnumMap, EnumSet. Shared between threads: the concurrent ones, on choosing a concurrency tool.
ClassOrderCost of the main operationsNulls
ArrayListIndexget(i) O(1); add at end amortised O(1); insert, remove, contains O(n)Yes
LinkedListIndexEnds O(1); get(i) O(n), and slow even thenYes
ArrayDequeInsertionBoth ends O(1)No
PriorityQueueHeappeek O(1); offer, poll O(log n); contains O(n)No
HashMap, HashSetNoneO(1) on average; a crowded bin falls back to a treeOne null key
LinkedHashMap, LinkedHashSetInsertion, or accessO(1), plus a linked list through the entriesYes
TreeMap, TreeSetSortedO(log n), with floor, ceiling and range viewsNot as keys
EnumMap, EnumSetOrdinalO(1): an array, or a bit vectorNot as keys
ConcurrentHashMapNoneO(1); thread-safe without a global lockNo
CopyOnWriteArrayListIndexReads O(1) and lock-free; each write copies the arrayYes
Complexity is only half the costAn O(1) HashMap lookup with a slow hashCode, or an O(n) contains on a list inside a loop, decides more performance reviews than the table above. The DSA tab collects the library calls whose cost surprises people: hidden costs in the Java library.

ArrayList grows by half when full; LinkedList pays 24 bytes and a pointer chase per element

An ArrayList is an array with spare room. When it fills, it copies everything into an array 1.5 times larger, so appends are O(1) amortised. A LinkedList allocates a node per element, with links both ways. The textbook says linked lists win at inserts. On a modern CPU the array wins almost everything, because it is contiguous and the nodes are scattered across the heap.

ListGrowth.java · reads elementData by reflection, counts bytes per thread
// Run with: java --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED ListGrowth.java
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.util.*;

public class ListGrowth {
    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
    static Field elementData;

    static int capacity(ArrayList<?> list) throws IllegalAccessException {
        return ((Object[]) elementData.get(list)).length;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        elementData = ArrayList.class.getDeclaredField("elementData");
        elementData.setAccessible(true);

        var list = new ArrayList<Integer>();
        var growth = new StringBuilder("capacity " + capacity(list));
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            int before = capacity(list);
            list.add(i);
            if (capacity(list) != before) growth.append(" -> ").append(capacity(list));
        }
        System.out.println(growth + " (size " + list.size() + ")");
        list.trimToSize();
        System.out.println("after trimToSize: " + capacity(list));

        int n = 1_000_000;
        Integer[] boxes = new Integer[n];                   // box once, outside the measurements
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) boxes[i] = i + 1_000;

        long t = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        var grown = new ArrayList<Integer>();
        for (Integer b : boxes) grown.add(b);
        long grownBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - t;

        t = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        var presized = new ArrayList<Integer>(n);
        for (Integer b : boxes) presized.add(b);
        long presizedBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - t;

        t = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        var linked = new LinkedList<Integer>();
        for (Integer b : boxes) linked.add(b);
        long linkedBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - t;

        System.out.printf("bytes allocated per element: ArrayList grown %.1f, presized %.1f, LinkedList %.1f%n",
                grownBytes / (double) n, presizedBytes / (double) n, linkedBytes / (double) n);

        long sum = 0;
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sum += presized.get(n / 2);
        long arrayNs = System.nanoTime() - t0;
        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sum += linked.get(n / 2);
        long linkedNs = System.nanoTime() - t0;
        System.out.printf("1,000 x get(n/2): ArrayList %.2f ms, LinkedList %.0f ms (one run, sum %d)%n",
                arrayNs / 1e6, linkedNs / 1e6, sum);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · ListGrowth.java · the timings vary by run
capacity 0 -> 10 -> 15 -> 22 -> 33 -> 49 -> 73 -> 109 (size 100)
after trimToSize: 100
bytes allocated per element: ArrayList grown 14.6, presized 4.0, LinkedList 24.0
1,000 x get(n/2): ArrayList 0.17 ms, LinkedList 1268 ms (one run, sum 1002000000)
LineWhy
0 → 10 → 15 → 22A new list shares one empty array and allocates 10 slots on the first add. Each growth is old + old/2.
grown 14.6Each growth copies into a new array and discards the old one. The live list costs 4 to 6 bytes per element; the garbage costs the rest.
presized 4.0One reference per element, 4 bytes with compressed pointers. new ArrayList<>(n) when you know n.
LinkedList 24.0One node per element: a 12-byte object header and three 4-byte references (item, next, prev).
get(n/2)get(n/2) walks 500,000 nodes per call, from the nearer end, missing the cache at almost every step.
Default to ArrayListIteration, random access and appends are all fast, and the list itself needs a quarter or less of a linked list's memory. Even inserting into the middle is a System.arraycopy that moves bytes at memory speed, which beats walking to the node for most sizes.
Not a queue, eitherRemoving from the front of an ArrayList shifts every element: O(n). For a queue or a stack use ArrayDeque, which is a circular array and beats LinkedList at both ends too.
The one case for LinkedListMany inserts and removals in the middle of a long list, through a ListIterator you already hold. It is rare enough that Joshua Bloch, who wrote LinkedList, has said he never uses it.

A HashMap is an array of buckets, and the key's hash picks one bucket to search

put and get do the same three steps. Call hashCode(). Mix the high 16 bits into the low 16. Keep the low bits as the array index. Then only that one bucket is searched, comparing the stored hash first and calling equals only when the hashes match. That is why a lookup is O(1) on average, and why equals and hashCode must agree.

HashMapPeek.java · the index arithmetic, then the table itself
// Run with: java --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED HashMapPeek.java
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.util.*;

public class HashMapPeek {
    static Field table, next, key;

    static int spread(Object k) {                       // what HashMap.hash(key) computes
        if (k == null) return 0;
        int h = k.hashCode();
        return h ^ (h >>> 16);                          // fold the high bits into the low ones
    }

    static void dump(HashMap<?, ?> map) throws Exception {
        Object[] tab = (Object[]) table.get(map);
        System.out.println("table length " + tab.length + ", size " + map.size());
        for (int i = 0; i < tab.length; i++) {
            if (tab[i] == null) continue;
            List<Object> keys = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Object node = tab[i]; node != null; node = next.get(node)) keys.add(key.get(node));
            System.out.println("  bucket " + String.format("%2d", i) + ": " + keys);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        table = HashMap.class.getDeclaredField("table");
        table.setAccessible(true);
        Class<?> node = Class.forName("java.util.HashMap$Node");
        next = node.getDeclaredField("next");
        next.setAccessible(true);
        key = node.getDeclaredField("key");
        key.setAccessible(true);

        String k = "SKU-17";
        int h = k.hashCode();
        System.out.printf("hashCode     %32s  (%d)%n", Integer.toBinaryString(h), h);
        System.out.printf("h >>> 16     %32s%n", Integer.toBinaryString(h >>> 16));
        System.out.printf("spread       %32s%n", Integer.toBinaryString(spread(k)));
        System.out.printf("& (16 - 1)   %32s  -> bucket %d%n", Integer.toBinaryString(spread(k) & 15), spread(k) & 15);

        var stock = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
        for (String s : List.of("SKU-17", "apple", "banana", "cherry", "Aa", "BB", "plum"))
            stock.put(s, s.length());
        stock.put(null, 0);                             // allowed, always bucket 0
        dump(stock);
        System.out.println("iteration order: " + stock.keySet());
    }
}

hashCode     10010001111010100111000011110110  (-1846906634)
h >>> 16                     1001000111101010
spread       10010001111010101110000100011100
& (16 - 1)                               1100  -> bucket 12
table length 16, size 8
  bucket  0: [banana, Aa, BB, plum, null]
  bucket  1: [apple, cherry]
  bucket 12: [SKU-17]
iteration order: [banana, Aa, BB, plum, null, apple, cherry, SKU-17]
Design choiceWhy
Power-of-two tablehash & (n - 1) is a single AND, where hash % n is a division.
Spreading the hashThe mask keeps only the low bits. Keys whose hash codes differ only in high bits, such as many Float values, would all collide without it.
Hash stored in the nodeComparing two ints rejects most keys in a bucket before any equals call, and a resize never calls hashCode again.
Null keyHashes to 0, so it always lives in bucket 0. Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap reject it.
Iteration order is bucket orderThe keys came out as bucket 0, then 1, then 12: neither insertion order nor sorted, and it changes when the table resizes, on the next slide. Code that depends on HashMap order breaks on a JDK upgrade or a larger data set.

The table doubles at 75% full, and a crowded bucket turns into a red-black tree

When the size passes capacity × 0.75, the table doubles and every node moves to either its old index or old index + old capacity, decided by one bit of the stored hash. When one bucket collects too many keys, Java 8 and later convert it from a linked list into a red-black tree, so even a flood of colliding keys costs O(log n) per lookup instead of O(n). The demo watches both happen.

HashMapResize.java · normal growth, then eleven keys with one hash code
// Run with: java --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED HashMapResize.java
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.util.*;

public class HashMapResize {
    static Field table;

    static int length(HashMap<?, ?> map) throws IllegalAccessException {
        Object[] tab = (Object[]) table.get(map);
        return tab == null ? 0 : tab.length;
    }

    // Every key collides: the worst case that treeification exists for.
    record BadKey(int id) implements Comparable<BadKey> {
        @Override public int hashCode() { return 42; }
        @Override public int compareTo(BadKey o) { return Integer.compare(id, o.id); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        table = HashMap.class.getDeclaredField("table");
        table.setAccessible(true);

        var map = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
        System.out.println("new HashMap: table length " + length(map) + " (allocated on first put)");
        List<String> orderAt12 = null;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 25; i++) {
            int before = length(map);
            map.put("order-" + i, i);
            if (i == 12) orderAt12 = new ArrayList<>(map.keySet()).subList(0, 6);
            if (length(map) != before) System.out.println("put #" + i + ": table " + before + " -> " + length(map));
        }
        System.out.println("first keys at size 12: " + orderAt12);
        System.out.println("first keys at size 25: " + new ArrayList<>(map.keySet()).subList(0, 6));

        var bad = new HashMap<BadKey, Integer>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 11; i++) {
            int before = length(bad);
            bad.put(new BadKey(i), i);
            Object[] tab = (Object[]) table.get(bad);
            Object bin = tab[42 & (tab.length - 1)];
            System.out.println("colliding key " + String.format("%2d", i) + ": table " + before + " -> " + tab.length
                    + ", bin is a " + bin.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        var sized = new HashMap<String, Integer>(1_000);
        sized.put("x", 1);
        System.out.println("new HashMap<>(1_000): table length " + length(sized)
                + "; HashMap.newHashMap(1_000): " + length(put(HashMap.newHashMap(1_000))));
    }

    static HashMap<String, Integer> put(HashMap<String, Integer> m) { m.put("x", 1); return m; }
}
