Constant in HashMapValueSeen above
Default capacity, load factor16, 0.75The 13th put passes 16 × 0.75 = 12 and doubles the table; the 25th passes 24.
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD8Adding a 9th key to a bin with 8 asks for a tree.
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY64Below 64 slots, resizing is tried first: keys 9 and 10 doubled the table instead. At 64, key 11 made the tree.
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD6A tree bin split by a resize back to 6 nodes or fewer becomes a list again.
The capacity argument is not a sizenew HashMap<>(1_000) makes 1,024 slots with a threshold of 768, so it still resizes at the 769th entry. HashMap.newHashMap(1_000) 19 sizes the table for 1,000 entries. Before 19, pass (int) (n / 0.75f) + 1.
Why trees, and their limitsTreeification arrived in Java 8 (JEP 180) to blunt hash-flooding attacks, where crafted keys all collide. Tree bins order nodes by hash, then by compareTo if the keys are Comparable. Colliding keys that are not comparable can still need a search of both subtrees. A TreeNode is about twice the size of a Node.
Resizes are cheap, but not freeEach resize allocates a new table and walks every node, but never calls hashCode again: the stored hash decides the new index. Under concurrent writes a plain HashMap resize can lose entries. Java 7's head insertion could even create a cycle that spun a CPU forever. Use ConcurrentHashMap.

LinkedHashMap remembers order; TreeMap keeps keys sorted and answers range questions

LinkedHashMap is a HashMap with a doubly linked list threaded through its entries, in insertion order or, if you ask, access order. That second mode plus one overridden method is an LRU cache. TreeMap is a red-black tree: every operation is O(log n), and in exchange it can find the nearest key, the first or last entry, or a whole range.

OrderedMaps.java · three orders, an LRU cache, price bands by weight
import java.util.*;

public class OrderedMaps {
    // An LRU cache in eight lines: access order plus an eviction hook.
    static class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private final int capacity;
        LruCache(int capacity) {
            super(16, 0.75f, true);                       // true = access order, not insertion
            this.capacity = capacity;
        }
        @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> skus = List.of("tea", "apple", "milk", "bread", "eggs");
        Map<String, Integer> hash = new HashMap<>(), linked = new LinkedHashMap<>(), tree = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String s : skus) { hash.put(s, s.length()); linked.put(s, s.length()); tree.put(s, s.length()); }
        System.out.println("HashMap       " + hash.keySet());
        System.out.println("LinkedHashMap " + linked.keySet() + "  insertion order");
        System.out.println("TreeMap       " + tree.keySet() + "  sorted");

        var cache = new LruCache<String, String>(3);
        cache.put("a", "A");
        cache.put("b", "B");
        cache.put("c", "C");
        cache.get("a");                                   // a becomes the most recently used
        cache.put("d", "D");                              // evicts the eldest: b
        System.out.println("LRU after get(a), put(d): " + cache.keySet());

        // Shipping price by weight band: the band starts at the key, in kg.
        NavigableMap<Double, Integer> bands = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0.0, 4, 2.0, 7, 5.0, 12, 10.0, 20, 30.0, 45));
        for (double kg : new double[] {0.4, 2.0, 7.5, 31})
            System.out.println(kg + " kg -> band " + bands.floorKey(kg) + " costs " + bands.floorEntry(kg).getValue());
        System.out.println("ceilingKey(7.5) " + bands.ceilingKey(7.5) + ", higherKey(10.0) " + bands.higherKey(10.0)
                + ", lowerKey(0.0) " + bands.lowerKey(0.0));
        System.out.println("headMap(5.0) " + bands.headMap(5.0) + ", tailMap(10.0, true) " + bands.tailMap(10.0, true));
        System.out.println("subMap(2.0, 10.0) " + bands.subMap(2.0, 10.0) + ", descending " + bands.descendingKeySet());
        System.out.println("pollFirstEntry " + bands.pollFirstEntry() + ", now first " + bands.firstKey());
    }
}

Access order makes get a writeIn access-order mode every get moves an entry, so it is a structural change. Iterating while calling get throws ConcurrentModificationException, and two threads that only read can still corrupt the list. The thread-safe version is on the LLD tab's LRU cache.
floorEntry is a lookup tableTax brackets, shipping bands, rate cards, time-based price lists: store each band's start as a key and floorEntry(x) finds the band for any x in O(log n). That replaces a chain of ifs that someone has to keep in order.
Views write throughheadMap, tailMap and subMap are views: removing from one removes from the map, and putting a key outside the range throws IllegalArgumentException: key out of range. For a sorted map shared between threads, use ConcurrentSkipListMap.

A TreeSet decides equality with compareTo, so a careless comparator deletes data

HashSet is a HashMap whose values are all one shared dummy object, so it uses hashCode and equals. TreeSet is a TreeMap, and it never calls equals: two elements that compare as 0 are the same element. Sort by length and every word of the same length is a duplicate.

SetsDemo.java · three orders, two vanishing acts, BigDecimal
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.*;

public class SetsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> fruit = List.of("pear", "Apple", "fig", "apple", "plum", "kiwi");
        System.out.println("HashSet       " + new HashSet<>(fruit));
        System.out.println("LinkedHashSet " + new LinkedHashSet<>(fruit));
        System.out.println("TreeSet       " + new TreeSet<>(fruit) + "  (uppercase sorts first)");

        Set<String> byLength = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(String::length));
        byLength.addAll(fruit);
        System.out.println("TreeSet by length          " + byLength + "  <- three fruits vanished");
        Set<String> byLengthThenName = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(String::length)
                .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        byLengthThenName.addAll(fruit);
        System.out.println("by length, then by name    " + byLengthThenName);

        Set<String> ignoreCase = new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
        ignoreCase.addAll(fruit);
        Set<String> exact = new HashSet<>(fruit);
        System.out.println("case-insensitive TreeSet   " + ignoreCase + ", contains(\"APPLE\") " + ignoreCase.contains("APPLE")
                + "; HashSet contains(\"APPLE\") " + exact.contains("APPLE"));

        List<BigDecimal> prices = List.of(new BigDecimal("2.0"), new BigDecimal("2.00"));
        System.out.println("BigDecimal 2.0 and 2.00: HashSet size " + new HashSet<>(prices).size()
                + ", TreeSet size " + new TreeSet<>(prices).size()
                + "  (equals " + prices.get(0).equals(prices.get(1)) + ", compareTo " + prices.get(0).compareTo(prices.get(1)) + ")");

        try {
            Set.of("a", "b", "a");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Set.of with a duplicate: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Three fruits vanishedpear, plum and kiwi all have four letters, so to the length comparator they are one element: the first is kept and the others are dropped without an error. Always break ties down to a total order: .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()).
BigDecimal disagrees with itself2.0 and 2.00 have different scales, so equals is false while compareTo is 0. The same two prices make a HashSet of 2 and a TreeSet of 1. Normalise with stripTrailingZeros(), or choose one collection on purpose.
When inconsistency is the pointA TreeSet with String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER is a case-insensitive set by design: it found "APPLE" where the HashSet did not. That is legitimate, but it breaks the Set contract, so do not pass it to code that expects equals semantics.

ArrayDeque is the stack and the queue; PriorityQueue is a heap that only looks sorted at the top

ArrayDeque is a circular array with O(1) operations at both ends, which makes it the right stack, the right FIFO queue and the right double-ended queue. PriorityQueue is a binary heap stored in an array: the smallest element (by its comparator) is always at the head, while the rest are only partly ordered. Every queue method comes in two forms, one that throws and one that returns a special value.

Queues.java · stacks, FIFO, heaps, top-k, the two method families
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;

public class Queues {
    record Task(String name, int priority) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        stack.push("a"); stack.push("b"); stack.push("c");
        Stack<String> legacy = new Stack<>();
        legacy.push("a"); legacy.push("b"); legacy.push("c");
        System.out.println("ArrayDeque as stack " + stack + ", pop " + stack.pop());
        System.out.println("java.util.Stack     " + legacy + ", pop " + legacy.pop() + "  (iterates bottom first)");

        Queue<String> fifo = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of("first", "second", "third"));
        System.out.println("queue poll " + fifo.poll() + ", peek " + fifo.peek() + ", left " + fifo);

        PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(7, 3, 9, 1, 4, 8));
        System.out.print("PriorityQueue toString " + heap + ", poll order");
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) System.out.print(" " + heap.poll());
        System.out.println();

        int k = 3;
        PriorityQueue<Integer> topK = new PriorityQueue<>();       // a min-heap holding the k largest
        for (int n : new int[] {5, 12, 3, 41, 8, 27, 19}) {
            topK.offer(n);
            if (topK.size() > k) topK.poll();                      // drop the smallest
        }
        List<Integer> largest = new ArrayList<>(topK);
        largest.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        System.out.println("top 3 " + largest);

        PriorityQueue<Task> work = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority).reversed()
                .thenComparing(Task::name));
        work.addAll(List.of(new Task("email", 1), new Task("refund", 5), new Task("invoice", 5), new Task("audit", 3)));
        System.out.print("by priority:");
        while (!work.isEmpty()) System.out.print(" " + work.poll().name());
        System.out.println();

        Queue<String> empty = new ArrayDeque<>();
        System.out.println("empty: poll " + empty.poll() + ", peek " + empty.peek());
        try { empty.remove(); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("empty: remove -> NoSuchElementException"); }
        try { empty.offer(null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("ArrayDeque.offer(null) -> NullPointerException"); }

        Queue<String> bounded = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
        bounded.add("x");
        System.out.println("full: offer " + bounded.offer("y"));
        try { bounded.add("y"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("full: add -> " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}

java.util.StackIt extends Vector, so every call takes a lock, and it inherits get(i) and add(i, e), which let code reach past the top. It even iterates bottom first, so its toString is the reverse of ArrayDeque's. Use Deque<E> stack = new ArrayDeque<>().
The heap is not sortedtoString printed [1, 3, 8, 7, 4, 9]: the array in heap order, where each parent is no larger than its children. Only repeated poll gives sorted order, at O(log n) each. Iterating a PriorityQueue, or streaming it, gives the heap order.
Top k in O(n log k)Keep a min-heap of size k and evict its smallest whenever it overflows; what remains are the k largest. Interviewers ask for it constantly: heap and top-k in the DSA tab has the problems. ArrayDeque rejects null, because poll uses null to mean empty.

Change a collection while iterating it and the iterator throws, except when it silently skips

Every non-concurrent collection counts its structural changes in a field called modCount. An iterator remembers the count it started with and checks it on each next(); a mismatch throws ConcurrentModificationException. The name misleads: one thread is enough. And the check is best-effort, as the second case below shows.

FailFast.java · what throws, what silently skips, and the safe ways
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FailFast {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> basket = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea", "milk", "sugar", "eggs"));
        try {
            for (String item : basket)
                if (item.equals("milk")) basket.remove(item);           // structural change mid-loop
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
            System.out.println("remove(\"milk\") in for-each: ConcurrentModificationException");
        }

        List<String> quiet = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea", "milk", "sugar", "eggs"));
        List<String> visited = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String item : quiet) {
            visited.add(item);
            if (item.equals("sugar")) quiet.remove(item);              // the second-to-last element
        }
        System.out.println("remove(\"sugar\"): no exception, visited " + visited + ", left " + quiet);

        List<String> viaIterator = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea", "milk", "sugar", "eggs"));
        for (Iterator<String> it = viaIterator.iterator(); it.hasNext(); )
            if (it.next().startsWith("s")) it.remove();                // the iterator's own remove
        List<String> viaRemoveIf = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea", "milk", "sugar", "eggs"));
        viaRemoveIf.removeIf(s -> s.length() == 3);
        System.out.println("Iterator.remove " + viaIterator + ", removeIf " + viaRemoveIf);

        ListIterator<String> li = viaIterator.listIterator();
        while (li.hasNext()) {
            String s = li.next();
            li.set(s.toUpperCase());
            if (s.equals("tea")) li.add("lemon");                      // insert after the current one
        }
        System.out.println("ListIterator set/add " + viaIterator);

        Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("tea", 0, "milk", 4, "eggs", 0));
        try {
            for (String sku : stock.keySet()) if (stock.get(sku) == 0) stock.remove(sku);
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
            System.out.println("HashMap remove during keySet loop: ConcurrentModificationException");
        }
        stock.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);
        System.out.println("entrySet().removeIf " + stock);

        Map<String, Integer> live = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2));
        for (String key : live.keySet()) live.put(key + key, 0);       // weakly consistent: no exception
        System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap put during iteration: size " + live.size());

        List<String> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("audit", "email"));
        int seen = 0;
        for (String l : listeners) { listeners.add(l + "-copy"); seen++; }   // iterates a snapshot
        System.out.println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: iterated " + seen + ", now holds " + listeners.size());
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · FailFast.java
remove("milk") in for-each: ConcurrentModificationException
remove("sugar"): no exception, visited [tea, milk, sugar], left [tea, milk, eggs]
Iterator.remove [tea, milk, eggs], removeIf [milk, sugar, eggs]
ListIterator set/add [TEA, lemon, MILK, EGGS]
HashMap remove during keySet loop: ConcurrentModificationException
entrySet().removeIf {milk=4}
ConcurrentHashMap put during iteration: size 4
CopyOnWriteArrayList: iterated 2, now holds 4
Why "sugar" did not throwFor-each calls hasNext() before every next(), and ArrayList.hasNext() is just cursor != size. Removing the second-to-last element makes size 3 just as cursor reaches 3, so the loop ends. next(), which does the check, is never called, and eggs is never visited. No exception, wrong result.
To change while iteratingUse
Remove matching elementsremoveIf 8, or Iterator.remove()
Replace or insert in a listListIterator.set, add; or replaceAll
Remove map entriesentrySet().removeIf, or computeIfPresent returning null
Add to what you iterateCollect into a new list, then addAll after the loop
Fail-fast is not a safety netThe Javadoc calls the exception best-effort: use it to find bugs, never to rely on for correctness. Between threads a plain collection may not throw at all, and give wrong data or corrupt itself instead. That needs a concurrent collection or a lock, not an iterator check.
Weakly consistent and snapshot iteratorsConcurrentHashMap's iterators never throw and may or may not show changes made during the loop: it grew to 4 entries while being iterated. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates the array as it was when the loop started, so it saw 2 elements and the list ended with 4.

An unmodifiable view still changes underneath you; an immutable copy never does

Collections.unmodifiableList wraps a list and blocks writes through the wrapper only: the owner of the original can still change it, and the view shows every change. List.of and List.copyOf build lists that nobody can change. They also reject null, which surprises people the first time contains(null) throws. Java 21 gave the ordered collections one shared interface for their ends.

Unmodifiable.java · views, copies, their classes, the sequenced methods
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Unmodifiable {
    static String name(Object o) { return o.getClass().getName().replace("java.util.", ""); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> source = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
        List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
        List<String> copy = List.copyOf(source);
        source.add("c");
        System.out.println("after source.add(c): view " + view + ", copy " + copy);
        try { view.add("x"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("view.add -> UnsupportedOperationException"); }

        try { List.of("x", null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("List.of(\"x\", null) -> NullPointerException"); }
        try { List.of("x").contains(null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("List.of(\"x\").contains(null) -> NullPointerException"); }
        System.out.println("Stream.toList keeps nulls: " + Stream.of("x", null).toList());

        System.out.println("List.of(1, 2)               " + name(List.of(1, 2)));
        System.out.println("List.of(1, 2, 3)            " + name(List.of(1, 2, 3)));
        System.out.println("Stream.toList()             " + name(Stream.of(1).toList()));
        System.out.println("Collectors.toList()         " + name(Stream.of(1).collect(Collectors.toList())) + " (mutable, but not promised)");
        System.out.println("Collections.unmodifiableList " + name(view));
        List<Integer> fixed = List.of(1, 2, 3);
        System.out.println("List.copyOf of an immutable list is the same object: " + (List.copyOf(fixed) == fixed));

        List<String> steps = new ArrayList<>(List.of("placed", "paid", "shipped"));
        System.out.println("getFirst " + steps.getFirst() + ", getLast " + steps.getLast() + ", reversed " + steps.reversed());
        steps.reversed().addFirst("delivered");                       // a view: writes go to steps
        steps.addFirst("created");
        System.out.println("after reversed().addFirst and addFirst: " + steps);

        LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> recent = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        recent.put("b", 2);
        recent.put("c", 3);
        recent.putFirst("a", 1);
        System.out.println("LinkedHashMap " + recent + ", firstEntry " + recent.firstEntry()
                + ", pollLastEntry " + recent.pollLastEntry() + ", reversed keys " + recent.sequencedKeySet().reversed());
        try { List.of().getFirst(); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("List.of().getFirst() -> NoSuchElementException"); }
    }
}

reversed() is a viewWrites through it go to the original: steps.reversed().addFirst("delivered") appended to steps. On an empty collection, getFirst throws NoSuchElementException rather than returning null.
Set.of and Map.of orderTheir iteration order is randomised once per JVM run, on purpose, so that no code comes to depend on it. A test that passes on your machine and fails in CI with the same data is often this.

The utility classes save a loop each, and each one has a trap that comes up in interviews

Arrays and Collections hold the sorting, searching, copying and wrapping methods. Most are one-liners you should reach for instead of writing loops. A few behave in ways that look like bugs until you know the rule: Arrays.asList on an int[], a binary search on unsorted data, and equals on arrays.

Utilities.java · asList, stable sorting, binary search, array equality
import java.util.*;

public class Utilities {
    record Order(String id, String status, int day) {
        @Override public String toString() { return id + "/" + status + "/d" + day; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] ids = {3, 1, 2};
        List<int[]> oops = Arrays.asList(ids);                  // one element: the int[] itself
        List<Integer> boxed = Arrays.stream(ids).boxed().toList();
        System.out.println("Arrays.asList(int[]) size " + oops.size() + "; boxed " + boxed);

        String[] codes = {"b", "a", "c"};
        List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList(codes);              // fixed-size, backed by the array
        fixed.set(0, "z");
        System.out.println("set through the list changed the array: " + Arrays.toString(codes));
        try { fixed.add("d"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("Arrays.asList(...).add -> UnsupportedOperationException"); }

        List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Order("o1", "PAID", 3), new Order("o2", "NEW", 1),
                new Order("o3", "PAID", 1), new Order("o4", "NEW", 2), new Order("o5", "PAID", 2)));
        orders.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Order::day));
        orders.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::status));        // stable: day order kept within a status
        System.out.println("stable sort by status after day " + orders);

        int[] sorted = {10, 20, 30, 40};
        System.out.println("binarySearch 30 -> " + Arrays.binarySearch(sorted, 30)
                + ", 25 -> " + Arrays.binarySearch(sorted, 25) + " (= -(insertion point 2) - 1)");
        int[] unsorted = {40, 10, 30, 20};
        System.out.println("binarySearch on unsorted data for 40 -> " + Arrays.binarySearch(unsorted, 40));

        int[] a = {1, 2}, b = {1, 2};
        System.out.println("a == b " + (a == b) + ", a.equals(b) " + a.equals(b) + ", Arrays.equals " + Arrays.equals(a, b));
        System.out.println("2-D toString " + Arrays.toString(new int[][] {{1}, {2}}).replaceAll("@[0-9a-f]+", "@…")
                + ", deepToString " + Arrays.deepToString(new int[][] {{1}, {2}}));

        List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "x", "z", "x"));
        Collections.shuffle(tags, new Random(42));               // seeded: the same order every run
        System.out.println("frequency(x) " + Collections.frequency(tags, "x") + ", nCopies " + Collections.nCopies(3, "-")
                + ", shuffled " + tags + ", max " + Collections.max(tags) + ", disjoint " + Collections.disjoint(tags, List.of("q")));

        List<String> withNulls = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("b", null, "a"));
        withNulls.sort(Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println("nullsFirst " + withNulls);
    }
}

MethodThe rule
Arrays.asList(T...)A fixed-size list backed by the array: set writes through, add and remove throw. On an int[], T is int[], so you get a list of one array.
Arrays.sortPrimitives: dual-pivot quicksort. Objects: TimSort, which is stable, so sorting by day and then by status keeps the day order within each status.
Arrays.binarySearchRequires sorted input; on unsorted data the answer is meaningless. A miss returns -(insertion point) - 1, always negative.
Array equals, hashCode, toStringInherited from Object: identity. Use Arrays.equals, Arrays.hashCode, Arrays.toString, and the deep versions for nested arrays.
Collections.shuffle(list, rnd)Pass a seeded Random when a test needs the same order every run.

Arrays, worth knowing

fill, setAll, copyOf, copyOfRange, stream, parallelSort, mismatch 9, compare 9. System.arraycopy is the fast primitive under most of them.

Collections, worth knowing

frequency, nCopies, disjoint, max and min with a comparator, reverse, swap, rotate, and the empty…, singleton…, unmodifiable…, checked… and synchronized… wrappers.

synchronizedList is half the jobEach method takes a lock, but iteration is many calls, so you must hold synchronized (list) around the whole loop yourself or risk ConcurrentModificationException. A concurrent collection is usually the better fix: see copy-on-write and lock-free collections.

A thread is always in one of six states, and an interrupt is a request it must choose to honour

getState() reports one of six values. RUNNABLE covers running on a CPU, waiting for one, and blocking inside most native I/O. Interrupting a thread only sets a flag: blocking methods notice it, throw InterruptedException and clear it, and computing code must check it itself. Nothing can stop a thread from outside. Thread.stop() has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20.

ThreadStates.java · each state on cue, then two ways to answer an interrupt
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class ThreadStates {
    static void waitFor(Thread t, Thread.State s) throws InterruptedException {
        while (t.getState() != s) Thread.sleep(1);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object lock = new Object();
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            System.out.println("inside run()        " + Thread.currentThread().getState());
            try {
                Thread.sleep(200);                           // TIMED_WAITING
                synchronized (lock) { }                      // BLOCKED while main holds the lock
                release.await();                             // WAITING
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "worker");

        System.out.println("after new           " + worker.getState());
        synchronized (lock) {
            worker.start();
            waitFor(worker, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING);
            System.out.println("in sleep(200)       " + worker.getState());
            waitFor(worker, Thread.State.BLOCKED);
            System.out.println("at synchronized     " + worker.getState());
        }
        waitFor(worker, Thread.State.WAITING);
        System.out.println("in await()          " + worker.getState());
        release.countDown();
        worker.join();
        System.out.println("after run() returns " + worker.getState());

        Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                Thread.sleep(60_000);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.out.println("sleeper woke with InterruptedException; flag is now "
                        + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();          // restore it for whoever runs next
                System.out.println("sleeper restored the flag: " + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());
            }
        });
        sleeper.start();
        waitFor(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING);
        sleeper.interrupt();
        sleeper.join();

        Thread spinner = new Thread(() -> {
            long spins = 0;
            while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) spins++;   // CPU work must poll the flag
            System.out.println("spinner saw the flag and stopped: " + (spins > 0));
        });
        spinner.start();
        Thread.sleep(50);
        spinner.interrupt();
        spinner.join();

        Thread virtual = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 1).start(() -> { });
        virtual.join();
        Thread heartbeat = Thread.ofPlatform().name("heartbeat").daemon().unstarted(() -> { });
        System.out.println(virtual.getName() + " virtual=" + virtual.isVirtual() + " daemon=" + virtual.isDaemon()
                + "; " + heartbeat.getName() + " daemon=" + heartbeat.isDaemon());
    }
}

in sleep(200)       TIMED_WAITING
at synchronized     BLOCKED
in await()          WAITING

sleeper woke with InterruptedException; flag is now false

spinner saw the flag and stopped: true
vt-1 virtual=true daemon=true; heartbeat daemon=true
Never swallow an interruptA method that throws InterruptedException clears the flag first, as line 7 of the output shows. An empty catch means a shutdown request, or a Future.cancel(true), is lost, and the thread runs on. Either rethrow it or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before returning.
RUNNABLE does not mean busyA thread blocked in a socket read or a JDBC call shows as RUNNABLE in a thread dump, because the JVM cannot see inside native code. Two hundred RUNNABLE threads in SocketInputStream.read usually means a slow dependency, not a CPU problem.
Daemon threadsThe JVM exits when only daemon threads are left, without running their finally blocks. Virtual threads are always daemon threads. The builders 21 Thread.ofPlatform() and Thread.ofVirtual() set names, daemon status and handlers in one place.

Without a happens-before edge, another thread may never see your write

The Java Memory Model (JLS chapter 17) defines when a write in one thread must be visible to a read in another. In between, the compiler, the JIT and the CPU may keep values in registers, reorder instructions and buffer stores, as long as no single thread can tell. Two threads can tell. The promise in return: a program with no data races behaves as if its actions ran in one sequential order.

Visibility.java · a flag that one thread sets and another never sees
public class Visibility {
    static boolean plainStop;                      // no happens-before between writer and reader
    static volatile boolean volatileStop;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread plain = new Thread(() -> {
            long spins = 0;
            while (!plainStop) spins++;            // the JIT may read plainStop once, outside the loop
            System.out.println("plain reader stopped after " + spins + " spins");
        });
        plain.setDaemon(true);                     // so the JVM can still exit
        plain.start();
        Thread.sleep(500);                         // long enough for the loop to be compiled
        plainStop = true;
        plain.join(2_000);
        System.out.println("plain flag: reader still running 2 s after the write? " + plain.isAlive());

        Thread reader = new Thread(() -> {
            long spins = 0;
            while (!volatileStop) spins++;         // a volatile read on every iteration
            System.out.println("volatile reader stopped" + (spins > 0 ? "" : " at once"));
        });
        reader.start();
        Thread.sleep(500);
        volatileStop = true;
        reader.join(2_000);
        System.out.println("volatile flag: reader still running? " + reader.isAlive());
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · Visibility.java · the same on every run here
plain flag: reader still running 2 s after the write? true
volatile reader stopped
volatile flag: reader still running? false
What goes wrongExample
VisibilityThe JIT compiled while (!plainStop) into a loop that reads the field once. Legal: nothing in the loop synchronises, so no other thread's write has to be seen.
ReorderingWrites and reads swap places, in the compiler or the CPU. The next slide catches it happening tens of thousands of times.
Atomicitycount++ is a read, an add and a write; a thread can lose the race between them. On 32-bit JVMs a non-volatile long or double can even tear into two halves (JLS 17.7).
Fixed by accident is not fixedPut a System.out.println in the plain loop and it usually stops, because PrintStream synchronises internally. Remove the logging and the bug returns. The definition to remember: a data race is two accesses to one variable, at least one a write, not ordered by happens-before.

Happens-before is the only ordering promise between threads, and it is created at specific points

If action A happens-before action B, then B sees A's effects and everything that happened before A. The JLS defines a small set of these edges, java.util.concurrent documents more, and the relation is transitive. Without an edge, any outcome the hardware can produce is legal, including one that no interleaving of the source lines could produce: both reads below returning 0.

Reordering.java · the store-buffering test, plain fields against volatile ones
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

// The store-buffering test: each thread writes one variable, then reads the other.
// If every thread's actions happened in program order, at least one read would see a 1.
public class Reordering {
    static int x, y, r1, r2;                       // plain fields
    static volatile int vx, vy;                    // volatile fields
    static int vr1, vr2;
    static final AtomicInteger round = new AtomicInteger(), finished = new AtomicInteger();

    static Thread side(int trials, Runnable body) {
        return new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 1; i <= trials; i++) {
                while (round.get() != i) Thread.onSpinWait();   // start each trial together
                body.run();
                finished.incrementAndGet();
            }
        });
    }

    static int run(boolean useVolatile, int trials) throws InterruptedException {
        round.set(0);
        Thread a = useVolatile ? side(trials, () -> { vx = 1; vr1 = vy; }) : side(trials, () -> { x = 1; r1 = y; });
        Thread b = useVolatile ? side(trials, () -> { vy = 1; vr2 = vx; }) : side(trials, () -> { y = 1; r2 = x; });
        a.start();
        b.start();
        int bothZero = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= trials; i++) {
            x = y = vx = vy = 0;
            finished.set(0);
            round.set(i);                          // release both threads
            while (finished.get() != 2) Thread.onSpinWait();
            if (useVolatile ? vr1 == 0 && vr2 == 0 : r1 == 0 && r2 == 0) bothZero++;
        }
        a.join();
        b.join();
        return bothZero;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        int trials = 200_000;
        System.out.printf("plain fields:    both reads saw 0 in %,d of %,d trials%n", run(false, trials), trials);
        System.out.printf("volatile fields: both reads saw 0 in %,d of %,d trials%n", run(true, trials), trials);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25, x86-64 · Reordering.java · the plain count varies by run
plain fields:    both reads saw 0 in 22,217 of 200,000 trials
volatile fields: both reads saw 0 in 0 of 200,000 trials
Reading the resultIf each thread's write came before its read, the second read to run would have to see a 1. Yet with plain fields both saw 0 in tens of thousands of trials: each write sat in a store buffer while the next read went ahead. With volatile, the JVM puts a fence after each write, and the impossible result never appeared in 200,000 trials. x86 reorders only a store with a later load; ARM servers such as Graviton reorder more, so racy code that works on a laptop can fail in production.
Thishappens-before
Each action in a threadEvery later action in that thread (program order)
Unlocking a monitorEvery later lock of the same monitor
A volatile writeEvery later read of that variable
t.start()Everything thread t does
Everything thread t doesAnother thread's return from t.join()
The end of a constructorReads of that object's final fields by other threads, if this did not escape
A class's static initialiserAny use of the class
java.util.concurrent edgeMeans
Putting into a concurrent collectionVisible to the thread that gets or removes that element
executor.submit(task)Visible to the task when it starts
A task's actionsVisible after future.get() returns
countDown(), release(), unlock()Visible after the matching await(), acquire(), lock() returns
Completing a CompletableFutureVisible to its dependent stages
Piggybacking on transitivityWrite the data in plain fields, then write a volatile flag. A reader that sees the flag also sees the data: write data → write flag (program order) → read flag (volatile) → read data (program order). This is how BlockingQueue, Future and safe publication work, and it is why you rarely need volatile on every field.

volatile gives visibility and ordering for one variable, never atomicity for a sequence of steps

Every read of a volatile field sees the most recent write to it, and everything written before that write. That makes it right for a stop flag, or for a reference to an immutable snapshot that one thread replaces and many read. It does nothing for count++, which is a read, an add and a write: two threads can both read 41 and both write 42.

VolatileDemo.java · lost updates, then two lazy singletons done right
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class VolatileDemo {
    static volatile int volatileCount;
    static int lockedCount;
    static final AtomicInteger atomicCount = new AtomicInteger();
    static final Object lock = new Object();

    // Double-checked locking: correct only because the field is volatile.
    static final class Config {
        private static volatile Config instance;
        final String region;
        private Config() { region = "eu-west"; }
        static Config get() {
            Config c = instance;                     // one volatile read on the fast path
            if (c == null) {
                synchronized (Config.class) {
                    c = instance;
                    if (c == null) instance = c = new Config();
                }
            }
            return c;
        }
    }

    // The holder idiom: lazy and thread-safe, with no volatile and no lock.
    static final class Rates {
        private Rates() { }
        private static final class Holder { static final Rates INSTANCE = new Rates(); }
        static Rates get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int threads = 4, each = 1_000_000;
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) {
            for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < each; i++) {
                        volatileCount++;                  // read, add, write: three steps
                        atomicCount.incrementAndGet();    // one atomic step
                        synchronized (lock) { lockedCount++; }
                    }
                });
        }
        System.out.printf("expected      %,d%n", threads * each);
        System.out.printf("volatile ++   %,d%n", volatileCount);
        System.out.printf("AtomicInteger %,d%n", atomicCount.get());
        System.out.printf("synchronized  %,d%n", lockedCount);

        var configs = ConcurrentHashMap.<Config>newKeySet();
        var rates = ConcurrentHashMap.<Rates>newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) pool.submit(() -> { configs.add(Config.get()); rates.add(Rates.get()); });
        }
        System.out.println("1,000 concurrent callers saw " + configs.size() + " Config and " + rates.size() + " Rates instance");
    }
}

volatile guaranteesvolatile does not give
Each read sees the latest writeAtomic read-modify-write: ++, +=, check-then-set
Writes before a volatile write are visible after a read of itA consistent view of two fields at once
Atomic 64-bit reads and writes of long and doubleMutual exclusion of any kind
Why double-checked locking needs itinstance = new Config() is three steps: allocate, construct, assign. Without volatile, the assignment may become visible before the constructor's writes, so a thread on the fast path sees a non-null Config whose region is still null. The local c saves a second volatile read.
The holder idiom needs nothingThe JVM initialises Holder on first use, exactly once, under its own lock, and class initialisation creates a happens-before edge. Lazy, thread-safe and free after the first call. An enum is simpler still: singleton, the safe ways.
Good usesA volatile boolean running checked by a worker loop. A volatile reference to an immutable config, replaced whole on reload. Counters belong in AtomicLong or LongAdder, on atomics and CAS.

synchronized is a re-entrant lock on an object, and wait and notify are its waiting room

Every object has a monitor. A synchronized block takes it on entry and releases it on exit, even when an exception leaves the block, and each release happens-before the next acquire. wait() releases the monitor and sleeps until another thread calls notify or notifyAll on the same object. Together they build any blocking structure, which is why the JDK built BlockingQueue so you do not have to.

WaitNotify.java · a bounded buffer from one monitor, re-entrancy, the owner rule
import java.util.*;

public class WaitNotify {
    // A bounded buffer built from the monitor alone.
    static final class Buffer<T> {
        private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final int capacity;
        private int maxSeen;
        Buffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

        synchronized void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
            while (items.size() == capacity) wait();   // a loop, never an if
            items.addLast(item);
            maxSeen = Math.max(maxSeen, items.size());
            notifyAll();                               // wake consumers (and other producers)
        }
        synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException {
            while (items.isEmpty()) wait();
            T item = items.removeFirst();
            notifyAll();
            return item;
        }
        synchronized int maxSeen() { return maxSeen; }
    }

    static final class Counter {
        private int n;
        synchronized void add() { n++; }
        synchronized void addTwice() { add(); add(); }   // re-entrant: the same thread holds the lock
        synchronized int get() { return n; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var buffer = new Buffer<Integer>(2);
        List<Integer> consumed = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) buffer.put(i);
                buffer.put(-1);
                buffer.put(-1);                            // one stop signal per consumer
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        Runnable consumer = () -> {
            try {
                for (int item; (item = buffer.take()) != -1; ) consumed.add(item);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        };
        Thread c1 = new Thread(consumer), c2 = new Thread(consumer);
        producer.start(); c1.start(); c2.start();
        producer.join(); c1.join(); c2.join();
        List<Integer> sorted = new ArrayList<>(consumed);
        Collections.sort(sorted);
        System.out.println("consumed " + sorted.size() + " items, sum " + sorted.stream().mapToInt(i -> i).sum()
                + ", buffer never held more than " + buffer.maxSeen());

        var counter = new Counter();
        counter.addTwice();
        System.out.println("re-entrant addTwice: " + counter.get());

        Object monitor = new Object();
        try {
            monitor.wait();                                // without holding the monitor
        } catch (IllegalMonitorStateException e) {
            System.out.println("IllegalMonitorStateException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        synchronized (monitor) {
            System.out.println("holdsLock inside synchronized: " + Thread.holdsLock(monitor));
            monitor.wait(10);                              // releases the monitor while it waits
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · WaitNotify.java
consumed 20 items, sum 210, buffer never held more than 2
re-entrant addTwice: 2
IllegalMonitorStateException: current thread is not owner
holdsLock inside synchronized: true

The rules

  • A synchronized instance method locks this; a static one locks the Class object. They are different locks.
  • The lock is re-entrant: the thread that holds it can enter it again, so addTwice calling add works.
  • Call wait, notify and notifyAll only while holding that object's monitor, or get IllegalMonitorStateException.
  • Always wait in a loop that rechecks the condition. Wakeups can be spurious, and another thread may take the item between the notify and your return from wait.
  • Prefer notifyAll. notify wakes one arbitrary waiter, which may be a producer when only a consumer can make progress.
Lock on a private objectLocking this in a public class lets any caller take your lock too. Use private final Object lock = new Object(). Never lock a string literal or a boxed number: they are shared across the JVM, and javac's lint flags the boxed case ([synchronization] on JDK 21, [identity] on 25), as concurrency bugs shows.
Virtual threads and synchronizedOn JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pinned a virtual thread to its carrier. JDK 24 removed that (JEP 491), so synchronized is fine again on 24 and later. Virtual threads under the hood measures both.
When to use it todaysynchronized is still the simplest correct lock for short critical sections. For waiting, use BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch or a Condition. Hand-written wait and notify belong in interviews and in libraries.

ReentrantLock does what synchronized does, plus timeouts, interruption, fairness and several conditions

The locks in java.util.concurrent.locks are ordinary objects. You lock and unlock them yourself, which means you must unlock in finally, and in return you can give up after a timeout, abandon the wait when interrupted, and hold several wait queues on one lock. Read-write locks and StampedLock go further for data that is read far more often than written.

Locks.java · tryLock, lockInterruptibly, re-entrancy, readers together, optimistic reads
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class Locks {
    static final class Point {                       // StampedLock's optimistic read
        private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
        private double x, y;
        void move(double dx, double dy) {
            long stamp = sl.writeLock();
            try { x += dx; y += dy; } finally { sl.unlockWrite(stamp); }
        }
        double distance(Runnable between) {
            long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();     // no lock taken at all
            double cx = x, cy = y;
            between.run();                           // lets the demo slip a write in here
            if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {               // a write happened: fall back to a real read lock
                System.out.println("optimistic read invalidated, retrying under the read lock");
                stamp = sl.readLock();
                try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
            }
            return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        CountDownLatch held = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Thread holder = new Thread(() -> {
            lock.lock();
            try { held.countDown(); done.await(); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            finally { lock.unlock(); }
        });
        holder.start();
        held.await();
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        boolean got = lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        System.out.printf("tryLock(100 ms) while another thread holds it: %b after ~%d ms%n",
                got, Math.round((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e8) * 100);

        Thread impatient = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                lock.lockInterruptibly();
                lock.unlock();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.out.println("lockInterruptibly gave up when interrupted");
            }
        });
        impatient.start();
        while (!lock.hasQueuedThread(impatient)) Thread.sleep(1);
        impatient.interrupt();
        impatient.join();
        done.countDown();
        holder.join();

        lock.lock();
        lock.lock();
        System.out.println("held twice by one thread: holdCount " + lock.getHoldCount());
        lock.unlock();
        lock.unlock();

        ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
        AtomicInteger reading = new AtomicInteger(), peak = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch allIn = new CountDownLatch(3);
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    rw.readLock().lock();
                    try {
                        peak.accumulateAndGet(reading.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
                        allIn.countDown();
                        allIn.await();                    // all three readers hold the lock at once
                        reading.decrementAndGet();
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                    finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
                    return null;
                });
            allIn.await();
            Future<Integer> writer = pool.submit(() -> {
                rw.writeLock().lock();                   // waits until every reader is gone
                try { return reading.get(); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
            });
            System.out.println("readers inside together: " + peak.get() + "; readers left when the writer got in: " + writer.get());
        }

        var p = new Point();
        p.move(3, 4);
        System.out.println("distance " + p.distance(() -> { }));
        System.out.println("distance " + p.distance(() -> p.move(3, 4)));
    }
}

ReentrantReadWriteLock

Any number of readers together, or one writer alone: three readers held it at once above, and the writer waited until they left. A read lock can be taken while holding the write lock (downgrading), never the reverse: upgrading deadlocks. Only worth it when reads are long and frequent.

StampedLock

tryOptimisticRead() takes no lock: read the fields, then validate(stamp). If a write slipped in, as the demo forced, retry under a real read lock. Fastest for tiny read-mostly sections. Not re-entrant, and it has no conditions.

Which to picksynchronized by default. ReentrantLock when you need a timeout, interruption or two conditions, such as notFull and notEmpty in a bounded buffer. The LLD tab's locks, atomics and collections puts them to work in designs.

Compare-and-set updates a value without a lock, by retrying whenever it loses a race

A CAS is one CPU instruction (lock cmpxchg on x86): if the value is still what I read, set it to my new value, and tell me whether that worked. Wrap it in a loop and you have a lock-free update. Under heavy contention many threads keep failing and retrying, which is what LongAdder avoids by giving each thread its own cell to increment.

Atomics.java · a CAS loop, the helpers, LongAdder, ABA, VarHandle
import java.lang.invoke.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class Atomics {
    static final AtomicLong highest = new AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE);

    static void recordMax(long value) {              // the compare-and-set loop
        long current;
        do {
            current = highest.get();
            if (value <= current) return;
        } while (!highest.compareAndSet(current, value));   // lost a race: read again, retry
    }

    static final class Seat {                        // CAS on an ordinary field, via a VarHandle
        volatile String holder;
        static final VarHandle HOLDER;
        static {
            try { HOLDER = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Seat.class, "holder", String.class); }
            catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); }
        }
        boolean claim(String who) { return HOLDER.compareAndSet(this, null, who); }
    }

    static long time(int threads, Runnable work) throws InterruptedException {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) pool.submit(work);
        }
        return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { long v = (i * 7919L) % 10_007; pool.submit(() -> recordMax(v)); }
        }
        System.out.println("max recorded by 10,000 racing tasks: " + highest.get());

        AtomicInteger stock = new AtomicInteger(5);
        int left = stock.updateAndGet(s -> s > 0 ? s - 1 : s);          // never below zero
        int total = stock.accumulateAndGet(10, Integer::sum);
        System.out.println("updateAndGet " + left + ", accumulateAndGet " + total);

        AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong();
        LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();
        int threads = 8, each = 5_000_000;
        long atomicMs = time(threads, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < each; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); });
        long adderMs = time(threads, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < each; i++) adder.increment(); });
        System.out.printf("8 threads x 5M increments: AtomicLong %,d in %d ms, LongAdder %,d in %d ms (one run)%n",
                atomic.get(), atomicMs, adder.sum(), adderMs);

        // ABA: the value went A -> B -> A, and a plain CAS cannot tell.
        AtomicReference<String> top = new AtomicReference<>("A");
        AtomicStampedReference<String> stamped = new AtomicStampedReference<>("A", 0);
        String seen = top.get();
        int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
        String seenStamped = stamped.get(stampHolder);
        top.set("B"); top.set("A");                                     // another thread's changes
        stamped.set("B", 1); stamped.set("A", 2);
        System.out.println("plain CAS after A->B->A: " + top.compareAndSet(seen, "C")
                + ", stamped CAS: " + stamped.compareAndSet(seenStamped, "C", stampHolder[0], stampHolder[0] + 1));

        Seat seat = new Seat();
        System.out.println("VarHandle CAS: alice " + seat.claim("alice") + ", bob " + seat.claim("bob") + ", holder " + seat.holder);
    }
}

ClassUse it for
AtomicInteger, AtomicLongA counter or sequence that is also read often; incrementAndGet, compareAndSet
LongAdder, LongAccumulatorHot counters written by many threads and read rarely: metrics, request counts
AtomicReference<V>Swapping an immutable object: a config snapshot, a lock-free stack's top
AtomicStampedReferenceThe same, when A → B → A must be detected
VarHandle 9CAS on a field of your own class, with no wrapper object per instance
The function may run twiceupdateAndGet and accumulateAndGet retry the function each time the CAS fails, so it must be pure: no logging, no I/O, no counters of its own. ConcurrentHashMap.compute is the opposite case: it locks the bin and calls the function exactly once, so there the rule is to keep the function short.
ABAThe plain CAS succeeded because the value was A again, although two changes happened in between. That matters when the value stands for a version of something, such as a lock-free stack's top node. A stamp, or a fresh object for every state, makes each change distinct.
When a lock is betterSeveral variables that must change together, an invariant across fields, or long critical sections. A CAS covers one memory location. LongAdder's sum() is not an atomic snapshot either: it adds the cells while they keep changing.

A deadlock is a cycle of threads each holding the lock the next one needs, and the JVM can find it

Thread 1 holds account A's lock and waits for B's; thread 2 holds B's and waits for A's. Neither can move, and nothing will ever time out. A deadlock needs four conditions at once: exclusive locks, holding one while waiting for another, no way to take a lock away, and a cycle. Breaking any one prevents it. In practice you break the cycle with a global lock order.

Deadlock.java · a guaranteed deadlock, detected, then the ordered fix
import java.lang.management.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class Deadlock {
    static final class Account {
        final String id;
        final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        long balance = 100;
        Account(String id) { this.id = id; }
    }

    // Locks in argument order: transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) can deadlock.
    static void transferUnordered(Account from, Account to, CyclicBarrier bothHoldFirst) throws Exception {
        from.lock.lock();
        try {
            bothHoldFirst.await();                         // make the bad interleaving certain
            to.lock.lock();
            try { from.balance -= 10; to.balance += 10; } finally { to.lock.unlock(); }
        } finally { from.lock.unlock(); }
    }

    // Always lock in one global order, here by id: no cycle is possible.
    static void transferOrdered(Account from, Account to) {
        Account first = from.id.compareTo(to.id) < 0 ? from : to;
        Account second = first == from ? to : from;
        first.lock.lock();
        try {
            second.lock.lock();
            try { from.balance -= 10; to.balance += 10; } finally { second.lock.unlock(); }
        } finally { first.lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Account a = new Account("ACC-A"), b = new Account("ACC-B");
        CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(2);
        Thread t1 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("transfer-A-to-B").daemon().start(() -> {
            try { transferUnordered(a, b, barrier); } catch (Exception e) { }
        });
        Thread t2 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("transfer-B-to-A").daemon().start(() -> {
            try { transferUnordered(b, a, barrier); } catch (Exception e) { }
        });

        ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
        long[] ids;
        while ((ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads()) == null) Thread.sleep(10);
        for (ThreadInfo info : mx.getThreadInfo(ids)) {
            String lock = info.getLockName().replaceAll("@[0-9a-f]+", "");
            System.out.println(info.getThreadName() + " is " + info.getThreadState() + " on " + lock
                    + ", held by " + info.getLockOwnerName());
        }
        System.out.println("both still alive: " + (t1.isAlive() && t2.isAlive()));

        Account c = new Account("ACC-C"), d = new Account("ACC-D");
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                pool.submit(() -> transferOrdered(c, d));
                pool.submit(() -> transferOrdered(d, c));
            }
        }
        System.out.println("ordered locking: 20,000 opposite transfers finished, balances " + c.balance + " and " + d.balance);
    }
}

Found 1 deadlock.

Preventing it

Lock order: always acquire in one global order, by id as in transferOrdered. Timeouts: tryLock(timeout), release everything and retry. Fewer locks: one lock per aggregate, or a single-threaded owner fed through a queue. The database version, row locks taken in different orders, has the same cure.

Finding it

jcmd <pid> Thread.print or jstack <pid> prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with every thread in the cycle. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() sees ReentrantLock cycles too, which is why the demo above found one with no synchronized in it. Take three dumps a few seconds apart for anything slow.

Its relatives

Livelock: threads keep reacting to each other and get nowhere, such as two tryLock loops backing off in step; add random back-off. Starvation: a thread never gets the lock or the CPU. Pool starvation: tasks in a bounded pool block on other tasks queued in the same pool, and every thread waits.

Thread safety comes from not sharing, not mutating, or synchronising, in that order of preference

State that only one thread can reach needs no protection. State that never changes needs none either. Only shared, mutable state needs locks, atomics or concurrent collections, and each piece of it is a place where bugs and contention gather. The best concurrent design keeps that part small, and publishes everything else safely.

SafetyStrategies.java · a ThreadLocal leaking between pooled tasks, and the safe shapes
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class SafetyStrategies {
    static final ThreadLocal<String> CURRENT_USER = new ThreadLocal<>();

    static String handle(String user, boolean cleanUp) {
        if (user != null) CURRENT_USER.set(user);
        try {
            return "request for " + user + " runs as " + CURRENT_USER.get();
        } finally {
            if (cleanUp) CURRENT_USER.remove();               // always, in finally
        }
    }

    // Immutable and safely published through a final field: shareable as it is.
    record PriceList(Map<String, Long> cents) {
        PriceList { cents = Map.copyOf(cents); }
    }

    // Shared, mutable, published safely: a concurrent map in a final field.
    static final Map<String, Long> VIEWS = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    // DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe; SimpleDateFormat is neither.
    static final DateTimeFormatter ISO = DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) {   // one reused thread
            System.out.println(pool.submit(() -> handle("alice", false)).get());
            System.out.println(pool.submit(() -> handle(null, false)).get() + "  <- leaked from the last task");
        }
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) {
            System.out.println(pool.submit(() -> handle("alice", true)).get());
            System.out.println(pool.submit(() -> handle(null, true)).get());
        }

        var prices = new PriceList(Map.of("tea", 250L, "milk", 120L));
        List<String> totals = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (String sku : List.of("tea", "milk", "tea")) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    long sum = 0;                                  // stack-confined: no sharing at all
                    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) sum += prices.cents().get(sku);
                    totals.add(sku + "=" + sum);
                    VIEWS.merge(sku, 1L, Long::sum);
                });
            }
        }
        Collections.sort(totals);
        System.out.println("totals " + totals + ", views " + new TreeMap<>(VIEWS)
                + ", parsed " + LocalDate.parse("2026-10-07", ISO).getDayOfWeek());
    }
}

StrategyHow
Stack confinementLocals belong to one call on one thread: sum above is safe with no effort.
Thread confinementThreadLocal, or one owner thread fed through a queue (the actor style).
ImmutabilityRecords with copied components, final fields, List.copyOf: PriceList.
Thread-safe typesConcurrent collections, atomics, DateTimeFormatter instead of SimpleDateFormat.
LockingA lock around each invariant that spans more than one variable.
ThreadLocal in a poolPool threads live for the whole application, so a value set by one task is still there for the next one, here another user's identity. In an application server the same leak pins a whole web app's class loader in memory after a redeploy. Set and remove() in the same try / finally.
Publishing safelyAn object handed to another thread through a plain field may be seen half-built. Safe routes: a static initialiser, a volatile or AtomicReference field, a final field of a properly constructed object, a concurrent collection, or a lock both threads use.
ScopedValue replaces most ThreadLocalsFinal in JDK 25 (JEP 506): a value bound for the duration of one call, inherited by subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope, and impossible to leak because it is unbound when the call returns. With a million virtual threads, a ThreadLocal also means a million copies. See virtual threads under the hood.

An executor separates submitting work from running it, so threads become a resource you size once

A platform thread costs an OS thread, a reserved stack and tens of microseconds to start. Creating one per task pays that every time, and lets the load decide how many threads exist. An ExecutorService keeps a set of threads and a queue, so the same 10,000 tasks start 8 threads instead of 10,000. The factory methods in Executors each make a different trade-off, and some hide an unbounded queue or an unbounded thread count.

WhyExecutors.java · thread per task against a pool, named threads, what each factory builds
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class WhyExecutors {
    static long threadsStarted() { return ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getTotalStartedThreadCount(); }

    static String describe(ExecutorService e) {
        if (!(e instanceof ThreadPoolExecutor p)) return e.getClass().getSimpleName();
        int cap = p.getQueue().remainingCapacity();
        return String.format("core %d, max %s, queue %s (capacity %s)", p.getCorePoolSize(),
                p.getMaximumPoolSize() == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? "unbounded" : p.getMaximumPoolSize(),
                p.getQueue().getClass().getSimpleName(), cap == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? "unbounded" : cap);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int tasks = 10_000;
        long before = threadsStarted(), t0 = System.nanoTime();
        List<Thread> started = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) {
            Thread t = new Thread(() -> Math.sqrt(42));
            t.start();
            started.add(t);
        }
        for (Thread t : started) t.join();
        System.out.printf("new Thread per task: %,d threads started, %d ms%n",
                threadsStarted() - before, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000);

        before = threadsStarted();
        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.submit(() -> Math.sqrt(42));
        }                                                      // close() waits for every task (19+)
        System.out.printf("fixed pool of 8:     %,d threads started, %d ms (one run)%n",
                threadsStarted() - before, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000);

        ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("order-worker-", 1).factory();
        Set<String> names = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, named)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) pool.submit(() -> names.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()));
        }
        System.out.println("named threads that ran 30 tasks: " + names);

        try (ExecutorService fixed = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
             ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
             ExecutorService scheduled = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);
             ExecutorService stealing = Executors.newWorkStealingPool();
             ExecutorService virtual = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            System.out.println("newFixedThreadPool(4)       " + describe(fixed));
            System.out.println("newCachedThreadPool()       " + describe(cached));
            System.out.println("newScheduledThreadPool(2)   " + describe(scheduled));
            System.out.println("newWorkStealingPool()       " + describe(stealing));
            System.out.println("newVirtualThreadPerTask...  " + describe(virtual));
        }
    }
}

FactoryWhat it hides
newFixedThreadPool(n)An unbounded queue. Under overload it grows until OutOfMemoryError, and latency grows with it.
newSingleThreadExecutor()The same unbounded queue, with one thread: tasks run strictly in order.
newCachedThreadPool()No queue and no thread limit: a burst of slow tasks creates a thread for each one.
newScheduledThreadPool(n)A delay queue; see scheduled executors.
newWorkStealingPool()A ForkJoinPool sized to the cores, for CPU-bound work.
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() 21A new virtual thread per task: no queue, no limit. Bound the resource it calls instead.
Build production pools by handnew ThreadPoolExecutor(…) with a bounded queue, a named ThreadFactory and an explicit rejection policy makes overload visible as rejections instead of a growing heap. The next slide takes one apart.
Name your threadsA thread dump full of pool-7-thread-3 says nothing. Thread.ofPlatform().name("order-worker-", 1).factory() 21 makes the dump, the logs and the profiler point at the right pool.
close() and SpringExecutorService is AutoCloseable since 19: close() shuts down and waits, so try-with-resources works. In Spring, configure ThreadPoolTaskExecutor beans and name the one @Async uses: see async and scheduling.

A pool fills its core threads, then its queue, then its extra threads, and then it rejects

The order surprises almost everyone: a ThreadPoolExecutor adds threads beyond the core size only when the queue is full. With an unbounded queue the queue is never full, so the maximum pool size is never used and a fixed pool can only queue. The demo blocks every task so each decision stays visible.

PoolAnatomy.java · seven blocked tasks into core 2, queue 2, max 4
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolAnatomy {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Runnable blocker = () -> {
            try { release.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        };

        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                2, 4,                                   // core and maximum threads
                30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                   // idle time before extra threads die
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2),            // a bounded queue
                Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", 1).factory(),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());  // the default: throw

        for (int task = 1; task <= 7; task++) {
            int threads = pool.getPoolSize();
            String outcome;
            try {
                pool.execute(blocker);
                outcome = pool.getPoolSize() > threads
                        ? (threads < pool.getCorePoolSize() ? "new core thread" : "queue full, so an extra thread")
                        : "queued";
            } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
                outcome = "REJECTED: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName();
            }
            System.out.printf("task %d: %-37s threads %d, queued %d%n", task, outcome, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getQueue().size());
        }
        release.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("completed " + pool.getCompletedTaskCount() + ", largest pool " + pool.getLargestPoolSize());

        // CallerRunsPolicy: when full, the submitting thread runs the task itself (back-pressure).
        CountDownLatch release2 = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor polite = new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        polite.execute(() -> { try { release2.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } });
        polite.execute(() -> { });                                       // fills the queue
        polite.execute(() -> System.out.println("third task ran on: " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
        release2.countDown();
        polite.shutdown();
        polite.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
        double waitMs = 90, computeMs = 10;
        System.out.printf("sizing on %d cores: CPU-bound about %d threads; 90 ms waiting per 10 ms computing about %d%n",
                cores, cores, (int) (cores * (1 + waitMs / computeMs)));
    }
}

task 3: queued                                threads 2, queued 1
task 4: queued                                threads 2, queued 2
task 5: queue full, so an extra thread        threads 3, queued 2

Rejection policyWhen the pool is full
AbortPolicy (default)Throws RejectedExecutionException to the submitter
CallerRunsPolicyThe submitting thread runs the task itself, so it slows down: back-pressure for free
DiscardPolicyDrops the task silently. Almost never what you want
DiscardOldestPolicyDrops the oldest queued task and retries; for latest-value-wins work only

Sizing

  • CPU-bound: about one thread per core. More threads only add switching.
  • Blocking I/O: cores × (1 + wait time / compute time), from Goetz: 200 for the example above.
  • Little's law checks it: threads busy = arrival rate × time per task. 400 requests/s at 250 ms each keep 100 threads busy.
  • Then cap it by what the pool calls: 200 threads sharing a 20-connection database pool means 180 of them wait.

A Future is a handle to a result that may not exist yet, and shutting a pool down takes two decisions

submit returns a Future at once; get blocks until the task finishes, and rethrows its failure wrapped in ExecutionException. Two details cause most production surprises: a timed-out get does not stop the task, and an exception in a task whose Future nobody reads disappears without a trace. Shutting down means deciding what happens to queued work, and how long to wait for running work.

FutureShutdown.java · timeouts, cancellation, lost exceptions, shutdownNow
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FutureShutdown {
    static String slowQuote() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(5_000);
        return "quote";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

        Future<String> slow = pool.submit(FutureShutdown::slowQuote);
        try {
            slow.get(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            System.out.println("get(100 ms): TimeoutException; the task keeps running: done=" + slow.isDone());
        }
        System.out.println("cancel(true) " + slow.cancel(true) + ", state " + slow.state());

        Future<Integer> failing = pool.submit(() -> Integer.parseInt("12x"));
        try {
            failing.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("ExecutionException wraps " + e.getCause());
        }
        System.out.println("exceptionNow(): " + failing.exceptionNow().getClass().getSimpleName());

        Future<?> forgotten = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("nobody will see this"); });
        while (!forgotten.isDone()) Thread.sleep(1);
        System.out.println("submit() kept the exception inside the Future: state " + forgotten.state());

        Future<Integer> ok = pool.submit(() -> 6 * 7);
        System.out.println("resultNow() " + ok.get() + " / " + ok.resultNow());

        List<Callable<String>> calls = List.of(() -> "price", () -> "stock", () -> "tax");
        System.out.println("invokeAll: " + pool.invokeAll(calls).stream().map(Future::resultNow).toList());

        CountDownLatch busy = new CountDownLatch(1);
        pool.submit(() -> { busy.await(); return null; });
        pool.submit(() -> { busy.await(); return null; });   // both threads now busy
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) pool.submit(() -> "queued");
        List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow();     // interrupts the running two
        System.out.println("shutdownNow: " + neverStarted.size() + " queued tasks never ran; terminated "
                + pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
        try {
            pool.submit(() -> "late");
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("submit after shutdown: RejectedExecutionException");
        }

        ThreadFactory withHandler = r -> {
            Thread th = new Thread(r, "worker");
            th.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((x, e) -> System.out.println("uncaught handler got: " + e.getMessage()));
            return th;
        };
        try (ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(withHandler)) {
            single.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("thrown inside execute()"); });
        }
    }
}
