Future methodDoes
get(), get(timeout)Blocks for the result. The timed form throws TimeoutException and leaves the task running.
cancel(true)Stops a queued task from starting, and interrupts a running one, which must honour it.
state(), resultNow(), exceptionNow() 19Inspect a finished future without blocking or catching checked exceptions.
invokeAll, invokeAnyRun a batch and wait for all of them, or for the first success.
The exception nobody sawsubmit catches everything the task throws and stores it in the Future. If nobody calls get, nothing is logged: the forgotten task failed in silence. Use execute for fire-and-forget work, whose exceptions reach the thread's uncaught-exception handler, or catch and log inside the task.
Shutting down properlyshutdown() refuses new work and lets queued tasks finish. shutdownNow() also interrupts running tasks and returns the ones that never started. The usual sequence: shutdown, awaitTermination with a deadline, then shutdownNow. A pool of non-daemon threads that is never shut down keeps the JVM alive after main ends.
Timeouts end work, not just waitsAfter get(timeout) fails, call cancel(true), or the task keeps holding a thread and a connection. CompletableFuture composes timeouts and fallbacks more cleanly: the next slides.

CompletableFuture chains async steps without blocking, and the method name says sequence or parallel

A CompletableFuture is a Future you can attach the next step to. thenApply transforms the value, thenCompose starts another async call that depends on it, and thenCombine joins two calls that run at the same time. The timings below show the difference: two dependent 100 ms calls take 200 ms, and five independent 200 ms calls also take 200 ms.

CfCompose.java · four simulated services on a dedicated I/O pool
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class CfCompose {
    static final ExecutorService IO = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory());

    static void pause(long ms) {
        try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }
    static CompletableFuture<Long> priceOf(String sku) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(200); return sku.length() * 100L; }, IO);
    }
    static CompletableFuture<Integer> stockOf(String sku) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(200); return sku.equals("tea") ? 0 : 12; }, IO);
    }
    static CompletableFuture<String> customerTier(String id) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(100); return id.startsWith("vip") ? "GOLD" : "BASIC"; }, IO);
    }
    static CompletableFuture<Double> discountFor(String tier) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(100); return tier.equals("GOLD") ? 0.1 : 0.0; }, IO);
    }
    static long ms(long t0) { return Math.round((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e8) * 100; }   // to 100 ms

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        priceOf("warm-up").join();                       // start the pool threads, load classes
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        String label = priceOf("milk")
                .thenApply(cents -> String.format("%.2f", cents / 100.0))       // transform the value
                .join();
        System.out.println("thenApply   " + label + " after ~" + ms(t0) + " ms");

        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        double discount = customerTier("vip-7")
                .thenCompose(CfCompose::discountFor)                           // the next async call
                .join();
        System.out.println("thenCompose " + discount + " after ~" + ms(t0) + " ms (two calls in sequence)");

        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        String line = priceOf("bread")
                .thenCombine(stockOf("bread"), (p, s) -> p + " cents, " + s + " in stock")   // both at once
                .join();
        System.out.println("thenCombine " + line + " after ~" + ms(t0) + " ms (two calls in parallel)");

        t0 = System.nanoTime();
        List<String> skus = List.of("tea", "milk", "bread", "eggs", "jam");
        List<CompletableFuture<Long>> prices = skus.stream().map(CfCompose::priceOf).toList();
        CompletableFuture.allOf(prices.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();   // wait for all
        List<Long> all = prices.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();      // none block now
        System.out.println("allOf       " + all + " after ~" + ms(t0) + " ms (five calls in parallel)");

        CompletableFuture<String> fast = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(50); return "replica-b"; }, IO);
        CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { pause(300); return "replica-a"; }, IO);
        System.out.println("anyOf       " + CompletableFuture.anyOf(slow, fast).join());

        priceOf("jam").thenAccept(p -> System.out.println("thenAccept  saw " + p))
                      .thenRun(() -> System.out.println("thenRun     ran after it"))
                      .join();
        IO.shutdown();
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · CfCompose.java · times rounded to 100 ms
thenApply   4.00 after ~200 ms
thenCompose 0.1 after ~200 ms (two calls in sequence)
thenCombine 500 cents, 12 in stock after ~200 ms (two calls in parallel)
allOf       [300, 400, 500, 400, 300] after ~200 ms (five calls in parallel)
anyOf       replica-b
thenAccept  saw 300
thenRun     ran after it
MethodTakesLike
thenApply(fn)T -> UOptional.map
thenCompose(fn)T -> CompletableFuture<U>Optional.flatMap: one call after the other
thenCombine(other, fn)A second future and (T, U) -> VTwo calls at once, joined
allOf(…)Any number of futuresCompletes with Void when all have; then join each
anyOf(…)Any number of futuresThe first to complete, typed as Object
thenAccept, thenRunA consumer, a runnableThe end of a chain: side effects
thenApply with an async functiontier.thenApply(CfCompose::discountFor) compiles, and gives a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Double>>. Whenever the function itself returns a future, the method you want is thenCompose.
Start them, then waitallOf is fast because all five calls were started before anything waited. Calling priceOf(s).join() inside a loop starts each one only after the last has finished, and turns 200 ms into 1,000 ms.
Or write it blockingWith virtual threads, the same fan-out can be plain blocking code: a virtual thread per call and a Future each, as the LLD tab's virtual threads slide does. Choose by what your team can read and debug.

Failures travel down the chain wrapped in CompletionException, and each step runs on whatever thread is at hand

When a stage throws, every dependent stage completes exceptionally too, until one of them handles it. Three methods do the handling, and they differ in whether they can change the outcome. The other half of the story is threads: a non-async step runs on the thread that completed the previous one, or on the caller if that had already happened, and an async step with no executor runs in the common ForkJoinPool.

CfErrors.java · recovering, timing out, and which thread runs what
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class CfErrors {
    static String thread() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); }

    static CompletableFuture<Integer> failing() {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("inventory down"); });
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int recovered = failing().exceptionally(ex -> {
            System.out.println("exceptionally sees " + ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " wrapping " + ex.getCause().getMessage());
            return 0;                                                   // a fallback value
        }).join();
        System.out.println("recovered to " + recovered);

        String handled = failing().handle((value, ex) -> ex == null ? "stock " + value : "fallback").join();
        System.out.println("handle -> " + handled);

        try {
            failing().whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees the failure but cannot fix it")).join();
        } catch (CompletionException e) {
            System.out.println("join() throws CompletionException, cause " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }
        try {
            failing().get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("get() throws ExecutionException, cause " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }

        CompletableFuture<String> never = new CompletableFuture<>();
        try {
            never.orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join();         // Java 9
        } catch (CompletionException e) {
            System.out.println("orTimeout: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        System.out.println("completeOnTimeout: " + new CompletableFuture<String>()
                .completeOnTimeout("cached price", 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join());

        System.out.println("supplyAsync with no executor runs on: " + CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CfErrors::thread).join());
        CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x");
        System.out.println("thenApply on a completed future runs on: " + done.thenApply(v -> thread()).join());
        CompletableFuture<String> later = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            return "y";
        });
        CompletableFuture<String> after = later.thenApply(v -> thread());
        System.out.println("thenApply registered before completion runs on: " + after.join());
        System.out.println("thenApplyAsync runs on: " + done.thenApplyAsync(v -> thread()).join());
        System.out.println("common pool parallelism: " + ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism()
                + " on " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " cores");
    }
}

MethodRuns whenCan change the outcome
exceptionally(fn)Only on failureYes: returns a fallback value
handle((v, ex) -> …)AlwaysYes: maps either outcome to a new value
whenComplete((v, ex) -> …)AlwaysNo: for logging and metrics; the failure carries on
exceptionallyCompose 12Only on failureYes: with another async call, such as a fallback service
orTimeout, completeOnTimeout 9When time runs outFail with TimeoutException, or complete with a default
Unwrap before you inspectA failure from an async stage arrives wrapped: exceptionally saw a CompletionException whose cause was the real IllegalStateException. join throws that unchecked wrapper, get a checked ExecutionException. Test ex.getCause(), not ex.
Blocking work in the common poolWith no executor, supplyAsync uses the common pool: 19 threads on this 20-core machine, shared with every parallel stream in the JVM. Twenty slow HTTP calls there stall everything else. Pass an executor for anything that blocks, as CfCompose does with IO.
cancel does not interruptCompletableFuture.cancel(true) completes the future with a CancellationException but does not interrupt the thread running the task, which carries on. If the work must stop, check a flag or use a Future from an ExecutorService.

ForkJoinPool splits work recursively and lets idle threads steal it, so every core stays busy

A fork/join task splits itself in two until the pieces are small, forks one half and computes the other. Each worker keeps its forked tasks in its own deque and works from the top. A worker with nothing to do steals from the bottom of someone else's deque, where the oldest and largest pieces are. Parallel streams and CompletableFuture's default executor both run on this machinery, in the common pool.

ForkJoin.java · a RecursiveTask, and the pool that parallel streams use
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;
import java.util.stream.LongStream;

public class ForkJoin {
    static final LongAdder TASKS = new LongAdder();

    static final class Sum extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
        private final long[] data;
        private final int from, to;
        Sum(long[] data, int from, int to) { this.data = data; this.from = from; this.to = to; }

        @Override protected Long compute() {
            TASKS.increment();
            if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {                     // small enough: just do it
                long s = 0;
                for (int i = from; i < to; i++) s += data[i];
                return s;
            }
            int mid = (from + to) >>> 1;
            Sum left = new Sum(data, from, mid), right = new Sum(data, mid, to);
            left.fork();                                      // push onto this worker's deque
            long r = right.compute();                         // work on the other half ourselves
            return left.join() + r;                           // often run by us, sometimes stolen
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long[] data = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000).toArray();
        ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(8);
        long total = pool.invoke(new Sum(data, 0, data.length));
        System.out.printf("sum %,d from %,d tasks; steals: %,d (varies by run)%n", total, TASKS.sum(), pool.getStealCount());
        pool.close();

        Set<String> threads = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
        long parallel = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 2_000_000).parallel()
                .peek(i -> threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName().replaceAll("\\d+$", "N")))
                .sum();
        System.out.println("parallel stream sum " + parallel + " ran on " + threads);
        System.out.println("common pool parallelism " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()
                + " (cores - 1; the caller thread joins in)");
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · ForkJoin.java · the steal count varies by run
sum 50,000,005,000,000 from 2,047 tasks; steals: 28 (varies by run)
parallel stream sum 2000001000000 ran on [ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N, main]
common pool parallelism 19 (cores - 1; the caller thread joins in)

Writing a fork/join task

  • Fork one half, compute the other. Forking both and joining both leaves the current worker idle.
  • Pick a threshold. Too small and task overhead dominates; too large and cores sit idle at the end. 10,000 elements gave 2,047 tasks here.
  • Join in reverse order of forking, so the worker usually pops its own task instead of waiting.
  • RecursiveTask<V> returns a value; RecursiveAction does not.
Do not block in itFork/join assumes tasks compute. A task that waits on I/O or a lock holds a worker, and the common pool has only cores − 1 of them for the whole JVM. If blocking is unavoidable, wrap it in ForkJoinPool.managedBlock so the pool can add a thread meanwhile.
Parallel streamsThe output shows a parallel stream running on common-pool workers and on main: the calling thread joins in, which is why the pool is sized to cores − 1. When that helps and when it hurts is on how a parallel stream runs.

Fixed rate keeps a timetable, fixed delay keeps a gap, and either one stops for good after an exception

ScheduledExecutorService runs tasks after a delay or periodically, on a small thread pool. The two periodic methods differ only when a run takes longer than the period, which in production is exactly when it matters. And both share one dangerous rule: if a run throws, the task is never scheduled again, and nothing is logged.

Scheduling.java · rate against delay, a task that throws, java.util.Timer
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class Scheduling {
    static long t0;
    static long at() { return Math.round((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 5e7) * 50; }   // to 50 ms

    static void work(long ms) {
        try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2)) {
            List<Long> rate = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(), delay = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
            t0 = System.nanoTime();
            ScheduledFuture<?> r = ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> { rate.add(at()); work(150); }, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            ScheduledFuture<?> d = ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { delay.add(at()); work(150); }, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            Thread.sleep(1_000);
            r.cancel(false);
            d.cancel(false);
            System.out.println("150 ms task, period 100 ms, start times in ms:");
            System.out.println("  scheduleAtFixedRate     " + rate);
            System.out.println("  scheduleWithFixedDelay  " + delay);

            AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger();
            ScheduledFuture<?> fragile = ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
                if (runs.incrementAndGet() == 3) throw new IllegalStateException("feed unavailable");
            }, 0, 20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            Thread.sleep(300);
            System.out.println("a periodic task that threw on run 3 ran " + runs.get() + " times in 300 ms; done=" + fragile.isDone());
            try {
                fragile.get();
            } catch (ExecutionException e) {
                System.out.println("  the exception was kept in the future: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
            }
        }

        Timer timer = new Timer("legacy-timer", true);
        timer.schedule(new TimerTask() {
            @Override public void run() { throw new IllegalStateException("one bad task"); }
        }, 0);
        Thread.sleep(100);
        try {
            timer.schedule(new TimerTask() { @Override public void run() { } }, 0);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("java.util.Timer after one task threw: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

  scheduleWithFixedDelay  [0, 250, 500, 750]
a periodic task that threw on run 3 ran 3 times in 300 ms; done=true

Exception in thread "legacy-timer" java.lang.IllegalStateException: one bad task
	at Scheduling$1.run(Scheduling.java:41)
	at java.base/java.util.TimerThread.mainLoop(Timer.java:572)

MethodNext run startsHere
schedule(task, delay)Once, after the delay
scheduleAtFixedRate(…, period)Previous start + period; at once if the run overran. Runs never overlap.Every 150 ms: as soon as each run ends
scheduleWithFixedDelay(…, delay)Previous end + delayEvery 250 ms: 150 work + 100 gap
One exception ends the scheduleThe task that threw on its third run never ran again: its future is done, and the exception waits inside it for a get nobody calls. Wrap every periodic body in try / catch (Exception e) that logs, so one bad run does not stop the feed for good.
java.util.Timer is worseOne thread runs every task, so a slow task delays all the others, and one exception kills that thread: every later schedule fails with Timer already cancelled. It also follows the wall clock, so a clock change shifts its timetable. The scheduled executor uses System.nanoTime.
In a clusterEvery instance runs its own schedule, so a nightly job on four pods runs four times. Use a lock such as ShedLock, or a scheduler with a shared store. Spring's @Scheduled uses a single thread by default. See batch and scheduling.

A virtual thread is a continuation run on a few carrier threads, and blocking takes it off its carrier

A virtual thread since 21 is a java.lang.Thread whose stack lives on the heap. The JDK schedules virtual threads onto a ForkJoinPool of carrier threads, one per core by default. When a virtual thread blocks in sleep, socket I/O, a lock or a queue, its frames are saved to the heap and the carrier is free to run another. That is how 100,000 threads each sleeping for a second finish in about two seconds on 20 carriers.

VirtualInternals.java · carriers change, and few carriers serve many threads
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualInternals {
    static String carrier() {                       // "VirtualThread[#29]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3"
        String s = Thread.currentThread().toString();
        return s.substring(s.indexOf('@') + 1);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var moved = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++)
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    String before = carrier();
                    Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(50));      // unmount, then mount again later
                    if (!carrier().equals(before)) moved.incrementAndGet();
                    return null;
                });
        }
        System.out.println("virtual threads that woke up on a different carrier: " + moved.get() + " of 20 (varies by run)");

        Set<String> carriers = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1));      // unmounts: the carrier runs others
                    carriers.add(carrier());
                    return null;
                });
        }
        System.out.printf("100,000 virtual threads slept 1 s each: %.1f s in total, on %d carrier threads (%d cores)%n",
                (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9, carriers.size(), Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · VirtualInternals.java
virtual threads that woke up on a different carrier: 20 of 20 (varies by run)

Pinning.java · one carrier, ten threads each sleeping 100 ms while holding a lock
// Run with: java -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1 Pinning.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

// One carrier thread, ten virtual threads, each sleeping 100 ms while holding its own lock.
public class Pinning {
    static long run(boolean useSynchronized) throws InterruptedException {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
                Object monitor = new Object();
                ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    if (useSynchronized) {
                        synchronized (monitor) { sleep(); }        // pinned on JDK 21 to 23
                    } else {
                        lock.lock();
                        try { sleep(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
    }

    static void sleep() {
        try { Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(100)); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println(Runtime.version().feature() + ": synchronized " + run(true) + " ms, ReentrantLock " + run(false) + " ms");
    }
}
Output on JDK 21, then on JDK 25 · Pinning.java
21: synchronized 1104 ms, ReentrantLock 116 ms
25: synchronized 127 ms, ReentrantLock 103 ms
PinningA virtual thread that cannot unmount holds its carrier while it waits. On JDK 21 to 23 that happened inside synchronized: with one carrier, ten 100 ms sleeps ran one after another, for over a second. JDK 24 fixed it (JEP 491), and on 25 they overlap again. Native code and foreign calls still pin. The JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned reports where.
Where they do not helpCPU-bound work: there are still only as many carriers as cores. Pooling them: they are cheap, so create one per task. Unlimited fan-out: 100,000 threads can open 100,000 connections, so bound the downstream with a Semaphore or a connection pool, as the LLD slide does.
The companionsScopedValue is final in JDK 25 (JEP 506) and replaces most ThreadLocal use. StructuredTaskScope runs subtasks as one unit that fails and cancels together; it is still a preview API in 25 (JEP 505), so this tab's code does not use it.

ConcurrentHashMap locks one bin at a time, and its compound methods are atomic per key

Since Java 8 a ConcurrentHashMap is a hash table much like HashMap, made safe bin by bin. Reads take no lock at all. A write into an empty bin is a single compare-and-set; a write into a non-empty bin locks only that bin's first node. A resize is shared out among the threads that write during it. What it cannot make atomic is two separate calls, such as get followed by put.

ChmDemo.java · HashMap against ConcurrentHashMap, then the atomic methods
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class ChmDemo {
    static void inParallel(int threads, Runnable work) throws InterruptedException {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) {
            for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) pool.submit(work);
        }
    }

    // Eight daemon threads write one plain HashMap. Any of three things can happen; report which did.
    static String racyHashMap() throws InterruptedException {
        Map<Integer, Integer> plain = new HashMap<>();
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger();
        Queue<String> errors = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        List<Thread> writers = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) {
            Thread w = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().unstarted(() -> {
                for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) { int k = next.getAndIncrement(); plain.put(k, k); }
            });
            w.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> errors.add(e.getClass().getSimpleName()));
            writers.add(w);
            w.start();
        }
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 5_000_000_000L;
        for (Thread w : writers) w.join(Math.max(1, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000));
        long stuck = writers.stream().filter(Thread::isAlive).count();
        if (stuck > 0) return stuck + " writer(s) still running after 5 s, looping in a corrupted bin";
        if (!errors.isEmpty()) return "writers threw " + new TreeSet<>(errors);
        return String.format("size %,d", plain.size());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("HashMap, 400,000 distinct keys from 8 threads: " + racyHashMap());
        Map<Integer, Integer> concurrent = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger();
        inParallel(8, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) { int k = next.getAndIncrement(); concurrent.put(k, k); } });
        System.out.printf("ConcurrentHashMap, the same keys: size %,d%n", concurrent.size());

        Map<String, Integer> racy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(), atomic = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        inParallel(8, () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                Integer old = racy.get("hits");                   // get, then put: two steps
                racy.put("hits", old == null ? 1 : old + 1);
                atomic.merge("hits", 1, Integer::sum);            // one atomic step per key
            }
        });
        System.out.printf("800,000 increments: get-then-put %,d, merge %,d%n", racy.get("hits"), atomic.get("hits"));

        AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger();
        Map<String, String> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++)
                pool.submit(() -> cache.computeIfAbsent("rates", k -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return "loaded"; }));
        }
        System.out.println("1,000 concurrent computeIfAbsent calls ran the loader " + loads.get() + " time(s)");

        try {
            concurrent.put(null, 1);
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("put(null, ...) -> NullPointerException");
        }
        Map<String, Integer> nested = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        try {
            nested.computeIfAbsent("a", k -> nested.computeIfAbsent("a", k2 -> 1));   // the map, from inside itself
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("computeIfAbsent inside computeIfAbsent: IllegalStateException: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> sales = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("tea", 40L, "milk", 75L, "jam", 12L));
        long total = sales.reduceValuesToLong(1, Long::longValue, 0L, Long::sum);    // parallel bulk operation
        String best = sales.search(1, (k, v) -> v > 50 ? k : null);
        System.out.println("reduceValues " + total + ", search " + best + ", mappingCount " + sales.mappingCount());
    }
}

ConcurrentHashMap, the same keys: size 400,000

Atomic per keyNot atomic
merge, compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresentget, then put: it lost increments above
putIfAbsent, replace(k, old, new), remove(k, v)containsKey, then put
Each single get, put, removeAnything across two keys
HashMap between threadsIt lost a large share of 400,000 distinct keys in the run above, with no exception. It can also throw from inside a resize, or corrupt a bin into a loop: in one run while this tab was written, a writer never finished, which is why the demo now gives them five seconds and reports what happened. Hashtable and Collections.synchronizedMap are correct, with one lock for the whole map.
Keep compute functions shortcomputeIfAbsent calls the loader once per absent key, while it holds that bin's lock. A slow remote call inside it stalls every writer to that bin. Touching the same map from inside the function is illegal: IllegalStateException: Recursive update.
Why no nullsA get returning null must mean absent. In a HashMap you can follow up with containsKey, but in a concurrent map the answer may change in between. mappingCount() returns a long estimate; the bulk methods take a parallelism threshold.

Copy-on-write makes reads free by making every write copy the whole array

CopyOnWriteArrayList never changes its array: each write builds a new one and swaps a volatile reference. Readers and iterators work on whichever array they started with, with no lock and no ConcurrentModificationException. The bill arrives on writes: 10,000 appends allocated 200 MB below. The other concurrent collections trade differently, using CAS-based linked structures.

CowDemo.java · snapshots, the write cost, a lock-free queue, a concurrent sorted map
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class CowDemo {
    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

    static long bytesFor(List<Integer> list, int adds) {
        long before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        for (int i = 0; i < adds; i++) list.add(i);
        return MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("audit", "email"));
        Iterator<String> snapshot = listeners.iterator();
        listeners.add("sms");                                  // a write copies the array
        List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>();
        snapshot.forEachRemaining(seen::add);
        System.out.println("iterator made before add(\"sms\") sees " + seen + "; list is " + listeners);
        try {
            listeners.iterator().remove();
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator.remove -> UnsupportedOperationException");
        }

        System.out.printf("10,000 adds allocate: ArrayList %,d bytes, CopyOnWriteArrayList %,d bytes%n",
                bytesFor(new ArrayList<>(), 10_000), bytesFor(new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(), 10_000));

        Queue<Integer> jobs = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) {
                int base = p * 1_000;
                pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) jobs.offer(base + i); });   // lock-free
            }
        }
        System.out.println("ConcurrentLinkedQueue after 4 producers: " + jobs.size() + " jobs (size() walks the whole queue)");

        ConcurrentSkipListMap<Integer, String> slots = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            for (int h = 9; h <= 17; h++) { int hour = h; pool.submit(() -> slots.put(hour * 100, "free")); }
        }
        System.out.println("ConcurrentSkipListMap: next slot after 12:30 is " + slots.ceilingKey(1230)
                + ", first " + slots.firstKey() + ", afternoon " + slots.tailMap(1300).keySet());

        List<Integer> shared = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)));
        int sum = 0;
        synchronized (shared) {                               // required: iteration is many calls
            for (int n : shared) sum += n;
        }
        System.out.println("synchronizedList iterated under its own lock: sum " + sum);
    }
}

ClassBuilt onUse it for
CopyOnWriteArrayList, …ArraySetAn array copied on every writeRead constantly, changed rarely: listeners, routing tables, feature flags
ConcurrentLinkedQueue, …DequeA lock-free linked list (CAS on the links)An unbounded queue shared by many threads, with no waiting
ConcurrentSkipListMap, …SetA lock-free skip list, O(log n)A sorted map shared between threads: the concurrent TreeMap
ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()A ConcurrentHashMapA concurrent HashSet
Collections.synchronizedListOne lock around every methodLegacy code; iterate inside synchronized (list)
The write cost is quadraticEach add copies n references, so n appends copy about n²/2 of them: 10,000 adds made 200 MB of garbage against 327 KB for an ArrayList. Fine for a list of 12 listeners changed at startup; a disaster for a log of events.
Snapshot means staleThe iterator made before add("sms") never saw it. That is the point, and also the trap: a reader can act on an element that was removed a moment ago. Snapshot iterators cannot remove either.
size() is not free everywhereConcurrentLinkedQueue.size() walks the whole queue, and its answer may be stale before it returns. Use isEmpty(), or keep a separate counter. A queue that needs a bound or blocking is a BlockingQueue.

A BlockingQueue is a hand-off with back-pressure: producers wait when it is full, consumers when it is empty

Every producer-consumer design in Java is a BlockingQueue underneath, including every ThreadPoolExecutor. Its value is in the blocking: put waits for space and take waits for an element, so a fast producer is slowed to the consumers' pace instead of filling the heap. Each method also comes in throwing, non-blocking and timed forms.

BlockingQueues.java · four method forms, the implementations, poison pills
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BlockingQueues {
    record Reminder(String text, long dueAtMs) implements Delayed {
        @Override public long getDelay(TimeUnit unit) {
            return unit.convert(dueAtMs - System.currentTimeMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        }
        @Override public int compareTo(Delayed o) {
            return Long.compare(getDelay(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS), o.getDelay(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
        }
    }

    static final String POISON = "__STOP__";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<String> bounded = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
        bounded.put("a");
        bounded.put("b");
        System.out.println("full queue: offer -> " + bounded.offer("c")
                + ", offer(50 ms) -> " + bounded.offer("c", 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
        Thread taker = new Thread(() -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(100); bounded.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        taker.start();
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        bounded.put("c");                                      // blocks until the taker makes room
        System.out.printf("put blocked for ~%d ms until a take made room%n", Math.round((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e8) * 100);
        taker.join();

        SynchronousQueue<String> handoff = new SynchronousQueue<>();
        System.out.println("SynchronousQueue offer with no taker -> " + handoff.offer("x") + ", size " + handoff.size());

        System.out.println("LinkedBlockingQueue() capacity: " + new LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity());

        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        DelayQueue<Reminder> reminders = new DelayQueue<>(List.of(new Reminder("in 150 ms", now + 150),
                new Reminder("in 50 ms", now + 50), new Reminder("in 100 ms", now + 100)));
        System.out.print("DelayQueue releases:");
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) System.out.print(" [" + reminders.take().text() + "]");
        System.out.println();

        PriorityBlockingQueue<Integer> urgent = new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 3));
        System.out.println("PriorityBlockingQueue take -> " + urgent.take());

        BlockingQueue<String> work = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(100);
        List<String> done = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        int consumers = 3;
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(consumers)) {
            for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (String job; !(job = work.take()).equals(POISON); ) done.add(job);
                    return null;                                // a poison pill ends each consumer
                });
            for (int i = 1; i <= 30; i++) work.put("job-" + i);
            for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) work.put(POISON);
        }
        System.out.println("poison pills: 3 consumers finished " + done.size() + " jobs and stopped");
    }
}

ThrowsReturnsBlocksTimes out
Insertaddofferputoffer(e, t, unit)
Removeremovepolltakepoll(t, unit)
Examineelementpeek
ImplementationShape
ArrayBlockingQueueBounded array, one lock. The predictable choice; optionally fair.
LinkedBlockingQueueLinked nodes, separate locks for put and take, so more throughput. Unbounded unless you pass a capacity: 2,147,483,647 above.
SynchronousQueueNo capacity: each put waits for a take. The cached thread pool's queue.
PriorityBlockingQueueUnbounded heap: the smallest element first.
DelayQueueUnbounded; an element can be taken only once its delay has expired.
LinkedTransferQueuetransfer waits until a consumer has received the element.
Bound every queueAn unbounded queue turns overload into memory growth and seconds of hidden latency, and the first symptom is an OutOfMemoryError. A bounded one turns it into blocked producers or rejections, which the caller can see and act on.
Stopping consumersPut one poison pill per consumer after the last real item, as above, or interrupt them with shutdownNow. The LLD tab builds the pattern by hand: producer-consumer and deadlock.

Latches, barriers, semaphores and phasers coordinate threads so you never write wait and notify

Five classes in java.util.concurrent exist only to make threads wait for each other in a particular shape. Pick by the shape: one event that many threads wait for, a group that meets repeatedly, a limit on how many may proceed, a group whose size changes, or two threads swapping data. Each is built on the same internal queue as ReentrantLock.

Synchronizers.java · all five, each in its typical shape
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class Synchronizers {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // CountDownLatch: a start gate for N workers, and a finish line for the coordinator.
        CountDownLatch startGate = new CountDownLatch(1), finished = new CountDownLatch(5);
        AtomicInteger started = new AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    startGate.await();                         // everyone waits for the gun
                    started.incrementAndGet();
                    finished.countDown();
                    return null;
                });
            System.out.println("before countDown: " + started.get() + " started");
            startGate.countDown();
            finished.await();
            System.out.println("after the gate opened and all finished: " + started.get() + " started; latch count " + finished.getCount());
        }

        // CyclicBarrier: 3 parties meet each round; the barrier action runs once per round.
        List<String> rounds = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        AtomicInteger round = new AtomicInteger();
        CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> rounds.add("round " + round.incrementAndGet() + " merged"));
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) {
            for (int p = 0; p < 3; p++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int r = 0; r < 2; r++) barrier.await();   // reused: no reset needed
                    return null;
                });
        }
        System.out.println("CyclicBarrier: " + rounds);

        // Semaphore: at most 3 callers inside at any moment.
        Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(3);
        AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), peak = new AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++)
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    permits.acquire();
                    try {
                        peak.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
                        Thread.sleep(10);
                        inside.decrementAndGet();
                    } finally { permits.release(); }
                    return null;
                });
        }
        System.out.println("Semaphore(3): 50 tasks, at most " + peak.get() + " inside at once");

        // Phaser: parties register and leave between phases.
        Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1);                          // the coordinator
        List<String> log = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) {
            for (int w = 1; w <= 3; w++) {
                int id = w;
                phaser.register();
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();             // phase 0: everyone loaded
                    if (id == 3) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); return; }   // leaves after phase 0
                    log.add("worker " + id + " in phase " + phaser.getPhase());
                    phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
                });
            }
            phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();                     // wait for phase 0
            phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();                     // and phase 1
            phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
        }
        Collections.sort(log);
        System.out.println("Phaser: " + log + ", terminated " + phaser.isTerminated());

        // Exchanger: two threads swap buffers.
        Exchanger<String> exchanger = new Exchanger<>();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            Future<String> a = pool.submit(() -> exchanger.exchange("full buffer"));
            Future<String> b = pool.submit(() -> exchanger.exchange("empty buffer"));
            System.out.println("Exchanger: filler got the " + a.get() + ", drainer got the " + b.get());
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · Synchronizers.java
before countDown: 0 started
after the gate opened and all finished: 5 started; latch count 0
CyclicBarrier: [round 1 merged, round 2 merged]
Semaphore(3): 50 tasks, at most 3 inside at once
Phaser: [worker 1 in phase 1, worker 2 in phase 1], terminated true
Exchanger: filler got the empty buffer, drainer got the full buffer
ClassShapeReusable
CountDownLatchWait until a count reaches zero: a start gate, or "these N tasks are done"No
CyclicBarrierN threads wait for each other, then an optional action runs once per roundYes
SemaphoreAt most N permits out at once: a concurrency limitYes
PhaserLike a barrier, but parties register and leave between phasesYes
ExchangerTwo threads meet and swap one object eachYes
Semaphore with virtual threadsThe natural way to bound a downstream: 50 virtual threads, a Semaphore(3), and never more than three calls in flight. Release in finally. A permit has no owner, so any thread can release it, which also means a missing release is never caught for you.
Broken barriersIf one party of a CyclicBarrier is interrupted or times out, every other party gets BrokenBarrierException and the barrier stays broken until reset(). A latch has no such failure mode, and also no way back: it cannot count up again.
Often there is a simpler toolWaiting for N submitted tasks is invokeAll, or allOf on CompletableFutures. Waiting for one thread is join. Reach for a latch when the threads are not yours to join, such as in a test that starts a server.

Name the problem first; the tool follows from it

Most concurrency questions, in interviews and in code review, reduce to a handful of needs. Each need has one tool that fits it and one tool people reach for instead, which is usually where the bug comes from. Read the right-hand column as the list of things to look for in a review.

I need toUseInstead of
Stop a worker loop from another threadvolatile boolean, or interrupt itA plain field, which the loop may never re-read
Count events from many threadsLongAdder; AtomicLong if read oftenvolatile long and ++
Update one value from its old valueAtomicReference.updateAndGet with an immutable valueRead, compute, then set
Keep an invariant across several fieldssynchronized or ReentrantLock around every accessMaking each field volatile
Wait for a lock, but not foreverReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout)synchronized, which cannot time out
Share a map between threadsConcurrentHashMap with merge and computeHashMap, or get then put
Load a cache entry once per keycomputeIfAbsentcontainsKey, then put
Share a list that is read far more than writtenCopyOnWriteArrayListsynchronizedList, iterated without its lock
Hand work from producers to consumersA bounded BlockingQueueA list and wait / notify
Limit concurrent calls to a dependencySemaphore, or a sized connection poolA small thread pool used as a limiter
Run tasks in the backgroundA ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and named threadsnew Thread per task, or newFixedThreadPool's unbounded queue
Handle many blocking I/O tasks at onceVirtual threads 21A platform pool of hundreds of threads
Split CPU-bound work across coresForkJoinPool, or a parallel streamMore threads than cores
Compose async calls with timeouts and fallbacksCompletableFuture on your own executorBlocking get() calls in sequence
Run something periodicallyScheduledExecutorService, with a try/catch in the taskjava.util.Timer
Wait for N things to finishinvokeAll, allOf or CountDownLatchPolling a counter in a loop
Carry per-request contextScopedValue 25, or a ThreadLocal removed in finallyA ThreadLocal that is never removed
The order to think inCan it be unshared? Can it be immutable? Is there a thread-safe class that already does this? Only then: which lock, and what exactly does it protect. Write that last answer in a comment beside the lock.
Where the designs liveThe LLD tab uses these tools in full designs: a thread-safe LRU cache and a token-bucket rate limiter. The interview questions on locks and synchronizers test the choices on this page.

javac compiles to bytecode for an abstract stack machine; the JVM interprets it, then compiles the hot parts

A .class file holds bytecode: instructions for a stack machine that exists only in the JVM specification. The JVM loads it, verifies it, links it, and starts by interpreting it. Methods that turn out to be hot are compiled to machine code, first quickly by C1 and then thoroughly by C2. If an assumption behind compiled code stops being true, the JVM throws that code away and interprets again.

Bytecode.java · a small method, and the class file's own header
import java.io.DataInputStream;
import java.io.InputStream;

public class Bytecode {
    static int total(int[] prices, int discount) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int p : prices) sum += p;
        return sum - discount;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("total = " + total(new int[] {250, 120, 90}, 60));
        try (InputStream raw = Bytecode.class.getResourceAsStream("Bytecode.class");
             DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(raw)) {
            int magic = in.readInt();
            int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(), major = in.readUnsignedShort();
            System.out.printf("class file: magic %X, version %d.%d (%d = Java %d)%n",
                    magic, major, minor, major, major - 44);
        }
        System.out.println("running on " + System.getProperty("java.vm.name") + " " + Runtime.version());
    }
}

Reading the bytecodeMeans
iconst_0, istore_2Push the int 0, pop it into local slot 2 (sum). Slot 0 is prices, slot 1 discount.
arraylength, ialoadThe enhanced for became an index loop over a copy of the array reference.
if_icmpge 35, goto 11The loop test and the jump back: no structured loops in bytecode.
iadd, isub, ireturnPop two ints, push the result; return the top of the stack.
The same Order class compiled with --release 25, run on JDK 21
Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class Order
	java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: Order has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0
Class file versionsThe major version is the Java release plus 44: 52 is Java 8, 55 is 11, 61 is 17, 65 is 21, 69 is 25. A JVM runs any older version and refuses newer ones, so build with --release set to the oldest JDK you deploy on. --release also checks the API you call, which -target alone does not.

A class is loaded on demand by a chain of loaders, and its identity includes the loader that defined it

Classes are loaded lazily, the first time code needs them. Each loader asks its parent first and defines the class itself only if the parent cannot, so java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader and cannot be replaced from the classpath. A loaded class is then linked, and initialised (its static initialiser run) only on its first active use. At run time a class is its name plus its loader.

ClassLoading.java · the chain, lazy initialisation, two loaders and one name
import java.net.URL;
import java.net.URLClassLoader;

public class ClassLoading {
    public static class Tariffs {                           // public: see the last part
        static { System.out.println("  Tariffs static initialiser runs, in " + Tariffs.class.getClassLoader().getName()); }
        public Tariffs() { }
        static final int VAT_PERCENT = 20;                          // a constant: no initialisation
        static int lookups = 0;
    }

    static String loader(Class<?> c) {
        ClassLoader l = c.getClassLoader();
        return c.getName() + " -> " + (l == null ? "bootstrap (null)" : l.getName());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println(loader(String.class));
        System.out.println(loader(java.sql.Connection.class));
        System.out.println(loader(ClassLoading.class));
        System.out.println("parent chain: app -> " + ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader().getParent().getName()
                + " -> " + ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader().getParent().getParent());

        System.out.println("reading the constant VAT_PERCENT = " + Tariffs.VAT_PERCENT);
        Class<?> loadedOnly = Class.forName("ClassLoading$Tariffs", false, ClassLoading.class.getClassLoader());
        System.out.println("forName(name, false, loader) loaded " + loadedOnly.getSimpleName() + " without initialising it");
        System.out.println("now touching a non-constant static field:");
        Tariffs.lookups++;
        System.out.println("  lookups = " + Tariffs.lookups);

        // Two loaders that do not delegate to each other each define their own class with the same name.
        URL classes = ClassLoading.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation();
        try (var first = new URLClassLoader("first", new URL[] {classes}, null);
             var second = new URLClassLoader("second", new URL[] {classes}, null)) {
            Class<?> a = first.loadClass("ClassLoading$Tariffs"), b = second.loadClass("ClassLoading$Tariffs");
            Object instance = a.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
            System.out.println("same name, two loaders: a == b " + (a == b) + ", b.isInstance(object of a) " + b.isInstance(instance)
                    + ", a == Tariffs.class " + (a == Tariffs.class));
        }
    }
}

new, a static method call, reading or writing a non-constant static fieldReading a static final compile-time constant: javac copied its value
Class.forName(name)Class.forName(name, false, loader), loader.loadClass(name)
Initialising a subclass (the superclass goes first)Tariffs.class, or declaring a variable of the type
X cannot be cast to XThe same class file defined by two loaders gives two unrelated classes: a == b is false and casting between them throws ClassCastException with both names identical. It happens when a library is both in an app server and in the web app, or in plugin systems and test frameworks.
Class loader leaksA class keeps its loader alive, and the loader keeps every class it defined, with their static fields. One ThreadLocal or JDBC driver registration that outlives a redeployed web app keeps the whole old app in Metaspace. After a few redeploys: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.
Each loader, its own staticsThe first loader's copy of Tariffs ran its static initialiser again, with its own lookups. Lazy initialisation is also what makes the holder idiom thread-safe: the JVM runs a class's initialiser exactly once, under a lock.

Each thread has its own stack; everything else is shared, and each area fails with its own error

The JVM's memory is not just the heap. Each thread has a stack of frames holding its locals and operands. The heap holds every object. Metaspace holds class metadata, the code cache holds JIT-compiled code, and direct buffers, thread stacks and the GC's own structures live outside the heap altogether. When one area runs out, the error message names it, and the message tells you where to look.

MemoryAreas.java · the pools, then four of the ways to run out
// Run with: java -Xmx64m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1m MemoryAreas.java
import java.lang.management.*;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.util.*;

public class MemoryAreas {
    static int depth;
    static void recurse() { depth++; recurse(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (MemoryPoolMXBean pool : ManagementFactory.getMemoryPoolMXBeans())
            System.out.printf("%-8s %s%n", pool.getType() == MemoryType.HEAP ? "heap" : "non-heap", pool.getName());

        try {
            recurse();
        } catch (StackOverflowError e) {
            System.out.println("StackOverflowError after about " + (depth / 1_000) * 1_000 + " frames (varies with -Xss and the JIT)");
        }

        List<long[]> hoard = new ArrayList<>();
        try {
            while (true) hoard.add(new long[1_000_000]);          // 8 MB each, all kept reachable
        } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {
            int held = hoard.size();
            hoard = null;                                         // release it so the program can go on
            System.out.println("OutOfMemoryError: " + e.getMessage() + " (after " + held + " x 8 MB)");
        }
        try {
            long[] huge = new long[Integer.MAX_VALUE];
            System.out.println(huge.length);
        } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {
            System.out.println("OutOfMemoryError: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(2 * 1024 * 1024);           // off-heap, capped by MaxDirectMemorySize
        } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {
            System.out.println("OutOfMemoryError: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        MemoryUsage heap = ManagementFactory.getMemoryMXBean().getHeapMemoryUsage();
        System.out.println("heap max " + heap.getMax() / (1024 * 1024) + " MB, set by -Xmx64m");
    }
}

The message saysLook at
Java heap spaceA leak or an undersized heap: take a heap dump (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError)
GC overhead limit exceededParallel GC spent nearly all its time collecting and recovered almost nothing: the same causes
MetaspaceToo many classes: generated proxies, or a class loader leak after redeploys
Requested array size exceeds VM limitAn array near Integer.MAX_VALUE elements, usually a bug in a size calculation
Cannot reserve … direct buffer memoryOff-heap buffers from Netty, NIO or a driver, past MaxDirectMemorySize
unable to create native threadOS or container limits on threads or memory, not the heap
StackOverflowErrorRecursion without a base case, or a very deep but valid one: raise -Xss
In a container, heap is not the whole billThe process uses the heap plus Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers and the GC's own structures. A container sized to exactly -Xmx gets killed by the kernel with no Java error at all. The Spring Boot tab works through the sizing: JVM memory.

Garbage is whatever cannot be reached from a GC root, and four kinds of reference decide what counts as reachable

The collector does not count references. It starts from the roots (every thread's locals, static fields, JNI handles and held monitors), marks everything it can reach, and reclaims the rest. That is why a cycle of objects that point at each other is still garbage. The java.lang.ref classes let code hold an object without keeping it alive, which is how caches, canonical maps and native-resource cleanup work.

References.java · weak, soft, cycles, WeakHashMap, Cleaner
// Run with: java -Xmx64m References.java
import java.lang.ref.*;
import java.util.*;

public class References {
    static final class Node {
        Node other;
        final byte[] payload = new byte[1024];
    }

    static void collect() throws InterruptedException {
        System.gc();                                    // a request; G1 runs a full collection here
        Thread.sleep(100);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object strongTarget = new Object();
        WeakReference<Object> weak = new WeakReference<>(new Object());
        WeakReference<Object> weakButHeld = new WeakReference<>(strongTarget);
        SoftReference<byte[]> soft = new SoftReference<>(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
        collect();
        System.out.println("after a GC: weak cleared " + (weak.get() == null) + ", weak to a held object cleared "
                + (weakButHeld.get() == null) + ", soft cleared " + (soft.get() == null));

        List<byte[]> pressure = new ArrayList<>();
        try {
            while (true) pressure.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
        } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {
            pressure.clear();
        }
        System.out.println("after memory pressure: soft cleared " + (soft.get() == null) + " (cleared before any OutOfMemoryError)");

        Node a = new Node(), b = new Node();
        a.other = b;
        b.other = a;                                    // a cycle
        WeakReference<Node> cycle = new WeakReference<>(a);
        a = null;
        b = null;
        collect();
        System.out.println("an unreachable cycle was collected: " + (cycle.get() == null));

        Map<Object, String> sessions = new WeakHashMap<>();
        Object key = new Object();
        sessions.put(key, "session data");
        System.out.println("WeakHashMap size with the key held: " + sessions.size());
        key = null;
        collect();
        System.out.println("WeakHashMap size after the key became unreachable: " + sessions.size());

        Cleaner cleaner = Cleaner.create();
        Object resource = new Object();
        cleaner.register(resource, () -> System.out.println("Cleaner action ran: release the native handle"));
        resource = null;
        collect();
        System.out.println("strongTarget kept alive to the end: " + (strongTarget != null));
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · References.java
after a GC: weak cleared true, weak to a held object cleared false, soft cleared false
after memory pressure: soft cleared true (cleared before any OutOfMemoryError)
an unreachable cycle was collected: true
WeakHashMap size with the key held: 1
WeakHashMap size after the key became unreachable: 0
Cleaner action ran: release the native handle
strongTarget kept alive to the end: true
ReferenceCleared whenUse
Strong (ordinary)Never, while reachableEverything
SoftReferenceThe JVM needs memory; always before an OutOfMemoryErrorMemory-sensitive caches, though a bounded cache is usually better
WeakReferenceThe next collection that finds no strong pathWeakHashMap keys, listeners, canonical maps
PhantomReferenceAfter the object is finalised; get() always returns nullCleanup of native resources, which Cleaner 9 wraps

Generations

Most objects die young, so new objects go into a small young generation that is collected often and cheaply, by copying the few survivors. Objects that survive several collections move to the old generation, which is collected rarely. Every collector in the JDK except Epsilon builds on this idea.

The collectors

G1: the default since 9, region-based, with a pause-time goal. ZGC: pauses under a millisecond at any heap size, generational since 21 and only generational since 24. Parallel: throughput for batch work. Serial: small heaps. Choosing and reading one: garbage collection.

System.gc() and finalizeSystem.gc() is a request the JVM may ignore, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC makes it a no-op; this demo relies on G1 honouring it. finalize() is deprecated for removal (JEP 421, 18): it ran late, or never, and could resurrect objects. Use try-with-resources, then Cleaner as a safety net.

The JIT compiles what runs hot, optimises it with what it has seen, and undoes it when it was wrong

HotSpot starts every method in the interpreter and counts calls and loop iterations. Hot methods are compiled by C1, which also records which types and branches actually occur, and then by C2, which uses that profile to inline, unroll loops and remove allocations. The first call below took milliseconds; the two-thousandth took tens of microseconds. That gap is why a freshly started service is slow, and why naive benchmarks lie.

Jit.java · warm-up, and an allocation the JIT removes
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;

public class Jit {
    record Point(double x, double y) {
        double length() { return Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y); }
    }

    static double walk(int steps) {                 // one Point per step, and none escapes it
        double total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) {
            Point p = new Point(i, i + 1);
            total += p.length();
        }
        return total;
    }

    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long[] nanos = new long[5];
        double sink = 0;
        for (int round = 0; round < 2_000; round++) {
            long t0 = System.nanoTime();
            sink += walk(10_000);
            long ns = System.nanoTime() - t0;
            if (round == 0) nanos[0] = ns;
            if (round == 1) nanos[1] = ns;
            if (round == 10) nanos[2] = ns;
            if (round == 100) nanos[3] = ns;
            if (round == 1_999) nanos[4] = ns;
        }
        System.out.printf("walk(10,000) took %d, %d, %d, %d, %d microseconds on runs 1, 2, 11, 101, 2000%n",
                nanos[0] / 1_000, nanos[1] / 1_000, nanos[2] / 1_000, nanos[3] / 1_000, nanos[4] / 1_000);

        long before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        sink += walk(1_000_000);
        long bytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        System.out.printf("walk(1,000,000) once warm allocated %,d bytes for 1,000,000 Points (sink %.0f)%n", bytes, Math.floor(sink));
    }
}

67   91       3       Jit$Point::length (23 bytes)
67   92       4       Jit$Point::<init> (15 bytes)
68   90       3       Jit$Point::<init> (15 bytes)   made not entrant: not used
68   93       4       Jit$Point::length (23 bytes)
68   91       3       Jit$Point::length (23 bytes)   made not entrant: not used
71   94 %     3       Jit::walk @ 4 (40 bytes)
72   95       3       Jit::walk (40 bytes)

76   94 %     3       Jit::walk @ 4 (40 bytes)   made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower level

In the PrintCompilation linesMeans
First two columnsMilliseconds since start, then the compile task's id
Tier 3, then 4C1 with profiling, then C2. Tier 0 is the interpreter; tiers 1 and 2 are rarely used C1 variants.
% and @ 4On-stack replacement: the loop at bytecode index 4 was compiled while walk was still running, and the frame switched over mid-loop.
made not entrantThat compiled version is retired: replaced by a better tier, or invalidated because an assumption stopped holding (deoptimisation).
OptimisationHere
InliningPoint.length() and the constructor were compiled into walk, which is what lets the next one work.
Escape analysisNo Point leaves its iteration, so C2 kept its fields in registers: 0 bytes allocated, against 32 MB with the analysis switched off.
SpeculationCalls are inlined for the classes seen so far, behind a cheap check; a new class arriving triggers deoptimisation.
Why naive benchmarks lieA loop timed with System.nanoTime measures the interpreter, then a compile, then code that may have removed the work entirely because its result is unused. Use JMH, which forks JVMs, warms up, and consumes results with a Blackhole.
Warm-up in productionThe first requests after a deploy run interpreted and trigger compiles that compete for CPU. Send synthetic traffic before marking an instance ready, or keep enough capacity that slow instances do not matter.
Starting warmerClass data sharing, and Project Leyden's AOT cache, store loaded classes and, from JDK 25, method profiles from a training run (JEPs 483, 514, 515). GraalVM native image compiles everything ahead of time. Both are on startup time.

Every object pays a header and rounds up to 8 bytes, so a boxed int costs four times an int

On a 64-bit HotSpot with a heap under 32 GB, an object starts with a 12-byte header: an 8-byte mark word for the hash, locking and GC age, and a 4-byte compressed class pointer. Fields follow, and the total rounds up to a multiple of 8. References are 4 bytes. JDK 25 can shrink the header to 8 bytes with compact object headers (JEP 519), an opt-in product flag. The per-object rows below count allocated bytes; the map line measures heap in use after a full GC.

ObjectSize.java · bytes per object, then a map against an array
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.IntFunction;

public class ObjectSize {
    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

    record Money(long cents) { }
    record Line(int qty, long cents) { }

    // Average bytes per object over many allocations, so the measurement itself is noise.
    static long each(IntFunction<Object> make) {
        int n = 100_000;
        Object[] keep = new Object[n];                     // allocated first: not counted
        long before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) keep[i] = make.apply(i);
        long bytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        return Math.round(bytes / (double) n);
    }

    static long liveHeap() {
        System.gc();
        return ManagementFactory.getMemoryMXBean().getHeapMemoryUsage().getUsed();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("compact object headers: " + ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().getInputArguments()
                .contains("-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders"));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "new Object()", each(i -> new Object()));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "Integer (not cached)", each(i -> Integer.valueOf(1_000 + i)));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "Long", each(i -> Long.valueOf(1_000 + i)));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "record Money(long)", each(i -> new Money(i)));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "record Line(int, long)", each(i -> new Line(i, i)));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "new int[0]", each(i -> new int[0]));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "new int[10]", each(i -> new int[10]));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "new Object[10]", each(i -> new Object[10]));
        System.out.printf("%-26s %3d bytes%n", "String.valueOf(10_000 + i)", each(i -> String.valueOf(10_000 + i)));

        int n = 1_000_000;                                 // retained size, measured after a full GC
        long base = liveHeap();
        Map<Integer, Integer> boxed = HashMap.newHashMap(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) boxed.put(i + 1_000, i + 1_000);
        long mapBytes = liveHeap() - base;
        base = liveHeap();
        int[] plain = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) plain[i] = i;
        long arrayBytes = liveHeap() - base;
        System.out.printf("1M int->int entries kept alive: HashMap %d bytes each, int[] %d bytes each (%d, %d)%n",
                mapBytes / n, arrayBytes / n, boxed.size(), plain.length);
    }
}

new Object[10]              56 bytes

Integer (not cached)        16 bytes
Long                        16 bytes
record Money(long)          16 bytes
record Line(int, long)      24 bytes
new int[0]                  16 bytes
