#BugSymptomFix
1A static SimpleDateFormat shared by request threadsWrong dates and odd exceptions under load, never in testsDateTimeFormatter, which is immutable
2containsKey then put, even on a ConcurrentHashMapAn expensive initialisation runs twice or morecomputeIfAbsent
3A parallel stream adding to an ArrayListLost elements, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionCollect: toList(), collect(…); no shared mutable state
4Lazy initialisation with if (x == null) x = load()Loaded several times; another thread may even see a half-built objectThe holder idiom, a volatile double-check, or eager initialisation
5Tasks that wait for subtasks in the same bounded poolEvery thread waits, nothing progresses: a hang with no deadlock in the dumpA separate pool for subtasks, CompletableFuture chaining, or ForkJoinPool
6synchronized on an Integer, a String literal or this in a public classUnrelated code shares the lock: contention or a surprise deadlockprivate final Object lock = new Object()
Testing for racesRun the code with many threads released together by a latch, as here, and repeat it. For memory-model bugs, OpenJDK's jcstress tool runs millions of trials on purpose. A passing single-threaded test proves nothing about any of these.
The tools that prevent themEvery fix in the table comes from one page: choosing a concurrency tool. The memory-model reasons behind bug 4 are on happens-before.

Leaks and waste rarely crash a test; they show up days later as a full pool, a slow GC or an OutOfMemoryError

A garbage collector frees memory nobody can reach, so a Java leak is memory something still reaches by mistake: a static map, a registered listener, an unclosed resource. Waste is the milder cousin: code that allocates far more than it needs, making the collector work harder. The numbers below are allocated or retained bytes, measured, and they do not change from run to run.

ResourceBugs.java · unclosed resources, boxing, regexes, caches, listeners
// Run with: java -Xmx512m ResourceBugs.java
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class ResourceBugs {
    static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean MX =
            (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

    static final class Connection implements AutoCloseable {
        static int open;
        Connection() { open++; }
        void query(String sql) { if (sql.contains("bad")) throw new IllegalStateException("syntax error"); }
        @Override public void close() { open--; }
    }

    static void leaky(String sql) {
        Connection c = new Connection();
        c.query(sql);                                       // throws: close() is never reached
        c.close();
    }
    static void safe(String sql) {
        try (Connection c = new Connection()) { c.query(sql); }
    }

    static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();             // grows forever
    static final List<Consumer<String>> LISTENERS = new ArrayList<>();    // never unregistered
    static final Pattern SKU = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}");

    static WeakReference<byte[]> openPage() {
        byte[] page = new byte[10 * 1024 * 1024];
        LISTENERS.add(event -> { if (event.equals("refresh")) System.out.println(page.length); });   // captures page
        return new WeakReference<>(page);
    }                                                       // the page's owner is gone after this returns

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (String sql : List.of("select 1", "bad sql", "select 2", "bad again")) {
            try { leaky(sql); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { }
        }
        System.out.println("1 without try-with-resources: " + Connection.open + " connections leaked out of 4");
        Connection.open = 0;
        for (String sql : List.of("select 1", "bad sql", "select 2", "bad again")) {
            try { safe(sql); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { }
        }
        System.out.println("  with it: " + Connection.open + " leaked");

        long before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        Long boxed = 0L;
        for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) boxed += i;                   // a new Long every time
        long boxedBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        long plain = 0;
        for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) plain += i;
        long plainBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        System.out.printf("2 summing 1M values: Long %,d bytes allocated, long %,d (same sum: %b)%n",
                boxedBytes, plainBytes, boxed == plain);

        String[] skus = new String[10_000];
        for (int i = 0; i < skus.length; i++) skus[i] = "ABC-" + (1_000 + i % 9_000);
        before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        int matched = 0;
        for (String s : skus) if (s.matches("[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}")) matched++;   // compiles the regex each call
        long matchesBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        before = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
        int matched2 = 0;
        for (String s : skus) if (SKU.matcher(s).matches()) matched2++;
        long patternBytes = MX.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;
        System.out.printf("3 10,000 regex checks: String.matches %,d bytes, precompiled Pattern %,d (%d, %d matched)%n",
                matchesBytes, patternBytes, matched, matched2);

        for (int request = 0; request < 150; request++)
            CACHE.put("report-" + request, new byte[1024 * 1024]);          // one entry per distinct key
        System.out.println("4 unbounded static cache after 150 requests: " + CACHE.size() + " MB held, and never released");
        CACHE.clear();

        WeakReference<byte[]> watch = openPage();
        System.gc();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println("5 a 10 MB page dropped by its owner, but its listener is still registered: reachable "
                + (watch.get() != null));
        LISTENERS.clear();
        System.gc();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println("  after removing the listener: reachable " + (watch.get() != null));
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · ResourceBugs.java
1 without try-with-resources: 2 connections leaked out of 4
  with it: 0 leaked
2 summing 1M values: Long 24,000,256 bytes allocated, long 0 (same sum: true)
3 10,000 regex checks: String.matches 11,280,000 bytes, precompiled Pattern 1,360,168 (10000, 10000 matched)
4 unbounded static cache after 150 requests: 150 MB held, and never released
5 a 10 MB page dropped by its owner, but its listener is still registered: reachable true
  after removing the listener: reachable false
#BugFix
1close() after the work, skipped by any exceptiontry-with-resources, for every AutoCloseable
2A Long accumulator in a loop: 24 bytes per iterationA primitive; watch for boxing in generic code and streams
3String.matches, split with a regex, replaceAll in a loopA static final Pattern, compiled once
4A static map used as a cache, keyed by request dataA bounded cache with eviction: Caffeine, or an LRU LinkedHashMap
5A listener registered and never removedUnregister in close(); return a handle from register
The listener holds the pageThe lambda captured page, the static list holds the lambda, so 10 MB stayed reachable after its owner forgot it. Event buses, observer lists, caches of callbacks and inner classes (with their hidden this$0) all leak this way. The weak reference showed the page was freed only once the listener went.
Leaks that are not memoryThe two leaked connections in case 1 would be pool connections in a real service: after enough failures the pool is empty and every request waits for its timeout. ThreadLocals in pools leak data between requests, as thread-safety strategies showed.
Finding themA heap that does not drop back after full collections is the sign. Take a heap dump and look at the dominator tree: the culprit is usually one map or list with millions of entries. The Spring Boot tab walks through it: memory leaks.

Three questions that open almost every Java interview

These thirty questions are the core-Java questions that keep recurring in 2025 and 2026 interviews, from screening calls to senior deep-dives. Each has a 30-second answer to say first and a go deeper paragraph for the follow-up, and each links to the slides in this tab that cover it, with the code that proves it.

How to practise with theseRead the question, look away, and answer out loud for thirty seconds. Then compare with the 30-second answer: whatever you left out is your study list, and the links under each answer open the slide that covers it. The browser's Back button returns you here.
Q1

Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

30-second answerAlways pass-by-value. For a primitive, the value copied is the number; for an object, the value copied is the reference. So a method can change the object the caller passed in, because both references point at it, but assigning a new object to the parameter only moves the method's own copy. That is why you cannot write a swap(a, b) in Java.

Go deeper: Draw the two stack frames and the one heap object. "Objects are passed by reference" is the answer interviewers are listening for as a mistake: in a pass-by-reference language the callee could rebind the caller's variable, and Java cannot. Strings and wrappers look as if they were copied because they are immutable, so no method can change them at all. To return two values, return a record.

In this tabPass-by-valuePrimitives and wrappers

Q2

Why is String immutable, and what is the string pool?

30-second answerEvery method that seems to modify a String returns a new one. That makes strings safe to share between threads, safe as hash keys (the hash is cached), and safe for security checks, because a path or class name cannot change after it was checked. It also lets the JVM pool them: identical literals and compile-time constants share one instance. new String(…) always makes a new object, and intern() returns the pooled one.

Go deeper: The pool has been in the heap since Java 7. "ord" + "er" is folded by javac into the literal, so it is the pooled instance; part + "er" is built at run time and is not. Hence == on strings passes tests and fails on input. Since Java 9 a Latin-1 string uses one byte per character (compact strings). And += in a loop copies everything each time: 57.8 MB against 98 KB for StringBuilder in this tab's demo.

In this tabStrings and the pool

Q3

What is the difference between == and equals, and why must hashCode be overridden with equals?

30-second answer== compares primitives by value and objects by identity: is it the same object? equals compares meaning, as each class defines it; Object's default is identity. Hash collections pick a bucket by hashCode and call equals only inside it. If two equal objects have different hash codes they land in different buckets, so a HashSet holds both "duplicates" and contains fails. Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

Go deeper: Name the contract: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, false for null. Then the traps: a hash code built from a mutable field loses the entry when the field changes; instanceof equality across a subclass that adds fields breaks symmetry; equals(Order) is an overload, not an override, which @Override catches. javac's -Xlint:overrides warns about equals without hashCode. A record generates both correctly.

In this tabThe Object contractEquality bugs

Three questions on how Java resolves methods and types

Interviewers use these to tell apart candidates who know the rules from those who know the vocabulary. Each answer has a mechanism behind it, and saying the mechanism is what scores: compile time against run time, and what erasure leaves behind.

Q4

What is the difference between overloading and overriding, and what cannot be overridden?

30-second answerOverloading is several methods with one name and different parameters; javac chooses one at compile time from the declared types of the arguments. Overriding is a subclass redefining an inherited method with the same signature; the JVM chooses at run time from the receiver's actual class. Static methods cannot be overridden, only hidden; private methods are not inherited; final methods and constructors cannot be overridden. Fields are never polymorphic.

Go deeper: Overload resolution has three phases: widening only, then boxing, then varargs, so pay(5) calls pay(long) rather than pay(Integer). An override may return a subtype (covariant), may not narrow access, and may not throw broader checked exceptions. In bytecode, overrides are reached through invokevirtual or invokeinterface, which look up the receiver's class; static calls are invokestatic.

In this tabOverloading and overridingDynamic dispatch

Q5

Abstract class or interface: which, and when, now that interfaces have default methods?

30-second answerAn interface is a type any class can adopt, any number at once. It can have default, static and private methods, but no instance state and no constructor, so it cannot enforce an invariant. An abstract class can hold state and a constructor, and a class can extend only one. Make the type callers depend on an interface; add an abstract class only when implementations share state or a fixed algorithm, the template method pattern.

Go deeper: Default methods exist so interfaces can grow without breaking implementers: that is how Java 8 added stream() to Collection. When two defaults collide, a superclass method wins, then the more specific interface, and otherwise the class must override and choose with X.super.m(). The JDK pairs both: List and AbstractList. Mention composition over inheritance as the usual alternative to both.

In this tabAbstract classes and interfacesComposition (LLD)

Q6

What is type erasure, and what is PECS?

30-second answerjavac checks generic types, inserts the casts, and then erases the type arguments, so List<String> and List<Integer> are the same ArrayList class at run time. You therefore cannot write new T(), create a T[], or test instanceof List<String>. PECS is how to type parameters: producer extends, consumer super. Read Ts from a ? extends T; write Ts into a ? super T.

Go deeper: Erasure was chosen so generic code could run alongside pre-Java-5 code. Declarations keep their generic signatures in the class file, which is how Jackson's TypeReference recovers Map<String, List<Integer>>. Generics are invariant while arrays are covariant, so arrays check every store at run time (ArrayStoreException). Raw types and unchecked casts cause heap pollution, and the ClassCastException appears far from the cause.

In this tabType erasurePECSGenerics traps

Three questions about failing safely and staying unchanged

Exception questions test judgement as much as rules: when to make a caller deal with something, and how to keep the cause when you translate. The immutability question is a checklist question, and a missing item is easy to spot.

Q7

Checked or unchecked exceptions: what is the difference, and when do you use each?

30-second answerChecked exceptions, subclasses of Exception but not of RuntimeException, must be caught or declared, and javac enforces it. Use them for recoverable conditions at a boundary the caller can act on, such as I/O or a timeout. Unchecked ones, RuntimeException and Error, need no declaration: programming errors and failures no caller can fix. Modern code, and Spring, favour unchecked domain exceptions, translated from checked ones at the boundary, keeping the cause.

Go deeper: Checked-ness exists only in the compiler; the JVM never checks it. Checked exceptions do not mix with lambdas, because the standard functional interfaces declare none. Never catch Error except to log at the top of a thread. A static initialiser that throws gives ExceptionInInitializerError once, then NoClassDefFoundError forever. Catching InterruptedException must restore the interrupt flag.

In this tabThe hierarchyDesigning exceptionsStreams and checked exceptions

Q8

What does try-with-resources do that a finally block does not?

30-second answerIt closes every AutoCloseable it declares, in reverse order, however the body exits. If the body throws and close() throws too, the body's exception propagates and the close failure is attached to it with addSuppressed. A hand-written finally that calls close() lets the close failure replace the original, so the log shows the symptom and loses the cause. It also skips a resource that is null.

Go deeper: A return inside finally discards any exception in flight, and javac's [finally] lint is the only warning. finally does not run on System.exit or a killed process. Since Java 9 an effectively final variable can be the resource. Make close() idempotent, because wrappers often close what they wrap. ExecutorService (19) and HttpClient (21) are AutoCloseable too.

In this tabtry-with-resources

Q9

How do you make a class immutable?

30-second answerMake the class final, or give it a private constructor and factories. Make every field private and final, with no setters; a change returns a new instance. Copy every mutable input in the constructor, for example with List.copyOf, and prefer immutable types such as Instant over Date. Never return mutable internals. A record does most of this, but you still copy mutable components in its compact constructor.

Go deeper: The payoffs: no locks needed, safe sharing and caching, stable hash keys, and final fields mean other threads see the object fully built. The traps: Collections.unmodifiableList is a view the owner can still change; List.copyOf is shallow, so the elements must be immutable too; and a non-final class can be subclassed into something mutable. String and the wrappers are the textbook examples.

In this tabImmutable classesRecordsThe drill

The HashMap questions, asked in every Java interview at every level

"How does HashMap work?" is the most common core-Java question there is. A junior answer describes buckets. A strong answer adds the hash spreading, the resize rule, Java 8's tree bins and what goes wrong with mutable keys, which is what the next two questions probe.

Q10

How does HashMap work internally?

30-second answerIt is an array of buckets whose length is a power of two, 16 by default. put calls hashCode, mixes the high 16 bits into the low ones, and masks with length - 1 to choose a bucket. It walks that bucket comparing the stored hash, then equals, and replaces the value or appends a node. When the size passes capacity × 0.75 the table doubles. get repeats the same lookup. Both are O(1) on average.

Go deeper: A power of two lets the index be one AND instead of a division, and spreading the hash keeps keys that differ only in high bits from colliding. On resize each node stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, decided by one bit of the stored hash, so hashCode is never called again. The null key lives in bucket 0. Iteration follows bucket order, which changes on resize. new HashMap<>(1000) still resizes at 769 entries; HashMap.newHashMap(1000) (19) does not.

In this tabHashing and bucketsResize and treeify

Q11

What happens when keys collide, and what did Java 8 change?

30-second answerColliding keys share a bucket as a linked list, so a lookup there is linear in the number of colliding keys. Since Java 8, adding to a bucket that already holds 8 nodes converts it into a red-black tree, making it O(log n), but only once the table has at least 64 slots; a smaller table resizes instead. A tree bin that shrinks to 6 nodes or fewer on a resize becomes a list again. Java 8 also switched to appending new nodes at the tail.

Go deeper: The change (JEP 180) defends against hash-flooding attacks, where crafted keys all collide. In this tab's demo, with every key hashing to 42, the 9th and 10th keys doubled the table to 32 and then 64, and the 11th made the tree. Tree bins order by hash, then compareTo if the keys are Comparable. A TreeNode is about twice the size of a Node. A bad hashCode is a performance cliff, never a correctness bug.

In this tabResize and treeifyWrite your own HashMap

Q12

Why should HashMap keys be immutable?

30-second answerThe map files each entry under its key's hash at the moment of insertion. If a field that hashCode uses changes later, the key now hashes to a different bucket: get and remove look in the wrong place and fail, while the entry stays in the map, unreachable. That is a wrong answer and a memory leak at once. String, records of immutable types and Instant cannot drift.

Go deeper: The demo in this tab mutates a Date key: get returns null while the map still reports size 1. The same holds for HashSet elements and for the fields a TreeMap comparator reads. If a key must change, remove it, change it, then put it back. A record is only a safe key if its components are immutable too: a List component reopens the problem.

In this tabEquality bugsThe Object contract

Three collections questions that test whether you have measured anything

Each of these has a textbook answer and a real one. The textbook says linked lists are good at inserts and fail-fast iterators catch concurrent changes. The real answers, backed by this tab's measurements, are what interviewers hope to hear.

Q13

ArrayList or LinkedList: when would you choose LinkedList?

30-second answerAlmost never. ArrayList is a resizable array: O(1) get, amortised O(1) appends, O(n) inserts in the middle by shifting, and 4 bytes per reference. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(1) at the ends or at an iterator's position, but O(n) get with a cache miss per node, and 24 bytes per node. For a queue or a stack, ArrayDeque beats both. LinkedList only wins for many middle inserts through an iterator you already hold.

Go deeper: ArrayList grows by half when full and allocates its first 10 slots lazily; presize it when you know the size. In this tab's measurement, 1,000 calls to get(n/2) on a million elements took a fraction of a millisecond on ArrayList and over a second on LinkedList. Even middle inserts are usually faster on the array, because System.arraycopy moves memory faster than the list can walk to the node.

In this tabArrayList and LinkedListQueues and deques

Q14

What is a ConcurrentModificationException, and how do you avoid it?

30-second answerNon-concurrent collections count their structural changes, and an iterator checks that count on each next(). If anything other than the iterator itself changed the collection, it throws, even in a single thread, for example list.remove(x) inside a for-each loop. Avoid it with Iterator.remove, removeIf, a ListIterator, collecting the changes and applying them after the loop, or a concurrent collection.

Go deeper: The check is best-effort, not a guarantee. Removing the second-to-last element of an ArrayList during a for-each ends the loop silently and skips the last element, because hasNext() only compares the cursor with the size. Concurrent collections never throw: ConcurrentHashMap's iterators are weakly consistent, and CopyOnWriteArrayList's iterate a snapshot. For maps, use entrySet().removeIf.

In this tabFail-fast iteratorsCopy-on-write

Q15

HashMap, Hashtable, synchronizedMap or ConcurrentHashMap?

30-second answerHashMap is not thread-safe and allows a null key and null values. Hashtable is legacy: every method locks one shared lock, and it rejects nulls. Collections.synchronizedMap wraps any map in one lock, but iteration and compound actions still need your own locking. ConcurrentHashMap reads without locking, locks one bin per write, offers atomic compute, merge and putIfAbsent, and rejects nulls. For a shared map, it is the default.

Go deeper: Nulls are banned because a null from get must mean absent: in a concurrent map you cannot follow up with containsKey safely. Even on a ConcurrentHashMap, get then put is a race; the demo lost increments that merge did not. A plain HashMap shared by eight writers lost a large share of 400,000 keys with no exception. Java 7's version used segments; Java 8 rewrote it around bins.

In this tabConcurrentHashMapWhich collection

Three memory-model questions that separate senior candidates from the rest

Most candidates can say "volatile means visible". These questions ask why visibility is not automatic, what exactly volatile promises, and why one famous idiom was broken for years. The demos in this tab give you a concrete story for each.

Q16

What is the Java Memory Model, and what does happens-before mean?

30-second answerThe JMM, chapter 17 of the language specification, defines when a write in one thread is guaranteed to be visible to a read in another. Without synchronisation the compiler, the JIT and the CPU may keep values in registers, reorder instructions and buffer stores, so another thread can see stale or out-of-order values. Happens-before is the guarantee: if A happens-before B, B sees A and everything before it. A program with no data races behaves as if it ran in one sequential order.

Go deeper: List the edges: unlocking a monitor before a later lock of it, a volatile write before a later read of it, Thread.start, join, the end of a constructor for final fields, and the java.util.concurrent hand-offs. Then tell the demo: with plain fields, a store-buffering test saw both threads read 0 in tens of thousands of 200,000 trials, a result no interleaving allows; with volatile, never. x86 reorders only a store with a later load; ARM reorders more.

In this tabThe memory modelHappens-before

Q17

What does volatile guarantee, and when is it not enough?

30-second answerA read of a volatile field sees the latest write to it, and everything the writing thread did before that write. It also stops the compiler and CPU reordering around it, and makes 64-bit long and double reads and writes atomic. It does not make a compound action atomic: count++ on a volatile still loses updates. Use it for flags and for publishing immutable snapshots; use an atomic or a lock for read-modify-write and for invariants across fields.

Go deeper: In the demo, four threads each incremented a volatile counter a million times and it ended below 4,000,000, while AtomicInteger and synchronized were exact. Making an array reference volatile does not make its elements volatile: use AtomicIntegerArray. A volatile write costs a memory fence; reads are almost free on x86. The plain flag in the visibility demo never stopped its reader, because the JIT read it once, outside the loop.

In this tabvolatileAtomics and CAS

Q18

Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

30-second answerinstance = new Config() is three steps: allocate, run the constructor, publish the reference. Without volatile, the publication can become visible to another thread before the constructor's writes, so a thread taking the unsynchronised fast path sees a non-null reference to a half-built object. volatile adds the happens-before edge from the constructor to every reader. Simpler still: the holder idiom, or an enum.

Go deeper: The first null check sits outside the lock so that, once initialised, readers never take it; the second, inside, stops two threads both creating one. Copy the field into a local to avoid a second volatile read. The holder idiom works because the JVM initialises a class lazily, exactly once, under a lock, and class initialisation is itself a happens-before edge. If every field of the object is final, a racy reader still sees those fields fully set, but relying on that is fragile.

In this tabDouble-checked lockingClass initialisationSingletons (LLD)

Three questions about choosing the right waiting tool

Interviewers ask these to see whether you reach for the simplest correct tool. The strong answer names the default, then the specific feature that would justify something heavier, and one failure mode of each.

Q19

synchronized or ReentrantLock?

30-second answerBoth are re-entrant mutual-exclusion locks with the same memory semantics. synchronized is part of the language: it releases itself, even on an exception, and each object has one wait set. ReentrantLock is a class you must unlock in finally, and in return it offers tryLock with a timeout, lockInterruptibly, optional fairness, several Conditions and introspection. Default to synchronized; use ReentrantLock when you need one of those features.

Go deeper: On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pinned a virtual thread to its carrier: in this tab's demo, ten sleeps on one carrier took over a second with synchronized and about 100 ms with ReentrantLock. JDK 24 removed that difference. tryLock with a timeout is also a deadlock escape hatch. For read-mostly data there are ReadWriteLock and StampedLock. Lock a private final object, never this in a public class.

In this tabExplicit locksPinning

Q20

What is the difference between wait and sleep, and why must wait be called in a loop?

30-second answersleep pauses the thread for a time and keeps every lock it holds. wait releases the monitor of the object it is called on, blocks until notify, notifyAll, a timeout or an interrupt, then takes the monitor back before returning, and must be called while holding that monitor. Always wait in a while loop that rechecks the condition: wakeups can be spurious, notifyAll wakes every waiter, and another thread may change the state before you run.

Go deeper: Calling wait without the monitor throws IllegalMonitorStateException: current thread is not owner. notify wakes one arbitrary waiter, possibly one that cannot proceed, so prefer notifyAll, or Conditions with separate wait sets. In real code, a BlockingQueue or a latch does all of this for you. Both sleep and wait respond to interrupts by throwing InterruptedException.

In this tabwait and notifyBlockingQueue

Q21

CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier or Semaphore?

30-second answerA CountDownLatch is one-shot: threads wait until a count reaches zero, as a start gate or to wait for N tasks. A CyclicBarrier makes a fixed group of threads wait for each other, round after round, with an optional action each time. A Semaphore hands out N permits, limiting how many threads proceed at once, with no owner per permit. A Phaser generalises the first two for groups whose size changes.

Go deeper: If one party at a barrier is interrupted or times out, the others get BrokenBarrierException until reset(). A latch cannot count up again. A semaphore is the natural way to bound a slow dependency from virtual threads: in the demo, 50 tasks behind Semaphore(3) never had more than three inside. Often a simpler tool fits: invokeAll, CompletableFuture.allOf or join.

In this tabSynchronizersChoosing a tool

Three questions about running work in the background, and the defaults that hurt

Every service runs background work, and these questions check that you know what the convenient defaults do under load. The answers that score name the trap in the default: an unbounded queue, a shared common pool, a carrier thread that cannot be released.

Q22

How does a ThreadPoolExecutor decide to queue, grow or reject, and why is newFixedThreadPool risky?

30-second answerOn each execute: if fewer than the core number of threads are running, start a core thread; otherwise offer the task to the queue; if the queue is full and there are fewer than the maximum threads, start an extra one; otherwise call the rejection handler, which throws by default. Extra threads appear only when the queue is full. newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue, so it never grows and never rejects: under overload the queue, the latency and the heap grow until something fails.

Go deeper: Build pools explicitly: a bounded queue, named threads, and a deliberate policy. CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread run the task, which slows producers down for free. newCachedThreadPool has the opposite problem: no queue and no thread limit. Size CPU-bound pools near the core count and I/O-bound ones by cores × (1 + wait/compute), then cap by what they call, such as the database pool. Monitor queue length, not just thread count.

In this tabThreadPoolExecutorWhy executors

Q23

Future or CompletableFuture, and what is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose?

30-second answerA Future can only be blocked on, polled or cancelled. A CompletableFuture can also be completed by hand and composed: attach steps that run when it completes, combine several, recover from errors and add timeouts, all without blocking a thread. thenApply maps the result with a plain function, T -> U. thenCompose takes a function that returns another future, T -> CompletableFuture<U>, and flattens it, like flatMap.

Go deeper: thenCombine joins two futures running at once, and allOf waits for many: five 200 ms calls took 200 ms in the demo because all were started before anything waited. Failures arrive wrapped in CompletionException; exceptionally and handle recover, whenComplete only observes. Without an executor, async stages run in the shared common pool, so never put blocking I/O there. cancel(true) does not interrupt the running task.

In this tabCompositionErrors and threads

Q24

What are virtual threads, and when do they not help?

30-second answerVirtual threads, final in Java 21, are ordinary Thread objects that the JDK schedules onto a small pool of carrier threads, one per core by default. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, a sleep or a lock, it is unmounted and its carrier runs another, so blocking thread-per-request code scales to hundreds of thousands of concurrent tasks. They do not speed up CPU-bound work, should never be pooled, and need explicit limits on the resources they call.

Go deeper: In the demo, 100,000 virtual threads each sleeping one second finished in about two seconds on 20 carriers. Pinning: on JDK 21 to 23 a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized held its carrier; JDK 24 fixed that, and native calls still pin. A million threads means a million ThreadLocal copies, which is why ScopedValue became final in 25. In Spring Boot 3.2 and later, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true switches request handling to them.

In this tabVirtual threadsVirtual threads (LLD)

Three questions about what the JVM is doing underneath your code

JVM questions come up most in senior and production-focused rounds, often as "tell me about an OutOfMemoryError you fixed". Answer with the model first, then the evidence you would collect: the error message, a heap dump, a GC log, a thread dump.

Q25

What are the JVM's memory areas, and how do StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError differ?

30-second answerEach thread has a program counter and a stack of frames holding locals and operands. Shared areas are the heap, split into young (Eden and two survivor spaces) and old generations; Metaspace for class metadata; the code cache for compiled code; and native memory for direct buffers, thread stacks and the GC's own structures. StackOverflowError means one thread's stack is full, usually from runaway recursion. OutOfMemoryError means an area could not satisfy an allocation, and its message names the area.

Go deeper: Know the messages: Java heap space, Metaspace, Cannot reserve … direct buffer memory, unable to create native thread, Requested array size exceeds VM limit. Each points at a different cause and flag: -Xmx, MaxMetaspaceSize, MaxDirectMemorySize, OS limits, a size bug. In a container the process needs the heap plus everything else, so a limit equal to -Xmx gets the process killed. Always run with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.

In this tabMemory areasJVM memory (Boot)

Q26

How does the garbage collector decide what is garbage, and why are heaps generational?

30-second answerBy tracing, not by counting references. Starting from the GC roots (every thread's locals, static fields, JNI references and held monitors), the collector marks everything reachable and reclaims the rest, including cycles that point only at each other. Most objects die young, so new objects go into a young generation that is collected often and cheaply by copying the few survivors; long-lived ones are promoted to the old generation and collected rarely. G1 is the default collector; ZGC targets sub-millisecond pauses.

Go deeper: A Java memory leak is an object that is still reachable by mistake: a static map, a listener, a ThreadLocal. Soft references are cleared before any OutOfMemoryError, weak ones at the next collection, and phantom ones drive Cleaner. System.gc() is only a request. finalize is deprecated for removal. Choosing between G1, ZGC and Parallel depends on the latency and throughput goals, and is measured from GC logs.

In this tabGC rootsGarbage collection (Boot)

Q27

What happens between "java -jar" and your first line of main, and why are the first requests slow?

30-second answerThe launcher starts the JVM, which sets up the runtime and the collector, then loads the main class through the application class loader, which delegates to the platform and bootstrap loaders. The class is linked (verified, prepared, resolved) and initialised (its static initialisers run), and main starts in the interpreter. Other classes load lazily when first used, and hot code is compiled by C1 and then C2. Early requests pay for class loading, initialisation and interpretation: that is warm-up.

Go deeper: In the demo the first call of a method took milliseconds and the two-thousandth tens of microseconds. A class built for a newer JDK fails here with UnsupportedClassVersionError. Class data sharing and Leyden's AOT cache (JDK 24 and 25) store loaded classes and method profiles from a training run to start warmer; GraalVM native image compiles ahead of time. In Kubernetes, only report ready after warm-up traffic.

In this tabSource to running codeClass loadingThe JIT

Three questions about the Java that came after 8

These test whether you have kept up, and whether you use new features with judgement. A good answer is specific: the release, what the feature replaces, and a case where you would not use it.

Q28

What has changed in Java since 8 that you actually use?

30-second answerBy 11: var, the List.of factories, HttpClient and the new String helpers. By 17: records, text blocks, switch expressions, instanceof patterns, sealed classes and helpful NullPointerException messages. By 21: virtual threads, pattern matching in switch with record patterns, and sequenced collections. In 25: scoped values, flexible constructor bodies, compact source files and compact object headers. Plus the runtime: G1 by default, container awareness, and JFR included free.

Go deeper: Say what broke on an upgrade you did: reflection into JDK internals closed in 16 and 17, the Java EE modules removed in 11, libraries built for a newer class file version. Explain the cadence: a feature release every six months and an LTS every two years, with previews behind --enable-preview until they are final. Structured concurrency is still a preview in 25.

In this tabEach LTSThe new syntaxJava 25

Q29

When would you not use a record?

30-second answerA record is a transparent, shallowly immutable carrier: a final class whose private final fields are its components, with a canonical constructor, accessors and value-based equals, hashCode and toString, built into the language. Do not use one when you need mutable state, inheritance from a class, hidden or derived state stored in fields, or framework contracts such as JPA entities, which need a no-argument constructor and proxies. Use it for DTOs, events, keys, projections and value objects.

Go deeper: Validate and copy in the compact constructor, because a record holding a caller's List is not immutable. An array component makes equals compare identity. Records deserialize through their canonical constructor, so validation runs there too, unlike ordinary classes. Lombok's @Value gives similar classes through an annotation processor, with more knobs and a build-time dependency.

In this tabRecordsSerialization

Q30

What problem do sealed classes and pattern matching solve together?

30-second answerA sealed type lists exactly which classes may extend it, so the compiler knows the complete set. A switch over it, matching types and deconstructing records, can then be checked for exhaustiveness: no default is needed, and adding a new subtype breaks every switch that does not handle it, at compile time. Together they give Java algebraic data types: a closed hierarchy of records, handled by one switch per operation instead of a visitor.

Go deeper: Permitted subclasses must be final, sealed or non-sealed. Guards use when, case null handles null, and a case that can never match is a dominance error. If a new subtype arrives without recompiling the switch, it throws MatchException. The design trade-off: sealed types and switches when the set of types is fixed and operations keep coming; an interface method when new types keep coming.

In this tabSealed typesThe Java 21 toolkit (LLD)

Core-Java coding questions test whether your code survives two threads, a null and a follow-up

The drills in this section are the ones Java interviews set over and over: an immutable class, a hash map from scratch, two threads in turn, parallel calls with timeouts, a concurrent counter, and a bug hunt. The code matters less than the way you get there. Interviewers score the questions you ask, the invariant you state, whether you test your own code, and how you answer "and now make it thread-safe".

The five steps, out loud

  1. Pin the contract. Inputs, nulls, sizes, ordering, and above all: is it used by one thread or many? Each answer changes the design.
  2. State the invariant. "Each key lives in exactly one bucket, chosen by its hash." "Exactly one thread prints at a time, odd first." Code is easier to check against a sentence.
  3. Write compilable Java. Real types, real imports, generics where they belong. A record or a final class with private final fields is a quick signal of care.
  4. Test it in front of them. A main with the normal case, an edge case and a failing input. For concurrency, repeat the run, and say why the code cannot race.
  5. Name the cost and the next step. Time and space, then the follow-up you would expect: resize, thread safety, back-pressure, timeouts.
DrillWhat it really tests
Immutable classDefensive copies, final, the difference between a view and a copy
Your own HashMapequals and hashCode, resizing, collisions, a generic API
Odd/even printerMonitors, waiting in a loop, hand-off between threads
Parallel callsComposition, timeouts, fallbacks, which failures are fatal
Word counterAtomic updates, no shared mutable state, checking the answer
Spot the bugReading code for what it does, not what it says
What sinks candidatesCoding before asking whether it must be thread-safe. if instead of while around wait. A HashMap shared between threads "because it's only a counter". Never running the code, so the interviewer finds the off-by-one.
How to use these slidesRead the prompt in the heading, close the slide, write your version, and run it. Then compare. Every listing here compiles with javac --release 21 -Xlint:all and checks itself, so its output is the bar to meet.
Stream-heavy questions"Group employees by department", "find the second-highest salary": those live in the Streams tab's coding drills, and algorithm questions in the DSA tab.

Drill: "make this Booking class immutable", and prove that it is

You get a class with a setter, a Date, and a list it shares with its callers. A full answer fixes six things and shows each fix working: the caller's list, the getter's list, the Date, the setter, subclassing, and invalid input. Then it adds value-based equality, because an immutable object is usually a value.

DrillImmutable.java · the given class, the answer, and the attacks
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;

public class DrillImmutable {
    // The class you are given: "make this immutable".
    static class Booking {
        private String guest;
        private Date checkIn;
        private List<String> rooms;
        Booking(String guest, Date checkIn, List<String> rooms) { this.guest = guest; this.checkIn = checkIn; this.rooms = rooms; }
        String guest() { return guest; }
        Date checkIn() { return checkIn; }
        List<String> rooms() { return rooms; }
        void setGuest(String guest) { this.guest = guest; }
    }

    // The answer.
    static final class ImmutableBooking {                          // 1 final: no mutable subclass
        private final String guest;                                // 2 private final fields
        private final LocalDate checkIn;                           // 3 an immutable type, not Date
        private final List<String> rooms;

        ImmutableBooking(String guest, LocalDate checkIn, List<String> rooms) {
            this.guest = Objects.requireNonNull(guest, "guest");
            this.checkIn = Objects.requireNonNull(checkIn, "checkIn");
            if (rooms.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("at least one room");
            this.rooms = List.copyOf(rooms);                       // 4 copy in; also rejects null rooms
        }
        String guest() { return guest; }
        LocalDate checkIn() { return checkIn; }
        List<String> rooms() { return rooms; }                     // 5 already unmodifiable
        ImmutableBooking withGuest(String newGuest) {              // 6 change = new object
            return new ImmutableBooking(newGuest, checkIn, rooms);
        }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof ImmutableBooking b && guest.equals(b.guest) && checkIn.equals(b.checkIn) && rooms.equals(b.rooms);
        }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(guest, checkIn, rooms); }
        @Override public String toString() { return guest + " " + checkIn + " " + rooms; }
    }

    static String attempt(Runnable attack) {
        try { attack.run(); return "changed it"; }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { return "blocked"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> rooms = new ArrayList<>(List.of("101"));
        Date date = new Date(0);
        Booking given = new Booking("Ana", date, rooms);
        rooms.add("102");
        date.setTime(86_400_000L);
        given.rooms().add("103");
        given.setGuest("Bo");
        System.out.println("given class after 4 outside changes: " + given.guest() + " " + given.checkIn().toInstant() + " " + given.rooms());

        List<String> rooms2 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("101"));
        ImmutableBooking b = new ImmutableBooking("Ana", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 8), rooms2);
        rooms2.add("102");
        System.out.println("caller adds to its list: " + b.rooms());
        System.out.println("getter's list .add():    " + attempt(() -> b.rooms().add("103")));
        ImmutableBooking renamed = b.withGuest("Bo");
        System.out.println("withGuest: " + renamed + ", original still " + b);
        System.out.println("equal by value: " + b.equals(new ImmutableBooking("Ana", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 8), List.of("101"))));
        for (Runnable bad : List.<Runnable>of(() -> new ImmutableBooking(null, LocalDate.EPOCH, List.of("1")),
                () -> new ImmutableBooking("X", LocalDate.EPOCH, List.of()),
                () -> new ImmutableBooking("X", LocalDate.EPOCH, Arrays.asList("1", null)))) {
            try { bad.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + e.getMessage()); }
        }
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · DrillImmutable.java
given class after 4 outside changes: Bo 1970-01-02T00:00:00Z [101, 102, 103]
caller adds to its list: [101]
getter's list .add():    blocked
withGuest: Bo 2026-10-08 [101], original still Ana 2026-10-08 [101]
equal by value: true
rejected: NullPointerException guest
rejected: IllegalArgumentException at least one room
rejected: NullPointerException null
StepCloses
1 final classA subclass that adds a setter or overrides rooms()
2 private final fieldsReassignment, including by this class's own code later
3 LocalDatedate.setTime(…) by anyone who held the Date
4 List.copyOf inThe caller's later add; also rejects null elements
5 return the unmodifiable copyrooms().add(…) from readers
6 withGuestThe need for a setter at all
The record versionSay it next: record Booking(String guest, LocalDate checkIn, List<String> rooms) with a compact constructor holding the same checks and rooms = List.copyOf(rooms). It gives steps 1, 2 and the equality for free. The interviewer often wants to hear that you know both.
Follow-up: "what if Room were a class?"List.copyOf copies references, not rooms. If Room is mutable, the booking is not immutable either: copy each room, or make Room immutable too. Immutability is only as deep as the types you hold.
Follow-up: "why bother?"Thread safety without locks, safe as map keys, safe to cache and share, and simpler reasoning: nothing changes behind your back. The background is on writing an immutable class.

Drill: "implement a HashMap with put, get and remove", in about sixty lines

Interviewers ask for this because it touches everything: generics, equals and hashCode, arrays of a generic type, collisions, resizing and null keys. Aim for separate chaining, a power-of-two table, a stored hash per node and a resize at 75% full. Then prove it, here by running 100,000 random operations against java.util.HashMap and comparing every answer.

MyHashMap.java · the map, and a randomised check against the JDK's
import java.util.*;

// Separate chaining, power-of-two table, resize at 0.75, null key allowed.
public class MyHashMap<K, V> {
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final int hash;
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> next;
        Node(int hash, K key, V value, Node<K, V> next) { this.hash = hash; this.key = key; this.value = value; this.next = next; }
    }

    private Node<K, V>[] table = newTable(16);
    private int size;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private static <K, V> Node<K, V>[] newTable(int n) { return (Node<K, V>[]) new Node<?, ?>[n]; }

    private static int hash(Object key) {
        if (key == null) return 0;
        int h = key.hashCode();
        return h ^ (h >>> 16);                                   // spread the high bits
    }

    public V get(Object key) {
        int h = hash(key);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[h & (table.length - 1)]; n != null; n = n.next)
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) return n.value;
        return null;
    }

    public V put(K key, V value) {
        int h = hash(key), i = h & (table.length - 1);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next)
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) { V old = n.value; n.value = value; return old; }
        table[i] = new Node<>(h, key, value, table[i]);           // prepend: O(1)
        if (++size > table.length * 3 / 4) resize();
        return null;
    }

    public V remove(Object key) {
        int h = hash(key), i = h & (table.length - 1);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i], prev = null; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next)
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) {
                if (prev == null) table[i] = n.next; else prev.next = n.next;
                size--;
                return n.value;
            }
        return null;
    }

    public int size() { return size; }

    private void resize() {
        Node<K, V>[] old = table;
        table = newTable(old.length * 2);
        for (Node<K, V> head : old)
            for (Node<K, V> n = head, next; n != null; n = next) {
                next = n.next;
                int i = n.hash & (table.length - 1);             // the stored hash: no hashCode call
                n.next = table[i];
                table[i] = n;
            }
    }

    int capacity() { return table.length; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyHashMap<String, Integer> mine = new MyHashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> real = new HashMap<>();
        Random random = new Random(7);                           // seeded: the same run every time
        int mismatches = 0;
        for (int op = 0; op < 100_000; op++) {
            String key = random.nextInt(20) == 0 ? null : "k" + random.nextInt(5_000);
            int kind = random.nextInt(3), value = random.nextInt();
            Object a, b;
            if (kind == 0) { a = mine.put(key, value); b = real.put(key, value); }
            else if (kind == 1) { a = mine.get(key); b = real.get(key); }
            else { a = mine.remove(key); b = real.remove(key); }
            if (!Objects.equals(a, b) || mine.size() != real.size()) mismatches++;
        }
        System.out.println("100,000 random put/get/remove against java.util.HashMap: " + mismatches
                + " mismatches; size " + mine.size() + ", capacity " + mine.capacity());

        MyHashMap<String, String> collide = new MyHashMap<>();
        collide.put("Aa", "first");
        collide.put("BB", "second");                             // same hashCode: same bucket
        System.out.println("colliding keys: " + collide.get("Aa") + ", " + collide.get("BB") + "; remove(Aa) -> "
                + collide.remove("Aa") + ", get(BB) still " + collide.get("BB"));
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · MyHashMap.java
100,000 random put/get/remove against java.util.HashMap: 0 mismatches; size 2485, capacity 4096
colliding keys: first, second; remove(Aa) -> first, get(BB) still second
ChoiceSay why
Power-of-two lengthThe index is hash & (length - 1), no division
h ^ (h >>> 16)The mask uses only low bits; this lets the high bits count
Hash stored in the nodeCheap rejection before equals; resize never calls hashCode
Objects.equalsHandles the null key, which hashes to bucket 0
Prepend on insertO(1), after the scan that checked the key is absent
new Node<?, ?>[n] and one castGeneric arrays cannot be created; one unchecked cast, suppressed at the smallest scope

Complexity

get, put and remove are O(1) on average, O(n) if every key collides. A resize is O(n), but doubling makes it O(1) amortised per insert. Memory: the table plus one node per entry.

Follow-ups to expect

"Make the worst case O(log n)": tree bins, as Java 8 did. "Make it thread-safe": one lock is easy, lock striping or per-bin locking is what ConcurrentHashMap does. "Iterate it": walk the table, and track a modification count to fail fast.

Test it the way it was tested hereA randomised comparison against a trusted implementation, with a seeded Random, finds edge cases you would not think to write. Add deliberate collisions ("Aa" and "BB") and the null key. The real one's internals are on HashMap internals.

Drill: "print 1 to 10 with two threads, one odd and one even, in order"

The classic hand-off problem. Each thread must wait for its turn and then pass the turn on, with no busy-waiting and no missed signals. Give two solutions: one with a monitor and wait/notifyAll, which shows you understand the mechanism, and one with two semaphores, which shows you would not write the first in production.

OddEven.java · wait/notify, then semaphores, then 200 repeat runs
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class OddEven {
    static final int MAX = 10;

    // Solution 1: one monitor, a shared counter, wait in a loop.
    static final class Printer {
        private int next = 1;
        private final List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        synchronized void print(boolean odd) throws InterruptedException {
            while (true) {
                while (next <= MAX && (next % 2 == 1) != odd) wait();   // not my turn
                if (next > MAX) { notifyAll(); return; }
                out.add(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ":" + next++);
                notifyAll();                                            // wake the other thread
            }
        }
    }

    // Solution 2: two semaphores pass the turn back and forth.
    static List<String> withSemaphores() throws InterruptedException {
        Semaphore oddTurn = new Semaphore(1), evenTurn = new Semaphore(0);
        List<String> out = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        Thread odd = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 1; i <= MAX; i += 2) { oddTurn.acquire(); out.add("odd:" + i); evenTurn.release(); }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }, "odd");
        Thread even = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 2; i <= MAX; i += 2) { evenTurn.acquire(); out.add("even:" + i); oddTurn.release(); }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }, "even");
        odd.start(); even.start();
        odd.join(); even.join();
        return out;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Printer p = new Printer();
        Thread odd = new Thread(() -> { try { p.print(true); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "odd");
        Thread even = new Thread(() -> { try { p.print(false); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "even");
        odd.start(); even.start();
        odd.join(); even.join();
        System.out.println("wait/notify: " + p.out);
        System.out.println("semaphores:  " + withSemaphores());

        boolean allInOrder = true;
        for (int run = 0; run < 200; run++) {                            // repeat: races show up in repetition
            List<String> r = withSemaphores();
            for (int i = 0; i < MAX; i++) if (!r.get(i).endsWith(":" + (i + 1))) allInOrder = false;
        }
        System.out.println("200 more runs, every one in order: " + allInOrder);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · OddEven.java
wait/notify: [odd:1, even:2, odd:3, even:4, odd:5, even:6, odd:7, even:8, odd:9, even:10]
semaphores:  [odd:1, even:2, odd:3, even:4, odd:5, even:6, odd:7, even:8, odd:9, even:10]
200 more runs, every one in order: true

What to say while writing it

  • The invariant: next is the number to print, and only the thread whose parity matches may print it.
  • while, not if: a thread can wake spuriously, or wake when it is still not its turn.
  • notifyAll: with only two threads notify works, but notifyAll stays correct when the problem grows to three.
  • Termination: the last thread must wake the other, or it waits forever; the next > MAX check handles both.
  • Semaphores: a permit is the turn. Odd starts with it; each thread releases the other's.
Follow-up: three threads, round robinGeneralise the monitor version: thread k of n prints when next % n == k. Or use n semaphores in a ring, or one ReentrantLock with a Condition per thread, so each signal wakes exactly the next thread.
Why repeat the runA concurrency bug can pass a single run and fail one time in a hundred. Two hundred repeated runs, all in order, is evidence; one run is a hope. Say this, and the interviewer hears that you have debugged threads before.
The mechanismssynchronized, wait and notify explains the monitor and why waits sit in loops; synchronizers covers Semaphore and its relatives.

Drill: "a product page needs price, stock and reviews; call them in parallel, within 300 ms"

The question is really about failure. Price is required: without it the page cannot render, so a late price is an error. Stock and reviews are optional: a failure or a timeout should give a fallback, not a broken page. The answer starts all three calls at once, gives each its own policy, and combines them, so the page takes as long as its slowest permitted wait.

ParallelCalls.java · three services, three failure policies, one deadline
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ParallelCalls {
    record ProductPage(long priceCents, int stock, String reviews) { }

    static final ExecutorService IO = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory());

    static <T> CompletableFuture<T> call(String name, long ms, T result, boolean fails) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            if (fails) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is down");
            return result;
        }, IO);
    }

    static ProductPage load(boolean stockDown) {
        CompletableFuture<Long> price = call("pricing", 150, 1299L, false)
                .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                       // required: fail if late
        CompletableFuture<Integer> stock = call("inventory", 100, 7, stockDown)
                .exceptionally(ex -> -1);                                     // optional: -1 means unknown
        CompletableFuture<String> reviews = call("reviews", 800, "4.6 stars", false)
                .completeOnTimeout("reviews unavailable", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);   // optional: default
        return price.thenCombine(stock, (p, s) -> new long[] {p, s})
                .thenCombine(reviews, (ps, r) -> new ProductPage(ps[0], (int) ps[1], r))
                .join();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        load(false);                                                        // warm up the pool
        for (boolean stockDown : new boolean[] {false, true}) {
            long t0 = System.nanoTime();
            ProductPage page = load(stockDown);
            long ms = Math.round((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e8) * 100;
            System.out.println(page + " in ~" + ms + " ms" + (stockDown ? " (inventory failed)" : ""));
        }
        try {
            call("pricing", 600, 1L, false).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join();
        } catch (CompletionException e) {
            System.out.println("a required call past its deadline: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        IO.shutdownNow();
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · ParallelCalls.java · times rounded to 100 ms
ProductPage[priceCents=1299, stock=7, reviews=reviews unavailable] in ~300 ms
ProductPage[priceCents=1299, stock=-1, reviews=reviews unavailable] in ~300 ms (inventory failed)
a required call past its deadline: TimeoutException
CallPolicyMethod
Pricing, 150 msRequired: fail the page if it is lateorTimeout(300 ms)
Inventory, 100 msOptional: unknown stock if it failsexceptionally(ex -> -1)
Reviews, 800 msOptional: a placeholder if it is latecompleteOnTimeout(…, 300 ms)
Reading the resultBoth pages took about 300 ms: the reviews call is slow, so the page waits for its deadline and uses the placeholder. Sequential calls would have taken 150 + 100 + 800 = 1,050 ms. The second page shows the inventory failure absorbed as stock=-1.
Use your own executorThese calls block, so they run on a dedicated IO pool, never the common ForkJoinPool. Name its threads, size it for the calls in flight, and shut it down. With virtual threads, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() fits too.
Follow-ups to expect"Cancel the slow call when we give up": orTimeout completes the future but does not stop the work, so pass a timeout to the HTTP client too. "Retry pricing once": compose with exceptionallyCompose 12. "Add a circuit breaker": that is Resilience4j's job.
The mechanismscomposition and errors and threads. At architecture level, the reference deck's resilience slide sets the same timeouts and fallbacks per dependency.

Drill: "count word frequencies across many lines, using all the cores"

There are three good answers and one common wrong one. The wrong one shares a HashMap, or does get then put on a ConcurrentHashMap, and loses counts. The good ones either share nothing (a parallel stream that collects), or share a concurrent map updated atomically. The answer that scores best checks itself: all three results below are compared against a plain sequential count.

WordCount.java · sequential, parallel stream, pool plus LongAdder, all compared
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class WordCount {
    static List<String> lines() {                                    // 20,000 lines of seeded random words
        String[] vocab = {"order", "ship", "pay", "refund", "cart", "stock", "price", "tax", "the", "a"};
        Random r = new Random(42);
        return IntStream.range(0, 20_000)
                .mapToObj(i -> IntStream.range(0, 12).mapToObj(j -> vocab[r.nextInt(vocab.length)]).collect(Collectors.joining(" ")))
                .toList();
    }

    static Stream<String> words(String line) { return Arrays.stream(line.toLowerCase().split("\\s+")).filter(w -> !w.isEmpty()); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> lines = lines();

        Map<String, Long> sequential = new HashMap<>();                 // 1 the baseline
        for (String line : lines) words(line).forEach(w -> sequential.merge(w, 1L, Long::sum));

        Map<String, Long> parallel = lines.parallelStream()             // 2 a parallel stream, no shared state
                .flatMap(WordCount::words)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

        ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // 3 a pool and a shared map
        int chunk = 1_000;
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int from = 0; from < lines.size(); from += chunk) {
                List<String> part = lines.subList(from, Math.min(from + chunk, lines.size()));
                pool.submit(() -> part.forEach(line -> words(line)
                        .forEach(w -> counts.computeIfAbsent(w, k -> new LongAdder()).increment())));
            }
        }
        Map<String, Long> pooled = new HashMap<>();
        counts.forEach((w, n) -> pooled.put(w, n.sum()));

        System.out.println("words counted: " + sequential.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()
                + ", distinct " + sequential.size());
        System.out.println("parallel stream matches: " + sequential.equals(parallel) + ", pool + LongAdder matches: " + sequential.equals(pooled));

        List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> top3 = sequential.entrySet().stream()
                .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
                .limit(3).toList();
        System.out.println("top 3: " + top3);
    }
}
Output on JDK 25 · WordCount.java
words counted: 240000, distinct 10
parallel stream matches: true, pool + LongAdder matches: true
top 3: [order=24196, refund=24087, cart=24059]
ApproachWhy it is correctWhen
1 merge into a HashMapOne threadSmall input; and always as the reference answer
2 groupingByConcurrent in a parallel streamThe collector owns the concurrent map; your code shares nothingThe data is already in memory
3 computeIfAbsent(…).increment() on LongAdderscomputeIfAbsent is atomic per key; LongAdder handles contention on hot wordsWork arrives from many producers, or from files, or over time
The answer that loses countsmap.put(w, map.getOrDefault(w, 0L) + 1) from several threads: two threads read 41 and both write 42. It loses nothing in a single-threaded test. On a ConcurrentHashMap use merge(w, 1L, Long::sum); with very hot keys, the LongAdder version.
Follow-up: the top k wordsSort the entries by count descending, with a tie-break on the word so the order is stable, and take k: shown above. For millions of distinct words, keep a min-heap of size k instead: O(n log k).
Follow-up: the input is 50 GBStream it line by line with Files.lines, in chunks handed to a bounded pool, so memory holds the counts and not the file. Beyond one machine, the same shape is map-reduce, or a Kafka Streams aggregation.

Drill: five short snippets, each with one bug the compiler accepts

Code-reading rounds hand you a few lines and ask what they print, or what is wrong. Each snippet below is a line or two from real code, with the comment saying what the author meant. Find the bug before reading the answers. Every snippet compiles cleanly with -Xlint:all.

1 · remove the zero quantities
List<Integer> qty = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0, 0, 5, 0, 7));
for (int i = 0; i < qty.size(); i++)
    if (qty.get(i) == 0) qty.remove(i);                    // Bug 1: remove empty lines
2 · a fallback region
Optional<String> configured = Optional.of("eu-west");
String region = configured.orElse(loadDefault());         // Bug 2: a default, if missing
3 · the average order value
int totalCents = 1_000, orders = 3;
double average = totalCents / orders;                       // Bug 3: average order value
4 · build the report in the background
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("4 report built on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
worker.run();                                               // Bug 4: build it in the background
5 · the label "A1 band"
char grade = 'A';
String label = grade + 1 + " band";                         // Bug 5: "A1 band"
Output on JDK 25 · SpotTheBug.java · bug, then fix
1 after removing zeros by index: [0, 5, 7]
  removeIf: [5, 7]
2 region eu-west, but loadDefault() ran 1 time(s)
  orElseGet ran it 0 time(s)
3 average 333.0  ->  333.3333333333333
4 report built on main
4 report built on Thread-0
5 label 66 band  ->  A1 band
#The bugThe fix
1Removing at i shifts the next element into i, and i++ skips it, so two zeros in a row leave one behind.removeIf, an Iterator, or loop backwards
2orElse(loadDefault()) evaluates its argument first, every time, even when the value is present. A database call there runs on every request.orElseGet(SpotTheBug::loadDefault), which runs only when empty
3totalCents / orders is integer division; the result is truncated before it is widened to double.Cast one operand: (double) totalCents / orders; for money, BigDecimal
4run() just calls the method on the current thread: the report was built on main, blocking it.start(), or better, submit it to an executor
5grade + 1 is evaluated first, as char plus int: 65 + 1 = 66. Concatenation only starts when a String appears, from the left.Start with a string: "" + grade + 1, or String.valueOf(grade) + 1
More of the sameThe pitfalls section is a longer bug hunt, by category: equality, concurrency and resources. In an interview, read the snippet aloud line by line before answering: most of these are found by saying what each line does.

Read the question for its shape, and the Java tool follows

Most core-Java coding prompts are one of about twenty shapes in disguise. Spot the shape in the first minute and the first line of the answer is already decided. This table is the one to revise from the night before.

If the question saysReach forWatch out for
"…an immutable / value object"A record, or a final class with copies in and outMutable components; Date; arrays
"…as a map key" or "…in a set"equals and hashCode from the same immutable fieldsequals(MyType) overloads; mutable fields
"…sorted by X, then Y"Comparator.comparing(…).thenComparing(…)a - b comparators; ties that drop TreeSet elements
"…the k largest / most frequent"A min-heap PriorityQueue of size kSorting everything when n is huge
"…least recently used cache"LinkedHashMap in access order with removeEldestEntryIt is not thread-safe, even for reads
"…nearest price band / slot"TreeMap.floorEntry, ceilingKeyA chain of ifs
"…a stack" or "…a queue"ArrayDequeStack, LinkedList, remove(0) on an ArrayList
"…thread-safe singleton"An enum, or the holder idiomDouble-checked locking without volatile
"…count from many threads"LongAdder, AtomicLong, ConcurrentHashMap.mergevolatile and ++; get then put
"…threads take turns / print in order"Semaphores in a ring, or a lock with one Condition per threadif around wait; a final thread that never wakes the other
"…producer and consumer"A bounded BlockingQueue, with poison pills to stopUnbounded queues; wait/notify by hand
"…at most N at a time"SemaphoreA missing release in finally
"…wait for all N tasks"invokeAll, CompletableFuture.allOf, CountDownLatchStarting each task only after the last finished
"…call services in parallel, with a timeout"CompletableFuture on your own executor, orTimeout, completeOnTimeoutThe common pool; timeouts that do not stop the work
"…run every N seconds"ScheduledExecutorServiceTimer; a task exception that silently ends the schedule
"…rate limiter"A token bucket refilled from System.nanoTimeA timer thread per client
"…parse dates / money"java.time with an explicit zone; BigDecimal from stringsSimpleDateFormat shared; double; YYYY
"…read a big file"Files.lines in try-with-resources, or a BufferedReaderreadAllLines on gigabytes; an unclosed stream

The whole Stream API, and the failure behind each method

A reference for java.util.stream as it stands in JDK 25. It covers every method on Stream and the primitive streams, all 44 Collectors, the Gatherers that became final in Java 24, and the Optional that the search and reduce operations return. It ends with the stream questions interviewers ask most often, and the coding problems they set, solved.

57

methods on Stream: 40 instance, 9 static and 8 inherited from BaseStream. Every one is in the index on slide 3, linked to the slide that covers it.

44

factory methods on Collectors, from toList to teeing. Slide 4 lists them all, along with the five Gatherers and every Optional method.

25

JDK 25, the current LTS, is the target. JDK 26 ships the identical stream API. Anything added after Java 8 carries a since tag.

How to use it

  • Arrow keys move through slides; C opens contents, where each topic is its own section.
  • since 16 marks an API added after Java 8, with the release that added it. No tag means Java 8.
  • Slide 5 runs a real pipeline one element at a time. Step through it before reading the rest of How a stream runs; the next five slides assume you have.
  • Preparing for an interview? Read Interview questions, then work the Coding drills with the solutions covered. Every answer links back to the slide that goes deeper.
How the API slides are writtenEvery method gets three things: what it does, a real line of code, and the failure it causes when used wrongly. The examples compile on JDK 25; the two listings marked "trimmed" or "simplified" show only the shape of JDK internals. Where a slide quotes an output or an exception message, it is what the JVM actually printed.

A stream is a recipe, not a container

A collection holds elements. A stream holds none. It describes work: where the elements come from, what happens to each one, and what to produce at the end. Nothing runs until a terminal operation asks for a result, and then it runs exactly once.

The running example on every API slide
record Line(String sku, int qty, double price) {}
record Order(String id, String customer, String status,
             double total, List<Line> lines) {}

List<String> bigSpenders = orders.stream()   // source: nothing copied
        .filter(o -> o.total() > 500)        // recorded, not run
        .map(Order::customer)                // recorded, not run
        .distinct()                          // recorded, not run
        .sorted()                            // recorded, not run
        .toList();                           // runs all of the above, once
CollectionStream
Holds elementsYes, in memoryNo. Elements flow through it
Work happensWhen you call a methodOnly when a terminal op runs
IterationExternal: you write the loopInternal: the library drives it
ReusableAs often as you likeOnce
SizeFiniteCan be infinite
Changes the sourceadd, remove doNever. It builds a new result
Where the one-shot rule bitesStoring a Stream in a field or passing it to two methods. The second consumer throws. Store the collection, or a Supplier<Stream<T>>, and call .stream() each time you need one: a fresh pipeline costs a few small objects.

Every method on Stream, in one table

Fifty-seven methods, grouped by what they are. Kind says when the method runs. Stateful means it has to remember elements it has already seen. Short-circuit means it can finish without reading the whole source, which is what lets it work on an infinite stream.

Two nested types complete itStream.Builder<T> (add, accept, build) builds a stream element by element, and Stream.Builder exists for each primitive stream too. IntStream.IntMapMultiConsumer and its long and double cousins since 16 are the functional interfaces that the primitive mapMulti takes.

Everything the stream methods hand work to

A collect call is only as good as the Collector you pass it, and the search operations return an Optional. This is the rest of the API, grouped by what each method produces.

Collectors · 44 static methodsProducesCovered in
toList() · toSet() · toCollection(supplier) · toUnmodifiableList() 10 · toUnmodifiableSet() 10A collectionCollections
toMap ×3 · toUnmodifiableMap ×2 10 · toConcurrentMap ×3A map, one value per keytoMap
joining() · joining(delimiter) · joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix)A StringNumbers and strings
counting() · summingInt/Long/Double · averagingInt/Long/Double · summarizingInt/Long/Double · minBy · maxByA number, a statistics object or an OptionalNumbers and strings
reducing(op) · reducing(identity, op) · reducing(identity, mapper, op)One valueDownstream

teeing(c1, c2, merger) 12Two collectors in one pass, mergedteeing

Collector · Gatherer 24 · Gatherers 24

Collector<T, A, R>: supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher, characteristics, and two Collector.of factories. The characteristics are CONCURRENT, UNORDERED and IDENTITY_FINISH.

Gatherer<T, A, R>: initializer, integrator, combiner, finisher, andThen. Factories: of ×3, ofSequential ×4, and defaultInitializer, defaultCombiner, defaultFinisher. Nested types: Integrator (of, ofGreedy), Integrator.Greedy and Downstream (push, isRejecting).

Gatherers: windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan, mapConcurrent.

Custom CollectorsBuilt-in gatherersYour own gatherer

Optional · OptionalInt · OptionalLong · OptionalDouble

Create: of, ofNullable, empty. Test: isPresent, isEmpty 11. Unwrap: get, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow() 10, orElseThrow(supplier). Act: ifPresent, ifPresentOrElse 9. Transform: map, flatMap, filter, or 9, stream 9.

The primitive versions have no map, flatMap, filter or or, and unwrap with getAsInt, getAsLong and getAsDouble.

StreamSupport: stream, intStream, longStream and doubleStream, each from a Spliterator or from a Supplier of one: 8 methods for turning your own data structure into a stream.

OptionalStreamSupport

Elements travel down the pipeline one at a time

The obvious mental model is wrong. A stream does not filter the whole list, then map the whole list, then collect. It takes one element and pushes it through every stage as far as it goes, then takes the next. That one fact explains laziness and short-circuiting, and it is why sorted() costs what it does. Pick a pipeline, press Next, and predict each step before you see it.

Pulled from the source
Calls per stage
Result

Vertical, not horizontal

In pipeline 2, filter and map take turns: fig is dropped before kiwi is even read. No list of filtered elements exists at any point, which is why a stream over a million rows needs no more memory than a stream over ten.

Pulled by the terminal operation
